case_name: A. Sreenivasa Reddy vs. Rakesh Sharma & Anr.
text: Case: A. Sreenivasa Reddy vs. Rakesh Sharma & Anr.. Date: 8th August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. A. Sreenivasa Reddy was charged with conspiracy, cheating, forgery, and using forged documents, punishable under Sections 120-B, 420, 468, and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The primary allegation was that A. Sreenivasa Reddy, while serving as an Assistant General Manager at SBI, conspired with other co-accused to cheat the bank by sanctioning a corporate loan of Rs. 22.50 crore to M/s Sven Genetech Limited and diverted the funds for personal benefits. The High Court rejected the petition filed by A. Sreenivasa Reddy and declined to quash the criminal proceedings instituted against him. A. Sreenivasa Reddy challenged the High Court's order on the grounds that the investigation was flawed and the charges were based on insufficient evidence. He argued that the sanction to prosecute him was initially declined and later reviewed without proper justification. The CBI registered an FIR against A. Sreenivasa Reddy and other co-accused, conducted the investigation, and filed the chargesheet in the Court of the Principal Special Judge (CBI Cases) at Hyderabad. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's decision was justified and upheld the rejection of the petition, emphasizing that the investigation had revealed sufficient material evidence to proceed with the trial. The Supreme Court highlighted that the requirement for sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC applies only to public servants who are not removable from their office save by or with the sanction of the government. In this case, the Court found that the provisions of Section 197 were not applicable. The Supreme Court decided that the prosecution for the offences under the IPC should continue, even though the sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 was declined. The Court emphasized that the IPC offences could be prosecuted independently. The Supreme Court noted that the outcome of the departmental inquiry, which exonerated A. Sreenivasa Reddy, did not have a bearing on the criminal proceedings under the IPC. The Court emphasized that the charges in the departmental inquiry were different from the criminal charges. The Supreme Court directed the Special Judge for CBI Cases at Hyderabad to dispose of the case within a period of three months from the date of receipt of the order, ensuring a speedy trial. The Supreme Court emphasized that the CBI conducted a thorough investigation, recording the statements of 65 witnesses and collecting 545 documents, which formed the basis for the charges against A. Sreenivasa Reddy and other co-accused.

case_name: A.G. Perarivalan vs State, Through Superintendent of Police CBI/SIT/MMDA, Chennai, Tamil Nadu
text: Case: A.G. Perarivalan vs State, Through Superintendent of Police CBI/SIT/MMDA, Chennai, Tamil Nadu. Date: 18th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. A.G. Perarivalan was convicted for offences under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), the Arms Act, 1951, the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, the Passport Act, 1967, the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, and the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (TADA) for his involvement in the assassination of former Prime Minister Rajeev Gandhi. A.G. Perarivalan was sentenced to death by the designated TADA Court. The Supreme Court commuted A.G. Perarivalan's death sentence to life imprisonment on 18th February 2014. The Tamil Nadu Government proposed remission of A.G. Perarivalan's sentence due to his having already undergone a sentence of 23 years and in view of Section 435 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), which requires consultation with the Central Government as the case was investigated by the CBI. The Governor of Tamil Nadu referred the State Cabinet's recommendation for remission to the President of India on 25th January 2021, rather than taking a decision himself. The Supreme Court set A.G. Perarivalan at liberty forthwith, deeming him to have served his sentence in connection with Crime No. 329 of 1991, and cancelled his bail bonds. The Supreme Court emphasized that the advice of the State Cabinet is binding on the Governor in matters of remission under Article 161 of the Constitution and that the Governor's action of referring the recommendation to the President was contrary to the constitutional scheme.

case_name: AMEET LALCHAND SHAH AND OTHERS v. RISHABH ENTERPRISES AND ANOTHER
text: Case: AMEET LALCHAND SHAH AND OTHERS v. RISHABH ENTERPRISES AND ANOTHER. Date: 3rd May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The dispute arises from a series of agreements related to the commissioning of a 2 MWp Photovoltaic Solar Plant at Dongri, Raksa, District Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh, involving allegations of fraud, misrepresentation, and breach of trust. The central agreements are the Equipment and Material Supply Contract (01.02.2012), Engineering, Installation, and Commissioning Contract (01.02.2012), Sale and Purchase Agreement (05.03.2012), and the Equipment Lease Agreement (14.03.2012). The Delhi High Court dismissed the application, holding that the agreements between the parties are not inter-connected with the principal agreement dated 05.03.2012 and therefore, the parties cannot be referred to arbitration. The Supreme Court held that all four agreements were inter-connected for the single purpose of commissioning the 2 MWp Photovoltaic Solar Plant, and therefore, the dispute should be referred to arbitration. The Supreme Court stated that the allegations of fraud were not serious enough to avoid arbitration and that the arbitrator could examine the allegations regarding fraud. The Supreme Court directed the appellants to pay the arrears of lease rent and future lease rent for the equipment at the rate of Rs.28,26,000/- per month until the disposal of the arbitration proceedings.

case_name: APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. vs Shakti International Fashion Linkers & Ors.
text: Case: APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. vs Shakti International Fashion Linkers & Ors.. Date: 14th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the cheques issued by Shakti International Fashion Linkers to APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. were dishonored due to insufficient funds, leading to a violation of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The amount involved was Rs. 9,55,574, which was to be paid through a cheque that was dishonored due to a 'stop payment' instruction. The Trial Court acquitted the respondents, stating that there was no legal liability as the payment through the card was not established and proved, and the payments were prior to the issuance of the card. The High Court dismissed the application for leave to appeal, confirming the Trial Court's decision to acquit the respondents. The Supreme Court reiterated that under Section 139, there is a presumption that a cheque was issued for discharge of a debt or liability unless the contrary is proved, and this presumption is rebuttable. The Supreme Court quashed the acquittal orders of the lower courts, held the respondents guilty under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and imposed a sentence of three months' simple imprisonment with a fine. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to pay a sum of Rs. 19,11,148 to the original complainant by way of compensation within eight weeks. The dishonor of the cheque with the reason 'stop payment' was considered significant as it indicated a deliberate action by the drawer to prevent payment, rather than an issue of insufficient funds. The complainant argued that there is a mandatory presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act that the cheque was issued for a legally enforceable debt or liability, which the accused failed to rebut. The Supreme Court affirmed that the burden of proof lies on the accused to rebut the presumption that a cheque was issued for discharge of a debt or liability under Section 139 of the N.I. Act.

case_name: Aarif & Ors. vs. The State of Rajasthan & Anr.
text: Case: Aarif & Ors. vs. The State of Rajasthan & Anr.. Date: 19th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Aarif and the other appellants were charged with offences punishable under Sections 148, 341, 323, 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The incident occurred on 22nd February 2017, when Aarif, Javed, and several others assaulted the complainant's father with iron rods, resulting in his death and causing injuries to the complainant's mother. The Trial Court exercised power under Section 319 of the CrPC based on the evidence provided by PW-1, the widow of the deceased, and directed that the appellants, who were not named in the charge sheet, should be proceeded against with the accused named in the charge sheet. The High Court set aside the Trial Court's initial order under Section 319 of the CrPC and directed that the Trial Court should record the evidence of all eyewitnesses before reconsidering the application under Section 319. The Supreme Court found that the evidence of PW-1 was not sufficient to confirm the order under Section 319 of the CrPC. The witness admitted to not disclosing the incident to the police immediately despite being in the hospital where a police outpost was present. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned orders dated 8th June 2022 and 4th April 2023, dismissing the application under Section 319 of the CrPC against the appellants. The Supreme Court clarified that the observations made in its judgment regarding the testimony of eyewitnesses were only for the limited purpose of deciding the issue of applicability of Section 319 of the CrPC and should not affect the ongoing trial.

case_name: Abdul Ahad and Ors. vs. Union of India and Ors.
text: Case: Abdul Ahad and Ors. vs. Union of India and Ors.. Date: 17th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the students who were admitted to the Glocal Medical College through private counseling, contrary to the centralized counseling mandated by the State of Uttar Pradesh, should be allowed to continue their studies despite their admission being declared illegal by the Medical Council of India (MCI). The review petitioners contended that they were duly qualified as they had cleared the NEET examination and were admitted through the counseling conducted by the Glocal Medical College. They argued that they had already completed the first and second year of their MBBS course, and it would be unjust to cancel their admissions at this stage. The State of Uttar Pradesh argued that the admissions were conducted through private counseling, which was not permissible as per the centralized counseling mandated by the State. They contended that the admissions were a result of collusion between the Glocal Medical College and the students, and therefore, the students were not entitled to any equitable relief. The Supreme Court held that the private counseling conducted by Glocal Medical College was illegal and contrary to the centralized counseling mandated by the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Court emphasized that the admissions through private counseling were not permissible in law and must be considered illegal. The Supreme Court dismissed the review petitions, stating that the students' admissions were illegal, and no sympathy could be shown to those who entered through backdoor methods. The Court upheld the MCI's discharge order and emphasized the need to maintain the purity of the admission process. The Supreme Court dismissed all pending applications, including the applications for intervention and impleadment, stating that they were without merit.

case_name: Abdul Ansar v. State of Kerala
text: Case: Abdul Ansar v. State of Kerala. Date: 5th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 308 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) could be sustained. The appellant was Abdul Ansar, and the respondent was the State of Kerala. Accused No. 1 was the driver of the bus, the appellant (Accused No. 2) was the conductor, and Accused No. 3 was the cleaner. PW-1 Josia, a schoolgirl, fell and came under the bus's rear wheel when the bus started moving after the appellant rang the bell, causing her to sustain serious injuries. The Additional Sessions Judge acquitted the driver (Accused No. 1) but convicted the appellant (Accused No. 2) and the cleaner (Accused No. 3) under Section 308 read with Section 34 of IPC, sentencing them to four years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The High Court acquitted Accused No. 3 but confirmed the conviction of the appellant under Section 308 of IPC, reducing his sentence to one year and imposing a fine of Rs. 50,000. The appellant's counsel argued that the offence of attempt to commit culpable homicide was not established and highlighted that the cleaner had been acquitted, making the conviction of the appellant unsustainable. The Supreme Court held that the offence of attempt to commit culpable homicide was not made out as the appellant did not have the required intention or knowledge, and instead found the appellant guilty under Section 338 of IPC. The Supreme Court sentenced the appellant to six months of simple imprisonment under Section 338 of IPC and directed him to pay a total compensation of Rs. 75,000 to the victim, PW-1. The Supreme Court directed the appellant to pay Rs. 50,000 already deposited and an additional Rs. 25,000 as compensation to the victim, PW-1. The appellant has already undergone incarceration for 36 days.

case_name: Abhimeet Sinha & Ors. vs. High Court of Judicature at Patna & Ors.
text: Case: Abhimeet Sinha & Ors. vs. High Court of Judicature at Patna & Ors.. Date: 6th May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The common challenge was to the constitutionality of the Rules stipulating minimum qualifying marks in the viva voce test as part of the selection criteria for appointment to the District Judiciary in Bihar and Gujarat. The writ petitioners alleged a violation of their fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India due to the prescribed minimum qualifying marks for the viva voce test. The recruitment processes for District Judge (Entry Level) direct from Bar Examination (2015) in Bihar and the post of Civil Judge (2019 and 2022 Advertisement) in Gujarat were under scrutiny. The Bihar Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1951 were amended to include a screening test, a written main test, and an interview for selection, with specific minimum qualifying marks for each stage. The court concluded that prescribing minimum qualifying marks for interviews is permissible and not in violation of the All India Judges (2002) decision. The court upheld the validity of Clause 11 of the Bihar Rules, 1951 and Rule 8(3) of the Gujarat Rules, 2005. The writ petitions were dismissed, and the court upheld the legality of the selection processes in Bihar and Gujarat.

case_name: Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua
text: Case: Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua. Date: 7th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court of Delhi had correctly exercised its revisional power under the proviso to Section 25B(8) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, in setting aside the Rent Controller's order denying leave to defend to the tenant. The respondent sought leave to defend on three primary grounds: (i) questioning the appellant's title over the property; (ii) claiming the property belonged to the Government of India under the Enemy Property Act, 1968; and (iii) asserting the availability of alternative accommodations for the appellant. The learned Rent Controller dismissed the application for leave to defend, holding that the respondent could not question the appellant's title, the claim of alternative accommodation was vague, and the Enemy Property Act did not apply to the property in question. The High Court allowed the revision, holding that there were triable issues regarding the availability of alternative accommodation and that the appellant's denials were vague. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court had overstepped its revisional jurisdiction, which is limited to ensuring that the Rent Controller's order is according to law, without substituting its own findings for those of the Rent Controller. The Supreme Court set aside the order of the High Court and restored the order of the learned Rent Controller, thereby dismissing the application for leave to defend and upholding the eviction order. The Supreme Court noted that the proceedings under the Enemy Property Act were not relevant to the eviction case, as the claim had already been dismissed by the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, and subsequent proceedings were stayed by the High Court.

case_name: Abu Salem Abdul Kayyum Ansari vs. The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Abu Salem Abdul Kayyum Ansari vs. The State of Maharashtra. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Abu Salem was charged with threatening a party in a civil dispute, extracting money, and murdering Pradeep Jain upon failure to make the payment. Additionally, he was involved in the Bombay Bomb Blasts, transporting illegal arms and explosives. The extradition request included a solemn sovereign assurance that Abu Salem would not face the death penalty or imprisonment for more than 25 years if extradited. This assurance was critical for obtaining Portugal's agreement to extradite Abu Salem. The Designated Court, Mumbai convicted Abu Salem and sentenced him to life imprisonment under various provisions of law, taking into account the assurance given to Portugal that he would not face the death penalty. The Supreme Court emphasized that while the Judiciary must impose sentences according to Indian law, the Executive must comply with international obligations, ensuring that the sentence aligns with the assurance given to Portugal. The Supreme Court directed that Abu Salem's detention period should be counted from 12th October 2005, when he was handed over to Indian authorities, and not from the date of his initial detention in Portugal. The Supreme Court of Portugal confirmed the extradition of Abu Salem for specific offences and emphasized that he could not be prosecuted for any other offences not included in the extradition request. The Government of India, through an affidavit, assured that it would abide by the assurance given to Portugal, ensuring that Abu Salem would not be imprisoned for more than 25 years. The Portuguese Courts stated that violating the 'principle of speciality' could lead to the annulment of the extradition authorization, making Abu Salem's presence in India illegal and subjecting India to potential international legal consequences. The Indian Government relied on Article 72 of the Constitution, which allows the President to grant pardons, reprieves, and commutations, along with Sections 432 and 433 of the Cr.P.C., which permit the government to remit or commute sentences. The Supreme Court of India concluded that the Government of India must advise the President to exercise his powers under Article 72 to commute Abu Salem's sentence to ensure it does not exceed 25 years, in compliance with the assurance given to Portugal.

case_name: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited vs. The Board of Trustees of Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority & Ors.
text: Case: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited vs. The Board of Trustees of Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority & Ors.. Date: 5th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the disqualification of Adani Ports from participating in two tenders issued by Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA) due to the termination of a Concession Agreement by Visakhapatnam Port Authority was justified. Adani Ports argued that the termination of the Concession Agreement by Visakhapatnam Port Authority was a counterblast to their earlier termination of the same agreement, and that the issue of termination was still pending before the Arbitral Tribunal. Adani Ports sought a declaration that the termination of the Concession Agreement should not be treated as a disqualification for participating in any future tenders issued by public authorities. The Supreme Court observed that the termination of the Concession Agreement was a matter pending before the Arbitral Tribunal and should not be treated as a disqualification for participating in any other tenders issued by public authorities. A broad consensus was reached that the termination of the Concession Agreement by Visakhapatnam Port Authority would not be treated as a disqualification for Adani Ports in future tenders, and Adani Ports agreed not to claim any right to participate in the two specific tenders in question. The Supreme Court disposed of the Civil Appeal by observing that the termination of the Concession Agreement shall not be treated as a disqualification for future tenders. The Writ Petition was dismissed as withdrawn with the liberty to challenge the validity of the RFQ clause before the High Court. Clause 2.2.8 of the RFQ documents was significant because it was the basis for disqualifying Adani Ports due to the termination of the Concession Agreement. The Supreme Court allowed Adani Ports the liberty to challenge the validity of this clause before the High Court.

case_name: Additional Commissioner Revenue vs. Akhalaq Hussain and Another
text: Case: Additional Commissioner Revenue vs. Akhalaq Hussain and Another. Date: 3rd March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the exchange deed between Akhalaq Hussain and Mangal Singh, a Scheduled Tribe member, violated the provisions of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (U.P. ZA & LR) Act. The High Court of Uttarakhand decided that Section 161 of the U.P. ZA & LR Act, which requires permission for land exchange, did not apply to the exchange deed in question because the exchange was done through a registered document with paid stamp duty. The Supreme Court held that Section 157-B, which prohibits the transfer of land by Scheduled Tribe members to non-Scheduled Tribe individuals, applied to the exchange deed, rendering it void. The Assistant Collector's order declared the exchange deed void due to the lack of prior permission required under Section 161 of the U.P. ZA & LR Act and ordered the land to be vested in the State Government. The respondents argued that the land was not agricultural land and thus did not fall under the U.P. ZA & LR Act, relying on the exchange deed's recitals and the state's counter affidavit. The Supreme Court stated that the land is deemed agricultural in the absence of a declaration under Section 143 of the U.P. ZA & LR Act changing its nature from agricultural to abadi land. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation, stating that the provisions of Section 157-B apply to exchanges and bar the transfer of land by Scheduled Tribe members to non-Scheduled Tribe individuals. The Supreme Court held that the lack of prior permission from the Assistant Collector as required by Section 161 rendered the exchange void. The Supreme Court ruled that the land involved in the void exchange deed would vest in the State Government as per Section 167 of the U.P. ZA & LR Act.

case_name: Afjal Ali Sha @ Abjal Shaukat Sha vs. State of West Bengal & Ors.
text: Case: Afjal Ali Sha @ Abjal Shaukat Sha vs. State of West Bengal & Ors.. Date: 17th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the criminal trial S.T. No. 1 (03) of 2020, arising out of FIR No. 495 of 2019, should be transferred from the Court of Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Tamluk, Purba Medinipur, West Bengal, to a competent court in the State of Assam, due to concerns about the possibility of a fair trial in West Bengal. The allegations were that the deceased, Kurban Sha, was shot in the neck by unknown assailants while working in the office of a political party. The FIR was lodged under Section 302 read with Section 120B of the IPC and Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act against Respondent No. 2 and others. The investigation concluded that Respondent Nos. 3 to 11 were also involved in the offence along with Respondent No. 2. A chargesheet was filed against them, and charges were framed under Sections 302 read with 120B IPC and Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act. The trial commenced in September 2020. The Governor of West Bengal issued a notification directing the Public Prosecutor to withdraw the criminal proceedings against the respondents, citing political and personal vendetta. This was followed by the Public Prosecutor moving an application to withdraw the prosecution, which was allowed by a Link Judge, leading to the acquittal of the respondents. The Calcutta High Court observed that the State's action was arbitrary and unreasoned, noting that the prosecution's withdrawal lacked justification and appeared to be influenced by mala fide intentions. The High Court set aside the notification and the Link Judge's order, reinstating the trial. The petitioner raised concerns about the change of Public Prosecutor four times, harassment of prosecution witnesses and relatives of the deceased, threats to witnesses, and attempts to influence the trial. The petitioner feared that a fair trial would not be possible in West Bengal. The Supreme Court decided that there was no legal necessity to transfer the trial outside West Bengal. The Court issued directions to ensure the fairness of the trial, including appointing a Special Public Prosecutor, providing security to the petitioner and key witnesses, and transferring the trial to the Court of Chief Judge, City Sessions Court at Calcutta. The Supreme Court directed that the trial be transferred to the Court of Chief Judge, City Sessions Court at Calcutta, to be conducted by the Chief Judge on a weekly basis. The State was directed to appoint a Special Public Prosecutor, provide security to the petitioner and witnesses, and transfer the respondents in custody to the Central Jail at Calcutta. The Supreme Court requested the Learned Portfolio Judge of the Calcutta High Court to regularly monitor and supervise the trial proceedings, ensuring compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court's decision aimed to ensure a fair and unbiased trial by transferring the trial to a different court within West Bengal, appointing a Special Public Prosecutor, and providing necessary security to the petitioner and witnesses, while also involving the High Court in monitoring the trial.

case_name: Agra Development Authority vs Anek Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Agra Development Authority vs Anek Singh & Ors.. Date: 20th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the acquisition proceedings for the land in question should be deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. The High Court held that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013, because the compensation was not actually paid to the landowners. The Agra Development Authority argued that the possession of the land was already taken over, the land was mutated in the revenue records, and development works had been carried out on the land in question. The High Court relied on the decision because it held that the acquisition proceedings would lapse if compensation was not actually paid to the landowners, a precedent set in the Pune Municipal Corporation case. The Supreme Court's decision in Indore Development Authority vs Manoharlal & Ors. overruled the Pune Municipal Corporation case, clarifying that if either possession was taken or compensation was paid, the acquisition would not lapse. The Supreme Court ruled that depositing the compensation with the Special Land Acquisition Officer satisfies the requirement of payment, and thus the acquisition proceedings did not lapse. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's judgment, dismissing the writ petition filed by the original writ petitioners, thereby upholding the acquisition proceedings. This decision may ensure that land acquisition cases are not deemed to have lapsed merely due to the non-payment of compensation directly to landowners, provided the compensation is deposited with the appropriate authority. Land acquisition authorities should ensure that either possession of the land is taken or compensation is properly deposited with the appropriate authority to avoid lapses in acquisition proceedings. The Supreme Court found the High Court's reliance on the overruled Pune Municipal Corporation decision to be erroneous and corrected this by applying the principles from the Indore Development Authority case. The Supreme Court clarified that Section 24(2) should be interpreted such that acquisition proceedings do not lapse if either possession has been taken or compensation has been deposited with the appropriate authority, thus ensuring the continuity of valid acquisition processes.

case_name: Ahsan vs. State of U.P.
text: Case: Ahsan vs. State of U.P.. Date: 29th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the quantum of the sentence of life imprisonment awarded to Ahsan under Section 307 IPC was justified considering the facts and circumstances of the case. Ahsan was charged with offences under Sections 452, 307/34, 316/34, and 504 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). On 8th October 2004, Ahsan, along with co-accused Manshad and Kamil, entered the house of Iliyas' uncle armed with pistols, and shot at Iliyas' cousin Istekhar, niece Rukhsana (who was pregnant), and son-in-law Shahzad, causing severe injuries. The Trial Court convicted Ahsan under Sections 452, 307/34, 316/34, and 504 IPC, sentencing him to seven years' rigorous imprisonment for Section 452, life imprisonment for Section 307/34, ten years' rigorous imprisonment for Section 316/34, and two years' rigorous imprisonment for Section 504 IPC, with all sentences to run concurrently. The High Court dismissed Ahsan's appeal, upholding the Trial Court's judgment of conviction and sentence. Ahsan's main argument was that since the victim Shahzad survived the gunshot injury, the courts should have imposed a sentence under the first part of Section 307 IPC, which could extend only up to ten years and fine, instead of life imprisonment. The Supreme Court dismissed Ahsan's appeal, finding no merit in the argument for reducing the sentence, and upheld the life imprisonment awarded by the lower courts considering the grievous nature of the gunshot injury caused to the victim Shahzad.

case_name: Ajai alias Ajju etc. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Ajai alias Ajju etc. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 15th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves the appeal of four accused, Ajai alias Ajju, Braj Pal, Ravi, and Mukesh, who were convicted for the murder of Vijay Pal Singh, his wife Smt Rajesh, their son Nishant, and their son-in-law Mangal Singh, as well as for attempting to murder Smt Pinky. The High Court commuted the death penalty awarded by the Trial Court to life imprisonment for all the accused. The prosecution's story involved a complaint by Braj Pal Singh, who reported that his brother Vijay Pal Singh, his wife, their son, and their son-in-law were found dead with their necks cut, and Smt Pinky was found injured. The accused were allegedly involved in the assault due to enmity. The appellants argued that Smt Pinky, the solitary eye-witness, was unreliable due to enmity, and there was no corroborative evidence. They also pointed out that the names of the assailants were not initially disclosed, and the dog squad was used, indicating unknown assailants. The Supreme Court found Smt Pinky's testimony to be reliable, noting that her injuries were not challenged, and she had no reason to falsely implicate the accused. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals by the accused and upheld the life imprisonment sentence. The appeals for enhancement of the sentence to death penalty by the State were also dismissed. Smt Pinky sustained multiple injuries, including amputated fingers, cut wounds on her hand, forearm, face, and neck, as well as a lacerated wound on her ear. The investigation led to the recovery of blood-stained weapons and clothes, and the mobile phone of the deceased Nishant from the accused. These items were sent for forensic examination. The prosecution believed Smt Pinky's account because she was an injured witness with no reason to falsely implicate the accused, and her testimony was consistent and corroborated by the injuries and recoveries made. The Supreme Court stated that the use of the dog squad was justified as the names of the assailants were not known at the time of the initial investigation, and this did not impact the credibility of the prosecution's case. The High Court commuted the death sentence awarded by the Trial Court to life imprisonment for the accused, considering various factors and legal precedents.

case_name: Ajanta LLP vs Casio Keisanki Kabushiki Kaisha d/b/a Casio Computer Co. Ltd.
text: Case: Ajanta LLP vs Casio Keisanki Kabushiki Kaisha d/b/a Casio Computer Co. Ltd.. Date: 4th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Ajanta LLP could seek modification of a consent decree based on an alleged typographical error in the settlement agreement concerning the trademark 'FX-991ES PLUS/ FX/ 991'. Casio sought a permanent injunction to restrain Ajanta from manufacturing, importing, marketing, and selling the impugned product 'ORPAT FX-991ES PLUS', and requested mandatory injunctions for the recall and destruction of such products, as well as inspection of accounts for damages. Ajanta LLP filed the application seeking correction of an alleged typographical error in the settlement agreement which they claimed was intended to pertain only to the trademark 'FX-991ES PLUS/ FX-991' and not 'FX-991ES PLUS/ FX/ 991'. The High Court dismissed Ajanta LLP's application for modification of the judgment, leading Ajanta LLP to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court interpreted the correspondence to show that the settlement agreement was reached after detailed consultation and there was no ambiguity or misunderstanding regarding the use of the trademark terms 'FX-991ES PLUS/ FX/ 991'. The Supreme Court affirmed that a consent decree cannot be modified or altered unless there is a patent or obvious mistake, fraud, or misrepresentation, and held that the misunderstanding claimed by Ajanta LLP did not meet this threshold. The Supreme Court decided that there was no typographical error that warranted modification of the settlement agreement, as the agreement was clear and agreed upon by both parties after thorough consultation. This judgment may ensure that parties are more meticulous in drafting and agreeing to settlement terms, as courts are likely to uphold the original terms unless there is clear evidence of a patent or obvious mistake, fraud, or misrepresentation. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal, reaffirming that the settlement agreement terms should remain as originally agreed upon by both parties. The judgment emphasizes that typographical errors in legal agreements must be clear and obvious to warrant modification, and parties must provide substantial evidence of such errors for courts to consider alterations. The Supreme Court clarified that courts have inherent powers to rectify consent decrees to ensure they are free from clerical or arithmetical errors, but such powers are limited to obvious mistakes, fraud, or misrepresentation.

case_name: Ajmal vs. The State of Kerala
text: Case: Ajmal vs. The State of Kerala. Date: 12th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ajmal and the other accused were charged under sections 143, 147, 148 IPC read with section 149 IPC. Their conviction and sentence under sections 341, 323, 324, 427, and 302 read with section 34 IPC were confirmed. The incident occurred on 27th January 2008 when the deceased, Varkeychen @ George Thomas, was attacked by the accused, including Ajmal, with sticks and bricks after a verbal altercation over vehicles overtaking. The Sessions Court convicted Ajmal and sentenced him to life imprisonment, which was confirmed by the High Court. However, the High Court acquitted some other accused. The appellant's counsel argued that the accused did not have any premeditation or intention to commit murder and that the incident was a result of a sudden altercation. The Supreme Court found the testimonies of the eyewitnesses (PW-1, PW-2, and PW-4) reliable as they were consistent and supported the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court noted that the failure to examine three independent eyewitnesses did not affect the prosecution's case, as the testimonies of PW-1, PW-2, and PW-4 were found to be sufficient and reliable. The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction of Ajmal under section 302 IPC was not sustainable and modified the conviction to section 304 Part II IPC, considering the absence of premeditation and the nature of the injuries inflicted. The Supreme Court ordered that Ajmal be released forthwith as he had already undergone several years of incarceration, unless he was required in connection with any other case. The Supreme Court noted that there was no formation of an unlawful assembly with the common object of committing murder, and accordingly, the appellants were acquitted from the charge of unlawful assembly under section 149 IPC. The Supreme Court observed that the sticks and brick used in the assault were not premeditated deadly weapons but were picked up spontaneously during the altercation, which contributed to the decision to modify the conviction to section 304 Part II IPC.

case_name: Ajmer Singh & Ors. vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Ajmer Singh & Ors. vs. State of Haryana. Date: 11th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants were charged under Sections 148, 323, 325, and 307 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for causing injuries during a fight. The trial court convicted the appellants and sentenced them to six months rigorous imprisonment under Sections 148 and 323 read with Section 149 IPC, two years under Section 325 read with Section 149 IPC, and seven years under Section 307 read with Section 149 IPC. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellants but later modified the sentence under Section 307 read with Section 149 IPC from seven years to five years of rigorous imprisonment. The incident was triggered when Surender Singh tried to drive his tractor-trolley through a disputed passage, leading to a confrontation and subsequent fight involving lathi and spade blows. The complainant party, including Rajesh Kumar, Jagdish Chand, Lajwanti, Ravi Kumar, and Sanjeev Kumar, sustained injuries from lathi and spade blows during the fight. The appellants claimed that the complainant party was the aggressor, provoked by the usage of the passage, and that they acted in self-defense during a free fight involving both parties. The Supreme Court noted that both parties suffered injuries and that the appellants' injuries had not been adequately considered by the lower courts, highlighting the mutual nature of the altercation. The Supreme Court acknowledged that the passage in question was owned by the Gram Panchayat and not the complainant party, as established by a civil suit decision. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellants, ruling that the injuries on both sides and the nature of the fight did not justify the convictions. The appeals were allowed, and the appellants' bail bonds were discharged. The Supreme Court considered the mutual injuries, the ownership of the passage, the lack of premeditation, and the failure of the lower courts to adequately consider the defense's evidence in reversing the conviction.

case_name: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.. Date: 21st February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court erred in allowing additional evidence in the First Appeal without giving the appellant an opportunity to rebut or explain the additional evidence, which led to the setting aside of the trial court's decree in a partition suit. The trial court decreed the partition suit, declaring that the plaintiffs were entitled to a 1/4th share in the joint family properties described in Schedule B, C, and D of the plaint. The High Court set aside the trial court's judgement after accepting additional evidence, which included sale deeds indicating that a partition had already occurred in the family. The High Court ruled that there was no unity of title and possession between the parties based on this evidence. The Supreme Court ruled that the High Court should have given the appellant an opportunity to rebut the additional evidence or explain the alleged admissions in the sale deeds. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and remanded the case for fresh consideration. The Supreme Court instructed the High Court to decide the First Appeal afresh, giving the appellant an opportunity to lead evidence in rebuttal or explain the alleged admissions in the additional evidence. The Supreme Court expected the High Court to conclude the process expeditiously within six months. The procedural error committed by the High Court was that it admitted additional evidence and proceeded to decide the appeal without giving the appellant an opportunity to rebut the additional evidence or explain the alleged admissions, thereby violating the principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court simultaneously admitted additional evidence and decided the First Appeal on the same day, without providing the appellant an opportunity to respond to the new evidence, which was a procedural irregularity.

case_name: Alka Chandewar vs. Shamshul Ishrar Khan
text: Case: Alka Chandewar vs. Shamshul Ishrar Khan. Date: 6th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was correct in its interpretation of Section 27(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, concerning the enforcement of interim orders passed by the Arbitral Tribunal. The sole Arbitrator passed an interim order on 7th October 2010, stating that no further flats were to be disposed of without the leave of the Arbitral Tribunal. Shamshul Ishrar Khan allegedly transferred five flats on 14th October 2010, in breach of the interim order dated 7th October 2010. The High Court held that Section 27(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, does not empower the Tribunal to make representations to the Court for contempt for orders, including interim orders, passed by the Arbitrator, except in respect of taking evidence. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 27(5) to include persons guilty of any contempt to the Arbitral Tribunal during the conduct of arbitral proceedings, not just those failing to attend in accordance with the court process. The Supreme Court held that interim orders passed by the Arbitral Tribunal should have teeth and be enforceable; otherwise, the provision would be rendered otiose. The Supreme Court noted that sub-section (2) of Section 17 was added by the Amendment Act of 2015, making interim orders of the Arbitral Tribunal enforceable as orders of the Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Bombay High Court, and remanded the matter back to the High Court to decide the alleged contempt on facts.

case_name: All India Bank Officers' Confederation vs. The Regional Manager, Central Bank of India, and Others
text: Case: All India Bank Officers' Confederation vs. The Regional Manager, Central Bank of India, and Others. Date: 7th May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Section 17(2)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and Rule 3(7)(i) of the Income Tax Rules, 1962, which treat interest-free or concessional loans provided by banks to their employees as taxable perquisites, were valid. The appellants challenged these provisions on the grounds of excessive and unguided delegation of essential legislative functions to the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and argued that Rule 3(7)(i) was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution as it used the Prime Lending Rate (PLR) of the State Bank of India (SBI) as the benchmark. The High Courts of Madras and Madhya Pradesh upheld the validity of Section 17(2)(viii) and Rule 3(7)(i), dismissing the writ petitions filed by the bank officers' associations and staff unions challenging these provisions. The Supreme Court concluded that Section 17(2)(viii) and Rule 3(7)(i) did not result in an excessive delegation of legislative functions. The Court held that the provisions clearly reflected legislative policy and provided sufficient guidance to the rule-making authority. The Supreme Court held that using SBI's PLR as the benchmark for computing the taxable value of interest-free or concessional loans was not arbitrary or irrational. The Court noted that SBI's rates impact other banks and that a single clear benchmark ensures consistency and prevents unnecessary litigation. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upheld the High Courts' judgements, and validated the provisions of Section 17(2)(viii) of the Income Tax Act and Rule 3(7)(i) of the Income Tax Rules.

case_name: Amar Nath Jha vs. Nand Kishore Singh & Etc.
text: Case: Amar Nath Jha vs. Nand Kishore Singh & Etc.. Date: 3rd August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the appeal against the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction of Nand Kishore Singh and Maheshwar Singh for the offences under Section 396 IPC and the finding that Mintu Kumar @ Mintu Singh was a juvenile at the time of the offence. The prosecution's case was that on the night of 21st-22nd April 1999, 30-40 unknown persons committed dacoity in the houses of the informant (PW9) and his uncle Madhukant Jha (deceased), during which Madhukant Jha was killed by a gunshot. The High Court found that the prosecution's case was not believable due to lack of proper identification, recovery of stolen articles, and essential facts missing from the FIR. It also found that Mintu Kumar @ Mintu Singh was a juvenile at the time of the offence. The High Court criticized the inadequacy of the Test Identification Parade (TIP) as only Mintu Singh, a minor, was subjected to it, and none of the weapons used in the dacoity were recovered. The Supreme Court rejected the informant's attempt to withdraw the special leave petitions, stating that proceedings in a criminal case, especially of this nature, cannot depend on the whims of the informant. The Supreme Court noted that the recovery of stolen articles was limited and the identification of these articles by witnesses was suspicious, which cast doubt on the credibility of the allegations. The Supreme Court viewed the absence of certain essential facts in the FIR, such as the presence of key witnesses, as creating suspicion and undermining the prosecution's case. The High Court's finding that Mintu Kumar @ Mintu Singh was a juvenile at the time of the offence, based on a medical examination, was significant as it resulted in his case being referred to the Juvenile Justice Board. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgement, dismissing the appeals and confirming the acquittal of Nand Kishore Singh and Maheshwar Singh, and the finding that Mintu Kumar @ Mintu Singh was a juvenile. The Supreme Court stated that appellate courts should not casually overturn an acquittal, especially when the High Court has provided detailed reasoning and the prosecution failed to explain certain missing links in the alleged offence. The Supreme Court found the High Court's judgement to be the only possible view due to the prosecution's failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and the detailed reasons provided by the High Court for the acquittal.

case_name: Amar Nath Neogi vs State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Amar Nath Neogi vs State of Jharkhand. Date: 10th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Amar Nath Neogi, a senior citizen and not a government servant, should be granted anticipatory bail in a case where the final report had already been filed. Amar Nath Neogi was charged under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The investigation in the case against Amar Nath Neogi had been completed, and the final report had been filed. The Supreme Court directed Amar Nath Neogi to surrender before the Court of competent jurisdiction within two weeks and stated that he should be released on bail upon executing a bond of Rs. 50,000 with two solvent sureties of the same amount. The Supreme Court questioned the need for anticipatory bail since Amar Nath Neogi was a senior citizen who had never been in government service, and the investigation was already completed with the final report filed. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal, directing Amar Nath Neogi to surrender and be released on bail as specified, and disposed of any pending applications with no orders as to costs. Amar Nath Neogi was required to execute a bond of Rs. 50,000 with two solvent sureties of the same amount as a condition for his bail. The case was presided over by Justice Kurian Joseph and Justice R. Banumathi. Amar Nath Neogi was directed to surrender before the Court of competent jurisdiction where the final report had been filed, within two weeks from the date of the judgment.

case_name: Ambalal Parihar vs State of Rajasthan & Ors.
text: Case: Ambalal Parihar vs State of Rajasthan & Ors.. Date: 16th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the second to fourth respondents committed gross abuse of process of law and forum shopping by filing a Civil Writ Petition to club eight FIRs and seek relief from coercive action. Six FIRs were registered against the second to fourth respondents at the instance of the appellant, Ambalal Parihar. The second to fourth respondents sought a writ of mandamus to club the eight FIRs and consolidate them into one, and to prevent any coercive action against them in connection with all eight FIRs. The High Court's Single Judge ordered that no coercive action shall be taken against the second to fourth respondents in connection with all eight FIRs. The appellant alleged that the respondents filed the Civil Writ Petition to avoid the roster Judge who had not granted interim relief in the petitions under Section 482 of CrPC, and this was a classic case of forum hunting. The Supreme Court viewed the filing of the Civil Writ Petition as a gross abuse of process of law and a clear instance of forum hunting. The Supreme Court set aside and dismissed the High Court's order in the Civil Writ Petition No. 6277 of 2023. The Supreme Court imposed costs of Rs. 50,000 on the second to fourth respondents, to be paid to the Rajasthan State Legal Services Authority. The Supreme Court directed that the conduct of the second to fourth respondents be brought to the notice of the concerned Court hearing the petitions under Section 482 CrPC and that a copy of the order be placed in all eight petitions. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order in the Civil Writ Petition, and imposed costs on the second to fourth respondents.

case_name: Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. vs K.S. Infraspace LLP & Anr.
text: Case: Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. vs K.S. Infraspace LLP & Anr.. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the dispute between Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. and K.S. Infraspace LLP qualified as a commercial dispute within the meaning of Section 2(1)(c) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. K.S. Infraspace LLP filed the application seeking an order to return the plaint to be presented in the appropriate court, arguing that the dispute did not qualify as a commercial dispute. The Commercial Court rejected the application on 17th October 2018, deciding that the dispute was a commercial dispute. The High Court set aside the Commercial Court's order, directed that the plaint be returned to be presented in the appropriate court, and concluded that the dispute did not qualify as a commercial dispute. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion that the immovable property involved was not being used exclusively in trade or commerce, and therefore, the dispute did not qualify as a commercial dispute. The Supreme Court directed that the plaint be returned to the appellant to be presented in the appropriate court having jurisdiction. The Supreme Court clarified that a commercial dispute involves agreements relating to immovable property used exclusively in trade or commerce and that the property must be actually used for such purposes at the time of the dispute. The decision may ensure that only disputes involving property actually used in trade or commerce are classified as commercial disputes, thus maintaining the efficiency of the Commercial Courts. Parties should consider whether the immovable property involved in the dispute is actually used exclusively in trade or commerce at the time of the dispute. Misclassifying a dispute as a commercial dispute could lead to jurisdictional challenges and delays in the resolution process. The principles may encourage parties to ensure that their suits clearly qualify as commercial disputes under the Act to avoid dismissal or transfer to a non-commercial court.

case_name: Ameena Begum vs The State of Telangana & Ors.
text: Case: Ameena Begum vs The State of Telangana & Ors.. Date: 4th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the detention order dated 24th March 2023 against Ameena Begum's husband under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986, was justified and lawful. Ameena Begum's husband was detained on grounds of being a habitual offender involved in multiple criminal activities, including outraging the modesty of women, cheating, extortion, obstructing public servants, robbery, and criminal intimidation, as per the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986. Ameena Begum submitted a representation on 29th March 2023 under Section 10 of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986, seeking revocation of the detention order. The Advisory Board opined that there was sufficient cause for the detention of the detenu, leading the Government to issue an order on 20th May 2023, confirming the detention for 12 months from the date of detention, i.e., 27th March 2023. Ameena Begum's counsel argued that the High Court's judgement suffered from factual and legal errors and that the detention order was not justified, both substantively and procedurally. The Supreme Court emphasized that not all breaches of law lead to public disorder. Public disorder must affect the community at large, whereas breaches of law affecting only individuals fall under 'law and order'. The Supreme Court found the detention order invalid because the incidents cited were isolated acts affecting individuals and did not pose a threat to public order. The Court also noted that the existing legal framework was sufficient to address such acts without resorting to preventive detention. The Supreme Court suggested that preventive detention laws should not be used as a substitute for the ordinary criminal justice system and should be invoked only in cases where there is a clear and present danger to public order. The ruling may lead to more stringent scrutiny of detention orders, ensuring they are not used arbitrarily and are only applied in cases of genuine public order threats, thereby protecting individual liberties. The Supreme Court quashed the detention order and directed the immediate release of Ameena Begum's husband, holding that the detention was unjustified and not in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court highlighted that future preventive detention orders must strictly adhere to legal requirements, ensure proper application of mind, and differentiate clearly between issues of 'law and order' and 'public order'.

case_name: Amina Marwa Sabreen A (Minor) and Others vs State of Kerala and Others
text: Case: Amina Marwa Sabreen A (Minor) and Others vs State of Kerala and Others. Date: 24th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the petitioners, being non-Keralite residents of Tamil Nadu, should be given preference for admission in minority medical institutions in Kerala despite their low All India ranking in NEET-UG. The petitioners are Amina Marwa Sabreen A (Minor) and two others, belonging to the Muslim minority community and residents of Tamil Nadu. The petitioners challenged the Press Release because it mandated centralized counseling for all medical seats in Kerala, including those in minority institutions, which they believed should conduct their own counseling. The Ordinance provides for the regulation of admission and fixation of fees for private medical educational institutions in Kerala, and includes provisions for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes. The petitioners argued that the Ordinance and Press Release unfairly preferred Keralite students over non-Keralite students for admissions to medical colleges in Kerala, including minority institutions. The petitioners requested the Supreme Court to quash the Press Release dated 1st July 2017 and direct the Directorate General of Health Services to conduct admissions to minority medical institutions on an all-India basis. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground of maintainability, citing the lack of specific prayers and pleadings challenging the Government Order dated 30th January 2017. The G.O. detailed the admission procedures for professional courses in Kerala, categorizing students as Keralite, Non-Keralite Category I (NK I), and Non-Keralite Category II (NK II), and specifying eligibility criteria for each category. The petitioners were ineligible because they were categorized as Non-Keralite Category II (NK II), which excluded them from eligibility for admission to medical and allied courses in Kerala. The decision may reinforce the state's authority to include minority institutions in centralized counseling, potentially limiting the autonomy of such institutions in their admission processes. The dismissal could discourage similar challenges from non-Keralite students and affirm the preferential treatment of Keralite students in the state's admission policies.

case_name: Aminuddin vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Aminuddin vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 15th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court's order granting bail to the second respondent in a murder case was justified, considering the seriousness of the offence and the evidence presented. The second respondent was charged with murder under Section 302 of the IPC for the killing of the appellant's son with knives. The appellant was the father of the deceased. The postmortem report revealed that the deceased had sustained eight ante mortem injuries, which caused his death. The Sessions Judge rejected the bail application, noting the direct charge of murder, the seriousness of the crime, and the injuries mentioned in the postmortem report. The High Court granted bail citing the larger mandate of Article 21 of the Constitution of India, without providing specific reasons related to the case. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order did not pass muster as it failed to consider relevant factors such as the seriousness of the offence and the evidence presented. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in Mahipal vs. Rajesh Kumar, emphasizing the need for Judges to provide reasoned decisions when granting or refusing bail. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail and directed the second respondent to surrender forthwith. The Supreme Court disposed of all pending applications related to this case.

case_name: Amit Sachan & Anr. Vs. Bar Council of Uttar Pradesh, Lucknow & Ors.
text: Case: Amit Sachan & Anr. Vs. Bar Council of Uttar Pradesh, Lucknow & Ors.. Date: 24th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the cancellation and rescheduling of the election of the Awadh Bar Association due to unruly behavior during the election process held on 14th August 2021. The High Court canceled the election due to unruly behavior, misbehavior with female lawyers, and a breach of protocol during the polling process, which led to security issues in the premises of the High Court. The High Court directed the implementation of the 'one Bar one Vote' principle, the display of voter lists, the prohibition of canvassing through distribution of visiting cards, pamphlets, and hosting dinner parties, and the formulation of a 'code of conduct' for elections. The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions, agreeing with the High Court's decision to hold fresh elections to maintain the purity of the election process, despite the petitioners' argument about the difficulty of bringing back nearly 4,500 members for voting during the pandemic. The Supreme Court noted that the misbehavior and unruly conduct of some advocates during the elections, including tearing ballot papers and pushing female lawyers, cannot be tolerated and must be deprecated. The Supreme Court emphasized that the legal profession is noble and crucial for the administration of justice, and the independence of the Bar must be maintained to ensure a strong judicial system. The High Court took suo moto cognizance due to the unruly behavior of advocates that led to security concerns and intervention by officers and police to maintain order, thereby disrupting the election process. The High Court directed the Awadh Bar Association to prohibit canvassing through visiting cards, pamphlets, posters, and hosting dinner parties, and to debar members involved in misbehavior during the elections. The decision may lead to stricter enforcement of election rules and conduct to prevent misbehavior and ensure a fair and orderly election process, potentially reducing incidents of unruly behavior in future elections. The decision reinforces the importance of maintaining the purity of elections and the conduct of Bar Associations, ensuring that only genuine voters and regularly practicing advocates participate in the election process, thereby upholding the integrity and independence of the Bar.

case_name: Amit Vashistha vs. Suresh & Anr.
text: Case: Amit Vashistha vs. Suresh & Anr.. Date: 31st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the complaint filed under Section 228 of the IPC for obstructing judicial proceedings under Section 7A of the Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, was maintainable. The allegations were that Suresh obstructed and interfered with the adjudication proceedings by abusing and attempting to assault the Presiding Officer, leading to the filing of a complaint under Section 228 IPC. The High Court acquitted Suresh on the grounds that the adjudication proceedings under Section 7A of the Employees Provident Funds Act were not conducted before a court, thus the complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(i) Cr.P.C. was not maintainable. The appellant argued that the proceedings under Section 7A were judicial proceedings, and therefore, the complaint under Section 228 IPC was maintainable as the proceedings should be considered as being conducted before a court. The Supreme Court held that the proceedings under Section 7A are indeed judicial proceedings as defined under Section 2(i) of the Cr.P.C., and thus, they can be equated with proceedings before a court for the purpose of Section 195(1)(b)(i) Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, reinstated the conviction of the respondent under Section 228 IPC, and upheld the initial punishment imposed by the Magistrate.

case_name: Amol Vitthalrao Kadu vs. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: Case: Amol Vitthalrao Kadu vs. State of Maharashtra & Ors.. Date: 10th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the Investigating Officer could be held personally liable for the compensation awarded to the family of Pravin, who died in police custody, without a prior determination of liability. The Investigating Officer was held liable by the High Court for the compensation amount awarded to the family of Pravin, who allegedly died an unnatural death while in police custody. The High Court directed the State to pay Rs. 7 lakhs as compensation to Pravin's family and recover the amount from the Investigating Officer-in-charge of the case at the time of Pravin's death. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's order, stating that the compensation could only be recovered from the Investigating Officer after the liability was fixed and determined in the pending proceedings. The Supreme Court noted that proceedings were pending to determine the liability for Pravin's death and directed that the State could recover the compensation from the erring officials only after the liability was established. The Supreme Court referred to the principles established in the D.K. Basu vs. State of West Bengal case, emphasizing that monetary compensation is an effective remedy for the infringement of the fundamental right to life by public servants. The Supreme Court reiterated that the defense of sovereign immunity is not available to the State for the acts of its officials that infringe upon the fundamental rights of citizens, and the State is vicariously liable for their actions. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part, modifying the High Court's order to state that the compensation amount should be recovered from the concerned officials only after their liability is determined. The Supreme Court directed that the compensation already paid to Pravin's family by the State should not be recovered from the Investigating Officer until the liability is determined in the pending proceedings. The D.K. Basu case established that compensation for the infringement of fundamental rights by public servants is a well-accepted remedy, emphasizing the State's vicarious liability and the need for compensatory, rather than punitive, relief.

case_name: Amritlal vs Shantilal Soni & Ors.
text: Case: Amritlal vs Shantilal Soni & Ors.. Date: 28th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main accusation was that Shantilal Soni & Ors. committed offences punishable under Section 406 read with Section 34 and Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) by refusing to return 33.139 Kg of silver entrusted to them by the appellant Amritlal. The Judicial Magistrate First Class, Khachrod, took cognizance of the offences on 4th December 2012 and framed charges against the accused on 12th September 2013. The High Court held that taking cognizance of the offence on 4th December 2012 was barred by limitation since the alleged incident occurred on 4th October 2009, and quashed the proceedings under Sections 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC). The Supreme Court relied on the principle laid down by the Constitution Bench in the case of Sarah Mathew v. Institute of Cardio Vascular Diseases, which stated that for computing the period of limitation under Section 468 CrPC, the relevant date is the date of filing the complaint or the date of institution of prosecution, not the date on which the Magistrate takes cognizance. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order dated 6th March 2019, dismissed the petition filed before the High Court, and directed the trial magistrate to proceed with the trial expeditiously. The Supreme Court directed that any attempt by the accused-respondents to delay or obstruct the trial would lead to coercive proceedings, including the possible cancellation of bail and imposition of monetary conditions equivalent to the present value of the property involved. The parties were directed to appear before the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Khachrod, District Ujjain on 1st April 2022.

case_name: Amy Mehta vs. State of Karnataka & Anr.
text: Case: Amy Mehta vs. State of Karnataka & Anr.. Date: 17th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in releasing the accused on bail despite the seriousness of the allegations and the gravity of the offences under Sections 376, 354, 328, and 120B of the IPC. The prosecutrix alleged that the accused mixed a substance in her drink, causing her to lose consciousness, and then committed a sexual act on her while she was intoxicated. The High Court reasoned that the complaint was filed after five days, the matter of intoxicating the prosecutrix and subjecting her to a sexual act was to be determined at trial, and the accused had been in custody since 11th February 2022, with no need for further custodial interrogation. The Supreme Court found the decision unsustainable because the High Court failed to consider the seriousness of the allegations, the gravity of the offences, and the material collected during the investigation. It also noted that the High Court did not properly appreciate the delay in filing the FIR and the prosecutrix's efforts to lodge the complaint. The Supreme Court noted that the delay in filing the FIR could be due to the prosecutrix needing time to recover from the shock and that this aspect should be considered at the time of trial, not as a basis for granting bail. The Supreme Court instructed the High Court to consider the bail application afresh, taking into account the seriousness of the offence, the material collected during the investigation, and the statement of the prosecutrix recorded under Section 161 of the Cr.PC, which are now part of the chargesheet. The Supreme Court directed the accused to surrender before the concerned court/jail authority within one week from the judgement date and instructed the High Court to decide the bail application afresh thereafter. The Supreme Court emphasized that while considering bail applications, courts must consider the seriousness of the offence, the gravity of the allegations, and the material collected during the investigation, ensuring that justice is served both to the accused and the victim. The Supreme Court viewed the High Court's consideration of the need for further custodial trial as irrelevant when deciding on the bail application under Section 439 of the Cr.PC. It noted that this consideration might be relevant in anticipatory bail applications but not in regular bail applications. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order releasing the accused on bail and remitted the matter to the High Court to consider the bail application afresh in accordance with the law and the relevant material collected during the investigation.

case_name: Anand Kumar Tiwari & Ors. vs. High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Anand Kumar Tiwari & Ors. vs. High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 12th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the determination of inter-se seniority between directly recruited and promotee District Judges in Madhya Pradesh. The petitioners sought to quash the amendment made on 08.06.2005 to the Madhya Pradesh Uchchtar Nyayik Sewa (Bharti Tatha Seva Sharten) Niyam, 1994, and the order dated 27.10.2015, which determined the inter-se seniority of direct recruited and promotee District Judges. The petitioners contended that the seniority list wrongly showed them below the District Judges who were promoted through the Limited Competitive Examination (LCE). The High Court based its decision on the date of appointment, resolving that District Judges promoted through LCE on 02.09.2009 should be given seniority over those directly recruited on 10.09.2009. The 2017 Rules specified that 65% of the posts should be filled by promotion on merit-cum-seniority, 10% by promotion through LCE, and 25% by direct recruitment from eligible advocates. Seniority would be determined based on a roster system. The petitioners argued that the delay in amending the seniority rules as directed by the Supreme Court should not be detrimental to their interests, and the 2017 Rules should be applied retrospectively to determine seniority based on a roster system. The Supreme Court held that the petitioners were not entitled to retrospective application of the 2017 Rules, as Rule 11(1) stated that the relative seniority of members holding substantive posts before the commencement of the Rules would remain unchanged. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's use of the principle of continuous officiation, stating that in the absence of specific rules for determining inter-se seniority, the date of appointment or promotion could be used. The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions, upholding the High Court's seniority list issued on 27.10.2015, which placed the promotee District Judges above the direct recruits. The judgment reinforces the application of continuous officiation and the adherence to the seniority rules in effect at the time of appointments or promotions, providing clarity on the determination of inter-se seniority in the absence of specific rules. The respondents argued that the delay was due to the pendency of an SLP before the Supreme Court, and the 2017 Rules were eventually implemented prospectively to address the seniority determination based on a roster system.

case_name: Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board vs. CCL Products (India) Limited
text: Case: Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board vs. CCL Products (India) Limited. Date: 22nd July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board's invocation of three bank guarantees furnished by CCL Products was justified and whether the National Green Tribunal (NGT) was correct in directing the refund of the amounts covered by these guarantees. The Pollution Control Board received complaints about environmental pollution caused by CCL Products and, after a Task Force Committee review, issued directions on 26th August 2011 for CCL to improve its existing systems and comply with specific environmental standards. The Task Force Committee directed CCL to improve its effluent treatment plant (ETP), install flow meters and energy meters, store treated effluents in lined lagoons, use treated effluents on its own land, and ensure no discharge of effluents outside the premises. The Board found certain violations during inspections and decided to invoke the bank guarantees due to CCL Products' non-compliance with the directions issued to ensure environmental standards. The National Green Tribunal held that the invocation of the bank guarantees was unwarranted as the principles of natural justice were not followed. It directed the Pollution Control Board to refund the amounts to CCL Products. The Supreme Court set aside the NGT's judgement, stating that the invocation of the bank guarantees was justified as they were unconditional and issued to secure compliance with environmental norms. The court emphasized that bank guarantees constitute independent contracts, and their invocation should be upheld unless there is evidence of fraud or irretrievable injustice. The Supreme Court reasoned that the Pollution Control Board had followed due process by issuing show cause notices and conducting hearings. It found that the bank guarantees were invoked in terms of the conditions stipulated, and the Board's actions were to secure compliance with environmental standards.

case_name: Anees vs. The State Govt. of NCT
text: Case: Anees vs. The State Govt. of NCT. Date: 3rd May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. Anees was convicted of the offence punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his wife, Saira. The investigation revealed that the marital relationship was strained due to the deceased's behavior of leaving the house without permission and returning late. On the night of the incident, an altercation led to Anees inflicting stab injuries on Saira, resulting in her death. Their minor daughter, Shaheena, was the sole eyewitness. Shaheena, the minor daughter, was the sole eyewitness to the incident. She initially stated that she saw her father inflicting knife injuries on her mother but later turned hostile during the trial, claiming that thieves had attacked her parents. The post-mortem report revealed multiple incised wounds and stab wounds on Saira's body, including deep injuries to the abdomen, liver, and heart, which were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The courts found the appellant's explanation that two intruders had attacked his wife to be false. The appellant failed to provide any details about the alleged intruders and did not disclose this to the Investigating Officer immediately after the incident. The knife used in the commission of the crime was discovered at the instance of Anees from a drain outside his house. The discovery, corroborated by the forensic analysis of blood-stained clothes matching the blood group of the deceased, was significant evidence against Anees. The trial court concluded that the appellant, Anees, was guilty of the murder of his wife, Saira, and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000. In default of payment, he was to undergo further rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court dismissed Anees' appeal, affirming the judgement and order of conviction passed by the trial court. The High Court found that the appellant's failure to disclose the details of the incident and his false explanation were additional links in the chain of circumstantial evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, agreeing that the circumstantial evidence and the appellant's conduct pointed to his guilt. The court emphasized the applicability of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, noting that the appellant failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the incident. The Supreme Court highlighted the principle that when a crime occurs inside a house, the burden of proof shifts to the accused to provide a satisfactory explanation. The failure to do so, coupled with false explanations, can be used to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court stated that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a prima facie case based on reasonable inferences. If the accused fails to offer a reasonable explanation, the court can draw an adverse inference, adding an additional link to the chain of circumstances proving guilt.
