case_name: Aneesh Kumar V.S. & Ors. vs State of Kerala & Ors.
text: Case: Aneesh Kumar V.S. & Ors. vs State of Kerala & Ors.. Date: 24th April 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether the candidates from the first Ranked List (RL-I) are entitled to be appointed to the 93 Non-Joining Duty (NJD) vacancies reported after the list expired. The RL-I was considered expired on 1st June 2016 because the last batch of candidates advised from it commenced training on 1st May 2016, and the list's validity ended one month after this date, as per Rule 13 of the Kerala Public Service Commission Rules of Procedure, 1976. The Division Bench concluded that the RL-I expired on 19th July 2016 due to the interim orders that caused its life to be extended. The Supreme Court observed that the maxim does not apply in this case because the candidates had already obtained all vacancies they were entitled to during the life of RL-I, even if there were no litigations or interim orders. The candidates filed appeals in the Supreme Court challenging the Full Bench's decision that the RL-I had expired before the 93 NJD vacancies were reported. The decision to treat RL-I as expired excluded the candidates from being advised for the 93 NJD vacancies reported after the expiration of RL-I, affecting their employment opportunities. The Supreme Court clarified that a Ranked List expires one month after the commencement of training of the last batch of candidates advised from the list. The case underscores the importance of strict adherence to the validity period of Ranked Lists and emphasizes that judicial intervention or delays cannot extend the statutory lifespan of such lists. The appellants sought a direction under Article 142 to accommodate them against the existing vacancies, citing equity and fairness due to the delays caused by litigation. The Supreme Court reasoned that the RL-I had expired before the vacancies were reported, and the appellants had no legal claim to these vacancies under the statutory rules. The Commission might consider establishing clearer timelines for reporting vacancies and processing appointments to ensure that all vacancies are filled within the validity period of Ranked Lists.

case_name: Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. vs. MMTC Ltd.
text: Case: Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. vs. MMTC Ltd.. Date: 17th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main agreement was a Long Term Agreement (LTA) dated 7th March 2007, where Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. agreed to supply certain quantities of freshly mined and washed 'German Creek', 'Isaac', and 'Moranbah North' coking coal to MMTC Ltd. The main issues of dispute were whether MMTC Ltd. committed a breach of contract by not lifting the agreed quantity of coking coal, and whether Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. was in breach for not supplying the contracted quantity of coal. The Majority Award concluded that MMTC Ltd. committed a breach of contract by not lifting 454,034 metric tonnes of coking coal within the Fifth Delivery Period. The Majority Award found that Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. was at all material times in a position to perform its obligations under the Agreement by supplying the requisite quantities of coal in a timely manner. The Majority Award ordered MMTC Ltd. to pay damages to Anglo American Metallurgical Coal Pty Ltd. in the sum of USD 78,720,414.92, with additional interest and costs. The Division Bench of the High Court of Delhi set aside the Majority Award and the judgment of the Single Judge, concluding that the Majority Award was based on no evidence and was therefore perverse. The Supreme Court of India concluded that the Majority Award was a detailed award based on facts, and the Division Bench had arbitrarily picked out three emails to arrive at a faulty conclusion, acting as a court of appeal.

case_name: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 13th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellant Anil Bhardwaj was correctly deemed unsuitable for the post of District Judge (Entry Level) due to a pending criminal case under Section 498A/406/34 IPC, despite his subsequent acquittal. Anil Bhardwaj was deemed unsuitable for the post due to the pendency of a criminal case filed by his wife under Section 498A/406/34 IPC, as noted in his attestation form and verified by the police report. The appellant argued that his case for appointment should have been reconsidered following his acquittal on 18th September 2019, as he had disclosed the pending FIR in his application and had not concealed any information. The Supreme Court held that the appellant's subsequent acquittal did not automatically entitle him to reconsideration for the post. The Court emphasized that judicial service candidates must have impeccable character and integrity, and the pending case at the time of selection justified the Committee's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the Committee's determination of his unsuitability was valid and justified based on the pending criminal case at the time of selection. Yes, the Supreme Court noted that the appellant's acquittal had washed away any stigma associated with the criminal case, ensuring that his future prospects were not tainted by the prior allegations.

case_name: Anil Kumar Singh vs. Vijay Pal Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Anil Kumar Singh vs. Vijay Pal Singh & Ors.. Date: 30th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the plaintiff, Anil Kumar Singh, could withdraw his suit under Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the orders of the Trial Court and the Revision Court, which had allowed the withdrawal. The dispute related to a land bearing numbers 629-A/0.0320 hectares and 629-B/1.5820 hectares situated in the village of Asyoli Pargana, Bangar, Tehsil and District Hardoi (UP). The appellant, Anil Kumar Singh, claimed ownership of 3/4th of the suit land, while the remaining 1/4th belonged to Ajit Pratap Singh. The Trial Court allowed Anil Kumar Singh's application to withdraw the suit under Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, subject to the payment of Rs. 350/- as costs to Vijay Pal Singh. The suit was dismissed as withdrawn with the condition that no further suit on the same cause of action could be filed. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Vijay Pal Singh, set aside the orders of the Trial Court and the Revision Court, and directed Anil Kumar Singh to place Vijay Pal Singh in possession of the suit land. The Supreme Court held that the High Court committed a jurisdictional error in setting aside the orders of the Trial Court and the Revision Court. The High Court was not justified in interfering with the appellant's right to withdraw the suit under Order XXIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order of the High Court, and restored the orders of the Trial Court and the Revision Court, which permitted Anil Kumar Singh to withdraw the suit.

case_name: Anil Kumar Yadav vs State (NCT) of Delhi & Anr.
text: Case: Anil Kumar Yadav vs State (NCT) of Delhi & Anr.. Date: 14th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the cancellation of bail granted to Anil Kumar Yadav and other accused by the High Court of Delhi, which was challenged by the appellants in the Supreme Court. The incident occurred on 21st October 2015, where Rohit Bansal and his friends were assaulted by the accused at Shanghai Club, Hauz Khas, leading to the death of Rupesh Tanwar and injuries to Rohit Bansal. The trial court granted bail to Anil Kumar Yadav based on the lack of specific role attributed to him, as seen in the CCTV footage, and the fact that he had been in custody for about sixteen months. The High Court cancelled the bail citing that the trial court's decision was based on irrelevant considerations, such as discrepancies in the CCTV footage and the period of incarceration, which did not justify granting bail in a serious crime like murder. The prosecution argued that the accused were involved in a serious crime, as evidenced by witness testimonies, CCTV footage, and the recovery of incriminating articles from the accused. They emphasized the potential for the accused to tamper with evidence and intimidate witnesses. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court correctly set aside the trial court's decision, as the latter had granted bail on erroneous grounds and without considering the serious nature of the crime and the evidence against the accused. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upheld the High Court's decision to cancel the bail, and directed the accused to surrender before the Committal Court within one week from the date of the order.

case_name: Anil Kumar vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: Anil Kumar vs. State of Kerala. Date: 1st November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Anil Kumar was charged under Sections 302 and 498A of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his wife and for causing mental and physical harassment. The incident occurred on 26th September 2010, when Anil Kumar allegedly set his wife on fire after she poured kerosene on herself during a quarrel. The wife later succumbed to her burn injuries. The FIR stated that the deceased wife poured kerosene on herself due to unbearable mental and physical harassment by Anil Kumar, and he then set her on fire with the intention to kill her. Anil Kumar's defense was that his wife had a suicidal tendency and had previously tried to harm herself. He claimed that she set herself on fire and he attempted to douse the flames. Both the trial court and High Court rejected Anil Kumar's defense, relying on the evidence of frequent quarrels and harassment, as well as the dying declarations of the deceased. The dying declarations stated that Anil Kumar assaulted the deceased, who then poured kerosene on herself. Anil Kumar then ignited a matchstick and set her on fire, saying 'You Die'. The Supreme Court held that Section 302 IPC was applicable as the act of setting the deceased on fire was premeditated and intentional, thereby not qualifying for the lesser charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-II IPC. The Supreme Court interpreted the evidence of past quarrels and harassment as indicative of a pattern of abusive behavior, which supported the prosecution's case that the act was intentional and premeditated. The Supreme Court dismissed Anil Kumar's appeal, upheld his conviction and life imprisonment sentence under Section 302 IPC, and one year of rigorous imprisonment under Section 498A IPC, with both sentences running concurrently. The Supreme Court noted that Anil Kumar, who is in jail, may apply for remission in accordance with the prevailing policy of the State.

case_name: Anita Rani vs. Ashok Kumar & Ors.
text: Case: Anita Rani vs. Ashok Kumar & Ors.. Date: 16th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Anita Rani filed two money suits: one for the recovery of Rs.10,48,000/- and another for Rs.67,31,000/-. The first suit involved a loan given to the respondents which was partially repaid, while the second suit involved unauthorized withdrawals from her joint bank account with her son. The trial court dismissed both suits. In the first suit, it was held that the plaintiff failed to establish the loan and the suit was barred by limitation. In the second suit, the court found that the payments were part of a real estate business and a settlement was reached, dismissing the fraud allegations. The First Appellate Court allowed Anita Rani's appeals, granting decrees in both suits for the recovery of the amounts claimed with interest. The court ruled in favor of Anita Rani, setting aside the trial court's dismissal of her suits. The High Court allowed the second appeals filed by the respondents, resulting in the dismissal of both money suits filed by Anita Rani. The High Court also directed Anita Rani to refund Rs.55,00,000/- paid by the respondents with interest. The Supreme Court found that the High Court and the trial court went on the wrong track by accepting the respondents' plea of full and final settlement without sufficient evidence. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court overlooked key aspects and set aside the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed Anita Rani's appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the First Appellate Court's decrees in both suits. The Supreme Court also awarded costs of Rs.50,000/- to Anita Rani and ordered the release of the deposited amount with interest.

case_name: Anjana Saraiya vs The State of U.P. & Ors.
text: Case: Anjana Saraiya vs The State of U.P. & Ors.. Date: 12th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the cancellation of Anjana Saraiya's allotment of Plot No. 415 in the Organized Development Scheme, Phase-III, Pilkhuwa, District Ghaziabad, due to delayed installment payments was justified. Anjana Saraiya cited her husband's continuous ill-health and resulting financial crisis as reasons for her inability to pay the fourth to seventh installments on time. Despite these challenges, she managed to secure the money and clear all dues, including interest, before receiving the cancellation notice. The High Court of Allahabad dismissed Anjana Saraiya's writ petition, stating that she did not fulfill the terms and conditions of the allotment scheme by failing to pay the installments regularly and on time. The Supreme Court found that Anjana Saraiya's delay in payment was not deliberate or willful, considering her financial difficulties and the ill-health of her husband. The Court allowed her to regularize the account by paying an additional sum of Rs. 2 lakhs as compensation for the delayed payment, thus setting aside the cancellation order. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to hand over the vacant possession of the plot to Anjana Saraiya and execute the necessary documents within a period of four weeks after she deposits the additional sum of Rs. 2 lakhs within six weeks from the date of the judgment. Anjana Saraiya had deposited a total sum of Rs. 3,84,546 (including interest) against the total value of Rs. 2,70,000 for the plot. This demonstrated her bonafides and influenced the Supreme Court's decision to allow her to regularize the account and set aside the cancellation order.

case_name: Anjum Ara vs The State of Bihar and Others
text: Case: Anjum Ara vs The State of Bihar and Others. Date: 8th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue in the case is the challenge against the appointment of Anjum Ara as Anganwari Sevika and the subsequent cancellation of her appointment by the Appellate Authority. Anjum Ara's appointment was challenged on the basis that her father was a Panchayat Teacher, earning Rs.6,000 per month, which allegedly disqualified her under Clause 4.9 of the 2011 Anganwari Sevika Guidelines. The initial appeal by respondent No.8 was allowed by the Appellate Authority, setting aside the appointment of Anjum Ara. The High Court struck down Clause 4.9 of the 2011 Anganwari Sevika Guidelines as it was found to be in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court found the decisions unsustainable because once Clause 4.9 was struck down by the High Court, it ceased to exist, and it was not necessary for Anjum Ara to challenge its validity separately. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgments and orders, set aside the Appellate Authority's order, and directed the reinstatement of Anjum Ara as Anganwari Sevika.

case_name: Ankush Maruti Shinde and Others vs. State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Ankush Maruti Shinde and Others vs. State of Maharashtra. Date: 5th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue is the confirmation of the death sentence imposed by the Sessions Court on Ankush Maruti Shinde and others for the crimes of robbery, murder, and gang rape. The impugned judgement was passed by the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court. The Sessions Court convicted six accused under various sections of the IPC, including robbery, murder, and gang rape, and sentenced them to death. The Bombay High Court altered the death sentences of accused nos. 3, 5, and 6 to life imprisonment, while confirming the death sentences for accused nos. 1, 2, and 4. The Supreme Court recalled its judgement due to the lack of opportunity for accused nos. 3, 5, and 6 to be heard before deciding on the appeals for enhancement of their sentences. The prosecution stated that seven to eight unknown persons entered Trambak's hut, threatened and assaulted the family members, robbed them, and committed gang rape. The prosecution relied on oral evidence from witnesses, medical evidence, and identification of the accused in test identification parades. PW1 (Manoj Satote) was the complainant and an eyewitness, while PW8 (Vimalabai) was also an eyewitness and a victim who survived the assault. The defense argued that the identification of the accused was unreliable due to poor lighting conditions, lack of forensic evidence, and the possibility of mistaken identity. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals of accused nos. 1, 2, and 4, confirming their death sentences, and restored the death sentences of accused nos. 3, 5, and 6 as initially imposed by the Sessions Court.

case_name: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
text: Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari. Date: 5th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the settlement of all disputes and litigations between Anu Bhandari and Pradip Bhandari, including the dissolution of their marriage by mutual consent. There were twenty-three cases pending before various courts, including Trial Courts, the High Court, the Supreme Court, and the Consumer Forum. The mediation efforts were facilitated by Hon'ble Mrs. Justice Lisa Gill, Judge of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, and Ms. Meenakshi Arora, learned Senior Counsel, appointed by the Supreme Court as a Mediator. The mediation efforts led to an amicable settlement between the parties, resulting in the resolution of all their disputes and the filing of a mutual consent divorce petition. The Supreme Court quashed several pending cases and dismissed others in terms of the settlement, effectively ending all civil and criminal litigations between the parties. Mr. Pradip Bhandari was directed to transfer his share in agricultural land situated in Village Golpura, Tehsil and District Panchkula to Ms. Anu Bhandari, their daughter Bhuvi Bhandari, and their son Vibhu Bhandari. The Supreme Court restrained both parties from instituting any fresh litigation in respect of the subject matter without the Court's leave. The Supreme Court actively facilitated the settlement through mediation and directed the parties to appear before it, leading to the resolution of disputes and the grant of mutual consent divorce.

The Supreme Court restrained both parties from instituting any fresh litigation in respect of the subject matter without the Court's leave.
The Supreme Court actively facilitated the settlement through mediation and directed the parties to appear before it, leading to the resolution of disputes and the grant of mutual consent divorce.

case_name: Anuj Singh @ Ramanuj Singh and Manoj Singh vs. The State of Bihar
text: Case: Anuj Singh @ Ramanuj Singh and Manoj Singh vs. The State of Bihar. Date: 22nd April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Trial Court convicted Anuj Singh and Manoj Singh under Section 307 read with Section 34 IPC and under Section 27 of the Arms Act, sentencing them to five years of Rigorous Imprisonment under Section 307 and three years under Section 27 of the Arms Act, along with fines. The High Court modified the conviction of Anuj Singh and Manoj Singh under Section 307 read with Section 34 IPC to Section 324 IPC, reducing the sentence to two years of Rigorous Imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000. The conviction under Section 27 of the Arms Act was confirmed. The incident involved an altercation over the repairing of a wall on the roadside, during which the appellants Anuj Singh and Manoj Singh allegedly fired shots at the informant, causing injuries. The key evidence included the testimony of the injured informant (PW-6) and other witnesses who confirmed that Anuj Singh and Manoj Singh were present at the scene with firearms and caused injuries to the informant. The medical examination revealed gunshot wounds on the informant's right forearm and left leg, which were confirmed to be caused by firearms. The defense argued that Manoj Singh was not present at the scene as he was posted at Islampur Block as a junior engineer, supported by the testimony of defense witnesses. The Supreme Court observed that minor contradictions in the witnesses' testimonies do not discredit their overall reliability and should not be a ground to reject their testimony. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the convictions and sentences under Section 324 IPC and Section 27 of the Arms Act, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of medical evidence in corroborating the prosecution's case, noting that the injuries confirmed by the medical examination aligned with the testimonies of the eyewitnesses. The Supreme Court acknowledged the existence of previous enmity due to a land dispute, which was evident from the altercation and subsequent actions of the appellants.

case_name: Anushka Rengunthwar & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Anushka Rengunthwar & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 3rd February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue raised by the petitioners is the restriction imposed by the notification dated 4th March 2021, which limits Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) cardholders to compete only for seats reserved for Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and supernumerary seats in medical entrance exams like NEET-UG, rather than competing with Indian citizens for all seats. Before the notification dated 4th March 2021, OCI cardholders had the right to appear for NEET-UG exams and compete for medical seats on par with Indian citizens, under the notifications dated 11th April 2005 and 5th January 2009. The petitioners argue that the notification dated 4th March 2021 violates the doctrine of non-retrogression because it reverses the rights previously granted to OCI cardholders, reducing their ability to compete for medical seats, which they had enjoyed since 2005. The notification dated 4th March 2021 restricts OCI cardholders to only NRI quota and supernumerary seats, denying them the opportunity to compete with Indian citizens for general seats in medical entrance exams, which limits their educational opportunities significantly. The Union of India justifies the notification by stating that it aims to protect the limited educational seats for Indian citizens, ensuring that foreigners, including OCI cardholders, do not take away these opportunities, thus prioritizing Indian citizens' rights in educational admissions. The Supreme Court acknowledged the petitioners' grievances about the sudden change in their rights and the impact on their educational careers. The Court examined the balance between the State's sovereign rights and the individual rights of the OCI cardholders, particularly focusing on the principle of non-retrogression and the reasonableness of the classification imposed by the notification.

case_name: Anversinh @ Kiransinh Fatesinh Zala vs State of Gujarat
text: Case: Anversinh @ Kiransinh Fatesinh Zala vs State of Gujarat. Date: 12th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The High Court of Gujarat overturned his conviction under Section 376 IPC but upheld the charges of kidnapping under Sections 363 and 366 IPC, maintaining a sentence of five years rigorous imprisonment. Anversinh was accused of kidnapping a minor girl with the intention of marriage and subjecting her to sexual intercourse against her will. The trial court concluded that the prosecutrix was a minor, aged 16 years, 3 months, and 6 days at the time of the incident, and her consent was irrelevant for the charges of kidnapping. The defense argued that there was a consensual love affair between Anversinh and the prosecutrix, and she had left her parents' home willingly to be with him. The Supreme Court noted that the consent of a minor is immaterial under Section 361 IPC and upheld the conviction for kidnapping, emphasizing the protective nature of the law regarding minors. The Supreme Court reduced the sentence to the period of imprisonment already undergone by Anversinh, considering factors like the absence of force, the age of the accused, and the passage of time. The key reasons included the lack of force used in the kidnapping, the young age of the accused at the time, the long passage of time since the incident, and the rehabilitation of the accused who had no prior or subsequent criminal record.

case_name: Anwar @ Bhugra vs State of Haryana
text: Case: Anwar @ Bhugra vs State of Haryana. Date: 29th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of Anwar @ Bhugra under Sections 394 and 397 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 25 of the Arms Act was justified based on the evidence presented. Anwar @ Bhugra was initially charged under Sections 394 and 397 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 25 of the Arms Act. The prosecution's case was that Anwar @ Bhugra, along with two other accused, waylaid and robbed Jahid (PW-4) near the cremation ground and inflicted injuries with a drant, knife, and pistol. Anwar @ Bhugra's defense was that the incident was fabricated, and there were inconsistencies and doubts in the prosecution's evidence, including the recovery of the pistol. The Supreme Court found the recovery of the pistol doubtful because the memo of personal search stated that nothing was recovered from Anwar @ Bhugra at the time of his arrest, contradicting the recovery memo of the pistol. The Supreme Court found inconsistencies in the statements of prosecution witnesses Jahid (PW-4), Jain Singh (PW-5), and Harun Ali (PW-6), who provided conflicting accounts of the incident and the recoveries. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence of Anwar @ Bhugra under Sections 394 and 397 IPC and Section 25 of the Arms Act, and acquitted him of all charges. The ruling emphasizes the importance of consistency in recovery memos and witness statements, potentially leading to more stringent scrutiny of evidence in future cases involving recovery of weapons. The ruling highlights the need for credible and consistent witness statements, which may result in more careful examination and cross-examination of witnesses in future trials to ensure reliability. The Supreme Court suggested that the handling of evidence should be meticulous, and any discrepancies between personal search memos and recovery memos should be resolved to maintain the integrity of the prosecution's case. The ruling could lead to improved law enforcement practices, ensuring that the evidence collected is consistent and reliable, thereby reducing the chances of wrongful convictions based on flawed evidence.

case_name: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia
text: Case: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia. Date: 20th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether a DNA test could be ordered to determine the paternity of Master 'X', the second child born to Aparna during her marriage with Ajinkya, amidst allegations of adultery. Ajinkya sought a DNA test to ascertain the paternity of Master 'X' based on allegations that Aparna was in an adulterous relationship with Kshitij Bafna, and a DNA test from a private laboratory indicated that Ajinkya was not the biological father. The Family Court allowed the application for a DNA test, stating that the respondent had made out a prima-facie case justifying the exercise of discretion to direct a DNA test. Aparna argued that the respondent had not made out a prima-facie case requiring a DNA test, and that such a test would violate the presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act and infringe on the child's right to privacy. The High Court upheld the Family Court's order for a DNA test, stating that the direction did not violate fundamental rights and that a DNA test was a legitimate means to establish the truth in the matter of paternity. The Supreme Court highlighted that Section 112 provides a presumption of legitimacy for children born during a valid marriage, which can only be rebutted by strong evidence of non-access. The Court also discussed that DNA tests should not be ordered routinely but only when absolutely necessary to resolve the controversy. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and the Family Court's order for a DNA test, stating that there was insufficient material to dislodge the presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, and that the DNA test was not justified in this case.

case_name: Aparna Bhat & Ors. vs. State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Aparna Bhat & Ors. vs. State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 18th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the bail condition imposed by the Madhya Pradesh High Court, requiring the accused to visit the complainant's house with a Rakhi thread and other symbolic gestures, was appropriate. The challenged bail condition required the accused to visitthe complainant's house, tie a Rakhi band to her, promise to protect her, and give monetary gifts. The appellants argued that such bail conditions trivialize the trauma undergone by survivors of sexual assault and adversely affect their dignity. They also contended that these conditions reflect entrenched patriarchal and misogynistic attitudes. The Supreme Court found the bail condition to be wholly unacceptable as it dilutes and erodes the offence of sexual harassment by transforming the accused into a protector through a judicial mandate. The Supreme Court directed that bail conditions should not mandate or permit contact between the accused and the victim and should avoid reflecting stereotypical or patriarchal notions about women. It emphasized protecting the complainant from any further harassment. The Supreme Court emphasized that judges should avoid any language or reasoning that diminishes the offence and trivializes the survivor. It stated that such conduct undermines the guarantee of fair justice to all, especially victims of sexual violence. The Supreme Court mandated the inclusion of a gender sensitization module in the foundational training of judges and continuing education programs. It also directed the National Judicial Academy to develop these training modules in consultation with relevant experts. The Supreme Court directed that the complainant should be immediately informed of the grant of bail to the accused and a copy of the bail order should be provided to the complainant within two days. The Supreme Court firmly stated that courts should not suggest or entertain any notions of compromise or mediation between the prosecutrix and the accused, as it is beyond their powers and undermines the dignity of the survivor. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned bail condition imposed by the Madhya Pradesh High Court, expunging it from the record, and disposed of the appeal accordingly.

case_name: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
text: Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.. Date: 31st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Central Government's decision to debar the petitioner's medical college from admitting students for two years and to encash the bank guarantee was justified. The Central Government debared the college based on a negative recommendation from the Medical Council of India (MCI), citing deficiencies in faculty and resident doctors during inspections. The OC, constituted under the Supreme Court's directions, reviewed the compliance submitted by the college and initially approved the scheme for the academic session 2016-17, but later noted deficiencies in subsequent inspections. The Supreme Court observed that the deficiencies noted by MCI were marginal and that the Central Government's decision to debar the college for two years was excessive. The court emphasized the need for proportionality in administrative decisions. The Supreme Court set aside the Central Government's decision to debar the college from admitting students for two years and allowed the college to admit students for the academic session 2017-18, subject to fulfilling conditions imposed by the Oversight Committee. The Supreme Court allowed the Medical Council of India or the Competent Authority of the Central Government to inspect the college as deemed fit and to take appropriate action if any deficiencies were found in the future, after giving the college an opportunity to address them. The Supreme Court quashed the decision to debar the college from admitting students and extended the cut-off date for admissions to 5th September 2017, allowing the college to participate in the ongoing counselling process for the academic session 2017-18.

case_name: Apoorva Arora & Anr. vs State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.
text: Case: Apoorva Arora & Anr. vs State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.. Date: 19th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants are the actors, casting director, scriptwriters, creator of the web-series 'College Romance,' and the media company that owns the YouTube channel on which the web-series was hosted. The appellants were alleged to have produced, transmitted, and published obscene and sexually-explicit material online under Sections 67 and 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The High Court dismissed the petition to quash the FIR and upheld the registration of the FIR under Sections 67 and 67A of the IT Act, stating that the content was capable of appealing to prurient interests and was hence obscene. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR on the grounds that the material in question did not meet the threshold for obscenity or sexually explicit content under Sections 67 and 67A of the IT Act, as it did not arouse sexual feelings or prurient interest, nor did it involve any sexually explicit acts. The FIR was registered due to the content in Season 1, Episode 5 of the web-series 'College Romance,' titled 'Happily F****d Up,' which was alleged to contain vulgar and obscene language. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court incorrectly equated vulgarity and profanities with obscenity and failed to follow the proper judicial process to objectively assess whether the material was obscene. The Supreme Court emphasized the 'community standard test,' which considers whether the material as a whole, when taken in context, has the tendency to deprave and corrupt, rather than focusing solely on vulgar or profane language.

case_name: Aprajita Chakraborty vs. Anirban Biswangri
text: Case: Aprajita Chakraborty vs. Anirban Biswangri. Date: 5th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the transfer petition filed by the petitioner-wife seeking to transfer the marriage petition filed by the respondent-husband from the Court of Civil Judge (S.D.)/Family Court at Thane, Maharashtra to the Court of competent jurisdiction at Gaya, Bihar. The Supreme Court issued a notice and passed an interim order staying further proceedings pending before the Court of Civil Judge (S.D.)/Family Court at Thane, Maharashtra. The Supreme Court allowed the transfer petition, transferring Marriage Petition No.474 of 2021 from the Civil Judge (S.D.)/Family Court at Thane, Maharashtra to the Court of competent jurisdiction at Gaya, Bihar. The Court at Thane, Maharashtra was directed to immediately transmit the entire case record to the Court of District Judge, Gaya, who in turn shall assign the matter to a Court of competent jurisdiction. The Supreme Court directed the Court at Gaya to explore the possibility of settlement between the parties through the process of mediation. The Supreme Court directed the Registry to send a copy of the order immediately to both the Courts for compliance.

case_name: Aqeel Ahmad vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Another
text: Case: Aqeel Ahmad vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Another. Date: 5th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the challenge to the High Court's orders granting bail to Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil, who were accused in the murder of Khursheed Ahmad. Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil were charged under Sections 147, 148, 149, 302, 336, and 427 of the IPC for the murder of Khursheed Ahmad. The High Court granted bail to Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil based on the fact that other co-accused had been granted bail and general allegations were made against all accused without specific roles assigned. The appellant argued that the High Court did not properly consider the seriousness of the crime, the respondents' involvement, and the threat to the appellant as an eyewitness, and that bail was granted without detailed consideration of the facts. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's bail orders and directed Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil to surrender to custody within 10 days, finding that the bail was granted without proper consideration of the facts. The post-mortem report indicated that Khursheed Ahmad was severely assaulted, with fractured ribs and injuries sufficient to cause death, which highlighted the seriousness of the crime and the respondents' involvement. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court improperly granted bail to Abdullah and Nasir by merely referring to bail orders of co-accused without detailed consideration of their specific involvement in the crime. The Supreme Court directed Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil to surrender to custody within 10 days and clarified that they could apply for fresh bail applications at an appropriate stage, which would be considered on their own merits. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for not properly considering the detailed facts and material on record when granting bail to the respondents, which led to the setting aside of the bail orders. The Supreme Court referenced its decision to cancel the bail granted to co-accused Neyaz Ahmad on 28th April 2023, highlighting its relevance to the challenge against the bail orders for Abdullah, Nasir, and Muzammil.

case_name: Arcelor Mittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. vs. Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd.
text: Case: Arcelor Mittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. vs. Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd.. Date: 14th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue is whether the Court has the power to entertain an application under Section 9(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, once an Arbitral Tribunal has been constituted and the meaning of the expression 'entertain' in Section 9(3) of the Arbitration Act. The Cargo Handling Agreement between Arcelor Mittal and Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd. was for Cargo Handling at Hazira Port, and it included an arbitration clause for settling disputes. Arcelor Mittal invoked the arbitration clause by a notice of arbitration dated 22nd November 2020 and approached the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act for the appointment of an Arbitral Tribunal. The Respondent, Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd., contended that the disputes were not arbitrable and claimed that the total amount due and payable by Arcelor Mittal was Rs.673.84 crores, inclusive of interest. The Gujarat High Court dismissed the application filed by Arcelor Mittal under Article 227 of the Constitution, holding that the Commercial Court has the power to consider whether the remedy under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act is inefficacious and pass necessary orders under Section 9. The Supreme Court held that the word 'entertain' in Section 9(3) means the entire process up to its final adjudication and passing of an order on merits. Therefore, if the application is already entertained and arguments are heard, the Court can proceed to pass an order even after the Arbitral Tribunal is constituted.

case_name: Archana Rana vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and another
text: Case: Archana Rana vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and another. Date: 1st March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the quashing of the chargesheet and the entire proceedings of Case Crime No. 153 of 2016, which involved allegations against Archana Rana and her husband under Sections 419, 420, 323, 504, and 506 of the IPC. The allegations were that Archana Rana's husband took Rs. 5,00,000 from the complainant for getting his son employed, and when the employment did not materialize, Archana Rana assaulted and threatened the complainant and his son when they asked for the money back. They were charged under Sections 419, 420, 323, 504, and 506 of the IPC. The High Court dismissed Archana Rana's application to quash the chargesheet and the entire criminal proceedings. Archana Rana argued that the FIR and chargesheet did not constitute a case against her for the offences under Sections 419 and 420 IPC, as the allegations did not meet the necessary ingredients for these offences. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings against Archana Rana for the offences under Sections 419 and 420 IPC, finding that the allegations did not constitute the necessary ingredients for these offences. No, the Supreme Court only quashed the proceedings for the charges under Sections 419 and 420 IPC. The proceedings for the charges under Sections 323, 504, and 506 IPC were not quashed and were allowed to continue. The Supreme Court referenced this case to outline the necessary ingredients to constitute an offence under Section 420 IPC, emphasizing that cheating is an essential element for such an offence. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings against Archana Rana for the offences under Sections 419 and 420 IPC, as the allegations did not meet the necessary ingredients for these offences. The Supreme Court allowed the criminal proceedings for the charges under Sections 323, 504, and 506 IPC to continue in the Court of the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Azamgarh, as per the chargesheet. Archana Rana was charged under Sections 419, 420, 323, 504, and 506 of the IPC in Case Crime No. 153 of 2016.

case_name: Arnab Manoranjan Goswami vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: Case: Arnab Manoranjan Goswami vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.. Date: 27th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Arnab Manoranjan Goswami sought three substantive reliefs: a writ of Habeas Corpus for illegal arrest and wrongful detention, the quashing of the FIR registered on 5 May 2018 under Sections 306 and 34 of the IPC, and the quashing of the arrest memo. The case involved the suicide of Anvay Naik, who left a note accusing Arnab Goswami and two others of not paying dues amounting to Rs. 83 lacs, Rs. 4 crores, and Rs. 55 lacs, respectively, which led to severe mental pressure on him. The High Court declined to grant interim bail to Arnab Goswami and posted the hearing of the petition for quashing the FIR on 10 December 2020, stating that he could seek regular bail under Section 439 of the CrPC. The Supreme Court held that Section 20-A(1) of the TADA Act is mandatory and no information about the commission of an offence under TADA can be recorded without prior approval of the District Superintendent of Police. The Supreme Court concluded that the arrest of Arnab Goswami was illegal as it was rooted in malice and lacked compliance with legal procedures, particularly the re-opening of investigation without judicial sanction. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of protecting personal liberty, noting that the High Court failed to evaluate whether the allegations in the FIR disclosed an offence under Section 306 of the IPC. The Supreme Court granted interim bail to Arnab Goswami, recognizing the failure of the High Court to consider the prima facie evaluation of the FIR's allegations. The Supreme Court noted that the re-investigation ordered by the Home Department was without judicial sanction and emphasized that further investigation must comply with legal provisions. The Supreme Court referred to cases like State of Haryana vs. Bhajan Lal, Madan Mohan Singh vs. State of Gujarat, and S.S. Chheena vs. Vijay Kumar Mahajan to support the principles of quashing FIRs and the evaluation of allegations. The Supreme Court concluded that the FIR against Arnab Goswami did not prima facie constitute an offence under Section 306 of the IPC, as there was no direct or indirect act of instigation or involvement leading to the suicide of Anvay Naik.

case_name: Arun Kumar Jagatramka vs. Jindal Steel and Power Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: Arun Kumar Jagatramka vs. Jindal Steel and Power Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 15th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether a person who is ineligible under Section 29A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) to submit a resolution plan is also barred from proposing a scheme of compromise and arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT held that a person ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC to submit a resolution plan is also barred from proposing a scheme of compromise and arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. This decision was rendered in favor of Jindal Steel and Power Limited (JSPL) and reversed the earlier decision of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). Arun Kumar Jagatramka challenged the NCLAT decision on the grounds that Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not place any embargo on any person for submitting a scheme. He argued that the NCLAT's interpretation of Section 29A of the IBC into Section 230 amounted to a judicial reframing of legislation. The Supreme Court concluded that the prohibition in Section 29A and Section 35(1)(f) of the IBC also applies to a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 when the company is undergoing liquidation under the IBC. Consequently, the appeals and the writ petition were dismissed, upholding the constitutional validity of Regulation 2B of the Liquidation Process Regulations.

case_name: Arun Kumar Niranjan vs District Basic Education Officer & Ors.
text: Case: Arun Kumar Niranjan vs District Basic Education Officer & Ors.. Date: 25th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Arun Kumar Niranjan was working as a teacher before he was promoted to the post of Headmaster. Arun Kumar Niranjan did not join the duty because the promotion was to a rural inconvenient area. The charges against Arun Kumar Niranjan were not taking charge in the original school after the cancellation of the promotion, defying the instructions of the A.B.S.A., Development Block: Kaunch, and defying the Developmental Orders. The amended rule stated that if any teacher refuses the promotion within both aforesaid backward areas, that teacher would not be promoted till the upcoming three years and again after three years, the promotion of that teacher would be considered as per prescribed rules. The learned Single Judge took the view that for declining to accept the promotion and refusing to join duty on account of promotion in the year 2007, the appellant cannot be visited with any penal consequences by relying on the order issued in the year 2010. The Division Bench concluded that the actual promotion of the appellant was after the introduction of the amended rules in January 2010, and therefore, set aside the order of the learned Single Judge. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment of the Division Bench because the appellant was being proceeded against for his conduct in the year 2007, before the introduction of the new rules in 2010. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment of the Division Bench and restored the judgment of the learned Single Judge, while vacating the order on costs passed by the learned Single Judge.

case_name: Arun Singh & Others vs. State of U.P. through its Secretary & Another
text: Case: Arun Singh & Others vs. State of U.P. through its Secretary & Another. Date: 10th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case dealt with whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the petition to quash the charges under Section 493 IPC and Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, despite a prior compromise between the parties. The complainant alleged that after finalizing the marriage, the accused misled his daughter into believing they were married, established physical relations, and subsequently demanded dowry of Rs. 5 Lakhs. The appellants argued that the allegations in the FIR were fabricated after a prior compromise was reached, and the charges did not disclose the ingredients necessary for an offence under Section 493 IPC. The Supreme Court quashed the charge under Section 493 IPC, ruling that the FIR did not disclose any deceitful inducement leading to a belief in lawful marriage. The Court upheld the charges under Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, stating that the allegations in the FIR disclosed cognizable offences related to dowry demands. The Supreme Court emphasized that offences involving public interest or societal impact, like dowry-related offences, cannot be quashed solely based on a compromise between private parties.

case_name: Aruna vs. The State of Maharashtra and Others
text: Case: Aruna vs. The State of Maharashtra and Others. Date: 27th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the appellant, Aruna's, challenge against her disqualification as President of the Municipal Council, Kundalwadi, due to the Committee's refusal to verify her caste certificate under Rule 14 of the Maharashtra Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, De-notified Tribes (Vimukta Jatis), Nomadic Tribes, Other Backward Classes and Special Category (Regulation of Issuance and Verification of) Caste Certificate Rules, 2012. The High Court dismissed Aruna's petitions because it declined to interfere with the District Caste Verification Committee's order that refused to verify her caste certificate, thereby disqualifying her from her elected post under Section 9A of the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965. Aruna argued that her caste certificate was validly issued by the competent authority in Maharashtra under Rule 6(1)(a) and that the Committee erred in refusing to verify it based on the incorrect application of Rule 14, which deals with certificates issued by authorities in other states. The Supreme Court held that the Committee and the High Court posed the wrong question and arrived at an erroneous conclusion. The Committee could not decline to verify a valid caste certificate issued under Rule 6(1)(a) by the competent authority in Maharashtra. The Supreme Court decided not to reinstate Aruna as her elected tenure was ending in December 2021. Instead, it molded the relief prospectively, recognizing her caste status as 'Munnur Kapu' in Maharashtra from 22nd November 2016 and set aside the High Court's order.

case_name: Arvind Kumar @ Nemichand & Ors. vs. State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Arvind Kumar @ Nemichand & Ors. vs. State of Rajasthan. Date: 22nd November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the conviction of the accused for the murder of Ladduram and others, based on the evidence and circumstances, was justified. The prosecution's case was that Surjaram and his associates attacked Ladduram and others with weapons such as farsi, barchi, lathi, bhala, and sword due to a dispute over a pathway, resulting in multiple deaths and injuries. The defense argued that the accused had sustained multiple injuries and were acting in private defense, and that these injuries were not adequately considered during the investigation. The trial court convicted five of the accused, acquitted two, and sentenced the convicted individuals to life imprisonment for the murder of Ladduram and others. The High Court acquitted one more accused, confirming the conviction of the remaining four, and dismissed the appeals against the acquittal. The Supreme Court criticized the investigation for being defective and colorable, noting the suppression of facts such as the injuries suffered by the accused and the existence of a dispute over the pathway. The disputed pathway, which was claimed by Surjaram and blocked to prevent access to the deceased's lands, was a significant factor in the conflict, leading to the violent confrontation. The Supreme Court found that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not reliable due to material contradictions, the suppression of key facts, and the interested nature of the witnesses. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the convictions and sentences of the accused, and directed that the accused be acquitted. The Supreme Court found that the injuries sustained by the accused, which were substantial and not explained by the prosecution, supported the defense's claim of acting in private defense and led to doubts about the prosecution's case.

case_name: Arvind Singh vs. The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Arvind Singh vs. The State of Maharashtra. Date: 24th April 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Arvind Singh and Rajesh Daware were accused of kidnapping and murdering an 8-year-old boy named Yug, as well as demanding ransom from his father. The complainant, Dr. Mukesh Ramanlal Chandak, was the father of the victim, Yug. Yug was kidnapped from his housing society, 'Guru Vandana Apartment', by a boy wearing a red half-sleeve T-shirt and white pants, who took him on a black scooty. The prosecution relied on the testimony of witnesses who saw the accused with Yug, CCTV footage from a petrol pump, and the recovery of the dead body and other incriminating items based on the accused's disclosure statements. The motive was revenge against Dr. Chandak, as Arvind Singh had grievances against him for allegedly paying a meagre salary and confronting him about overcharging patients. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and death sentence of Arvind Singh and Rajesh Daware for kidnapping and murdering Yug.

case_name: Asfaq vs State of Rajasthan and Others
text: Case: Asfaq vs State of Rajasthan and Others. Date: 11th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the denial of parole to the appellant, Asfaq, who was convicted under the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (TADA) and sentenced to life imprisonment. Asfaq had applied for parole, which was rejected multiple times by various authorities, leading to the present appeal. The authorities rejected Asfaq's parole application on the grounds that releasing him on parole could lead to untoward incidents in society, affect young generations adversely, pose a threat to those who had deposed against him, and potentially endanger Asfaq's own life due to public anger and annoyance. The High Court of Rajasthan dismissed Asfaq's writ petition for parole, stating that parole cannot be claimed as a matter of right, especially in cases involving serious and heinous crimes. The High Court suggested that Asfaq could approach the Supreme Court for appropriate relief. The Supreme Court of India found the High Court's dismissal of Asfaq's parole application to be inappropriate and not meeting the test of law. The Supreme Court held that conviction for a serious and heinous crime cannot be the sole reason for denying parole and emphasized the need to consider parole applications on merits, taking into account the possibility of reformation. The Supreme Court outlined that parole should be granted to allow prisoners to maintain family and social ties, as part of the reformation process. The Court emphasized that parole decisions should balance public interest with the convict's potential for reformation and good conduct, and should not be denied solely based on the nature of the offense. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the rejection of Asfaq's parole application at this stage, but allowed for the possibility of reapplying for parole in the future when the external environment changes for the better and after a reasonable period of time has passed.

case_name: Asharam Tiwari vs State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Asharam Tiwari vs State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 12th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Asharam Tiwari was convicted under Sections 302/34, 324/34, 325/34, and 323 of the IPC for life imprisonment and other lesser punishments. The incident occurred on 23rd October 2006 when Asharam Tiwari and his co-accused assaulted PW-1, his family, and PW-1's brother Ramdas over a land dispute, resulting in the death of two people and injuries to others. The victims were PW-1, his wife PW-4, their son Ramashankar (who died during treatment), their minor daughter, and PW-1's brother Ramdas (who was shot dead). The defense argued that Asharam Tiwari was only armed with a lathi, did not share common intention with the other accused, and was falsely implicated at the behest of the village sarpanch. They also claimed his alibi was not properly considered. The prosecution argued that the common intention was evident from the fact that all four accused came armed together, assaulted PW-1 and his family, and then proceeded to kill Ramdas. The recovery of bloodstained lathi and clothes also indicated common intention. Ramdas sustained a contusion on his right arm, a contusion on his left arm, a lacerated wound on his right brow, an ingress injury in his stomach, and an egress injury on his back. Ramashankar sustained an incised wound in the temporal area, a fracture and blood clotting, a stitched injury on the parietal area, an incised wound on the left shoulder, and injuries on the neck and forehead. The court found PW-1 and PW-4 to be reliable and truthful witnesses, and saw no reason for them to falsely implicate someone, especially given that the deceased was their own minor son. PW-2, the son of the second deceased, was also found to be a reliable eye-witness. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upheld the conviction of Asharam Tiwari, and suggested that he could apply for premature release considering his age and time served. The Supreme Court advised that if Asharam Tiwari applies for premature release, the authorities should consider it in accordance with the law, given that he had completed over 14 years of custody and was 72 years old.

The defense argued that Asharam Tiwari was only armed with a lathi, did not share common intention with the other accused, and was falsely implicated at the behest of the village sarpanch. They also claimed his alibi was not properly considered.

The prosecution argued that the common intention was evident from the fact that all four accused came armed together, assaulted PW-1 and his family, and then proceeded to kill Ramdas. The recovery of bloodstained lathi and clothes also indicated common intention.
Ramdas sustained a contusion on his right arm, a contusion on his left arm, a lacerated wound on his right brow, an ingress injury in his stomach, and an egress injury on his back.

Ramashankar sustained an incised wound in the temporal area, a fracture and blood clotting, a stitched injury on the parietal area, an incised wound on the left shoulder, and injuries on the neck and forehead.

The court found PW-1 and PW-4 to be reliable and truthful witnesses, and saw no reason for them to falsely implicate someone, especially given that the deceased was their own minor son. PW-2, the son of the second deceased, was also found to be a reliable eye-witness.
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upheld the conviction of Asharam Tiwari, and suggested that he could apply for premature release considering his age and time served.

The Supreme Court advised that if Asharam Tiwari applies for premature release, the authorities should consider it in accordance with the law, given that he had completed over 14 years of custody and was 72 years old.

case_name: Ashim @ Asim Kumar Haranath Bhattacharya vs. National Investigation Agency
text: Case: Ashim @ Asim Kumar Haranath Bhattacharya vs. National Investigation Agency. Date: 1st December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant, Ashim @ Asim Kumar Haranath Bhattacharya, should be granted post-arrest bail, which had been previously rejected by the trial court and the High Court. The charges against the appellant included Sections 120B, 121, 121A, 122 of the IPC, Section 25(1A) of the Arms Act, 1959, Section 5 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, and Sections 18, 20, 40(1)(b)(c) of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967. The FIR was initially lodged on 1st March 2012 under various sections of the IPC, Arms Act, and Explosive Substances Act. The appellant has been in custody since 6th July 2012, amounting to over nine and a half years as an undertrial prisoner. The Supreme Court observed that the charges were framed only after seven years of filing the charge-sheet and that the trial has been significantly delayed, affecting the appellant's right to a speedy trial. There were 298 prosecution witnesses listed in the charge sheet, but the respondent indicated that only 100 to 105 witnesses were likely to be examined. The Supreme Court directed that the State of West Bengal should designate more dedicated courts of Sessions as Special Courts for the trial of offences specified in the schedule appended to the Act 2008, and the Central Government should take up the issue in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court of Calcutta. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the trial court to release the appellant on post-arrest bail within three days, subject to appropriate conditions to ensure his availability for trial. The Supreme Court emphasized that deprivation of personal liberty without ensuring a speedy trial is inconsistent with Article 21 of the Constitution of India, and undertrials cannot be indefinitely detained pending trial. The Supreme Court noted that the trial was being conducted at a very slow pace, with hearings taking place only one day a month, which frustrated the purpose of designating special courts for speedy trials under the Act 2008.

case_name: Ashish Kumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Ashish Kumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 31st January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Ashish Kumar, who had the qualifications of a graduate and post-graduate in Psychology, was eligible for the post of 'Psychologist' in the Social Welfare Department, despite not possessing a training qualification like L.T./B.T.B.Ed. Ashish Kumar's application was initially rejected because he did not have the training qualification (L.T./B.T.B.Ed.) which the respondents argued was necessary as per the advertisement. The High Court dismissed Ashish Kumar's appeal, agreeing with the respondents that the qualification required was both a graduate degree in Psychology and a training qualification like L.T./B.T.B.Ed. The Supreme Court interpreted the advertisement to mean that the qualifications of graduation in Psychology, L.T./B.T.B.Ed., were alternative and not cumulative. Therefore, Ashish Kumar was eligible with his qualifications. The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the High Court and directed the respondents to issue an appointment order to Ashish Kumar for the post of 'Psychologist' within two months.

case_name: Ashok G. Rajani vs. Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Ashok G. Rajani vs. Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 22nd September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) was correct in not restraining the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) from proceeding with the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s Seya Industries Limited, despite the settlement reached between the parties. The NCLAT issued a notice of the appeal but did not restrain the IRP from proceeding with the CIRP. However, it restrained the IRP from constituting a Committee of Creditors (CoC) until the next hearing date. The parties reached an amicable settlement on 8th August 2021, and entered into a formal settlement agreement, which was submitted to the NCLT, requesting the withdrawal of the CIRP application under Section 12A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The Supreme Court set aside the NCLAT's interim order because it held that before the constitution of the CoC, there is no bar to withdrawal of an application for CIRP if the parties have settled their disputes, and the application for withdrawal should be considered under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules. The Supreme Court directed the NCLT to take up the settlement application and decide it in light of the observations made, allowing the settlement to be considered and the CIRP application to be withdrawn. The impact of the Supreme Court's decision was to provide relief to the Corporate Debtor, M/s Seya Industries Limited, by allowing the withdrawal of the CIRP application based on the settlement, thus enabling the company to continue its business operations without the impediment of ongoing insolvency proceedings.

case_name: Ashok Gulabrao Bondre vs. Vilas Madhukarrao Deshmukh & Ors.
text: Case: Ashok Gulabrao Bondre vs. Vilas Madhukarrao Deshmukh & Ors.. Date: 12th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ashok Gulabrao Bondre alleged that the respondents committed offences of forgery by preparing false documents, specifically a personal recognizance bond and a surety bond, in Criminal Case No. 19 of 2003. The Judicial Magistrate First Class dismissed the complaint on 6th November 2004, stating that such a complaint could not be filed except in writing by the concerned court or a subordinate one. The Additional Sessions Judge found the allegations serious but held that the complaint could not proceed without the involvement of the concerned court under Section 340 of the CrPC. The court directed the appellant to file an application under Section 340 CrPC for a preliminary enquiry. The High Court rejected the application filed under Section 482 CrPC, leading to the appeal before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court referred to its Constitution Bench decision in Iqbal Singh Marwah and another v. Meenakshi Marwah and another, concluding that Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC applies only when the offence is committed with respect to a document after it has been produced or given in evidence in court proceedings. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the Revisional Court and the High Court, remitting the matter back to the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ramtek, for consideration on merits within one year from the date of the judgment. The Supreme Court directed the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ramtek, to decide the complaint on its merits as expeditiously as possible and within one year from the date of the judgment.

case_name: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
text: Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.. Date: 11th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the mandatory requirement for judicial officers to pass a higher grade Hindi examination for confirmation and increment, as per the Bihar Civil Service (Judicial Branch) Training and Departmental Examination Rules, 1963, applied under the Jharkhand Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 2004. Rule 21(b) stipulated that successful passing of an examination conducted by the Judicial Academy under the directions and guidance of the High Court was the only condition precedent for confirmation of the trainees as Civil Judges, Junior Division (Munsif)/Civil Judges, Senior Division (Subordinate Judges). The High Court held that passing the higher grade Hindi examination was mandatory for confirmation and increments, relying on Rule 7 of the Bihar Government Servant (Hindi Examination) Regulation, 1968, and Rule 27(a) of the Bihar Civil Service (Judicial Branch) Training and Departmental Examination Rules, 1963. The Supreme Court held that the 1963 Bihar Rules could not be read into the 2004 Jharkhand Rules, as the latter were in supersession of all earlier Rules and did not explicitly require passing the higher grade Hindi examination as a condition for confirmation. The Supreme Court concluded that the 2004 Jharkhand Rules did not mandate passing the higher grade Hindi examination for confirmation, and any such prescription should have been explicitly included in the Rules. The Supreme Court directed that the appellants were entitled to increments and other mandatory benefits from their date of appointment and should be covered under the old pension scheme, which was applicable at the time of their entry into service in 2011. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the respondents to remit the differential mandatory benefits to the appellants within three months.

case_name: Ashok Kumar Singh Chandel vs State of U.P.
text: Case: Ashok Kumar Singh Chandel vs State of U.P.. Date: 4th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main charges were for the murder of five individuals, causing injuries to others, and creating public disturbance with intent to harm the Shukla family due to long-standing political rivalry. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused, citing various inconsistencies and doubts regarding the prosecution's evidence and witness testimonies. The High Court overturned the acquittal, convicting all the accused for the offences under Sections 148, 302 read with 149, and 307 read with 149 of the IPC, and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The key pieces of evidence included witness testimonies, the First Information Report (FIR), recovery of weapons, medical reports of injuries, and the ballistic report. The defense argued that the witness testimonies were inconsistent, the FIR was ante-dated, the evidence was manipulated, and the accused were falsely implicated due to political rivalry. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgment, agreeing that the prosecution had provided sufficient evidence to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the accused and confirmed the life imprisonment sentences imposed by the High Court.

case_name: Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh vs. State of Gujarat
text: Case: Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh vs. State of Gujarat. Date: 7th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the conviction of Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC, Section 307 IPC read with Section 34 IPC, and under Section 25(c) of the Arms Act was sustainable based on the evidence presented. Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh was charged with offences under Sections 302, 307, 120B IPC read with Section 34 IPC, 143, 147, 148, 149, 506(II), 323 and 504 IPC, under Section 25(c) of the Arms Act, and under Section 3(1)(x) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. On 23rd November 1997, Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh and others were involved in a dispute over ploughing a disputed road, which led to an altercation with the complainant and his family. During the incident, gunshots were fired by the accused, resulting in the death of Somiben and injuries to Ramanbhai and Nandaben. The High Court affirmed the conviction of Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh under Sections 302 and 307 IPC read with Section 34 IPC and under Section 25(c) of the Arms Act, but acquitted him under Section 3(1)(x) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh argued that there was no evidence of electric light at the time of the incident to identify the assailants, and there were contradictions in the prosecution's case regarding who fired the gunshots. He also pointed out the absence of definite evidence linking the fatal injuries to the weapon recovered from him. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC, Section 307 IPC read with Section 34 IPC, and under Section 25(c) of the Arms Act, and ordered his immediate release, giving him the benefit of doubt. The Supreme Court found that there were doubts about the identification of the assailants due to darkness at the time of the incident, contradictions in the prosecution's case, and the absence of definite evidence linking the fatal injuries to the weapon recovered from Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh.

case_name: Ashoo Surendranath Tewari vs. The Deputy Superintendent of Police, EOW, CBI & Anr.
text: Case: Ashoo Surendranath Tewari vs. The Deputy Superintendent of Police, EOW, CBI & Anr.. Date: 8th September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary allegation was regarding the diversion of funds through the MSME Receivable Finance Scheme operated by SIDBI, where 12 payments amounting to Rs.1,64,17,551/- were fraudulently made to an incorrect bank account. Ashoo Surendranath Tewari allegedly received an email containing RTGS details for the fraudulent account, which he forwarded to Accused No.5, and subsequently signed various cheques that facilitated the diversion of funds. He was discharged because no sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act was obtained, and the Special Judge found no need for sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. in this case. The High Court concurred with the Special Judge that there was no need for sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. for prosecuting Ashoo Surendranath Tewari. The CVC found that Ashoo Surendranath Tewari appeared to be a victim of Muthukumar's plot and was not involved in the fraud, supporting the Competent Authority's view that no sanction for prosecution was required. The Supreme Court emphasized that the standard of proof in criminal proceedings is higher than in departmental proceedings and that the findings in the CVC report, which exonerated Ashoo Surendranath Tewari on merits, were crucial. The Supreme Court relied on precedents such as P.S. Rajya vs. State of Bihar and Radheshyam Kejriwal vs. State of West Bengal, which highlight the higher standard of proof required in criminal cases and the relevance of exoneration in departmental proceedings. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the High Court and the Special Judge, and discharged Ashoo Surendranath Tewari from the offences under the Penal Code. The Supreme Court concluded that, given the detailed findings of the CVC report and the circumstances of the case, the chances of conviction in a criminal trial appeared to be bleak. The CVC report played a significant role in the Supreme Court's decision as it detailed that Ashoo Surendranath Tewari was likely a victim of Muthukumar's fraud and had taken steps to mitigate the impact, which supported his non-involvement in the crime.

case_name: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuriya & Anr. vs M/S. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
text: Case: Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuriya & Anr. vs M/S. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. Date: 8th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the dishonour of a cheque issued by the appellants for Rs. 10,00,000 due to insufficient funds, and the subsequent legal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The High Court dismissed the petition because the appellants, as directors of the company, were deemed responsible for the conduct of the business and thus liable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The appellants received a total amount of Rs. 1,50,19,831 from the respondent through various cheques between 23rd November 2007 and 12th March 2009. The appellants argued that they were non-executive directors and were not responsible for the day-to-day conduct of the business, thus they should not be held vicariously liable under Section 138 of the NI Act. The High Court observed that the directors, being responsible for the business conduct of the company, were liable for the dishonoured cheque under Section 138 of the NI Act, and their defense of being non-executive directors was not sufficient to absolve them. The dispute arose when a cheque issued by the appellants towards part payment of a financial agreement was dishonoured due to insufficient funds, leading the respondent to file a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants, as directors responsible for the company's business conduct, were vicariously liable for the dishonoured cheque under Section 138 of the NI Act. After the dishonour of the cheque, the appellants were issued a legal notice demanding payment, which they refused to accept, leading to the filing of the complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act. The trial court took cognizance of the complaint, issued summons to the appellants, and granted them bail on furnishing security. If similar cheques issued by the appellants were dishonoured in the future, they could face additional legal proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act, and their defense of being non-executive directors might not suffice to absolve them of liability. To avoid future legal issues, the appellants should ensure that sufficient funds are available in the company's accounts when issuing cheques, and they should closely monitor the financial transactions and obligations of the company.

case_name: Ashutosh Samanta (D) by LRS. & Ors. vs. Sm. Ranjan Bala Dasi & Ors.
text: Case: Ashutosh Samanta (D) by LRS. & Ors. vs. Sm. Ranjan Bala Dasi & Ors.. Date: 14th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the letters of administration could be granted for the will of Gosaidas Samanta, despite the significant delay in filing the petition and the absence of the original attesting witnesses. The trial court allowed the petition for letters of administration, relying on the depositions of the testator's sons and other evidence that supported the validity of the will. The Calcutta High Court affirmed the trial court's decision, upholding the grant of letters of administration based on the evidence presented. The appellants argued that the significant delay in seeking letters of administration should render the petition non-maintainable and questioned the genuineness of the will due to suspicious circumstances.
