case_name: Ashwani Kumar & Anr. vs The State of Punjab
text: Case: Ashwani Kumar & Anr. vs The State of Punjab. Date: 28th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of Ashwani Kumar and his co-accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code should be upheld. Ashwani Kumar and his co-accused were charged with murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution's case was that Ashwani Kumar was found pressing the neck of his wife while his co-accused was hitting her with a brick, leading to her death. Ashwani Kumar's defense was that he acted out of sudden provocation after finding his wife with another man, leading to a physical altercation that resulted in her death. The Trial Court convicted them based on the testimony of police officers who witnessed the crime and the forensic evidence that supported the prosecution's case. The key pieces of evidence included the eyewitness testimony of the police officers and the medical report indicating multiple stab wounds and blunt force trauma consistent with the prosecution's narrative. The Supreme Court did not find the defense credible and upheld the findings of the lower courts, stating that the evidence provided by the police officers was consistent and reliable. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence of Ashwani Kumar and his co-accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The ruling reinforces the importance of consistent and reliable eyewitness testimony and forensic evidence in upholding convictions for serious crimes like murder. The Supreme Court observed that there was no motive for the police officers to falsely implicate the appellants, and their testimony was found to be credible and trustworthy. The Supreme Court advised that the credibility of police testimony should be carefully evaluated, especially when it aligns with forensic evidence and other corroborative testimonies.

case_name: Asian Hotels (North) Ltd. vs. Alok Kumar Lodha & Ors.
text: Case: Asian Hotels (North) Ltd. vs. Alok Kumar Lodha & Ors.. Date: 12th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's order permitting the amendment of the plaint to declare mortgages and charges on the entire premises as void ab initio and to implead mortgagee banks/financial institutions was correct. The High Court allowed the applications, permitting the original plaintiffs to amend their plaints to declare the mortgages/charges on the entire premises as void ab initio and to implead the mortgagee banks/financial institutions. Asian Hotels (North) Ltd. argued that the mortgages were created since 1982, well before the licenses were granted to the plaintiffs, and that the plaintiffs had no locus or right to challenge these mortgages. They also argued that the amendment would change the nature of the suit and result in misjoinder of causes of action and parties. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court committed a serious error in allowing the applications for amendment and impleadment, stating that the plaintiffs had no locus to challenge the mortgages and that such an amendment would change the nature of the suit. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's orders allowing the applications under Order 6 Rule 17 and Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appeals filed by Asian Hotels (North) Ltd. were allowed. The Supreme Court reasoned that the original plaintiffs' rights as perpetual license holders were yet to be adjudicated, and thus, they could not challenge the mortgages/charges on the entire premises. The Court emphasized that permitting such an amendment would alter the nature of the suit and result in a misjoinder of causes of action.

case_name: Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd. vs Central Bureau of Investigation
text: Case: Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd. vs Central Bureau of Investigation. Date: 28th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether an order framing a charge by a Special Judge under the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act, being an interlocutory order, can be assailed under Article 226/227 of the Constitution of India. The charges against Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd. included Section 120B read with Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 477A of IPC and Section 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) was the complainant that alleged wrongful loss caused to it by the use of fake invoices of Oil Companies relating to the transportation of Bitumen for road works in Delhi during 1997 and 1998. The Special Judge, CBI, concluded that there was a prima facie case against the appellant and the other accused, and thus directed the framing of charges. The appellants filed a Criminal Revision against the order framing charge, which was later converted into a Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 352 of 2010 before the Delhi High Court. The Supreme Court directed that any stay of proceedings in trial courts granted by higher courts would automatically lapse after six months unless extended by a specific speaking order, to ensure that trials do not remain pending for an unduly long period. The decision set a precedent that challenges to orders of charge should be entertained only in the rarest of rare cases to correct a patent error of jurisdiction, ensuring a speedy trial process in corruption cases. The Supreme Court emphasized that any stay on proceedings should not exceed six months unless extended by a speaking order, and matters should be decided on a day-to-day basis to prevent undue delays. The Supreme Court clarified that the inherent power under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised sparingly and only in rarest of rare cases to prevent misuse, ensuring that the trial process is not unduly hampered. The judgement could streamline the process of handling corruption cases by limiting the scope for challenging orders framing charges, thereby reducing delays and ensuring swifter justice. The judgement indicates that framing of charges can proceed based on the prima facie evidence and material brought on record, without requiring a detailed appreciation of the evidence as would be necessary at the trial stage.

case_name: Asok Pande vs Supreme Court of India
text: Case: Asok Pande vs Supreme Court of India. Date: 11th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main relief sought by Asok Pande is the issuance of a writ of mandamus to the Supreme Court of India to evolve a set procedure for constituting benches and allotment of jurisdiction to different benches. Additionally, he seeks specific rules for the constitution of benches in the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court. Asok Pande seeks the constitution of various specific benches, including the Supreme Criminal Court, Supreme PIL Court, Supreme Tax Court, Supreme Service Court, Supreme Land Dispute Court, and Supreme Miscellaneous Matter Court. Asok Pande has grievances against the Allahabad High Court related to a contempt proceeding against him. He alleges that a bench was improperly constituted, leading to his suspension from practice and a ban on his entry into the high court. The Supreme Court expressed disapproval of Asok Pande's aspersions on the judges of the High Court, stating that the allegations were unwarranted and not based on any judicial order. The court emphasized that questioning the conduct of judicial proceedings in a writ petition under Article 32 was inappropriate. Article 145 of the Constitution governs the rule-making power of the Supreme Court, allowing it to make rules for regulating the practice and procedure of the court with the approval of the President. The Supreme Court reiterated that the Chief Justice is the Master of the Roster and has the exclusive prerogative to constitute benches and allocate cases. This authority is necessary for the efficient transaction of the administrative and judicial work of the court. The Supreme Court found the relief sought by Asok Pande to be misconceived because it would intrude into the exclusive duty and authority of the Chief Justice to constitute benches and allocate cases. Furthermore, the court stated that no mandamus can issue to direct a body or authority vested with rule-making power to make rules in a particular manner. The court rejected the petitioner's suggestions about the composition of benches in the High Courts, emphasizing that there should be no distinction between judges drawn from the Bar and those from the district judiciary. Both are appointed under Article 217 of the Constitution and perform the same functions.

case_name: Atbir vs. State of NCT of Delhi
text: Case: Atbir vs. State of NCT of Delhi. Date: 29th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Atbir was originally sentenced to death for the murder of his step-mother, step-brother, and step-sister. The sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment by the Honourable President of India, with the condition that Atbir would remain in prison for the remainder of his natural life without parole or remission. Atbir filed a writ petition challenging the order of the Director General of Prisons, which denied his request for furlough, citing the conditions set by the Honourable President of India that he would remain in prison for the remainder of his natural life without parole or remission. The Director General of Prisons denied Atbir's request for furlough based on the Honourable President's order that Atbir would remain in prison for the remainder of his natural life without parole and without remission. Additionally, Atbir had not earned the last three Annual Good Conduct Reports. The High Court of Delhi dismissed Atbir's writ petition, stating that since he was not entitled to any remission of any kind, he was also not entitled to furlough, as his sentence required him to remain in prison for the remainder of his natural life. The Supreme Court found the reasoning of the High Court and the Director General of Prisons to be incorrect. The Court held that even if Atbir's sentence did not allow for remission, it did not automatically disqualify him from being eligible for furlough under the Delhi Prison Rules, 2018. The Supreme Court differentiated between furlough and parole by stating that furlough is a reward for good conduct and is counted towards the sentence, whereas parole is temporary release for a specific purpose and does not count towards the sentence. Under the Delhi Prison Rules, 2018, a prisoner must have good conduct in prison, should have earned rewards in the last three Annual Good Conduct Reports, and must continue to maintain good conduct. The prisoner should also not be a habitual offender and must be a citizen of India. The Supreme Court directed the Director General of Prisons to reconsider Atbir's request for furlough in accordance with the law and the Delhi Prison Rules, 2018. The Court expected the decision to be made expeditiously, preferably within two months from the date of the judgement. The Delhi Prison Rules, 2018 provide the framework and criteria for determining a prisoner's eligibility for furlough. These rules emphasize good conduct in prison and stipulate that furlough can be granted as a reward for maintaining such conduct, thereby encouraging prisoners to reform. The Supreme Court's judgement reflects the principles of reformation and rehabilitation by recognizing that good conduct in prison should be rewarded with furlough, even if the prisoner is not eligible for remission. This approach encourages prisoners to maintain good behavior and aids their reintegration into society. The Supreme Court's judgement overturns the previous denials of furlough to Atbir and requires the Director General of Prisons to reconsider his request based on the criteria set forth in the Delhi Prison Rules, 2018. This opens the possibility for Atbir to be granted furlough if he meets the eligibility requirements.

case_name: Atma Ram Properties Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
text: Case: Atma Ram Properties Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.. Date: 6th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether property tax recoverable from the tenant under Section 67(3) of the NDMC Act can be treated as part of the rent for seeking eviction of a tenant who defaults in its payment. The appellant terminated the tenancy of the respondent through a legal notice and filed a suit for possession of the tenanted premises, citing the increased rent due to property tax. The Court held that the Delhi Rent Control Act, as a special enactment with a non-obstante clause, prevails over the NDMC Act in landlord-tenant disputes, and property tax cannot be treated as part of the rent for eviction purposes. The Court predicted that treating property tax as part of rent for eviction purposes would undermine the protective intent of the Delhi Rent Control Act and lead to unfair evictions. The Court relied on the fact that Section 67(3) of the NDMC Act only allows recovery of property tax as rent but does not override the provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, which bars eviction based on such recovery.

case_name: Atma Singh vs. Gurmej Kaur & Ors.
text: Case: Atma Singh vs. Gurmej Kaur & Ors.. Date: 13th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Gurmej Kaur, who remarried after the death of her husband Narain Singh, was entitled to inherit the estate of her son Pal Singh under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, despite the provisions of the Hindu Widow's Re-Marriage Act, 1856. Atma Singh argued that Gurmej Kaur, having remarried, lost her right to inherit the property of Narain Singh and his lineal descendants, including Pal Singh, according to the Hindu Widow's Re-Marriage Act, 1856. The High Court ruled that although Gurmej Kaur lost her rights in Narain Singh's estate upon her remarriage, she retained her right to inherit her son Pal Singh's estate under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which provides an overriding effect over previous laws. The Supreme Court interpreted that the Hindu Widow's Re-Marriage Act, 1856, disqualified a widow from inheriting her deceased husband's property or his lineal successors' property upon remarriage. However, this did not affect her right to inherit her own son's estate under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Supreme Court concluded that Gurmej Kaur, as the mother of Pal Singh and a Class I heir under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, was entitled to inherit his estate despite her remarriage. The Court upheld the decisions of the lower courts. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in Smt. Kasturi Devi vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation, which held that a mother cannot be divested of her interest in her son's property either on the ground of unchastity or remarriage.

case_name: Aurangabad Municipal Corporation vs. Jayant S/O Sarvottamrao Kharwadkar & Ors.
text: Case: Aurangabad Municipal Corporation vs. Jayant S/O Sarvottamrao Kharwadkar & Ors.. Date: 21st November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the reversion of Jayant S/O Sarvottamrao Kharwadkar from the post of Town Planner to Sectional Engineer by the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation was valid, considering the alleged violation of principles of natural justice. Jayant Kharwadkar was appointed as Junior Engineer in 1985 and transferred to the Planning Department as Planning Assistant in 1988. He was promoted to Assistant Town Planner in 1997 and confirmed as Town Planner in 1999. His reversion to Sectional Engineer was ordered by the Municipal Commissioner in 2002 without a hearing. The High Court allowed a review petition, setting aside the Municipal Commissioner's order of reversion and reinstating Jayant Kharwadkar as Town Planner. The High Court emphasized that the reversion was ordered without a hearing, violating principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was correct in setting aside the reversion order due to the violation of natural justice principles. The Supreme Court quashed the Municipal Commissioner's reversion order, noting the lack of a proper hearing for the respondent. The Supreme Court directed the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation to initiate any further proceedings against Jayant Kharwadkar in accordance with law, ensuring adherence to principles of natural justice, and to complete the process within a stipulated timeframe to avoid prolonged uncertainty. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the reversion order dated 28th August 2002, reinstating Jayant Kharwadkar as Town Planner and allowing the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation to take lawful action if necessary, within a specified timeframe.

case_name: Aureliano Fernandes Vs. State of Goa and Others
text: Case: Aureliano Fernandes Vs. State of Goa and Others. Date: 12th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge against the dismissal of Aureliano Fernandes from his position at Goa University following allegations of sexual harassment. Aureliano Fernandes was dismissed based on the findings of the Standing Committee for Prevention of Sexual Harassment at Workplace, which concluded that he had committed acts of sexual harassment. Aureliano Fernandes raised objections about the composition of the Committee, alleging bias, and claimed that he was not given a fair opportunity to defend himself. The High Court upheld the dismissal, rejecting Aureliano Fernandes' claims of procedural unfairness and bias in the inquiry process. The counsel argued that the inquiry was conducted in haste, without giving Aureliano Fernandes adequate opportunity to defend himself, and that the Committee was improperly constituted. The Supreme Court upheld the inquiry process, stating that Aureliano Fernandes was given adequate opportunities to present his case and that the principles of natural justice were followed. The decision underscores the importance of adhering to procedural fairness and natural justice in disciplinary actions, while also highlighting that the composition of inquiry committees should be impartial. case_name: Avishek Raja & Ors. vs Sanjay Gupta
text: Case: Avishek Raja & Ors. vs Sanjay Gupta. Date: 19th June 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the non-implementation of the Majithia Wage Board Award by various newspaper establishments and whether this constituted contempt of court. The Act regulates the conditions of service of working journalists and other newspaper employees, including entitlement to gratuity, hours of work, leave, and wage fixation through a Wage Board. The Majithia Wage Board recommended revised wages for working journalists and non-journalist employees, which were accepted by the Central Government on 25th October 2011 and notified on 11th November 2011. The Supreme Court upheld the recommendations of the Majithia Wage Board, dismissing the writ petitions challenging the wage revisions and confirming their legality. The petitioners filed contempt petitions alleging that the respondents did not implement the Majithia Wage Board Award, as approved and notified by the Central Government. The Supreme Court recognized financial constraints but clarified that the inability to pay due to financial difficulties must be distinguished from heavy cash losses, which could justify withholding payment of arrears. The Supreme Court did not find the newspaper establishments guilty of contempt, as their non-implementation stemmed from a misunderstanding of the Award, not wilful disobedience. The Supreme Court clarified that the Wage Board Award must be implemented in full, including for contractual employees, and that all allowances should include variable pay. Newspaper establishments should fully implement the Wage Board Award as clarified by the Supreme Court, including paying arrears and applying the wage revisions to all eligible employees. The decision reinforces the legal requirement for newspaper establishments to comply with Wage Board recommendations and clarifies that financial difficulties alone are not sufficient grounds for non-compliance. The Supreme Court viewed such undertakings as involuntary and under duress, thus non est in law, and emphasized that employees are entitled to the wages recommended by the Wage Board.

case_name: Avneesh Chandan Gadgil & Anr. vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce & Ors.
text: Case: Avneesh Chandan Gadgil & Anr. vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce & Ors.. Date: 24th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to an appeal under Section 30 of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, concerning the condonation of delay in filing an appeal against an order passed by the Recovery Officer. The DRAT set aside the order of the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) which had condoned the delay in filing the appeal under Section 30 of the Act, 1993, by applying Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The DRAT held that Section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable to such appeals. The High Court of Delhi quashed the order of the DRAT and restored the order of the DRT, which had condoned the delay by applying Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The High Court relied on the decision in A.R. Venugopal Alias R. Venugopal vs. Jotheeswaran & Ors. The Supreme Court considered the precedent set in International Asset Reconstruction Company of India Limited vs. Official Liquidator of Aldrich Pharmaceuticals Limited & Ors., which held that Section 5 of the Limitation Act is specifically excluded from appeals under Section 30 of the Act, 1993. The Supreme Court held that Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply to appeals under Section 30 of the Act, 1993. The Court quashed the High Court's judgment and restored the DRAT's order, which had set aside the DRT's condonation of delay. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the High Court's judgment, and restored the DRAT's order. The Court held that the delay in filing the appeal under Section 30 of the Act, 1993, could not be condoned by applying Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

case_name: Avtar Singh & Anr. vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Avtar Singh & Anr. vs. State of Punjab. Date: 23rd March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Avtar Singh and another were convicted under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, for unauthorized possession of gas cylinders and allegedly selling them at a higher price than prescribed. The trial court sentenced the appellants to six months of imprisonment along with a fine of Rs 500 each. The main evidence against the appellants was the testimony of two official witnesses who deposed in favor of the prosecution, as none of the independent witnesses or alleged buyers supported the prosecution's case. The appellants argued that under the Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Order, 1988, only specified officers and those authorized by the Central or State Government had the power to seize gas cylinders, and the Sub-Inspector of Police was not authorized to take such action. The High Court upheld the trial court's decision and confirmed the appellants' conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court held that the Sub-Inspector of Police did not have the authority to seize the gas cylinders under the Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Order, 1988, and therefore the proceedings initiated by him were unauthorized and had to be struck down. The Supreme Court emphasized that when a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, it must be done in that way or not at all, and other methods are necessarily forbidden. The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the High Court and the trial court, and consequently, the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act were set aside, discharging their bail bonds. The key reason was the lack of authority and power with the Sub-Inspector of Police to take action under the relevant order, making the proceedings initiated by him unauthorized. The State argued that the appellants were rightly convicted for unauthorized possession of gas cylinders and should not be allowed to go free due to a technical default in the seizure process. The Supreme Court stated that when a power is given to do something in a certain way, it must be done in that specific way, or it should not be done at all, citing the principle from the case Dharani Sugars and Chemicals Ltd. vs. Union of India and Ors.

text: Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.. Date: 15th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the termination of Avtar Singh from service in the CRPF for not disclosing his involvement in a criminal case was justified. Avtar Singh was terminated from service for suppressing the fact that he was involved in a criminal case when he filled out the verification form during his appointment process. Avtar Singh was charged under Sections 323, 324 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Avtar Singh was acquitted by the trial court on 2nd May 1994, but an appeal against the acquittal was pending at the time of his termination. The Supreme Court's earlier judgement stated that employees must truthfully disclose any involvement in criminal cases, whether it results in conviction, acquittal, or is pending. The employer can take action based on the nature of the offense and the circumstances of the case. The Supreme Court directed the Appointing Authority to reconsider Avtar Singh's case in light of the principles laid down in the 2016 judgement and to pass a speaking order after considering the subsequent developments in the criminal case. A 'speaking order' is a detailed order in which the Appointing Authority must provide reasons for their decision after considering all relevant factors and giving Avtar Singh an opportunity to be heard.

case_name: Ayurved Vikas Mandal vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: Case: Ayurved Vikas Mandal vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.. Date: 12th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the State of Gujarat should absorb the 23 teachers who were working in an aided college that was converted into a self-financing institution and whether the institution should be responsible for their salaries and arrears. The State of Gujarat set the condition that the employees of the institution should be continued as such, and only on that condition was the permission granted for the conversion of the college into a self-financing institution. The High Court of Gujarat directed that the 23 teachers should be absorbed into government service. However, the State government contended that implementing this direction would set a wrong precedent and affect the chances of direct recruits. In the affidavit, the State government stated that it had decided to accommodate 16 employees of the trust in available vacancies in other Grant-in-Aid Ayurveda Colleges in the State, with 7 employees already retired. The trust was required to pay the salaries and allowances for these employees from the date the trust stopped paying until their absorption by the State. The Supreme Court directed that the entire arrears be cleared within three months and that the pension papers for the 7 retired employees be forwarded to the government for processing. The Court also allowed the trust to mobilize funds by disposing of or mortgaging property to comply with the payment directions. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal in terms of the affidavit filed by the State, directing that the judgment should not be treated as a precedent and emphasizing that the arrears should be cleared within three months without any further extension.

case_name: B V Seshaiah vs. The State of Telangana & Anr.
text: Case: B V Seshaiah vs. The State of Telangana & Anr.. Date: 1st February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the appeal against the High Court's decision to dismiss the revision petitions and confirm the conviction of the appellants under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The allegation against the appellants was that they took money from Respondent No. 2 under the guise of making investments and made wrongful gains for their profits. The appellants and Respondent No. 2 agreed to settle the dispute amicably through a Memorandum of Understanding, which included a clause for arbitration if the dispute was not resolved amicably. Clause 8 of the Memorandum of Understanding stated that any dispute should be resolved amicably, and if not, it should be referred to a sole arbitrator, whose decision would be final and binding. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions and confirmed the conviction because Respondent No. 2 failed to file a compromise petition as agreed upon in the Memorandum of Understanding. The Supreme Court viewed the settlement as a compounding of the offence and stated that the appellants could not be convicted based on the orders of the lower courts when the parties had agreed to settle the dispute amicably or through arbitration. The Supreme Court cited the case of M/S Meters and Instruments Private Limited & Anr. vs. Kanchan Mehta, which held that the nature of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is primarily related to a civil wrong and is compoundable. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court cannot override the compounding of offences when the law clearly allows the parties to settle the dispute through such means. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the order of conviction passed by the trial court, and left it open for the parties to settle their dispute as per the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding. The Supreme Court noted that Respondent No. 2 was duty-bound to file a compromise petition before the High Court, and by failing to do so, he withheld key information that led to the unwarranted confirmation of the appellants' conviction.

case_name: B. Nagoji Rao vs The Special Land Acquisition Officer & Anr.
text: Case: B. Nagoji Rao vs The Special Land Acquisition Officer & Anr.. Date: 20th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the disparity in compensation for land acquired, where land growing sugarcane received lower compensation compared to adjacent land growing arecanut trees. B. Nagoji Rao was awarded Rs.2.38 Lacs per acre for his land growing sugarcane. The adjacent land growing arecanut trees was awarded Rs.10.08 Lacs per acre. B. Nagoji Rao contended that the land value should be based on the quality of the land and not on the crop grown at the time of the Section 4(1) notification. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgments and remitted the matter to the High Court for fresh consideration based on the quality of the land and not the crop grown. The Supreme Court highlighted the need for the High Court to consider evidence regarding the quality of the soil in the appellants' land compared to the adjacent lands. If the High Court found B. Nagoji Rao's land to be of the same quality, he would be entitled to similar compensation as the land growing arecanut trees. The Supreme Court stipulated that B. Nagoji Rao would not be entitled to statutory benefits for the period of delay in filing the appeal before the High Court or the Supreme Court. The decision could ensure that land valuation for compensation considers the quality of the land rather than the crop grown, potentially leading to fairer compensation assessments in future land acquisition cases. Landowners should provide clear evidence of the quality of their land and ensure that such evidence is considered in compensation assessments, rather than relying solely on the type of crop grown at the time of acquisition. The Supreme Court found it necessary to remit the matter because the quality of the soil and its impact on land value required detailed examination, which was not available before them.

case_name: B. S. Hari Commandant vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: B. S. Hari Commandant vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 13th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The criminal appeal number was 1890 of 2014. B. S. Hari was a Commandant in the Border Security Force. The incident involved the recovery of Jerrycans of Acetic Anhydride, a controlled substance, from Pakistani territory and fields owned by Indian civilians near the border. B. S. Hari was charged under Sections 40 and 46 of the Border Security Force Act, related to civil offences committed in contravention of Section 25 of the NDPS Act. The General Security Force Court found B. S. Hari guilty of the second and third charges, sentencing him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, and dismissal from service. The counsel argued that the charges against B. S. Hari were not proved, as the main accused were either given relief or discharged due to lack of evidence. It was also argued that the trial was a nullity without proper sanction from the Central Government. The Supreme Court found the punishment disproportionately harsh and set aside the conviction and sentence, ordering that B. S. Hari is entitled to full retiral benefits from the date of his superannuation. The Supreme Court's decision was based on the lack of direct evidence against B. S. Hari and the disproportionate nature of the punishment considering his long service without blemish and the fact that the main accused were let off.

case_name: Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute vs Radhu Vithoba Barde
text: Case: Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute vs Radhu Vithoba Barde. Date: 15th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute was entitled to a decree for specific performance of the agreement to sell land, despite the land being subject to restrictions under Section 36A of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, which requires permission for transfer of land from a tribal to a non-tribal. The agreement to sell dated 31st July 2001 involved Radhu Vithoba Barde agreeing to sell his land of 80R situated at Block No.41/1, Mandve (Bk), Tq. Sangamner, to Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute for a total consideration of Rs.2,25,000/-, out of which Rs.2,20,000/- was paid by the plaintiff. The defendant, Radhu Vithoba Barde, denied the plaintiff's claims and argued that the agreement to sell and the subsequent handing over of possession were invalid due to the lack of prior sanction under Section 36A of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code. The trial court refused the decree for specific performance but granted the alternative relief of refunding Rs.2,20,000/- with interest. The First Appellate Court affirmed this judgment but increased the interest rate from 6% to 14% and directed the plaintiff to hand over possession to the defendant. The High Court dismissed the second appeal, ruling that a decree for specific performance could not be granted due to the restriction under Section 36A of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, which requires prior sanction for transfer of land from a tribal to a non-tribal. The Supreme Court held that the requirement for prior sanction under Section 36A applies to the execution of the sale deed and not the agreement to sell itself. The Court concluded that the plaintiff could seek specific performance, and upon obtaining the decree, the necessary sanction could be sought before executing the sale deed. The Supreme Court modified the judgments of the lower courts, granting the decree for specific performance to Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute, subject to obtaining the necessary sanction under Section 36A of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code before executing the sale deed.

case_name: Babasaheb Maruti Kamble vs. State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Babasaheb Maruti Kamble vs. State of Maharashtra. Date: 1st November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Babasaheb Maruti Kamble was charged with offences under Sections 302, 376(2)(f), and 342 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The trial court awarded Babasaheb Maruti Kamble a death penalty for the offence under Section 302, IPC, life imprisonment for the offence under Section 376(2)(f), and simple imprisonment for two months for the offence under Section 342. The High Court upheld the conviction and confirmed the death sentence of Babasaheb Maruti Kamble on 9th/10th July 2014. The Supreme Court initially dismissed the special leave petition in limine on 6th January 2015. Babasaheb Maruti Kamble filed a review petition seeking review of the order dismissing his special leave petition in limine, arguing that a case involving a death sentence should not be dismissed without recording reasons. The Supreme Court allowed the review petition, recalled the order of 6th January 2015, and restored the special leave petition to its original number. They also commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment with a cap of 20 years rigorous imprisonment. case_name: Babji vs State of Andhra Pradesh
text: Case: Babji vs State of Andhra Pradesh. Date: 9th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Babji's conviction under Section 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act was justified, based on allegations of demanding and accepting money to influence the confirmation of an airline ticket. Babji was accused of demanding Rs. 2,100 from PW-4, Sumeet Asthana, to secure a confirmed airline ticket, which was against the actual fare of Rs. 1,646. PW-4 filed a complaint with the Vigilance Officer, leading to an investigation. The prosecution relied on the complaint filed by PW-4 and the testimony of PW-2, who accompanied PW-4. The evidence aimed to show that Babji demanded and accepted money to influence a public servant for confirming the airline ticket. Both the trial court and the High Court found Babji guilty under Section 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, concluding that he demanded and accepted money for influencing the confirmation of an airline ticket. Babji's defense argued that the prosecution's evidence was vague and did not clearly establish that the money was received to influence a public servant. They contended that there was no convincing evidence linking the payment to any act by a public servant. The Supreme Court observed that the prosecution's evidence was insufficient to prove that Babji received the money to induce a public servant to act in his official capacity. The Court noted the lack of convincing evidence showing that Babji's actions were intended to influence a public servant. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside Babji's conviction under Section 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Court acquitted Babji and discharged his bail bonds, concluding that the prosecution failed to establish the necessary elements of the offence.

case_name: Badri Vishal Pandey and Ors. vs. Rajesh Mittal and Ors.
text: Case: Badri Vishal Pandey and Ors. vs. Rajesh Mittal and Ors.. Date: 4th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the respondents complied with the order passed by the Supreme Court on 7th September 2015, which required the re-engagement of retrenched workmen as daily wage workers/muster roll employees based on seniority. The order directed that the respondents should take the petitioners, who were retrenched workmen, on daily wage basis as per the office order dated 7th April 2015 and list contained therein. The workmen were retrenched due to the paucity of work orders and financial constraints faced by U.P. Jal Nigam, leading to the termination of services for those appointed after 31st March 1989. The Supreme Court found that the respondents had not willfully disobeyed the order, as they had re-engaged some of the retrenched workmen and published advertisements to re-engage others based on seniority. The Supreme Court stated that the order dated 7th September 2015 should not be interpreted based on the impressions of the petitioners, but on the explicit terms of the order, which did not mandate immediate reinstatement but re-engagement as per the seniority list and availability of work. The re-engagement of retrenched workmen is governed by Section 6Q of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which mandates giving preference to retrenched workmen over others when new employment opportunities arise. The Supreme Court dismissed the contempt petitions, concluding that there was no willful disobedience of its order dated 7th September 2015 by the respondents. The Supreme Court directed that the services of the workmen who had already been re-engaged by the respondents should not be affected by the dismissal of the contempt petitions.

case_name: Baidyanath Yadav vs. Aditya Narayan Roy & Ors.
text: Case: Baidyanath Yadav vs. Aditya Narayan Roy & Ors.. Date: 19th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appointment of Baidyanath Yadav to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) for the Selection Year 2014 should be quashed in favor of Aditya Narayan Roy, whose name was not recommended by the State Screening Committee despite being recommended by the departmental minister. The High Court ruled that the State Screening Committee failed to record and disclose reasons for not recommending Aditya Narayan Roy, and directed the committee to recommend his name to the UPSC within two weeks. The High Court quashed Baidyanath Yadav's appointment, stating that the process lacked objectivity and fairness. Baidyanath Yadav argued that the High Court erred in giving undue weight to the serial order of names placed before the State Screening Committee. He contended that non-disclosure of reasons by the selection committee did not vitiate their decision, as there were no rules or administrative instructions requiring such disclosure. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's direction was beyond its jurisdiction. The Court held that the High Court should have directed a reassessment of all candidates by the State Screening Committee rather than ordering the recommendation of a specific candidate. The Supreme Court concluded that there was no bias, mala fide, or arbitrariness in the selection process conducted by the State Screening Committee. The Court emphasized that it is not within the jurisdiction of the High Court or Supreme Court to re-assess the merit of candidates selected by an expert body unless there is evidence of procedural impropriety. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision and allowed the appeals filed by Baidyanath Yadav and the State of Bihar. The Court upheld the selection of Baidyanath Yadav to the IAS for the Selection Year 2014 and dismissed the claims of Aditya Narayan Roy.

case_name: Ballu @ Balram @ Balmukund and Another vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Ballu @ Balram @ Balmukund and Another vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 2nd April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants were charged under Sections 302, 201, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of Mahesh Sahu and concealing evidence. Mahesh Sahu was in a love relationship with Anita, the sister of appellant Ballu @ Balram @ Balmukund. The prosecution alleged that due to the enmity arising from Mahesh Sahu's relationship with Anita, the appellants caused his death on 7th June 1992 and attempted to conceal the evidence. The prosecution relied on the testimony of witnesses, including Govind (PW-7), who saw the appellant dragging a dead body, and Sumitra Bai (PW-6), who saw blood stains being washed at the scene. The trial court acquitted the appellants, stating that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. The High Court reversed the trial court's judgement, convicting the appellants under Sections 302, 201/34 IPC, and sentencing them to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in reversing the acquittal without sufficient grounds, as the trial court's judgement was based on a detailed examination of evidence. The Supreme Court emphasized that an appellate court should interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court's findings are perverse or impossible. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, reinstating the trial court's acquittal of the appellants and discharging their bail bonds. The Supreme Court found that the prosecution witnesses, including Beni Prasad (PW-1) and Sumitra Bai (PW-6), had given inconsistent and exaggerated statements, leading to doubts about their reliability. The Supreme Court reiterated that circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain leading to no other conclusion but the guilt of the accused, which the prosecution failed to establish in this case.

case_name: Balwant Singh (D) through LR vs. Dungar Singh (D) through LRs
text: Case: Balwant Singh (D) through LR vs. Dungar Singh (D) through LRs. Date: 12th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue was whether the arbitral award dividing the family properties between the brothers Balwant Singh and Dungar Singh should be upheld as a rule of court despite objections from Balwant Singh. Balwant Singh objected to the arbitral award on grounds that the arbitrators conducted the proceedings hurriedly and did not allow sufficient time for him to present his case, rendering the award unclear and unjustifiable. The District Judge dismissed the application to make the arbitral award a rule of the court, citing procedural irregularities and insufficient clarity in the award. The High Court overturned the District Judge's decision, holding that the arbitral award was valid, clear, and made with mutual consent, and declared it as a rule of the court. The interpretive issue was whether an arbitral award made by close relatives of the parties could be considered unbiased and valid when no allegations of misconduct were raised against the arbitrators. This judgment reinforces the validity of arbitral awards made with mutual consent and encourages the resolution of family property disputes through arbitration.

case_name: Balwant Singh vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Balwant Singh vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 3rd May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the inordinate delay in deciding the mercy petition of the petitioner, Balwant Singh, warranted the commutation of his death sentence to life imprisonment. Balwant Singh was convicted and sentenced to death for his involvement in a bomb blast on 31st August 1995, which resulted in the death of the then Chief Minister of Punjab, Shri Beant Singh, and 16 others, and injured several more. The petitioner argued that the delay of more than 10 years in deciding his mercy petition was inordinate and caused him undue mental agony, thus entitling him to the commutation of his death sentence to life imprisonment. The respondent argued that the petitioner himself had not filed any mercy petition and that the pending appeals of co-accused in the Supreme Court were relevant to the consideration of the mercy petition. The Supreme Court acknowledged the delay but noted that the petitioner had not personally filed the mercy petition and that various factors, including national security and law and order considerations, influenced the decision to defer the petition. Thus, the Court did not grant the relief sought by the petitioner. The Supreme Court directed that the competent authority should re-evaluate the mercy petition in due course, taking into account the relevant circumstances and security considerations. The petition was disposed of with these observations.

case_name: Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority vs Birla Super Bulk Terminal & Ors.
text: Case: Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority vs Birla Super Bulk Terminal & Ors.. Date: 27th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority (BIAAPA) could levy betterment charges on the lands allotted by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development (KIAD) Act. The High Court held that the lands allotted by KIADB for industrial purposes were not subject to the betterment charges under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act as the KIAD Act is a special Act and would prevail over the general law of the KTCP Act. The Supreme Court decided that BIAAPA had the authority to levy betterment charges under the KTCP Act as the development activities and land use changes fall under the jurisdiction of the Planning Authority, including the industrial lands allotted by KIADB. The non-obstante clause in Section 76-M of the KTCP Act declares that the provisions of the Act and the rules, regulations, and bye-laws made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent contained in any other law, thus supporting BIAAPA's authority to levy charges. The High Court exempted the respondents from paying betterment charges on the basis that the KIAD Act, being a special Act, would override the general provisions of the KTCP Act, and that the industrial lands were already developed and did not require further development charges. The Supreme Court viewed that both the KTCP Act and the KIAD Act operate in different fields with different objectives, and there was no inconsistency or overlap that would negate the authority of BIAAPA under the KTCP Act. The counsel for BIAAPA argued that the KTCP Act governs the entire planning and development of buildings within Karnataka, including industrial areas, and that the authority to levy betterment charges under Section 18 of the KTCP Act is applicable to all lands within its jurisdiction. The Supreme Court directed the first respondent to pay Rs.1,48,29,173/- to BIAAPA with interest at the rate of 6% from the date of the demand (17th September 1998) within two months, failing which the respondent would be liable to pay interest at the rate of 12% thereafter. The Supreme Court applied the principle that a statute is best interpreted when its purpose is understood, and that both the KTCP Act and the KIAD Act must be harmoniously construed to give effect to the legislative intent and avoid reducing the legislation to futility.

case_name: Bank Employees Union vs. Rajarshi Shahu Govt. Servants Co-operative Bank Ltd.
text: Case: Bank Employees Union vs. Rajarshi Shahu Govt. Servants Co-operative Bank Ltd.. Date: 6th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellant, a Registered Trade Union, had the locus to prefer an application to modify a standing order that applies to the employees of the respondent under Section 38(2) of the Maharashtra Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The original standing order mandated that every employee shall retire from service on attaining the age of 55 years, with possible extensions not exceeding one year at a time or three years in total at the discretion of the president. The agreements changed the retirement age from 55 years to 58 years. The Additional Labour Commissioner allowed the alteration to the Standing Order clause No. 22(7) to change the retirement age to 58 years. The Industrial Court allowed the appeal on the ground that only an employee, as defined under the Maharashtra Industrial Relations Act, could apply for the alteration of a standing order, and the Registered Union had no locus to do so. The Supreme Court ruled that the technical objection as to the union's locus standi could not be countenanced and set aside the order of the Industrial Court, thereby allowing the union to file the application under Section 38(2) of the Maharashtra Industrial Relations Act. The Supreme Court ordered that all consequential benefits as a result of this judgement be given to the employees of the respondent within six months from the date of the judgement.

case_name: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh
text: Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh. Date: 21st June 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Baljit Singh was entitled to compassionate appointment in the Bank of Baroda following his father's death in harness. The High Court set aside the judgment of the First Appellate Court and restored the judgment of the Trial Court, which granted Baljit Singh's claim for compassionate appointment. Baljit Singh's application was based on the 1998 Scheme for compassionate appointments issued by the Bank of Baroda, which allowed for such appointments in the case of an employee's death in harness. The appellant Bank argued that Baljit Singh did not meet the financial eligibility criteria and that the High Court failed to consider the factual aspects of the case properly. The Supreme Court ruled that Baljit Singh did not meet the financial eligibility criteria as the family's monthly income exceeded 60% of the deceased employee's last drawn emoluments, thus disqualifying him from compassionate appointment under the Scheme. The Supreme Court acknowledged that Baljit Singh had completed the 8th standard during his father's lifetime and was therefore eligible for the post of Peon, but this did not affect his ineligibility based on the family's financial status. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed Baljit Singh's suit for compassionate appointment.

case_name: Basavaraj alias Basavannappa Parmeshwar Bangargir vs. State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Basavaraj alias Basavannappa Parmeshwar Bangargir vs. State of Maharashtra. Date: 1st October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Basavaraj was convicted under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of his father. The alleged motive was a grudge Basavaraj nursed against his father regarding his claim to a share in the agricultural lands of the deceased. The conviction was based on circumstantial evidence, as there were no eyewitnesses to the occurrence. The postmortem report confirmed that the death was caused by cardio-respiratory failure due to multiple deep incised wounds over the scalp, face, and neck, leading to obligogenic and neurogenic shock. Basavaraj was absconding after the incident and did not participate in the funeral rites of his father, which was considered an additional incriminating factor against him. The FSL report confirmed that the bloodstained clothes recovered from the appellant were indeed stained with human blood. The appellant argued that the conviction was based on surmises and conjectures, in the absence of any cogent and convincing evidence, and that the chain of circumstances was not conclusively established. The High Court justified the motive by stating that the appellant had a grudge against his father regarding agricultural lands, which established a clear motive for the crime. The testimonies of PW-2 and PW-8 were crucial in establishing the presence of the appellant in the agricultural fields on the night of the incident and his proximity to the crime scene. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the conviction and sentence of the appellant.

text: Case: Bayaji Sambhu Mali @ Borate (D) Through LRs. vs Nazir Mohammed Balal Zari Through GPA Holder & Ors.. Date: 12th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant was a deemed purchaser under Section 29 read with Section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, or whether the tenant was obliged to give notice under Section 32F(1A). The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant under Article 227 of the Constitution, challenging the order of the Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal. 'Tillers Day' on 1st April 1957 was significant because it was the date when the tenant claimed to be a deemed purchaser of the land, which was contested by the landlord, who was a minor at that time. The appellant argued that the application filed by the landlord for personal cultivation under Section 31(3) of the Act was dismissed, and subsequent appeals were also dismissed, reinforcing the tenant's claim as a deemed purchaser. The Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal decided that the tenant had not complied with the provisions of Section 32F of the Act, and therefore, the purchase in favor of the appellant was ineffective. The Supreme Court ruled that there was no requirement for the appellant to give notice under Section 32F(1A) because the appellant had already acquired a deemed status as a purchaser when the landlord's application was rejected. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant had produced certified copies of relevant documents in the review petition, which supported the appellant's claim that the landlord's application for possession had been rejected. case_name: Bhagwan Singh vs Dilip Kumar @ Deepu @ Depak and Another
text: Case: Bhagwan Singh vs Dilip Kumar @ Deepu @ Depak and Another. Date: 23rd August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main charges were gang rape, extortion, and making threats to make a rape video viral. The offences included Sections 376D, 384, 506 of the IPC, Section 326 of the POCSO Act, and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act. The High Court granted bail to Dilip Kumar and the other accused, requiring them to furnish a personal bond for Rs.1,00,000 with two sureties of Rs.50,000 each. Bhagwan Singh contended that the offences were heinous, involving gang rape of a minor, and that there was a high risk of the accused tampering with evidence and threatening witnesses, given their influence and power. The Supreme Court observed that the delay in filing the FIR, which was due to constant threats from the accused, could not be held against the prosecution, especially considering the circumstances and the minor victim's fear. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had erred by primarily considering the delay in filing the complaint and not adequately addressing the gravity of the allegations, the potential threat to witnesses, and the influence of the accused. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail and directed the accused to surrender before the jurisdictional court within two weeks. The Court allowed the accused to seek bail again after the recording of the remaining witnesses' evidence.

case_name: Bhagwani vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Bhagwani vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 18th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the conviction and death sentence of Bhagwani under Sections 363, 366A, 364, 346, 376D, 376A, 302, 201 of the IPC, and Section 5(g)(m) read with Section 6 of the POCSO Act should be upheld. Bhagwani and Satish were convicted for kidnapping, raping, and murdering an 11-year-old girl. The victim was found in an unconscious state with multiple injuries and signs of sexual assault. The prosecution presented circumstantial evidence, including the presence of Bhagwani and Satish at the crime scene, recovery of the victim's shawl and blanket, and the medical evidence showing rape and murder. The High Court upheld the conviction and death sentence imposed by the trial court on Bhagwani for the heinous crimes committed. The Supreme Court found the evidence to be consistent and sufficient to establish Bhagwani's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court noted that the chain of circumstances was complete and pointed conclusively to Bhagwani's involvement in the crimes. The Supreme Court noted that Bhagwani was not given a fair opportunity to defend himself as the trial court did not provide adequate time for legal representation, violating his right to a fair trial under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court considered Bhagwani's age (25 years), his lack of criminal antecedents, and the absence of evidence showing that he could not be reformed or rehabilitated. The Court also noted his conduct in jail. The Supreme Court commuted Bhagwani's death sentence to life imprisonment for a period of 30 years without remission, considering the heinous nature of the crime but also the potential for his reformation. The Supreme Court emphasized that sentencing should consider both the crime and the criminal, including the possibility of reformation and rehabilitation. The death penalty should be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases where alternative punishments are foreclosed. The victim had multiple injuries including scratches, contusions, and abrasions on various parts of her body, and evidence of severe sexual assault, including injuries to her genital and anal areas. The Supreme Court found that both the trial and high courts had correctly appreciated the evidence and followed legal principles in convicting Bhagwani. However, it highlighted the need for a fair trial and adequate legal representation, which was lacking.

case_name: Bhagwat Sharan (Dead Through LRS) vs. Purushottam & Ors.
text: Case: Bhagwat Sharan (Dead Through LRS) vs. Purushottam & Ors.. Date: 3rd April 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves a family lineage starting with Mangat Ram from Village Narnaul, Rajasthan, who had four sons: Madhav Prashad, Lal Chand, Ram Chand, and Umrao Lal. Madhav Prashad had no issues and adopted Hari Ram, son of Lal Chand. Ram Chand also had no issues and adopted Shriram, another son of Lal Chand. The plaintiff, Bhagwat Sharan, is the son of Radha Krishan, who was the son of Umrao Lal. The family branches in dispute are from the descendants of Madhav Prashad through Hari Ram and the descendants of Umrao Lal. The plaintiff, Bhagwat Sharan, claimed that the properties mentioned in the plaint were joint family properties owned by the Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and sought partition of the same by metes and bounds as per his share. He asserted that these properties were purchased and managed jointly by Madhav Prashad and Umrao Lal, and later by their descendants. The respondents contested that the properties were not joint family properties but were self-acquired properties of Madhav Prashad and Hari Ram. They denied the existence of any Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and asserted that the properties and business mentioned were individual acquisitions and not part of a joint family estate. The trial court decreed the suit in favor of the plaintiff, holding that all the properties were joint family properties and that the plaintiff had a 2.38% share in them. The court decided that the properties should be partitioned accordingly. The High Court set aside the trial court's decree of partition, ruling in favor of the contesting defendants. The High Court dismissed the plaintiff's application for condonation of delay, the application for review, and the application under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Supreme Court concluded that the plaintiff failed to prove the existence of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and that the properties in question were joint family properties. The Court emphasized that the burden of proof lay on the plaintiff to establish the HUF and its properties, which was not adequately done. Therefore, the appeals filed by the appellant were dismissed.

case_name: Bhagwat vs. State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Bhagwat vs. State of Maharashtra. Date: 19th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Bhagwat was convicted under Section 302 IPC for the murder of his wife by setting her on fire. The deceased sustained burn injuries on various parts of her body, including the head, face, neck, back, upper limbs, lower limbs, and anterior chest. The appellant argued that there were no eyewitnesses, the deceased died from accidental burns, and that he tried to save her, as evidenced by burns on his hand. He also claimed the dying declarations were inconsistent. The High Court acquitted Bhagwat of the charge under Section 498-A IPC regarding dowry demand. The third dying declaration, made in the presence of the Special Judicial Magistrate, was considered reliable and corroborative, leading to the conviction of the appellant. PW-7, the Special Judicial Magistrate, recorded the third dying declaration, and PW-8, the Doctor, certified the condition of the deceased at the time of the declaration. PW-1 Vijay and PW-9 testified that the appellant was often intoxicated and assaulted the deceased. They were present at the scene and saw their mother with burn injuries after being told to leave the room by the appellant. The first dying declaration was considered suspicious because it was recorded by a police officer without the signature of any doctor present, raising doubts about its authenticity. The court noted that the appellant's absconding for approximately three months after the incident was contrary to normal human behavior and undermined his claim of innocence. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the deceased's homicidal death, and there was no material evidence to support his claim of accidental burns or grave provocation.

case_name: Bhairon Sahai (D) Through LRs. vs. Bishamber Dayal (D) Through LRs. & Ors.
text: Case: Bhairon Sahai (D) Through LRs. vs. Bishamber Dayal (D) Through LRs. & Ors.. Date: 18th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the landlord, Bhairon Sahai, was entitled to seek eviction of the respondents on the grounds of parting with possession of the premises without the landlord's consent. The Rent Controller decided in favor of Bhairon Sahai, holding that Respondent No.1 had parted with possession of the premises in favor of Respondent No.2 without the landlord's consent, and directed the respondents to vacate the premises within two months. The Rent Control Tribunal, Delhi, reversed the findings of the Rent Controller, concluding that Respondent No.1, not Respondent No.2, was carrying on the business of a fair price shop, and the High Court of Delhi upheld this decision. The Supreme Court ruled that there had been parting of possession by Respondent No.1 in favor of Respondent No.2 without the landlord's consent, which was sufficient for eviction under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and allowed the appeal. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to vacate the premises within two months from the date of the judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appellant to receive the amount of Rs. 16,500/- that was deposited in the court registry during the pendency of the appeal.

case_name: Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. & Ors. vs. AMR-Dev Prabha & Ors.
text: Case: Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. & Ors. vs. AMR-Dev Prabha & Ors.. Date: 18th March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves a dispute over the validity of an auction process conducted by Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. (BCCL) for a tender, which was challenged by AMR-Dev Prabha on grounds of technical issues and alleged procedural irregularities during the auction process. The primary issue was the technical problems encountered during the e-auction process, which led to a re-auction. AMR-Dev Prabha argued that the re-auction was unjustified and contrary to the terms of the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT). The Division Bench of the High Court quashed the Letter of Acceptance issued by BCCL to RK Transport (the successful bidder after the re-auction) and directed a reconduction of the auction, citing serious procedural irregularities and technical issues. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by BCCL and RK Transport, setting aside the High Court's order. The Supreme Court held that there was no substantial procedural lapse that warranted the High Court's interference and that BCCL and C1-India (the e-auction facilitator) had acted in a bona fide manner. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition filed by AMR-Dev Prabha because it found that AMR-Dev Prabha's interest was purely commercial and not in public interest. The Court also noted that the initial auction process was affected by technical difficulties, which justified the resumption of the auction. The reports from CERT-In and the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) supported the conclusion that the auction process was not marred by collusion or malafide actions. These reports found that the technical problems were genuine and the resumption of the auction process was justified, which influenced the Supreme Court's decision to set aside the High Court's order.

case_name: Bharat Sher Singh Kalsia vs. State of Bihar & Anr.
text: Case: Bharat Sher Singh Kalsia vs. State of Bihar & Anr.. Date: 31st January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the petition filed by Bharat Sher Singh Kalsia to quash the FIR and subsequent criminal proceedings related to alleged forgery and fraud in the sale of land. The allegations were that Raj Kumar Karan Vijay Singh, using a Power of Attorney (PoA), sold off property belonging to the informant's family without obtaining the required signatures from the landowners/principals, and that the sale deed was fraudulent. The Trial Court found sufficient grounds to take cognizance of the offences under Sections 409, 467, 468, 471, and 420 of the IPC and issued process against the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appellant's petition, upholding the validity of the FIR and the subsequent criminal proceedings. The appellant argued that he was merely a vendee of the land and had no role in the alleged forgery. He contended that the Power of Attorney was valid at the time of the sale, the sale deed was executed with consideration, and the dispute was of a civil nature. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR and the order taking cognizance of the offences, finding that the appellant, as a bona fide purchaser, could not be held liable for any alleged misdeeds by the Power of Attorney holder, and that the matter was of a civil nature. The Supreme Court allowed the possibility for the Trial Court to summon the appellant under Section 319 of the CrPC if future evidence warranted his involvement, directing the Trial Court to act in accordance with the law.

text: Case: Bharat Stars Services Pvt Ltd. vs Harsh Dev Thakur & Anr.. Date: 28th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the challenge against the bail granted to the first respondent, Harsh Dev Thakur, in a case involving embezzlement of Rs. 2.78 Crores. Harsh Dev Thakur was accused of embezzling Rs. 2.78 Crores and transferring the money in the names of his wife, her brother, and her father, who are co-accused and absconding. The High Court granted bail to Harsh Dev Thakur, requiring him to deposit Rs. 50 Lakhs and meet other conditions. The State argued that there was a likelihood of Harsh Dev Thakur absconding once released on bail. The Supreme Court observed that the conditions imposed by the High Court were insufficient given the financial fraud of over Rs. 2.75 Crores and decided that more stringent conditions were necessary. The Supreme Court imposed additional conditions, including the requirement for Harsh Dev Thakur to furnish security for Rs. 75 Lakhs, deposit his passport with the trial court, and present himself at the jurisdictional police station once every week. The Supreme Court allowed the appellant to approach the trial court for withdrawal of the money, subject to conditions imposed by the trial court.

case_name: Bharatiya Janata Party, West Bengal vs State of West Bengal & Ors.
text: Case: Bharatiya Janata Party, West Bengal vs State of West Bengal & Ors.. Date: 9th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Bharatiya Janata Party sought a writ of mandamus directing the West Bengal State Election Commission to issue nomination forms to their candidates, enable submission of nomination papers through email, and provide police protection to their candidates. The Bharatiya Janata Party presented newspaper reports from the Times of India, the Statesman, and the Telegraph, detailing incidents of violence against their candidates while trying to obtain and submit nomination forms. The State Election Commission issued a notification providing additional venues for filing nomination papers, in response to the allegations of violence. The respondents argued that the writ petition was not maintainable as it was not filed by individual candidates and lacked specific details showing that any candidate was prevented from obtaining and filing nomination papers. The respondents cited the case of Bodula Krishnaiah vs State Election Commissioner, A.P., where the court held that once the election process is set in motion, the court should not interfere. The Supreme Court decided not to interfere in the ongoing election process, following the precedent that courts should not intervene once elections are set in motion. The Supreme Court suggested that political parties and candidates should approach the State Election Commissioner with their grievances, who is empowered to address issues related to the election process. The Supreme Court expressed hope that the State Election Commissioner would take appropriate steps to ensure free and fair elections, addressing any apprehensions and ensuring candidates are not deprived of their chance to contest. If the State Election Commissioner addresses the grievances, it could lead to a more orderly and fair election process, reducing incidents of violence and ensuring all candidates can participate without obstruction. Political parties should submit their grievances in writing to the State Election Commissioner, who is responsible for addressing such issues in accordance with the law. The decision reinforces the role of the State Election Commissioner in addressing election-related grievances and emphasizes that courts should refrain from interfering in the election process once it has begun.

case_name: Bharti AXA General Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Priya Paul & Anr.
text: Case: Bharti AXA General Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Priya Paul & Anr.. Date: 7th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the insurance claim for the accidental death of Priya Paul's son in a glider crash was valid under the Smart-Personal Accident-Individual Insurance Policy taken by the deceased. The insurance claim was rejected on the basis that the deceased was traveling in a motorized glider for sightseeing, which did not qualify as a standard aircraft and excluded the accident from the policy coverage. The NCDRC allowed the insurance claim, directing the insurer to pay Rs. 1 crore with interest, stating that the glider was an aircraft under the Aircrafts Act, 1934, and was duly licensed. The insurer argued that the glider was not a standard aircraft as it relied on aerodynamics to soar and that the deceased was not a fare-paying passenger in a regular scheduled airline or air charter company. The Supreme Court concluded that the term 'standard type of aircraft' was ambiguous and should be interpreted in favor of the insured, thus including the motorized glider as a standard type of aircraft under the policy. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by Bharti AXA General Insurance Co. Ltd., upheld the NCDRC's decision, and confirmed that the insurance claim was valid as the glider was a duly licensed aircraft and the deceased was a fare-paying passenger. The Supreme Court emphasized that insurance contracts require 'uberrima fides' or utmost good faith, meaning that the insured must fully disclose all relevant facts to the insurer. The decision sets a precedent that insurance policies with ambiguous terms should be interpreted in favor of the insured, potentially leading to more claims being upheld in cases involving non-standard aircraft. Bharti AXA General Insurance Co. Ltd. may need to revise its policy terms to clearly define exclusions and ensure that ambiguous terms are eliminated to avoid similar disputes in the future. case_name: Bharti Airtel Limited and Another vs. Vijaykumar V. Iyer and Others
text: Case: Bharti Airtel Limited and Another vs. Vijaykumar V. Iyer and Others. Date: 3rd January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether the right to claim set-off exists in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) when the Resolution Professional takes custody and control of all the assets of the corporate debtor under Section 25(2)(a) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). In April 2016, Bharti Airtel Limited and Bharti Hexacom Limited entered into eight spectrum trading agreements with Aircel Limited and Dishnet Wireless Limited for the purchase of the right to use spectrum in the 2300 MHz band, contingent on approval from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT). The TDSAT held that the DoT's demand of Rs.298 crores against the Aircel entities was untenable and directed the DoT to return the bank guarantees to the Aircel entities. However, the DoT did not return the bank guarantees and preferred a civil appeal. Bharti Airtel Limited wrote to the banks seeking confirmation of the cancellation of the bank guarantees and approached the Supreme Court, which directed the cancellation of the bank guarantees. Subsequently, Airtel made a payment of Rs.341.80 crores to the Aircel entities and set off Rs.145.20 crores against operational charges. The Adjudicating Authority held that Bharti Airtel Limited had the right to set off Rs.112.87 crores from the payment retained and due to the Aircel entities, a decision that was later challenged and overturned by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT). The Supreme Court concluded that the right to set-off is not automatic or self-executing under the IBC during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and dismissed the appeals filed by Bharti Airtel Limited, rejecting the claim for set-off.
