case_name: Bhartiben Chandrakantbhai Thakor vs State of Gujarat and Others
text: Case: Bhartiben Chandrakantbhai Thakor vs State of Gujarat and Others. Date: 27th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant, Bhartiben Chandrakantbhai Thakor, was appointed as an Auxiliary Nurse Midwife by the District Panchayat, Valsad on 15th January 1980. She submitted her resignation from service on 18th April 1993, but withdrew it on 23rd November 1993. Despite withdrawing her resignation, an order was passed on 23rd/26th December 1994 accepting her resignation with effect from 31st March 1993, which led to her filing a petition. By a judgment dated 12th October 2000, a Single Judge of the High Court of Gujarat set aside the order dated 23rd/26th December 1994 and directed that the appellant would be entitled to all consequential benefits. In a Letters Patent Appeal filed by the State of Gujarat, the Division Bench of the High Court found that the appellant had not been allowed to resume her duties for no fault of hers. However, the Division Bench directed that the appellant shall not be entitled to any benefits for the period for which the resignation was in force. On 8th April 2002 and 17th July 2002, orders were passed treating the period from 24th November 1993 to 30th March 2001 as unauthorized leave and considering it as a break in service without salary. These orders were later quashed by the High Court. The High Court, in its judgment dated 25th July 2006, held that no continuity of service could be granted on account of her absence from service over a period of 782 days. This judgment was affirmed by the Division Bench on 17th February 2009. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant should be treated to have completed the minimum pensionable service of 25 years. The pensionary dues payable to the appellant shall be computed on that basis, regardless of any previous orders by the State government. The arrears of pension payable to the appellant from the date of her voluntary retirement shall be paid within one month with interest at the rate of 6% per annum. The appeal was allowed and the impugned judgment of the High Court dated 17th February 2009 was set aside.

case_name: Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Ltd. vs Damodar Valley Corporation & Ors.
text: Case: Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Ltd. vs Damodar Valley Corporation & Ors.. Date: 23rd July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the tariff determined by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) under the Electricity Act, 2003, or the tariff determined by the Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) under the Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948, should prevail. The High Court upheld the tariff determined by the CERC, ruling that the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, took precedence over the Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948, for tariff determination. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity also upheld the CERC's tariff determination, agreeing that the 2003 Act superseded the 1948 Act in matters of tariff. The key provisions included Sections 32, 37, 38, 39, and 40, which dealt with financial aspects such as expenditure, depreciation, allowances, and interest payments, relevant to tariff determination. The Supreme Court interpreted the proviso to mean that the provisions of the Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948, that are not inconsistent with the Electricity Act, 2003, shall continue to apply to the Corporation. The Supreme Court held that the specific provisions of the 1948 Act, which were consistent with the 2003 Act, would continue to apply, but any inconsistencies would be resolved in favor of the 2003 Act. The Supreme Court affirmed that the CERC had the jurisdiction to determine the tariff for DVC under the Electricity Act, 2003, thereby overriding the tariff set by DVC under the 1948 Act. The CERC considered various factors including capital cost, return on equity, interest on loans, depreciation, operational norms, and fuel price adjustment while determining the tariff. The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the CERC and the Appellate Tribunal, confirming that the tariff determined by the CERC under the Electricity Act, 2003, would prevail over the tariff determined by DVC under the Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948.

case_name: Bhawna Bai vs Ghanshyam and Others
text: Case: Bhawna Bai vs Ghanshyam and Others. Date: 3rd December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the charges framed by the trial court against the respondents for the murder of Gopal Saran should be quashed as decided by the High Court. The charges framed against the respondents were under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of Gopal Saran. According to the prosecution, Gopal Saran was last seen with the respondents, who took him to the field where his dead body was later found. The prosecution alleged that the respondents consumed liquor with Gopal Saran and that he was found dead in their field the next morning. The High Court quashed the charges against the respondents, stating that the trial court failed to apply its judicial mind and give concise reasons for framing the charges. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in quashing the charges, noting that the trial court had sufficient grounds for framing the charges based on the allegations in the charge sheet. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision and restored the charges framed by the trial court against the respondents, directing the trial to proceed. The Supreme Court emphasized that at the stage of framing charges, the court only needs to see if there is a prima facie case against the accused and does not need to conduct an elaborate inquiry or consider whether the trial is likely to end in conviction. The prosecution mentioned the 'last seen together' circumstance, the recovery of the dead body in the respondents' field, the absence of immediate information to the police or the victim's family, and prior quarrels between the deceased and the respondents. The Supreme Court held that the trial court's role in framing charges is to evaluate if there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, and that detailed reasoning is not required at this stage. The Supreme Court directed the Second Additional Sessions Judge, Mandleswar, to proceed with the trial in accordance with law and clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.

case_name: Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil vs K. Madan Mohan Rao & Ors.
text: Case: Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil vs K. Madan Mohan Rao & Ors.. Date: 24th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the election petition filed by K. Madan Mohan Rao against Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil disclosed any cause of action and whether it was barred in law, thus liable to be rejected. The allegations included that Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil furnished false information in Form 26 (election affidavit), that the Returning Officer did not follow Election Commission guidelines, and that there were irregularities in the publication of information regarding pending criminal cases against the appellant. Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil applied for the rejection on the grounds that the mandatory requirements under Sections 81 and 81(3) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 were not followed and that the petition did not disclose how the nomination paper was improperly accepted. The High Court dismissed the application for rejection, stating that only the averments in the petition and the accompanying documents could be considered and not any other materials brought on record during the proceedings. Bhim Rao Baswanth Rao Patil filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court of India challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, stating that the High Court correctly appreciated the law relating to Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC and dismissed the appellant's application. The Supreme Court clarified that only the pleadings and the accompanying documents in the election petition can be considered for the purpose of Order VII Rule 11, CPC, and any other materials brought on record during the proceedings cannot be taken into account. The decision reinforces the importance of strict adherence to procedural rules and guidelines in election petitions and ensures that only the initial pleadings and documents are considered for the purpose of rejection under Order VII Rule 11, CPC. Candidates should ensure accurate and complete disclosure of all required information in Form 26 (election affidavit), adhere to Election Commission guidelines, and provide clear documentation of any criminal cases or convictions to avoid legal challenges. The Supreme Court highlighted that the acceptance of election petitions should be based solely on the pleadings and accompanying documents, and any additional materials brought during the proceedings should not influence the decision under Order VII Rule 11, CPC. The decision could lead to more stringent adherence to procedural requirements in election disputes, ensuring that all necessary information is disclosed at the initial stages and preventing the use of extraneous materials to influence the outcome of such petitions.

case_name: Bhisham Lal Verma vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Bhisham Lal Verma vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 30th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether a second petition under Section 482 of the CrPC is maintainable on grounds that were available for challenge at the time of filing the first petition under the same section. Bhisham Lal Verma was charged with offences under Sections 409, 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120B of the IPC, and Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, related to irregularities in the construction of toilets under the Integrated Low-Cost Sanitation Scheme and embezzlement of public funds. The Allahabad High Court dismissed the second petition, stating that it was not maintainable since the petitioner had already filed a previous petition under Section 482 CrPC challenging the government's sanction order, and he could not challenge the charge sheet and cognizance order later. The Supreme Court agreed with the view that successive petitions under Section 482 CrPC should not be allowed as it would enable an accused to stall proceedings by filing multiple petitions, raising one plea after another, even though all such pleas were available at the first instance. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition, holding that the second petition under Section 482 CrPC was not maintainable, and upheld the Allahabad High Court's decision. The Supreme Court expressed its appreciation and gratitude to Mr. S. Nagamuthu, learned amicus curiae, for his able and scholarly assistance in the case.

case_name: Bhoopendra Singh vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
text: Case: Bhoopendra Singh vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.. Date: 29th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The second respondent was charged under Sections 147, 148, 149, 323, 341, 307, 302, and 336 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), and Sections 3/25 and 4/25 of the Arms Act 1959 for the murder of Daansingh. The High Court granted bail to the second respondent based on her prolonged custody (three years and ten months), the absence of an overt act assigned to her, and the grant of bail to co-accused Vijay Pal. The court also noted the variance in the prosecution story regarding her presence and anticipated delay in the trial's conclusion. The appellant argued that the second respondent was involved in the conspiracy to murder Daansingh by constantly communicating with the sharp-shooter and her son using multiple SIM cards, and that she was the custodian of the weapons used in the crime. The appellant also highlighted that there was no change in circumstances to warrant the grant of bail after the previous applications were denied. The charge-sheet provided evidence that the second respondent used multiple mobile numbers to stay in contact with the co-accused, Prahlad (the hired sharp-shooter), and her son, Anek Singh. Additionally, it was found that she was the custodian of the weapons stored at the rental premises where she resided. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision erroneous as it failed to consider the seriousness of the crime and the specific role attributed to the second respondent. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court's observation that no overt act was assigned to the second respondent was incorrect, given the evidence presented in the charge-sheet. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail to the second respondent, rejecting her bail application and directing her to surrender on or before 7th November 2021. The Supreme Court clarified that its observations were solely for the purpose of considering the bail application and would not affect the merits of the case or the pending trial.

case_name: Bhupesh Rathod vs. Dayashankar Prasad Chaurasia & Another
text: Case: Bhupesh Rathod vs. Dayashankar Prasad Chaurasia & Another. Date: 10th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was validly filed on behalf of the company despite objections regarding its format and authorisation. The trial court acquitted the respondent on the grounds that there was no document except a promissory note to show the loan was granted, and the Board Resolution authorising the complaint was not signed by the board members. The Supreme Court ruled that the format of the complaint, which described the complainant as the Managing Director of the company, was valid and not a fundamental defect. The Supreme Court noted that the respondent did not dispute his signatures on the cheques and failed to provide an alternative explanation for why the cheques were issued. The Court held that the absence of a loan agreement was not critical since the respondent did not present any alternative explanation for the cheques, and the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act applied. The Supreme Court sentenced the respondent to one year of imprisonment and imposed a fine of twice the cheque amount, with the option to suspend the sentence if an additional payment of Rs. 1,60,000 was made to the appellant within two months. The Supreme Court emphasized that technical objections regarding complaint format should not be used to evade financial liability when the substantive elements of the offence are proven.

case_name: Bijay Kumar Singh & Others vs. Amit Kumar Chamariya & Others
text: Case: Bijay Kumar Singh & Others vs. Amit Kumar Chamariya & Others. Date: 22nd October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants were liable for eviction on the grounds of non-payment of arrears of rent under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997. The Supreme Court interpreted that the deposit of arrears of rent, accompanied by an application for determination, is a mandatory requirement to avoid eviction under Section 7(2) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997. The Court predicted that allowing tenants to bypass statutory requirements for depositing arrears would undermine the legislative intent and lead to judicial uncertainty. The Court held that the Single Judge should have maintained judicial decorum by referring the matter to a larger Bench for clarity on conflicting interpretations. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, affirming the High Court’s decision that the appellants failed to comply with mandatory provisions of the tenancy law.

case_name: Biju K.K. vs Cochin University of Science and Technology, Kochi & Ors.
text: Case: Biju K.K. vs Cochin University of Science and Technology, Kochi & Ors.. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Biju K.K. was wrongfully denied marks for his experience as a daily wager when applying for the post of Technical Assistant Grade-II and whether the appointment of other candidates was in compliance with the eligibility criteria. The Supreme Court remitted the matter to the learned Single Judge to reconsider whether the Selection Committee was justified in awarding marks for experience and whether Biju K.K.'s service as a daily wager should have been considered. Biju K.K. approached the High Court by filing a writ petition because he was awarded fewer marks for his experience, which affected his position in the rank list, and he contended that other candidates who were appointed did not meet the requisite qualifications. The Supreme Court directed the Single Judge to reconsider the writ petition on merits, specifically whether the Selection Committee's decision on awarding marks for experience and the eligibility criteria for other candidates were justified, and to allow the parties to produce additional documents within four weeks. text: Case: Bikash Manna vs. The State of West Bengal. Date: 30th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Bikash Manna should be granted protection under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. in connection with FIR No. 261 of 2017. The FIR number was 261, and it was registered on 2nd April 2017 at Police Station Domjur, Howrah, West Bengal. The Supreme Court ordered that in case Bikash Manna was arrested in connection with FIR No. 261 of 2017, he should be released on bail upon furnishing a self-bond and depositing a sum of Rs. 10 Lakhs before the Court. The condition was that Bikash Manna had to deposit Rs. 10 Lakhs before the Court and cooperate with the investigation, among other conditions under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. The de-facto complainant had no objection to granting protection to Bikash Manna under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C., provided he could withdraw the amount deposited before the Court. The Supreme Court allowed the de-facto complainant to withdraw the amount deposited along with interest and ordered that Bikash Manna be released on bail if arrested, subject to the conditions under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. and executing a bond of Rs. 25,000 with two sureties. Bikash Manna was required to execute a bond to the tune of Rs. 25,000 with two sureties of the like amount. Bikash Manna was required to cooperate with the investigation and comply with the conditions under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. The pending applications, if any, were disposed of by the Supreme Court. The de-facto complainant was represented by Mr. Pijush K. Roy, who submitted that the complainant was only interested in getting his money and did not want to prosecute the appellant.

case_name: Binay Kumar Dalei & Ors. v. State of Odisha & Ors.
text: Case: Binay Kumar Dalei & Ors. v. State of Odisha & Ors.. Date: 2nd March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue raised by the Rural Organisation for Social Empowerment (Respondent No.8) was to cancel the stone quarry leases granted pursuant to an advertisement dated 17th August 2017, and to ensure no further leases were granted in the Kuldiha Wildlife Sanctuary and the eco-sensitive zone linked to it. The NGT called for a report from the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (HoFF) after conducting an inspection of the Eco-Sensitive Zone surrounding the Kuldiha Wildlife Sanctuary. Based on the report, the NGT directed the State Government to take steps to bring the entire corridor within the ambit of the eco-sensitive zone and prohibit ingress into the zone. The appellants contended that their stone quarries were not among the 11 quarries that had ingressed into the eco-sensitive zone, and they argued that their quarries were situated on the other side of the hillock, thus there was no reason to stop their operation. They also claimed that the NGT refused to hear their interests before passing the order. The State of Odisha submitted that the mining operations would be permitted only after the implementation of the Comprehensive Wildlife Management Plan. They also stated that the process for declaring the traditional elephant corridor as a conservation reserve was in an advanced stage of consideration. The Supreme Court directed the State of Odisha to implement the Comprehensive Wildlife Management Plan as suggested by the Standing Committee of NBWL before permitting any mining activity in the eco-sensitive zone. The State was also directed to complete the process of declaring the traditional elephant corridor as a conservation reserve as per Section 36A of the Wildlife Protection Act. The appellants requested the Supreme Court to direct the Government to compensate them for the losses incurred during the period they were not permitted to carry out mining operations despite holding a valid lease. However, the Supreme Court did not issue such directions but allowed the appellants to approach the Government for redressal of their grievances.

case_name: Bir Singh vs. Delhi Jal Board & Ors.
text: Case: Bir Singh vs. Delhi Jal Board & Ors.. Date: 30th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case is 'Bir Singh vs. Delhi Jal Board & Ors.' The main issues addressed in this judgment pertain to the entitlement of a Scheduled Caste person to benefits or concessions in employment when moving from one state to another. The Supreme Court held that a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste in relation to a particular state is not entitled to the benefits or concessions allowed to Scheduled Caste candidates in employment in another state. The Court considered the Constitution Bench judgments in 'Marri Chandra Shekhar Rao vs. Dean, Seth G.S. Medical College and others' and 'Action Committee on Issue of Caste Certificate to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the State of Maharashtra and another vs. Union of India and another'. The key question referred to the larger Bench was whether a Presidential Order issued under Article 341(1) or Article 342(1) has any bearing on the State's action in making provisions for the reservation of appointments or posts in favor of any Backward Class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. The Civil Appeal No. 4494 of 2006 was disposed of by the larger Bench of the Supreme Court by order dated 6th August 2014, in light of the High Court's findings that the impugned order suffered from apparent illegality as the appointing authority was the University, and the State Government had no power to ask for cancellation of an appointment made in accordance with the advertisement. The Supreme Court interpreted Articles 341 and 342 to mean that the specification of castes or tribes as Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes in relation to a State or Union Territory is binding and cannot be varied except by law made by Parliament. This specification is necessary to prevent the benefits of reservation from being misused by those who migrate from one State to another. The Court observed that if a member of a Scheduled Caste or Tribe from one State were to claim reservation benefits in another State, it would deprive the original residents of the reservation benefits intended for them, thereby disrupting the allocation and purpose of such reservations.

case_name: Bir Wati & Ors. vs. Union of India & Anr.
text: Case: Bir Wati & Ors. vs. Union of India & Anr.. Date: 17th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the reference petition filed by the appellants under the Land Acquisition Act was barred by limitation and if they were still entitled to seek re-determination of compensation under Section 28-A of the Act. The appellants were not aware of the passing of the award because they were neither present when the award was passed, nor were they served with the notice of the award under Section 12(2) of the Land Acquisition Act. They also did not receive any notice in the name of the deceased Jugal Kishore. The application for reference to the Civil Court was dismissed by the Additional District Judge on 21st April 2005, and this dismissal was upheld by the High Court on 9th March 2006, both on the grounds that it was barred by limitation. The Supreme Court allowed the appellants to make an application to the concerned Collector under Section 28-A of the Act within three months from the date of receipt of the judgment. The Court directed that the application should seek compensation based on the enhanced compensation awarded to other similarly situated landowners. The Supreme Court considered the peculiar facts and circumstances, such as the death of the bread earner during the proceedings, the illiteracy of the appellants, their unawareness of the award and legal procedures, and the expiration of three months' time to apply under Section 28-A. The Supreme Court stipulated that the appellants would not be entitled to claim any interest due to the delay on their part. The Collector was directed to decide the application within three months and release the payment of compensation after proper verification of the appellants' family relations with the original claimant.

case_name: Birbal Choudhary @ Mukhiya Jee vs. State of Bihar
text: Case: Birbal Choudhary @ Mukhiya Jee vs. State of Bihar. Date: 6th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants were convicted under the provisions of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for committing offences punishable under Sections 364A, 34, 395, and 412. The Sessions Court sentenced Krishna Bihari Singh and Jawahar Koiry to death penalty, but the High Court commuted their sentence to imprisonment for 20 years. The crime involved the abduction of Ajay Shanker Mishra, Manoj Singh, and Raju Mishra for extracting ransom. The victims were kidnapped and held in captivity while a ransom demand was made. The prosecution led 22 witnesses as part of its evidence, including testimonies from the victims, the informant, and various business associates. Test Identification Parades (TIPs) and the recovery of ransom money also played a significant role in establishing the case. The informant, Arun Kumar Mishra, lodged the written report about the abduction and was also a key witness during the trial. He provided critical information about the kidnapping and the ransom demands. The High Court opined that the actions of all the appellants were driven by common intention, and it confirmed the conviction of the appellants, modifying the sentence to imprisonment for 20 years. The Sessions Court convicted all the accused persons under Sections 364A, 34, 395, and 412 IPC, sentencing them to various terms of imprisonment. Two appellants, Krishna Bihari Singh and Jawahar Koiry, were initially sentenced to death, which was later commuted to 20 years by the High Court. The Test Identification Parade (TIP) played a significant role in identifying the accused. The victims identified several appellants during the TIP, which was conducted under the supervision of a Metropolitan Magistrate. The prosecution presented evidence including a letter written by PW-17 during confinement, signed by PW-20, and the testimony of the informant about the ransom demands made by the accused using a mobile phone. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions and the modified sentences of 20 years of rigorous imprisonment for the appellants, dismissing the appeals.

case_name: Birendra Prasad Sah vs The State of Bihar & Anr.
text: Case: Birendra Prasad Sah vs The State of Bihar & Anr.. Date: 8th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was filed within the statutory period. The amounts of the two cheques were Rs 36,00,000 and Rs 13,00,000. The appellant issued a second legal notice because despite repeated requests to the postal department, no acknowledgment of the first notice was furnished. The Chief Judicial Magistrate condoned the delay in filing the complaint and took cognizance of the matter. The High Court quashed the complaint, stating it was not filed within the statutory period of thirty days. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the complaint to the trial court. The MSR Leathers case established that successive notices are permissible under Section 138, which was relevant to the argument that the second legal notice was valid. The High Court erred by not considering the sufficient cause shown for the delay in filing the complaint as indicated in paragraphs 7 and 8 of the appellant's complaint. The appellant did not receive proof of service despite making repeated queries with the postal department. The potential outcome of the trial will depend on the merits of the case, which will be adjudicated upon during the trial. The restoration of the complaint allows the appellant to pursue the case further in the trial court, potentially leading to a resolution based on the merits of the case.

case_name: Bishambhar Prasad vs. M/s Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Bishambhar Prasad vs. M/s Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 20th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the allotment of industrial land in Kota, Rajasthan, to M/s Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. (APPL) was valid and whether the cancellation of permissions and approvals by the State Government and RIICO was justified. The legal dispute was triggered by the cancellation of permissions and approvals granted to M/s Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. by the State Government and RIICO, following a review by a Cabinet Committee set up after a change in government. The High Court quashed the cancellation of the land allotment and the permissions granted to APPL, stating that the State Government and RIICO had not followed due procedure and had violated principles of natural justice. The State of Rajasthan and RIICO argued that the land allotted to APPL remained with the State Government, the approvals for conversion to commercial use violated the Model Code of Conduct, and the process of cancellation was within their rights and powers. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's view that APPL was not given a fair opportunity to defend itself, and the cancellation of the allotment without issuing a show cause notice or hearing APPL was a violation of the principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court decided that the allocation of the land to APPL was valid and that the permissions for conversion granted by RIICO were in accordance with the Master Plan and the 1979 Rules. The cancellation by the State Government and RIICO was set aside. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Rajasthan, RIICO, and the workers' unions, upholding the High Court's judgment that the cancellation of the land allotment and permissions to APPL was invalid, and directed the reinstatement of the allotment and permissions.

case_name: Board of Trustees for the Port of Calcutta vs The Port Tenants Welfare Association & Ors.
text: Case: Board of Trustees for the Port of Calcutta vs The Port Tenants Welfare Association & Ors.. Date: 27th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the interest rate for the payment of arrears of rent should be fixed at 6% per annum or at a higher rate as per the rate schedule fixed by the Board under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. The High Court granted the facility of 36 installments for payment of arrears of rent and fixed the interest rate at 6% per annum. The appellant challenged the decision because they believed the interest rate should have been 15 to 18% in terms of the rate schedule fixed by the Board under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement regarding the fixation of interest at 6% per annum, but also decided that no further levy would be imposed as the respondents had already paid interest at that rate. The Supreme Court invoked its jurisdiction under Article 142 to give a quietus to the controversy, considering the long duration of the dispute and the desire to bring finality to the matter. The Supreme Court made it clear that this judgement should not be treated as a precedent for the purpose of fixation of rent or interest rates, as it was constrained to pass the order based on the specific facts and circumstances of the case. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgement regarding the interest rate, and directed that no further interest would be levied since the respondents had already paid as per the High Court's rate. The decision could influence future disputes by emphasizing the importance of context-specific judicial discretion and ensuring that judgements are not automatically used as precedents without considering the unique facts of each case. Parties should ensure that agreements regarding rent and interest rates are clear, adhere to the statutory provisions, and consider the potential for judicial discretion in case of disputes. The Supreme Court clarified that while the rate schedule fixed by the Board under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, suggests higher interest rates, judicial discretion can be applied based on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.

case_name: Bohatti Devi vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Bohatti Devi vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 30th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's decision to grant bail to the respondent No. 2, who is accused of offences under Sections 302 and 120B IPC, was justified. The respondent No. 2 is accused of offences under Sections 302 (murder) and 120B (criminal conspiracy) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision unsustainable because the High Court did not consider the seriousness and gravity of the offence, the relevant material in the charge sheet, and the fact that a non-bailable warrant was issued against the accused. The respondent No. 2 had initiated proceedings to quash the criminal case against him under Section 482 Cr.P.C., which were dismissed by the High Court and subsequently by the Supreme Court. A non-bailable warrant was issued, and he was arrested in 2021. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for considering the bail granted to co-accused Vicky and Sarvesh @ Mangal without properly assessing the specific roles and allegations against respondent No. 2. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order granting bail to respondent No. 2 and directed him to surrender within two weeks, failing which a non-bailable warrant would be issued. The Supreme Court instructed the trial court to conduct the trial in accordance with the law and based on the evidence, without being influenced by the Supreme Court's observations while considering the bail application. The respondent No. 2 was accused of conspiring to murder, under Sections 302 and 120B IPC, which involved serious and grave charges. The Supreme Court emphasized that the gravity of the offence is crucial in bail decisions to ensure that serious allegations, especially those involving murder and conspiracy, are not trivialized and justice is appropriately served. The Supreme Court directed respondent No. 2 to surrender before the concerned Jail Authority/Court within two weeks, failing which a non-bailable warrant would be issued against him.

text: Case: Bombay Mercantile Cooperative Bank Ltd. vs M/S U.P. Gun House & Ors.. Date: 22nd January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the auction and sale of the mortgaged property by the Cooperative Bank to recover a loan taken by M/S U.P. Gun House was valid despite claims of improper notice service. M/S U.P. Gun House took a loan of Rs. 2,00,000 from the Cooperative Bank in 1996 to establish a firearms business. The loan was declared an NPA on 30th February 2002 because an amount of Rs. 2,39,812.41 was due and payable by M/S U.P. Gun House. The Cooperative Bank issued a notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 22nd March 2006, took symbolic possession of the property on 9th July 2009, and later took physical possession and auctioned the property. The property was auctioned on 31st December 2012, and Abdul Haleem Siddiqui was the highest bidder with a bid of Rs. 42,00,000. The sale was later challenged by M/S U.P. Gun House but was upheld by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court directed the Cooperative Bank to pay Rs. 54,00,000 to M/S U.P. Gun House in full and final settlement of all claims, to be paid within five weeks from the date of the order. The Supreme Court upheld and confirmed the sale of the property in favor of Abdul Haleem Siddiqui, the auction purchaser, and set aside the orders of the lower courts that had quashed the auction.

case_name: Brijesh Kumar & Another vs. Shardabai (Dead) by LRS. & Ors.
text: Case: Brijesh Kumar & Another vs. Shardabai (Dead) by LRS. & Ors.. Date: 1st October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the plaintiff's suit for adverse possession over the suit lands was valid, and if the High Court was correct in restoring the Trial Court's decree favoring the plaintiff's adverse possession claim. The Trial Court decreed the plaintiff's suit for adverse possession, holding that the plaintiff had perfected his title by continuous, hostile, and uninterrupted possession for more than 12 years adverse to that of the original landowners. The First Appellate Court reversed the Trial Court's decree, holding that the Trial Court had overlooked documentary evidence and arrived at an erroneous conclusion of adverse possession based solely on oral evidence. The High Court allowed the second appeal, reversing the First Appellate Court's decision and restoring the Trial Court's decree that favored the plaintiff's claim of adverse possession. The appellants argued that the findings of the First Appellate Court were final and the High Court should not have reappraised the evidence in the second appeal. They contended that the plaintiff never acquired title by adverse possession as the original owner sold the lands to Urmila Devi before the expiry of twelve years. The Supreme Court concluded that the plaintiff's claim of adverse possession was unsustainable. The Court found that the Khasra entries relied upon by the plaintiff were suspicious and based on fraud and forgery, and that the plaintiff failed to establish peaceful, open, and continuous possession necessary for a claim of adverse possession. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and restored the order of the First Appellate Court, thereby dismissing the plaintiff's suit for adverse possession.

case_name: Brijmani Devi vs. Pappu Kumar & Anr.
text: Case: Brijmani Devi vs. Pappu Kumar & Anr.. Date: 17th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to Pappu Kumar, the respondent-accused, who was charged with the murder of Rupesh Kumar, the appellant's son. The FIR No. 93/2020 was lodged by Brijmani Devi after she witnessed Pappu Kumar shooting her son Rupesh Kumar on the night of 19th February 2020 while he was sleeping on the rooftop of their house. Pappu Kumar had previously attempted to murder Rupesh Kumar in 2017, leading to FIR No. 316/2017 being lodged against him for causing serious bullet injury to Rupesh Kumar. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision because the High Court's orders were cryptic and lacked proper reasoning, failing to consider the seriousness of the allegations, the respondent's criminal antecedents, and the potential threat to the appellant and witnesses. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court granted bail without adequate reasoning, not taking into account the severity of the allegations, the respondent's history of absconding, and the possibility of him threatening the witnesses. The Supreme Court cancelled the bail granted to Pappu Kumar and directed him to surrender before the concerned jail authorities within two weeks.

case_name: C. Doddanarayana Reddy (Dead) By LRS. & Ors. vs C. Jayarama Reddy (Dead) By LRS. & Ors.
text: Case: C. Doddanarayana Reddy (Dead) By LRS. & Ors. vs C. Jayarama Reddy (Dead) By LRS. & Ors.. Date: 14th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the plaintiff, C. Jayarama Reddy, was entitled to a 1/4th share in the suit property, claiming he was a minor at the time of his father's death and continued to be a member of the joint Hindu family. The plaintiff claimed that he was a minor at the time of his father's death in 1963 and did not understand the contents of the release deed he signed on 15th June 1963, which allegedly severed his ties with the joint family. The plaintiff presented a School Leaving Certificate (Ex.P/1) to prove his date of birth, but did not produce any school official or headmaster to verify the authenticity of the certificate. The trial court found that the plaintiff was not a minor at the time of the release deed, relying on the registered release deed (Ex.D/1) which mentioned the plaintiff's age as about 22 years and a registered marriage deed (Ex.D/2) indicating the plaintiff's age as 24 years. The High Court ruled that the School Leaving Certificate (Ex.P/1) was admissible as proof of age under Section 35 of the Evidence Act and concluded that the plaintiff was a minor at the time of the release deed, thus declaring the release deed null and void. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in interfering with the concurrent findings of the trial court and the First Appellate Court, which had held that the plaintiff failed to prove his minority and dismissed the plaintiff's suit. The Supreme Court emphasized that the School Leaving Certificate needed to be properly authenticated and the date of birth recorded therein needed to be corroborated by reliable and trustworthy evidence, which was not done in this case.

case_name: C. Venkata Swamy vs H.N. Shivanna
text: Case: C. Venkata Swamy vs H.N. Shivanna. Date: 4th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary suits involved were O.S. No. 6640/1996 filed by C. Venkata Swamy for a declaration and permanent injunction regarding the suit land, and O.S. No. 2150/1992 filed by H.N. Shivanna for a similar claim on the same land. The trial court dismissed the suit filed by C. Venkata Swamy (O.S. No. 6640/1996) and decreed the suit filed by H.N. Shivanna (O.S. No. 2150/1992). The High Court of Karnataka dismissed the appeals filed by C. Venkata Swamy and affirmed the judgement of the trial court. The Supreme Court remanded the case back to the High Court because the Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the appeals cursorily without proper appreciation of evidence, discussing the issues, and providing adequate reasoning as required under Section 96 and Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Supreme Court emphasized that the first Appellate Court has a duty to fully reappreciate evidence, provide independent conclusions, and address all issues and arguments with detailed reasoning, as first appeals are a valuable right of litigants. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to decide the appeals afresh on merits in accordance with the law, without being influenced by the Supreme Court's observations, and to ensure expeditious disposal of the appeals.

case_name: C.S. Gopalakrishnan & Ors. vs. The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.
text: Case: C.S. Gopalakrishnan & Ors. vs. The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.. Date: 9th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Tamil Nadu Industrial Purposes Act and Highways Act were arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution when compared to the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition Act, 2013. C.S. Gopalakrishnan argued that the acquisition proceedings under the Industrial Purposes Act were arbitrary and that the prolonged delay in issuing the Section 3(1) Notice after the initial Public Notice infringed upon his property rights. The Court found that while there were delays in issuing notices under the Tamil Nadu Industrial Purposes Act, these did not invalidate the acquisition proceedings due to the protections afforded by the Validation Act of 2019. The Supreme Court stated that challenges based on procedural irregularities should be addressed in individual cases and not as a broad attack on the validity of the state laws. The Supreme Court concluded that the Tamil Nadu Highways Act was not arbitrary and served its purpose of enabling efficient and timely land acquisitions for infrastructure projects.

case_name: C.S. Ramaswamy vs V.K. Senthil & Ors.
text: Case: C.S. Ramaswamy vs V.K. Senthil & Ors.. Date: 30th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respective suits filed by the plaintiffs for cancellation of the sale deeds executed in favor of the defendant were barred by the law of limitation. The plaintiffs claimed that the sale deeds executed in favor of C.S. Ramaswamy were obtained by fraudulent misrepresentation, and they sought to have these sale deeds declared null and void. The trial court rejected the applications because it found that the issue of limitation was a mixed question of law and facts, which could not be decided at the preliminary stage. The High Court dismissed the civil revision petitions and confirmed the orders passed by the trial court, rejecting the applications filed under Order VII Rule 11 CPC. C.S. Ramaswamy argued that the suits were filed after a lapse of more than 10 years from the date of execution of the sale deeds, and thus, were clearly barred by the law of limitation. The plaintiffs argued that they came to know about the fraudulent nature of the sale deeds only in April 2015, and they filed the suits immediately thereafter, making them within the limitation period as per Section 17 of the Limitation Act. The Supreme Court found the allegations of fraud to be vague and not specific, and it was not satisfied with the plaintiffs' explanation of how they came to know about the fraud only in 2015. The Supreme Court allowed the applications under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, rejecting the plaints on the ground that the suits were barred by the law of limitation. The decision could set a precedent that vague allegations of fraud are insufficient to extend the limitation period, emphasizing the need for clear and specific evidence of fraud and the timing of its discovery. Parties should ensure they file suits within the prescribed limitation period and provide clear, specific evidence of any alleged fraud, including the timing and manner of its discovery, to avoid their suits being barred by limitation. The Supreme Court emphasized this to prevent misuse of legal provisions by making vague claims of fraud, ensuring that only genuine cases with clear evidence are allowed to proceed, thereby maintaining the integrity of the legal process.

case_name: CBI vs. B.B. Agarwal & Ors.
text: Case: CBI vs. B.B. Agarwal & Ors.. Date: 18th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main allegation was that B.B. Agarwal and the other respondents, including two companies, defrauded Punjab National Bank (PNB) to the tune of approximately Rs. 15 crores through a public issue of their companies. The CBI filed charges under Section 120B read with Sections 409, 420, 468, and 471 of the IPC, and Section 13(2) read with Section 13(i)(c) and (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The High Court of Delhi quashed the criminal proceedings against the respondents under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., concluding that there was no criminality issue involved following the settlement of the case between the parties. The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings after the parties settled their accounts and the Debt Recovery Tribunal, Mumbai, disposed of the recovery suit based on the settlement. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the CBI, agreeing with the High Court that there was no surviving criminality issue and that continuing the trial would be an abuse of process. The Supreme Court noted that the settlement between PNB and the two companies resulted in the payment of Rs. 12.20 crores to PNB, and there were no outstanding dues, which justified quashing the criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court viewed that there was no criminality issue involved after the settlement and that prosecuting the respondents further would be unnecessary and unjust. The civil suits filed by PNB against the companies were settled through a one-time settlement, and the Debt Recovery Tribunal, Mumbai, disposed of the cases based on this settlement. The CBI argued that the criminal case should be brought to its logical end on merits, irrespective of the civil settlement between the parties. The CBI relied on the decision in Rumi Dhar (Smt.) vs. State of West Bengal & Anr., which held that criminal proceedings should continue to their logical conclusion despite civil settlements. The Supreme Court distinguished this case by noting that there was no surviving issue of criminality after the settlement, unlike in the precedent cited, where the issue of criminality persisted.

case_name: CCE, Aurangabad vs. M/s Videocon Industries Ltd.
text: Case: CCE, Aurangabad vs. M/s Videocon Industries Ltd.. Date: 29th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The dispute concerned the classification of LCD panels imported by Videocon Industries, with the revenue arguing they were parts of televisions under Chapter 85.29, while the assessee claimed they were liquid crystal devices under Chapter 90.13. The revenue argued that the LCD panels were primarily used in televisions and should be classified under Chapter 85.29 as parts of televisions, citing their principal use as a determining factor. The Supreme Court upheld the CESTAT's classification of LCD panels under Chapter 90.13 and dismissed the revenue's appeals, providing finality to the classification dispute. The judgment is likely to serve as a precedent for similar classification disputes, emphasizing the importance of specific descriptions in tariff classifications over general descriptions. The Court clarified that LCD panels, being liquid crystal devices, fall under Chapter 90.13 as they are not more specifically provided for under other headings, overriding the revenue's reliance on their principal use.

case_name: Captain Pramod Kumar Bajaj vs. Union of India and Another
text: Case: Captain Pramod Kumar Bajaj vs. Union of India and Another. Date: 3rd March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Captain Pramod Kumar Bajaj was aggrieved by the judgment passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, which upheld the order of his compulsory retirement passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal and the Central Board of Direct Taxes. The compulsory retirement was based on the decision of the President of India, communicated by the Central Board of Direct Taxes, citing Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules, which allows for compulsory retirement in the public interest. Captain Pramod Kumar Bajaj was a Permanent Commissioned Officer in the Indian Army who later qualified for the Civil Services Examination in 1989 and was appointed to the Indian Revenue Service. He was promoted to the rank of Commissioner in the Department of Income Tax in 2012. The three main arguments were: (1) The presence of bias in the decision-making process; (2) The compulsory retirement was punitive and intended to deprive him of an appointment as Member ITAT; (3) His service records were consistently 'Outstanding' with no adverse entries, which contradicts the decision to retire him compulsorily. The court noted that while there were allegations of bias and malice, particularly against the Chairman of the CBDT, these allegations could not be looked into as the concerned officer was not made a party in the proceedings to clarify his stand. The Supreme Court quashed the order of compulsory retirement, holding it as punitive and not in the public interest. The court set aside the adverse consequences of the order and allowed the appeal.

case_name: Caretel Infotech Ltd. vs. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Caretel Infotech Ltd. vs. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited & Ors.. Date: 9th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The e-public tender was for setting up call centres to receive, record, and reply to information enquiries and complaints from LPG customers of IOC, HPC, and BPC. Caretel Infotech Ltd. contended that the blacklisting clause did not apply to them as they had not been blacklisted at the time of submitting their bid on 19th December 2017. They argued that the blacklisting occurred later, on 22nd February 2018. The Supreme Court noted that there were serious disputes regarding the Business Continuity Certificate, which required cross-examination of deponents. It stated that such disputes should not be resolved through writ proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution of India but rather through civil suit proceedings. The Supreme Court held that the show cause notice issued on 5th December 2017 did not amount to the initiation of blacklisting proceedings. The notice only asked Caretel Infotech Ltd. to show cause why blacklisting should not be initiated, which meant that actual blacklisting had not yet begun. The Supreme Court interpreted Clause 20 to require specific disclosure in the provided format, which did not include the initiation of blacklisting proceedings. It concluded that Caretel Infotech Ltd. could not be penalized for not disclosing the show cause notice as the format did not mandate it. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by Caretel Infotech Ltd., setting aside the impugned order of the Division Bench and dismissing the writ petition filed by respondent No.3, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited.

case_name: Cdr Amit Kumar Sharma etc vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Cdr Amit Kumar Sharma etc vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 20th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) could adjudicate on the validity of the selection proceedings for Permanent Commission (PC) in the Indian Navy when relevant material was disclosed only to the AFT in a sealed cover. The Supreme Court held that the non-disclosure of relevant material to the affected party and its disclosure in a sealed cover to the AFT caused substantial prejudice to the officers and violated principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court directed that the vacancies must be determined correctly and that the appellants' objections regarding the determination of vacancies should be considered by the AFT. The Supreme Court noted that the selection board proceedings were not disclosed to the appellants, which prevented them from challenging the findings of the AFT. The Court emphasized the need for transparency and fairness in the adjudication process. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment of the AFT and remanded the case back to the AFT for fresh adjudication, directing that the material should be disclosed to the appellants to enable a fair hearing. The Supreme Court directed that the officers who were protected by interim orders of the Court shall continue to have the benefit of those orders pending the disposal of the proceedings before the AFT, and thereafter for a period of eight weeks to allow for any further appeals. The Supreme Court emphasized the principles of natural justice, transparency, and fairness, stating that all material relied upon by either party in the course of a judicial proceeding must be disclosed to the affected party.

The Supreme Court directed that the vacancies must be determined correctly and that the appellants' objections regarding the determination of vacancies should be considered by the AFT.

text: Case: Central Board of Trustees vs. M/s Indore Composite Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 26th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the Division Bench of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh was justified in dismissing the writ petition filed by the Central Board of Trustees regarding the order of the Employees Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal that set aside the demand for damages under Section 14B of the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. The Central Board of Trustees issued an order under Section 7A on 15th April 2010, directing M/s Indore Composite Pvt. Ltd. to deposit Rs. 87,204/- for non-payment of provident fund contributions for the year 2005-2006 on wages lesser than the minimum wages prescribed for employees under the category of semi-skilled. The Employees Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by M/s Indore Composite Pvt. Ltd. and set aside the order dated 21st January 2015 passed by the Central Board of Trustees, which demanded damages and allied dues of Rs. 91,585/- for delayed payments. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh dismissed the writ petition filed by the Central Board of Trustees, affirming the order of the Employees Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and remanded the case back to the Division Bench of the High Court for a fresh decision on the merits, in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court instructed the High Court to decide the writ petition afresh on merits, strictly in accordance with the law, and uninfluenced by any observations made by the Supreme Court.

case_name: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) vs. Thommandru Hannah Vijayalakshmi @ T. H. Vijayalakshmi
text: Case: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) vs. Thommandru Hannah Vijayalakshmi @ T. H. Vijayalakshmi. Date: 8th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the FIR filed against Thommandru Hannah Vijayalakshmi for possession of assets disproportionate to her known sources of income should be quashed. The charges included being in possession of disproportionate assets under Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and abetment under Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. Thommandru Hannah Vijayalakshmi, a Commissioner of Income Tax, was accused of possessing assets disproportionate to her known sources of income, along with her spouse, during the check period from 1st April 2010 to 29th February 2016. The High Court quashed the FIR, stating that a Preliminary Enquiry should have been conducted by the CBI before registering the FIR. The CBI argued that a Preliminary Enquiry was not mandatory and that the FIR was registered based on reliable source information. The Supreme Court held that a Preliminary Enquiry is not mandatory in all corruption cases and that an FIR can be filed if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision to quash the FIR, allowing the CBI to proceed with its investigation. The Supreme Court emphasized that the CBI must follow its manual and guidelines but noted that failure to conduct a Preliminary Enquiry does not invalidate an FIR if it discloses a cognizable offence. The CBI Manual provides guidelines for investigations, including the procedure for Preliminary Enquiries, but it is not a statutory requirement overriding the Criminal Procedure Code. The Supreme Court acknowledged the potential harm but reiterated that a Preliminary Enquiry is not mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence, thus balancing the need for fair investigation with the protection of public servants' reputations. The Supreme Court directed the CBI to continue its investigation in accordance with the law, ensuring adherence to the procedural requirements while investigating the allegations against Thommandru Hannah Vijayalakshmi.

case_name: Central Bureau of Investigation vs Arvind Khanna
text: Case: Central Bureau of Investigation vs Arvind Khanna. Date: 17th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR and charge sheet against Arvind Khanna for receiving foreign contributions without prior permission under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976. The allegations were that Arvind Khanna received a sum of Rs. 9,04,84,770 from eight foreign entities without obtaining prior permission from the Central Government, in violation of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976. Arvind Khanna's defense was that the funds received were gifts from his father, Mr. Vipin Khanna, who is an Indian passport holder, and that the foreign entities through whom the funds were sent were holding the funds on behalf of his father. The High Court of Delhi quashed the FIR and charge sheet, stating that the material on record was not sufficient to frame a charge against Arvind Khanna, and provided liberty to the Central Government to compound the case under Section 41(1) of the FCRA, 2010. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. by recording findings on disputed facts and allowing the petition based on the defense put forth by Arvind Khanna. The Supreme Court set aside the Revisional Court's order dated 20th August 2011, which had taken cognizance under the FCRA, 1976, and remitted the matter back to the Revisional Court for fresh consideration after issuing notice to Arvind Khanna. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the trial court to proceed with the case from the stage it was stopped, uninfluenced by the findings and observations made by the High Court. The ruling could lead to more stringent scrutiny of defenses based on the source of foreign contributions and ensure that courts exercise their jurisdiction appropriately, especially in cases involving violations of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act. The ruling emphasizes the importance of lower courts adhering to procedural norms and refraining from making detailed factual assessments during preliminary stages, which may affect the handling of foreign contribution cases by ensuring proper legal processes are followed. The Supreme Court clarified that the High Court should not exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to make detailed factual assessments or preempt the trial court's jurisdiction, emphasizing the need for proper judicial restraint. The Supreme Court directed the Revisional Court to issue notice to Arvind Khanna and conduct a fresh hearing, providing him an opportunity to be heard before making any further decisions.

case_name: Central Bureau of Investigation vs P.S. Jayaprakash & Ors.
text: Case: Central Bureau of Investigation vs P.S. Jayaprakash & Ors.. Date: 2nd December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting anticipatory bail to the respondents, who were accused of multiple offences, including conspiracy, under the IPC. The respondents were accused of offences punishable under Sections 120B, 167, 218, 330, 323, 195, 348, 365, 477A, and 506 of the IPC. The High Court granted anticipatory bail to the respondents, who were all officials of the Kerala Police or the Intelligence Bureau at the relevant time. The High Court granted anticipatory bail primarily on the grounds that the FIR was filed after a significant delay and did not consider the individual roles of the accused. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not adequately consider the allegations, the roles played by the accused, or the recommendations of the D.K. Jain Committee. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's orders granting anticipatory bail and remitted the matters back to the High Court for fresh consideration. The D.K. Jain Committee, headed by a former judge of the Supreme Court, was tasked with recommending appropriate actions against the erring officials involved in the 1994 espionage case against ISRO scientist S. Nambi Narayanan. The Supreme Court noted that the delay in filing the FIR was due to the recommendations made by the D.K. Jain Committee and the directions of the Supreme Court, not due to any lapse on the part of the CBI. The Supreme Court directed that the respondents should not be arrested for five weeks or until the High Court decides their anticipatory bail applications, provided they cooperate with the investigation. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider the anticipatory bail applications afresh, strictly in accordance with law and on their own merits, without being influenced by the interim arrangement.

case_name: Central Bureau of Investigation vs. M. Sivamani
text: Case: Central Bureau of Investigation vs. M. Sivamani. Date: 1st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the proceedings against M. Sivamani based on a bar under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC. The investigation was initiated after allegations that the claim for compensation in a motor accident case was false, leading to a direction by the Madras High Court to the CBCID and later to the CBI to investigate the matter. The charges included Sections 120-B r/w 182, 420, 468, 468 r/w 471 IPC and 13(2) r/w 13(i)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 r/w 511 IPC. M. Sivamani, an advocate, was accused of misrepresentation and producing false evidence, knowing the true facts of the incident. The respondent moved the petition pleading a bar under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC, arguing that cognizance of the offense under Section 182 IPC could not be taken except on a complaint in writing from the concerned public servant. The High Court quashed the proceedings, holding that a written complaint from the competent authority was essential, which was not fulfilled in this case. The CBI argued that the High Court's direction to investigate the matter by itself should be seen as fulfilling the requirement of a complaint by a public servant, given the public interest involved. The Supreme Court interpreted that the bar is to prevent frivolous or vexatious proceedings by private parties, and it should not apply when the investigation is directed by the High Court in public interest. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, allowing the CBI's appeal and directing that the proceedings be concluded within six months. The Supreme Court reasoned that the direction by the High Court to the CBI to investigate should be treated as equivalent to a written complaint by a public servant, thus bypassing the bar under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC. This judgment clarifies that the bar under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC does not apply when an investigation is initiated at the direction of a High Court, emphasizing the need to prevent misuse of the provision to hinder justice.

case_name: Central Bureau of Investigation vs. Mrs. Pramila Virendra Kumar Agarwal & Anr.
text: Case: Central Bureau of Investigation vs. Mrs. Pramila Virendra Kumar Agarwal & Anr.. Date: 25th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. They were charged under Section 13(1)(e) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and Section 109 of the IPC for accumulating disproportionate assets to their known sources of income. The High Court allowed the criminal revision application of accused No. 2 (Mrs. Pramila Virendra Kumar Agarwal) and discharged her, while dismissing the criminal revision application filed by the CBI against the discharge of accused No. 1 (Mr. Virendra Kumar Agarwal). The High Court discharged her on the grounds that the Investigating Officer did not provide an opportunity for the accused to explain the disproportionate assets and that the sanction for prosecution was defective. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court's conclusion regarding the defective sanction for prosecution was premature and that such matters should be considered during the trial. The Supreme Court held that the explanation of disproportionate assets should be considered during the trial, not at the discharge stage. The trial court should evaluate the evidence presented to establish whether the assets were indeed disproportionate. The charge sheet detailed the assets as follows: Beginning of the check period assets valued at Rs. 1,30,000; end of the check period assets valued at Rs. 1,34,45,426; total assets found during the check period at Rs. 1,33,15,426; total income during the check period at Rs. 51,02,106; total expenditure at Rs. 24,75,874; likely savings at Rs. 26,26,232; resulting in disproportionate assets of Rs. 1,06,89,194. The Supreme Court noted that clubbing the assets of both accused (husband and wife) was not justified if they had independent sources of income. This aspect should be thoroughly examined during the trial. The Supreme Court indicated that the issue of the validity of the sanction for prosecution could only be fully addressed during the trial. It emphasized that the presence of a sanction, even if allegedly defective, required a detailed examination in the trial court. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and the Special Court's order, restoring the proceedings in Special Case No. 21 of 2010 to the file of the Special Court. It directed that all contentions on merits be left open for consideration during the trial. The Supreme Court reiterated that the consideration of evidence and charges should be thorough and detailed, with all explanations and defenses evaluated during the trial. The process should ensure that justice is served based on the merits of the case.

case_name: Central Coalfields Limited vs. Smt. Parden Oraon
text: Case: Central Coalfields Limited vs. Smt. Parden Oraon. Date: 9th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the rejection of the request for compassionate appointment of Smt. Parden Oraon's son, following the disappearance and presumed civil death of her husband, who was an employee of Central Coalfields Limited. Smt. Parden Oraon's husband, an Operator Helper at Gidi Washery, went missing on 3rd October 2002. After obtaining a civil death decree in 2012, she sought compassionate appointment for her son in January 2013, which was rejected by Central Coalfields Limited. The High Court of Jharkhand allowed the writ petition, quashed the termination order of the respondent's husband, and directed Central Coalfields Limited to consider the claim for compassionate appointment of her son. Central Coalfields Limited rejected the request citing that the respondent's husband was already dismissed from service and that the policy decision made in 2013 stated that compassionate appointments could not be provided to dependents of missing employees. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by Central Coalfields Limited, setting aside the High Court's judgment, and concluded that the respondent's son could not be given compassionate appointment due to the significant lapse of time since the respondent's husband went missing. The Supreme Court found that the National Coal Wage Agreement did not contain any clause preventing compassionate appointment in cases of civil death or dual employment within the family. However, the court ultimately ruled against the appointment due to the long delay since the disappearance of the respondent's husband.

case_name: Centrum Financial Services Limited vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
text: Case: Centrum Financial Services Limited vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.. Date: 28th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused, Jayant Kumar Jain, in connection with FIR No. 128 of 2019 for offences under Sections 409, 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120B IPC. The parties involved were Centrum Financial Services Limited (appellant), State of NCT of Delhi (respondent), and Jayant Kumar Jain (respondent No. 2). Jayant Kumar Jain was charged with offences under Sections 409, 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120B IPC for misappropriating funds and siphoning off Rs. 25 crores through shell companies. Centrum Financial Services Limited, a non-banking financial company (NBFC), lodged an FIR against M/s Sri Aranath Logistics Limited and its Managing Director, Jayant Kumar Jain, alleging misappropriation of a loan amount of Rs. 25 crores, which was diverted to fake/shell companies instead of being used for the intended business purposes. The High Court allowed the bail application of Jayant Kumar Jain, directing his release on bail, primarily on the grounds that the case arose out of a commercial transaction and was based on documents already seized. The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court failed to consider the serious nature of the allegations, the modus operandi of siphoning off funds through shell companies, and the evidence collected during the investigation which indicated a systematic fraud. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's reasoning was insufficient and mechanical, as it did not consider the nature of the accusations, the material collected during the investigation, and the serious allegations of siphoning off funds through shell companies. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order granting bail to Jayant Kumar Jain and directed him to surrender before the concerned court/jail authority forthwith. The Supreme Court stated that after surrender, it would be open for Jayant Kumar Jain to move an appropriate application for bail before the High Court afresh after a period of three months, which shall be considered by the High Court on its own merits and in accordance with law. The Supreme Court discussed the principles of granting and canceling bail, emphasizing that the High Court must exercise its discretion judiciously, considering the nature and gravity of the accusations and the material evidence collected during the investigation.

case_name: Chairman and Managing Director FCI and Ors vs. Jagdish Balaram Bahira and Ors
text: Case: Chairman and Managing Director FCI and Ors vs. Jagdish Balaram Bahira and Ors. Date: 6th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue addressed was whether individuals who had falsely claimed to belong to a Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe, or other backward class were entitled to retain the benefits of public employment or admission obtained on the basis of such claims, even after their claims had been invalidated. The Supreme Court emphasized that the constitutional policy of reservations aims to redress social exclusion, economic deprivation, and political alienation of historically disadvantaged classes, ensuring that only genuine beneficiaries receive these benefits. The Court noted that the capture of affirmative action benefits by individuals who do not genuinely belong to the beneficiary groups constitutes a serious fraud on the Constitution, depriving genuine beneficiaries of their legitimate entitlements. The Court examined whether equities that arise due to the passage of time could be protected under judicial review. However, the Court ultimately emphasized that fraudulent claims cannot be sustained, regardless of the passage of time. The State of Maharashtra enacted the Maharashtra Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, De-Notified Tribes (Vimukta Jatis), Nomadic Tribes, Other Backward Classes and Special Backward Category (Regulation of Issuance and Verification of) Caste Certificate Act, 2000, which established procedures for obtaining and verifying caste certificates and imposed penalties for false claims. case_name: Chairman-Cum-Managing Director ONGC Ltd. & Ors. vs. Consumer Education Research Society & Ors.
text: Case: Chairman-Cum-Managing Director ONGC Ltd. & Ors. vs. Consumer Education Research Society & Ors.. Date: 9th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether there is a relationship of consumer and service provider between the employees of ONGC who are part of the Self Contributory, Post Retirement and Death in Service Benefits Scheme, 1991, and ONGC. The NCDRC held that the employees of ONGC who were part of the Scheme were consumers of ONGC, and awarded various amounts and costs in favor of the claimants. The Supreme Court concluded that there is no consumer-service provider relationship between the employees and ONGC because the Scheme is managed and run by a Trust and not by ONGC, and any service rendered is by the Trust, not ONGC. The Scheme required contributions from the employees based on their salary and age, and was managed by a Trust consisting of trustees nominated by the Chairman of ONGC and representatives from the Association of Scientific and Technical Officers (ASTO). The Supreme Court set aside the costs imposed by the NCDRC but directed ONGC to pay the amounts payable (excluding costs) under the impugned orders to the claimants within 8 weeks. The Supreme Court directed ONGC to pay the amounts payable under the orders of the NCDRC to the claimants within 8 weeks, excluding the costs that were set aside.

case_name: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
text: Case: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.. Date: 2nd March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the rollback of the retirement age from 60 to 58 years by the appellant, ITI Limited, was valid and whether clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders conferred any right on employees to continue in service till the age of 60 years. The High Court of Karnataka held that the rollback of the retirement age from 60 to 58 years was valid but stated that the rollback should not affect the existing rights recognized under clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders. The Supreme Court held that clause 17(7)(iii) is an enabling provision that allows the appellant to continue an employee in service up to the age of 60 years, subject to medical fitness, but it does not confer any right on employees to seek continuation as a matter of right. ITI Limited cited financial losses and recommendations from a consultant, M/s. Price Waterhouse Coopers, to reduce manpower costs as reasons for rolling back the retirement age from 60 to 58 years. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's judgment by clarifying that clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders does not confer any right on employees to seek continuation in service till the age of 60 years, and the clause only provides discretionary power to the appellant. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, upholding the validity of the rollback of the retirement age and clarifying the interpretation of clause 17(7)(iii) while dismissing any claims for continuation of employment based on this clause.
