case_name: Chaitra Nagammanavar vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.
text: Case: Chaitra Nagammanavar vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.. Date: 2nd May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appointment of Chaitra Nagammanavar as an Assistant Professor was valid, given that the university had specified that the selection would be based on the Karnataka State Civil Services (Unfilled Vacancies Reserved for SCs and STs) Rules, 2001, which gives preference to candidates within the age bracket of 29-40 years. Her appointment was challenged because she was selected based on merit, whereas another candidate, Respondent No. 7, who was within the preferred age bracket of 29-40 years as per the 2001 Rules, was not selected. The Single Judge of the High Court set aside Chaitra Nagammanavar's appointment and directed that Respondent No. 7, who was within the preferred age bracket as per the 2001 Rules, be appointed instead. The Division Bench confirmed the order of the Single Judge, upholding that Respondent No. 7 should be appointed in accordance with the 2001 Rules, and dismissed the appeals filed by Chaitra Nagammanavar and the university. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, agreeing with the High Court's decision that the university must follow the 2001 Rules for the appointment, thereby directing that Respondent No. 7 should be appointed instead of Chaitra Nagammanavar. The Supreme Court suggested that the university consider creating a supernumerary post to accommodate Chaitra Nagammanavar, due to the extraordinary situation where she continued in office during the subsistence of the writ proceedings and subsequent appeals.

case_name: Chaitu Lal vs. State of Uttarakhand
text: Case: Chaitu Lal vs. State of Uttarakhand. Date: 20th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Chaitu Lal was charged with offences under Section 354 IPC (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty) and Section 511 read with Section 376 IPC (attempt to commit rape). On 12th January 1991, Chaitu Lal, in a drunken state, entered the house of the complainant-victim, who is his aunt, and attempted to molest her by lifting her petticoat and trying to commit rape. The incident was witnessed by the complainant's daughter and other villagers who intervened. The Sessions Judge convicted Chaitu Lal under Section 354 IPC, sentencing him to one year of rigorous imprisonment, and under Section 511 read with Section 376 IPC, sentencing him to two years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 200. The High Court dismissed Chaitu Lal's appeal and upheld the conviction and sentences passed by the Sessions Judge. Chaitu Lal argued that he was framed by the complainant-victim due to existing enmity, the FIR was delayed by three days, and there was insufficient evidence to prove the offence under Section 511 read with Section 376 IPC. The Supreme Court noted that the delay in filing the FIR was justified as the complainant first traveled to meet her husband in Nandprayag and then traveled to Chamoli to register the complaint. The delay did not adversely affect the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the convictions and sentences imposed by the lower courts, concluding that the guilt of Chaitu Lal had been established beyond reasonable doubt.

case_name: Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi vs. State Rep. by Inspector of Police
text: Case: Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi vs. State Rep. by Inspector of Police. Date: 24th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi was charged with the offense under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Ramamurthy. The trial court convicted Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The High Court upheld the trial court's conviction and sentence of life imprisonment for Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi under Section 302 IPC. The main evidence against Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi was the extra-judicial confession recorded by the Tahsildar, Salem (P.W.12), and the recovery of the Maruti van, weapon, and blood-stained clothes based on his confession. The Supreme Court found the extra-judicial confession to be suspicious and unreliable, noting that it was unusually detailed and seemed to be crafted to support the prosecution's case. The High Court disbelieved the circumstances of motive, abduction by the accused, conspiracy, and recovery of articles, relying solely on the extra-judicial confession. The Supreme Court observed that key witnesses, including P.W.8 and P.W.11, had turned hostile, and the prosecution failed to provide reliable matching of blood groups for the recovered material objects, further weakening the case against Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi. The Supreme Court concluded that it would be unsafe to convict Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi and award life imprisonment based solely on the extra-judicial confession, given that all other circumstances remained unproved. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment convicting Chakarai @ Chakaravarthi, acquitted him of all charges, and ordered his immediate release if he was not required in any other case. The Supreme Court highlighted that extra-judicial confessions should be treated with caution and must be corroborated by other reliable evidence, especially when they form the sole basis for conviction.

case_name: Champa Lal Dhakar vs. Naval Singh Rajput & Ors.
text: Case: Champa Lal Dhakar vs. Naval Singh Rajput & Ors.. Date: 4th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the charges framed under Section 307 IPC against the respondents by the trial court and directing the trial court to reconsider its order. The trial court framed charges against the accused under Sections 147, 148, 451, 325/149, 307/149, 294/149, and 506/149 of the IPC. The High Court quashed the charge under Section 307 IPC because it found that no case was made out for an attempt to murder based on the injuries sustained by the complainant, which were not life-threatening. The complainant sustained injuries on the nose, including a fracture of the nasal bone. The High Court directed the trial court to reconsider its order regarding the framing of charges and to take further steps in accordance with the law, suggesting that a charge under Section 325/149 IPC should have been framed instead. The appellant argued that the High Court committed a manifest error in quashing the charge under Section 307 IPC, asserting that the accused intended to commit murder as evidenced by the attack by 17 to 18 persons. The Supreme Court observed that, based on the evidence and the medical certificate, it could not be said that the accused had the intention to cause the death of the complainant, thus agreeing with the High Court's decision to quash the charge under Section 307 IPC. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court did not commit any error in setting aside the order of the trial court framing the charge under Section 307 IPC, and thus, upheld the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant, agreeing with the High Court's view that the case did not warrant a charge under Section 307 IPC. The legal significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it reinforced the principle that charges should be framed based on the intention and the nature of the injuries sustained, ensuring that the charges are appropriate to the evidence presented.

case_name: Chanchalpati Das vs The State of West Bengal & Anr.
text: Case: Chanchalpati Das vs The State of West Bengal & Anr.. Date: 18th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Chanchalpati Das and Madhu Pandit Das were charged under Sections 468, 471, 406, and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for forgery, using forged documents, criminal breach of trust, and criminal conspiracy. The incident involved the alleged theft and illegal transfer of a 42-seat deluxe bus from ISKCON Kolkata to ISKCON Bengaluru without proper authorization. The High Court dismissed both criminal revision applications, refusing to quash the charge-sheet filed against the appellants. The appellants argued that the prosecution was an attempt to harass them, there was no substantial evidence to support the charges, and the complaint was filed after an inordinate delay of eight years. The Supreme Court noted that the inordinate delay of eight years in filing the complaint was unexplained and suggested misuse and abuse of the process of law to settle personal scores. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings pending against the appellants in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Alipore, and directed the respondent-complainant to pay a cost of Rs. 1,00,000. The Supreme Court emphasized that frivolous and malicious litigations should be discouraged to prevent abuse of the judicial process and to ensure that genuine cases are heard in a timely manner.

case_name: Chandan Banerjee & Ors vs. Krishna Prosad Ghosh & Ors.
text: Case: Chandan Banerjee & Ors vs. Krishna Prosad Ghosh & Ors.. Date: 21st September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the classification within the same cadre of Sub-Assistant Engineers (SAEs) for the purpose of appointment to supernumerary posts, which was claimed to violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The circular prescribed separate conditions for diploma and degree holder Sub-Assistant Engineers (SAEs) for supernumerary appointments as Assistant Engineers (AEs) and was upheld by the Division Bench of the High Court of Calcutta. The Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition, declaring the circular arbitrary and unconstitutional, and held that the classification violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Division Bench reversed the Single Judge's decision, upholding the validity of the circular and the subsequent gradation list, stating that classification on the basis of educational qualifications for supernumerary appointments was valid. KMC created supernumerary posts to rectify the stagnation faced by SAEs who had not been promoted despite having completed 20 to 25 years of service and to motivate them by providing promotional avenues. The Supreme Court upheld the Division Bench's decision, stating that the circular and gradation list did not suffer from arbitrariness and discrimination and dismissed the appeal.

case_name: Chander Bhan (D) Through LR Sher Singh vs Mukhtiar Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Chander Bhan (D) Through LR Sher Singh vs Mukhtiar Singh & Ors.. Date: 3rd May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the plaintiff-appellant was entitled to specific performance of the agreement to sell 16 kanals of land or whether the respondents were protected as bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. On 10th November 2002, the appellant and respondent no. 3 entered into an agreement to sell 16 kanals of land for a total consideration of Rs. 8 lakhs, with Rs. 2.50 lakhs paid at the time of agreement and the remaining Rs. 5.50 lakhs to be paid at the time of execution of the sale deed by 10th November 2004. The appellant filed a suit for permanent injunction to prevent respondent no. 3 from alienating the suit property after receiving information that respondent no. 3 was likely to sell the property. On 28th July 2003, respondent no. 3 executed a release deed in favor of his son, Harvinder Singh (respondent no. 4), which was followed by a mutation sanction. This action led to the subsequent sale of the land to Mukhtiar Singh and Baljeet Singh (respondent nos. 1-2) on 16th June 2004. The trial court decreed the suit in favor of the appellant, directing respondent no. 3 to accept the balance sale consideration and execute the agreement to sell. The court also noted that respondents no. 3 and 4 had refused to testify, leading to an adverse inference against them. The High Court reversed the decisions of the trial court and the first appellate court, dismissing the suit for specific performance but granting the appellant a refund of the earnest money with interest, holding that respondents no. 1 and 2 were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration. The Supreme Court held that the doctrine of lis pendens applied, as the suit for permanent injunction was filed before the execution of the release deed, making the subsequent alienation by respondent no. 3 to respondent no. 4 and then to respondents no. 1 and 2 invalid against the appellant's interest. The Supreme Court rejected the claim of respondents no. 1 and 2 of being bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration, as the transactions were executed during the pendency of the suit and were thus subject to the doctrine of lis pendens. The Supreme Court found no substantial reason for the High Court to base its decision primarily on the deposition of PW-7, emphasizing that the transactions were invalid due to the doctrine of lis pendens, regardless of the knowledge of the injunction order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and upheld the decree in favor of the appellant. The court directed respondent no. 3 to accept the balance sale consideration and execute the sale deed in favor of the appellant within three months. The Supreme Court reinforced that the doctrine of lis pendens aims to maintain the status quo during litigation and prevent actions by any party that could affect the subject matter of the suit, thereby upholding equity and justice.

case_name: Chandrika (Dead) by LRs. vs. Sudama (Dead) Thr. LRs. & Ors.
text: Case: Chandrika (Dead) by LRs. vs. Sudama (Dead) Thr. LRs. & Ors.. Date: 15th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the name of Rajbali, the appellant's predecessor-in-title, was rightly entered in the revenue records for the disputed land despite lacking any right, title, or interest. The Revenue Authorities concluded that Rajbali's name could not have been entered in the revenue records due to the lack of any right, title, or interest in the land, and directed it to be deleted. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by Chandrika, thereby affirming the orders of the Consolidation Officer, Settlement Officer Consolidation, and Deputy Director of Consolidation. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on the grounds that the findings of the Revenue Authorities and the High Court were based on proper appreciation of evidence, consistent with the revenue entries, and supported by reasons. The Supreme Court stated that the concurrent findings of fact by the Revenue Authorities and the High Court were binding and called for no interference. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no merit in the arguments presented by the appellants' counsel and upholding the previous decisions.

case_name: Chattar Singh & Ors. vs. Madho Singh (D) & Ors.
text: Case: Chattar Singh & Ors. vs. Madho Singh (D) & Ors.. Date: 6th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the land recorded as 'Charnoi' (common land for grazing cattle) vested in the State on the abolition of intermediaries on 2nd October 1951 or was saved from vesting in favor of the proprietor as a grove under Section 5(f) of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Zamindari Act. The Board of Revenue, in its order dated 2nd December 1959, set aside the orders of the Tehsildar, Sub-Divisional Officer, and Additional Commissioner, and held that Kalusingh, the ex-zamindar, was entitled to get the land in his name as Bhumiswami under Section 5(f) of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act. The High Court reversed the findings of the First Appellate Court, holding that the land was recorded as Charnoi land and therefore vested in the State. The Court relied on khasra entries, which showed the land as Charnoi and included an admission that the villagers had been grazing their cattle on the land. The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 4 of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act caused all land, including Charnoi land, to vest in the State. Section 5(f) did not confer rights on the ex-zamindar over common land recorded as Charnoi, as such land was reserved for public purposes like grazing cattle and could not be claimed as a grove. The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' claim that the land was a grove, stating that the land was primarily used for grazing cattle and therefore classified as Charnoi. The Court emphasized that common land for public purposes vested in the State and could not be retained by the ex-zamindar or his legal representatives. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's judgment that the Charnoi land vested in the State and rejecting the appellants' claim that it was a grove. The Court found no merit in the appellants' arguments and affirmed the correctness of the High Court's decision.

case_name: Chherturam @ Chainu vs. State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Chherturam @ Chainu vs. State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 13th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the conviction of Chherturam @ Chainu under Section 302 of the IPC for the murder of his father was justified or if it should be considered under Section 304 Part-I of the IPC due to lack of premeditation and sudden quarrel. On the night of 26th and 27th July 2010, Chherturam @ Chainu, under the influence of alcohol, had a quarrel with his father Goienda. In the presence of their neighbor Chamruram (PW-8) and his brother (PW-4), Chherturam assaulted his father with a piece of Nagar Wood, leading to his father's death. The post-mortem examination revealed multiple injuries caused by a hard and blunt object, resulting in hemorrhagic shock. The injuries included several contusions and fractures, indicating a brutal assault. The Additional Sessions Judge convicted Chherturam @ Chainu under Section 302 IPC for murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 1,000, and an additional four months of rigorous imprisonment in default of payment. The High Court dismissed Chherturam @ Chainu's appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence given by the Additional Sessions Judge. Chherturam @ Chainu's counsel argued that the incident occurred during a sudden quarrel under the influence of alcohol without premeditation, and thus should be considered under Section 304 Part-I IPC instead of Section 302 IPC. The Supreme Court concluded that the nature and brutality of the injuries inflicted by Chherturam @ Chainu did not warrant application of Exception 4 of Section 300 IPC. Therefore, the conviction under Section 302 IPC was upheld, but the Court directed the State to consider his case for remission after completing the mandatory sentence period.

case_name: Chhote Lal vs. Rohtash & Ors.
text: Case: Chhote Lal vs. Rohtash & Ors.. Date: 14th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The accused were charged with offences under Sections 148, 201/149, and 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code, with the maximum punishment being life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000, in default of which they would undergo further imprisonment of six months. On 4th November 2000, Kishan Sarup was returning from duty with the complainant when they were attacked by the accused who chased them with a car, assaulted Kishan Sarup with knives and iron rods, and then took him away in their car. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the accused, leading to their acquittal. The appellant argued that the appellate court should be slow in upsetting the conviction, especially in light of the evidence on record, particularly the testimony of the eyewitness (complainant). The Supreme Court found that the sole eyewitness (complainant) did not see anyone killing or burning the victim, and his presence during the incident appeared doubtful. His testimony alone was not sufficient to uphold the conviction. The Supreme Court noted discrepancies such as the complainant not intervening to save his son, the absence of injuries on the complainant, and inconsistencies regarding the use of weapons and the presence of the eyewitness during the incident. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to acquit the accused, stating that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, both through circumstantial evidence and the testimony of the eyewitness.

case_name: Chowgule and Company Private Limited vs. Goa Foundation & Ors.
text: Case: Chowgule and Company Private Limited vs. Goa Foundation & Ors.. Date: 30th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The legal proceedings were triggered by the rampant exploitation of natural resources in the Iron Ore mining sector in the State of Goa, which led to the appointment of Justice M.B. Shah as a Commission of Inquiry. His reports resulted in the suspension of all mining operations in Goa and the revocation of environmental clearances for 137 mines. In Goa Foundation-I, the Supreme Court held that all iron ore and manganese ore leases had expired on 22nd November 2007, and any mining operations carried out after that date were illegal. The Court ruled that mining lease renewals required a second express order from the State Government and must be in the interest of mineral development. In Goa Foundation-II, the Supreme Court concluded that the State of Goa was obliged to grant fresh mining leases, not second renewals, and that the Ministry of Environment and Forests needed to issue fresh environmental clearances. The second renewals of mining leases were quashed for being hasty and not in the interest of mineral development. The mining leaseholders contended that the Supreme Court's order did not restrict the transportation of minerals already mined before 15th March 2018. They argued that the prohibition was only on mining operations after that date, not on the transportation of previously mined ore. The State of Goa decided to permit the transportation of minerals mined before 15th March 2018, provided that the royalty was paid. This decision was challenged by Goa Foundation, leading to an interim order from the High Court suspending all transportation of minerals. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and upheld the State of Goa's decision to permit the transportation of minerals mined before 15th March 2018. The Court directed that all transportation must be completed within six months and that the State ensure only royalty-paid minerals are transported.

case_name: Citizens for Green Doon & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Citizens for Green Doon & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 14th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary project involved was the Chardham Mahamarg Vikas Pariyojna, aimed at improving connectivity to pilgrimage sites in Uttarakhand by widening roads. The main environmental concern was the potential harm to the fragile Himalayan ecosystem, including deforestation, landslides, and ecological degradation. The Supreme Court upheld the implementation of the 2018 MoRTH Circular, requiring adherence to Intermediate Lane Width standards for environmentally sensitive areas. The Union of India argued that wider roads with the DL-PS standard were necessary for national security to facilitate swift troop and equipment movement to border areas. The Court directed compensatory afforestation at a ratio of ten trees planted for every tree cut, with monitoring to ensure survival and growth of the saplings.

case_name: Commanding Officer, Railway Protection Special Force, Mumbai vs Bhvanaben Dinshbhai Bhabhor & Others
text: Case: Commanding Officer, Railway Protection Special Force, Mumbai vs Bhvanaben Dinshbhai Bhabhor & Others. Date: 26th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Commissioner awarded Rs. 4,33,820 along with 9% interest, payable within 30 days of the order, for the accidental death of the constable during employment. The appellant argued that under Section 2(1)(n) of the 1923 Act, a member of the Armed Forces of the Union is excluded from the definition of a 'workman,' and as RPF is declared an Armed Force, the claim was not maintainable. The Supreme Court stated that declaring the RPF as an Armed Force of the Union did not intend to exclude its members from the benefits of the Employees Compensation Act, as they are deemed railway servants under the Railways Act, 1989. The Supreme Court held that the provisions of the Employees Compensation Act, 1923, apply to RPF members, as they are considered railway servants and not explicitly excluded by the Act. The judgement affirms that RPF members are entitled to compensation under the Employees Compensation Act, 1923, providing clarity on their eligibility despite being declared part of the Armed Forces.

case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax, Noida vs. M/S. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax, Noida vs. M/S. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 10th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the assessable value of imported aluminum scrap declared by the respondent, which was rejected by the Assessing Officer leading to a reassessment with an increased value. The Assessing Officer found the declared transaction value to be low and reassessed the value by considering the grades of aluminum scrap and the quantum of other metals present. The CESTAT allowed the respondent's appeal, rejecting the enhancement of the assessable value by the Revenue and restoring the assessable value as declared by the respondent in the Bills of Entry. The Tribunal found that the Assessing Officer did not properly examine the evidence available with the department for enhancing the assessable value and failed to establish that the price was not the sole consideration of the transaction value. The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's decision, agreeing that the declared transaction value should be accepted unless cogent reasons are provided to reject it, and that the Assessing Officer failed to provide such reasons. The Supreme Court emphasized that the assessable value must be based on the price actually paid or payable for the goods, as per Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, and that the declared transaction value can only be rejected with valid reasons and evidence. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue and upheld the Tribunal's decision, thereby accepting the assessable value declared by M/S. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading Pvt. Ltd.

case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise, Haldia vs. M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd.
text: Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Haldia vs. M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd.. Date: 14th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves the Commissioner of Central Excise, Haldia accusing M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd. of manufacturing and clearing products like Foots Oil, Pressed Wax, and Pressed Paraffin Wax without paying excise duty, and the subsequent legal dispute over whether these activities constituted 'manufacture' under the Central Excise Act, 1944. On 23rd September 2005, a search was conducted at the registered office and factory premises of M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd. by the Central Excise officers, leading to a Show Cause Notice being issued on 21st March 2006, demanding unpaid excise duty and alleging that the company was manufacturing goods without following due procedure. The CESTAT dismissed the appeal on 31st May 2017, concluding that the process undertaken by M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd. did not amount to 'manufacture' under the Central Excise Act, 1944, and thus, no excise duty was payable. The High Court directed the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise to decide on the preliminary objection regarding jurisdiction before addressing the merits of the case. The Assistant Commissioner concluded that the matter could proceed under the Central Excise Act. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by the Commissioner of Central Excise, set aside the orders of the Appellate Authority and the CESTAT, and directed that the proceedings pursuant to the Show Cause Notice dated 21st March 2006 be taken to a logical conclusion. M/s. Krishna Wax (P) Ltd. was given three weeks to respond to the Show Cause Notice. The Supreme Court set aside the orders because it found that the appellate proceedings were premature, as the issue of whether the process amounted to 'manufacture' under the Central Excise Act had not been properly adjudicated following the Show Cause Notice. The Court emphasized that such determinations should occur after allowing the concerned party to respond to the notice.

case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise, Indore vs M/S Grasim Industries Ltd.
text: Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Indore vs M/S Grasim Industries Ltd.. Date: 11th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the various charges realized by the Assessees, such as packing charges, wear and tear charges, facility charges, service charges, delivery and collection charges, rental charges, repair and testing charges, should be included in the assessable value for the purpose of levy of excise duty under Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Commissioner of Central Excise argued that these charges should be included in the assessable value as they contribute to the value of the excisable goods and are essential for their marketability. The Supreme Court held that packing charges should be included in the assessable value as they are necessary to make the goods marketable. The Supreme Court decided that charges for wear and tear, facility, and service should be included in the assessable value as they are incurred in relation to the manufacture and marketability of the goods. The court addressed that delivery and collection charges, being related to the post-manufacturing stage, should still be included in the assessable value if they are necessary to place the goods in the hands of the customer. The Supreme Court's stance was that rental, repair, and testing charges should be included in the assessable value as they contribute to the value addition of the excisable goods. The Supreme Court emphasized the principle that the value for excise duty should reflect the price at which the goods are sold in the course of wholesale trade and must include all elements that enhance the value of the goods. The final decision of the Supreme Court was that all charges realized by the Assessees, which contribute to making the goods marketable and are part of the transaction value, should be included in the assessable value for the purpose of levy of excise duty.

case_name: Commissioner of Central Excise, Raipur vs M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation
text: Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Raipur vs M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation is liable to pay service tax on the services rendered as 'Consulting Engineer Services' to M/s Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. (BALCO) during the period from August 2003 to November 2005. M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation provided 'Design Engineering Services' and 'Project Management & Technical Services' under a contract dated 26th April 2003. The Commissioner of Central Excise, Raipur issued a show cause notice demanding service tax, interest, and penalties because M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation allegedly did not pay service tax on the services rendered and did not obtain Service Tax Registration. The total service tax demand confirmed was Rs. 10,42,71,437/- along with interest, and penalties under Sections 76, 77, and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994. The CESTAT set aside the service tax demand by holding that during the relevant period of dispute, the respondent, being a body corporate, was not covered under the definition of 'Consulting Engineer'. The key argument is that the definition of 'Consulting Engineer' under Section 65 (31) of the Finance Act, 1994, should include a body corporate, and the CESTAT's interpretation excluding the body corporate is incorrect. The Commissioner cited the Karnataka High Court's decision in Tata Consultancy Services v. Union of India and the Calcutta High Court's decision in M.N. Dastur Limited v. Union of India, which held that companies providing engineering services are liable to pay service tax. M/s Sepco Electric Power Construction Corporation filed an appeal with the CESTAT, challenging the service tax demand and penalties imposed by the Commissioner of Central Excise, Raipur. The decision could clarify whether a body corporate providing consulting engineer services is liable for service tax, impacting similar cases and providing a precedent for future disputes. The Commissioner might need to issue clear guidelines and notifications specifying that bodies corporate are included in the definition of 'Consulting Engineer' to ensure compliance and prevent similar disputes. The Supreme Court found it problematic because excluding a body corporate from the definition creates an unjustifiable distinction and goes against the legislative intent of taxing all entities providing engineering services.

case_name: Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai vs. M/S Ganpati Overseas
text: Case: Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai vs. M/S Ganpati Overseas. Date: 6th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether the Customs, Excise, and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) was justified in holding that the enhancement of the value of imported goods and the penalties imposed by the Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication-1), Mumbai on the respondents could not be sustained and consequently setting aside the same. The show cause notice was issued by the Additional Director General, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, New Delhi, based on secret information that M/S Ganpati Overseas had imported tuners from Hong Kong at grossly under-invoiced prices, thereby evading huge customs duty. Mr. Suresh Chandra Sharma admitted that the rate of tuners per piece as shown in the invoices by M/S Arise Enterprises did not reflect the actual price and had deliberately mentioned a lower price with the intention of saving customs duty. Mr. Yashpal Sharma confirmed the factum of importing goods at prices much lower than the actual price to evade customs duty. The investigation revealed that M/S Ganpati Overseas had imported twenty consignments during 1997-98 and 1998-99 at under-invoiced prices, resulting in evasion of customs duty amounting to approximately twenty-five to thirty lakhs rupees. The CESTAT set aside the enhancement of the value of the imported goods and the penalties imposed by the Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication-1), Mumbai, finding that the initial export declarations could not form the basis for enhancing the value of the goods. The respondents contended that the statements made under Section 108 of the Customs Act were obtained through coercion and duress, and thus, were not voluntary. The second set of export declarations filed by the foreign supplier showed the price of goods matching the price declared in the import invoices, which was accepted by the Hong Kong customs authority with the imposition of a penalty. This undermined the basis of the initial export declarations used to enhance the value of the goods. The CESTAT rejected the initial export declarations because they were unattested photocopies and the foreign supplier had filed a second set of declarations with corrected prices that matched the import invoices, which were accepted by the Hong Kong customs authority. case_name: Commissioner of Customs vs. M/S. Atul Automations Pvt. Ltd. and Others
text: Case: Commissioner of Customs vs. M/S. Atul Automations Pvt. Ltd. and Others. Date: 24th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the import of Multi-Function Devices (MFDs) by the respondents was in violation of the Foreign Trade Policy and the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016. The Commissioner of Customs held that the imports were in violation of the Foreign Trade Policy as they were made without the necessary prior authorization and classified the MFDs as 'other wastes' under the Waste Management Rules, imposing a redemption fine and ordering the consignment for re-export. The Tribunal ruled that the MFDs did not constitute 'waste' under the Waste Management Rules as they had a utility life of 5 to 7 years. It directed the release of the consignment under Section 125 of the Customs Act, reducing the redemption fine and penalties. The High Court held that the MFDs correctly fell in the category of 'other wastes' under the Waste Management Rules and could be imported with restrictions, requiring necessary authorizations. The Supreme Court concluded that Section 125 of the Customs Act vests discretion in the authority to levy fine in lieu of confiscation and that this discretion should be harmoniously read with the Foreign Trade Act, permitting the redemption of restricted goods imported without authorization upon payment of the market value. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court and Tribunal's orders for the release of the MFDs on payment of the market value and penalties, while directing the respondents to deposit a bond without sureties for 90% of the enhanced valuation of the goods.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata vs. Batanagar Education and Research Trust
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata vs. Batanagar Education and Research Trust. Date: 2nd August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the cancellation of the registration of Batanagar Education and Research Trust under Section 12AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, due to alleged misuse of the status conferred by the registration. The cancellation was based on findings from a survey conducted on the Trust, which indicated that a major part of the donations received were not genuine and were in the nature of accommodation entries. The Trust was also found to be involved in returning the donations in cash through intermediaries. The ITAT found that the Trust's activities were not genuine and upheld the cancellation of its registration under Section 12AA(3) of the Income Tax Act. The Tribunal noted that the Trust was involved in money laundering and hawala activities. The High Court of Calcutta set aside the orders of the CIT and ITAT, restoring the Trust's registration. The High Court held that the Revenue failed to establish that the Trust was involved in any illegal, immoral, or irregular activities. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, restored the orders of the CIT and ITAT, and upheld the cancellation of the Trust's registration. The Supreme Court concluded that the Trust had misused its status by returning substantial donations in cash, indicating that the donations were bogus. The Supreme Court found that the Trust received donations by cheque, out of which substantial amounts were returned in cash to the donors, demonstrating that the donations were not genuine. The Court highlighted the misuse of the status conferred by Sections 12AA and 80G of the Income Tax Act.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata vs. Jagannath Gupta Family Trust
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata vs. Jagannath Gupta Family Trust. Date: 1st February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the cancellation of registration of the respondent-trust under Section 12AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, due to alleged bogus donations, was justified. The Commissioner initiated proceedings based on a survey conducted at the School of Human Genetics and Population Health (SHGPH), Kolkata, which revealed a donation entry of Rs. 37,00,000 to the respondent-trust, alleged to be bogus and involving money laundering. The Trust argued that the proceedings were contrary to natural justice as they were not given an opportunity to cross-examine the donor's representative, whose statement was used as the basis for the allegations. The ITAT set aside the cancellation order, stating that the Trust should be given an opportunity to cross-examine the donor's representative, and remanded the matter for fresh consideration. The High Court quashed the cancellation order, holding that a single alleged bogus donation was insufficient to prove that the Trust's activities were not genuine or in accordance with its objects. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, stating that the High Court's reasoning was erroneous and contrary to the plain language of Section 12AA(3) of the Income Tax Act. The case was remanded back to the Commissioner for fresh consideration. The Supreme Court directed the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata to reconsider the case on its own merits, without being influenced by the observations of the appellate authority, the High Court, or the Supreme Court in this order.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax (TDS), Kanpur & Anr. vs. Canara Bank
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax (TDS), Kanpur & Anr. vs. Canara Bank. Date: 2nd July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Canara Bank was liable to deduct tax at source on the interest paid to New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) on its fixed deposits, under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Revenue argued that NOIDA was not exempt from TDS on interest income under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as it was not a corporation established by a Central, State, or Provincial Act. The High Court of Allahabad ruled that NOIDA was exempt from TDS on interest income under Section 194A(3)(iii)(f) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as it was a corporation established by the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976. The High Court based its decision on the interpretation that NOIDA, being constituted under the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, qualified as a corporation established by a State Act, thus exempting it from TDS under Section 194A(3)(iii)(f). The Supreme Court held that the term 'established by or under an Act' includes entities that owe their existence to an Act, confirming that NOIDA, established by the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, was covered under this provision. The Supreme Court concluded that NOIDA was exempt from TDS on interest income under Section 194A(3)(iii)(f) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, affirming the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue, upholding the High Court's decision that NOIDA was exempt from TDS on interest income paid by Canara Bank.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax II vs. M/S Modipon Ltd.
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax II vs. M/S Modipon Ltd.. Date: 24th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the advance deposit of central excise duty in the Personal Ledger Account (PLA) qualifies as actual payment of duty under Section 43B of the Income Tax Act, 1961, entitling the assessee to claim a deduction. The Court considered whether the consistent practice of the assessee, accepted by the Revenue in prior years, should allow the deduction under Section 43B for the advance deposits in the disputed assessment years. The Court interpreted that Section 43B aims to ensure actual payment of taxes rather than accrual-based deductions, and the advance deposit in the PLA constitutes such payment as the amount is credited to the government and irretrievably lost to the assessee. The ruling affirmed that advance deposits for excise duty in the PLA are to be treated as actual payments, setting a precedent for similar cases and ensuring consistency in tax deductions under Section 43B. The Supreme Court clarified that PLA deposits are actual payments within the meaning of Section 43B, as they are credited to the Revenue, and the assessee loses control over the funds upon deposit.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.. Date: 24th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Inland Container Depots (ICDs) operated by Container Corporation of India Ltd. qualified for deduction under Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court of Delhi held that the ICDs operated by Container Corporation of India Ltd. were eligible for deductions under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Commissioner of Income Tax argued that the activities undertaken by the assessee did not fall within the definition of 'infrastructure facility' as per Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act and that the CBDT's notification allowing such deductions was no longer valid after the amendment in 2001. The Supreme Court ruled that ICDs could be considered 'inland ports' for the purposes of Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act, based on their function and the notifications issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that Container Corporation of India Ltd. was entitled to claim deductions under Section 80-IA for the income earned from the ICDs. The Supreme Court reasoned that the ICDs performed functions similar to those of ports, such as customs clearance, and were notified as 'infrastructure facilities' by the CBDT. Therefore, they qualified for tax deductions under Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act. The court's decision confirmed that the notifications issued by the CBDT, which classified ICDs as 'infrastructure facilities' eligible for tax deductions, remained valid and effective even after the amendments made by the Finance Act, 2001.

case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax-I vs. M/s Rashtradoot (HUF)
text: Case: Commissioner of Income Tax-I vs. M/s Rashtradoot (HUF). Date: 27th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's dismissal of the Revenue's appeal for lack of substantial questions of law was appropriate in the context of income tax proceedings initiated against the respondent based on a search operation. The income tax proceedings were initiated against M/s Rashtradoot (HUF) following a search operation conducted by the Income Tax Department on 4th September 1997, covering the block period from 1st April 1987 to 4th September 1997. The ITAT ruled in favor of the respondent (M/s Rashtradoot (HUF)), allowing their appeal against the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the Revenue's appeal, affirming the ITAT's order and ruling that the appeal did not involve any substantial questions of law. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court did not provide any reasons for dismissing the appeal and failed to frame any substantial questions of law, which are required under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the High Court, directing it to decide the appeal afresh on merits, frame substantial questions of law, and provide detailed reasoning in accordance with Section 260A of the Income Tax Act. The Supreme Court did not express any opinion on the merits of the case, stating that the High Court should decide the appeal uninfluenced by any observations made by the Supreme Court.

case_name: Committee of Management vs The Director of Higher Education & Ors.
text: Case: Committee of Management vs The Director of Higher Education & Ors.. Date: 5th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Dr. Ramesh Chandra Mishra, Dr. Ravindra Nath Mishra, and Dr. Bachau Prasad Pathak were appointed as ad hoc Lecturers at Lala Laxmi Narain Degree College, Sirsa, Allahabad. The High Court erroneously decided that the respondents were entitled to be treated as ad hoc Lecturers and directed the Directorate of Higher Education to pay them the salary of ad hoc Lecturers. The Supreme Court held that the High Court's decision was incorrect as the respondents were only appointed as part-time Lecturers and not as ad hoc Lecturers. The Supreme Court found no evidence that the respondents applied pursuant to the advertisement dated 12th January 1988. The Supreme Court stated that the respondents submitted independent applications between August 1988 and December 1989 for the post of part-time Lecturer, which were accepted by the College for a fixed period of three months on a fixed salary. The High Court directed the Directorate of Higher Education to inquire into the payment of salary to the respondents as ad hoc Lecturers and take steps for payment of outstanding salary to them, based on the assumption that they were appointed as ad hoc Lecturers. The Supreme Court concluded that there was no evidence that the respondents worked beyond April 1990 and that they had no right to be regularized as Lecturers. The respondents were only part-time Lecturers and not ad hoc Lecturers. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the Committee of Management, setting aside the High Court's order and the subsequent order passed by the Special Secretary on 8th September 1997, which had regularized the respondents' services. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in interpreting that the respondents were appointed pursuant to the advertisement dated 12th January 1988, and therefore, their claim to be treated as ad hoc Lecturers was unfounded.

case_name: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.
text: Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.. Date: 19th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The petitioners sought a writ of mandamus directing the Union of India to appoint a regular Director of CBI forthwith by following the procedure laid down in section 4A of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946. They also sought to quash the order dated 10th January 2019 appointing Mr. Nageshwar Rao as the interim Director of CBI. The petitioners alleged that Mr. Nageshwar Rao was appointed as interim Director of CBI in an arbitrary and illegal manner, bypassing the High Powered Selection Committee, and in violation of the established procedure under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946. The petitioners argued that there was a lack of transparency in the appointment process of the CBI Director. They emphasized the need for proper recording and public availability of deliberations and rational criteria for shortlisting and selection, as required under the RTI Act. The Supreme Court found that the appointment of Mr. Nageshwar Rao as interim Director of CBI was authorized by the High Powered Selection Committee through a resolution dated 9th/10th January 2019, and therefore, it was not unauthorized or illegal. The Supreme Court directed that transparency must be maintained in the process of shortlisting, selection, and appointment of the CBI Director, in line with previous directions to ensure that the process is not undermined by secrecy. The court noted that tweets made by the petitioners' counsel claimed that the minutes of the High Powered Selection Committee meeting were forged and misleading. However, the court refrained from commenting on these tweets, as the issue was part of a separate contempt petition. The court found that the petitioners had received responses to their RTI applications, informing them of the procedures and seniority criteria for the selection of the CBI Director. The court saw no grounds to interfere based on the RTI concerns raised by the petitioners. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition, finding no grounds to interfere, as the regular Director of CBI had already been appointed, satisfying the main prayer of the petitioners.

case_name: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India
text: Case: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India. Date: 9th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main contention was to declare the 'right to die with dignity' as a fundamental right within the fold of 'right to live with dignity' guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The petition sought directions for the implementation of 'Living Wills' for terminally ill patients. The petition sought directions to ensure that persons of deteriorated health or terminally ill patients could execute a document titled 'My Living Will and Attorney Authorisation' for appropriate action when admitted to a hospital with a serious illness. It also requested the appointment of a committee to issue guidelines for 'Living Wills'. It was argued that individual autonomy, including the right to die with dignity, is an inextricable facet of Article 21 of the Constitution and is also part of the fundamental conception of liberty and privacy. The Supreme Court recognized the ethical, social, and legal dilemmas faced by families and doctors in end-of-life situations, emphasizing the need for a legal framework to alleviate these issues and ensure the right to die with dignity. The Supreme Court acknowledged the potential for abuse by beneficiaries and the fears of collusion among treating physicians. It highlighted the need for stringent guidelines and oversight to prevent misuse while ensuring the patient's rights. The Supreme Court concluded that the law permits accelerating the process of dying sans suffering when life is on the path of inevitable decay, under certain circumstances, while balancing ethical, social, and legal considerations.

case_name: Competition Commission of India vs. M/s Fast Way Transmission Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Competition Commission of India vs. M/s Fast Way Transmission Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 24th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue was whether M/s Fast Way Transmission Pvt. Ltd., a group of Multi-System Operators (MSOs), abused their dominant position in the cable TV market of Punjab and Chandigarh by unlawfully terminating an agreement with a broadcaster, thus denying market access. The broadcaster alleged that M/s Fast Way Transmission Pvt. Ltd. terminated their agreement arbitrarily, resulting in a denial of market access, which violated Sections 3 and 4 of the Competition Act, 2002. The Competition Commission of India investigated the complaint, found a violation of Section 4(2)(c) of the Competition Act due to abuse of dominant position, and imposed a penalty of Rs. 8,40,01,141 on M/s Fast Way Transmission Pvt. Ltd. The Appellate Tribunal overturned the penalty imposed by the Competition Commission, stating that there was no violation of Sections 3 or 4 since the broadcaster was not in direct competition with the MSOs. The interpretive issue was whether the denial of market access under Section 4(2)(c) of the Competition Act applied only between direct competitors or could extend to situations involving dominant entities and their dependencies.

case_name: Council of Architecture vs. Mr. Mukesh Goyal & Ors
text: Case: Council of Architecture vs. Mr. Mukesh Goyal & Ors. Date: 17th March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal question was whether Section 37 of the Architects Act 1972 merely prohibits the use of the title 'Architect' by individuals not registered with the Council of Architecture or if it also prohibits unregistered individuals from practicing architecture and its cognate activities. The appellant is the Council of Architecture. The first respondent, Mr. Mukesh Goyal, was working as an Architectural cum Planning Assistant in the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA). The Supreme Court held that Section 37 of the Architects Act does not prohibit individuals not registered under the Architects Act from undertaking the practice of architecture and its cognate activities. Section 37 of the Architects Act 1972 prohibits individuals not registered with the Council of Architecture from using the title and style of 'Architect'. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court of Allahabad that Section 37 of the Architects Act does not prohibit unregistered individuals from practicing architecture. The Supreme Court held that NOIDA cannot promote or recruit individuals who do not hold a degree in architecture recognized by the Architects Act to a post that uses the title or style of 'architect'. The Supreme Court held that NOIDA can change the nomenclature of the post to any alternative as long as it does not violate the provisions of the Architects Act by using the style and title of 'architect'. The implication is that unregistered individuals can continue to practice architecture and its cognate activities, but they cannot use the title or style of 'Architect'.

case_name: D. N. Joshi (D) Thr. LRs. & Others vs. D.C. Harris & Another
text: Case: D. N. Joshi (D) Thr. LRs. & Others vs. D.C. Harris & Another. Date: 3rd July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the gift deed dated 31st May 1949, by Akhtari Begum in favor of Zamir Ahmad, and whether it was accompanied by possession, which would determine the ownership and the right to seek eviction of the appellants from the suit premises. The High Court found that the gift deed dated 31st May 1949 was valid and was accompanied by possession, thereby granting Zamir Ahmad ownership of the suit property. The High Court of Uttarakhand allowed the second appeal filed by the respondents, decreeing their suit for eviction and confirming their ownership of the suit property. The trial court initially dismissed the suit for eviction because it found the gift deed invalid as it was not accompanied by delivery of possession and thus no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the gift deed was valid and that the respondents were entitled to evict the appellants from the suit property. The amendment application allowed by the High Court in 2006 permitted the respondents to add substantial questions of law to their second appeal, which played a crucial role in the final decision favoring the respondents. The appellants argued that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by deciding the second appeal without formulating substantial questions of law initially and by re-appreciating evidence to overturn concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts.

case_name: D.K. Agrawal vs. Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
text: Case: D.K. Agrawal vs. Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. Date: 23rd September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Disciplinary Committee found D.K. Agrawal guilty of professional and other misconduct, recommending his removal from the membership register for five years. The High Court confirmed the recommendations of the Council, ordering the permanent removal of D.K. Agrawal from the membership register of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. The Supreme Court set aside the recommendations and orders of the Council and the High Court, remitting the matter back to the Council for fresh consideration and disposal. The judgment underscores the necessity for the Council to independently evaluate disciplinary reports and provide detailed reasons for its findings, ensuring adherence to principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court clarified that the Council must independently assess evidence and submissions, and its recommendations must be reasoned and supported by detailed findings.

case_name: DBS Bank Limited Singapore vs Ruchi Soya Industries Limited & Anr.
text: Case: DBS Bank Limited Singapore vs Ruchi Soya Industries Limited & Anr.. Date: 3rd January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court clarified that dissenting financial creditors are entitled to monetary compensation equivalent to their security interest's liquidation value, rather than enforcing the security directly. The Court reaffirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom in approving resolution plans is paramount, but it must ensure that dissenting creditors receive at least the minimum liquidation value. The Court held that there was no conflict, as Section 30(2)(b) safeguards the rights of dissenting creditors, while Section 30(4) governs the CoC's commercial decisions. The Court referred the matter to a larger bench to resolve conflicts in prior judgments, particularly concerning the interpretation of dissenting financial creditors' rights under Section 30(2)(b)(ii).

case_name: DKG Buildcon Private Ltd. vs. The Adjudicating & Enquiry Officer, S.E.B.I
text: Case: DKG Buildcon Private Ltd. vs. The Adjudicating & Enquiry Officer, S.E.B.I. Date: 14th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue addressed in the case is the non-compliance with summons issued by SEBI for the production of documents and furnishing of information during an investigation into the manipulation of share prices and aiding Ketan Parekh in rigging the securities market. The SEBI investigation concluded that DKG Buildcon Private Ltd. and other entities had facilitated Ketan Parekh in manipulating the securities market. SEBI imposed a penalty of rupees one crore on DKG Buildcon for non-compliance with the summons. The Supreme Court upheld the penalty because DKG Buildcon failed to comply with multiple summons issued by SEBI, which obstructed the investigation. The court found that the penalty was justified and within the provisions of Section 15A(a) of the SEBI Act, considering the severity of the offences and the non-cooperative attitude of DKG Buildcon. SEBI justified the imposition of the penalty by citing that DKG Buildcon had willfully failed to respond to the summons and furnish necessary documents and information, thus obstructing the investigation. The penalty aimed to be a deterrent against such non-compliance. The allegations against DKG Buildcon included transferring shares of Shonkh Technology International Ltd. to entities controlled by Ketan Parekh, who then manipulated the securities market by creating artificial volumes and synchronized trading to inflate share prices. Before imposing the penalty, SEBI issued multiple summons to DKG Buildcon to furnish information and documents and appear before the Investigating Authority. Due to DKG Buildcon's repeated non-compliance, SEBI initiated adjudication proceedings and issued a show cause notice before finally imposing the penalty.

case_name: Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. vs. M/S Navigant Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. vs. M/S Navigant Technologies Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 2nd March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the period of limitation for filing a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, starts from the date of the draft award circulation or from the date the signed copy of the award was provided. The arbitration was triggered by the termination of a Service Level Agreement dated 2nd May 2011 by the appellant corporation, which led to disputes being referred to a three-member tribunal. The arbitral tribunal (2:1) allowed the claims of the respondent company. The third arbitrator disagreed with the majority and provided a separate dissenting opinion. The appellant argued that the limitation period should commence from the date the signed copy of the award was provided (19th May 2018), not from the date the draft award was circulated (27th April 2018). The Supreme Court held that the period of limitation for filing objections would commence from the date the signed copy of the award was provided to the parties (19th May 2018). Therefore, the objections filed by the appellant were within the prescribed period. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the Civil Court and the High Court, and restored the petition filed under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, to the file of the Court of District and Sessions Judge, Hissar, Haryana, to be decided on merits.

case_name: Damodar Valley Corporation vs Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Others
text: Case: Damodar Valley Corporation vs Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Others. Date: 3rd December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue addressed in this case is the challenge by Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) against the order of the Appellate Tribunal which dismissed their appeal against the tariff order determined by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). The appeal was maintained under Section 125 of the Electricity Act 2003. Damodar Valley Corporation is entrusted with multifarious functions including the generation, transmission, and distribution of electrical energy (both hydro and thermal), as well as operating schemes for irrigation, water supply, drainage, and flood control in the Damodar river and its tributaries. The initial appeal filed by Damodar Valley Corporation was allowed by the Appellate Tribunal, which remanded the matter to the Central Commission for de novo consideration of the tariff order dated 3rd October 2006. The two main contentions raised by Damodar Valley Corporation were: (1) the Commission and the Appellate Tribunal did not give the benefit of Section 38 of the DVC Act in the computation of tariff, and (2) the improper treatment of cumulative depreciation as repayment of loan, thereby reducing the notional loan component in the capital cost. Section 38 of the DVC Act states that the Corporation shall pay interest on the amount of capital provided by each participating Government, which is deemed part of the Corporation's expenditure. The case involves whether this interest on capital should be considered in addition to other tariff elements such as interest on loan and return on equity. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant (Damodar Valley Corporation) had not made out a case for interference and that the orders of the Commission and the Appellate Tribunal were upheld.

case_name: Dasanglu Pul vs Lupalum Kri
text: Case: Dasanglu Pul vs Lupalum Kri. Date: 19th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the nomination paper of Dasanglu Pul, the returned candidate, was improperly accepted due to non-disclosure of properties belonging to her deceased spouse in the affidavit filed with her nomination. The High Court declared Dasanglu Pul's election void because she did not disclose her deceased husband's properties in her affidavit filed with the nomination paper, which was deemed a defect of substantial character under Section 36(2)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Dasanglu Pul argued that according to the custom of the Mishmi tribe, only the first wife would succeed to the properties of the deceased husband, and she had no claim over the properties of her late husband, hence she marked 'not applicable' in the relevant column of Form 26. The Supreme Court considered the customary rights of the Mishmi tribe, noting that Dasanglu Pul had no claim over her deceased husband's properties as per the tribe's customs, and thus her indication of 'not applicable' in Form 26 did not amount to a substantial defect. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, ruling that the non-disclosure did not amount to a substantial defect, and restored Dasanglu Pul's election as the member of the Legislative Assembly from the 45-Hayuliang (ST) Assembly Constituency. The Supreme Court ruled that the non-disclosure in Form 26 did not materially affect the result of the election as contemplated under Section 100(1)(d)(iv) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, thereby rejecting the claim that the nomination acceptance was improper.

case_name: Dashrath Sahu vs. State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Dashrath Sahu vs. State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 29th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of Dashrath Sahu under Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act was justified and whether the rejection of the application under Section 320 CrPC was lawful. Dashrath Sahu was charged with offences under Sections 451, 354 of the IPC, and Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act for assaulting a woman belonging to a Scheduled Caste with the intent to dishonor or outrage her modesty. The Special Judge convicted Dashrath Sahu under Sections 451 and 354 of the IPC and Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act, sentencing him to one year of simple imprisonment and a fine. The High Court allowed the joint application to the extent of the offences punishable under Sections 354 and 451 IPC, acquitting Dashrath Sahu of those charges, but rejected the application for the offence under Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act, reducing his imprisonment from one year to six months. The Supreme Court held that for an offence under Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act, the intention must be to dishonor or outrage the modesty of a person specifically because they belong to a Scheduled Caste. In this case, it was found that the intention was not based on the victim's caste. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Masumsha Hasanasha Musalman vs. State of Maharashtra, which held that the offence must be committed against a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste specifically on the basis of their caste. The Supreme Court set aside and quashed the conviction of Dashrath Sahu under Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act, acquitted him of the charge, and discharged his bail bonds.

case_name: Dashrath Singh Chauhan vs. Central Bureau of Investigation
text: Case: Dashrath Singh Chauhan vs. Central Bureau of Investigation. Date: 9th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Dashrath Singh Chauhan was charged under Sections 7, 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The trial court convicted Dashrath Singh Chauhan under Sections 7, 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years and a fine of Rs.40,000. The main allegation was that Dashrath Singh Chauhan, an employee of Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking (DESU), demanded a bribe of Rs.4000 from the complainant for installing an electric connection in his factory. The prosecution's evidence included the testimony of a shadow witness and the recovery of the bribe money from Rajinder Kumar, who allegedly accepted the money on behalf of Dashrath Singh Chauhan. The High Court of Delhi dismissed the appeal filed by Dashrath Singh Chauhan and upheld his conviction and sentence. The counsel argued that once the charge of conspiracy was not proved and the co-accused was acquitted, Dashrath Singh Chauhan should also have been acquitted. Secondly, the conviction was based only on the evidence of a shadow witness and not on the acceptance of bribe money directly by Dashrath Singh Chauhan. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence under Sections 7, 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and acquitted Dashrath Singh Chauhan of the charges. The Supreme Court emphasized that the prosecution must prove both the demand and acceptance of bribe money by the accused, and in this case, the prosecution failed to prove the acceptance of bribe money by Dashrath Singh Chauhan. Rajinder Kumar, a co-accused and fellow employee of DESU, was alleged to have accepted the bribe money on behalf of Dashrath Singh Chauhan. However, he was acquitted of all charges. The Supreme Court found the evidence of the Investigating Officer unreliable due to his questionable integrity, as a bribe case had been directed against him by the High Court in another matter.

case_name: Dataram Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Dataram Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 6th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case dealt with the denial of bail to the appellant, Dataram Singh, despite no objections from the State and the complainant's strong opposition, raising questions about the exercise of judicial discretion in granting bail. Dataram Singh was charged under Sections 419, 420, 406, and 506 of the IPC for cheating and issuing a cheque for Rs. 18 lakhs that was stopped, violating Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Court emphasized the presumption of innocence and the principle that bail is the rule and jail is the exception. The courts denied bail citing the seriousness of the charges and the complainant's contention of being duped of a significant amount of money. The Supreme Court advised that judicial discretion in granting bail must be exercised judiciously, with a humane and compassionate approach, avoiding conditions that make bail illusory. The Court concluded that Dataram Singh cooperated during the investigation, was not arrested by the investigating officer, and posed no threat of absconding or tampering with evidence. The Court noted that overcrowded prisons exacerbate social problems and emphasized the need for humane bail decisions to prevent unnecessary incarceration. The Court clarified that it expressed no opinion on the merits of the allegations and left the matter to be decided by the trial court. The Court granted bail to Dataram Singh, subject to reasonable conditions to be set by the trial judge. The judgment reinforced that judicial discretion in bail matters must align with the principles of justice, equality, and compassion, avoiding mechanical denials of bail.

text: Case: Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade vs. State of Maharashtra. Date: 21st February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade was charged under Sections 302, 376(2)(f), 377, 363, 364, 367, and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, as well as under Sections 3, 4, 5(i) (l), and (m) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. The High Court confirmed the conviction of Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade and affirmed the sentence of death imposed on him. The case involved the kidnapping, rape, and murder of a young girl by Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade. The victim was found nude and still in front of the door of her tenement after being reported missing. The forensic evidence, including DNA analysis, established beyond reasonable doubt that the victim was raped by Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade. Eyewitnesses provided crucial information about seeing an old man carrying and dumping a white plastic bag, which was later identified as evidence linking Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade to the crime. The court held that there was no evidence to support the finding that the murder was pre-meditated, but upheld the conviction for murder based on the brutality of the crime and the age of the victim. The court identified that the accused-appellant was not given an effective hearing on the question of sentence and that there was a failure to elicit facts relevant to the existence of mitigating circumstances. The court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, considering the procedural lapses and the fact that the crime did not fall under the category of the rarest of rare cases. The court concluded that the possibility of reforming Dattatraya @ Datta Ambo Rokade was not considered by the trial court and emphasized the need for such consideration before imposing the death penalty. The court considered the lack of effective legal representation, the failure to present mitigating circumstances, and the absence of a real, effective, and meaningful hearing on the question of sentence.

case_name: Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
text: Case: Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.. Date: 10th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the tenancy and partnership between Pradeep Kumar and Subhash Chand ended with the death of Pradeep Kumar, leading to the deemed vacancy of the property under Section 12(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The appellants argued that the partnership between Pradeep Kumar and Subhash Chand ended automatically with the death of Pradeep Kumar on 21st May 2004, and therefore, the tenancy also ended under Section 12(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The High Court of Uttarakhand dismissed the review application on 23rd April 2008, stating that the grounds urged were different from those in the writ petition, and did not consider the subsequent events such as the death of Pradeep Kumar. Section 42(c) of the Partnership Act states that a partnership is dissolved by the death of a partner. The appellants argued that the partnership between Pradeep Kumar and Subhash Chand dissolved upon the death of Pradeep Kumar, and thus the tenancy should be deemed vacant. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, deemed the tenancy to have ended with the death of the partners, and ruled that the non-residential tenanted premises is deemed to be vacant. The appellants were allowed to proceed with remedies available under the law. The District Magistrate had permitted Subhash Chand to be inducted as a partner with Pradeep Kumar on 15th November 1982, which led to the signing of the partnership deed on 19th November 1982.
