case_name: Doddamuniyappa (Dead) Through LRs. Vs. Muniswamy & Ors.
text: Case: Doddamuniyappa (Dead) Through LRs. Vs. Muniswamy & Ors.. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the compromise dated 25th March 1976, entered into by the original defendants, bound the rights of the plaintiffs and whether the suit property was a joint family property. The original parties involved in the compromise were Doddamuniyappa (defendant no. 1) and the sons of Chikkanna (respondent nos. 7, 8, and 9 - original defendant nos. 2, 3, and 4). The High Court decided that the suit property was a joint family property and the compromise entered into without the consent of the plaintiffs (grandsons of Chikkanna) did not bind their rights. The appellants argued that the property was not a joint family property but an absolute property of the original defendants, and the compromise entered into was valid and binding. The Supreme Court ruled that the compromise did not bind the plaintiffs (respondent nos. 1 to 6) as they were not parties to it, and the property, being joint family property, could not be compromised without their consent. The Supreme Court emphasized that property inherited from a father by his sons becomes joint family property in the hands of the sons and their descendants. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgement, confirming that the suit property was joint family property and the compromise did not bind the rights of the plaintiffs. The judgement reinforces that compromises involving joint family property require the consent of all interested parties, and the rights of descendants must be respected in family property disputes. Parties should ensure that all members of the joint family, including descendants with potential inheritance rights, are consulted and give their consent before entering into any compromise involving joint family property. This judgment may lead to more stringent requirements for family consent in property deals, ensuring that the rights of all family members are protected, and prevent unilateral compromises in joint family properties. The Supreme Court clarified that descendants have an inherent right in joint family property, and any compromise or transaction involving such property without their consent is not legally binding on them.

case_name: Dominic Alex Fernandes (D) Through LRS. & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Dominic Alex Fernandes (D) Through LRS. & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 17th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the tenancy of a property, whose ownership was acquired by a person to whom the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA) applies, would be treated as 'illegally acquired property' and subjected to forfeiture under SAFEMA. The appeal arose from the forfeiture of property owned by Krishna Budha Gawde, who was detained under COFEPOSA. The appellants, who claimed to be bona fide tenants, challenged the forfeiture, arguing that their tenancy rights should not be terminated by the forfeiture. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that the tenancy did not survive the forfeiture under Section 7(3) of SAFEMA. The Supreme Court held that the rights of a bona fide tenant do not automatically terminate by forfeiture of property under SAFEMA. The Court noted that the competent authority must independently determine the tenancy rights of the appellants. The Supreme Court ruled that for forfeiture under SAFEMA, there must be a direct nexus between the property and the illegal activities of the person to whom the Act applies. The appellants, being bona fide tenants without such a nexus, could not have their rights terminated without proper adjudication. The Supreme Court referred to several cases, including C.B. Gautam vs. Union of India, Amratlal Prajivandas vs. Union of India, and Fatima Mohd. Amin vs. Union of India, to support the principle that bona fide rights of tenants or holders of property should not be adversely affected without due process. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remitted the matter to the competent authority for an independent adjudication of the appellants' tenancy rights in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court directed the competent authority to pass an appropriate order regarding the tenancy rights of the appellants, considering their claim of being bona fide tenants and having no nexus with the illegal activities of Krishna Budha Gawde. The legal significance was that once the property was vested in the Central Government under SAFEMA, it was considered free from all encumbrances. However, the Supreme Court clarified that bona fide tenancy rights must be independently adjudicated and could not be summarily extinguished. The Supreme Court noted that the appellants claimed to be bona fide tenants paying rent under the Bombay Rent Act and were not aware of proceedings under SAFEMA and COFEPOSA. The Court emphasized the need for the competent authority to consider these claims independently.

case_name: Dr Naresh Kumar Mangla vs Smt. Anita Agarwal & Ors.
text: Case: Dr Naresh Kumar Mangla vs Smt. Anita Agarwal & Ors.. Date: 17th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the anticipatory bail granted to the accused in the dowry death case of Dr. Deepti Mangla should be canceled and the investigation transferred to the CBI. The accused were charged under Sections 498A, 304-B, 323, 506, and 313 of the IPC and Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The FIR was filed by Dr. Naresh Kumar Mangla, father of the deceased Dr. Deepti Mangla, alleging dowry harassment, physical abuse, and eventual dowry death of his daughter. The Allahabad High Court granted anticipatory bail to the parents-in-law, brother-in-law, and sister-in-law of the deceased, which was later challenged in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in granting anticipatory bail without proper consideration of the seriousness of the allegations and the materials on record. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail and canceled the bail granted to the accused. The Supreme Court directed that the investigation be transferred to the CBI for further investigation. The key allegations included dowry harassment, physical abuse, financial exploitation, and the unnatural death of Dr. Deepti Mangla due to the actions of her in-laws. The alleged suicide note was contested in its authenticity, and the Supreme Court noted deficiencies in the police investigation regarding its genuineness. The Supreme Court highlighted the need for a thorough investigation into the financial transactions between the deceased, her in-laws, and the role these played in the alleged dowry harassment. The Supreme Court emphasized that superior courts have the authority to direct further or de novo investigations when the initial investigation is found to be deficient or biased, ensuring justice is served.

case_name: Dr. Ashok Sinha vs. The State of Tripura & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Ashok Sinha vs. The State of Tripura & Ors.. Date: 19th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the State government should administer the Tripura Medical College as a government institution or through an independent society, and whether the fees charged and admission procedures should be aligned with other government medical colleges in the North East. The High Court of Tripura directed the State government to either reconstitute the managing committee of the Tripura Medical College to ensure administrative control by the Society or retain control with all consequences within three months. Following the High Court's direction, the State government reconstituted the Society for the Tripura Medical College, which has its own recruitment rules and pay structure, while maintaining some government representation to ensure proper channeling of finances. The petitioner, Dr. Ashok Sinha, contended that despite the earlier directions, the situation had not changed, and he challenged the admission procedure and fees charged, arguing they should be at par with other government medical colleges in the North East. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, finding that the constitution of the Society had been recast with both government and non-governmental nominees, and it was functioning as an independent entity with government oversight in financial matters. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, stating that it would not be appropriate to determine the correctness of the policy decision taken by the State government, which included running the Tripura Medical College through a hybrid model of administration. The Supreme Court suggested that grievances regarding the fees could be considered by the regulatory committee constituted in the State, as it would not be possible for the Court to determine the reasonableness of the fees without underlying material.

text: Case: Dr. Gajendra Singh vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the penalty of removal from service imposed on Dr. Gajendra Singh, a Branch Manager at the United Insurance Company, for issuing an insurance cover note without collecting the premium was justified. Dr. Gajendra Singh was alleged to have issued an insurance cover note (No. 543675) without collecting any premium, causing financial loss to the insurance company when a claim was filed based on this cover note after an accident. Dr. Gajendra Singh explained that he issued the cover note based on the assurance from the insured that the premium would be sent through his person. However, the insured applied for another policy with a cheque that later bounced. The departmental inquiry found the charges against Dr. Gajendra Singh to be proven, and the disciplinary authority imposed the penalty of removal from service without disqualification from future employment. The High Court of Allahabad dismissed Dr. Gajendra Singh's writ appeal, upholding the disciplinary authority's decision to remove him from service. The Supreme Court found that the penalty of removal from service was disproportionate to the charge and misconduct held to be proved, given Dr. Gajendra Singh's long, unblemished service record. The Supreme Court quashed the penalty of removal from service and remitted the matter to the disciplinary authority to impose any other appropriate punishment lesser than removal from service, to be completed within three months.

case_name: Dr. J. Vijayan & Others vs. The State of Kerala & Others
text: Case: Dr. J. Vijayan & Others vs. The State of Kerala & Others. Date: 2nd August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the State of Kerala was obligated to enhance the retirement age of university teachers to 65 years in accordance with the University Grants Commission (UGC) Regulations, 2010. The UGC Regulations, 2010, stipulated that the age of superannuation for teachers in central universities and other institutions maintained and/or funded by the UGC should be enhanced to 65 years. The State of Kerala adopted the UGC Regulations but did not enhance the retirement age of university teachers to 65 years, citing its discretion to decide on service conditions for its employees. The Kerala High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellants, upholding the State Government's decision not to enhance the retirement age to 65 years. The Supreme Court observed that the regulation of the age of superannuation falls within the exclusive domain of the State Government's policy-making power and is not mandatorily governed by UGC Regulations. The Supreme Court upheld the concurrent findings of the Division Bench and the Single Bench of the Kerala High Court, dismissing the appeal and supporting the State's decision to maintain the retirement age at 56 years for teachers in aided colleges and 60 years for university teachers. The Supreme Court affirmed that State Governments have the discretion to adopt UGC Regulations partially and are not bound to implement the entire scheme, including the enhanced retirement age.

case_name: Dr. Jaya Thakur vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Jaya Thakur vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 11th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Dr. Jaya Thakur sought a writ, order, or direction in the nature of certiorari for quashing the order dated 17th November 2021, which extended the tenure of the Director of Enforcement beyond the specified period. The petition challenged the Central Vigilance Commission (Amendment) Act, 2021, the Delhi Special Police Establishment (Amendment) Act, 2021, and the Fundamental (Amendment) Rules, 2021, along with the extension orders dated 17th November 2021 and 17th November 2022. In the Common Cause (2021) judgment, the Supreme Court directed that no further extension shall be granted to the Director of Enforcement beyond the period specified in the initial appointment. Dr. Jaya Thakur argued that the extensions violated the Supreme Court's direction in the Common Cause (2021) judgment and that the amendments were contrary to the principles of insulating the Director of Enforcement from government influence, thus undermining the independence of the office. The Union of India argued that the extensions were necessary for public interest, particularly citing the ongoing mutual evaluation of India by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), which required continuity in leadership for effective representation and completion of the evaluation process. The Supreme Court examined whether the amendments were within the legislative competence of the Parliament and whether they violated any fundamental rights or other constitutional provisions. The court reiterated the principles of judicial review, emphasizing that a law could be invalidated only on grounds of lack of legislative competence or violation of constitutional provisions. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Central Vigilance Commission (Amendment) Act, 2021, the Delhi Special Police Establishment (Amendment) Act, 2021, and the Fundamental (Amendment) Rules, 2021, stating that the legislative amendments did not violate constitutional principles or judicial directives. The extensions granted to the Director of Enforcement were deemed valid and in public interest.

case_name: Dr. Joe Joseph & Ors. vs. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Joe Joseph & Ors. vs. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.. Date: 8th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the implementation of the Dam Safety Act, 2021, which deals with the surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance of dams, including the Mullaperiyar Dam, and the establishment of a multi-tier institutional mechanism for ensuring the safe functioning of dams. The Dam Safety Act, 2021, mandated the constitution of a National Committee and a National Dam Safety Authority (NDSA) to oversee the safety and maintenance of dams. The Act also specified that the NDSA would act as the State Dam Safety Organisation and be responsible for surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance of dams. The Supervisory Committee, constituted by the Supreme Court, was tasked with the surveillance, inspection, operation, and maintenance of the Mullaperiyar Dam. This committee included representatives from the Central Water Commission and the states of Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The Supreme Court decided that the existing Supervisory Committee would continue its tasks until the NDSA becomes fully operational. case_name: Dr. Kriti Lakhina and Others vs. State of Karnataka and Others
text: Case: Dr. Kriti Lakhina and Others vs. State of Karnataka and Others. Date: 4th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge to Clause 4.1 of the Information Bulletin issued by the Directorate of Medical Education and the Karnataka Examinations Authority, which imposed domicile restrictions for admission to post-graduate medical and dental courses in Karnataka. Clause 4.1 required candidates to be of Karnataka origin and have studied MBBS or BDS in a medical or dental college located in Karnataka or outside Karnataka, with certain domicile conditions. The petitioners argued that Clause 4.1 was unconstitutional as it arbitrarily imposed domicile requirements, thereby violating the principle of equality and depriving them of the opportunity to compete for admission to post-graduate courses despite having completed their MBBS/BDS from colleges in Karnataka. The State of Karnataka argued that the eligibility conditions were necessary to ensure that the State's requirement for skilled human resources was met, especially given the large number of vacancies in public health care institutions and medical colleges. The Supreme Court held Clause 4.1 to be invalid as it violated Article 14 of the Constitution. The Court directed the State of Karnataka and the concerned authorities to modify the Information Bulletin to comply with this judgement and complete the admission process within the stipulated timeline. The Court relied on the decision in Vishal Goyal and Others vs. State of Karnataka and Others, which similarly held that imposing domicile requirements for admission to post-graduate courses was unconstitutional.

case_name: Dr. Lakshman vs The State of Karnataka & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Lakshman vs The State of Karnataka & Ors.. Date: 17th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the criminal complaints filed by Dr. Lakshman against the respondents-accused under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. Dr. Lakshman accused the respondents of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and conspiracy related to the sale of land at Ballur village, for which he had paid Rs.9 crores, but the respondents failed to deliver the promised land. The High Court quashed the complaints on the grounds that there was a novation of contract, the appellant had already filed a civil suit for recovery of the advance, and the complaints were related to civil disputes rather than criminal offenses. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, stating that the High Court had erred in its decision by entering into disputed facts and ignoring the allegations of cheating and criminal conspiracy, which warranted a trial. The agreements were significant because they formed the basis of Dr. Lakshman's complaint, where he alleged that the respondents failed to procure and transfer the promised land, leading to the charges of cheating and breach of trust. The respondents allegedly deceived Dr. Lakshman by including land in the agreements that they had already sold to a third party and issuing cheques as security that were from a closed account, indicating fraudulent intentions. The cheques were issued as security for the advance payment made by Dr. Lakshman. However, the cheques were from an account that was closed before the agreements were made, which supported the allegations of fraud. The Supreme Court stated that whether there was a novation of contract due to the subsequent agreement was a matter to be decided at trial and not at the stage of quashing the proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court emphasized that the presence of an element of cheating and fraud could make a case both civil and criminal. Hence, the High Court's view that the matter was purely civil was incorrect, and the criminal proceedings should not have been quashed. The Supreme Court directed that the trial court proceed with the complaints in accordance with law and decide the matters on their merits without being influenced by the observations of the High Court.

case_name: Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences vs. Dr. Yerra Trinadh & Others
text: Case: Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences vs. Dr. Yerra Trinadh & Others. Date: 4th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in ordering the re-evaluation of answer scripts in absence of any provision for re-evaluation in the relevant rules. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh ordered the re-evaluation of the answer scripts of students who appeared in the post-graduation diploma course, which the University contested as there was no provision for re-evaluation in the relevant rules. Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences contended that there was no provision for re-evaluation in the relevant rules and that the High Court was not justified in ordering the re-evaluation while exercising powers under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court disapproved the practice of the High Court calling for answer scripts and ordering re-evaluation in absence of any provision in the relevant rules, and held that such orders are unsustainable. The Supreme Court acknowledged that the University had adopted a digital evaluation process, which had been subsequently improved and approved by the High Court in a recent decision, and that all precautions were being taken to ensure accurate evaluation. The Supreme Court held that the results declared for the original writ petitioners after re-evaluation or supplementary examinations shall not be disturbed, even though the order for re-evaluation was quashed. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the orders of the High Court and the Division Bench directing re-evaluation of the answer scripts, but maintained that the results of the students who passed after re-evaluation would not be affected.

case_name: Dr. Nazrul Islam vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Nazrul Islam vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 28th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the disciplinary proceedings initiated against Dr. Nazrul Islam could continue after his retirement from service. Dr. Nazrul Islam contended that the disciplinary proceedings against him could not continue once he had retired from service. The Union of India cited Rule 6(1) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958, which allows for the continuation of departmental proceedings for the purpose of withholding pension or gratuity if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct. Rule 6(1) allows the Central Government to withhold a pension or gratuity, either in full or in part, and to recover any pecuniary loss caused to the Government if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct or negligence during their service. Dr. Nazrul Islam argued that the Inquiry Report did not find him guilty of any grave misconduct, and therefore, the proceedings could not be continued under Rule 6(1). The Supreme Court directed the Central Government to give Dr. Nazrul Islam an opportunity of hearing before passing final orders on recovery, if any, and to conclude the disciplinary proceedings expeditiously, within six months. The Supreme Court emphasized that the Central Government must consult the Union Public Service Commission before passing any order under Rule 6(1) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958. If the Central Government does not conclude the disciplinary proceedings within the stipulated time, the proceedings shall be deemed to have been dropped, as directed by the Supreme Court. This judgement might ensure that disciplinary proceedings against retired officials are conducted within a reasonable timeframe and that the officials are given a fair opportunity to defend themselves before any recovery from pension or gratuity is ordered. The Supreme Court found Dr. Nazrul Islam's contention unappreciable because the Inquiry Report had already been submitted, and it was now for the Central Government to take a decision as per the procedure prescribed under the Rules. Consulting the Union Public Service Commission is significant because it ensures an additional layer of scrutiny and fairness before any decision affecting the pension or gratuity of a retired official is made.

text: Case: Dr. Prerit Sharma & Ors. vs. Dr. Bilu B.S. & Ors.. Date: 27th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court directed that counselling for Super Specialty Medical Courses for the academic year 2020-2021 proceed without providing reservations for in-service doctors. The Act provided for 40% reservation for in-service doctors but had not been implemented for several years, and the State of Kerala expressed its inability to implement it for the 2020-2021 academic year due to administrative challenges. The Supreme Court predicted that implementing reservations would be detrimental to the interests of meritorious candidates as it would reduce 50% of available seats in Tamil Nadu for Super Specialty Medical Courses. The Supreme Court clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the validity of GOMS No.462 of 07.11.2020 and limited its decision to the academic year 2020-2021. The State of Kerala argued that it was practically impossible to introduce new reservation norms as the admission process for Super Specialty Medical Courses for the 2020-2021 academic year was already at an advanced stage.

case_name: Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala vs. Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur & Anr.
text: Case: Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala vs. Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur & Anr.. Date: 1st October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala was negligent in performing the surgery on Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur, resulting in complications and subsequent suffering for the patient. Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur alleged that Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala performed a general surgery without her consent, failed to perform the surgery properly, resulting in post-operative complications including dysentery, loss of appetite, and jaundice, and necessitated another surgery to remove remaining stones. Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala defended himself by stating that he performed the surgery as per standard medical practice, obtained consent from the patient's husband for the conventional surgery after noticing complications during the laparoscopic procedure, and denied any negligence or carelessness in his conduct. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission held Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala guilty of negligence and awarded a total compensation of Rs. 2 lakhs to Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the National Commission, and restored the order of the State Commission, which had dismissed the complaint against Dr. S.K. Jhunjhunwala, finding no merit in the allegations of negligence. The Supreme Court applied the Bolam test and principles from the case of Jacob Mathew vs. State of Punjab, emphasizing that a doctor is not liable for negligence simply because something went wrong, but only if it is proven that the doctor lacked the requisite skill or failed to exercise reasonable competence. The Supreme Court observed that there was no need for additional consent as per clause 4 of the Consent Form signed by Mrs. Dhanwanti Kaur, which allowed the performing doctor to undertake any necessary procedure if complications arose during the operation.

case_name: Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan vs The State of Maharashtra & Anr.
text: Case: Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan vs The State of Maharashtra & Anr.. Date: 20th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellant, Dr. Subhash K. Mahajan, could be prosecuted under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 for denying sanction for prosecution against two government officials. Dr. Subhash K. Mahajan was accused because he denied sanction for prosecution against two officials who had adverse entries in their confidential report against a scheduled caste employee, Bhaskar Karbhari Gaidwad, who then lodged a complaint against him under the Act. The charges included offences under Sections 3(1)(ix), 3(2)(vi), and 3(2)(vii) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and Sections 182, 192, 193, 203, and 219 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court rejected Dr. Subhash K. Mahajan's petition to quash the proceedings, stating that the allegations under the Atrocities Act needed to be tried. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for a preliminary inquiry before arresting a public servant under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, to prevent misuse of the law. The Supreme Court stated that prior sanction for prosecution is mandatory for public servants under the Atrocities Act to protect them from frivolous and false complaints. The Supreme Court quashed the proceedings against Dr. Subhash K. Mahajan, stating that no case was made out under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The Supreme Court highlighted that public servants should be protected from unnecessary and frivolous prosecution, ensuring their actions taken in official capacity are not unduly challenged under the Atrocities Act. The Supreme Court directed that preliminary inquiry and approval from the appointing authority are required before registering an FIR against public servants under the Atrocities Act to prevent misuse. The Supreme Court concluded that while protecting the rights of victims under the Atrocities Act is crucial, it is equally important to prevent the misuse of the Act against innocent public servants.

case_name: Dr. Vijay Mallya vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
text: Case: Dr. Vijay Mallya vs. State Bank of India & Ors.. Date: 31st August 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Dr. Vijay Mallya was guilty of contempt of court for failing to disclose his assets and violating the restraint orders passed by the High Court of Karnataka and the Supreme Court. Dr. Vijay Mallya was found guilty of contempt on two counts: (a) disobeying the Supreme Court's orders by not disclosing full particulars of his assets, and (b) violating the express orders of restraint passed by the High Court of Karnataka, which prevented him from transferring, alienating, or disposing of his properties. Dr. Vijay Mallya transferred USD 40 million out of his account shortly after receiving it, despite an oral undertaking and subsequent court orders preventing such actions. Additionally, he failed to disclose the existence of the bank account and details of the transferred amount. Dr. Vijay Mallya argued that he was required to disclose his assets as of 31st March 2016 and claimed that any violation pertained to the High Court's orders, not the Supreme Court's. He also contended that he had filed a reply to the banks' response, which the Supreme Court had not considered. The Supreme Court acknowledged that it was an error to state that no reply was filed by Dr. Vijay Mallya. However, upon review, the Court found that the reply did not contradict the banks' claims or provide any substantial defense against the charges of contempt. The Supreme Court dismissed the review petitions, finding no error apparent on the record to justify interference. The Court directed Dr. Vijay Mallya to appear before it on 5th October 2020 for hearing regarding the proposed punishment for contempt.

case_name: Duncans Industries Ltd. vs. A. J. Agrochem
text: Case: Duncans Industries Ltd. vs. A. J. Agrochem. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court held that insolvency resolution under the IBC focuses on revival and continuation of the corporate debtor, whereas 'winding up' under the Tea Act pertains to liquidation. The Court directed that in case of any conflict, the provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, would prevail over the Tea Act, 1953. The Court stated that Section 238 of the IBC gives the Code overriding effect over any inconsistent provisions in other laws, including the Tea Act. The Court interpreted that the IBC aims to ensure revival and continuation of corporate entities in a time-bound manner, whereas the Tea Act addresses sector-specific issues like management of tea estates. The Supreme Court ruled that the insolvency proceedings initiated by A. J. Agrochem under Section 9 of the IBC were maintainable without requiring prior consent from the Central Government.

case_name: Dushyant N. Dalal and Another vs Securities and Exchange Board of India
text: Case: Dushyant N. Dalal and Another vs Securities and Exchange Board of India. Date: 4th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether interest could be recovered on orders of penalty and disgorgement of unlawful gains under the SEBI Act, 1992, when the amounts remained unpaid. SEBI alleged that Dushyant N. Dalal and Mrs. Puloma D. Dalal manipulated the demand for shares in the retail individual investor category, denying other investors their legitimate shares in IPOs, resulting in an unlawful gain of Rs. 4.05 crores. SEBI directed them to disgorge the unlawful gain of Rs. 4.05 crores, pay an additional Rs. 1.95 crores as interest, and barred them from accessing the securities market for 45 days. The SAT dismissed the appeal and upheld SEBI's order, which included the disgorgement and interest payments. The Supreme Court clarified that interest could be awarded in equity on amounts due, under the principles of the Interest Act, 1978 and Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, even if not explicitly provided in the SEBI Act. The Supreme Court held that interest on penalties under the SEBI Act could be levied prospectively from the date of the amendment (18th July 2013) that introduced Section 28A, and not retrospectively. The Supreme Court concluded that the SEBI order dated 21st July 2009 did not explicitly include future interest payments, thus future interest was not applicable if the amount was not paid within the stipulated time. The judgment may ensure that future SEBI orders explicitly include provisions for future interest payments, preventing ambiguity and ensuring compliance with equity principles. The Supreme Court directed that the attachment of bank accounts by SEBI was justified and that the appellants must comply with the payment of the penalty and interest as directed. The Supreme Court suggested that future SEBI orders should clearly state the conditions for interest accrual and penalties to ensure transparency and compliance with legal and equitable principles. The judgment reinforces the importance of compliance with SEBI regulations and the potential financial consequences of market manipulation, including the obligation to pay interest on penalties and disgorged amounts.

The Supreme Court concluded that the SEBI order dated 21st July 2009 did not explicitly include future interest payments, thus future interest was not applicable if the amount was not paid within the stipulated time.
The judgment may ensure that future SEBI orders explicitly include provisions for future interest payments, preventing ambiguity and ensuring compliance with equity principles.
The Supreme Court directed that the attachment of bank accounts by SEBI was justified and that the appellants must comply with the payment of the penalty and interest as directed.
The Supreme Court suggested that future SEBI orders should clearly state the conditions for interest accrual and penalties to ensure transparency and compliance with legal and equitable principles.

The judgment reinforces the importance of compliance with SEBI regulations and the potential financial consequences of market manipulation, including the obligation to pay interest on penalties and disgorged amounts.

case_name: E S Krishnamurthy & Ors. vs M/s Bharath Hi Tech Builders Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: E S Krishnamurthy & Ors. vs M/s Bharath Hi Tech Builders Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 14th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appeal was filed under Section 62 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016. The main issue was whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) can dismiss a petition under Section 7 of the IBC based on the fact that the corporate debtor has initiated the process of settlement with the financial creditors, without applying its mind to the merits of the petition. The NCLT declined to admit the petition and instead directed the respondent to settle the claims within three months. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's order and found no merit in the appeal against the NCLT's decision. The NCLT directed the corporate debtor to settle the remaining claims as expeditiously as possible but not later than three months and allowed the remaining petitioners to approach the Adjudicating Authority again if they were aggrieved by the settlement process. The Supreme Court concluded that the NCLT and NCLAT had acted outside the scope of their jurisdiction under Section 7(5) of the IBC by directing the parties to settle rather than deciding the petition based on the merits.

text: Case: E. Sivakumar vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 10th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the illegal manufacture and sale of Gutkha and Pan Masala containing tobacco and/or nicotine. The High Court issued a writ of mandamus to transfer the investigation of the criminal case concerning the illegal manufacture and sale of Gutkha and Pan Masala to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). E. Sivakumar was named as an accused because of his alleged involvement in the crime under investigation while he was posted as a Food Safety Officer in the Food Safety and Drug Administration Department, Ministry of Health. The grounds of challenge were: (i) the previous decisions of the Coordinate Bench of the same High Court were disregarded, (ii) the petitioner was not given an opportunity of hearing, (iii) no special circumstances were noted for transferring the investigation to the CBI, and (iv) the writ petition filed was politically motivated. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's decision to transfer the investigation to the CBI, emphasizing that the petitioner was named in the FIR and that the previous rejections of similar requests did not preclude the High Court from ordering the transfer.

case_name: E. Sivakumar vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: E. Sivakumar vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 18th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the transfer of investigation of a criminal case concerning the illegal manufacture and sale of Gutkha and Pan Masala, containing tobacco and/or nicotine, from the State Vigilance Commission of Tamil Nadu to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The petitioner challenged the decision on the grounds that the transfer of investigation to the CBI had already been considered and rejected by the High Court in two previous writ petitions, the petitioner was not given an opportunity of hearing, no special circumstances were noted for transferring the investigation, and the public interest litigation was politically motivated. The High Court reasoned that a fair investigation was necessary due to the involvement of high-ranking officials and the extent of the conspiracy transcending beyond the State of Tamil Nadu. The Court found it imperative to issue a writ of mandamus to transfer the investigation to the CBI to ensure an impartial and comprehensive investigation. The Supreme Court concluded that the petitioner, being named as an accused in the FIR, did not have the right to be heard at the stage of investigation. The Court found that the lack of hearing did not render the High Court's judgment a nullity. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had distinguished the previous decisions and provided a detailed analysis justifying the transfer of investigation to the CBI. The Court found that the High Court's decision was consistent with the legal position and did not disregard the previous rulings. The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the public interest litigation was politically motivated, noting that the High Court had considered this issue and found the petition to be genuine. The Court emphasized that the transfer of investigation was necessary to ensure a fair and impartial investigation.

case_name: Ebha Arjun Jadeja & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat
text: Case: Ebha Arjun Jadeja & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat. Date: 16th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The charges were under Section 25(1B)(a) and 27 of the Arms Act, 1959, and under Section 3 and 5 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (TADA Act). The main legal issue was whether the initiation of proceedings under the TADA Act was valid without prior approval of the District Superintendent of Police as required under Section 20-A(1) of the TADA Act. The prosecution stated that Police Inspector C.J. Singh, during a night round, received information about Ebha Arjun Jadeja's arrival in the village and set up a naka. Ebha Arjun Jadeja and two others were found with arms and were arrested. The items recovered included a foreign-made 9mm beretta pistol, a 32 bore foreign-made revolver, three live cartridges, one fired cartridge, and five live cartridges. The Designated TADA Court dismissed the application filed by the accused, stating that there was compliance with Section 20-A(1) of the TADA Act. The Supreme Court held that Section 20-A(1) of the TADA Act is mandatory and that no information about the commission of an offence under TADA Act can be recorded without prior approval of the District Superintendent of Police. The Supreme Court referred to the cases of Rangku Dutta @ Ranjan Kumar Dutta vs. State of Assam, Anirudhsinhji Karansinhji Jadeja & Anr. vs. State of Gujarat, and Ashrafkhan & Anr. vs. State of Gujarat. The Supreme Court concluded that the proceedings initiated without compliance with Section 20-A(1) of the TADA Act were vitiated and the appellants were to be discharged from the offences under the TADA Act. The Supreme Court made it clear that the appellants could still be prosecuted under the provisions of the Arms Act, despite being discharged from the offences under the TADA Act. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Designated TADA Court, and discharged the appellants from the offences under the TADA Act, while allowing for prosecution under other applicable laws.

case_name: Electrosteel Castings Limited vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Electrosteel Castings Limited vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.. Date: 26th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the suit filed by Electrosteel Castings Limited was maintainable in light of the bar under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Electrosteel Castings Limited filed the suit to declare that UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited acquired no rights under an Assignment Deed dated 30.06.2018, and to declare a possession notice dated 19.06.2019 as null and void. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal by Electrosteel Castings Limited, confirming the dismissal of the suit as not maintainable under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act. Electrosteel Castings Limited argued that the assignment agreement dated 30.06.2018 was fraudulent and that the assignee, UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited, could not be considered a secured creditor since the debt was allegedly discharged under the approved resolution plan of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The Supreme Court found that the allegations of fraud were made without specific particulars and seemed to be a clever drafting strategy to circumvent the bar under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the suit was not maintainable due to the bar under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act and dismissed the appeal, allowing Electrosteel Castings Limited to seek remedies under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT).

case_name: Enforcement Directorate vs. Kapil Wadhawan & Anr.
text: Case: Enforcement Directorate vs. Kapil Wadhawan & Anr.. Date: 27th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the date of remand should be included or excluded when computing the 60/90 day period for default bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The Bombay High Court granted default bail to the respondents, holding that the date of remand should be included in computing the 60-day period, making the chargesheet filed on the 61st day invalid. The Enforcement Directorate appealed, arguing that the date of remand should be excluded when calculating the 60-day period for filing the chargesheet. The Supreme Court upheld the Bombay High Court’s decision, ruling that the date of remand must be included in computing the remand period for default bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The Supreme Court emphasized that personal liberty is a fundamental right and the law should protect against prolonged incarceration due to procedural delays in filing chargesheets. The Court stated that the General Clauses Act does not apply to the computation of the remand period under Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The Court interpreted the legislative intent as ensuring a balance between expeditious investigation by authorities and safeguarding the accused's right to liberty. The Court highlighted that any restriction on personal liberty must adhere to principles of fairness, reasonableness, and procedural safeguards under Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The prosecution argued for excluding the date of remand, while the defense contended that it should be included for determining the 60-day period for default bail. The Supreme Court directed that the accused's right to default bail must be upheld as their applications were filed within the stipulated period before the chargesheet was submitted.

case_name: Erudhaya Priya vs. State Express Transport Corporation Ltd.
text: Case: Erudhaya Priya vs. State Express Transport Corporation Ltd.. Date: 27th July 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. On 16th August 2011, Erudhaya Priya was traveling from Chennai to Bangalore in a bus owned by the respondent corporation. The bus collided with a stationary lorry on the Kolar Bangalore National Highway, resulting in multiple injuries to passengers, including Erudhaya Priya, and the death of the bus conductor. Erudhaya Priya sustained grievous injuries, including fractures in the arms and legs, and suffered a disability of 31.1% of the whole body. The MACT held the respondent liable to pay compensation to Erudhaya Priya, calculating a total of Rs. 35,24,288/- based on various heads including loss of earning power, medical expenses, and pain and suffering, along with interest at 7.5% per annum from the date of the petition until realization. The High Court reduced the compensation to Rs. 25,00,000/-, reasoning that the multiplier method for quantifying loss of earning power was incorrectly applied without proper evidence of how the injuries affected Erudhaya Priya's earning capacity as a software engineer. Erudhaya Priya claimed an enhancement of compensation to Rs. 41,69,831/- under various heads and a revised interest rate of 12% per annum. The Supreme Court awarded Erudhaya Priya a compensation of Rs. 41,69,831/- along with simple interest at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of application until payment.

case_name: Ex. Ct. Mahadev vs The Director General, Border Security Force & Ors.
text: Case: Ex. Ct. Mahadev vs The Director General, Border Security Force & Ors.. Date: 14th June 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Ex. Ct. Mahadev, who was convicted of murder under Section 46 of the BSF Act and sentenced to life imprisonment, was justified in his plea of self-defense. Ex. Ct. Mahadev was convicted for the murder of a civilian named Nandan Deb, whom he shot dead with his INSAS rifle during a patrolling duty in a rubber plantation near the Bangladesh border on 5th June 2004. Ex. Ct. Mahadev claimed he acted in self-defense when confronted by a group of armed intruders, including Nandan Deb, who were smuggling across the border and threatened his life. The High Court of Delhi dismissed Ex. Ct. Mahadev's writ petition, upholding the General Security Force Court's conviction and sentencing, and rejected his plea of self-defense. The Supreme Court accepted Ex. Ct. Mahadev's plea of self-defense, modifying his conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC and setting him free for the period already undergone. The Supreme Court considered the preponderance of probabilities, the uneven terrain of the rubber plantation, and the imminent threat posed by armed intruders, concluding that Mahadev acted in a knee-jerk reaction to save his life.

case_name: Executive Officer, Arulmigu Chokkanatha Swamy Koil Trust, Virudhunagar vs. Chandran & Ors.
text: Case: Executive Officer, Arulmigu Chokkanatha Swamy Koil Trust, Virudhunagar vs. Chandran & Ors.. Date: 10th February 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the property claimed by the plaintiff, Chandran, was rightfully his, despite the temple's assertion of ownership and possession over the same property for a long duration. Chandran sought a declaration of his ownership of 2 acres and 73 cents of land in Survey No. 188 and a mandatory injunction to correct revenue records to reflect his ownership. The High Court reversed the judgements of the trial court and the First Appellate Court, which had dismissed Chandran's suit, and instead decreed in favor of Chandran, directing corrections to the revenue records. The Supreme Court upheld the findings of the trial court and the First Appellate Court that the plaintiff, Chandran, failed to prove his title to the suit property and that the temple was the rightful owner in possession. The Supreme Court found the High Court's judgement erroneous because it failed to address the issue of non-joinder of a necessary party (Janaki Ammal) and wrongly decreed the suit without proper evidence of Chandran's title and possession. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgement of the High Court, and restored the judgement of the trial court and the First Appellate Court, thereby dismissing Chandran's suit.

case_name: Extra Judicial Execution Victim Families Association vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Extra Judicial Execution Victim Families Association vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 14th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involved allegations of 1,528 fake encounter deaths in Manipur by police and armed forces personnel, raising questions about constitutional violations. The Supreme Court directed the registration of FIRs for the 32 deaths where Commissions of Inquiry found evidence of excessive or retaliatory force by the police and armed forces. The Judicial Inquiry and High Court category examined 37 cases, with several resulting in compensation being awarded to the victims’ families. The NHRC reviewed 20 cases of alleged fake encounters, recommending compensation in several and requesting further investigation in others. The Court rejected the argument that delays in investigation justified inaction, emphasizing that crimes involving deaths must not be ignored due to the passage of time. The Supreme Court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to lodge FIRs, investigate, and file charge sheets where necessary. The Court deemed it inappropriate to involve the Manipur Police in the investigations due to allegations of their complicity in some of the fake encounters. The Court stated that the NHRC's guidelines and directives were vital for maintaining transparency and accountability, and their enforcement was necessary to uphold human rights. The Court rejected this argument, stating that access to justice is a constitutional right and public interest litigation enables third parties to seek justice for the victims. The Court reiterated that the rule of law is fundamental to constitutional democracy and must be upheld even in cases involving armed forces and security personnel.

case_name: FERRODOUS ESTATES (PVT.) LTD. vs. P. GOPIRATHNAM (DEAD) & ORS.
text: Case: FERRODOUS ESTATES (PVT.) LTD. vs. P. GOPIRATHNAM (DEAD) & ORS.. Date: 12th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The suit was for specific performance of an agreement to sell the suit property between the appellant and the respondents. The agreement to sell was dated 12th June 1980. FERRODOUS ESTATES contended that the respondents failed to obtain the necessary permissions from the competent authorities under the Tamil Nadu Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1978, which were required to complete the sale transaction. The learned Single Judge decreed the suit in favor of FERRODOUS ESTATES, directing the respondents to execute the sale deed within two months, failing which the sale deed would be executed by the court. The Division Bench held that since the agreement was considered void ab initio due to the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, its repeal did not revive the agreement, and thus, specific performance could not be granted. The Division Bench awarded FERRODOUS ESTATES a compensation of Rs. 2 crores instead of specific performance of the agreement. The Supreme Court held that the agreement to sell was not void ab initio and could be enforced, subject to obtaining necessary permissions, and thus reversed the Division Bench's decision.

case_name: Fainul Khan & Ors. vs. State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Fainul Khan & Ors. vs. State of Jharkhand. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants were convicted under Sections 302/149, 323/149, and 147 IPC, and sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder and other offences. The deceased was assaulted with spears and lathis, resulting in fatal injuries, while two eyewitnesses also sustained injuries during the attack. The appellants contended that the charges were defective, key incriminating questions were not put to them under Section 313 CrPC, and that there were inconsistencies in the prosecution's evidence. P.W.7 and P.W.8 were injured eyewitnesses who testified about the assault on the deceased and themselves during the incident. The Court held that the defective charge under Section 147 IPC did not prejudice the appellants, as they were aware of the charges and evidence against them. The medical evidence supported the testimonies of P.W.7 and P.W.8, corroborating their accounts of the injuries sustained during the incident. The Court found that relevant questions were put to the appellants, and there was no evidence of material prejudice or failure of justice. The defense argued that the absence of injury reports discredited the witnesses, but the Court deemed it a case of defective investigation rather than a basis to doubt their credibility. The Court ruled that the appellants shared a common object to commit the offence, as evidenced by their coordinated actions during the assault. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of the appellants and dismissed their appeals, directing them to surrender to serve the remainder of their sentences. The Court emphasized balancing the rights of the accused to a fair trial with the rights of the victim and society for justice, rejecting unwarranted presumptions of prejudice.

case_name: Faizabad-Ayodhya Development Authority vs. Dr. Rajesh Kumar Pandey & Ors.
text: Case: Faizabad-Ayodhya Development Authority vs. Dr. Rajesh Kumar Pandey & Ors.. Date: 6th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The authority was unable to declare the award due to interim orders issued by the High Court, which prevented further proceedings in the acquisition process. The Supreme Court held that the period of interim orders must be excluded, as these orders imposed limitations on the acquiring authority's ability to proceed with the award declaration. The Court applied principles such as 'no one should be prejudiced by an act of the Court' and 'the law does not compel the impossible' to justify excluding delays caused by court-imposed stays. The judgment reinforces that delays caused by court orders cannot be attributed to the acquiring authority and ensures fairness in applying compensation provisions. The Court clarified that Section 24 of the 2013 Act applies only when an award under Section 11 of the 1894 Act has not been made due to inaction, and not when court orders have caused delays.

case_name: Federation Haj PTOs of India vs. Union of India
text: Case: Federation Haj PTOs of India vs. Union of India. Date: 4th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue raised is the eligibility conditions and other provisions contained in the Haj Policy 2019-2023 formulated by the Government of India. The Haj Policy 2019-2023 was formulated based on data collected and compiled in a study by IIT Delhi, after inviting and considering suggestions and comments from stakeholders including PTOs/HGOs. Changes included renaming HGOs to Haj Group Organisers, reducing security deposit amounts, modifying the distribution formula for seat allocation, and introducing a mid-term review of the policy. The petitioners argued that the turnover requirements of Rs. 5 crores and Rs. 3 crores respectively were exceptionally high and could lead to high package rates for pilgrims, which may not be in their interest. The Supreme Court held that the policy decision was based on both experience and financial strength, and it was not manifestly arbitrary or unreasonable. The court emphasized that policy decisions are best left to the Executive. The Supreme Court directed that the petitioner's case should be considered by the competent authority, taking into account the peculiar facts and circumstances, as the petitioner was prevented from achieving the turnover due to the respondent's actions. The Supreme Court cited the principle that judicial review of policy decisions is very limited and courts should not interfere unless the policy is against a statute, offends the Constitution, or is manifestly arbitrary, capricious, or mala fide. The Supreme Court disposed of all the writ petitions, directing the competent authority to consider the petitioner's case in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 93 of 2019 and make necessary orders within a week.

case_name: Fedrick Cutinha vs State of Karnataka
text: Case: Fedrick Cutinha vs State of Karnataka. Date: 18th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was correct in overturning the trial court's acquittal of Fedrick Cutinha and Krishnappa Naika @ Kittu Naika and convicting them for murder and causing grievous injuries. They were charged under Sections 302 and 326 read with Section 34 of the IPC for murder and causing grievous injuries. The trial court acquitted all eleven accused persons, including Fedrick Cutinha and Krishnappa Naika, for lack of evidence beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court overturned the trial court's acquittal and convicted Fedrick Cutinha and Krishnappa Naika, sentencing them to life imprisonment for murder and five years for causing grievous injuries. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court failed to provide good reasons for deviating from the trial court's findings and did not establish that the trial court's acquittal was perverse. The Supreme Court emphasized that appellate courts should not interfere with acquittal orders unless there is gross perversity in appreciating the evidence, as there is a double presumption of innocence in favor of the acquitted. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of Fedrick Cutinha and Krishnappa Naika, restoring the trial court's acquittal. The incident occurred on 11th September 1999, involving an attack during the polling day for the Lok Sabha and Assembly Elections, where several individuals were assaulted with knives and iron rods, leading to the death of Lingappa Naika. According to the prosecution, Fedrick Cutinha threw chili powder on Umanath Naika's face, assaulted Balachandra with an iron rod, and kicked Jagdish, but he was not alleged to have caused fatal injuries. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court failed to provide an opportunity for the accused to be heard on the quantum of sentence before sentencing them, which is required under Section 235(2) of the CrPC.

case_name: Fekan Yadav vs. Satendra Yadav @ Boss Yadav & Ors.
text: Case: Fekan Yadav vs. Satendra Yadav @ Boss Yadav & Ors.. Date: 19th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting anticipatory bail to respondents 1 and 2 in a case involving the alleged kidnapping of the appellant's son, Bittu Kumar. The respondents were accused of kidnapping the appellant's son, Bittu Kumar, on 3rd January 2017, following threats made by respondent no. 1 to make the appellant issueless. The appellant argued that given the gravity of the accusations and the ongoing investigation, the High Court was not justified in granting anticipatory bail to respondents 1 and 2, as their custodial interrogation was necessary. The High Court granted anticipatory bail to the respondents, without assigning detailed reasons, which was later challenged by the appellant in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not consider the gravity of the accusations and the necessity for custodial interrogation, thus setting aside the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail to the respondents. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order dated 27th April 2017, and revoked the anticipatory bail granted to respondents 1 and 2.

case_name: Food Corporation of India & Ors. vs. Abhijit Paul
text: Case: Food Corporation of India & Ors. vs. Abhijit Paul. Date: 18th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the demurrages imposed on the Food Corporation of India (FCI) by the Railways can be recovered by the FCI from the contractors as 'charges' recoverable under clause XII (a) of the contract. Both the Single Judge and the Division Bench of the High Court of Tripura held that demurrages cannot be recovered as a charge by the FCI from the contractors under the clauses of the contract. The contract was for transporting foodgrains from railway siding, Churaibari in Assam, to Food Security Depot Chandrapur in Tripura, on a regular basis for a period of two years. The FCI demanded reimbursement of the amount of demurrages imposed on it by the Railways due to the contractor's inability to provide trucks at railway sidings, which inhibited the FCI from unloading foodgrains from railway wagons within the 'free time' specified by the Railways. The writ petition was allowed by the Single Judge of the High Court, which held that the FCI was only entitled to recover losses incurred due to the contractor's dereliction of duties under the contract, but not for losses causally distant from the contractor's actions. The Corporation was directed to settle its claims through a civil suit of recovery. The Supreme Court concluded that the expression 'charges' in clause XII (a) of the contract did not include liability for demurrages, and hence, the FCI cannot impose and collect demurrages from the contractors.

case_name: Fr. Issac Mattammel Cor-Episcopa vs. St. Mary's Orthodox Syrian Church & Ors.
text: Case: Fr. Issac Mattammel Cor-Episcopa vs. St. Mary's Orthodox Syrian Church & Ors.. Date: 6th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court's interim order was passed in direct contravention of its binding decision in K.S. Varghese, which is against judicial discipline and propriety. The Court clarified that the 1934 Constitution governs the affairs of Malankara Church, and no individual parish church can adopt a new constitution or parallel system of administration. The Court predicted that non-compliance with its judgments would lead to chaos, undermine judicial discipline, and create unnecessary litigation. The Court emphasized that judgments in representative suits, such as the 1995 judgment and the K.S. Varghese case, are binding on all concerned parties, including parishioners and church authorities. The Court directed all pending litigations on similar disputes to be decided in line with its decision in K.S. Varghese and to avoid further deviation from binding precedents.

case_name: Future Coupons Private Limited & Ors. vs. Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC & Ors.
text: Case: Future Coupons Private Limited & Ors. vs. Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC & Ors.. Date: 15th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The legal dispute was initiated by Amazon due to a sale transaction between Future Retail Limited (FRL) and the Reliance Group, which Amazon claimed violated their agreements with Future Coupons Private Limited (FCPL). Amazon initiated arbitration proceedings before the Singapore International Arbitration Center (SIAC) and sought an emergency relief to prevent the transaction. The Delhi High Court, by order dated 21st December 2020, concluded that the regulatory authorities had to pass appropriate orders considering the representations of both FRL and Amazon before granting approvals for the transaction between FRL and the Reliance Group. The Emergency Arbitrator, by order dated 25th October 2020, injuncted FRL from taking any steps to materialize the deal with Reliance, including proceedings before various regulatory authorities. The Arbitral Tribunal later dismissed the applications filed by FRL and FCPL to vacate this award. The Supreme Court of India allowed the NCLT proceedings to continue without culminating in a final order of sanction of the scheme, as per its order dated 22nd February 2021. Later, the court issued detailed orders for reconsideration by the Delhi High Court on the matter. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) had approved the scheme following the filing of the FRL suit. However, the proceedings for the final sanctioning of the scheme by NCLT were pending. The Supreme Court granted liberty to FRL to approach the Delhi High Court to seek continuation of the NCLT proceedings beyond the 8th stage (Meeting of Shareholders and Creditors) and requested the High Court to consider all contentions and pass appropriate orders expeditiously.

case_name: Future Coupons Private Limited & Ors. vs. Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC & Ors.
text: Case: Future Coupons Private Limited & Ors. vs. Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC & Ors.. Date: 1st February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves multiple civil appeals arising from the dispute between Future Coupons Private Limited (FCPL), Future Retail Limited (FRL), and Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC. The appeals challenge various orders of the Delhi High Court related to the Amazon-Future dispute, specifically concerning arbitration agreements, shareholding agreements, and the sale of retail assets to the Reliance Group. Amazon entered into Shareholder and Share-Subscription Agreements with FCPL on 22nd August 2019, intending to acquire a 49% stake in FCPL. These agreements included an arbitration agreement to settle disputes according to the Arbitration Rules of the Singapore International Arbitration Center (SIAC). In March 2020, FRL's Board decided to sell its retail businesses and assets to the Reliance Group for over Rs. 25,000 crores due to business downturns caused by COVID-19 lockdowns and the risk of insolvency due to outstanding loans of about Rs. 20,000 crores. This sale aimed to alleviate FRL's financial position and protect employment for around 25,000 employees of the Future Group. Amazon initiated arbitration proceedings before the SIAC and sought an emergency relief to prevent FRL and FCPL from proceeding with the transaction. On 25th October 2020, the Emergency Arbitrator passed an interim award in favor of Amazon, directing FRL and FCPL to maintain the status quo regarding the transaction. The Emergency Arbitrator's interim award was challenged in the Delhi High Court, which resulted in contrasting orders. Amazon's enforcement of the award was initially upheld, but later appeals and legal proceedings, including hearings in the Supreme Court, addressed the validity and enforcement of the interim award and arbitration agreements. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the learned Single Judge dated 2nd February 2021 and 18th March 2021, which enforced the Emergency Arbitrator's interim award. The Court remitted the matter back to the Delhi High Court for reconsideration on its own merits, emphasizing the need for proper adherence to principles of natural justice and procedural fairness. The Supreme Court addressed two main legal questions: (1) Whether an Emergency Arbitrator's Award falls within the contemplation of the Arbitration Act, and (2) Whether an order passed under Section 17(2) of the Arbitration Act, in enforcement proceedings, is appealable under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act. The Court affirmed that the Emergency Arbitrator's Award is valid under the Arbitration Act and that no appeal lies against an enforcement order under Section 17(2).

case_name: G. Saraswathi & Anr. vs. Rathinammal & Ors.
text: Case: G. Saraswathi & Anr. vs. Rathinammal & Ors.. Date: 15th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Division Bench of the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellants' Letters Patent Appeal, which sought specific performance of an agreement. The Trial Court decreed the appellants' suit for specific performance of the agreement by judgment/decree dated 3rd July 1984. The Single Bench of the High Court allowed the respondents' appeal, set aside the judgment/decree of the Trial Court, and dismissed the appellants' suit by judgment/decree dated 30th October 1998. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the Letters Patent Appeal by order dated 21st April 2004, confirming the judgment and decree of the Single Bench. The Supreme Court set aside the order because the Division Bench dismissed the appeal cursorily without dealing with any issues or arguments and without providing reasoning, which did not conform to the requirements of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Supreme Court directed the Division Bench of the High Court to decide the appeal afresh on merits in accordance with the law, providing reasoned judgments and dealing with the issues and arguments presented by the parties. No, the Supreme Court refrained from making any observations on the merits of the controversy, leaving it to the High Court to decide the appeal strictly in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to ensure the expeditious disposal of the appeal, noting that the appeal was quite old.

case_name: GOOGLE INDIA PRIVATE LIMITED VERSUS M/S. VISAKHA INDUSTRIES AND ANOTHER
text: Case: GOOGLE INDIA PRIVATE LIMITED VERSUS M/S. VISAKHA INDUSTRIES AND ANOTHER. Date: 10th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves Google India Private Limited, the appellant, who is the second accused in a criminal complaint filed by Visakha Industries, the first respondent. The complaint involves allegations of defamation through articles posted in the Ban Asbestos India group hosted by Google. The complaint seeks to invoke Sections 120B, 500, and 501 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The first accused is alleged to be the Coordinator of Ban Asbestos India, a group hosted by Google India Private Limited, and is accused of posting defamatory articles against Visakha Industries. The appellant made over the legal notice to its parent entity, Google LLC, which owns the Google Group platforms. Google LLC replied to the legal notice and requested specific URLs of the objectionable content from the complainant. The civil suit was initially dismissed, but the complainant succeeded in the first appeal, and the suit was decreed. However, the High Court allowed the second appeal, dismissing the suit against the appellant. The High Court found that the appellant could not claim exemption under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, either before or after its amendment, as the appellant did not take action to block the defamatory content despite being notified. The appellant argued that it is not the intermediary as it does not provide Google Groups services, which are provided by its parent company, Google LLC. The appellant also claimed that it is only a reseller of Google LLC Ads program in India. The Supreme Court noted that an intermediary is not liable for third-party information or data unless it has actual knowledge of the content or fails to remove or disable access to the material after being notified by a court order or a government agency. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by Google India Private Limited, holding that the appellant did not take action to block the defamatory content despite being notified and thus could not claim exemption under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act.

case_name: GPSK Capital Private Limited vs. The Securities and Exchange Board of India
text: Case: GPSK Capital Private Limited vs. The Securities and Exchange Board of India. Date: 20th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether GPSK Capital Private Limited was entitled to exemption from payment of registration fees for the period for which the individual Srikant Mantri had already paid fees after converting his individual membership to a corporate entity. GPSK Capital Private Limited argued that since Srikant Mantri had already paid the fees as an individual member, the company, after converting the individual membership to a corporate entity, should be exempt from paying the fees again. SEBI held that the company did not satisfy the conditions of Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations because Srikant Mantri was not a whole-time director during the relevant period, and hence the company was not eligible for fee exemption. The SAT affirmed SEBI's decision, stating that the company failed to meet the conditions under Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations, and thus was not entitled to the fee exemption. The Supreme Court upheld the decisions of SEBI and the SAT, concluding that GPSK Capital Private Limited did not fulfill the required conditions and was therefore not entitled to the fee continuity benefits. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because GPSK Capital Private Limited failed to prove that it satisfied the conditions laid out in Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations, particularly that Srikant Mantri was not a whole-time director during the relevant period. The Supreme Court clarified that a stock broker must obtain a separate certificate of registration from SEBI for each stock exchange where they operate, and must pay the ad valorem fee prescribed for each certificate of registration. The Supreme Court noted that SEBI's policy aimed to encourage brokers to corporatize to ensure better regulatory control and transparency. However, the court affirmed that the benefits of fee exemption were only available if the conditions specified, such as the whole-time directorship and shareholding requirements, were met.

SEBI held that the company did not satisfy the conditions of Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations because Srikant Mantri was not a whole-time director during the relevant period, and hence the company was not eligible for fee exemption.
The SAT affirmed SEBI's decision, stating that the company failed to meet the conditions under Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations, and thus was not entitled to the fee exemption.

The Supreme Court upheld the decisions of SEBI and the SAT, concluding that GPSK Capital Private Limited did not fulfill the required conditions and was therefore not entitled to the fee continuity benefits.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because GPSK Capital Private Limited failed to prove that it satisfied the conditions laid out in Para 4 of Schedule III of the Regulations, particularly that Srikant Mantri was not a whole-time director during the relevant period.

The Supreme Court clarified that a stock broker must obtain a separate certificate of registration from SEBI for each stock exchange where they operate, and must pay the ad valorem fee prescribed for each certificate of registration.

The Supreme Court noted that SEBI's policy aimed to encourage brokers to corporatize to ensure better regulatory control and transparency. However, the court affirmed that the benefits of fee exemption were only available if the conditions specified, such as the whole-time directorship and shareholding requirements, were met.

case_name: GULF OIL CORPORATION LTD. vs. THE STATE OF TELANGANA & ORS.
text: Case: GULF OIL CORPORATION LTD. vs. THE STATE OF TELANGANA & ORS.. Date: 13th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the leasehold rights of Gulf Oil Corporation Ltd. on the land granted to Sri Udasin Mutt by the Nizam of Hyderabad could be evicted under the provisions of the Telangana Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987. Gulf Oil Corporation Ltd. argued that they had valid lease agreements for the land, executed with the permission of the government, and that the leases were for industrial purposes, not agricultural land. The State of Telangana argued that the land in question was agricultural land and, according to Section 82 of the Telangana Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, any lease of agricultural land to non-landless poor individuals was automatically canceled. The Endowments Tribunal concluded that the land was agricultural land, and thus the lease agreements were null and void under Section 82 of the 1987 Act, as they were not approved by the government. The Supreme Court upheld the decisions of the Endowments Tribunal and the High Court, concluding that the leases were invalid as the land was agricultural and the lease agreements lacked prior government approval as required by the law. The Supreme Court emphasized that any lease of agricultural land belonging to charitable or religious institutions must have prior government approval, and failure to obtain such approval renders the lease null and void. The Supreme Court stated that even if the land was used for non-agricultural purposes, it did not change the nature of the land being classified as agricultural, and thus the lease agreements were still subject to the provisions of the 1987 Act. The land in question was originally granted as inam land by the Nizam of Hyderabad to Sri Udasin Mutt in 1873 and was subsequently leased to M/s Indian Detonators, the predecessor of Gulf Oil Corporation Ltd., for industrial use.
