case_name: Gadadhar Chandra vs. The State of West Bengal
text: Case: Gadadhar Chandra vs. The State of West Bengal. Date: 15th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Gadadhar Chandra's conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC was justified, given the involvement of another accused, Arjun Mondal, in the murder of Purna Chandra Ghosh. The appellant, Gadadhar Chandra, and the other accused, Arjun Mondal, were jointly involved in the incident leading to the death of Purna Chandra Ghosh. Gadadhar Chandra was charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC for the murder of Purna Chandra Ghosh. The evidence against Gadadhar Chandra included the testimony of PW1, who witnessed the appellant brandishing a knife and threatening to assault PW1 while Arjun Mondal stabbed the deceased. Gadadhar Chandra's counsel argued that Section 34 IPC was not applicable as there was no prior concert or pre-arranged plan to kill the deceased, and the appellant did not actively participate in the stabbing. The Supreme Court found the prosecution's case doubtful due to the non-examination of two crucial eyewitnesses, Susanta Kr. Chandra and Rabu, who were present with the appellant and Arjun before the incident. The non-recovery of the knife used by Gadadhar Chandra weakened the prosecution's case, as the knife allegedly used by Arjun was recovered, but not the one used by the appellant. The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the ingredients of Section 34 IPC, which pre-supposes a prior concert and a pre-arranged plan, and therefore, the appellant's conviction under this section was not justified. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgments and orders of the High Court and Sessions Court, acquitted Gadadhar Chandra of the charges against him, and allowed the appeal. The prosecution's case was that Gadadhar Chandra and Arjun Mondal attacked Purna Chandra Ghosh near the railway gate, with Arjun stabbing the deceased while Gadadhar brandished a knife and threatened PW1. The Supreme Court directed that all pending applications, if any, stand disposed of along with the main appeal.

case_name: Gaddipati Divija & Anr. vs. Pathuri Samrajyam & Ors.
text: Case: Gaddipati Divija & Anr. vs. Pathuri Samrajyam & Ors.. Date: 18th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in allowing Respondent No. 1's appeal and decreeing the suit for specific performance by holding that the deceased G. Venugopala Rao and his legal heirs failed to perform their obligation with regard to getting the property measured and demarcated, while Respondent No. 1 was always ready and willing to perform her part of the contract by paying the balance sale consideration. The appellants were Gaddipati Divija and another minor child, represented by their maternal grandmother. They were the minor children of G. Venugopala Rao. The Trial Court partly decreed and partly dismissed the suit, holding that the Plaintiff was entitled to recover the advance amount of Rs. 4,00,000/- paid towards sale consideration with future interest, but not entitled to specific performance of the contract. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the Trial Court's judgment, and decreed the suit for specific performance, directing the legal heirs of G. Venugopala Rao to execute the sale deed in favor of Respondent No. 1 after demarcating the property and receiving the balance sale consideration. The appellants sought to recall the judgment on the ground that they were not heard during the proceedings. However, the High Court noted that there was no representation on behalf of the appellants despite multiple opportunities and dismissed the recall petition. G. Venugopala Rao was obligated to measure and demarcate the suit schedule property within three months, following which Respondent No. 1 was to pay the balance sale consideration. The High Court held that Respondent No. 1 was always ready and willing to perform her part of the contract by paying the balance sale consideration, and that this was supported by her conduct and the testimony of her husband. Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, requires the plaintiff to aver and prove that they have performed or have always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract. In this case, the High Court found that Respondent No. 1 fulfilled this requirement, while the appellants and their predecessor failed to perform their obligations.

case_name: Gajanan Marotrao Nimje & Ors. vs The Reserve Bank of India & Ors.
text: Case: Gajanan Marotrao Nimje & Ors. vs The Reserve Bank of India & Ors.. Date: 11th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants, who were appointed under the Scheduled Tribe (ST) quota but later found not to belong to the ST category, should be terminated from service and have their benefits recovered. The Division Bench of the High Court directed the termination of the appellants from service and the recovery of all benefits they had earned, as they did not belong to the Scheduled Tribe category. The earlier judgment dated 1st November 2012 protected the appointments of employees who had been confirmed in service before 28th November 2000, provided they gave an undertaking to give up their claim as belonging to Scheduled Tribes and agreed to be treated as General Category employees. The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in passing an omnibus order for termination and recovery of benefits, especially considering the long service of the appellants and the absence of any fraud at the time of their appointment. The Supreme Court ordered that the appellants be placed below the last general category candidate as of 28th November 2000 and continue as such until their superannuation. The benefits earned after 28th November 2000 as reserved category candidates would be surrendered or recovered. The Supreme Court ruled that there would be no recovery of any benefits from employees who had already superannuated. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to dispose of all contempt proceedings against the officers of the Reserve Bank of India for non-implementation of the impugned judgment dated 13th April 2018, and indicated that the notification dated 24th December 2013 should be reconsidered.

case_name: Gajubha Jadeja Jesar vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Gajubha Jadeja Jesar vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 10th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the project proponent's Cold Rolled Coils unit required prior environmental clearance under the Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) notification dated 14th September 2006. The NGT concluded that the Cold Rolled Coils unit required an environmental clearance and initially stayed all activities of the project. However, the NGT later allowed the unit to operate for one year to obtain the necessary clearance, based on a recommendation from the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC). The EAC recommended granting a one-year grace period for the Cold Rolled Coils unit to obtain the required environmental clearance, given the ambiguity in the EIA notification and the fact that the unit was already operating with consent from the State Pollution Control Board. The Ministry filed an affidavit supporting the EAC's recommendation, agreeing to provide a one-year grace period for units like the Cold Rolled Coils unit to obtain environmental clearance, addressing the ambiguity in the EIA notification. The Supreme Court upheld the NGT's decision, recognizing that the NGT acted within its jurisdiction to ensure sustainable development. The Court noted that the ambiguity in the EIA notification justified the one-year grace period for compliance. The Supreme Court quashed the closure notice issued by the Gujarat State Pollution Control Board, allowing the Cold Rolled Coils unit to operate within the one-year period to obtain the necessary environmental clearance as per the amended EIA notification. The Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 3116 of 2020 and allowed Civil Appeal No. 3576 of 2020, permitting the Cold Rolled Coils unit to continue operating under the one-year grace period to obtain environmental clearance and quashing the closure notice.

case_name: Ganesan vs. State Represented by its Inspector of Police
text: Case: Ganesan vs. State Represented by its Inspector of Police. Date: 14th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ganesan was accused of offences punishable under Section 7 read with Section 8 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, involving the sexual molestation of a minor girl. The trial court convicted Ganesan under Section 7 of the POCSO Act and sentenced him to three years rigorous imprisonment, along with an order to pay rupees one lakh as compensation to the victim. The High Court modified the trial court's compensation order, directing the State to pay the compensation to the victim and recover it from Ganesan if it found he had sufficient means. Ganesan's counsel argued that no sufficient opportunity was given to the accused before the High Court, as the legal aid counsel was appointed and heard within four days. The Supreme Court found the victim's testimony to be trustworthy, unblemished, and of sterling quality, thereby justifying the conviction based on her sole testimony. The Supreme Court dismissed Ganesan's appeal, upholding the conviction and the three-year rigorous imprisonment sentence as imposed by the trial court.

case_name: Gangadhar alias Gangaram vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Gangadhar alias Gangaram vs. State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 5th August 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Gangadhar was charged under Section 8C read with Section 20(b)(ii)(c) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act for the recovery of 48 Kgs 200 gms of cannabis (ganja). The trial court convicted Gangadhar, sentencing him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment with a default stipulation. Gangadhar was convicted based on the presumption of ownership of the house where the ganja was recovered, supported by the 2008 voters' list, despite his defense that he had sold the house to co-accused Gokul Dangi. The Supreme Court found the investigation flawed because it failed to verify the sale agreement, did not investigate the village panchayat records, and relied on a 2008 voters' list without confirming the current ownership. The sale agreement dated 12th June 2009, which Gangadhar presented the day after the search, indicated that he had sold the house to Gokul Dangi. However, the police did not investigate its genuineness. The Supreme Court stated that the presumption of possession under the NDPS Act is rebuttable and does not dispense with the prosecution's obligation to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court found that the evidence of ownership and possession was inconclusive and flawed, as the investigation did not properly verify the sale agreement or the panchayat records. The Supreme Court emphasized that the prosecution must establish a prima facie case beyond reasonable doubt before the burden of proof shifts to the accused. In this case, the prosecution failed to meet this burden. The Supreme Court set aside Gangadhar's conviction and acquitted him, directing his immediate release unless wanted in any other case. The Supreme Court criticized the police investigation as extremely casual, perfunctory, and shoddy, which denied Gangadhar the right to a fair investigation and trial. The Supreme Court's decision led to the acquittal and immediate release of Gangadhar, concluding that he had suffered incarceration for an offence he had not committed due to a flawed investigation.

case_name: Garg Builders vs. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited
text: Case: Garg Builders vs. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited. Date: 4th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellant, Garg Builders, was entitled to pendente lite interest on the award amount despite the interest barring clause in the contract. Clause 17 of the contract stipulated that no interest shall be payable by BHEL on Earnest Money Deposit, Security Deposit, or on any moneys due to the contractor. The Arbitrator awarded pendente lite interest at the rate of 10% per annum to Garg Builders on the award amount from the date of filing of the claim petition until the realization of the award amount, stating there was no prohibition in the contract regarding such interest. The Delhi High Court, both the Single Judge and Division Bench, set aside the Arbitrator's award regarding pendente lite interest, stating that Clause 17 of the contract expressly barred such interest and the Arbitrator had exceeded his jurisdiction. The Supreme Court held that under Section 31(7)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, if the contract expressly bars payment of interest, the Arbitrator does not have the power to award pendente lite interest. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, confirming that the Arbitrator's award of pendente lite interest was not sustainable due to the express prohibition in the contract. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Garg Builders, upholding the High Court's decision to set aside the award of pendente lite interest, and directed both parties to bear their own costs.

case_name: Gas Point Petroleum India Limited vs Rajendra Marothi & Ors.
text: Case: Gas Point Petroleum India Limited vs Rajendra Marothi & Ors.. Date: 10th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the auction sale of the property of National Ginni Enterprises was valid, given the objections raised by Gas Point Petroleum India Limited regarding alleged irregularities in the auction process. Gas Point Petroleum India Limited raised objections that the auction sale violated Order 21 Rule 84 and Order 21 Rule 85 of the CPC, as the auction purchaser did not deposit 25% of the sale amount immediately and the balance 75% within the prescribed 15-day period. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh dismissed the objections raised by Gas Point Petroleum India Limited, restored the order passed by the Executing Court, and set aside the lower Appellate Court's order, stating that the appellant failed to establish any irregularity or fraud in the auction sale. The Supreme Court found that there was non-compliance with the mandatory provisions of Order 21 Rule 84 and Order 21 Rule 85 of the CPC, as the auction purchaser did not deposit the required amounts within the stipulated time frame, rendering the auction sale invalid. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order, set aside the auction sale, and restored the lower Appellate Court's order, allowing Gas Point Petroleum India Limited's objections and declaring the auction sale invalid due to non-compliance with the relevant provisions of the CPC. The Supreme Court directed that it would be open for the respondent (auction purchaser) to get back the amount deposited by him, which was lying with the Executing Court. The Supreme Court emphasized that the provisions of Order 21 Rule 84 and Rule 85 of the CPC are mandatory, and non-compliance with these provisions renders the auction sale invalid. The purchaser must deposit 25% of the sale amount immediately and the balance within 15 days from the date of the sale.

case_name: Gaurav Aseem Avtej vs U.P. State Sugar Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Gaurav Aseem Avtej vs U.P. State Sugar Corporation Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 20th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the land leased by the plaintiffs to M/s Shiv Prasad Banarasi Das Sugar Mills vested in the State Government under the Uttar Pradesh Sugar Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1971, and whether the plaintiffs were entitled to evict the defendant-corporation and recover arrears of rent. The plaintiffs contended that the land in dispute, which was leased out for parking vehicles, did not vest in the State Government under the 1971 Act, and that they retained ownership and rights to evict the defendants and recover arrears of rent. The Trial Court partially decreed the suit, allowing recovery of arrears of rent but refusing eviction. The First Appellate Court reversed the Trial Court's decision, decreeing the suit in favor of the plaintiffs and ordering eviction of the defendant-corporation. The High Court allowed the second appeals, reversing the First Appellate Court's decision and dismissing the suit, holding that the land vested in the State Government under the 1950 Act and the 1971 Act, and that the plaintiffs had lost all rights to the property. The Supreme Court interpreted that under the 1971 Act, all lands held or occupied for the purposes of the factory, including those held on lease, vested in the State Government. The Court emphasized that the intention of the legislature was to secure all assets used for the factory's purposes. The Supreme Court held that the 1950 Act was not applicable to the land in dispute as it was being used for non-agricultural purposes prior to the Act's enforcement, and the land was declared as non-agricultural under Section 143 of the Act in 1972. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision that the land vested in the State Government under the 1971 Act. The Court also stated that the plaintiffs could pursue any available remedies for compensation for their lands.

The plaintiffs contended that the land in dispute, which was leased out for parking vehicles, did not vest in the State Government under the 1971 Act, and that they retained ownership and rights to evict the defendants and recover arrears of rent.

The Trial Court partially decreed the suit, allowing recovery of arrears of rent but refusing eviction. The First Appellate Court reversed the Trial Court's decision, decreeing the suit in favor of the plaintiffs and ordering eviction of the defendant-corporation.

The High Court allowed the second appeals, reversing the First Appellate Court's decision and dismissing the suit, holding that the land vested in the State Government under the 1950 Act and the 1971 Act, and that the plaintiffs had lost all rights to the property.

The Supreme Court interpreted that under the 1971 Act, all lands held or occupied for the purposes of the factory, including those held on lease, vested in the State Government. The Court emphasized that the intention of the legislature was to secure all assets used for the factory's purposes.

The Supreme Court held that the 1950 Act was not applicable to the land in dispute as it was being used for non-agricultural purposes prior to the Act's enforcement, and the land was declared as non-agricultural under Section 143 of the Act in 1972.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision that the land vested in the State Government under the 1971 Act. The Court also stated that the plaintiffs could pursue any available remedies for compensation for their lands.

case_name: Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 18th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the application filed under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) by the Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. was within the period of limitation, given that the right to sue accrued on 21st July 2011 when the account was declared NPA. The NCLT applied Article 62 of the Limitation Act, which provides a 12-year limitation period for enforcing payment of money secured by a mortgage, and concluded that the application was within limitation. Therefore, the NCLT admitted the Section 7 application. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, following its earlier judgments, and held that the limitation period for the purposes of the IBC would begin running only on and from 1st December 2016, the date when the IBC came into force. The appellant argued that Article 137 of the Limitation Act, a residuary article providing a three-year limitation period, should apply. Since the right to sue accrued on 21st July 2011, the application filed in 2017 was time-barred. The Supreme Court held that Article 62 of the Limitation Act does not apply to applications under Section 7 of the IBC, which are applications and not suits. Instead, Article 137 applies, and since the right to sue accrued on 21st July 2011, the application filed in 2017 was time-barred. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the NCLT and NCLAT, and ruled that the application filed under Section 7 of the IBC was time-barred.

case_name: General Manager East Coast Railway Rail Sadan & Anr. vs. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd.
text: Case: General Manager East Coast Railway Rail Sadan & Anr. vs. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd.. Date: 22nd July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary dispute was regarding the appointment of an arbitrator to adjudicate the dispute between the parties arising out of a contract/agreement dated 29th November 2018. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. sought an interim injunction against the encashment of the Performance Bank Guarantee and forfeiture of the security deposit. The appellants challenged the jurisdiction of the Orissa High Court based on Section 42 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which stipulates that once an application under the Act is made in a court, that court alone has jurisdiction over the arbitral proceedings and all subsequent applications. The Orissa High Court appointed an arbitrator to adjudicate the dispute between the parties, observing that since the appellant, East Coast Railways, did not oppose the appointment of an arbitrator in principle, relegating the respondent to the appropriate High Court would only delay the adjudication of the disputes. The Supreme Court held that the Orissa High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration Act, as the respondent had earlier initiated proceedings under Section 9 of the Act in the court at Visakhapatnam, which meant only the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati had jurisdiction. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the judgment and order of the Orissa High Court, and observed that it would be open for the respondent to submit an application under Section 11(6) of the Act before the competent High Court having jurisdiction, namely the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati.

case_name: Geo Varghese vs The State of Rajasthan & Anr.
text: Case: Geo Varghese vs The State of Rajasthan & Anr.. Date: 5th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the FIR under Section 306 IPC for abetment of suicide filed against Geo Varghese, a Physical Training Teacher, should be quashed. The complainant, mother of the deceased student, alleged that her son committed suicide due to mental harassment and humiliation meted out by Geo Varghese, particularly on 19th and 25th April 2018. The suicide note mentioned 'THANKS GEO (PTI) OF MY SCHOOL' and other statements indicating the student's mental state but did not directly attribute specific acts of harassment by Geo Varghese. The defense argued that the FIR did not disclose any specific acts of harassment or abetment by Geo Varghese that would constitute an offence under Section 306 IPC. They emphasized that disciplining students is part of a teacher's duty and does not amount to instigation to commit suicide. The Supreme Court concluded that there were no specific allegations or evidence indicating that Geo Varghese intended to provoke or instigate the student to commit suicide. Thus, the ingredients of Section 306 IPC were not satisfied. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR against Geo Varghese, stating that continuing the prosecution would be an abuse of the process of law and that the allegations did not prima facie constitute an offence under Section 306 IPC.

case_name: Girraj vs Kiranpal and Others
text: Case: Girraj vs Kiranpal and Others. Date: 8th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the bail granted to five respondent-accused who were allegedly involved in the murder of Girraj's two sons during an incident on 29th November 2019. The High Court granted bail to the accused on the basis of parity, as a co-accused, Narendra, had previously been granted bail. The accused were charged under Sections 147, 148, 149, 302, 307, 323, 342, and 508 of the Indian Penal Code 1860, and Sections 27 and 30 of the Arms Act. The Supreme Court cancelled the bail granted to the accused, stating that the High Court's decision was based on extraneous considerations and was contrary to settled legal principles. The bail was cancelled because the High Court granted it on the basis of parity without considering the seriousness of the offense and the specific allegations against the accused. The High Court justified the bail by stating that there was no criminal history of the accused and that the indiscriminate firing made it difficult to determine who caused the injuries. The cancellation of bail for the co-accused Narendra by the Supreme Court led to the cancellation of bail for the other accused, as their bail was granted on the basis of parity with Narendra. The incident involved the ambush and murder of Girraj's sons, Gajendra and Akash, by the accused, who blocked their passage with a bullock cart and attacked them with firearms. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court failed to consider the seriousness of the offense and the specific allegations against the accused, and granted bail based on extraneous considerations. The Supreme Court directed the accused to surrender within 24 hours of the order being uploaded and granted them the liberty to apply for bail afresh before the High Court. If the accused reapply for bail before the High Court, the outcome will depend on the High Court's consideration of the Supreme Court's observations and the seriousness of the offense.

case_name: Glocal Medical College and Super Speciality Hospital & Research Centre vs. Union of India and Another
text: Case: Glocal Medical College and Super Speciality Hospital & Research Centre vs. Union of India and Another. Date: 1st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the cancellation of conditional permission granted for the establishment of medical colleges and the debarment of these colleges from admitting students for the academic years 2017-18 and 2018-19. The Government of India cancelled the conditional permission for the establishment of the medical colleges, debarred them from admitting students for the next two academic years (2017-18 and 2018-19), and authorized the Medical Council of India (MCI) to encash the bank guarantees submitted by the colleges. The MCI pointed out several deficiencies in the colleges during its inspection on 21st and 22nd December 2016, leading to the recommendation that the colleges be debarred from admitting students and that their bank guarantees be encashed. The Oversight Committee, constituted by the Supreme Court, intervened in the process, permitted the colleges to submit compliance inputs afresh, and eventually recommended the confirmation of the conditional letter of permission for the colleges after dismissing the deficiencies pointed out by the MCI. The Supreme Court set aside the cancellation of permission and debarment of the colleges, stating that the Central Government's decision was unsustainable in law and facts, and ordered a fresh consideration of the materials on record, taking into account the recommendations/views of the MCI, Hearing Committee, DGHS, and the Oversight Committee.

case_name: Gopinathan vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: Gopinathan vs. State of Kerala. Date: 22nd June 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Gopinathan was charged under Section 55(g) and 8(1) read with 8(2) of the Abkari Act for manufacturing arrack. The trial court convicted Gopinathan and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for 5 years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, in default, rigorous imprisonment for 1 year for each offence. The High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for 2 years and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, in default, rigorous imprisonment for 6 months. Gopinathan was apprehended by the police on 25th February 2007 while engaged in manufacturing arrack at a place called Kochethupara in Perunad village. The police seized 40 liters of arrack and 3750 liters of wash from the site. The Supreme Court considered the overall aspects, including the time elapsed since the incident (15 years), Gopinathan's age (63 years), and the absence of criminal antecedents, while modifying the sentence to simple imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- on both counts. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction but modified the sentence to simple imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, in default, simple imprisonment for six months. The Supreme Court found no reason to deviate from the High Court's view, as the evidence presented by PW-1 and PW-3 was credible and nothing significant was elicited from their cross-examination. The Supreme Court directed that all pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of. Gopinathan was arrested for being engaged in the illegal activity of manufacturing arrack in a remote area. The police seized 40 liters of arrack and 3750 liters of wash, which were crucial evidence in proving Gopinathan's involvement in the illegal manufacturing of arrack.

case_name: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs Mother Superior Adoration Convent
text: Case: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs Mother Superior Adoration Convent. Date: 1st March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether buildings used for residential accommodation for nuns and hostels for students qualify for exemption from building tax under Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975. Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975 exempts buildings used principally for religious, charitable, or educational purposes from building tax. The Government of Kerala argued that residential accommodation for nuns and hostels for students are for residential purposes and do not directly involve religious or educational activities, thus not qualifying for exemption under Section 3(1)(b). The Kerala High Court decided to exempt the buildings in question, ruling that the residential accommodations for nuns and hostels for students are integral to religious and educational activities. The Supreme Court concluded that buildings used for residential accommodation for nuns and hostels for students, if used principally for religious or educational purposes, qualify for exemption under Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act. The Government of Kerala filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision to exempt the buildings used by the Mother Superior Adoration Convent from building tax. The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'principally' to mean that the dominant purpose of the building's use must be for religious, charitable, or educational purposes, allowing some incidental residential use. The Supreme Court clarified that if the residential use of a building is integrally connected to its educational or religious purposes, such as nuns residing in a convent for religious training or students living in a hostel for education, the building can be exempted from tax. The decision may lead to more religious and educational institutions claiming tax exemptions for buildings used principally for religious, charitable, or educational purposes, even if they have some residential use. Religious and educational institutions should ensure that the primary use of their buildings is for religious, charitable, or educational purposes and that any residential use is incidental and integrally connected to these primary purposes. The Kerala government should assess whether the hostels are used principally for educational purposes, considering the integral connection between the students' accommodation and their education, to determine eligibility for tax exemptions.

case_name: Government of Maharashtra (Water Resources Department) vs M/S Borse Brothers Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: Government of Maharashtra (Water Resources Department) vs M/S Borse Brothers Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 19th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the judgment in N.V. International v. State of Assam lays down the law correctly regarding the period of limitation for filing appeals under section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The appellant, Government of Maharashtra, argued that the rationale or logic contained in N.V. International should apply only to appeals from section 34 orders, but not to orders passed under other sections such as sections 8, 9, 16, and 17 of the Arbitration Act. The respondent, M/S Borse Brothers Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd., argued that the Government of Maharashtra had not provided a satisfactory explanation for the delay of 131 days in filing the appeal and had not appeared before the High Court with clean hands. The Supreme Court decided that the period of limitation for filing appeals under section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, should not exceed 120 days, including a grace period of 30 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act, aligning with the objective of speedy resolution of disputes in arbitration. The appeals filed by the Government of Maharashtra and Union of India were dismissed by the High Courts of Bombay and Delhi, respectively, for failing to condone the delay in filing the appeals beyond the 120-day period.

case_name: Government of NCT of Delhi & Anr. vs. Shakeel Ahmed & Ors.
text: Case: Government of NCT of Delhi & Anr. vs. Shakeel Ahmed & Ors.. Date: 9th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The High Court of Delhi declared that the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013. The High Court's decision was based on the precedent set by the case of Pune Municipal Corporation and Anr. vs. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki and Ors., which was subsequently overruled by the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors. The Constitution Bench ruled that the word 'or' in Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013, should be read as 'nor' or 'and', meaning that land acquisition proceedings do not lapse if either possession has been taken or compensation has been paid. The appellant argued that possession of the land in question was taken on 4th March 1983, and therefore, the land acquisition proceedings should not be deemed to have lapsed. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's judgement and order, ruling that the land acquisition proceedings had not lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013, and restored the validity of the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The main issue was whether the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, regarding the land in question, were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

case_name: Govind Prasad Kejriwal vs. State of Bihar
text: Case: Govind Prasad Kejriwal vs. State of Bihar. Date: 31st January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Govind Prasad Kejriwal was charged with offences under Sections 323, 341, and 379 of the IPC. The original complaint was filed by Gopal Prasad, the brother of Ramesh Kumar, who was a partner in Kejriwal Films, along with the accused. The dispute was related to a partnership firm called Kejriwal Films and involved allegations of conspiracy, theft, and misappropriation of partnership property. The complainant alleged that Govind Prasad Kejriwal and others broke the locks of Savera Chitra Mandir, removed valuable items, and threatened the complainant. The trial court initially dismissed the complaint, but it was later revived by the Sessions Court, and the trial court took cognizance of the offences under Sections 323, 341, and 379 IPC. Govind Prasad Kejriwal argued that the allegations were part of a civil dispute given a criminal color and that the charges did not constitute any offence under Sections 323, 341, and 379 IPC. The Supreme Court viewed the dispute as purely civil in nature and considered the criminal proceedings an abuse of process of law and the Court. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings against Govind Prasad Kejriwal, setting aside the orders of the trial court and the High Court. The Supreme Court justified its decision by stating that none of the ingredients for the offences under Sections 323, 341, and 379 IPC were satisfied, and continuing the proceedings would be an abuse of process. Relevant actions included an earlier FIR lodged by Govind Prasad Kejriwal against Ramesh Kumar for theft, and a title suit filed by Ramesh Kumar which was later dismissed. The Supreme Court addressed the principle that civil disputes should not be converted into criminal cases, and the legal system should not be used to settle civil disputes through criminal proceedings.

case_name: Govindammal (Dead) By Lrs. and Ors. vs. Vaidiyanathan and Ors.
text: Case: Govindammal (Dead) By Lrs. and Ors. vs. Vaidiyanathan and Ors.. Date: 23rd October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants were Govindammal (Dead) By Lrs. and others, and the respondents were Vaidiyanathan and others. The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the 'A schedule' property belongs to them or, alternatively, for partition of half share in the 'B schedule' property of which 'A schedule' is a part. The 'A schedule' property was allotted to Narayanaswamy and Manickam, the descendants of Pazanivelu Mudaliar, in a partition that took place on 21st July 1912. case_name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited vs. Mr. Amit Gupta & Ors.
text: Case: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited vs. Mr. Amit Gupta & Ors.. Date: 8th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue was whether the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) could prevent the termination of a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The default notices were issued under Article 9.2.1(e) and Article 9.2.1(a) of the PPA, citing the initiation of CIRP as an event of default and alleging operational and maintenance defaults. The NCLT restrained Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited from terminating the PPA, citing its importance in maintaining the Corporate Debtor as a going concern during CIRP. The issue was whether NCLT's jurisdiction extended to disputes arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution process, including the termination of PPAs. The NCLAT clarified that the termination of the PPA solely due to the initiation of CIRP would jeopardize the Corporate Debtor's ability to continue as a going concern. The Supreme Court upheld that the NCLT had jurisdiction to adjudicate on the matter as it arose directly from the insolvency resolution process of the Corporate Debtor.

case_name: Gulab vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Gulab vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 9th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Gulab was charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC for murder, while Idrish was charged under Section 302 of the IPC. The motive behind the murder was a previous enmity due to a fight between Hanifa and Idrish, which had led to Hanifa being accused in a criminal case. The prosecution presented the testimonies of three eyewitnesses (PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3) who stated that they saw Idrish shoot Hanifa after Gulab exhorted him to kill Hanifa, referring to him as an enemy. The High Court upheld Gulab's conviction because his presence at the crime scene and his act of exhorting Idrish to kill Hanifa demonstrated a common intention to commit the murder. The defense argued that there was an unexplained delay in lodging the FIR, that the eyewitnesses were interested witnesses due to their relationship with the deceased, and that there were inconsistencies in their testimonies. The Supreme Court found that the delay in lodging the FIR was satisfactorily explained due to the fear of the accused and the distance of the police station from the place of occurrence. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court and upheld by the High Court, thereby affirming the life imprisonment sentence for Gulab.

case_name: Guna Mahto vs. State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Guna Mahto vs. State of Jharkhand. Date: 16th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Guna Mahto was charged with the murder of his wife, Smt. Deomatiya Devi, under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and causing the disappearance of evidence under Section 201 IPC. The Trial Court convicted Guna Mahto of murdering his wife and sentenced him to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC and two years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 201 IPC. The High Court affirmed Guna Mahto's conviction based on the ocular evidence of witnesses Banaudhi Mahto (PW-2), Samodhi Yadav (PW-9), and Nandish Yadav (PW-10), despite the Investigation Officer not being examined. The prosecution presented evidence that Guna Mahto committed the murder of his wife and dumped her body in the village well. The dead body was recovered, and the post-mortem report indicated death by hemorrhage and shock due to injuries on the neck. The Supreme Court found the prosecution's case doubtful due to the non-examination of the Investigation Officer, lack of concrete evidence linking Guna Mahto to the crime, and reliance on hearsay evidence from the witnesses. The Supreme Court concluded that the evidence presented did not prove the guilt of Guna Mahto beyond reasonable doubt, emphasizing that suspicion alone cannot be the basis for conviction. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court and affirmed by the High Court, thereby acquitting Guna Mahto of the charges.

case_name: Guruviah & Ors. vs. The State represented by the Inspector of Police
text: Case: Guruviah & Ors. vs. The State represented by the Inspector of Police. Date: 20th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the conviction of the appellants under Sections 13(1)(d), 13(2), and 12 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The appellants were village assistants in the office of the village administrative officer. The appellants were accused of accepting illegal gratification for signing necessary papers to facilitate the transfer of an electric connection. The complaint was lodged by P.W.2 before the Additional Superintendent of Police (Vigilance and Anti-Corruption). The amount of illegal gratification demanded was Rs. 600. The appellants argued that they did not demand any illegal gratification and believed the money received was towards arrears of land tax. The prosecution argued that the appellants were in league with the village administrative officer and the circumstantial evidence pointed towards their involvement in obtaining illegal gratification. The Supreme Court held that the mere absence of direct evidence for demand and acceptance or conspiracy was irrelevant in view of the circumstantial evidence available, which pointed towards the appellants' involvement. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the conviction and sentence of the appellants, and directed them to surrender forthwith for serving out their remaining sentence. The Supreme Court rejected the defence that the appellants received the money in good faith towards arrears of land tax, noting that the land tax for the relevant period had already been cancelled by the State Government. The sodium carbonate solution test confirmed that the money recovered from the appellants was the same as that given to P.W.2 by the trap officials, thereby supporting the prosecution's case.

case_name: Gurwinder Singh vs State of Punjab & Another
text: Case: Gurwinder Singh vs State of Punjab & Another. Date: 7th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Gurwinder Singh, accused of involvement in terrorist activities and charged under various sections of the IPC, UAPA, and Arms Act, should be granted bail. Gurwinder Singh was charged under Sections 124A, 153A, 153B, 120-B of the IPC, Sections 17, 18, 19 of the UAPA, and Sections 25 and 54 of the Arms Act. The Special Judge denied bail on the grounds that there were reasonable grounds to believe the accusations against Gurwinder Singh were true, based on the disclosure statements and other evidence. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana upheld the Special Judge's decision to deny bail, citing the seriousness of the offences and the lack of examination of protected witnesses. Gurwinder Singh's counsel argued that the disclosure statements were insufficient to implicate him, his mobile phone did not contain incriminating evidence, and he had been in custody for five years without trial completion, which is contrary to the law laid down in KA Najeeb v. Union of India. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 43D(5) of the UAPA imposes strict conditions on granting bail, requiring courts to deny bail if there are reasonable grounds to believe the accusations are prima facie true. The communication records revealed consistent contact between Gurwinder Singh and Bikramjit Singh, supporting the accusation of their involvement in planning terrorist activities. The Supreme Court concluded that mere delay in trial for serious offences like those under the UAPA cannot be used as a ground to grant bail, especially when there is a risk of the accused influencing witnesses. This judgment reinforces the strict conditions for granting bail under the UAPA, making it more challenging for accused individuals to secure bail if there is prima facie evidence of their involvement in terrorist activities. Legal practitioners should consider the stringent bail conditions under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA and focus on disproving the prima facie evidence presented by the prosecution to increase the chances of bail. If bail were granted, there would be a significant risk that Gurwinder Singh could influence key witnesses, potentially hampering the judicial process and impacting the trial's outcome.

case_name: Gyan Prakash Arya vs. M/s Titan Industries Limited
text: Case: Gyan Prakash Arya vs. M/s Titan Industries Limited. Date: 22nd November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the order passed by the arbitrator under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, modifying the original award was beyond the scope and ambit of the arbitrator's jurisdiction. The dispute arose over the recovery of pure gold weighing 3648.80 grams, which M/s Titan Industries Limited claimed was in the possession of Gyan Prakash Arya. The respondent sought the return of the gold or its monetary value along with interest and damages. The original award directed Gyan Prakash Arya to return 3648.80 grams of pure gold along with interest at 18% per annum, calculated at Rs. 740 per gram from 24th July 2004 until the date of delivery. Alternatively, Arya was to pay the monetary value of the gold at Rs. 740 per gram with the same interest rate. The arbitrator modified the original award by substituting the value of gold from Rs. 740 per gram to Rs. 20,747 per 10 grams and made corresponding changes to the interest calculations. Gyan Prakash Arya argued that the modification went beyond correcting any arithmetical or clerical error, which is the only permissible scope under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. He contended that the modification introduced a new claim not part of the original award. The Supreme Court quashed the modification made by the arbitrator, stating it was beyond the scope of Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Court restored the original award dated 4th December 2010. The Supreme Court decided that there would be no order as to costs in the facts and circumstances of the case.

case_name: H.S. Goutham vs. Rama Murthy and Anr. Etc.
text: Case: H.S. Goutham vs. Rama Murthy and Anr. Etc.. Date: 12th February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the compromise decree obtained by H.S. Goutham in O.S. No. 3376 of 1995 was obtained by fraud, and whether the auction sale of the mortgaged property should be set aside. The original defendants contended that the decree dated 01.06.1995 was obtained by fraud and misrepresentation, and thus should be set aside. The Executing Court overruled the objections, stating that the judgment debtors failed to provide any evidence to support their claims of fraud and misrepresentation. The auction sale was confirmed in favor of H.M. Ravindra Kumar, the highest bidder, and a sale certificate was issued on 23.11.1999. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the consent decree, and remitted the suit to the Trial Court for fresh disposal, directing an inquiry into whether the decree was obtained by fraud. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in calling for a report, as it gave the judgment debtors an opportunity to fill in the lacuna, which was not permissible. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, upheld the consent decree, and confirmed the sale of the mortgaged property, stating that the objections of fraud and misrepresentation were not substantiated. The Supreme Court emphasized that an appeal against a consent decree is not maintainable under Section 96(3) of the CPC, as the decree was passed with the consent of the parties.

case_name: Hajabhai Rajashibhai Odedara vs State of Gujarat
text: Case: Hajabhai Rajashibhai Odedara vs State of Gujarat. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Hajabhai Rajashibhai Odedara was charged with offenses under Sections 302 (murder), 307 (attempt to murder), 328 (causing hurt by poison), 120B (criminal conspiracy), and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the IPC, and under the provisions of the Arms Act. The prosecution's case was that Hajabhai Rajashibhai Odedara and co-accused Jagrutiben conspired to kill Jagrutiben's family members. They allegedly strangled Simbhiben and Mukesh and attempted to kill Rajdeep by strangulation, leaving him under the belief that he had died. Rajdeep survived and provided a dying declaration implicating the accused. The trial court convicted Hajabhai Rajashibhai Odedara based on the deposition of Rajdeep (PW66), the sole eye-witness, and the recovery of a bottle of pesticide from the crime scene, which was purchased by the appellant. The court sentenced him to life imprisonment for the offenses under Sections 302, 307, and 328 IPC. The defense counsel argued that the conviction was solely based on the inconsistent statements of Rajdeep (PW66), who did not initially implicate the appellant. They also contended that the prosecution failed to prove the motive and that the story of the pesticide was not believable since no poison was found in the deceased's stomach. The Supreme Court observed that the prosecution's case was supported by the deposition of Rajdeep (PW66) and the recovery of the pesticide bottle purchased by the appellant. The Court found no reason to doubt the testimonies of the witnesses and the surrounding circumstances that implicated the appellant. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court and affirmed by the High Court. The Court upheld the life imprisonment sentence for the offenses committed by the appellant.

case_name: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 13th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary challenge was to the legality and validity of constituting a Delimitation Commission for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002 and the exercise of delimitation undertaken by the Commission. The order directed that all the provisions of the Constitution of India, as amended from time to time, shall apply in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir, subject to modifications made to Article 367. Clause (4) was added to Article 367, providing that the expression 'Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2)' in the proviso to clause (3) of Article 370 shall be read as 'Legislative Assembly of the State'. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 provided for the reorganisation of the State of Jammu and Kashmir by dividing it into two Union Territories: the Union Territory of Ladakh and the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. The Act came into force on 31st October 2019. The petitioners challenged the constitution of the Delimitation Commission on the grounds that it was appointed by usurping the jurisdiction of the Election Commission of India and was thus ultra vires the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (5) of Section 60 of the J&K Reorganisation Act. They also contended that it infringed clause (3) of Article 170 as well as Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court noted that there was no specific challenge to the constitutional validity of the provisions of the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 in the writ petition. Therefore, the Court proceeded on the footing that the 2019 Presidential Order, the said declaration, and the provisions of the J&K Reorganisation Act are valid. The Supreme Court concluded that Article 170, which deals with the composition of the Legislative Assemblies, forms part of Chapter III of Part VI of the Constitution and deals only with the State Legislature. Therefore, it has no application to the Legislatures of Union Territories, including the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. The Supreme Court held that there was nothing illegal about the delimitation exercise conducted by the Delimitation Commission for dividing the Union Territory into 90 constituencies on the basis of the 2011 census figures, as mandated by sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 62 of the J&K Reorganisation Act.

case_name: Hamdard Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (HIMSR) & Anr. vs. Union of India and Ors.
text: Case: Hamdard Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (HIMSR) & Anr. vs. Union of India and Ors.. Date: 8th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the denial of renewal permission for admission of the 5th batch (100 seats) in the MBBS course for the academic session 2016-17 by the Medical Council of India (MCI) and the Central Government due to deficiencies found during inspections. The MCI noted deficiencies such as the non-availability of a functional ventilator in the casualty, only 2 patients in the PICU on the day of assessment, only 2 static X-ray machines available against the requirement of 5, and other deficiencies detailed in the assessment report. The Central Government decided to debar HIMSR from admitting students for two academic sessions (2017-18 and 2018-19) and authorized the MCI to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crore offered by the petitioner. The Hearing Committee observed that the deficiency of faculty was marginal and within permissible limits, but it was not possible to validate the bed occupancy without physical verification. Despite these observations, the Ministry reiterated its earlier decision to debar the college. The Supreme Court found that the Central Government's order was mechanical and not in conformity with the Court's directions to record reasons. The Court noted that the Hearing Committee did not provide a conclusive opinion about the bed occupancy deficiency. The Supreme Court directed the MCI to send an inspection team to HIMSR within three months to verify the deficiencies. The petitioner college was to be informed of any deficiencies and given the opportunity to rectify them. The final decision was to be taken by the Competent Authority within one month of receiving the MCI's report. The Supreme Court ordered that the bank guarantee should not be encashed and should be kept alive until further orders from the Competent Authority of the Central Government.

The Central Government decided to debar HIMSR from admitting students for two academic sessions (2017-18 and 2018-19) and authorized the MCI to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crore offered by the petitioner.

The Hearing Committee observed that the deficiency of faculty was marginal and within permissible limits, but it was not possible to validate the bed occupancy without physical verification. Despite these observations, the Ministry reiterated its earlier decision to debar the college.

The Supreme Court found that the Central Government's order was mechanical and not in conformity with the Court's directions to record reasons. The Court noted that the Hearing Committee did not provide a conclusive opinion about the bed occupancy deficiency.

The Supreme Court directed the MCI to send an inspection team to HIMSR within three months to verify the deficiencies. The petitioner college was to be informed of any deficiencies and given the opportunity to rectify them. The final decision was to be taken by the Competent Authority within one month of receiving the MCI's report.
The Supreme Court ordered that the bank guarantee should not be encashed and should be kept alive until further orders from the Competent Authority of the Central Government.

case_name: Hameed Kunju vs. Nazim
text: Case: Hameed Kunju vs. Nazim. Date: 17th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the eviction order against the tenant, Nazim, passed by the Rent Controlling Court was valid and whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for a fresh trial. Hameed Kunju sought eviction on the grounds of arrears of rent and bona fide need for starting a business in the rented shop under Section 11(2)(b) and 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965. The Rent Controlling Court passed an ex parte eviction order against Nazim on 21st August 2007 due to his absence during the hearings and accepted the eviction petition on merits. The High Court allowed Nazim's writ petition, quashed the eviction order, and remanded the case to the Rent Controlling Court for a fresh trial, directing the court to allow Nazim to contest the eviction petition. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, holding that the High Court erred in entertaining the writ petition and interfering with the orders of the Rent Controlling Court and the Executing Court, and dismissed all applications filed by Nazim. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for speedy disposal of eviction cases, especially those claimed on the grounds of bona fide need, and awarded costs of Rs. 25,000 to be paid by Nazim to Hameed Kunju.

case_name: Hansaram vs. The State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Hansaram vs. The State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 4th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The dispute arose over the non-payment of Rs. 130 by Krishna Kumar Sahu to Hansaram for some material purchased from Hansaram's kirana shop. Hansaram and his son Virendra Sahu assaulted Krishna Kumar Sahu on the evening of 10th November 2005. Hansaram hit Ram Kumar Sahu on the head with a tangi near the field of Komal Singh, causing a severe injury. Ram Kumar Sahu was severely injured and later died in the hospital during the course of treatment. The police registered an offence under Section 307 IPC initially, which was later converted to Section 302 IPC after Ram Kumar Sahu's death. Hansaram claimed that he acted in self-defense after being attacked by Ram Kumar Sahu, Krishna Kumar Sahu, Dev Kumar Sahu, and Shail Kumar near the fields of Komal Singh. Hansaram sustained an incised wound on his head, contusions on his left thumb, pelvic region, and below the left knee. Dr. Hulesh Mandley (PW-19) conducted the post-mortem examination and found a lacerated wound on the deceased's head caused by a sharp-edged weapon. Dr. O.P. Shrivastava (PW-13) examined Hansaram and found multiple injuries on him. The Supreme Court set aside Hansaram's conviction under Section 302 IPC and instead convicted him under Section 304 (Part II) IPC, sentencing him to seven years of imprisonment. The Supreme Court found no evidence of premeditation and concluded that Hansaram did not intend to kill Ram Kumar Sahu, but acted in self-defense during a sudden quarrel. The Supreme Court ordered that if Hansaram had already completed the seven-year sentence, he should be released forthwith.

case_name: Hari Shankar Aggarwal vs State of Rajasthan & Anr.
text: Case: Hari Shankar Aggarwal vs State of Rajasthan & Anr.. Date: 10th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Hari Shankar Aggarwal was correctly impleaded as a nominee of the firm under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The complaint was filed based on an inspection conducted on 02.03.2002 at Oswal Traders Shop, alleging offences under Section 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. Hari Shankar Aggarwal's main defense was that he was not the nominee of the firm and that Devendra Singh Bhadauria had been nominated as the firm's nominee, which was communicated to the Chief Medical Officer, Mathura. Hari Shankar Aggarwal presented a letter dated 21.02.1995, which was received by the Chief Medical Officer on 21.10.1995, nominating Devendra Singh Bhadauria as the firm's nominee. The Special Judge did not accept the document dated 21.02.1995, stating that it was received on 21.10.1995, and had not been believed by the courts below. The Supreme Court observed that the nomination form in Form VIII was duly sent and received by the Chief Medical Officer and could not be rejected on the ground that it was sent on the company letterhead. The Supreme Court ruled that no cognizance could have been taken against Hari Shankar Aggarwal for the offence under Section 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and set aside the orders passed by the courts below. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the order taking cognizance and the orders passed by the lower courts, effectively acquitting Hari Shankar Aggarwal of the charges. The information from the Commercial Tax Department mentioned that Hari Shankar Aggarwal was the nominee, which was contradicted by the information from the Local Health Officer, stating that Devendra Singh Bhadauria was the nominee. The information from the Local Health Officer in Mathura was significant because it confirmed that Devendra Singh Bhadauria was the nominated director responsible for the firm, supporting Hari Shankar Aggarwal's defense. The Supreme Court concluded that there were no specific allegations against Hari Shankar Aggarwal apart from him being impleaded as a nominee, which was not supported by the evidence.

case_name: Haribhau vs The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Haribhau vs The State of Maharashtra. Date: 4th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of Haribhau under Sections 353, 504, and 294 read with Section 34 of the IPC was justified, and whether his sentence should be altered considering the circumstances. Haribhau and Babarao were charged under Sections 353, 504, and 294 read with Section 34 of the IPC, and under Section 3(1)(x) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The prosecution's case was that Haribhau, along with Babarao, assaulted and used abusive language against Bala Saheb Ingole, a teacher, when he was late to school. They also threatened him with injury endangering his life. The trial court convicted Haribhau and Babarao under Sections 353, 504, and 294 read with Section 34 of the IPC and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment. They were acquitted of the charge under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act. The High Court allowed the appeal for Babarao, acquitting him of all charges, but dismissed the appeal for Haribhau, upholding his conviction and sentence. Haribhau's main argument was that, considering his age, spotless career, lack of criminal antecedents, and the fact that he had already served one month of his sentence, the Supreme Court should reduce his sentence to the period already served and impose a higher fine instead. The Supreme Court altered Haribhau's sentence, reducing the jail term to the one month already served and increasing the total fine from Rs. 800 to Rs. 15,000 to be paid to the complainant, Bala Saheb Ingole. The Supreme Court directed Haribhau to deposit the fine amount in the Trial Court within one month for it to be paid to the complainant. Failure to deposit the fine would result in reviving the original jail sentence. The ruling may influence courts to consider the age, criminal history, and circumstances of the accused when deciding sentences for minor offences, potentially favoring fines over imprisonment. The judgement emphasizes a balanced approach by reducing the jail term and imposing a higher fine, acknowledging the need for punishment while also considering the potential for rehabilitation and the specific circumstances of the accused. Haribhau is no longer required to serve additional jail time beyond the one month already served, provided he pays the enhanced fine of Rs. 15,000 within the specified period.

case_name: Harinder Singh @ Hira vs. The State of Punjab
text: Case: Harinder Singh @ Hira vs. The State of Punjab. Date: 17th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves Harinder Singh, who was convicted for the murder of Gurdev Singh under Sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The trial court found Harinder Singh guilty of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment and imposed fines. Harinder Singh was the son of Lakhwinder Singh, the elder brother of Gurdev Singh's father. Sawinder Kaur, the mother of the deceased, filed a complaint after Gurdev Singh went missing and Chanan Singh informed her that Harinder Singh confessed to killing Gurdev Singh. Harinder Singh led the police to the location where he had buried Gurdev Singh's body, and it was recovered in the presence of witnesses. Evidence included Harinder Singh's confession, the recovery of Gurdev Singh's body at his instance, and statements from witnesses. Gurdev Singh had a chopped, incised wound on his forehead, nose, and both eyes, which was sufficient to cause death. The defense argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence, and the prosecution failed to establish the guilt of Harinder Singh beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence of Harinder Singh. Chanan Singh informed the complainant about Harinder Singh's confession and witnessed the recovery of the body. The Supreme Court concluded that the chain of circumstances led to only one inference: Harinder Singh was guilty of murdering Gurdev Singh.

case_name: Harish Chand vs. Smt. Urmila
text: Case: Harish Chand vs. Smt. Urmila. Date: 20th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the revision petition filed by Harish Chand for quashing and setting aside the order of the Family Court regarding maintenance. Harish Chand was working as a headmaster/senior teacher in a government school and was considered capable of maintaining the respondent, Smt. Urmila. The High Court dismissed the revision petition without setting out the facts, considering any submissions of the parties, or assigning any reasons, disposing of the petition in a cryptic manner. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order because it was passed in a cryptic manner without mentioning the facts, considering submissions of the parties, or assigning reasons, making it difficult to understand the factual background and reasoning behind the decision. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the High Court for deciding the revision petition afresh on merits, strictly in accordance with the law, and directed the High Court to dispose of the petition preferably within six months. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court neither set out the facts nor considered any submissions of the parties and did not assign any reasons for dismissing the revision petition, making it difficult to understand the background and reasoning behind the decision.

case_name: Harita Sunil Parab vs State of NCT of Delhi and Others
text: Case: Harita Sunil Parab vs State of NCT of Delhi and Others. Date: 28th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Harita Sunil Parab sought the transfer of two FIRs registered against the respondents from the courts in Delhi and Ghaziabad to a court of competent jurisdiction in Mumbai, Maharashtra. She cited her permanent residence in Mumbai, professional engagements as an advocate at the Mumbai High Court, difficulty in pursuing matters in Delhi due to threats from the accused, and the adverse impact on her professional engagements. The offences included Sections 354, 354A, 323, 506, 509, 379, 376, and 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The respondents argued that the accused and prosecution witnesses were all situated in Delhi, and transferring the cases to Mumbai would similarly hinder the respondents' professional engagements. The Supreme Court noted that if Harita Sunil Parab had any grievances regarding the investigation or apprehensions about her safety, she could file appropriate applications under the Code of Criminal Procedure before the concerned court or police, which would be dealt with on their merits. The Court emphasized that the convenience of the parties includes the convenience of the prosecution, other accused, witnesses, and the larger interest of society, and not just the petitioner. The Court found that the majority of the witnesses were in Delhi, making it impractical to transfer the case to Mumbai. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Gurcharan Das Chadha vs. State of Rajasthan, which stated that a case could be transferred if there was a reasonable apprehension of not getting a fair trial, but mere allegations were not sufficient without reasonable grounds. The Supreme Court concluded that the apprehensions of Harita Sunil Parab were not sufficient to warrant a transfer of the cases to Mumbai, and therefore, the transfer petitions were rejected. Harita Sunil Parab also filed a transfer petition for RTM-CR-641/2017, registered against her under Sections 145(B), 146, and 137 of the Railways Act, pending before the Special Railway Magistrate, Ratlam, to the Court of competent jurisdiction in Mumbai. The Supreme Court also rejected the transfer petition for the Railways Act case, stating similar grounds as the main case.

case_name: Harnek Singh & Ors. vs. Gurmit Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Harnek Singh & Ors. vs. Gurmit Singh & Ors.. Date: 18th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves allegations of medical negligence against Dr. Gurmit Singh and the Preet Surgical Centre & Maternity Hospital regarding the treatment and surgery of Mrs. Manjit Kaur, which led to her death. The SCDRC found Respondents 1 and 2 negligent and directed them to pay Rs. 15,44,000 jointly and severally, along with Rs. 10,000 as costs. The NCDRC dismissed the appeal of the complainants and allowed the appeal of the doctor and the hospital, holding that no medical negligence was proven. The Supreme Court found Dr. Gurmit Singh negligent, set aside the NCDRC's decision, and directed Respondents 1 and 2 to pay Rs. 25,00,000 with interest to the complainants. The MCI found that Dr. Gurmit Singh failed to exercise adequate medical competence, leading to a delay in diagnosing bowel perforation and subsequent deterioration of the patient. The Supreme Court awarded the complainants Rs. 25,00,000 with interest at 6% per annum from the date of the SCDRC order.

case_name: Harveer Singh & Anr. vs. State of U.P.
text: Case: Harveer Singh & Anr. vs. State of U.P.. Date: 15th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Harveer Singh and the other accused were prosecuted for the offences punishable under Sections 323, 324, 452, 504, and 506 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The Judicial Magistrate acquitted all the accused persons, including Harveer Singh and the other appellant, from all the charges on 1st May 2008. The Additional District and Sessions Judge, Mathura, convicted Harveer Singh and the other appellant for the offences under Sections 323, 324, and 452 IPC and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year with a fine of Rs 500 each. The appellants filed a criminal revision before the High Court of Allahabad challenging their conviction and sentence by the Additional District and Sessions Judge. The High Court of Allahabad dismissed the criminal revision ex parte, meaning it was dismissed without the appellants or their counsel being present. The main question considered by the Supreme Court was whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellants' revision ex parte without assigning any reasons. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not assign any reasons for dismissing the revision and thus remanded the case to the High Court for a fresh decision on merits. The Supreme Court instructed the High Court to decide the revision afresh on merits in accordance with law and preferably within six months. The Supreme Court interfered because the High Court failed to apply its judicial mind to the factual and legal aspects of the case and did not provide any reasoning in its dismissal of the revision. The Supreme Court's decision implies that the appellants' case will be re-evaluated by the High Court, giving them another opportunity to argue their case and potentially overturn their conviction. The Supreme Court viewed the High Court's dismissal of the revision ex parte, without assigning reasons, as inappropriate and necessitating a fresh consideration of the case on merits.

case_name: Haryana State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. & Ors. vs. Mr. Deepak Aggarwal & Ors.
text: Case: Haryana State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. & Ors. vs. Mr. Deepak Aggarwal & Ors.. Date: 28th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue involves the interpretation of the word 'initiated' in Section 24(1) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, with reference to land acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Party 'A' contends that the issuance and publication of a Notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 amounts to initiation of acquisition proceedings. Party 'B' argues that the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act marks the point of initiation. The court concluded that the word 'initiated' in Section 24(1) of the 2013 Act refers to the point of time when a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is issued and published in the official gazette. The court's interpretation ensures that more affected persons are entitled to higher compensation as determined under the 2013 Act and that ongoing public projects are protected from lapsing. The court held that Section 6 notifications under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 could be issued after 01.01.2014, provided the land acquisition proceedings were initiated before that date. The legislative intention behind the 2013 Act is to provide fair and just compensation for land acquisition while facilitating industrialization, infrastructure development, and urbanization projects.

case_name: Hazari Lal (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ramesh Kumar & Others
text: Case: Hazari Lal (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ramesh Kumar & Others. Date: 4th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the specific performance of an agreement to sell property executed in 1986 and the subsequent sale of the same property to Hazari Lal in 1999, which led to a legal dispute over the validity of the sale and the enforceability of the original agreement. The agreement to sell dated 24th September 1986 involved the sale of three properties (House Nos. 258, 259, and 260) in Sadar Bazar, Allahabad, for a total consideration of Rs 55,000, with Rs 5,000 paid as earnest money. The sale was to be completed upon obtaining permission from the Ceiling Department. The respondents filed the civil suit for specific performance of the 1986 agreement after the appellant purchased House Nos. 259 and 260 in 1999, claiming that the vendors had not informed them about obtaining permission from the Ceiling Department, which was a condition for completing the sale. The Trial Court decreed the suit in favor of the respondents, ordering specific performance of the 1986 agreement. This decision was upheld by both the First Appellate Court and the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments and decrees of the lower courts, dismissing the suit for specific performance filed by the respondents. The Court held that there was significant delay in filing the suit and that no permission from the Ceiling Department was required. The Supreme Court dismissed the suit because the respondents' predecessor had not taken timely action to enforce the agreement or to ensure that the vendors obtained the necessary permission from the Ceiling Department. The significant delay of over twelve years before filing the suit was a key factor in the dismissal.
