case_name: Hemant Kumar Verma & Ors. vs Employees State Insurance Corporation & Ors.
text: Case: Hemant Kumar Verma & Ors. vs Employees State Insurance Corporation & Ors.. Date: 22nd July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether junior resident doctors, who have completed their undergraduate medical courses at institutions run by the ESIC, should be included in the 'in-service' quota for postgraduate (PG) courses. The junior resident doctors contended that they should be considered as 'in-service' doctors for the purposes of the 50% reservation in PG courses, similar to the Insurance Medical Officers Grade-II (IMO-II), as they possess the same qualifications, entitlements, duties, and responsibilities. The ESIC argued that junior resident doctors are not 'in-service' doctors because they are serving a bond condition after completing their studies, unlike IMO-II doctors who are regular medical officers recruited through a selection process. The Supreme Court concluded that there is a clear distinction between junior resident doctors and IMO-II doctors. The junior residents are contractual employees serving a bond, whereas IMO-II doctors are regular employees recruited through a formal process. Thus, junior residents cannot claim the 'in-service' quota. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, finding no merit in the argument that junior resident doctors should be treated on par with IMO-II doctors for the purpose of the 'in-service' quota for PG courses. The Supreme Court noted that the decision to provide 'in-service' quota reservations lies within the policy domain of the respondent-authority (ESIC) and cannot be mandated by the Court. The policy decision to exclude junior resident doctors from the 'in-service' quota was deemed justified.

case_name: Hemantbhai Balvantbhai Patel vs The State of Gujarat and Another
text: Case: Hemantbhai Balvantbhai Patel vs The State of Gujarat and Another. Date: 24th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the criminal proceedings against the appellants for forging the signature of the complainant to withdraw money from a joint bank account should be quashed. The allegations were that Hemantbhai Balvantbhai Patel forged the complainant's signature to include his grandson in the joint bank account and then withdrew Rs. 10,50,000 from the account. The Gujarat High Court dismissed the petition to quash the criminal proceedings against the appellants. The Supreme Court opined that continuing the criminal proceedings would not be in the larger interest of the parties, considering the family relationship and the FSL report that supported the appellants' claims. The appellants offered to return the entire amount of Rs. 10,50,000 with 12% simple interest from 1st June 2007 to the complainant to resolve the dispute amicably. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings against both the appellants and the complainant, with the condition that the appellants return the amount with interest within one week. The complainant was the mother of appellant No.1 and the grandmother of appellant No.2. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of restoring cordial relations between the mother, son, and grandson, and used its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the criminal proceedings. The condition imposed was that the appellants return Rs. 10,50,000 with 12% simple interest from 1st June 2007 to the complainant within one week. The Supreme Court hoped to restore cordial relations between the family members involved in the dispute.

case_name: Hemudan Nanbha Gadhvi vs. State of Gujarat
text: Case: Hemudan Nanbha Gadhvi vs. State of Gujarat. Date: 28th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in convicting Hemudan Nanbha Gadhvi under Section 376(2)(f) IPC and sentencing him to ten years of rigorous imprisonment, after reversing his acquittal by the trial court. The victim was PW-2, a nine-year-old girl who was sexually assaulted on 20th February 2004. The key evidence included the FIR lodged by the victim's mother, the medical examination report confirming sexual assault, the presence of semen on the victim's clothes matching the appellant's blood group, and the identification of the appellant in the Test Identification Parade (T.I.P.). The trial court acquitted Hemudan Nanbha Gadhvi, as the victim and an eyewitness turned hostile during the trial and declined to identify the appellant in court. The High Court reversed the acquittal based on the medical evidence of sexual assault, the identification of the appellant in the T.I.P., and the presence of semen on the victim's clothes matching the appellant's blood group, despite the victim and eyewitness turning hostile. The appellant's counsel argued that the T.I.P. was only corroborative evidence and not substantive, that there was no direct evidence of the appellant being the perpetrator, and that the serological report was not formally exhibited or properly brought to the appellant's notice under Section 313 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court held that the T.I.P., supported by the medical report and the presence of the appellant's semen on the victim's clothes, was sufficient to establish the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court concluded that the serological report was admissible under Section 45 of the Evidence Act, 1872, and that the appellant was not prejudiced by its omission under Section 313 Cr.P.C. as the overall evidence against him was overwhelming. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's conviction of Hemudan Nanbha Gadhvi under Section 376(2)(f) IPC and the ten-year rigorous imprisonment sentence. The Supreme Court discussed the principles of dealing with hostile witnesses, the importance of corroborative evidence, and the necessity of balancing the presumption of innocence with the rights of the victim and societal interest in preserving the rule of law.

case_name: High Court of Tripura vs. Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee & Ors.
text: Case: High Court of Tripura vs. Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee & Ors.. Date: 6th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court of Gauhati's order directing the re-evaluation of Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee's answer papers for the selection to the post of Grade-I in Tripura Judicial Service was justified, especially given the absence of a provision for re-evaluation in the relevant rules. Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee's grievance was that some correct answers in his answer scripts were marked as incorrect, and he was not awarded any marks for some correct answers. This led to him falling short by 5 marks to qualify for the interview for the post of Grade-I in Tripura Judicial Service. The High Court of Gauhati allowed the review petition filed by Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee and directed the re-evaluation of his answer scripts for Papers I and II, finding that some correct answers were marked as incorrect and some correct answers were not awarded any marks. The High Court of Tripura argued that there was no provision for re-evaluation of answer scripts under the relevant rules governing the examination, and that the review petition was filed after an inordinate delay, making it unjustified to order re-evaluation. The Supreme Court of India set aside the High Court of Gauhati's re-evaluation order, holding that in the absence of a provision for re-evaluation in the relevant rules, the High Court was not justified in allowing the review petition and directing re-evaluation of the answer papers. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by the High Court of Tripura, set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court of Gauhati, and dismissed the review petition filed by Tirtha Sarathi Mukherjee, thereby upholding the original examination results.

case_name: Himachal Pradesh Bus Stand Management and Development Authority (HPBSM&DA) vs The Central Empowered Committee Etc. & Ors.
text: Case: Himachal Pradesh Bus Stand Management and Development Authority (HPBSM&DA) vs The Central Empowered Committee Etc. & Ors.. Date: 12th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the legality of the construction of a Bus Stand Complex in McLeod Ganj, Himachal Pradesh, which included a Hotel-cum-Restaurant structure, without obtaining the necessary environmental clearances. The CEC concluded that the construction of the Hotel-cum-Restaurant structure within the Bus Stand Complex was not permitted and violated the provisions of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and recommended its demolition. The NGT directed the demolition of the Hotel-cum-Restaurant structure, ordered the second respondent to pay a compensation of Rs. 15 lacs, and required the appellant to pay Rs. 10 lacs, among other compensations, due to the violations of environmental laws. The Supreme Court upheld the NGT's judgment, confirming the demolition of the Hotel-cum-Restaurant structure and stating that the construction was illegal and in violation of environmental norms. The District and Sessions Judge conducted an enquiry as directed by the Supreme Court and submitted a report highlighting that the Bus Stand Complex was constructed in violation of the Forest (Conservation) Act and without requisite permissions from the Town and Country Planning Department. The Supreme Court noted that the construction of the Hotel-cum-Restaurant structure in the eco-sensitive area exhibited a serious disregard for environmental laws, highlighting the importance of the environmental rule of law and the need for strict compliance with environmental regulations.

case_name: Himangni Enterprises vs. Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia
text: Case: Himangni Enterprises vs. Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia. Date: 12th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the disputes arising out of the lease deed between Himangni Enterprises and Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia were arbitrable under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The respondent, Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia, was seeking eviction of Himangni Enterprises from the premises in question, recovery of unpaid arrears of rent, and a permanent injunction. Himangni Enterprises filed the application under Section 8 of the Act, contending that the disputes should be resolved through arbitration as per the arbitration clause in the lease deed dated 31st August 2010. The Trial Court dismissed the application filed by Himangni Enterprises, holding that the civil suit for eviction and recovery of rent was maintainable in the Civil Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the Trial Court's decision, stating that the civil suit was maintainable despite the arbitration clause in the lease deed. Himangni Enterprises argued that the disputes should be referred to arbitration as per the arbitration clause in the lease deed and that the civil suit was barred under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Supreme Court held that disputes related to eviction and recovery of rent are not arbitrable and should be decided by the Civil Court, in line with its earlier decisions in Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. vs. Navrang Studios and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. vs. SBI Home Finance Ltd. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Himangni Enterprises, affirming the decisions of the Trial Court and the High Court, and directed the Civil Court to proceed with the trial of the suit on its merits. The judgment reinforces that landlord-tenant disputes, particularly those involving eviction and recovery of rent, are non-arbitrable and must be adjudicated by the Civil Court. The Supreme Court mentioned that broader public policy considerations, such as the statutory protection provided to tenants and the specific jurisdiction of Civil Courts in landlord-tenant disputes, justify the non-arbitrability of such disputes. The Supreme Court directed the concerned Civil Court to proceed with the trial of the suit on its merits, in accordance with the law, without being influenced by the observations made in the Supreme Court's judgment.

case_name: Himanshu Sharma vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Himanshu Sharma vs. State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 20th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in cancelling the bail granted to the appellants by another Single Judge of the same High Court. The appellants were charged under Sections 419, 420, 467, 468, 470, and 471 of the IPC and Section 25/27 of the Arms Act. The State sought the cancellation of bail on the grounds that the case had wider ramifications for national security and cybercrime, and the appellants were implicated based on confessional statements made by co-accused persons. The High Court reasoned that the independent role of the accused might vary, but collectively their role appeared challenging and had wider ramifications for national security and cybercrime. The Supreme Court noted that the exercise of jurisdiction by the Single Judge in cancelling the bail granted by another Single Judge was uncalled for and amounted to judicial impropriety/indiscipline. The Supreme Court highlighted that the learned Single Judge virtually reviewed the orders granting bail by examining the merits of the allegations, which was not appropriate. The Supreme Court observed that charges had already been framed, and the trial had commenced with seven witnesses examined, thus there was no requirement for further investigation. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the impugned orders dated 12th December 2023, which cancelled the bail granted to the appellants. The Supreme Court concluded that the orders cancelling bail were grossly illegal and did not stand up to scrutiny. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, reinstating the bail granted to the appellants and quashing the High Court's cancellation orders. The Supreme Court stated that the pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_name: Hospitality Association of Mudumalai v. In Defence of Environment and Animals and Ors.
text: Case: Hospitality Association of Mudumalai v. In Defence of Environment and Animals and Ors.. Date: 14th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the validity of the Tamil Nadu Government Notification G.O.(Ms.) No. 125, dated 31.08.2010, which notified an 'Elephant Corridor' in the Sigur Plateau of Nilgiris District and directed resort owners and private landowners to vacate the lands falling within the corridor. The appellants included the Hospitality Association of Mudumalai and its members, who are owners of resorts/guest houses and lands in the Nilgiris forest area. Some appellants were also owners of lands used for cultivation or had encroached upon government lands. The High Court of Madras upheld the validity of the Tamil Nadu Government's notification, directing resort owners and private landowners to vacate the lands within the notified elephant corridor and hand over the vacant possession to the District Collector, Nilgiris. The 'Elephant Corridor' in the Sigur Plateau of Nilgiris District is crucial for the migration of elephants between the Western and Eastern Ghats. It allows elephants to move freely between different forest areas, maintaining genetic diversity and reducing human-elephant conflict. The appellants argued that their lands do not fall within any scientifically recognized elephant corridor, and the identification of the corridor by the Expert Committee was erroneous. They also contended that the area notified as the corridor did not historically serve as an elephant migratory route. The Supreme Court appointed a 3-member Inquiry Committee to decide the objections of the appellants and others aggrieved by the actions of the District Collector, Nilgiris. The Committee was directed to consider objections, provide a hearing, and submit a report on the grievances and allegations regarding the elephant corridor.

case_name: I.C. Sharma vs. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
text: Case: I.C. Sharma vs. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.. Date: 10th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the insurance claim for the burglary that occurred in I.C. Sharma's house should be fully compensated despite the alleged under-insurance of the stolen items. The Insurance Company initially offered a sum of Rs. 3,500/- in November 2008, which I.C. Sharma refused to accept. Later, an amount of Rs. 29,920/- was offered, which was also not accepted by the appellant. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum dismissed the claim on the grounds that the articles mentioned were not included in the initial list provided to the Insurance Company. The State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission allowed the appeal and awarded a sum of Rs. 4,03,150/- to I.C. Sharma. The NCDRC ruled that the appellant was entitled to only Rs. 21,000/- for the stolen gold articles, Rs. 5,929/- for the Citizen watch, Rs. 7,000/- for repair of door latches, and Rs. 16,000/- for the stolen clothes after making appropriate deductions for under-insurance. The Supreme Court concluded that the principle of under-insurance should be applied when not all items under a particular category are stolen. However, if all items under a specific category are stolen, the insured should be compensated up to the insured value of those items. The Supreme Court awarded I.C. Sharma Rs. 1,00,500/- for jewellery and valuables, Rs. 66,000/- for electrical/mechanical appliances, Rs. 28,000/- for miscellaneous items, Rs. 7,000/- for repair of locks and doors, and an additional Rs. 25,000/- for compensation and litigation expenses, with interest at 12% per annum from 1st January 2009 until payment.

Sharma Rs. 1,00,500/- for jewellery and valuables, Rs. 66,000/- for electrical/mechanical appliances, Rs. 28,000/- for miscellaneous items, Rs. 7,000/- for repair of locks and doors, and an additional Rs. 25,000/- for compensation and litigation expenses, with interest at 12% per annum from 1st January 2009 until payment.

text: Case: IQ City Foundation & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 1st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the quashment of the order dated 31st May 2017 passed under Section 10-A of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 by the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and to grant permission to the petitioner College for 4th renewal for the academic year 2017-2018 to facilitate admission of the 5th batch (150 students) MBBS Course. The deficiencies included a shortfall in Teaching Faculty and Resident Doctors (4.5% and 3.50% respectively), issues with the Central Library not being air-conditioned, inadequate facilities in students' hostels, and lack of residential accommodation in RHTC, among others. The Hearing Committee recommended that the deficiencies were not such as to warrant disapproval at that stage of the college. The Central Government referred the matter back to the MCI to review the scheme in light of the recommendations of the Hearing Committee along with documents submitted by the petitioners and to furnish its recommendation. The compliance verification conducted by the Assessors on 21st March 2017 noted deficiencies such as a 15.90% deficiency of faculty, a 25.88% shortage of residents, and issues with patient admissions and hostel facilities. The Supreme Court ordered the Central Government to afford a further opportunity of hearing to the petitioners and also take the assistance of the newly constituted Oversight Committee, and thereafter take a decision within two weeks. The decision must contain reasons.

case_name: Ilavarasan vs. The Superintendent of Police & Ors.
text: Case: Ilavarasan vs. The Superintendent of Police & Ors.. Date: 28th August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the appellant's habeas corpus petition alleging that his wife, Mathithra, was forcibly taken away and coerced into marrying her maternal uncle, and that she was being restrained against her will. The High Court dismissed the habeas corpus petition and recorded adverse comments about the conduct of Advocates, stating that they are incapable of certifying marriages under Section 7A of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The Supreme Court directed the District Legal Services Authority to facilitate recording the statement of Mathithra, which confirmed that she married Ilavarasan of her own will and wished to reside with him. The report stated that Mathithra married Ilavarasan of her own will and was residing with him at Madurai. She was previously coerced into marrying her maternal uncle against her wishes. The Supreme Court held that the view expressed by the Madras High Court, which required public declaration for marriages under Section 7A, was erroneous. The Supreme Court emphasized that a public declaration is not required and that forcing such a condition would violate the rights under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court concluded that Mathithra wished to reside with Ilavarasan of her own free will and directed the respondents to ensure that she joins Ilavarasan. The Supreme Court noted that the concerns voiced by the High Court were not entirely unfounded, but emphasized that advocates should not undertake to solemnize marriages while acting as counsel. However, their role as witnesses in personal capacities cannot be ruled out.

case_name: Index Medical College, Hospital and Research Centre vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Index Medical College, Hospital and Research Centre vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 3rd February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court declared Rule 12 (8) (a) of the Madhya Pradesh Chikitsa Shiksha Pravesh Niyam, 2018 as violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court directed the State of Madhya Pradesh to initiate the process of filling up the 7 unfilled seats of the 1st year MBBS course in the mop-up round for the year 2020-21 by college level counselling within a period of 7 days from the order date. The private medical colleges challenged Rule 12 (8) (a) as it prevented them from filling up seats that fell vacant due to candidates not taking admission or resigning after the mop-up round, which they argued was an unreasonable restriction on their right to occupation under Article 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution of India. The State of Madhya Pradesh introduced Rule 12 (8) (a) to prevent manipulations in the admission process, ensuring that lesser meritorious candidates do not get admission in better colleges due to blocking of seats and subsequent resignations. The Supreme Court identified that implementing Rule 12 (8) (a) resulted in some seats remaining vacant, which was a national waste of resources and a huge financial burden on educational institutions.

case_name: Indian Bank and another vs Mahaveer Khariwal
text: Case: Indian Bank and another vs Mahaveer Khariwal. Date: 22nd January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the rejection of Mahaveer Khariwal's application for voluntary retirement by Indian Bank was lawful and in consonance with Regulation 29 of the Indian Bank Employees Pension Regulations, 1995. Indian Bank rejected the application on the grounds that Mahaveer Khariwal was not eligible for voluntary retirement under the Pension Regulations, 1995. Mahaveer Khariwal sought voluntary retirement due to personal reasons and requested a waiver of the three months' notice period as per Circular No. 32/97-98 dated 15th July 1997. The High Court quashed the bank's rejection of the voluntary retirement application and directed the bank to release Mahaveer Khariwal's retiral dues in accordance with the Pension Regulations, 1995, with interest at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of filing the writ petition. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, stating that the rejection of the voluntary retirement application was illegal and not in accordance with Regulation 29 of the Pension Regulations, 1995. Indian Bank failed to provide specific reasons for rejecting the voluntary retirement application and did not consider the request for curtailment of the notice period on merits as required by Sub-Regulation 3(b) of Regulation 29. The Supreme Court interpreted that the proviso to Sub-Regulation (1) of Regulation 29, which requires an employee to serve for a period of not less than one year after returning from deputation, did not apply to Mahaveer Khariwal as he was on transfer, not deputation. The decision emphasizes the need for employers to provide specific reasons when rejecting voluntary retirement applications and to consider requests for curtailment of notice periods on their merits, potentially impacting how future applications are processed. Employees should ensure that their applications comply with the requirements of Regulation 29, including providing a valid reason for curtailment of the notice period if applicable, and be prepared to challenge any rejections that do not follow due process. The Supreme Court clarified that rejections must be based on valid reasons and should comply with the procedural requirements of Regulation 29, including considering requests for curtailment of the notice period on their merits. Employers may need to review their procedures for handling voluntary retirement applications to ensure compliance with statutory regulations and provide clear, specific reasons for any rejections to avoid legal challenges.

case_name: Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 16th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue addressed was the challenge to the implementation of the 'One Rank One Pension' (OROP) policy for ex-servicemen of the defense forces, particularly the deviation from the principle of automatic pension revision to periodic intervals. The petitioners contended that the principle of OROP was replaced by 'one rank multiple pensions' and that the revision from automatic updates to periodic intervals was arbitrary and unconstitutional under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. The original definition of OROP was the payment of uniform pension to armed services personnel retiring in the same rank with the same length of service, irrespective of the date of retirement, with automatic revision of pension rates in case of future enhancements. The significant change was that instead of an automatic revision of pension rates, the revision would now occur at periodic intervals of every five years, effectively altering the initial principle of OROP. The Koshyari Committee recommended the implementation of OROP, defining it as a uniform pension for armed forces personnel retiring in the same rank with the same length of service, irrespective of their retirement date, with future pension enhancements automatically passed on to past pensioners. The Union Government justified the revised definition of OROP by stating that it was practical and feasible to revise the pension every five years, and that doing so annually would be administratively difficult and impracticable. The outcome of the case was that the Supreme Court of India upheld the revised definition of OROP as implemented by the Union Government, noting that the policy was a matter of executive decision and not open to judicial review on the grounds of being contrary to the original intent.

case_name: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur & Ors. Vs. Soutrik Sarangi & Ors.
text: Case: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur & Ors. Vs. Soutrik Sarangi & Ors.. Date: 28th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Soutrik Sarangi could be permitted to appear for the JEE (Advanced) 2021 despite having already secured admission in IIT Kharagpur in 2020 and the eligibility criteria restricting such attempts. Soutrik Sarangi approached the court challenging the eligibility criteria that prevented him from appearing in JEE (Advanced) 2021 because he had secured admission in IIT Kharagpur in 2020 but wanted to appear again for a better course. The eligibility criteria stated that a candidate who had taken admission in any IIT in a previous year was not eligible to appear in JEE (Advanced) again, regardless of whether they continued in the program or not. The Calcutta High Court allowed Soutrik Sarangi's petition, directing IIT to reconsider his eligibility and permit him to register for JEE (Advanced) 2021 if no decision was taken before the exam date. IIT argued that the eligibility criteria were neither illegal nor unconstitutional and were designed to prevent seat wastage and ensure fair opportunities for all candidates by avoiding multiple admissions and withdrawals. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, upholding the eligibility criteria that barred Soutrik Sarangi from appearing in JEE (Advanced) 2021 as he had already secured admission in IIT Kharagpur in 2020. The Supreme Court applied the principle that academic and administrative decisions made by expert bodies like IITs should be given deference unless they are shown to be plainly arbitrary or discriminatory. The Supreme Court noted that the criteria were established after extensive consultations, aimed at ensuring equitable access and avoiding seat wastage, and had been consistently applied over the years. The judgment reinforces the strict adherence to eligibility criteria, implying that candidates must carefully consider their decisions about accepting IIT admissions, as re-application restrictions will be enforced. IITs might further clarify their eligibility criteria and ensure that all candidates are fully aware of the implications of accepting an IIT seat, thus avoiding similar disputes in the future. The Supreme Court stated that courts should exercise caution and defer to the expertise of academic and administrative bodies in making decisions unless there is clear evidence of arbitrariness or discrimination.

case_name: Indian Oil Corporation Limited & Anr. vs. Kerala State Road Transport Corporation & Ors.
text: Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited & Anr. vs. Kerala State Road Transport Corporation & Ors.. Date: 7th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the policy decision taken by the Government of India regarding the withdrawal of diesel subsidies for bulk consumers, which affected the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation and others. The Kerala State Road Transport Corporation argued that the diesel price hike was arbitrary, illegal, and discriminatory. They claimed it violated Articles 12 and 14 of the Constitution of India and sought exemption from being treated as a bulk consumer. The Government of India justified the withdrawal of diesel subsidies for bulk consumers by stating that it was a necessary fiscal policy decision to reduce the subsidy burden on petroleum products, allocate more funds to social sector schemes, and ensure the country's long-term energy security. The Supreme Court held that policy decisions related to subsidies are not amenable to judicial review. The Court emphasized that subsidies are privileges and can be withdrawn at any time. It stated that no right exists to claim a subsidy, and such matters are within the domain of fiscal policy. The Supreme Court transferred all the writ petitions pending before various High Courts to itself and stayed the interim orders passed by the High Courts. It held that in such policy matters, no interim orders should have been passed by the High Courts. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petitions challenging the policy decision to withdraw diesel subsidies for bulk consumers and upheld the Government of India's policy. The appeals and transferred cases were disposed of accordingly.

case_name: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.
text: Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.. Date: 14th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the demand for payment of Entry Tax by the Indian Oil Corporation Limited under the Bihar Tax on Entry of Goods into Local Areas for Consumption, Use, or Sale Therein Act, 1993, and the subsequent disallowance of VAT set-offs. The Appellant argued that VAT should be set off against Entry Tax as previously allowed until 2014, and that retrospective reopening of assessments from 2008-09 based on audit objections was unjustified. The notification dated 4th May 2006 under the Bihar Value Added Tax Act, 2005, specifies that VAT on petroleum products sold by the Appellant to OMCs is levied at the point of sale by the OMCs to their retailers or consumers, affecting the claim for VAT set-offs by the Appellant. The audit objections led to the reopening of assessments from 2008-09 and disallowance of previously allowed set-offs, resulting in an Entry Tax demand of Rs. 1,683.03 crores for the assessment years 2008-09 to 2014-15. The broader implications include potential reassessment of tax liabilities for other oil marketing companies operating under similar circumstances, ensuring compliance with the clarified interpretation of the Entry Tax Act and VAT set-offs. The judgment reinforces that the second proviso to Section 3(2) of the Entry Tax Act is assessee-based and not goods-based, meaning the set-off is specific to the person liable to pay VAT and Entry Tax, not the goods being taxed.

case_name: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station
text: Case: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station. Date: 9th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the resignation of M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station from the dealership agreement with Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOC) was validly accepted by IOC, and whether the subsequent withdrawal of resignation by the dealership was legally effective. M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station requested to withdraw from the dealership due to their relocation to Bangalore for their children's education, and asked IOC to appoint new dealers within three months as per the agreement. IOC asked M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station to notarize the resignation letter, which was subsequently done and received by IOC on 16th November 2006. IOC then accepted the resignation on 18th November 2006 and requested the dealership to continue operations until alternative arrangements were made. The arbitrator found that IOC had validly accepted the resignation on 18th November 2006, and the subsequent withdrawal of the resignation by M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station on 11th December 2006 was not in accordance with law. The High Court set aside the arbitrator's award and ordered the restoration of the dealership to M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station, allowing them to seek damages from IOC if the dealership was not restored within three months. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and restored the arbitrator's award, concluding that the arbitrator's findings were plausible and not perverse. The court ruled that the High Court had acted illegally by interfering with the arbitrator's award and by ordering the restoration of the dealership. The letter dated 18th November 2006 was significant because it conveyed IOC's acceptance of the resignation, which the arbitrator found to be a valid acceptance, thereby rendering the subsequent withdrawal of resignation by M/S. Sathyanarayana Service Station legally ineffective.

case_name: Indian Railway Construction Company Limited vs. M/s National Buildings Construction Corporation Limited
text: Case: Indian Railway Construction Company Limited vs. M/s National Buildings Construction Corporation Limited. Date: 17th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The dispute centered around the termination of a contract for constructing a railway station-cum-commercial complex and the subsequent claims for forfeiture of security deposits and interest on advances. The NBCC sought the refund of two security deposits amounting to Rs. 5,57,486 and Rs. 60,85,840, which were forfeited by IRCON after terminating the contract. This judgment underscores the enforceability of forfeiture clauses when contractors fail to meet their obligations, potentially influencing similar contract disputes. The Court held that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under the Arbitration Act by interfering with the well-reasoned findings of the Arbitral Tribunal. The Supreme Court upheld the award of interest on advances by the Arbitral Tribunal but reduced the interest rate from 18% to 12%.

case_name: Indian Young Lawyers Association & Ors. vs. State of Kerala & Ors.
text: Case: Indian Young Lawyers Association & Ors. vs. State of Kerala & Ors.. Date: 13th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the exclusion of women aged 10 to 50 years from entering the Sabarimala Temple based on custom and usage violated constitutional rights, including Articles 14, 15, and 25. The case debated Articles 14 (equality before the law), 15 (prohibition of discrimination), 25 (freedom of religion), and 26 (rights of religious denominations) of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court referred the matter to a larger Constitution Bench to decide on critical questions concerning constitutional rights and essential religious practices. The judgment was expected to set a precedent for balancing gender equality with the right to manage religious affairs, potentially impacting practices in other places of worship. The Court sought to determine whether the Sabarimala Temple qualified as a religious denomination under Article 26 and if it could enforce practices excluding women as part of its essential religious customs.

case_name: Indu Bai & Ors. vs. State of Telangana & Ors.
text: Case: Indu Bai & Ors. vs. State of Telangana & Ors.. Date: 21st January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants, claiming to be pre-partition tenants, had the right to continue possession of land in Village Poppalguda, Ranga Reddy District, despite the State issuing an auction notice for the land. The appellants sought Patta rights over the disputed lands, measuring approximately 18 acres, and challenged the High Court's earlier decision to allow the auction of the land. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remitted the matter back to the High Court for reconsideration in accordance with the law. The High Court's reconsideration may result in a re-evaluation of the appellants' claims for Patta rights and the legality of the land auction. The Supreme Court clarified that the appellants were free to invoke other legal forums to address their grievances if they were not satisfied with the High Court's reconsideration.

case_name: Industrial Development Bank of India vs. Superintendent of Central Excise and Customs & Ors.
text: Case: Industrial Development Bank of India vs. Superintendent of Central Excise and Customs & Ors.. Date: 18th August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the customs authorities had the first right to sell imported goods under the Customs Act and adjust the sale proceeds towards payment of customs duty, despite the provisions of Section 529A and 530 of the Companies Act. During the period 1994-2000, IDBI granted financial assistance to M/s. Sri Vishnupriya Industries Limited, for which the company hypothecated movable properties and created an equitable mortgage of immovable properties. The customs authorities issued orders for the sale of warehoused goods for the recovery of customs duty and initiated steps for auctioning the imported goods. The single judge of the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that the customs authorities had not followed the procedure under the Customs Act, making the detention orders void ab initio. The court also observed that after the winding up order, the Official Liquidator was entitled to take possession of the company's properties. The full bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that customs authorities had the first right to sell imported goods and recover customs duty, which took precedence over the claims of secured creditors under Section 529A of the Companies Act. The Supreme Court held that Section 529A of the Companies Act, a non-obstante provision, overrides other conflicting provisions and grants priority to the debts due to secured creditors and workmen's dues over all other debts. The Supreme Court concluded that the customs authorities' right to recover customs duty does not override the priority given to secured creditors and workmen's dues under Section 529A of the Companies Act. The customs dues would fall under Section 530 of the Companies Act, which ranks below the debts specified in Section 529A. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court and ruled in favor of the appellant, IDBI, affirming the priority of secured creditors and workmen's dues over the customs authorities' claims.

case_name: Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (Gwalior) M.P. Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Gwalior
text: Case: Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (Gwalior) M.P. Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Gwalior. Date: 16th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Commissioner of Income Tax (CIT) had the authority to cancel the registration certificate granted to the appellant under Section 12A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The CIT issued a show cause notice to the appellant to explain why the registration certificate granted under Section 12A should not be canceled, citing factual grounds for the proposed cancellation. The ITAT allowed the appellant's appeal and set aside the CIT's order canceling the registration certificate, thereby restoring the certificate. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh allowed the appeal filed by the Revenue, setting aside the ITAT's order and restoring the CIT's order canceling the registration certificate. The Supreme Court held that the CIT had no express power to cancel the registration certificate once granted under Section 12A until the introduction of Section 12AA(3) by the Finance (No.2) Act 2004, which came into effect from 1st October 2004. The Supreme Court decided that Section 21 of the General Clauses Act did not apply to the CIT's order under Section 12A because the order was quasi-judicial in nature and not an executive or legislative order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and restored the ITAT's order. However, it noted that the CIT could exercise the power of cancellation under Section 12AA(3) from 1st October 2004 onwards.

case_name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India vs. Lalit Kumar Jain & Ors.
text: Case: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India vs. Lalit Kumar Jain & Ors.. Date: 29th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge to the notification dated 15th November 2019, which brought provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 into force concerning personal guarantors to corporate debtors. The Supreme Court transferred the writ petitions to avoid conflicting judgments by different High Courts and to provide an authoritative interpretation of the provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Court directed all High Courts to transfer pending writ petitions related to the notification to the Supreme Court and prohibited the filing of further writ petitions on the issue in High Courts. The Supreme Court's decision is likely to provide clarity and uniformity in the application of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, especially concerning personal guarantors to corporate debtors. The Court clarified that interim orders issued by High Courts in related cases would remain in effect until further orders by the Supreme Court.

case_name: Iqbal vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Iqbal vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 11th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Iqbal's conviction and four-year imprisonment for offences under Sections 399 and 402 IPC, read with Section 25 of the Arms Act, 1959, should be upheld. Iqbal was charged and convicted under Sections 399 (making preparation to commit dacoity) and 402 (assembling for the purpose of committing dacoity) IPC, read with Section 25 of the Arms Act, 1959. The trial court convicted Iqbal and sentenced him to four years of imprisonment. The District and Sessions Judge, Shahjahanpur, confirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the revision filed by Iqbal, as none appeared on his behalf during the hearing. The Supreme Court noted that the absence of Iqbal's counsel in the High Court was due to specific circumstances detailed by the appellant. The Supreme Court considered Iqbal's satisfactory conduct in jail, the absence of any other criminal cases against him, and his young age at the time of the incident in 1980. The Supreme Court limited Iqbal's sentence to the period already undergone and ordered his immediate release, provided he was not required to be detained in any other case. The Supreme Court decided to limit the sentence considering the long duration since the incident, Iqbal's young age at the time, his good conduct in jail, and the lack of other criminal cases against him. The Supreme Court instructed that Iqbal should be released forthwith if he was not otherwise required to be detained in any other case.

case_name: Iqram vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Iqram vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 16th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Iqram was charged with theft of electricity equipment belonging to the Electricity Department of the State of Uttar Pradesh under Section 136 of the Electricity Act and cognate provisions. Nine separate sessions trials were conducted against Iqram by the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Hapur. Iqram was convicted in all nine trials and sentenced to two years' simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1000 in each case, with the sentences running concurrently for certain offenses. Iqram's grievance was that the jail authorities were treating his sentences as consecutive rather than concurrent, leading to a total imprisonment period of 18 years. The High Court dismissed Iqram's petition, stating that under Section 427 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, each subsequent term of conviction should commence at the expiration of the previous sentence unless directed otherwise by the court. The Supreme Court identified that the trial court did not specifically exercise its discretion under Section 427(1) of the CrPC to direct that the subsequent sentences should run concurrently with the previous sentences. The Supreme Court emphasized that under Section 427(1) of the CrPC, the court has the discretion to order subsequent sentences to run concurrently with the previous sentences, and this discretion must be exercised judiciously. The Supreme Court addressed the potential miscarriage of justice by setting aside the High Court's judgement and directing that Iqram's sentences in the nine sessions trials should run concurrently, thereby reducing the total imprisonment period. The Supreme Court directed the jail authorities to act immediately upon the production of a certified copy of the order and ensure that Iqram's sentences run concurrently as per the Supreme Court's directive. Section 265-G of the CrPC states that the judgement delivered in a plea bargain shall be final and no appeal shall lie against such judgement, except through a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 or a Writ Petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. This provision was relevant as Iqram's case involved a plea bargain. The Supreme Court referenced the precedent set in the case of Mohd Zahid vs. State through NCB, which outlined the principles of law regarding concurrent and consecutive sentences under Section 427 of the CrPC. The overall outcome was that the Supreme Court allowed Iqram's appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed that the sentences in the nine sessions trials run concurrently, thereby significantly reducing his total imprisonment period.

case_name: Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar vs. State of Karnataka
text: Case: Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar vs. State of Karnataka. Date: 8th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the conviction and death sentence of Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar for the rape and murder of a five-year-old girl, R, was justified based on the circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution. Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar was charged under Sections 302 (murder), 376 (rape), 364 (kidnapping), 366A (procuration of minor girl), and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the Indian Penal Code. The key pieces of circumstantial evidence included: (i) the appellant taking the victim, R, from a neighbor's house; (ii) witnesses seeing the appellant carrying R and a gunny bag towards the Bennihalla stream; and (iii) the recovery of R's dead body in a gunny bag from Bennihalla based on the appellant's disclosure statement. Both the trial court and the High Court convicted Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar, with the trial court sentencing him to death and the High Court upholding the conviction and the death sentence. The defense highlighted discrepancies such as inconsistencies in the dates when witnesses claimed to have seen the appellant with the victim, and the initial police complaint not mentioning the appellant's involvement despite later claims by witnesses. The Supreme Court acknowledged the discrepancies but deemed them as not significant enough to create a reasonable doubt, considering the close-knit nature of the village community and the subsequent alignment of witness statements. The medical evidence included a postmortem report indicating asphyxia due to strangulation, signs of rape, and the body's condition aligning with the timeline of the alleged crime. The Supreme Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment with a stipulation that Irappa Siddappa Murgannavar shall not be entitled to premature release or remission until he has served at least 30 years of actual imprisonment. The Supreme Court considered factors such as the appellant's young age, lack of criminal antecedents, the potential for reformation, satisfactory conduct in prison, and the socio-economic background of the appellant. The Supreme Court emphasized that the chain of circumstantial evidence must be complete and conclusive, leading to only one inference of guilt and excluding all other hypotheses, to secure a conviction based on circumstantial evidence.

case_name: Irfan @ Naka vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Irfan @ Naka vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 23rd August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Irfan @ Naka was charged with offenses under Sections 302, 436, and 326-A of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his son Islamuddin, and his brothers Naushad and Irshad by setting them on fire. Irfan @ Naka appealed against the judgement and order of the High Court of Allahabad which confirmed the death sentence awarded to him by the Additional Sessions Judge for the murders. Irfan @ Naka was the father of one of the victims, Islamuddin, and the brother of the other two victims, Naushad and Irshad. The prosecution alleged that Irfan @ Naka had a strained relationship with the victims, particularly due to his second marriage, and on the night of 5th August 2014, he set fire to the room where the victims were sleeping, causing their deaths. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimonies from family members, dying declarations of the victims, and forensic evidence showing the presence of an inflammable substance used to start the fire. In their dying declarations, Irshad and Islamuddin stated that Irfan @ Naka locked the door from outside and set the room on fire with an inflammable substance, leading to their severe burn injuries and eventual deaths. The defense argued that the dying declarations were unreliable, that the evidence was circumstantial, and that Irfan @ Naka was falsely implicated due to family disputes over property. The Supreme Court found that the dying declarations were not reliable as they did not inspire confidence and were inconsistent with other evidence presented in the case. The Supreme Court acquitted Irfan @ Naka of all charges, stating that the prosecution failed to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that the benefit of doubt should go to the accused. The Supreme Court directed that Irfan @ Naka be released forthwith unless he was required to be detained in connection with any other case or cases.

case_name: Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd. vs. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd. vs. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 7th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the leave granted to Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd. to file a civil suit in the Calcutta High Court should be revoked based on the lack of territorial jurisdiction. The respondents argued that no part of the cause of action arose within the territorial jurisdiction of the Calcutta High Court and that it arose in Bangalore, thereby making the Calcutta High Court an inappropriate forum for the civil suit. The Single Judge of the High Court initially allowed the respondents' application and revoked the leave granted to the appellant to file the civil suit in the Calcutta High Court. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the Single Judge's order to revoke the leave granted to the appellant. The Supreme Court relied on the principle that questions of territorial jurisdiction should typically be raised in the written statement as part of the defense and not through an application for revocation of leave, as established in the cases of Secretary of State vs. Golabrai Paliram and Indian Mineral & Chemicals Co. vs. Deutsche Bank. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the Single Judge and the Division Bench, dismissed the application for revocation of leave, and granted liberty to the respondents to file their written statement in the suit to raise the plea of territorial jurisdiction. The Supreme Court directed the Single Judge of the High Court to frame appropriate issues in the suit, including the issue of territorial jurisdiction, and to proceed to answer them on their merits in accordance with the law.

case_name: Ishwarji Nagaji Mali vs. State of Gujarat
text: Case: Ishwarji Nagaji Mali vs. State of Gujarat. Date: 18th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Respondent no.2 was charged under Sections 302, 120(B), 114, and 304A of the IPC and under Sections 177, 184, and 134 of the Motor Vehicles Act. The incident involved the death of Daxaben, the wife of respondent no.2, who was allegedly hit by a speeding car while walking to Hanumanji Temple on 26th December 2020. The investigation revealed that respondent no.2 had conspired with others to kill his wife by hiring a driver to hit her with a car and make it appear as an accident. The father of the deceased preferred an appeal because the High Court granted bail to respondent no.2 without considering the seriousness of the charges and the evidence collected during the investigation. The High Court granted bail on the grounds that the case was based on circumstantial evidence, which it considered a weak piece of evidence, and there was no apprehension of respondent no.2 fleeing or tampering with evidence. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in granting bail without considering the material evidence and the seriousness of the offence, and it emphasized that circumstantial evidence can be strong enough to deny bail. The Supreme Court highlighted the insurance policy taken by respondent no.2, the call details showing communication between the conspirators, and the premeditated plan to kill Daxaben. The Supreme Court cited principles that emphasize the need to consider the nature and gravity of the offence, the evidence collected, and the likelihood of the accused interfering with the investigation while deciding on bail. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order granting bail to respondent no.2 and directed him to surrender before the concerned court/jail authorities within one week. The Supreme Court directed that the trial court should proceed with the trial of the case and decide it in accordance with law based on the evidence led by both sides.

The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order granting bail to respondent no.2 and directed him to surrender before the concerned court/jail authorities within one week.
The Supreme Court directed that the trial court should proceed with the trial of the case and decide it in accordance with law based on the evidence led by both sides.

case_name: J. Sekar @ Sekar Reddy vs. Directorate of Enforcement
text: Case: J. Sekar @ Sekar Reddy vs. Directorate of Enforcement. Date: 5th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves J. Sekar Reddy, Managing Partner of M/s SRS Mining, who deposited Rs 312.64 Crores in three bank accounts. The Income Tax Department conducted searches and seized Rs.106.98 Crores and 128.495 kg of gold. The CBI registered an FIR for various offenses, including money laundering under PMLA. The main issue was whether the proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) could continue despite the closure of the FIR for the scheduled offense due to lack of evidence. The High Court of Madras dismissed the petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C., which sought to quash the proceedings under the PMLA, holding that the commission of the scheduled offense is a fundamental pre-condition for initiating PMLA proceedings. The appellant argued that since the FIR for the scheduled offense was closed due to lack of evidence, the prosecution for offenses under PMLA was unsustainable. The CBI maintained that the seized currency notes, which were in the denomination of Rs. 2000, were part of the proceeds of crime and were not accounted for properly. The Adjudicating Authority refused to confirm the order of provisional attachment, stating that there was no material evidence to identify the bank officers who allegedly converted old currency notes into new ones. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the proceedings under PMLA, stating that the chances of proving the allegations in court were very bleak. The Supreme Court applied the principle that until allegations are substantiated and proven beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused must be presumed innocent. The court also referred to the judgement in Radheshyam Kejriwal vs. State of West Bengal, which states that if exoneration in adjudication proceedings is on merits, criminal prosecution on the same facts cannot continue. The Income Tax Department conducted searches, seized currency and gold, and later provided information that the seized new currency notes belonged to M/s SRS Mining and were recorded in the company's cash book. The department also confirmed that the tax on the seized amount was paid. The IT Department's letter dated 16th May 2019 clarified that the seized cash was accounted for and tax was paid, thus negating the allegations of money laundering. This letter played a crucial role in the Supreme Court's decision to quash the PMLA proceedings. The court found that the Enforcement Directorate did not present sufficient evidence to prove the allegations of money laundering beyond a reasonable doubt. The court noted that the reasonable belief of the Deputy Director was based on speculation and not on concrete evidence.

case_name: J.H. Patel (D) By LRS and Others vs. Nuboard Manufacturing Co. Ltd. & Others
text: Case: J.H. Patel (D) By LRS and Others vs. Nuboard Manufacturing Co. Ltd. & Others. Date: 26th September 2016. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge to the High Court's decision that allowed the management's writ petition and dismissed the workmen's writ petition against the Labour Court's award, which had granted 50% back-wages but denied reinstatement. The workmen, including J.H. Patel, were dismissed after they filed a criminal complaint against the company's officers for snatching away a subscription book. The company's officers were acquitted, and subsequently, the workmen were dismissed for filing a false report with the intent to misuse police powers. The Labour Court found that while the misconduct was proven, the dismissal was procedurally unfair as no departmental inquiry was held. Therefore, the Labour Court denied reinstatement but granted 50% back-wages from the date of dismissal until the judgment. The High Court set aside the Labour Court's award of back-wages, holding that the dismissal was justified based on the earlier criminal court decision that acquitted the company's officers. The Supreme Court observed that the Labour Court's judgment lacked discussion on the evidence presented by the management's witnesses, and it failed to explain why it concluded that the misconduct was proven. Hence, the Labour Court's findings could not be sustained. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, declared the termination of the workmen's services as unjustified, and awarded 50% back-wages with 6% interest per annum from the date of dismissal until superannuation or death, whichever is earlier. The Court provided an option for the respondents to pay 40% back-wages without interest if paid within three months.

case_name: J.S. Luthra Academy & Another vs. State of Jammu and Kashmir & Others
text: Case: J.S. Luthra Academy & Another vs. State of Jammu and Kashmir & Others. Date: 30th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the allotment of land to J.S. Luthra Academy was valid or whether it was arbitrary and needed to be quashed. The initial order was by the authority constituted under the J&K Wakf Act, 1978, which ordered the eviction of the Academy from the Wakf property in Jammu on 27th December 1995. The Jammu & Kashmir Special Tribunal granted an interim stay on the eviction order on 9th January 1996. The State Government considered allotting a piece of land in Channi Himmat, Jammu, to the Academy for shifting and running the school. The Writ Petitions questioned the allotment of land to the Academy, claiming it violated the original scheme and plan of the Channi Himmat Housing Colony. The Division Bench of the High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and quashed the allotment. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Division Bench, restored the judgment of the learned Single Judge, and allowed the Academy to retain the land with the modification that they pay for the two kanals of land initially allotted for free. The Supreme Court directed the Academy to pay Rs. 8,00,000 per kanal for the two kanals of land allotted for free, along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of allotment until the date of payment. The Supreme Court reasoned that the allotment was made in the public interest to avoid disrupting the education of hundreds of students and to ensure continuity of the school's operation, thereby justifying the deviation from the usual practice of auctioning the land.

case_name: JYOTI JAISWAL vs. NEERAJ KUMAR GUPTA
text: Case: JYOTI JAISWAL vs. NEERAJ KUMAR GUPTA. Date: 22nd November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the divorce petition filed by Neeraj Kumar Gupta in the Court of Ld. Additional District & Sessions Judge, Lalsot, District Dausa, Rajasthan, should be transferred to a competent court at Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh, at the request of Jyoti Jaiswal. The petitioner, Jyoti Jaiswal, argued for the transfer of the divorce petition to Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh, citing her convenience and potential difficulties in attending the court proceedings in Lalsot, Rajasthan. The Supreme Court considered the facts and circumstances of the case, the material on record, and concluded that the request for transfer was justified, thereby granting the transfer of the divorce petition to a competent court at Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The Supreme Court directed the Additional District and Sessions Court at Lalsot, Rajasthan, to transmit the entire record of the case to the transferee court at Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh, immediately. The Supreme Court instructed the transferee court at Ghazipur to decide the transferred case as expeditiously as possible. The Supreme Court allowed the transfer petition, ordering the transfer of the divorce petition from the Court of Ld. Additional District & Sessions Judge, Lalsot, District Dausa, Rajasthan, to a competent court at Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The Registry was directed to send a copy of the Supreme Court's order to both the courts (Lalsot and Ghazipur) immediately by e-mail for compliance.

case_name: Jadunath Singh vs Arvind Kumar & Anr.
text: Case: Jadunath Singh vs Arvind Kumar & Anr.. Date: 19th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. Jadunath Singh appealed the bail granted to the accused on the primary ground that they are dreaded criminals who have committed multiple murders, including the murder of a police constable during the course of the trial. The accused were charged under Sections 147, 148, 302/149, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code and were sentenced to life imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 20,000 each. On 11th February 2011, Arvind Kumar and others allegedly opened fire on Jadunath Singh, his son Rajvir, and others over a disputed plot, resulting in the deaths of Rajvir and Pawan Kumar and injuries to Ravita. The High Court granted bail to the accused based on their period of incarceration and the fact that two co-accused had already been granted bail. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not considered the relevant facts of the accused's involvement in the murder of a police constable and their subsequent absconding and resistance during arrest. The Supreme Court did not interfere with the bail granted to Arvind Kumar as he was not charge-sheeted in the murder case of the police constable. The Supreme Court set aside the bail granted to Chandra Kumar @ Chandu and Rishi Kumar, ordering them to surrender within two weeks or face coercive measures for taking them into custody. Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar were involved in the murder of police constable Ajay Kumar while in judicial custody, which significantly impacted their bail decision. The separate FIR charged Chandra Kumar and Rishi Kumar under Sections 302, 201, 120B, 34, and 224 of the IPC for the murder of police constable Ajay Kumar and related conspiracies. The High Court granted bail to the accused with the condition of furnishing a personal bond of Rs. 50,000 each along with two sureties.

case_name: Jafarudheen & Ors. vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: Jafarudheen & Ors. vs. State of Kerala. Date: 22nd April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the Division Bench of the High Court of Kerala's decision which confirmed the convictions and reversed the acquittals related to a political altercation leading to murder. The altercation involved members affiliated with CPI (M) and NDF (National Development Front). The altercation was a physical fight between CPI (M) members and NDF members, where the deceased reportedly assaulted A-3, leading to a conspiracy to kill the deceased. On 18th July 2002, the accused, armed with deadly weapons and traveling in an auto-rickshaw, a motorbike, and a jeep, attacked the deceased at his residence, resulting in his death and exploding country bombs. The charges included Sections 120-B, 143, 147, 148, 427, 460, 302 read with 149 IPC and Sections 3 and 5 of the Explosives Substances Act. The Trial Court convicted A-2, A-4, A-5, A-8, and A-9, while acquitting A-10 to A-16. It imposed various sentences including life imprisonment for the convicted. The High Court upheld the convictions of A-2, A-4, A-5, A-8, and A-9 and overturned the acquittal of A-10 to A-13, finding the Trial Court's acquittal of these accused erroneous. The Supreme Court highlighted the need for thorough scrutiny when reversing an acquittal, emphasizing the presumption of innocence and requiring strong reasons to overturn the Trial Court's decision. The Supreme Court noted that while a delay in sending the FIR to the Magistrate could lead to suspicion, it must be considered in light of the entire case and the explanations provided for the delay. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for credible evidence when considering recoveries under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, noting the potential for abuse and the requirement for careful scrutiny. The Supreme Court directed that the appeals filed by the convicted accused be considered afresh by the High Court, ensuring that the legal principles and the evidence on record were adequately scrutinized.

case_name: Jagbir Singh vs. State (N.C.T. of Delhi)
text: Case: Jagbir Singh vs. State (N.C.T. of Delhi). Date: 4th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Jagbir Singh was charged under Sections 302 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his wife by setting her on fire and for threatening her. The prosecution's case was that Jagbir Singh poured kerosene on his wife and set her on fire on 24th January 2008, leading to her death from burn injuries on 2nd February 2008. This act was allegedly driven by his illicit relationship with his brother's wife. The trial court found Jagbir Singh guilty under Sections 302 and 506 of the IPC, sentencing him to life imprisonment for murder and two years of rigorous imprisonment for criminal intimidation. The High Court of Delhi dismissed Jagbir Singh's appeal, upholding the trial court's conviction and sentence. There were multiple dying declarations. The initial statements did not implicate Jagbir Singh, but a later dying declaration on 27th January 2008 directly accused him of setting his wife on fire, which played a crucial role in his conviction. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction because it found the later dying declaration, which implicated Jagbir Singh, to be credible and supported by other evidence, such as the presence of kerosene on the clothes and the medical condition of the deceased. The appellant, Jagbir Singh, claimed that the fire was accidental, caused by a leaking petrol tank while he was trying to light a bidi, and that both he and his wife were injured in the process. He also argued that the dying declaration implicating him was a result of tutoring and conspiracy by his in-laws. The Supreme Court rejected the claim of conspiracy and tutoring, finding no substantial evidence to support the allegation. The Court found the dying declaration made by the deceased on 27th January 2008 to be voluntary and truthful. The Supreme Court noted that while a medical certificate confirming the fitness of the deceased to make the dying declaration is preferred, its absence is not necessarily fatal to the credibility of the declaration if the surrounding circumstances and evidence support its reliability. The Supreme Court dismissed Jagbir Singh's appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court and affirmed by the High Court.

case_name: Jagdish & Ors. vs. The State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Jagdish & Ors. vs. The State of Rajasthan. Date: 22nd February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the convictions and sentences of the appellants Jagdish and Prakash under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC should be upheld and whether their conviction under Section 397 of the IPC was justified. The charges against Jagdish and Prakash included Sections 302, 397, and 392 of the IPC, related to the murder, robbery, and abduction of the deceased Ram Chandra. The High Court upheld the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC but acquitted them of the charge under Section 397 IPC due to insufficient evidence. The prosecution presented evidence including the identification of Jagdish and Prakash by Shiv Bhagwan, blood-stained clothes found in the vehicle, and the recovery of Ram Chandra's dead body based on their disclosure statements. The Supreme Court found the identification of the appellants by Shiv Bhagwan credible and reliable, supporting the prosecution's case against Jagdish and Prakash. The Supreme Court convicted the appellants under Section 392 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced them to five years of imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 2000, and in default of payment, to undergo three months of simple imprisonment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by Bablu @ Balveer @ Roop Singh, setting aside his conviction and ordering his release unless required in any other case, due to lack of credible evidence directly linking him to the crime. The Supreme Court found inconsistencies and insufficient evidence in the prosecution's case against Bablu @ Balveer @ Roop Singh, particularly regarding the identification and recovery of evidence. The Supreme Court highlighted the importance of reliable and credible evidence for sustaining convictions, especially in cases involving severe penalties like life imprisonment and death sentences. The Supreme Court clarified that the dismissal of the appeals filed by Jagdish and Prakash would not prevent them from filing representation(s) for premature release/remission, which would be considered in accordance with law.

case_name: Jagjit Singh (D) Through LRS vs Amarjit Singh (D) Through his LRs
text: Case: Jagjit Singh (D) Through LRS vs Amarjit Singh (D) Through his LRs. Date: 13th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Amarjit Singh, the plaintiff, was entitled to specific performance of a contract for the purchase of a half share in a shop from Jagjit Singh, the defendant, despite alleged failure to prove readiness and willingness to perform the contract. The agreement dated 17th October 2000 involved the purchase of a half share in a shop for Rs. 1,50,000, with Rs. 1,30,000 paid in cash at the time of execution, and the balance to be paid by 30th March 2003 when the sale deed was to be executed and registered. The trial court dismissed the suit for specific performance, concluding that no agreement to sell had been executed between the parties. The first appellate court set aside the trial court's finding that no agreement was executed but concluded that the plaintiff failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the agreement. Thus, the suit for specific performance was dismissed. The High Court allowed the second appeal without framing any substantial question of law and reversed the appellate court's decision, holding that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.

case_name: Jagjit Singh vs State of Punjab
text: Case: Jagjit Singh vs State of Punjab. Date: 26th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant, Jagjit Singh, was the husband of the deceased, who died under unnatural circumstances along with her child by drowning in a river. Jagjit Singh was accused of subjecting his wife to cruelty and harassment related to dowry demands, which allegedly led to her unnatural death. The trial court convicted Jagjit Singh under Section 304-B IPC and sentenced him to 8 years of rigorous imprisonment, which was later reduced to 7 years by the High Court. The High Court upheld the conviction under Section 304-B IPC but reduced the sentence from 8 years to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment. The defense argued that the deceased took her life due to taunts from her sister about the appellant's financial status and not because of any dowry demands or harassment from the appellant. The Supreme Court found that there was sufficient evidence to establish dowry harassment soon before the death of the deceased, thus upholding the conviction under Section 304-B IPC. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and the reduced sentence of 7 years of rigorous imprisonment for Jagjit Singh under Section 304-B IPC.

case_name: Jahir Hak vs The State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Jahir Hak vs The State of Rajasthan. Date: 11th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Jahir Hak, who had been in custody for almost 8 years as an undertrial prisoner for offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, should be granted bail. Jahir Hak was charged under Sections 10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 18A, 18B, 19, 20, 23, and 38 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. Jahir Hak had been in custody for almost 8 years before the appeal was decided. At the time of the appeal, only 6 out of 109 witnesses had been examined, and the trial was expected to take at least 2 to 3 more years to conclude. The appellant argued that he had already been in custody for an extended period, the trial was progressing very slowly, and there was no significant evidence against him from the examined witnesses. The State argued that the offences were serious, and there was a need to protect witnesses who would testify during the trial. However, the State did not dispute that the examined witnesses' testimonies did not implicate the appellant. The court considered the precedent set in Union of India v. K. A. Najeeb (2021), where the Supreme Court granted bail to an accused who had been in jail for an extended period with little possibility of early completion of the trial. The court decided to grant bail to Jahir Hak, considering the long period of incarceration he had already undergone and the slow progress of the trial. The court directed that the appellant be released on bail subject to conditions that would be fixed by the trial court. The court clarified that its observations were made for the purpose of deciding the bail application and that the trial court would decide the case based on evidence and in accordance with the law. The court granted bail due to the appellant's long period of incarceration as an undertrial prisoner, the slow progress of the trial, and the fact that the evidence so far did not strongly implicate him.
