case_name: Kajal vs. Jagdish Chand & Ors.
text: Case: Kajal vs. Jagdish Chand & Ors.. Date: 5th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Kajal was a bright young girl of 12 years. She suffered serious injuries resulting in damage to her brain, leaving her with a very low IQ and severe weakness in all her limbs, severe hysteria, and severe urinary incontinence. Kajal suffered head injuries that resulted in her having an IQ of less than 20% of a child of her age and a social age of only a 9-month-old child. She has severe weakness in all her limbs, severe hysteria, and severe urinary incontinence. Her disability has been assessed as 100%. The MACT awarded Rs.11,08,501, and the High Court enhanced the award amount to Rs.25,78,501. The Supreme Court held that the notional income of Rs.15,000 per annum taken by the lower courts was not justified. Instead, they considered the minimum wages for a skilled workman, which with future prospects amounted to Rs.81,412.80 per annum. Using a multiplier of 18, the total was Rs.14,66,000. The Supreme Court awarded Rs.21,60,000 for attendant charges, considering she requires two attendants at a cost of Rs.10,000 per month for life. The Supreme Court increased the amount to Rs.15,00,000, considering the severe physical and mental disability Kajal suffers, including severe incontinence and the mental age of a nine-month-old child. The Supreme Court awarded Rs.5,00,000 for future medical expenses, considering her severe and lifelong medical needs. The Supreme Court awarded a total of Rs.62,27,000 to Kajal under various heads, including treatment expenses, loss of earnings, attendant charges, pain and suffering, loss of marriage prospects, and future medical treatment.

case_name: Kalabhai Hamirbhai Kachhot vs State of Gujarat
text: Case: Kalabhai Hamirbhai Kachhot vs State of Gujarat. Date: 28th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Kalabhai Hamirbhai Kachhot and other appellants were guilty of offences under Sections 302, 326, 324, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 135 of the Bombay Police Act for the murder of Gokalbhai. The accused allegedly ambushed Rajshibhai Maldebhai Karangiya, Mitesh Hardasbhai, and Gokalbhai Karsanbhai, attacking them with an axe and knives, resulting in the death of Gokalbhai. The Sessions Court convicted all the accused under Section 302 read with 34 IPC and Section 135 of the Bombay Police Act, sentencing them to life imprisonment and fines. The High Court confirmed the conviction but allowed the appeals partly by ordering all sentences to run concurrently and extended the benefit of Section 428 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellants' counsel argued that the conviction was based mainly on the testimony of chance witnesses with major contradictions and that the postmortem report did not match the injuries described. The Supreme Court found the testimony of the injured witnesses (PWs-18 and 19) natural and trustworthy, stating that minor discrepancies did not affect the credibility of their evidence. The Supreme Court noted that the identification was supported by the headlight of the motorcycle and the light from the farm, and that the accused and witnesses were from the same village, making identification credible. The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution proved the appellants' guilt beyond reasonable doubt, showing they committed the crime with common intention, supported by consistent and reliable witness testimony. The decision emphasizes the reliability of injured witness testimony and the importance of minor discrepancies not affecting the overall credibility, which could influence future rulings in similar cases. Legal practitioners should consider that minor discrepancies do not necessarily discredit witness testimonies if the core of the evidence remains consistent and trustworthy. Section 428 allows for the period of detention as under-trial prisoners to be set off against the sentence, which the High Court extended to the appellants, impacting the total time served.

case_name: Kale (Dead) Rep. Thr. LRs. vs. Union of India
text: Case: Kale (Dead) Rep. Thr. LRs. vs. Union of India. Date: 11th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves a dispute over the amount of land acquired by the State in Gajipur, Delhi, and the corresponding compensation paid to the landowners. The appellants claim that 45 Bigha 3 Biswas of their land was acquired, but they were compensated for only 36 Bigha 12 Biswas. The appellants' main grievance was that they were entitled to compensation for 45 Bigha 3 Biswas of land, but they were paid compensation for only 36 Bigha 12 Biswas, and they sought compensation for the remaining 9 Bigha of land. The Reference Court rejected the appellants' claim for additional compensation, concluding that only 36 Bigha 12 Biswas of land was acquired, and the appellants were already compensated for this amount. The High Court dismissed the appellants' revision petition, upholding the Reference Court's finding that only 36 Bigha 12 Biswas of land was acquired and that the appellants were adequately compensated for it. The Supreme Court concluded that the land measuring 36 Bigha 12 Biswas was acquired by the State, as evidenced by government records, and not 45 Bigha 3 Biswas as claimed by the appellants. The Court found no merit in the appellants' claim for additional compensation. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because the appellants failed to provide any documentary evidence to support their claim that 45 Bigha 3 Biswas of land was acquired. The Court agreed with the lower courts' findings that the acquired land was 36 Bigha 12 Biswas, for which compensation had already been paid.

case_name: Kalicharan & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Kalicharan & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 14th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issues were the omission to frame a proper charge in accordance with Section 213 of the Cr.P.C. and the failure of the Trial Judge to put material circumstances to the accused in their statements under Section 313 of the Cr.P.C. The charges included offenses under Section 148 IPC, Section 302 IPC, and Section 307 read with Section 149 IPC. Additionally, Yaad Prakash was charged under Section 25 of the Arms Act. The altercation occurred when Atar Singh was carrying soil with his bullock cart and was resisted by Kalicharan and his sons. The accused then returned with weapons and attacked the deceased Harpal Singh and others. Initially, it was alleged that Harpal Singh died due to bullet injuries caused by shots fired by Yaad Prakash. However, the prosecution witnesses later testified that Harpal Singh died from injuries caused by sharp weapons wielded by the accused. The Supreme Court found that the charges were misleading and not properly framed according to Section 213 of the Cr.P.C. Additionally, the important circumstances were not put to the accused in their statements under Section 313, causing serious prejudice. The Supreme Court set aside the convictions of Kalicharan, Yaad Prakash, and Shakuntala Devi and ordered their release unless required to be detained for any other offense. Diwan Singh's conviction was previously set aside by the Supreme Court on 1st July 2021, and he was acquitted. The Supreme Court stated that Sections 148 and 149 IPC could not be sustained as there was no assembly of five or more persons after excluding Diwan Singh, who was acquitted. PW-1 Atar Singh was the informant who witnessed the incident, and PW-2 Malkhan Singh was an eyewitness. Both provided key testimonies regarding the assault and the sequence of events. The Supreme Court concluded that the procedural errors, including the misleading charge and the failure to put material circumstances to the accused, caused serious prejudice and resulted in a failure of justice.

case_name: Kalinga @ Kushal vs. State of Karnataka By Police Inspector Hubli
text: Case: Kalinga @ Kushal vs. State of Karnataka By Police Inspector Hubli. Date: 20th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in convicting Kalinga @ Kushal for the murder of Master Hrithik despite the Trial Court's earlier acquittal. Kalinga @ Kushal was charged under Sections 201, 302, 363, and 364 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the alleged murder of Master Hrithik. On 3rd November 2002, Master Hrithik went missing. Despite searches, he was not found, leading PW-1 to file a missing complaint at PS Vidyanagar, Hubli. On 14th November 2002, Kalinga @ Kushal, in a drunken state, mentioned the incident. The next day, he confessed to PW-1, who then took him to the police station, leading to the filing of the complaint. The High Court justified convicting Kalinga @ Kushal by accepting the extra judicial confession made to PW-1 and the recovery of Hrithik's body from the well based on the appellant's information, despite the Trial Court's doubts about the reliability of the evidence. The Supreme Court highlighted discrepancies such as the absence of PW-1's mother and wife as witnesses, contradictions in the arrest account, unexplained differences in the description of clothes, and the unnatural conduct of PW-1 upon receiving information about his missing son. The Supreme Court found the extra judicial confession and the recovery of the body unreliable due to inconsistencies and lack of corroborative evidence, emphasizing that the prosecution failed to establish a coherent chain of circumstances. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's conviction of Kalinga @ Kushal and restored the Trial Court's acquittal, ordering the immediate release of the appellant if he was in custody.

case_name: Kallu Khan vs State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Kallu Khan vs State of Rajasthan. Date: 11th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Kallu Khan was charged under Sections 8 and 21 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. The Trial Court sentenced Kallu Khan to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs. 1,00,000. In default of payment of the fine, he was to undergo simple imprisonment for two years. The defense argued that the search and seizure were conducted by an unauthorized officer, no independent witnesses were involved, and there were contradictions in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses. During the search, a polythene bag containing 900 grams of brown substance resembling smack was found beneath the seat of Kallu Khan's motorcycle. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the default sentence from two years to one year. The Supreme Court found that the search and seizure were valid as they were conducted by a competent officer under Section 43 of the NDPS Act, and the recovery was a chance recovery from a public road. The Supreme Court held that the lack of independent witnesses did not invalidate the search and seizure, as the police witnesses' testimonies were consistent and credible. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the concurrent findings of the lower courts and affirming the conviction and sentence. The key evidence included the testimonies of police officers who conducted the search and seizure, the recovery of 900 grams of smack from Kallu Khan's motorcycle, and the procedural compliance during the search. No, the Supreme Court did not find any procedural irregularities in the handling of the seized contraband and ruled that the search and seizure were conducted lawfully. The Supreme Court noted that Kallu Khan had already served the sentence and paid the fine, and therefore, no further directions were necessary.

case_name: Kaloji Narayana Rao University of Health Sciences vs. Srikeerti Reddi Pingle & Ors.
text: Case: Kaloji Narayana Rao University of Health Sciences vs. Srikeerti Reddi Pingle & Ors.. Date: 16th February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondent student was eligible for admission to the MBBS course under the management quota for NRI candidates for the academic year 2020-21, based on her 12th-grade qualifications from Conrad High School, USA. The University alleged that the respondent student did not furnish proof of studying Biological Sciences in her qualifying examination (10+2 or equivalent) and therefore was ineligible for admission to the MBBS course. The High Court ruled that the student had completed her 12th grade with Biological Sciences as required, based on the certificates from Conrad High School and the Telangana State Board of Intermediate Education, and declared her eligible for admission. The University argued that the equivalence certificate did not sufficiently prove that the student had completed the necessary coursework in Biological Sciences to meet the eligibility criteria for the MBBS course. The Supreme Court observed that the MCI Regulations emphasize that candidates must have studied Physics, Chemistry, and Biology/Biotechnology, along with practical tests, during their 10+2 education or equivalent examination. The Supreme Court noted that the letters from Conrad High School stated that the respondent student completed an Advanced Placement (AP) Biology course in her 10th grade, which is typically equivalent to a first-year college-level course in the USA. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, ruling that the respondent student did not meet the eligibility criteria as specified by the MCI Regulations, which require continuous study of Biology/Biological Sciences in both 11th and 12th grades.

The University argued that the equivalence certificate did not sufficiently prove that the student had completed the necessary coursework in Biological Sciences to meet the eligibility criteria for the MBBS course.

The Supreme Court observed that the MCI Regulations emphasize that candidates must have studied Physics, Chemistry, and Biology/Biotechnology, along with practical tests, during their 10+2 education or equivalent examination.

The Supreme Court noted that the letters from Conrad High School stated that the respondent student completed an Advanced Placement (AP) Biology course in her 10th grade, which is typically equivalent to a first-year college-level course in the USA.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, ruling that the respondent student did not meet the eligibility criteria as specified by the MCI Regulations, which require continuous study of Biology/Biological Sciences in both 11th and 12th grades.

case_name: Kalyani (Dead) Through LRS. & Ors. vs. The Sulthan Bathery Municipality & Ors.
text: Case: Kalyani (Dead) Through LRS. & Ors. vs. The Sulthan Bathery Municipality & Ors.. Date: 26th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants were entitled to compensation for their land, which was used for the construction/widening of the Sulthan Bathery Bypass Road without receiving any compensation. The appellants claimed that they were assured compensation for their land, which they gave for the construction/widening of the road, but they never received any compensation despite multiple representations. The Sulthan Bathery Municipality contended that the appellants voluntarily gave their land without any claim for compensation and that there was no assurance given for compensation. The learned Single Judge ruled that there was no material on record to show that the appellants had voluntarily surrendered their land without compensation. The Judge held that the appellants were entitled to compensation for their land used for the construction/widening of the road, based on Article 300A of the Constitution. The Division Bench set aside the judgment of the Single Judge and dismissed the writ petition, stating that the appellants failed to prove that they were given assurance of compensation and that their claim was substantially delayed. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and order of the Division Bench, and restored the order of the Single Judge, recognizing the appellants' entitlement to compensation for their land used for the construction/widening of the road.

case_name: Kamala and Others vs. M.R. Mohan Kumar
text: Case: Kamala and Others vs. M.R. Mohan Kumar. Date: 24th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Kamala (Appellant No.1) was the legally wedded wife of M.R. Mohan Kumar (Respondent), thereby entitling her and her children to claim maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C. The Family Court held that Kamala was the legally wedded wife of M.R. Mohan Kumar and that their two children were born out of the wedlock. The court ordered M.R. Mohan Kumar to pay maintenance of Rs. 3,000 per month to Kamala and Rs. 2,500 per month to each of their children. Kamala presented several pieces of evidence, including photographs of herself with M.R. Mohan Kumar, birth certificates of their children listing M.R. Mohan Kumar as the father, and receipts acknowledging maintenance payments made by M.R. Mohan Kumar. M.R. Mohan Kumar denied that he had ever married Kamala and claimed that there was no valid marriage between them. He argued that Kamala's petition for maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C. was not maintainable as she was not his legally wedded wife. The High Court set aside the Family Court's order, stating that Kamala failed to prove that she was the legally wedded wife of M.R. Mohan Kumar. The High Court held that Kamala had not provided sufficient evidence to show that the marriage was solemnized according to customary rites. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision and reinstated the Family Court's order, holding that Kamala had provided sufficient evidence to establish her marriage to M.R. Mohan Kumar and that she and her children were entitled to maintenance. The Supreme Court emphasized that in proceedings under Section 125 Cr.P.C., a strict proof of marriage is not necessary as the proceedings are summary in nature and intended to prevent vagrancy and destitution. The Supreme Court presumed that Kamala and M.R. Mohan Kumar were living together as husband and wife, supported by the evidence of cohabitation and the birth certificates of their children. The Court held that such cohabitation raises a presumption of a valid marriage. The Supreme Court directed M.R. Mohan Kumar to pay the arrears of maintenance as ordered by the Family Court within two months and to continue paying the monthly maintenance as directed by the Family Court. The Supreme Court granted Kamala the liberty to move the Family Court for the enhancement of maintenance if required in the future.

case_name: Kamlesh Kalra vs. Shilpika Kalra & Ors.
text: Case: Kamlesh Kalra vs. Shilpika Kalra & Ors.. Date: 24th April 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the High Court's decision to quash the FIR under Sections 498A and 406 IPC, filed by Shilpika Kalra against her husband Manish Kalra, mother-in-law Kamlesh Kalra, and other in-laws. Shilpika Kalra and Manish Kalra got married on 28th July 2007. Shilpika Kalra alleged that her Stridhan articles were in possession of her mother-in-law Kamlesh Kalra, brother-in-law Avnish Kalra, and sister-in-law Suman Kalra, and that she faced harassment and demand for dowry. Charges under Section 406/34 IPC were framed against Manish Kalra and Kamlesh Kalra, and Manish Kalra was additionally charged under Section 498A IPC. Kamlesh Kalra and other in-laws sought to quash the FIR on the grounds that it was time-barred, filed much later than the period of limitation, and that the allegations did not constitute an offense under the cited sections. The High Court quashed the FIR under Section 498A IPC against Manish Kalra and Kamlesh Kalra, stating it was time-barred as it was filed beyond the limitation period of three years. The High Court held that Section 406 IPC is a continuing offense, and the non-return of Stridhan articles gives fresh cause of action every day, thus the charges under Section 406 IPC were not quashed against Kamlesh Kalra. The Supreme Court noted that the additional list of Stridhan articles submitted by Shilpika Kalra appeared to be an afterthought, filed more than seven years after the divorce petition and three years after the initial list. The Supreme Court found that the allegations of non-return of Stridhan articles were not sustainable in law, as the articles were already deposited with the police, and the FIR seemed to be a pressure tactic by Shilpika Kalra. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by Kamlesh Kalra, quashed the FIR under Sections 498A/406 IPC, and dismissed the appeal filed by Shilpika Kalra. The Supreme Court emphasized that filing criminal complaints as a pressure tactic constitutes an abuse of the process of the Court and should be discouraged to prevent misuse of legal provisions.

case_name: Kanailal Sarkar vs. The State of West Bengal
text: Case: Kanailal Sarkar vs. The State of West Bengal. Date: 4th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the conviction of Kanailal Sarkar under Section 306 IPC for abetting the suicide of his daughter-in-law, Laxmi Rani, was justified based on the evidence presented. Kanailal Sarkar was charged under Sections 302, 498-A, and 34 IPC for the murder and harassment of Laxmi Rani. The prosecution alleged that Kanailal Sarkar harassed Laxmi Rani, demanding money from her parents, and ultimately set her on fire by pouring kerosene on her. In her dying declaration, Laxmi Rani stated that her father-in-law, Kanailal Sarkar, poured kerosene on her and set her on fire. The trial court convicted Kanailal Sarkar under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted Kanailal Sarkar of the charge under Section 302 IPC but convicted him under Section 306 IPC for abetting the suicide of Laxmi Rani and sentenced him to five years of rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court observed that the dying declaration of Laxmi Rani, along with the testimonies of witnesses, supported the prosecution's case and justified the conviction under Section 306 IPC. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence of five years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 306 IPC. The Supreme Court directed Kanailal Sarkar to surrender to custody within four weeks to serve the remaining sentence, failing which he would be taken into custody. The Supreme Court ordered a copy of its decision to be sent to the concerned trial court for necessary action.

case_name: Kanchan Sharma vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Kanchan Sharma vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 17th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the criminal proceedings against Kanchan Sharma under Section 306 IPC and Section 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act should be quashed. Kanchan Sharma was accused of abetting the suicide of Vikas, who allegedly consumed poison after being harassed and abused with casteist slurs by Kanchan Sharma and her family. The complainant, Vijaydeep, alleged that Vikas was called to Kanchan Sharma's house where he was abused with casteist slurs and forcefully administered poison, leading to his death. The High Court dismissed Kanchan Sharma's application for quashing the criminal proceedings, stating that disputed questions of fact could not be adjudicated at that stage. Kanchan Sharma's counsel argued that there was no basis to proceed against her for the alleged offenses, as the deceased's actions were self-inflicted and not abetted by her. The Supreme Court found that there was no material evidence to show that Kanchan Sharma had any relation with the deceased or that she abetted his suicide. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the criminal proceedings against Kanchan Sharma, stating that there was no credible material to proceed with the trial. The Supreme Court reiterated that for a conviction under Section 306 IPC, there must be a clear act of instigation or aid to commit suicide, which was not evident in this case. This judgment emphasizes the need for substantial evidence linking the accused's actions directly to the suicide, ensuring that mere allegations without proof cannot sustain a conviction under Section 306 IPC. If similar cases lack substantial evidence of abetment, they are likely to be quashed by higher courts, reinforcing the principle that mere allegations are insufficient for conviction under Section 306 IPC. The Supreme Court highlighted the importance of examining the material evidence thoroughly and ensuring that the charges are not based on mere allegations without credible proof before proceeding with a trial.

case_name: Kanihya @ Kanhi (Dead) Through LRS. vs Sukhi Ram & Ors.
text: Case: Kanihya @ Kanhi (Dead) Through LRS. vs Sukhi Ram & Ors.. Date: 3rd May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellants' failure to deposit the full pre-emption amount within the time specified by the Trial Court, due to a minor shortfall of Rs 14, could be rectified by allowing a late deposit of the balance amount. The Trial Court decreed the pre-emption suit on 11th August 1988, directing the appellants to deposit a sum of Rs 9,214 minus 1/5th of the pre-emption amount already deposited, by 10th October 1988, failing which the suit would be dismissed. The shortfall of Rs 14 was due to an error in calculation, as the Trial Court had directed the deposit of Rs 7,600 instead of the required Rs 7,614. The High Court initially allowed the revision petition on 4th December 2008, invoking its inherent jurisdiction to correct the error and granted the appellants time to deposit the balance sum of Rs 14. The High Court allowed the Review Application, recalled its earlier order, and dismissed the revision petition on 26th October 2009, holding that the appellants' failure to deposit the full amount within the stipulated time could not be condoned. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the High Court and the Trial Court, allowed the appellants to deposit the deficit amount of Rs 14 on or before 20th May 2024, and directed the respondents to withdraw the entire amount deposited in court. The Supreme Court directed the appellants to pay a cost of Rs 1,00,000 to the respondents, to be deposited in the Trial Court along with the balance amount, as compensation for the prolonged litigation.

case_name: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.
text: Case: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.. Date: 24th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether it is necessary to seek probate or letter of administration in respect of a Will in terms of Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 in the National Capital Region of Delhi. The learned Single Bench allowed an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, holding that the suit for declaration and permanent injunction was not maintainable in view of Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that the bar under Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is not applicable and set aside the order of rejection of plaint, directing that both the suits be clubbed and common evidence be led together. The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires probate or letter of administration only for Wills made within the territories of Bengal, Madras, or Bombay, or for immovable properties situated within those territories, and is not applicable to Delhi. The Supreme Court held that it is not necessary to seek probate or letter of administration for Wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, or Jains in Delhi, as Delhi is not covered by the territories mentioned in Section 57(a) and (b) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the Division Bench's judgment that Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is not applicable to the National Capital Region of Delhi, and both suits should proceed with common evidence.

case_name: Kaptan Singh vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Others
text: Case: Kaptan Singh vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Others. Date: 13th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The private respondents were charged with offenses under Sections 147, 148, 149, 406, 329, and 386 of the IPC for the alleged involvement in a dispute over a plot of land owned by Munni Devi. Kaptan Singh, the power of attorney holder of Munni Devi, filed a complaint alleging that the respondents forcibly occupied the plot, demanded money, used abusive language, and physically assaulted him. The High Court quashed the proceedings, stating that the dispute was of a civil nature, and Kaptan Singh, being an outsider to the deal, had no locus to file the complaint. The Supreme Court held that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by quashing the criminal proceedings, as there were serious triable issues that required examination during the trial. The Supreme Court emphasized that the allegations made in the complaint, supported by the investigation and evidence collected by the police, warranted a trial and should not have been dismissed summarily by the High Court. The Supreme Court highlighted that the payment of Rs. 25 lakhs mentioned in the joint notarized affidavit, the alleged possession handed over to Mamta Gupta, and the existence of two conflicting documents of the same date were triable issues. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court failed to consider the material and evidence collected during the investigation, including the statements of witnesses and the complainant. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's conclusion, stating that Kaptan Singh, as the power of attorney holder of Munni Devi, had the right to file the complaint, and this aspect should be considered during the trial. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed that the trial should proceed further in accordance with law, emphasizing that the trial court should decide the case based on the evidence presented without being influenced by any observations made during the proceedings. The Supreme Court reiterated that the exercise of powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be done sparingly, carefully, and with caution, and should not be used to quash proceedings when there are serious triable issues that need to be addressed during the trial.

case_name: Karan Singh v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr.
text: Case: Karan Singh v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr.. Date: 22nd October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Karan Singh was entitled to pension and other benefits under the pension scheme introduced by the Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) despite having less than 10 years of qualifying service. Karan Singh claimed pension benefits based on the DTC's pension scheme introduced in 1993, arguing that his total service period, including training and regular appointment, should be counted towards qualifying service. The DTC calculated Karan Singh's qualifying service as 9 years, 1 month, and 25 days, excluding certain periods such as leave without pay, which did not meet the 10-year requirement for pension eligibility. The Central Administrative Tribunal initially directed the DTC to pay Karan Singh pension and other benefits, which was later set aside by the High Court. The High Court set aside the Central Administrative Tribunal's order, ruling that Karan Singh did not meet the minimum qualifying service requirement for pension under the DTC's scheme. The Supreme Court dismissed Karan Singh's appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that he did not have the required 10 years of qualifying service to be eligible for pension. The Supreme Court interpreted the rules to mean that the period of leave without pay should be excluded from qualifying service, and Karan Singh's service fell short of the 10-year requirement. Karan Singh objected to the exclusion of his training period and periods of leave without pay from the qualifying service, arguing that these should be included for pension eligibility. The decision reinforces the strict adherence to the qualifying service rules for pension eligibility, affecting other DTC employees with similar service records who may seek pension benefits. DTC might clarify and strictly enforce the rules regarding qualifying service for pension, ensuring that employees are aware of the criteria and exclusions to avoid similar disputes in the future. The Supreme Court concluded that periods of leave without pay should be excluded from the calculation of qualifying service, as these do not count towards pension eligibility under the rules.

text: Case: Karim Uddin Barbhuiya v. Aminul Haque Laskar & Ors.. Date: 8th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the election petition filed by Aminul Haque Laskar challenging the election of Karim Uddin Barbhuiya should be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC. The petition alleged corrupt practices and improper acceptance of Barbhuiya's nomination papers. Aminul Haque Laskar alleged that Karim Uddin Barbhuiya made false declarations regarding his educational qualifications, suppressed information about a diploma in engineering, and did not disclose bank loan details and un-liquidated provident fund dues. The Gauhati High Court dismissed the application filed by Karim Uddin Barbhuiya under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, which sought the rejection of the election petition filed by Aminul Haque Laskar. The main grounds of appeal were that the election petition did not disclose any material facts or cause of action, as it was based on bald allegations without supporting documents or reliable sources. It was also argued that the petition did not contain full particulars of the alleged corrupt practices. The Supreme Court concluded that the election petition lacked precise, specific, and unambiguous pleadings. It did not meet the requirements of Section 83(1)(a) and (b) of the Representation of the People Act, and therefore, the petition was dismissed. The key legal provisions discussed included Sections 83, 100, and 123 of the Representation of the People Act, which pertain to the contents of election petitions, grounds for declaring elections void, and definitions of corrupt practices, respectively. The judgment also referenced Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC for the rejection of petitions lacking cause of action. case_name: Kariman vs. State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Kariman vs. State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 22nd April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of Kariman under Section 302 IPC could be converted to Part I or Part II of Section 304 IPC, given the circumstances of the case. Kariman was charged and convicted under Section 302 IPC for the murder of his second wife, Dasmet Bai. On 11th September 1999, Kariman allegedly assaulted his second wife, Dasmet Bai, with fists and stones, causing her death. The incident was reported by Budhram, the uncle of the deceased, leading to Kariman's arrest and conviction. The trial court convicted Kariman and sentenced him to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC, which was affirmed by the High Court. Kariman's appeal to the Supreme Court questioned whether the conviction could be reduced to Section 304 IPC. Kariman's counsel argued that the incident was a result of a sudden quarrel, and there was no intention to kill. The injury caused was not sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, suggesting a conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC was more appropriate. The Supreme Court noted that the eyewitnesses (PW-4, PW-5, and PW-6) testified that Kariman chased and assaulted Dasmet Bai, but the genesis of the quarrel was not clear. The Court found no evidence of premeditation or cruelty. The Supreme Court concluded that the injury inflicted by Kariman was not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death and that the act was committed in the heat of the moment during a sudden quarrel. The Supreme Court modified Kariman's conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part II IPC, reducing the sentence to seven years of rigorous imprisonment, noting that Kariman had already served about 17 years in prison. The Supreme Court ordered that Kariman be released forthwith if his detention was not required in any other case, as he had already served the modified sentence period. The Supreme Court discussed the principles of modifying a conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 IPC, emphasizing the need to consider the intention and knowledge of the accused at the time of the incident.

case_name: Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Limited vs. JSW Energy Limited
text: Case: Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Limited vs. JSW Energy Limited. Date: 22nd November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether there was a concluded contract between Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Limited (KPTCL) and JSW Energy Limited regarding the tariff rate for the purchase of power before the Karnataka Electricity Reform Act, 1999 came into force. The High Court found that there was a concluded contract between KPTCL and JSW Energy Limited before the Karnataka Electricity Reform Act, 1999 came into force, based on the Government Order dated 12th May 1999. The High Court decided that the status of JSW Energy Limited's power plant was that of an Independent Power Producer (IPP) and not a Captive Power Plant (CPP). The High Court found the KERC's order flawed due to several errors in calculation and the Commission's failure to adhere to the principles of a negotiated single-part tariff, leading to a disproportionate loading of fixed charges on JSW Energy Limited. The High Court invoked the principle of waiver, noting that neither party insisted on the satisfaction of the condition precedent for a formal PPA before supplying power, and that the parties' conduct over three years indicated that the PPA was not considered essential. The High Court interpreted the proviso to Section 27(2) as indicating that a concluded contract regarding tariff between the parties before the Commission came into existence did not require a formal written document or a specific form. The High Court found merit in JSW Energy Limited's contention that the KERC failed to appreciate its rights grounded on the principles of promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation, contributing to the decision to allow the appeal.

case_name: Karnataka State Pollution Control Board vs. B. Heera Naik & Ors.
text: Case: Karnataka State Pollution Control Board vs. B. Heera Naik & Ors.. Date: 26th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Commissioner of the City Municipal Council and Chief Officers of the City Municipal Council could be prosecuted under Section 48 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The Karnataka State Pollution Control Board alleged that the respondents failed to renew the consent to discharge sewage effluent after the expiry date, did not provide a Sewage Treatment Plant, and continuously discharged untreated sewage into water bodies, violating Section 25 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. The High Court allowed the applications under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and quashed the proceedings initiated for the prosecution of the respondents by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the basis that the Commissioners of the Municipal Council and the Chief Officers of the City Municipal Council could not be prosecuted under Section 48 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, as they were not considered Heads of the Department. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation, holding that the Commissioners and Chief Officers of the Municipal Council could indeed be considered as Heads of the Department and therefore liable for prosecution under Section 48 of the Act. The Supreme Court emphasized that the Commissioners and Chief Officers, being Chief Executive Officers of the respective Corporation and Council, are responsible for ensuring compliance with the provisions of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and can be prosecuted for violations. The Supreme Court relied on its previous judgement in the case of V.C. Chinnappa Goudar vs. Karnataka State Pollution Control Board & Anr., which affirmed that the prosecution of Municipal Commissioners under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, does not require prior sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision to quash the complaints and directed the Magistrate/Metropolitan Magistrate to proceed with the complaints in accordance with the law. Section 47 of the Act is significant as it provides that any person responsible for the conduct of the business of the company, which includes municipal bodies, can be prosecuted for offenses committed under the Act. This provision was crucial in establishing the liability of the respondents. The Supreme Court concluded that the term 'Head of Department' under Section 48 of the Act includes Commissioners and Chief Officers of Municipal Councils, thereby making them liable for prosecution for non-compliance with the Act's provisions.

text: Case: Karshanbhai Ramjibhai Jaladiya vs. District Development Officer & Anr.. Date: 19th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The compensation initially awarded to the appellants was Rs. 1,85,000/- each, which was considered insufficient due to the prolonged litigation spanning over three decades and the service period of the workmen. The Supreme Court directed that Karshanbhai Ramjibhai Jaladiya shall be entitled to preferential appointment in case any future vacancy arises, either as Work Charged Clerk or as Carpenter, subject to eligibility. The Supreme Court instructed that the compensation amount of Rs. 6,50,000/- each, in addition to the amounts already paid, should be paid within a period of six weeks from the date of the judgment. case_name: Karuppanna Gounder vs. The State Represented by the Inspector of Police
text: Case: Karuppanna Gounder vs. The State Represented by the Inspector of Police. Date: 17th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Karuppanna Gounder was guilty of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the death of Chinnappa Gounder. Karuppanna Gounder and Chinnappa Gounder were neighbors who shared a common boundary and a well between their properties. The conflict arose when Karuppanna Gounder and his family were removing sand from their portion of the well, which led to an argument with Chinnappa Gounder's family over the sand being dropped on their passage. The main witnesses included PW-6, the son of the deceased, who witnessed the altercation and attack, and other eyewitnesses who testified to the events. The trial court convicted Karuppanna Gounder (A1) of murder under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. His son-in-law Rajendran (A2) was also convicted but the other accused were acquitted. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence of Karuppanna Gounder under Section 302 IPC but reduced Rajendran's conviction to causing simple injuries and awarded him three years rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court noted that the injuries on Chinnappa Gounder's head were consistent with the attack by Rajendran (A2) and other accused with iron rods, not just the hammer used by Karuppanna Gounder (A1). The post-mortem report revealed two relevant injuries: a laceration on the middle of the head and a compound fracture of the skull with brain matter exposed. The Supreme Court acquitted Karuppanna Gounder of the offence of murder but convicted him under Section 324 IPC. His sentence was modified to the period already undergone, and he was released on bail.

case_name: Kathi David Raju vs. The State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Kathi David Raju vs. The State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 5th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary allegation was that Kathi David Raju obtained a fake Scheduled Caste certificate of 'Yanadi' caste, whereas he actually belonged to the 'Telanga' caste, and used the fake certificate to secure employment. The Additional Junior Civil Judge, Bapatla, ordered a DNA test for Kathi David Raju, his mother, and his two brothers to verify his caste claim, which was challenged by Kathi David Raju. Kathi David Raju filed the application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the order for the DNA test, arguing that it was ordered on insufficient grounds and was a roving and fishing enquiry. The High Court dismissed Kathi David Raju's application, upholding the order for the DNA test. The Supreme Court found the order for the DNA test to be unsustainable because it was made without substantial investigation or sufficient grounds, viewing it as a roving and fishing enquiry. The Supreme Court set aside both the High Court's judgment and the Additional Junior Civil Judge's order for the DNA test, allowing for the possibility of reconsideration if substantial evidence is found in the future. The FIR alleged that Kathi David Raju obtained a fake Scheduled Caste certificate of 'Yanadi' caste, while he belonged to 'Telanga' caste, and used it to get a job as Additional Assistant Engineer in V.T.P.S. Electricity Generation Corporation. The police authorities requested a DNA test to verify Kathi David Raju's claim of being the son of 'Yedulcondalu' rather than 'Venkat Kotaiah' as stated in the FIR, to substantiate the allegation of obtaining a false caste certificate. Kathi David Raju's counsel cited the Andhra Pradesh (SC, ST, and BCs) Regulation of Issue of Community Certificates Act, 1993, which provides specific procedures for the cancellation of false community certificates and argued that the FIR was malicious. The Supreme Court suggested that the police authorities could request a DNA test in the future if they gather sufficient material evidence during their investigation to justify such a test. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment and the Additional Junior Civil Judge's order for the DNA test, but left open the possibility for the Court to reconsider the request if sufficient materials are found in the future.

case_name: Kavita Chandrakant Lakhani vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
text: Case: Kavita Chandrakant Lakhani vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.. Date: 24th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the charges under Section 366 IPC should be included against Respondent No. 2 for forcibly taking the appellant to his house and allegedly molesting her. Kavita Chandrakant Lakhani alleged that on 6th September 2003, after a birthday party, Respondent No. 2 forcibly took her to his house, removed her clothes, beat her with a waist belt, and touched her inappropriately. The Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate rejected the discharge application, leading to the committal of the case to the Sessions Court. The Sessions Court discharged Respondent No. 2 from charges under Sections 363, 366, and 506(ii) of the IPC. The High Court upheld the discharge, stating that mere abduction without intent to compel marriage or seduction to illicit intercourse does not fall under Section 366 IPC, and the additional allegations of molestation appeared to be an afterthought. The Supreme Court noted that the allegations of molestation were added later and lacked credibility. The Court found no intent of abduction for forced marriage or illicit intercourse, leading to the conclusion that the charge under Section 366 IPC was not maintainable. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to discharge Respondent No. 2 under Section 366 IPC, and directed the trial court to conclude the trial within six months.

case_name: Kazi Moinuddin Kazi Bashiroddin & Ors. vs The Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation & Anr.
text: Case: Kazi Moinuddin Kazi Bashiroddin & Ors. vs The Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation & Anr.. Date: 30th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation (MTDC) could withdraw an amount of Rs. 1,37,50,547/- which was deposited towards the enhanced amount of compensation for the land acquisition. MTDC claimed the amount was deposited by mistake because the Supreme Court's order dated 29th January 2018 did not require them to deposit the entire compensation amount awarded by the Reference Court. The High Court allowed MTDC to withdraw the amount of Rs. 1,37,50,547/- deposited on 20th March 2018, stating that the Supreme Court's order did not permit the withdrawal of the entire compensation amount. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's interpretation was incorrect and that the order dated 29th January 2018 should be applied on its substance rather than technicalities, intending that the entire enhanced compensation amount should reach the claimants. The original compensation issue was related to the acquisition of land comprising Gut Nos. 90 & 91 of Village Pimpaldari for the Ajanta Verul Development Project, where the appellants were dissatisfied with the compensation awarded by the Special Land Acquisition Officer and sought enhancement. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's order by directing that 50% of the enhanced compensation amount should be released without security and the remaining 50% with security, following the precedent set in a similar case. The Supreme Court emphasized that its orders should be understood on their pith and substance, avoiding technicalities, and that the interpretation should advance the cause of justice, particularly in matters of compensation for land losers. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order allowing MTDC to withdraw the deposited amount and rejected MTDC's application for withdrawal, ensuring that the appellants received the enhanced compensation as directed.

case_name: Kedar Nath Kohli (Dead) by LRs. vs. Baldev Singh
text: Case: Kedar Nath Kohli (Dead) by LRs. vs. Baldev Singh. Date: 27th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Kedar Nath Kohli, represented by his legal representatives, could claim possession of Plot No. 27 in Wazir Nagar, New Delhi, which was allegedly in the illegal possession of Baldev Singh. The appellant claimed that his father, Mehar Chand Kohli, was the original owner of Plot No. 27 and that the respondents had illegally trespassed and constructed on the land without authorization or consent. The respondent, Baldev Singh, claimed that he had purchased the property from Dharampal, s/o Haveli Ram, through a registered sale deed dated 15.9.1966, and that the property did not belong to the appellant. Both the trial court and the first appellate court dismissed the suit for possession filed by the appellant, and their judgments were confirmed by the High Court, which dismissed the appellant's Regular Second Appeal. The sale deed dated 15.9.1966 was crucial as it was produced by the respondent to show his ownership of Plot No. 27. However, the trial court summoned the original records and found discrepancies, indicating potential forgery. The Supreme Court found that the sale deed produced by the respondent was fabricated, as the original document from the Sub-Registrar's office did not match the respondent's claims and indicated that Baldev Singh was not the rightful owner of the property. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the High Court, first appellate court, and trial court, and decreed the suit filed by the original plaintiff Mehar Chand Kohli, granting possession of Plot No. 27 to the appellant.

The sale deed dated 15.9.1966 was crucial as it was produced by the respondent to show his ownership of Plot No. 27. However, the trial court summoned the original records and found discrepancies, indicating potential forgery.

The Supreme Court found that the sale deed produced by the respondent was fabricated, as the original document from the Sub-Registrar's office did not match the respondent's claims and indicated that Baldev Singh was not the rightful owner of the property.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the High Court, first appellate court, and trial court, and decreed the suit filed by the original plaintiff Mehar Chand Kohli, granting possession of Plot No. 27 to the appellant.

case_name: Kekhriesatuo Tep vs. National Investigation Agency
text: Case: Kekhriesatuo Tep vs. National Investigation Agency. Date: 12th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the bail granted to Kekhriesatuo Tep and other appellants by the Special Court, NIA, should be canceled as ordered by the Gauhati High Court. The Gauhati High Court canceled the bail on the grounds that the appellants had committed offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, which were serious in nature. The Supreme Court noted that the Special Judge had correctly distinguished between those who commit extortion voluntarily and those who are compelled to pay under threat, finding that the appellants were victims of extortion. The Special Court, NIA, found that the appellants had voluntarily cooperated with the investigation and surrendered all relevant documents, indicating no voluntary support for the outlawed organizations. The Supreme Court quashed the Gauhati High Court's order canceling the bail and reinstated the bail granted by the Special Court, NIA, finding no perverse or impossible view in the Special Court's decision. The FSL report showed that the receipts for the payments were in the appellants' handwriting, but the appellants claimed they were forced to make these payments under threat, which the court accepted. The Supreme Court interpreted that for an act to constitute an offence under Sections 39 and 40, it must be done with the intention of furthering the activities of a terrorist organization, which was not proven in this case. The Supreme Court distinguished between voluntary contributions to terrorist organizations and payments made under compulsion, finding the appellants' payments were made under duress. The appellants' voluntary cooperation with the investigation and their status as government servants with deep societal roots were factors that led the Supreme Court to uphold their bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashed the orders of the Gauhati High Court, and reinstated the bail granted by the Special Court, NIA, to the appellants.

case_name: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1)
text: Case: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1). Date: 3rd January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the debits made in the Profit & Loss Account of Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. with respect to the amount of surcharge on sales tax and turnover tax paid to the State Government should be disallowed under Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The High Court held that the levy of gallonage fee, licence fee, and shop rental (kist) with respect to FL-9 licences granted to the appellant falls within the purview of Section 40(a)(iib) and the amount paid in this regard is liable to be disallowed. The High Court ruled that the surcharge on sales tax and turnover tax is not a 'fee or charge' within the meaning of Section 40(a)(iib) and therefore cannot be disallowed under this provision. The assessment completed against the appellants for the assessment years 2014-2015 and 2015-2016 was set aside, and the matter was remitted to the Assessing Officer to pass revised orders after computing the liability in accordance with the High Court's position. The Supreme Court stated that the interpretation of Section 40(a)(iib) should be viewed from the nature of the undertaking on which the levy is imposed, not on the number of undertakings. This means that the levy of gallonage fee, licence fee, and shop rental (kist) is an exclusive levy on the State Government Undertakings and should be disallowed. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the surcharge on sales tax is a tax and not a 'fee' or 'charge'. Therefore, it is outside the scope of Section 40(a)(iib)(A) and (B) of the Income-tax Act and should not be disallowed.

case_name: Kerala State Road Transport Corporation vs. Akhilesh V.S. & Others
text: Case: Kerala State Road Transport Corporation vs. Akhilesh V.S. & Others. Date: 1st April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Corporation decided not to fill the vacancies due to a financial crunch and a skewed staff-to-bus ratio, despite having a rank list of eligible candidates. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in issuing a mandamus to fill the vacancies, as empanelment does not create an automatic right to appointment. The Court set aside the decision because the High Court’s directive disregarded the Corporation's valid reasons, such as financial constraints and operational needs. The Court stated that judicial review should not substitute the employer's discretion unless decisions are arbitrary, unreasonable, or illegal. The Court held that filling such vacancies is discretionary and subject to valid and germane reasons, without creating an indefeasible right for candidates on the rank list.

case_name: Kerala Transport Development Finance Corporation Limited vs. Basil T K & Ors.
text: Case: Kerala Transport Development Finance Corporation Limited vs. Basil T K & Ors.. Date: 31st January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the period during which the respondents (Basil T K and others) were kept out of service should be counted as 'notional service' for the purpose of seniority, promotion, and pay fixation, despite the High Court's directive that they should not receive monetary benefits for this period. The respondents were appointed as Assistant Managers on contract in 2000 and regularized in 2006. However, their regularization was canceled in 2007 due to the absence of a standard recruitment procedure and reservation for SC/ST candidates. After legal challenges, they were reinstated with continuity of service but without monetary benefits for the period they were out of service. The Single Judge directed that the period during which the respondents were out of service should be treated as notional service for the purpose of seniority and promotion. Consequently, the respondents were granted seniority above Aneesh Babu and directed to be promoted as Managers and Chief Managers with effect from the respective eligibility dates. KTDFCL argued that treating the period of absence as notional service would unfairly place the respondents above Aneesh Babu in the seniority list. They contended that the respondents should not receive any service benefits, including promotions, for the period they were out of service, as per the High Court's earlier judgment. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to treat the period out of service as notional service for seniority and promotion purposes. However, the Court clarified that the respondents would not be entitled to any arrears of salary for this period. The promotion to the post of Chief Manager would be governed by the applicable Service Rules and regulations. The Supreme Court directed that the promotion to the post of Chief Manager should be conducted in accordance with the applicable Service Rules and regulations, ensuring that the process is fair and based on the criteria set forth in those rules.

case_name: Ketan Kantilal Seth vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: Case: Ketan Kantilal Seth vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.. Date: 9th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the criminal cases pending against the petitioner in multiple states could be transferred to one court in Mumbai for a consolidated trial. There were 16 criminal cases pending against Ketan Kantilal Seth in Gujarat, Maharashtra, New Delhi, and West Bengal. The allegations were that Ketan Kantilal Seth and his associates, acting as directors of M/s Home Trade Limited, engaged in unauthorized transactions involving government securities and misappropriated funds. The petitioner argued that multiple trials in different states caused delays, huge expenses, and practical difficulties in securing the presence of witnesses and accused for trial. Most transactions and witnesses were based in Mumbai. The Supreme Court dismissed the intervention application, stating that the intervenor was neither a complainant in any of the cases nor directly involved, and thus had no locus to intervene in the petition. The Supreme Court allowed the transfer petitions, directing that all the specified criminal cases be transferred to the Principal Judge, Bombay City Civil and Sessions Court, Mumbai, and assigned to the appropriate court within its jurisdiction. The Supreme Court directed that the charges be framed within two months from the date of appearance of the accused and that the trials be concluded expeditiously, within two years, ensuring no prejudice to any accused.

case_name: Khaja Bilal Ahmed vs. State of Telangana & Ors
text: Case: Khaja Bilal Ahmed vs. State of Telangana & Ors. Date: 18th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Khaja Bilal Ahmed challenged the order of detention dated 25th October 2018 issued under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Boot-Leggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, etc., Act 1986. Khaja Bilal Ahmed was detained for being a 'Goonda' and habitually engaging in unlawful acts, including gruesome and heinous offences like murder, attempt to murder, rioting, and criminal trespass, which caused panic and terror among the public. Fourteen criminal cases were registered against Khaja Bilal Ahmed between 2007 and 2016. The bail application was allowed by the 14th Additional Metropolitan Magistrate on the ground that the investigating agency failed to complete the investigation within the period allowed by the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition challenging the order of detention on 13th June 2019. The appellant argued that the grounds relied upon by the Commissioner of Police were stale and had no proximate or live link between the antecedent activities and the detention order as they were from the years 2007 and 2012 except for Crime No. 178 of 2018. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgement and order of the High Court dated 13th June 2019 and quashed the detention order, finding that the detention order was based on stale and irrelevant grounds and that the confirmation order's existence was doubtful. The Advisory Board reported that there was sufficient cause for the detention of Khaja Bilal Ahmed, but the Supreme Court found issues with the confirmation process and the existence of the confirmation order. The Supreme Court noted that the previous criminal cases were referred to indicate the antecedent criminal history, but found that they were not relevant or valid grounds for the detention order as they were too old and did not provide a live link to the current situation. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement, quashed the detention order, and directed the release of Khaja Bilal Ahmed.

case_name: Khema @ Khem Chandra Etc. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Khema @ Khem Chandra Etc. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 10th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The judgement and order dated 30th April 2019, passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Appeal Nos. 6961, 7260, and 6227 of 2006, thereby dismissing the appeals filed by the appellants and confirming the judgment and order dated 28th September 2006 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Court No.4, Mathura. The appellants were convicted for offences punishable under Section 302 read with Section 149, Section 307 read with Section 149, and Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life with a fine of Rs. 5,000 each. On 27th April 2002, the deceased Prakash and his wife Kripa were going to extend invitations for their daughters' marriages when they were attacked by the accused persons near the house of accused Deepi, leading to the death of Prakash and injuries to others. The prosecution's case was based on the testimony of Omveer (PW-1) and Inder (PW-2), brothers of the deceased, and the recovery of weapons used in the crime on the basis of the memorandum of the accused. The main argument was that the appellants were falsely implicated, the key witnesses were unreliable, and the recoveries of weapons were fabricated. Additionally, the prosecution did not present key witnesses and evidence that could have provided the true genesis of the incident. The court found that Omveer (PW-1) could not have witnessed the incident as he was inside his house during the occurrence. Inder (PW-2), although an injured witness, had inconsistencies in his testimony regarding the timing of his injuries and medical examination. There were discrepancies regarding the time of Inder's (PW-2) injuries and his medical examination. The injury report stated 10:20 pm, but Inder claimed he was examined during the day, leading to inconsistencies in the evidence. The recoveries were found unreliable because the seizure memos were not signed by independent witnesses, and the memorandum statements under Section 27 of the Evidence Act were not placed on record. The court allowed the appeals, quashing the judgement and orders of the High Court and the trial court, and acquitted the appellants of all charges, directing their immediate release unless required in any other case. The court emphasized that it would re-appreciate evidence if the appreciation of evidence and findings were vitiated by errors of law or procedure, or where the conclusions were manifestly perverse, as in this case.

case_name: Khilendra Singh vs. Union of India Ministry of Agriculture
text: Case: Khilendra Singh vs. Union of India Ministry of Agriculture. Date: 28th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Khilendra Singh's appointment as Subject Matter Specialist (Crop Protection & Crop Psychology) was valid, given that his caste, Jaat, was not included in the Central List of OBCs at the time of his appointment. The appellant argued that he belongs to the Jaat caste, which falls within the category of Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and he was issued a certificate to this effect by the Tesildar. A show-cause notice was issued to Khilendra Singh because the community to which he belongs, Jaat, was not found in the Central List of OBCs, raising questions about the validity of his appointment to a post reserved for OBCs. The inquiry concluded that Khilendra Singh's caste, Jaat, was not in the Central List of OBCs for the State of Uttar Pradesh at the time of his appointment, leading to the termination of his services. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion ,that Khilendra Singh was not entitled to appointment in a post reserved for OBCs since the Jaat caste was not in the Central List of OBCs at the relevant time, though the Supreme Court provided different reasons for upholding the decision. The Jaat caste was included in the Central List of OBCs for the State of Uttar Pradesh in 2014, after Khilendra Singh's appointment and subsequent termination.

case_name: Khushwinder Singh vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Khushwinder Singh vs. State of Punjab. Date: 5th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the death penalty imposed on Khushwinder Singh for the murder of six family members was justified. Khushwinder Singh was convicted for the murders of six family members, including two children, on 26th June 2012, by pushing them into a canal after administering sleeping pills. Khushwinder Singh deceived the victims by promising to arrange for Rupinder Singh to go abroad and by claiming that a 'Baba' could help Gurinder Singh overcome his drinking habit. The evidence included the testimony of the complainant Jasmeen Kaur, the recovery of money and ornaments from the accused's house, and the last seen evidence placing the accused with the victims. The High Court upheld the conviction and death sentence imposed by the Sessions Court, confirming that the crime fell under the 'rarest of rare' category warranting capital punishment. The Supreme Court confirmed the death sentence due to the premeditated nature of the crime, the extreme brutality, and the fact that the accused meticulously planned and executed the murders in two stages. The Supreme Court found that the minor contradictions in witness testimonies did not affect the core of the prosecution's case and that the evidence was trustworthy and reliable.

case_name: Kirloskar Brothers Limited vs. Ramcharan and Ors.
text: Case: Kirloskar Brothers Limited vs. Ramcharan and Ors.. Date: 5th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the contractual labourers employed by a contractor, who was engaged by Kirloskar Brothers Limited, should be considered as employees of the principal employer (Kirloskar Brothers Limited) or the contractor. The Labour Court found that the respondents were employees of the contractor and not of Kirloskar Brothers Limited, and therefore rejected their claim for reinstatement by the principal employer. The Industrial Tribunal ruled that the contract labourers should be reinstated as employees of Kirloskar Brothers Limited, holding that a contract labourer automatically becomes an employee of the principal employer. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by Kirloskar Brothers Limited, confirming the judgement and order of the Industrial Tribunal. The Supreme Court found that there was no evidence to prove that the contract between Kirloskar Brothers Limited and the contractor was a sham. The Court emphasized that in the absence of a notification under Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the contract labourers could not automatically be considered employees of the principal employer. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the judgements of the High Court and the Industrial Tribunal, and restored the judgement of the Labour Court, which had found that the respondents were employees of the contractor, not Kirloskar Brothers Limited.

case_name: Kirpal Singh vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Kirpal Singh vs. State of Punjab. Date: 18th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Kirpal Singh's conviction under Sections 302 and 307 IPC for the murder of Balwinder Singh and the attempt to murder Sharan Kaur was justified, considering the reliability of the prosecution witnesses and evidence presented. On the night of 12th/13th November 1997, Balwinder Singh was sleeping in the chaubara of his house when Kirpal Singh and another assailant attacked him with a spade, resulting in severe head injuries. Sharan Kaur, who was sleeping downstairs, was also attacked by Kirpal Singh with a knife when she opened the door upon hearing a noise. The defense argued that the testimonies of Sharan Kaur (PW-5) and Daljit Singh (PW-6) were self-contradictory, unconvincing, and filled with inconsistencies. They also highlighted the failure to mention the second accused, Kulwinder Singh, in the initial FIR and subsequent petitions. The Supreme Court found the testimonies unreliable due to numerous contradictions, the unnatural conduct of the witnesses, and the lack of corroborative evidence. The Court noted that the story presented by the prosecution was inherently improbable and filled with inconsistencies. The Supreme Court acquitted Kirpal Singh, giving him the benefit of doubt due to the unreliable and uncorroborated testimonies of the prosecution witnesses. The Court set aside the judgements of the trial court and the High Court. The prosecution alleged that the motive for the murder was jealousy due to the successful halwai business of the deceased, Balwinder Singh, which was doing better than the accused's business. However, this motive was found to be weak and uncorroborated. The Supreme Court noted that the initial investigations by different police officers found the allegations by Sharan Kaur to be false and had filed closure reports. The Court found that the investigations were tainted and the subsequent allegations raised by Sharan Kaur lacked credibility.

case_name: Kishor Ghanshyamsa Paralikar (Dead) vs Balaji Mandir Sansthan Mangrul (Nath) & Anr.
text: Case: Kishor Ghanshyamsa Paralikar (Dead) vs Balaji Mandir Sansthan Mangrul (Nath) & Anr.. Date: 9th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the extension of time for depositing the balance of the sale consideration granted by the Trial Court was justified and whether the subsequent sale deed should be cancelled. The agreement was for the sale of agricultural land bearing Survey No.3, admeasuring 10 H, 50 R, situated at Village Murtizapur, Mangrulpir Taluk, District Washim, State of Maharashtra, for a total consideration of Rs.8,78,500. The High Court allowed the writ petition and set aside the orders passed by the Trial Court granting extension of time for depositing the balance of the sale consideration and cancelled the sale deed dated 12.01.2011. The Trial Court allowed the application for extension of time on 11.01.2011, permitting the appellant to deposit the balance amount, which was then deposited on the same day, leading to the execution of the sale deed on 12.01.2011. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the Trial Court's order permitting the appellant to deposit the balance amount of Rs.1,47,500. The Supreme Court clarified that Section 28 gives the vendor or lessor the right to rescind the contract for sale or lease of immovable property in the same suit if the purchaser or lessee fails to pay the purchase money within the period fixed by the decree or extended by the court. The appellant argued that there was only a delay of five days in depositing the balance sale consideration and that the Trial Court had exercised its discretion properly in granting the extension of time. This decision may ensure that Trial Courts retain the discretion to extend time for payment in specific performance decrees to prevent manifest injustice, even if there are minor delays in payment. Parties should ensure that they provide valid reasons for any delays in payment and seek extensions from the court promptly to avoid complications and potential rescission of the contract. The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in setting aside the Trial Court's extension order, as the Trial Court had exercised its discretion properly and assigned cogent reasons for granting the extension. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the Trial Court's order permitting the appellant to deposit the balance amount, thereby upholding the validity of the sale deed.

case_name: Kolkata West International City Pvt Ltd vs. Devasis Rudra
text: Case: Kolkata West International City Pvt Ltd vs. Devasis Rudra. Date: 25th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellant (Kolkata West International City Pvt Ltd) was liable to refund the amount paid by the respondent (Devasis Rudra) for a Row House, along with interest and compensation, due to the delayed possession beyond the agreed period. The Buyer's Agreement dated 2nd July 2007 stipulated that the appellant would hand over possession of the Row House to the respondent by 31st December 2008, with a grace period extending to 30th June 2009. The respondent sought possession of the Row House or, alternatively, the refund of the amount paid to the developer along with interest at 12% per annum, and compensation of Rs 20 lakhs. The SCDRC directed the appellant to refund the money paid by the respondent with interest at 12% per annum and awarded compensation of Rs 5 lakhs. The NCDRC reduced the compensation from Rs 5 lakhs to Rs 2 lakhs but upheld the refund of the money paid by the respondent with interest at 12% per annum. The Supreme Court held that it was unreasonable to expect the respondent to wait indefinitely for possession. By 2016, nearly seven years had elapsed since the agreed date, which was beyond a reasonable period.
