case_name: Kooli Saseendran & Ors. vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: Kooli Saseendran & Ors. vs. State of Kerala. Date: 17th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the acquittal of the appellants by the trial court and remanding the matter for fresh consideration. Kooli Saseendran and the other accused were charged with offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC, and Sections 3 and 5 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, for hurling bombs at Parayil Sasi, leading to his death. The prosecution's version was that on 12th October 1999, at about 8.30 a.m., Kooli Saseendran and others formed an unlawful assembly, armed with deadly weapons, and hurled bombs at Parayil Sasi, who received grievous injuries and died. The motive was political animosity as Parayil Sasi was an RSS activist and the accused were CPM workers. The trial court acquitted Kooli Saseendran and the other accused, finding the prosecution's evidence unreliable due to contradictions and deficiencies in the statements of key witnesses. The High Court set aside the trial court's acquittal and remanded the matter for fresh consideration, allowing both the prosecution and the defense to present fresh evidence. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision to remand the case unjustified, noting that the High Court did not find material evidence to convict the accused and remanding the case should not be done casually in criminal matters. The Supreme Court noted contradictions such as discrepancies in the statements of PW-1 and PW-3 regarding the events, the presence of Rajeevan's shop, and the involvement of the witnesses in other criminal activities on the same day. The Supreme Court highlighted the lack of prompt action and proper documentation by the police, such as the delay in lodging the FIR, not proving the daily diary report, and not examining important witnesses like the police officials at the picket post and Rajeevan. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the judgement of the High Court, and restored the trial court's acquittal of Kooli Saseendran and the other accused. The Supreme Court emphasized that the prosecution's failure to examine key witnesses like Rajeevan and the police officials present at the scene, and not producing crucial evidence like the daily diary report, significantly weakened the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for setting aside the well-reasoned judgement of the trial court in a casual manner without detailed discussion of the evidence, noting that remand should only be ordered in very rare circumstances in criminal cases.

case_name: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited Vs. Sanjiv Gupta & Others
text: Case: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited Vs. Sanjiv Gupta & Others. Date: 23rd September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondents violated the Supreme Court's order dated 7th May 2012 by not paying Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited (KMBL) the sum of Rs.4.5 crores from the sale proceeds of the property. KMBL filed contempt petitions alleging that the respondents failed to comply with the Supreme Court's order to pay Rs.4.5 crores to KMBL from the sale proceeds of the borrower's property. The High Court directed the borrower company to pay Rs.12 crores to Alchemist and Rs.6.5 crores to Kotak Mahindra, allowing creditors to recover the same by selling the land appurtenant to the plant and machinery, and further adjustments were to be made as directed. The Supreme Court ordered that Alchemist should sell the property and from the proceeds, pay Rs.4.5 crores to KMBL and retain Rs.9 crores, with any surplus to be deposited in the High Court. KMBL alleged that the sale was conducted in a clandestine manner, without informing KMBL about the sale dates and in violation of the High Court's directions. Alchemist contended that it was entitled to recover 98.12% of the total outstanding proceeds, and KMBL's share was only 1.88%, arguing that KMBL had already been paid Rs.2 crores, which was in excess of its due share. The Supreme Court directed Alchemist to deposit Rs.4.5 crores in the Court, stating that the issue of whether this amount was due to KMBL would be considered later. The Supreme Court closed the contempt petitions, directing that the deposited amount of Rs.4.5 crores be paid to KMBL, subject to the High Court's decision on the actual amount due to KMBL. The decision reinforces that compliance with court orders is mandatory and failure to do so can result in contempt proceedings, ensuring that all parties adhere to judicial directives. KMBL might pursue further legal action in the High Court to determine the exact amount due and ensure full compliance with the court's directives, potentially seeking additional damages if warranted. The Supreme Court clarified that Alchemist must pay the designated amounts to KMBL and retain its share, with any disputes regarding the sale process and amount due to be addressed by the High Court.

case_name: Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt Ltd (Now known as Krish Steel and Trading Pvt Ltd) vs. Venkatesan Sankaranarayan & Ors.
text: Case: Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt Ltd (Now known as Krish Steel and Trading Pvt Ltd) vs. Venkatesan Sankaranarayan & Ors.. Date: 1st March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the failure of Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt Ltd to implement the Resolution Plan for Tecpro Systems Limited, leading to the decision for the liquidation of Tecpro Systems by the NCLT and the subsequent appeal to the NCLAT and the Supreme Court. The Resolution Plan was approved by the Committee of Creditors with a majority of 89.92%. The appellant failed to fulfill its obligations, including the equity infusion, despite numerous opportunities over a period of six months. The NCLAT upheld the order of liquidation, noting that the appellant had failed to implement the Resolution Plan for over eight months and declined to exercise its jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016. The Supreme Court directed the appellant to deposit an amount of Rs 50 crores on or before 10 January 2021, to demonstrate its bona fides, and stated that failure to do so would result in the forfeiture of the Rs 20 crores already deposited. The Supreme Court dismissed the Civil Appeal, resulting in the forfeiture of the amount of Rs 20 crores and the reversion of management to the liquidator for taking steps in accordance with the law.

case_name: Krishan Chander & Anr. vs. State of Haryana & Ors.
text: Case: Krishan Chander & Anr. vs. State of Haryana & Ors.. Date: 17th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the land belonging to the appellants, which was acquired for the development of Sector 36 in Rohtak, should be released from the acquisition process as it had not been utilized for the intended public purpose. The appellants argued that their land, acquired under the notification dated 15th December 2006, was not utilized for the intended public purpose and remained vacant. They sought the release of their land similar to other lands that had been released from acquisition. The High Court dismissed the appellants' writ petition without directing notice to the respondents or considering the appellants' grievances in depth, leading the appellants to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should have conducted a deeper examination of the appellants' grievances, especially since the High Court's previous direction required the respondents to consider the release of the appellants' land if it was not likely to be utilized for public purposes. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider the appellants' writ petition, provide sufficient opportunity to both parties, and make a decision based on a detailed examination of the records and the relevant policy for the release of unutilized land. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order dismissing the writ petition and restored the petition for fresh consideration by the High Court, emphasizing that the High Court should secure the records and verify the facts before making a decision. The policy dated 26th October 2007, modified on 24th January 2011, pertained to the release of land over which residential buildings had been constructed. The High Court initially dismissed the appellants' petition based on this policy, stating that the appellants' land did not qualify for release as it was vacant. The Supreme Court noted that the collaboration agreement with M/s Sharad Farm and Holdings (P) Ltd. was an inter-se issue and did not affect the appellants' right to seek deletion of their land from the acquisition process.

case_name: Krishna Mohan Medical College and Hospital & Anr. vs Union of India and Another
text: Case: Krishna Mohan Medical College and Hospital & Anr. vs Union of India and Another. Date: 1st September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main challenge laid by the petitioners was against the order dated 31st May 2017, whereby the Union of India had directed the debarment of Krishna Mohan Medical College, Mathura from admitting students in the MBBS course for the academic years 2017-18 and 2018-19, and authorized the Medical Council of India (MCI) to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crores submitted by the petitioners. The court annulled the order dated 31st May 2017 and remitted the matter to the Central Government for fresh consideration of the materials on record, and after affording an opportunity of hearing to the petitioners' college, to deliver a reasoned decision on the issue of confirmation or otherwise of the conditional letter of permission (LOP) granted to them. The second inspection on 9th December 2016 was controversial because it was conducted close on the heels of the earlier inspection on 18th and 19th November 2016. The petitioners had already submitted a representation contradicting the findings of deficiencies recorded during the November inspection, and the matter was still pending consideration. During the inspection on 18th and 19th November 2016, the MCI found several deficiencies, including deficiencies in faculty at 32.31% and in residents at 34.78%, which were disputed by the petitioners. The court opined that the reasonable opportunity of hearing, as obligated by Section 10A(4) of the Indian Medical Council Act, was not adequately provided to the petitioners. The court emphasized the need for fairness in action and a just decision supplemented by reasons and rationale. The court decided to confirm the conditional LOP granted to the petitioner college on 12th September 2016 for the academic year 2016-17. However, the court directed the Central Government/MCI to conduct a fresh inspection of the college for the academic year 2018-19 and to furnish the report to the court within eight weeks.

case_name: Krishnamurthy @ Gunodu and Others vs. State of Karnataka
text: Case: Krishnamurthy @ Gunodu and Others vs. State of Karnataka. Date: 16th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants were rightly convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 and individually for the offences under Sections 447, 504, 506, and 341 of the IPC. The trial court convicted Krishnamurthy under Section 302 IPC and the co-accused under Sections 447, 504, 506, and 341 IPC. According to eyewitnesses, Krishnamurthy assaulted the deceased, Venkatarama, by kicking and stomping on his neck and chest after he had fallen down. The post-mortem report revealed that Venkatarama died from haemorrhagic shock due to multiple injuries, including fractured ribs and contusions to the neck and chest. The discrepancies were related to the exact actions of the accused, specifically who among them held Venkatarama's hands and legs, and their participation in the assault. The Supreme Court found that Thimmappa and Gopala had not participated in the assault after Venkatarama had fallen and were not responsible for his fatal injuries. The Supreme Court converted their conviction to under Section 323 read with Section 34 IPC, sentencing them to one year, and upheld their conviction for the individual offences under Sections 447, 504, 506, and 341 IPC. The Supreme Court modified Krishnamurthy's sentence to life imprisonment, setting aside the condition that it be till the end of his natural life without the possibility of remission. The appellants argued that their acquittal should be on parity with the juvenile 'A', but the Supreme Court rejected this argument, stating that each case must be decided on its own evidence and merits. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, modified the sentences for Thimmappa and Gopala, and upheld the life imprisonment for Krishnamurthy without the stipulation of life without remission. The Supreme Court directed that the sentences would run concurrently and the appellants would be entitled to the benefit of Section 428 of the CrPC for the period already undergone.

case_name: Kumer Singh vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.
text: Case: Kumer Singh vs. State of Rajasthan & Anr.. Date: 20th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court of Rajasthan erred in granting bail to the accused Kamlesh, Bhojraj Singh, and Arif who were charged with the murder of Sumer Singh. They were charged under Sections 147, 148, 341, 323, 307, 427, 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC for brutally killing Sumer Singh. The incident occurred on 16th August 2017 when Sumer Singh, a member of the Border Security Force on leave, was ambushed and brutally killed by the accused during the fair of Goganavami in Choti Roru village. The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court did not consider the brutality and seriousness of the crime and failed to provide sufficient reasons for granting bail to the accused. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not properly consider the seriousness of the crime, the number of injuries inflicted, and the overall brutality of the act when granting bail to the accused. The Supreme Court set aside the bail granted by the High Court, directing that the accused should surrender forthwith. The Supreme Court referred to the principles that bail should not be granted in cases of serious offenses without proper reasoning and consideration of the nature of the crime and its impact on society. The Supreme Court acknowledged the duration but emphasized that the seriousness of the crime and the manner in which it was committed outweighed the time already spent in custody. The Supreme Court directed the Sessions Judge to secure the compliance of the accused's surrender and ensure that the case proceeds without any delay. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's reasoning was insufficient and did not adequately address the severity and brutality of the crime, leading to the decision to set aside the bail.

case_name: Kusal Toppo vs. State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Kusal Toppo vs. State of Jharkhand. Date: 7th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The trial court convicted Kusal Toppo and the other accused for offences under Section 392, sentencing them to seven years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1000 each, with a default penalty of one year of rigorous imprisonment. They were also convicted under Section 302, receiving a sentence of life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.5000 each, with a default penalty of two years of rigorous imprisonment. The High Court upheld the trial court's convictions and sentences against the accused. The prosecution's case was based on the events of 4th December 1999, when a truck carrying Sita Devi was hijacked, and the bodies of Sita Devi, the driver, and the cleaner were found near the truck in Aamjharia Valley. The accused were implicated through extra-judicial confessions and witness testimonies. The Supreme Court noted that extra-judicial confessions are a weak form of evidence and cannot be relied upon solely for conviction without corroborative evidence. In this case, the extra-judicial confessions were not corroborated by any reliable evidence. The Supreme Court found that the recovery of the rope, based on the confession of one of the accused, was insufficient to link the accused to the crime, as the rope is a common item available everywhere and no forensic evidence connected it to the crime. The informant initially faced refusal from the Kuru Police Station to lodge the FIR. He was advised by the SP's office to lodge the FIR at the Chandwa Police Station, where the dead bodies were found, leading to the FIR being lodged on 7th December 1999. The defense argued that the extra-judicial confessions were weak evidence and could not be the sole basis for conviction without other reliable evidence establishing guilt. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the trial court and the High Court, acquitted the accused of all charges, and allowed the appeals. The Supreme Court acquitted the accused because the convictions were based on weak extra-judicial confessions without any corroborative evidence, and the only physical evidence, a rope, could not be conclusively linked to the crime.

case_name: Kush Kalra vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Kush Kalra vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 9th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the practice of affixing posters outside the residences of COVID-19 positive individuals violated their fundamental rights, including the right to privacy and dignity. The petitioner sought a writ of certiorari to quash the decision by various states and union territories to affix posters and a writ of mandamus to direct authorities to end the practice and protect the privacy of COVID-19 positive individuals. The Court dismissed the argument by observing that the central guidelines did not mandate such actions, and states had already withdrawn related directions, rendering the argument moot. The Supreme Court disposed of the petition, observing that no state or union territory is required to affix posters, and such practices should be avoided unless directed under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. The Court emphasized that affixing posters violated the dignity of individuals by exposing their health status to public scrutiny and gossip.

case_name: Kusha Duruka vs The State of Odisha
text: Case: Kusha Duruka vs The State of Odisha. Date: 19th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Kusha Duruka should be granted bail pending trial for being accused under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, for possessing 23.8 kg of Ganja. Kusha Duruka was charged under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, for possessing 23.8 kg of Ganja. The High Court granted bail to Kusha Duruka on the grounds of parity, as his co-accused Gangesh Kumar Thakur was granted bail earlier. The High Court's order did not mention that it was the second bail application filed by Kusha Duruka and did not reference the pending SLP before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court seriously deprecated the practice of granting bail without disclosing the pendency of an SLP and directed the original record of the bail application to be called for. The Supreme Court directed that all subsequent bail applications under Section 439 CrPC should be listed before the same judge who decided the earlier applications, and all details of previous bail applications must be disclosed. The Supreme Court proposed mandatory disclosure of previous bail application details, the pendency of other applications, and proper listing of subsequent applications to avoid discrepancies. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal as infructuous but imposed a token cost of Rs 10,000 on Kusha Duruka for the procedural oversight. The Supreme Court directed the Registrars General to place the order before the Chief Justices for correcting the system wherever required to avoid similar issues in future. This judgment could lead to stricter adherence to procedural rules and more transparency in the bail application process, reducing the chances of discrepancies and ensuring all relevant facts are disclosed. If similar procedural oversights occur, the Supreme Court may impose stricter penalties or cancel the bail, emphasizing the need for transparency and adherence to proper procedures.

case_name: Kutchi Lal Rameshwar Ashram Trust vs. Collector, Haridwar & Ors.
text: Case: Kutchi Lal Rameshwar Ashram Trust vs. Collector, Haridwar & Ors.. Date: 22nd September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the property in dispute, following the death of Mohan Lal without any heirs, vested in the government under Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Kutchi Lal Rameshwar Ashram Trust claimed that the property was purchased by Swamy Udhav Das in the name of his disciple, Mohan Lal, and that all movable and immovable properties were vested in the Trust as per the Swamy's will. The Collector, Haridwar, decided that the property in dispute vested in the government under Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as there was no heir to succeed to the property following the death of Mohan Lal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the Trust, upholding the Collector's decision that the property vested in the government due to the absence of legal heirs. The Supreme Court concluded that the Collector acted without jurisdiction in adjudicating the vesting of the property in the state government. Such an adjudication should have been done by a civil court with competent jurisdiction. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the High Court and the Collector, allowing the writ petition filed by the Trust. The Court ruled that the matter should be decided by a civil court.

case_name: LMJ International Ltd. vs Sleepwell Industries Co. Ltd.
text: Case: LMJ International Ltd. vs Sleepwell Industries Co. Ltd.. Date: 20th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The core issue involved the enforcement of two foreign arbitral awards under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which the petitioner contested on grounds of alleged procedural and substantive irregularities. The awards pertained to disputes over the quality of rice shipments and non-payment under contracts governed by GAFTA arbitration rules. The High Court deemed the foreign awards to be enforceable decrees, rejecting the petitioner's objections regarding procedural impropriety and fraud. The petitioner argued that the arbitration clause was improperly invoked, the arbitral tribunal was not constituted as per the agreement, and the awards were issued without proper notice or opportunity for the petitioner to present its case. The Supreme Court found no merit in the fraud claims, noting that the petitioner failed to substantiate allegations of concealment or procedural irregularities in obtaining the arbitral awards.

case_name: Lachhman Dass vs. Resham Chand Kaler and Anr.
text: Case: Lachhman Dass vs. Resham Chand Kaler and Anr.. Date: 23rd January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting regular bail to Resham Chand Kaler, who was accused of serious offences including murder and conspiracy. Resham Chand Kaler was charged under Sections 302, 307, 324, 148, and 149 of the IPC and Sections 25, 27, 54, and 59 of the Arms Act for the murder of Shingar Chand and inflicting injuries on others. The FIR alleged that Resham Chand Kaler, along with Kulbir Singh and others, attacked Harbilas and Shingar Chand, with Kulbir Singh firing a shot that killed Shingar Chand. The High Court granted bail on the grounds that the trial would take a long time to conclude and Resham Chand Kaler had been in custody since November 2015, without attributing any specific injury to him. The appellant argued that the nature of the crime was serious, involving criminal conspiracy, and that Resham Chand Kaler, being a British national, could tamper with the investigation and evade justice. The Supreme Court observed that a prima facie case was made out against Resham Chand Kaler, who was alleged to be the main conspirator and actively involved in the attack leading to Shingar Chand's death. The Supreme Court clarified that this case involved a legal challenge to the grant of bail for non-consideration of material on record, rather than a cancellation of bail due to breach of conditions. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail to Resham Chand Kaler and directed the concerned authorities to take him into custody immediately. The Supreme Court noted that Resham Chand Kaler being a British national should not influence the legal proceedings, as the law treats all accused equally regardless of their nationality. The Supreme Court also set aside the bail granted to the other accused persons linked to this case, finding that the High Court's orders were based on parity with Resham Chand Kaler's bail, which was not justified.

text: Case: Lakhan Singh vs. Amarjeet Singh & Anr.. Date: 6th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in allowing the accused-applicant, Amarjeet Singh, to present additional evidence regarding his plea of unsoundness of mind, which was not considered during the trial. The High Court allowed the application of Amarjeet Singh to present additional evidence and directed the Trial Court to take on record the additional evidence and documents, and then send the file back along with the additional evidence. Amarjeet Singh claimed that he was of unsound mind on the date of the incident, supported by OPD Reports and a Medical Store Bill from July 2011, and sought to examine doctors and his father who had the original records. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order allowing additional evidence, stating that the High Court did not consider the previous orders and evidence already on record and directed the High Court to reconsider the appeal on merits. The Trial Court, supported by medical reports and testimonies, found that Amarjeet Singh was fit to stand trial and dismissed the application regarding his unsoundness of mind, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2015. The Supreme Court restored the criminal appeal and the application for additional evidence for reconsideration by the High Court in accordance with the law, directing the parties to appear before the High Court on 10th January 2023. The Supreme Court allowed the interim arrangement made by the High Court to continue until the first date of appearance of the parties before the High Court.

case_name: Lakhvir Singh vs The State of Punjab & Anr.
text: Case: Lakhvir Singh vs The State of Punjab & Anr.. Date: 19th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants, who were convicted under Section 397 IPC, could be given the benefit of probation under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, considering their age at the time of the offense. The appellants were convicted for attempting to murder the complainant and robbing his taxi, resulting in injuries inflicted with a knife and a dagger. The trial court sentenced the appellants to undergo rigorous imprisonment for 7 years each. The appellants' counsel argued that since the appellants were under 21 years of age at the time of the offense, they should be given the benefit of probation under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958. The Supreme Court noted that the appellants committed a serious offense at a young age but had already served about half of their sentence, and the complainant had expressed forgiveness. The Supreme Court found that Section 6 of the Act, which restricts imprisonment of offenders under 21 years of age, did not apply since the appellants were above 21 years at the time of sentencing. The Supreme Court considered Sections 3 and 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, which allow the court to release offenders on probation of good conduct instead of sentencing them to imprisonment. The Supreme Court released the appellants on probation of good conduct under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, on completion of half their sentence, with conditions to maintain peace and good behavior. The appellants were required to enter into a bond with two sureties each, ensuring that they maintain peace and good behavior for the remaining part of their sentence, failing which they could be called upon to serve the remaining sentence.

case_name: Lalichan vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: Lalichan vs. State of Kerala. Date: 7th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Lalichan was charged under Sections 8(2) and 63 of the Kerala Abkari Act for illegal possession of 4.5 litres of arrack and 3.750 litres of Indian Made Foreign Liquor. The Trial Court convicted Lalichan under Sections 8(2) and 63 of the Kerala Abkari Act, sentencing him to one year of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 8(2) and a fine of Rs. 5,000 under Section 63. The High Court of Kerala confirmed Lalichan's conviction but reduced the sentence of simple imprisonment to nine months while maintaining the fines imposed by the Trial Court. The Supreme Court reduced Lalichan's sentence to the period already undergone, considering he was in custody for about thirty-five days, and confirmed the fines imposed by the lower courts. The Supreme Court directed Lalichan to pay the fines within four weeks if not already paid, confirming the penalties imposed by the Trial Court and the High Court. The primary legal issue addressed by the Supreme Court was whether the sentence imposed on Lalichan should be reduced considering the gravity of the offence and the time already spent in custody. The Supreme Court modified the sentence to the period already undergone by Lalichan, which was thirty-five days, while confirming the fines imposed by the Trial Court and the High Court.

case_name: Lance Nayak Raj Bahadur & Ors. vs. State of UP & Ors.
text: Case: Lance Nayak Raj Bahadur & Ors. vs. State of UP & Ors.. Date: 9th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants, who are constables and head constables, were entitled to promotion to the post of Sub-Inspector despite not securing the minimum required marks in each subject of the written examination as per the Uttar Pradesh Sub-Inspector and Inspector (Civil Police) Service Rules, 2008. The Rules specified that candidates must secure a minimum of 50% marks in each subject of the written examination to be eligible for promotion to the post of Sub-Inspector. The appellants argued that the requirement to secure 50% marks should be applied paper-wise rather than subject-wise, and since subjects 3 and 4 were part of the same paper, the aggregate marks should be considered instead of individual subject marks. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, stating that the selection process was undertaken without applying the reservation policy and that the 50% cut-off marks criteria must be applied subject-wise as per the rules. The Supreme Court held that the express language of the rules did not permit the interpretation suggested by the appellants and that candidates must secure a minimum of 50% marks in each subject to be eligible for promotion. The Supreme Court emphasized that merit is the key element in promotions through limited departmental examinations, and there can be no compromise or dilution of the criteria specified in the rules. The Supreme Court noted that the State had not prescribed any relaxed or different criteria for reserved category candidates and, therefore, no exception could be made for the appellants based on their reserved category status. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, stating that the appellants did not fulfill the criteria of securing 50% marks in each subject and, therefore, were not eligible for promotion. The judgment reinforces the importance of adhering to the specified criteria in promotion rules and ensures that merit-based promotions are not compromised by relaxing or diluting the required standards. The State of UP might consider reviewing and clarifying the promotion rules to avoid ambiguity and ensure that all candidates are aware of the specific requirements, including any relaxations for reserved categories if applicable.

case_name: Land Acquisition Collector vs. Jai Prakash Tyagi & Ors.
text: Case: Land Acquisition Collector vs. Jai Prakash Tyagi & Ors.. Date: 24th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the land acquisition proceedings for certain lands in the village of Wazirabad had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. The High Court declared that the land acquisition proceedings for the lands in question had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, primarily relying on the decision in Pune Municipal Corporation vs. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki. The Supreme Court's ruling in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal overruled the decision in Pune Municipal Corporation, which the High Court had relied upon. The Supreme Court clarified that the deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) occurs only if both possession has not been taken and compensation has not been paid for five years or more. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's judgment, ruling that there was no deemed lapse of the land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act. The Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the writ petition filed by the original writ petitioners. The Supreme Court directed that if the original landowners or interested persons had not been paid compensation, they should be paid in accordance with the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Their prayers for compensation should be considered according to the law and on their own merits. The Supreme Court interpreted the word 'or' in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act as 'and', meaning that for the deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings, both possession must not have been taken and compensation must not have been paid.

The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's judgment, ruling that there was no deemed lapse of the land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act. The Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the writ petition filed by the original writ petitioners.

The Supreme Court directed that if the original landowners or interested persons had not been paid compensation, they should be paid in accordance with the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Their prayers for compensation should be considered according to the law and on their own merits.

The Supreme Court interpreted the word 'or' in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act as 'and', meaning that for the deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings, both possession must not have been taken and compensation must not have been paid.

case_name: Latesh @ Dadu Baburao Karlekar vs. The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Latesh @ Dadu Baburao Karlekar vs. The State of Maharashtra. Date: 30th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's modification of the conviction of the accused from Section 302 IPC read with 149 IPC to Section 302 IPC read with 34 IPC, and the conviction of the other accused under Section 307 IPC, was justified. The appellants were Latesh @ Dadu Baburao Karlekar, Anil Ankush Gadekar, Vishnu Maruti Bule, Vijay @ Vijay Istriwala Ramdulari Nirmal, and Sunil Kashinath Chandanshiva. On 10th December 2006, between 10:20 pm to 10:30 pm, the appellants assaulted Jagdish Hingane (deceased) and his brother Vitthal Hingane (PW-2) with weapons like chopper, sword, sickle, and stick due to old enmity. The trial court convicted the accused under various sections, including Section 302 IPC read with 149 IPC, and sentenced them to life imprisonment and other punishments for different offences. The High Court partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the convictions under Sections 143, 144, 147, and 148 IPC, and modifying the convictions of appellants 1 to 3 to Section 302 read with 34 IPC, while maintaining the life sentence. The convictions of appellants 4 to 6 were changed to Section 307 read with 34 IPC. The appellants' counsel argued that the identification parade was not necessary, the FIR was filed with substantial delay, the alleged dying declaration was not part of the evidence, and the specific roles and weapons were not attributed to each accused. The Supreme Court found the evidence of PW-2 and PW-11 to be trustworthy and corroborated by other evidence, despite minor discrepancies. The Court emphasized the consistency and credibility of their testimonies. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to modify the convictions under Section 302 IPC read with 34 IPC for appellants 1 to 3 and maintained the life imprisonment sentence. The Supreme Court discussed the principles of joint liability under Section 34 IPC, emphasizing that specific roles and common intention must be established, and upheld the importance of corroborated eyewitness testimony in sustaining convictions.

case_name: Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India & Anr.
text: Case: Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India & Anr.. Date: 26th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The two central issues are: (i) Whether an action under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 can be initiated by the financial creditor against a corporate person concerning a guarantee offered for a loan account of the principal borrower, who is not a 'corporate person' within the meaning of the Code, and (ii) Whether an application under Section 7 of the Code filed after three years from the date of declaration of the loan account as Non-performing Asset (NPA) is barred by limitation. The Union Bank of India extended a term loan of Rs.9,60,00,000 (Rupees nine crore sixty lakhs) and an additional amount of Rs.2,45,00,000 (Rupees two crore forty-five lakhs) to M/s. Mahaveer Construction in 2007 and 2008, respectively. The loan accounts of M/s. Mahaveer Construction were declared as Non-performing Assets (NPAs) on 30th January 2010. After declaring the loan accounts as NPAs, the Union Bank of India issued a recall notice on 19th February 2010 to the principal borrower, M/s. Mahaveer Construction, and the corporate debtor, M/s. Surana Metals Limited, demanding repayment of the outstanding amount of Rs.12,35,11,548 (Rupees twelve crore thirty-five lakhs eleven thousand five hundred forty-eight). The corporate debtor, M/s. Surana Metals Limited, replied to the recall notice on 8th December 2018, stating that it was not the principal borrower nor owed any financial debt to the financial creditor and had not committed any default in repayment of the stated outstanding amount. The appellant challenged the maintainability of the application under Section 7 on the grounds that (i) the principal borrower was not a 'corporate person' and hence the Code could not be applied, and (ii) the application was barred by limitation as it was filed beyond the period of three years from the date of default. The Adjudicating Authority rejected the objections raised by the appellant, holding that the action could be initiated against the corporate debtor under Section 7 of the Code and that the application was within limitation due to the acknowledgment of debt by the corporate debtor on 8th December 2018. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) dismissed the appeal, affirming the decision of the Adjudicating Authority that the application under Section 7 of the Code was maintainable and not barred by limitation. The acknowledgment of debt by the corporate debtor on 8th December 2018 is significant because it extended the limitation period, making the application under Section 7 of the Code filed on 13th February 2019 within the permissible time frame. The court's decision implies that corporate guarantors can be held liable under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code for defaults committed by the principal borrower, even if the principal borrower is not a 'corporate person'. The liability of the guarantor is coextensive with that of the principal borrower. The court addressed the issue of limitation by stating that the acknowledgment of debt by the corporate debtor extended the limitation period. The application under Section 7 of the Code is not for recovery of the amount but for the resolution of insolvency, and the acknowledgment of debt renews the limitation period for initiating such proceedings.

case_name: Lekh Raj (Dead) Through L.Rs. & Ors. vs Ranjit Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Lekh Raj (Dead) Through L.Rs. & Ors. vs Ranjit Singh & Ors.. Date: 16th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the decree passed in 1965 regarding the agricultural land was executable despite objections raised by the judgment-debtors about its validity under the amended Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1973. The objections included claims that the execution was time-barred, that the decree became nullity due to the amendment in 1973, and that the decree holders had not deposited the required amount within the stipulated time. The Supreme Court concluded that the 1973 amendment did not impact the decree since the rights of the parties were finalized in 1965, well before the amendment came into effect. The Court rejected the argument as the amendment was retroactive, applicable only to pending cases or those initiated after 1973, and the decree in question had attained finality in 1965. The Supreme Court emphasized that the executing court cannot go behind the decree and must execute it as passed, without re-examining factual or legal objections already settled. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the judgment-debtors and upheld the validity of the execution proceedings, allowing the decree holders to proceed with the execution.

case_name: Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another Vs. Sunita
text: Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another Vs. Sunita. Date: 29th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondent, Sunita, was entitled to the Accident claim benefit under her late husband's life insurance policy despite the policy having lapsed due to non-payment of premium. The policy condition stated that the Accident claim benefit was payable only if the policy was in force at the time of the accident. The claim was rejected because the policy had lapsed in October 2011 due to non-payment of the premium, and it was not in force at the time of the accident on 6th March 2012. The District Forum allowed Sunita's claim for the Accident benefit based on the Ready reckoner issued by the Life Insurance Corporation. The NCDRC set aside the State Commission's order and confirmed the District Forum's decision, allowing Sunita's claim for the Accident benefit. The Supreme Court set aside the NCDRC's decision because the policy was not in force at the time of the accident, and the failure to disclose the accident when reviving the policy indicated bad faith on the part of the respondent. The Supreme Court emphasized that there is a requirement of 'uberrima fides' (good faith) in insurance contracts, meaning that the insured must act in good faith and disclose all relevant facts to the insurer. The Supreme Court stated that the terms of the insurance policy must be strictly construed and that it is not permissible to rewrite the contract while interpreting its terms. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the NCDRC's order, and rejected Sunita's claim for the Accident benefit. If Sunita's claim had been upheld, it could have set a precedent allowing policyholders to revive lapsed policies after an accident and claim benefits, potentially leading to increased disputes and financial liabilities for insurers. Insurance companies might tighten their policies and procedures to ensure stricter compliance with policy terms and conditions, especially regarding the disclosure of relevant facts when reviving lapsed policies.

case_name: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
text: Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.. Date: 30th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the state of Rajasthan has the power and jurisdiction to levy and collect stamp duty on insurance policies issued within the state. Life Insurance Corporation of India argued that the state of Rajasthan lacked legislative competence to impose stamp duty on insurance policies, as this power lies exclusively with the Parliament under Entry 91 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The High Court of Rajasthan upheld the imposition of stamp duty by the state government, stating that the state had the legislative competence to levy and collect stamp duty on insurance policies under the Rajasthan Stamp Law (Adaptation) Act, 1952. The Supreme Court ruled that the state of Rajasthan has the legislative competence to impose and collect stamp duty on insurance policies issued within the state, as per Entry 44 of List III, and the rate prescribed by the Parliament under Entry 91 of List I. The Supreme Court granted relief to the appellant by setting aside certain findings of the High Court and directing the state government not to demand and collect the specific amounts of stamp duty as per the orders dated 16.09.2004, 16.10.2004, 11.10.2004, 01.11.2004, and 28.10.2004. The Supreme Court held that the Rajasthan Stamp Law (Adaptation) Act, 1952 applies to the present case, as the insurance policies were issued between 1993-94 and 2001-02, prior to the 1998 Act coming into force.

case_name: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 7th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal challenge was the validity of Section 4(3) of the Uttar Pradesh Ministers (Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1981, as amended in 2016, which allowed former Chief Ministers to retain government accommodation for their lifetime. The 1997 Rules provided for the allotment of government accommodation to former Chief Ministers for their lifetime. However, these rules were struck down by the High Court earlier as being in conflict with the provisions of Section 4 of the 1981 Act. The State of Uttar Pradesh argued that the 2016 amendment provided a legitimate basis for allotting government accommodation to former Chief Ministers, asserting that these individuals formed a distinct class deserving of special privileges. The Supreme Court ruled that Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act was unconstitutional as it violated the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The court held that the provision created an arbitrary classification by treating former Chief Ministers as a special category, which was not supported by any constitutional principle. The Supreme Court referred to principles of equality and fraternity embodied in the Constitution, stating that public servants must act in a manner reflecting that ultimate authority is vested in the citizens. The court emphasized that privileges, rights, and benefits conferred on holders of public office must be reasonable, rational, and proportionate. The Supreme Court stated that once individuals demit public office, they are at par with common citizens. The court held that the classification of former Chief Ministers as a special category for the purpose of allotting government accommodation was arbitrary and discriminatory, thus violating Article 14 of the Constitution. The court's decision struck down Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act, rendering the 2016 amendment invalid. This ruling effectively nullified the provision allowing former Chief Ministers to retain government accommodation for their lifetime.

case_name: Lucknow Nagar Nigam vs. Kohli Brothers Colour Lab Pvt. Ltd. & Others
text: Case: Lucknow Nagar Nigam vs. Kohli Brothers Colour Lab Pvt. Ltd. & Others. Date: 22nd February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the property termed as 'enemy property' under the Enemy Property Act, 1968, vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property, is exempt from payment of property tax under the UP Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959. The High Court of Allahabad held that the assessee (Kohli Brothers Colour Lab Pvt. Ltd.) is exempt from payment of property tax under the UP Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, for the property termed as 'enemy property'. The property is an enemy property located on Mahatma Gandhi Marg, Lucknow, and was owned by the Raja of Mahmudabad, who migrated to Pakistan in 1947. A portion of the property is currently occupied and utilized for profit-generating purposes by Kohli Brothers Colour Lab Pvt. Ltd. Lucknow Nagar Nigam argued that the property is merely in the custody of the Custodian of Enemy Property and is not permanently vested in the Union Government. Therefore, it is liable to property tax as it is being used for commercial purposes by the assessee. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, ruling that the enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property is exempt from payment of property tax under the UP Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, as it is considered property of the Union and thus protected under Article 285 of the Constitution. The Custodian of Enemy Property, under the Ministry of Commerce, Government of India, issued a certificate stating that the subject property is enemy property vested with the Custodian, and therefore, the Custodian was obligated to pay house tax and other local taxes on behalf of this property. The court examined whether the statutory vesting of property as enemy property amounts to expropriation and transfer of ownership to the Union of India. It concluded that such vesting does confer ownership to the Union, making the property exempt from local taxes under Article 285 of the Constitution.

case_name: M. Durga Singh & Ors. vs Yadagiri & Ors.
text: Case: M. Durga Singh & Ors. vs Yadagiri & Ors.. Date: 18th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue is whether the appellants have the rightful ownership of 500 square yards of land in Survey No.87 of Lingampally Village and whether the respondents are land grabbers liable to be evicted. The suit was dismissed on 29th March 1975, with the trial court holding that the appellants had not been able to prove their title to the suit land. The Act allowed the Special Court to take cognizance of land grabbing cases and try disputes related to ownership and title to the land grabbed, whether the grabbing occurred before or after the commencement of the Act. The Special Court concluded that the appellants failed to establish ownership of the schedule property and that there was no material to prove their ownership. It also held that the respondents were not land grabbers. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because the appellants had engaged in continuous and fruitless litigation for several decades, taking several courts for a ride without establishing their claim. The appellants filed an application for restoration of the suit, which was also dismissed. They subsequently filed a revision petition, which was also dismissed. The multiple legal proceedings demonstrate the appellants' persistence but also highlight their misuse of the legal system by repeatedly filing suits without substantial evidence, causing prolonged litigation. The Special Court found the appellants' claim of ownership to be unsubstantiated, with vague descriptions and unclear boundaries of the land, making it difficult to ascertain the exact location of the disputed property. The decision reinforces the need for clear and substantial evidence in land dispute cases and discourages the misuse of the legal system through prolonged and baseless litigation. Parties should ensure they have clear and substantial evidence of ownership and title, understand the jurisdictional requirements, and avoid filing repetitive and baseless suits to prevent misuse of the legal system. The Supreme Court clarified that the appellants themselves approached the civil court and continued litigation despite knowing it was the wrong forum. The appellants should have withdrawn the suits and approached the correct forum earlier.

case_name: M. Elangovan vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: M. Elangovan vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 17th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant, M. Elangovan, was aggrieved because he was not granted promotion in respect of the 25% quota, which he argued should be based solely on seniority. The Union of India's counsel argued that even for the seniority channel, the incumbent should not have crossed the age limit as of the cut-off date. The Supreme Court found it difficult to appreciate the Union of India's submission and clarified that for promotions based on seniority, there cannot be any cut-off date. After the amendment on 30th January 1995, 25% of the vacancies for the Postman position are to be filled from amongst extra-departmental Agents with a minimum of 15 years of service based on their seniority. If there are not enough candidates, the vacancies are to be filled by direct recruits through an examination, where the cut-off date is applicable. The Supreme Court directed that if the appellant, M. Elangovan, is senior enough to be considered for the 25% of the vacancies, his case should be considered for promotion, and appropriate action should be taken within two months from the date of production of a copy of the judgment. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal with the observations and directions that the appellant's case should be considered for promotion based on seniority without any cut-off date.

text: Case: M. Kuppaswamy (D) through LRS. vs. R. Vandana. Date: 2nd April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The dispute was a civil matter related to an appeal against the judgment dated 13th April 2007 by the High Court of Karnataka, which was later resolved through mediation. The parties reached a settlement, and a Memorandum of Settlement dated 9th March 2018 was recorded and became part of the Supreme Court’s judgment. A Demand Draft for Rs.31,50,000 was handed over by the appellants to the respondent in terms of the settlement. The settlement underscores the Supreme Court's encouragement for mediation as an effective alternative dispute resolution mechanism. The appeal was disposed of in terms of the settlement, with no further legal proceedings or costs imposed.

case_name: M. Ramalingam vs. State Represented by Inspector of Police, SBE/CBI/ACB, Madras
text: Case: M. Ramalingam vs. State Represented by Inspector of Police, SBE/CBI/ACB, Madras. Date: 3rd October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. M. Ramalingam was charged under Section 120B and Section 420 IPC for conspiracy and cheating, involving the sanction of a jewel loan without pledging any jewel. T. Maran, the Branch Manager, sanctioned jewel loans to M. Ramalingam and others without actual jewels being pledged, thus facilitating the fraudulent activities. The conspiracy involved sanctioning jewel loans by making false entries in the jewel loan movement register, indicating that jewels were pledged when, in fact, they were not. The High Court upheld the conviction of M. Ramalingam under Section 120B and Section 420 IPC, finding sufficient evidence of his involvement in the conspiracy to cheat the bank. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of M. Ramalingam, finding no evidence to connect him to the fraudulent activities, and acquitted him of all charges. The prosecution relied on the jewel loan movement register and the testimony of bank officials to establish that loans were sanctioned without actual jewels being pledged. The Supreme Court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient to prove M. Ramalingam's involvement in the conspiracy and cheating beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court canceled T. Maran's bail and directed him to surrender and undergo the remaining part of his sentence. The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the involvement of the co-accused M. Ramalingam and N. Rajangam in the conspiracy, leading to their acquittal. N. Rajangam was acquitted by the Supreme Court, which set aside his conviction under Section 120B and Section 467 read with Section 471 IPC due to lack of evidence. The Supreme Court emphasized that the prosecution must prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt, and the lack of direct evidence connecting M. Ramalingam and N. Rajangam to the fraudulent activities warranted their acquittal.

case_name: M. Ravindran vs. The Intelligence Officer, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence
text: Case: M. Ravindran vs. The Intelligence Officer, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence. Date: 26th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the indefeasible right to 'default bail' under Section 167(2) of the CrPC was extinguished by the subsequent filing of an additional complaint by the investigating agency. M. Ravindran was charged under Section 8(c) read with Sections 22(c), 23(c), 25A, and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act). The basis for M. Ravindran's application for bail was that the investigation was not complete and the chargesheet had not been filed within the mandatory period of 180 days. The Trial Court granted bail to M. Ravindran on the ground that the court had no power to intervene with the indefeasible right conferred on him by the legislative mandate of Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The High Court cancelled the bail on the ground that the additional complaint was filed on the same day as the bail application and that the application for bail had not been disposed of by the time the additional complaint was filed. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, upholding M. Ravindran's right to default bail, and stated that the filing of the additional complaint after the bail application does not defeat the right to bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The Supreme Court interpreted that the indefeasible right under Section 167(2) of the CrPC is availed of the moment the accused files an application for bail and is prepared to offer bail. The Supreme Court viewed that the subsequent filing of an additional complaint by the investigating agency after the bail application does not extinguish the accused's right to default bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC. The Supreme Court emphasized that the timing of the filing of the bail application, specifically that it was filed after the completion of the mandatory period but before the additional complaint, was crucial in affirming the right to default bail. The broader legal principle established was that an accused's right to default bail cannot be defeated by subsequent actions of the investigating agency once the mandatory period for filing the chargesheet has elapsed and the bail application has been filed.

case_name: M. Vijayakumar vs. State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: M. Vijayakumar vs. State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 21st February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellant's conviction under Section 306 IPC for abetment of suicide was justified despite his acquittal under Sections 342 and 365 IPC by the High Court. M. Vijayakumar was charged under Sections 306, 342, and 365 IPC, while his co-accused were charged only under Sections 342 and 306 IPC. The High Court acquitted M. Vijayakumar of the charges under Sections 342 and 365 IPC but confirmed his conviction under Section 306 IPC, reducing his sentence to three years rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court emphasized that to convict someone under Section 306 IPC, it is necessary to prove that the accused had a clear mens rea to commit the offence, involving an active or direct act leading the victim to commit suicide. The prosecution's case was that the victim, Senthil Kumar, borrowed Rs. 2000 from M. Vijayakumar and was subsequently harassed by the appellant and others, leading to his abduction, wrongful confinement, and ultimately his suicide. The Supreme Court observed that the prosecution failed to establish the charges of abduction and wrongful confinement, as key witnesses were not examined, and the evidence presented did not support the prosecution's case. PW-2, the wife of the deceased Senthil Kumar, claimed that the appellant and others harassed her husband over the repayment of the borrowed amount, leading to his distress and eventual suicide. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in applying Section 106 of the Evidence Act, as the burden of proof should not have been shifted to the appellant without sufficient evidence from the prosecution. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction under Section 306 IPC, and acquitted M. Vijayakumar, discharging his bail bonds.

case_name: M.A. Antony @ Antappan vs. State of Kerala
text: Case: M.A. Antony @ Antappan vs. State of Kerala. Date: 12th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. M.A. Antony @ Antappan was accused of murdering six members of a family in the Manjooran House in Aluva Municipal Town, Ernakulam District, Kerala, on the night of 6th and 7th January 2001. He used a knife, axe, electrocuted, and strangulated the victims. The motive was financial. Antony needed money for employment abroad, and when the family members refused to give him money, he killed them. The Sessions Court in Ernakulam sentenced M.A. Antony @ Antappan to death by hanging. The High Court of Kerala confirmed the death sentence and dismissed Antony's appeal. The Supreme Court reconsidered the death sentence due to the socio-economic circumstances of the appellant, the possibility of his reformation, and the absence of evidence suggesting he was a hardened criminal. The Supreme Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment.

case_name: M.D. Frozen Foods Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Hero Fincorp Ltd.
text: Case: M.D. Frozen Foods Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Hero Fincorp Ltd.. Date: 21st September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants argued that the SARFAESI Act could not be applied retrospectively to debts classified as NPAs before the financial institution was notified under the Act. The Supreme Court rejected the claim, stating that the SARFAESI Act was procedural in nature and could be applied to live debts even if they became NPAs before the notification of the financial institution. The Court invoked principles of complementary remedies under Sections 35 and 37 of the SARFAESI Act, which allow for the coexistence of arbitration and SARFAESI proceedings without conflict. The Court ruled that NBFCs notified as financial institutions under the SARFAESI Act have the same rights and remedies as banks to recover secured debts through the Act. The Court observed that the SARFAESI Act provides an expeditious and effective mechanism for recovering secured debts, aligning with the legislative intent to streamline debt recovery processes.

case_name: M.D. Jain vs Bhagyavathi & Ors.
text: Case: M.D. Jain vs Bhagyavathi & Ors.. Date: 26th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether M.D. Jain should be discharged in a pending contempt proceeding where he was accused of tampering with court documents. The complaint was made by Bhagyavathi Jain, the former wife of M.D. Jain, alleging that M.D. Jain, in collusion with the court staff, had tampered with the court documents. The CBI investigation concluded that there was no evidence, even circumstantial, against M.D. Jain and others regarding the removal, tampering, and substitution of documents, and that the complaints made by Bhagyavathi Jain were false. The CBI report indicated that the court staff, particularly Shri Venkatachalam, failed to properly safeguard the case files, which facilitated the removal of documents, but there was no sufficient evidence to establish any cognizable offence. The High Court was of the view that the CBI inquiry was directed only against the court staff and that the filing of the 'B' report by the CBI could be used by the accused at the final hearing of the case. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court mistakenly viewed the CBI inquiry as being limited to the court staff, whereas the CBI report exonerated M.D. Jain, the appellant, from any involvement in the alleged tampering. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and allowed the appeal, requesting the High Court to reconsider the matter afresh in light of the CBI report exonerating M.D. Jain. Shri Venkatachalam was the custodian of the case files and was found by the CBI to have not taken proper care in safeguarding them, which facilitated the removal of documents. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to consider the matter afresh, taking into account the CBI report that exonerated M.D. Jain from any wrongdoing.

case_name: M.H. Uma Maheshwari & Ors. vs. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: M.H. Uma Maheshwari & Ors. vs. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 12th June 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in reducing the compensation awarded by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal to the appellants. The accident occurred on 16th July 2012 when S.T. Devaraju, the deceased, was traveling in a car that met with an accident. Devaraju suffered severe injuries and subsequently died. The Tribunal awarded a total compensation of Rs.65,60,347.20 to the appellants, which included amounts for loss of dependency, loss of consortium, loss of love and affection, and funeral expenses. The High Court reduced the compensation on the grounds that the deceased was over 50 years of age, thus future prospects should be calculated at 15% instead of 30%. The High Court also made adjustments for the compensation awarded under the heads of loss of consortium and love and affection. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in reducing future prospects to 15% because the age group of the deceased was considered to be between 40 to 50 years, which warrants a 30% addition for future prospects as per established legal precedents. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the compensation awarded by the Tribunal, deeming it just and reasonable. The Supreme Court noted that while the High Court found a double award for loss of consortium and love and affection, it did not justify reducing the total compensation. The Tribunal's award was seen as appropriate in its totality.

case_name: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 19th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary objective was to seek protection for two species of birds, the Great Indian Bustard and the Lesser Florican, which are on the verge of extinction due to hazards posed by overhead power lines. The petitioners sought interim directions to ensure predator-proof fencing, controlled grazing, to prevent the installation of overhead power lines, and to stop further construction of windmills and solar infrastructure in the habitats of the endangered birds. Overhead power lines are considered a threat because the Great Indian Bustard lacks frontal vision and cannot detect the power lines, leading to collisions and deaths. The Wildlife Institute of India reported that power line collisions are a significant cause of mortality for these birds. The Supreme Court suggested installing bird divertors on existing power lines and laying new power lines underground wherever technically feasible, especially in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard. The Supreme Court stated that both the State and Central Government have a duty to preserve endangered species and should provide the necessary funds for conservation efforts, including the undergrounding of power lines in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard. The committee was tasked with assessing the feasibility of laying underground power lines in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard and to provide technical evaluations on a case-by-case basis. The Supreme Court directed that all existing low voltage power lines in the priority and potential habitats of the Great Indian Bustard be converted to underground lines, and that future power lines should be laid underground wherever feasible. Bird divertors should be installed on all existing overhead lines.

case_name: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 26th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge to the withdrawal of a circular dated 23rd May 2009, which granted higher pay scales to Medical Officers, Dental Surgeons, and officers in the specialist cadre, and the recovery of excess amounts paid under this circular. The circular was withdrawn on the grounds that it was issued without the approval of the Finance Department and had financial implications that were not sanctioned by the appropriate authority. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the State of Madhya Pradesh, quashing the judgment of the learned Single Judge that had set aside the withdrawal of the circular and the recovery orders. The Supreme Court held that the State was not justified in ordering the recovery of excess amounts paid with interest, particularly as there was no misrepresentation by the employees, and the mistake was attributable to the Department/State. The Supreme Court directed that pay fixation and pension should be calculated as per the order dated 26th August 2008, as if the circular dated 23rd May 2009 was never issued, but no recovery of excess amounts already paid should be made. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's decision to uphold the recovery of excess amounts paid under the circular dated 23rd May 2009, but upheld the withdrawal of the circular itself.

case_name: M/S A.K. Sarkar & Co. & Anr. vs The State of West Bengal & Ors.
text: Case: M/S A.K. Sarkar & Co. & Anr. vs The State of West Bengal & Ors.. Date: 7th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants were correctly convicted under Section 16(1)(a)(i) read with Section 7 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for misbranding confectioneries. The allegations were that the appellants sold sugar boiled confectioneries that did not display the complete address of the manufacturer and the date of manufacturing, violating Rule 32(c) and (f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955. The Trial Court convicted the appellants, sentencing appellant no.2 and Amit Kumar Sarkar to six months of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1,000 each, while appellant no.1 was fined Rs.2,000. The appeal was dismissed by the District and Sessions Judge, but the conviction of Amit Kumar Sarkar was set aside, and he was acquitted. The High Court upheld the convictions but reduced the sentence of appellant no.2 from six months to three months of simple imprisonment. The appellants argued that Rule 32(c) and (f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules were not applicable to their case, claiming a misinterpretation of the law. The Supreme Court rejected the argument, stating that at the time of the offence, Rule 32(c) and (f) were indeed applicable, and the packets were correctly classified as misbranded. The Supreme Court discussed Article 20(1) of the Constitution, which prohibits retroactive criminal legislation but allows for lesser punishment if a new law provides for it. The Supreme Court considered the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and prescribes only monetary penalties for misbranding, leading to a reduction in the appellants' sentences. The Supreme Court converted the sentence of appellant no.2 from three months of simple imprisonment and a fine to just a fine of Rs.50,000, while upholding the fine of Rs.2,000 for appellant no.1.

case_name: M/S Bagalkot Udyog Limited vs. Shivashankargouda & Ors.
text: Case: M/S Bagalkot Udyog Limited vs. Shivashankargouda & Ors.. Date: 24th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The High Court directed the Executing Court to examine whether the renewal clause allowing an extension beyond 31st March 2013 was within the scope of the original decree. The respondents contested that the Executing Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by including a renewal clause for another 30 years starting 1st April 2013 in the draft lease deed. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was within its jurisdiction to entertain the matter under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and remand it back to the Executing Court for reconsideration. The Supreme Court left it to the Executing Court to decide whether the original decree limited the renewal of the lease deed up to 31st March 2013 or permitted further extensions. The Supreme Court predicted that if the Executing Court concludes that the lease could not be extended beyond 31st March 2013, it would effectively bring the matter to an end without continuity of proceedings.

The Supreme Court predicted that if the Executing Court concludes that the lease could not be extended beyond 31st March 2013, it would effectively bring the matter to an end without continuity of proceedings.

case_name: M/S Bhagwandas B. Ramchandani vs. British Airways
text: Case: M/S Bhagwandas B. Ramchandani vs. British Airways. Date: 29th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant, M/S Bhagwandas B. Ramchandani, is a sole proprietary concern engaged in the business of imports and exports. The cargo containing fruits and vegetables was damaged and destroyed due to bad weather conditions in London, which prevented the flight from departing to Canada. The appellant lodged a claim amounting to Rs 4,27,922/- for the destruction of the cargo sent on 30th June 2010 due to packaging and other issues. The appellant instituted a suit being OS No. 5164/2012 on 15th September 2012 before the City Civil Court, Mumbai, seeking recovery of Rs 9,17,642.56/- with interest at the rate of 21% per annum. The Trial Court framed a preliminary issue on the ground of limitation and held that the suit was not barred by limitation, as the period prescribed in Rule 30 of the Second Schedule to the Carriage by Air Act, 1972, could be calculated from 28th October 2010. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the respondent and held that the suit was barred by limitation, reasoning that the Air Act, 1972, being a special statute, had an overriding effect over the Limitation Act, 1963. The two substantial questions of law considered were: (1) The applicability of the Limitation Act, 1963, when the right itself is extinguished, and (2) Whether the provisions of the Carriage by Air Act, 1972, expressly exclude the Limitation Act, 1963.

case_name: M/S Bharti Airtel Limited vs. A.S. Raghavendra
text: Case: M/S Bharti Airtel Limited vs. A.S. Raghavendra. Date: 2nd April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case is about an employment dispute where A.S. Raghavendra, the respondent, alleged that his resignation from Bharti Airtel Limited was forced, and he should be considered a 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act. A.S. Raghavendra was appointed as the Regional Business Head (South) - Government Enterprise Services in Bharti Airtel Limited. The main legal issue was whether A.S. Raghavendra could be considered a 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act, which would allow him to seek relief for alleged forced resignation. The Supreme Court set aside the decisions of the High Court and the Single Judge, ruling that A.S. Raghavendra is not a 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act and restored the judgment of the Labour Court. A.S. Raghavendra filed a petition alleging that his resignation was forced, which led to conciliation proceedings that ultimately failed. The Labour Court rejected the claim on the grounds that A.S. Raghavendra was performing managerial duties and thus did not qualify as a 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act. The High Court initially decided that A.S. Raghavendra should be considered a 'workman' based on his lack of authority to appoint, dismiss, or conduct disciplinary inquiries against other employees. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation, stating that mere absence of authority to appoint or dismiss does not solely determine 'workman' status, especially for employees in high-ranking positions.

case_name: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 8th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the clauses in the contract that allowed GAIL to levy 'loss of transportation charges' on IPCL were valid and enforceable, considering IPCL had to lay down its own pipelines as mandated by the allocation letter from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. IPCL contended that the transportation charges levied by GAIL were arbitrary and unfair, as IPCL was mandated to lay its own pipelines for gas transportation and did not use GAIL's pipelines. They also claimed that the charges were contrary to the Government pricing orders and sought a refund of the 'loss of transportation charges' paid. GAIL defended the imposition of 'loss of transportation charges' by arguing that it had made significant investments in constructing its own infrastructure (the HBJ pipeline) and needed to recover legitimate maintenance costs. GAIL also argued that both parties were public sector enterprises at the time of contract signing and that the contract reflected mutual consensus. The Single Judge quashed the disputed clauses as being contrary to the Government pricing orders, unfair, and unconscionable. This decision was upheld by the Division Bench, which affirmed the Single Judge's observations and ruled in favor of IPCL. The Supreme Court concluded that the clauses allowing GAIL to levy 'loss of transportation charges' were arbitrary, unfair, and discriminatory, as IPCL was mandated to use its own pipelines and not GAIL's HBJ pipeline. The Court ruled that such charges violated Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which ensures the right to equality. The Supreme Court restricted the relief to a refund of transportation charges paid within three years prior to the filing of the writ petition by IPCL. The Court ordered that the refund should be made within two months from the judgment date, failing which it would carry an interest of 8% per annum.
