case_name: M/S Garment Craft vs. Prakash Chand Goel
text: Case: M/S Garment Craft vs. Prakash Chand Goel. Date: 11th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order allowing the application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, filed by Shailendra Garg, the sole proprietor of M/S Garment Craft. Shailendra Garg was unable to participate effectively because he was arrested and detained in judicial custody from 6th October 2015 to 6th May 2017, preventing him from leading evidence and communicating effectively with his counsel. The Additional District Judge allowed the application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code, setting aside the ex-parte decree and restoring the case to its original number for defence evidence. The Supreme Court found that the High Court overstepped its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 by reappreciating and substituting its own findings for those of the trial court, which had justifiably granted relief based on the appellant's incarceration and inability to participate in the trial. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to schedule three consecutive dates for the appellant to lead third-party evidence, file a list of witnesses and affidavit by way of evidence, and submit details of his assets within three weeks to protect the respondent's interests.

case_name: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.
text: Case: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.. Date: 1st February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Revisional Authority had the jurisdiction to reopen and revise the assessment orders passed by the Assessing Authority, classifying mosquito repellents as taxable at 4% instead of 10%. The appellant challenged the Revisional Authority's orders on the grounds that the assessment orders were legally correct, as they were based on the decision of the Haryana Tax Tribunal, which classified mosquito repellents containing 4% Alethrin as insecticides taxable at 4%. The Haryana Tax Tribunal's decision on 21st November 2001 held that mosquito repellents containing 4% Alethrin were classified as insecticides and were therefore subject to a concessional tax rate of 4%. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed the appellant's writ petition on the grounds that an alternative remedy of appeal under Section 33 of the Haryana Value Added Tax (VAT) Act was available, which the appellant had not pursued. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition without examining the merits of the challenge, particularly when the issue was purely legal and involved the jurisdiction of the Revisional Authority. The Supreme Court concluded that the Revisional Authority's orders were unsustainable because they ignored the binding decision of the Haryana Tax Tribunal and assumed jurisdiction without proper legal basis. The Supreme Court set aside the Revisional Authority's orders dated 2nd March 2009 for the assessment years 2003-04 and 2004-05, and upheld the orders of the Assessing Authority, restoring the classification of mosquito repellents as taxable at 4%.

case_name: M/S Hero Motocorp Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: M/S Hero Motocorp Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 17th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Union of India could be directed to adhere to the representation made in the Office Memorandum dated 7th January 2003, even after the enactment of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The Office Memorandum of 2003 provided that new industrial units and existing industrial units on substantial expansion in the States of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh would be entitled to 100% exemption from excise duty for 10 years from the date of commencement of commercial production. The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by Hero Motocorp Ltd., rejecting the claim of 100% budgetary support in lieu of the pre-existing 100% outright excise duty exemption. With the enactment of the CGST Act, the tax exemption benefits were reduced, and the GST Council decided that entities exempted from payment of indirect tax would pay tax in the GST regime, with any continued incentive administered through a reimbursement mechanism. The Budgetary Support Scheme provided to refund/reimburse the Central share of CGST and IGST to the affected eligible industrial units for the residual period in the North Eastern and Himalayan States, determined at 58% of CGST and 29% of IGST. Hero Motocorp Ltd. argued that the Union was bound by the promise made in the Office Memorandum of 2003 to provide 100% tax exemption, and the reduction to 58% was arbitrary and irrational. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, holding that the Union of India was not bound by the earlier representation after the enactment of the CGST Act and the changes brought by the GST regime. The Supreme Court emphasized that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot operate against a statute and the Government's duty to act in public interest, particularly when a new statutory regime like GST is introduced. The judgment suggests that companies must carefully consider the potential for legislative changes and not solely rely on government incentives, as these can be rescinded or altered by new statutory regimes. Companies should diversify their risk management strategies, not over-rely on government incentives, and anticipate potential changes in legislative frameworks to ensure financial stability and compliance. The Supreme Court stated that promissory estoppel cannot be applied to prevent the government from acting in the public interest or from implementing legislative changes such as the introduction of the GST regime.

case_name: M/S M.S.P.L. Limited vs. The State of Karnataka & Ors.
text: Case: M/S M.S.P.L. Limited vs. The State of Karnataka & Ors.. Date: 11th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Division Bench quashed the notifications due to procedural lapses, lack of adherence to environmental norms, and the acquisition serving private interests rather than public purposes. The Court observed that the Board failed to exercise due diligence, relying heavily on recommendations from the State High-Level Clearance Committee without independent evaluation. The Court directed strict adherence to statutory procedures, including environmental impact assessments and a transparent public purpose justification. The Court stated that the approval did not exempt the project from compliance with statutory provisions, including environmental clearances and procedural requirements. The Court emphasized that individual rights must yield to genuine public purposes but held that acquisitions solely benefitting private parties without public interest are unsustainable.

case_name: M/S Modi Naturals Ltd vs. The Commissioner of Commercial Tax UP
text: Case: M/S Modi Naturals Ltd vs. The Commissioner of Commercial Tax UP. Date: 6th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether M/S Modi Naturals Ltd is entitled to the full benefit of Input Tax Credit (ITC) claimed on goods purchased for manufacturing its final product, Rice Bran Oil (RBO), under the Uttar Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2008 (UP VAT Act). The years of assessment involved in the case were 2013-14 and 2015-16. M/S Modi Naturals Ltd manufactures Rice Bran Oil (RBO) and Physical Refined RBO, with a by-product of De-Oiled Rice Bran (DORB). The High Court ruled that M/S Modi Naturals Ltd was not entitled to the full benefit of ITC on the goods purchased for manufacturing RBO, holding that the ITC should be limited to the extent of tax payable on the sale value of the goods. The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'goods' under the UP VAT Act to include both taxable and exempt goods, and it held that the legislative intent was not to limit the scope of 'goods' to only taxable goods. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgement, and restored the orders of the Commercial Tax Tribunal, thereby entitling M/S Modi Naturals Ltd to claim the full amount of ITC. The Supreme Court held that the decision in M.K. Agro Tech Private Limited was not applicable to this case because the provisions of the Karnataka VAT Act, under which that decision was made, are distinct from the provisions of the UP VAT Act.

case_name: M/S Natesan Agencies (Plantations) vs. State Rep. by the Secretary to Government Environment and Forests Department
text: Case: M/S Natesan Agencies (Plantations) vs. State Rep. by the Secretary to Government Environment and Forests Department. Date: 20th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appellant's claim for damages for being deprived of using leased land, which was included in a wildlife sanctuary proposal but was later excluded without compensation. The Division Bench of the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the Single Judge, dismissing the appellant's suit for recovery of damages. The appellant claimed damages on the grounds that they were deprived of using the leased land due to its inclusion in a wildlife sanctuary proposal and were not compensated when the proposal was dropped. The learned Single Judge partly decreed the suit in favor of the appellant, holding them entitled to Rs. 86,88,000/- together with interest for being deprived of using the land. The Division Bench found no case for awarding damages as there was no unlawful dispossession or prevention from using the land by the State, and it was deemed that any misunderstanding by the appellant about their rights did not warrant compensation. The Division Bench allowed the appeal filed by the State Government, reversing the Single Judge's decree and dismissing the appellant's suit for damages. The Division Bench had prima facie doubts about the applicability of the Limitation Act to exclude the period during which the litigation was pending, but it ultimately did not delve into this question since the claim was rejected on merits.

case_name: M/S Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/S Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: M/S Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/S Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 26th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether a person who gives a term loan to a Corporate Person, free of interest, on account of its working capital requirements, is a Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). The NCLT dismissed the petition on the grounds that the loan given by M/S Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. was interest-free and, therefore, did not qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, dismissing the appeal on the grounds that the loan did not carry any interest and, therefore, could not be considered a 'financial debt'. The Supreme Court ruled that the definition of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC includes interest-free loans, as the term 'financial debt' covers any debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, which can include loans provided for business operations without interest. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgements of both the NCLAT and NCLT, and revived the petition under Section 7 of the IBC for fresh consideration in accordance with the law and the Supreme Court's findings. The Supreme Court directed that the petition under Section 7 of the IBC be decided afresh, taking into account the Court's interpretation that interest-free loans can qualify as 'financial debt'.

case_name: M/S Pahwa Plastics Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. vs. Dastak NGO and Ors.
text: Case: M/S Pahwa Plastics Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. vs. Dastak NGO and Ors.. Date: 25th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether an establishment employing about 8000 workers, set up with Consent to Establish (CTE) and Consent to Operate (CTO) from statutory authorities and having applied for ex post facto Environmental Clearance (EC), could be closed down pending the issuance of EC. The NGT held that manufacturing units like those of the appellants, which did not have prior EC, could not be allowed to operate, leading to the appeal in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court observed that ex post facto EC should not ordinarily be granted but can be allowed in exceptional circumstances if the units comply with environmental norms and stopping operations would have severe economic and livelihood impacts. The Supreme Court noted that the Haryana State Pollution Control Board (HSPCB) itself was under the misconception that prior EC was not necessary and that the appellants had applied for ex post facto EC. The Court allowed the units to continue operating pending the decision on their EC applications. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the NGT's order, and directed that the applications for EC be decided within one month. Pending the decision, the operation of the units was not to be interfered with. The Supreme Court's judgment allowed the manufacturing units to continue operations, emphasizing the importance of balancing environmental compliance with economic contributions and livelihood of employees.

case_name: M/S SCG Contracts India Pvt. Ltd. vs K.S. Chamankar Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: M/S SCG Contracts India Pvt. Ltd. vs K.S. Chamankar Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 12th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the written statement filed by the defendant could be taken on record after the lapse of the mandatory 120-day period stipulated by the Code of Civil Procedure as amended by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. The significance of the Order VII Rule 11 application was that it sought the rejection of the plaint, and the proceedings on this application caused a delay in the filing of the written statement by the defendant. The trial court initially allowed the written statement to be taken on record despite the lapse of the 120-day period, provided that the defendant paid costs of Rs. 25,000 to the plaintiff's counsel. The Supreme Court interpreted the amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure as mandating that the written statement must be filed within 120 days from the date of service of summons, beyond which the right to file the written statement is forfeited and the court has no power to extend this period. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the trial court and the High Court, ruling that the written statement filed by the defendant beyond the 120-day period should be taken off the record. The Supreme Court referred to the judgements in the cases of Bihar Rajya Bhumi Vikas Bank Samiti vs. State of Bihar and Canara Bank vs. N.G. Subbaraya Setty, which emphasized that statutory time limits must be strictly adhered to and are mandatory in nature. case_name: M/S Shree Daneshwari Traders vs. Sanjay Jain & Anr.
text: Case: M/S Shree Daneshwari Traders vs. Sanjay Jain & Anr.. Date: 21st August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Sanjay Jain was guilty under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for issuing cheques that were dishonored due to insufficient funds. Sanjay Jain was alleged to have issued several cheques to M/S Shree Daneshwari Traders as payment for commodities supplied, which were dishonored upon presentation due to insufficient funds. Sanjay Jain acknowledged the receipt of legal notices regarding the dishonored cheques but failed to make the payments or arrange for the amounts in satisfaction of the cheques issued. The Trial Court acquitted Sanjay Jain, stating that the cheques were issued as security for credit purchases and not for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by M/S Shree Daneshwari Traders, upholding the acquittal of Sanjay Jain by the Trial Court. The Supreme Court observed that the receipts presented by Sanjay Jain indicating cash payments did not negate the existence of a legally enforceable debt for which the cheques were issued. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, convicting Sanjay Jain under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and imposing a fine of Rs.2,97,150/-. The Supreme Court reasoned that the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act had not been sufficiently rebutted by Sanjay Jain, as the cheques were issued for the discharge of a debt. This judgement reinforces the legal principle that cheques issued for the discharge of a debt carry a statutory presumption of being for consideration, which must be rebutted with compelling evidence to avoid conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Supreme Court emphasized that courts must consider the statutory presumption in favor of the holder of the cheque and the need for the accused to provide substantial evidence to rebut this presumption in cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. If Sanjay Jain fails to pay the fine of Rs.2,97,150/- within twelve weeks, he will be taken into custody to serve the default sentence of six months' imprisonment.

case_name: M/S Siddhyvinayak Infrastructure vs. Kamalakar Jayant Srivastava & Anr.
text: Case: M/S Siddhyvinayak Infrastructure vs. Kamalakar Jayant Srivastava & Anr.. Date: 12th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main dispute was regarding the agreement for the purchase of a Twin Bungalow, where the complainant alleged that the developer did not fulfill the contractual obligations despite the payment made. The agreement was for the purchase of a Twin Bungalow with a super built-up area of 900 sq. ft. for a total sale consideration of Rs. 9,74,000, where Rs. 4,23,520 was to be paid in cash and the remaining Rs. 5,50,520 was to be financed through a loan. The bank sanctioned a loan of Rs. 6,40,000 in favor of the complainant on 24th November 2006, but the loan was never actually disbursed due to non-submission of necessary documents. The District Forum directed the developer to complete the construction of the bungalow and hand over possession to the complainant, along with compensation for physical and mental harassment and costs. The National Consumer Commission modified the order by directing the developer to provide possession of the house within one month and execute the Sale Deed after obtaining the Occupation Certificate, with the complainant required to pay the balance sale consideration. The Supreme Court directed the developer to refund Rs. 3,24,780 to the complainant with interest at 12% per annum, effectively ending the litigation and cancelling the obligation to execute the sale deed.

case_name: M/S Steel Authority of India Limited vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Bolpur
text: Case: M/S Steel Authority of India Limited vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Bolpur. Date: 28th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether M/S Steel Authority of India Limited was liable to pay interest on the duty amount of Rs. 15.66 crore for the clearances made during the period from July 2000 to December 2004. The company filed an appeal before the CESTAT after being served with a Show Cause Notice by the Commissioner of Central Excise, which demanded duty of Rs. 15.66 crore by invoking the extended period of limitation. The CESTAT dismissed the application filed by the company seeking rectification of its earlier order and maintained the appeal with regard to the penalty aspect while dismissing the appeal with regard to the duty demand. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by M/S Steel Authority of India Limited and upheld the decision of the CESTAT. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order and remitted the matter back to the CESTAT for consideration of the limited aspect of interest on the duty amount, noting that the issue of interest had not been addressed by any of the authorities.

case_name: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Government of N.C.T. of Delhi
text: Case: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Government of N.C.T. of Delhi. Date: 19th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether 'Pan Masala', which contains tobacco and gutka, covered by an Entry in the First Schedule to the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act 1957 (ADE Act), are taxable by the State under the Delhi Sales Tax Act 1975 and other related State acts. The conflicting precedents considered were Kothari Products Ltd. vs State of A.P., Radheshyam Gudakhu Factory vs State of Orissa, and Reliance Trading Co. vs State of Kerala on one side, and CST vs Agra Belting Works on the other. These cases provided differing interpretations on whether items covered by the ADE Act could be taxed under state laws. The Supreme Court concluded that 'Pan Masala' containing tobacco, covered by an Entry in the First Schedule to the ADE Act, could not be taxed by the State under the Delhi Sales Tax Act 1975 and other related State acts, as it falls under the exemption provided by the ADE Act. The Supreme Court reiterated that the ADE Act was enacted to provide for the levy and collection of additional duties of excise in respect of certain goods, replacing state sales taxes on those goods. Once goods are chargeable under the ADE Act, states cannot levy sales tax on the same goods. The Supreme Court referred to its previous judgments and emphasized that the majority decision of a Bench of larger strength would prevail over the decision of a Bench of lesser strength. The court should be guided by the strength of the Bench rather than the number of judges taking a particular view.

case_name: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi
text: Case: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi. Date: 4th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the taxability of pan masala or gutkha under state enactments, and whether state legislatures were empowered to levy sales tax on these articles in view of the provisions in the Constitution enabling the Union to levy additional duties of excise. The relevant central enactments were the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (CST Act), the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (CET Act), and the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act, 1957 (ADE Act). The appellants argued that state legislatures were not empowered to levy sales tax on gutkha in view of the constitutional provision enabling the Union to levy additional duties of excise. They also contended that the rate of state tax could not exceed the limit prescribed by the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The court held that state legislatures were competent to levy taxes on the sale or purchase of gutkha, and the levy of such sales taxes only meant that additional excise duty levied on such commodities by the Central Government would not be distributed among the states which had chosen to levy a tax on the sale of such articles. The court held that the provisions of the DST Act, particularly Sections 3, 4, and 7, were to be interpreted in such a way that goods listed as 'tax-free' under the Third Schedule would not be subject to sales tax unless specifically amended by the competent authority. The inclusion of gutkha in the taxable list was found to be valid. The 2001 amendment to the Central Excise Tariff Act included 'Pan Masala containing tobacco' under Chapter 24, which clarified that gutkha was a specific product and subject to different tax treatments compared to general chewing tobacco. This distinction affected how gutkha was classified and taxed under both central and state laws.

case_name: M/S VISTRA ITCL (INDIA) LTD & ORS. vs MR. DINKAR VENKATASUBRAMANIAN & ANR.
text: Case: M/S VISTRA ITCL (INDIA) LTD & ORS. vs MR. DINKAR VENKATASUBRAMANIAN & ANR.. Date: 4th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellants, as secured creditors with a pledge over shares, could claim rights as financial creditors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) after their earlier claim was rejected in 2017. The NCLT and NCLAT ruled that the appellants could not be considered financial creditors as their claim was based on pledged shares and they had not directly advanced any financial debt to the corporate debtor. The appellants argued that their claim constituted a financial debt under the IBC as the pledged shares were provided as security for loans benefiting the corporate debtor. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants were secured creditors to the extent of the pledged shares but could not be classified as financial creditors under the IBC since their relationship did not meet the statutory definition of financial debt. The Supreme Court directed that secured creditors holding pledged shares should have their claims evaluated within the framework of the IBC, but emphasized the distinction between financial and secured creditors. This judgment clarifies the limited rights of secured creditors holding pledged shares and reinforces the necessity for precise categorization under the IBC, impacting how resolution professionals and creditors approach such claims in insolvency proceedings.

case_name: M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.
text: Case: M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.. Date: 2nd June 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the enforcement of the second-tier arbitration award made by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in London, which contradicted the first-tier arbitration award made in India. The first-tier arbitration by the Indian Council of Arbitration resulted in a Nil Award, indicating that no amount was payable by Hindustan Copper Ltd. to Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. The ICC arbitration in London awarded Centrotrade $152,112.33 for the first shipment, $15,815.59 for demurrage on the first shipment, $284,653.53 for the second shipment, $82,733 in legal costs, and $29,000 for arbitration fees and expenses. Hindustan Copper Ltd. challenged the second-tier arbitration award on the grounds that it was contrary to public policy in India and that the arbitration agreement allowing for a two-tier arbitration process was invalid. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the two-tier arbitration agreement, stating that such a clause was permissible under Indian law. Yes, the Supreme Court enforced the second-tier arbitration award from the ICC in London, allowing Centrotrade to recover the awarded amounts. The Supreme Court's ruling was significant because it clarified the enforceability of two-tier arbitration clauses and reinforced India's commitment to honoring international arbitration awards, thereby promoting a pro-arbitration environment.

case_name: M/S. Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank & Anr.
text: Case: M/S. Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank & Anr.. Date: 31st August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, would prevail over the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings (Special Provisions) Act, 1958, in initiating the insolvency resolution process against Innoventive Industries Ltd. due to their default on loans. Innoventive Industries Ltd. claimed that their debt liabilities were temporarily suspended under two notifications issued under the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act, and hence, no debt was legally due at the time. The NCLT held that the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, would prevail over the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act, owing to the non-obstante clause in Section 238 of the Code, and admitted the application for initiating the insolvency resolution process against Innoventive Industries Ltd. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, stating that the Code and the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act operate in different fields and are not repugnant to each other. However, it also ruled that Innoventive Industries Ltd. could not use the Maharashtra Act to stall the insolvency resolution process under Section 7 of the Code. The Supreme Court found that the appeal at the behest of the erstwhile directors of Innoventive Industries Ltd. was not maintainable since the management of the company had been taken over by an interim resolution professional, rendering the directors without authority to file the appeal. The Supreme Court noted that the Code represents a paradigm shift in law, emphasizing that entrenched managements are no longer allowed to continue if they cannot pay their debts. The Court highlighted the objective of the Code to bring insolvency law under a single unified umbrella, to speed up the insolvency process, and to balance the interests of all stakeholders.

case_name: M/S. Jermyn Capital LLC Dubai vs. Central Bureau of Investigation & Ors.
text: Case: M/S. Jermyn Capital LLC Dubai vs. Central Bureau of Investigation & Ors.. Date: 17th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the order of the court allowing the appellant to withdraw the sum of Rs 38.52 crore along with 4 percent simple interest from 08.05.2006 till the date of actual payment should be modified. The appellant sought modification of the order dated 09.05.2023 to permit withdrawal of the amount along with the fixed deposit interest that had accrued thereon. The initial condition imposed by the Courts below required the appellant to furnish a bank guarantee for the release of the sum of Rs 38.52 crore. The appellant produced copies of various orders passed earlier by the Securities Appellate Tribunal and the Supreme Court, which directed that the sale proceeds be placed in bank fixed deposits to garner a higher rate of interest. The Supreme Court allowed the modification application, permitting the appellant to unconditionally withdraw the amount along with the fixed deposit interest accrued thereon. References were made to orders dated 08.05.2006 by the Securities Appellate Tribunal and orders dated 05.12.2008, 14.05.2009, and 16.11.2009 by the Supreme Court regarding the placement of sale proceeds in fixed deposits for higher interest. The appellant was represented by Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, Sr. Adv., Mr. Sunil Fernandes, AOR, and other advocates. The Supreme Court acknowledged that the fixed deposit interest accrued on the sale proceeds should be included in the amount to be withdrawn by the appellant. The Supreme Court's modification order effectively set aside the previous court condition requiring a bank guarantee for the release of the sum and allowed the unconditional withdrawal of the amount along with accrued interest. The Supreme Court highlighted the importance of modifying court orders to reflect the accurate financial entitlements of the parties involved, ensuring justice and adherence to previous judicial directives.

case_name: M/S. Meters And Instruments Private Limited & Anr. vs. Kanchan Mehta
text: Case: M/S. Meters And Instruments Private Limited & Anr. vs. Kanchan Mehta. Date: 5th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the proceedings for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can be regulated where the accused is willing to deposit the cheque amount. The High Court rejected the prayer of the appellants for compounding the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act on payment of the cheque amount and for exemption from personal appearance. The cheque amount was Rs.29,319/-. The cheque was returned unpaid for want of sufficient funds. The Magistrate observed that the case could not be tried summarily as a sentence of more than one year might have to be passed and decided to try the case as a summons case. The Supreme Court considered that the offence under Section 138 primarily related to a civil wrong and that the 2002 amendment made the offence compoundable. The Supreme Court stated that the trials under Section 138 are expected to be summary trials and can be regulated to ensure speedy resolution, including the possibility of closing proceedings if the cheque amount with interest and costs is paid. The Supreme Court established that the court has the discretion to close proceedings and discharge the accused if the complainant is duly compensated, even without the complainant's consent, under certain circumstances. The Supreme Court suggested that High Courts consider issuing directions to handle certain categories of Section 138 cases online to reduce the burden on courts and improve efficiency. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals, allowing the appellants to move the trial court afresh for any further order in light of the judgement.

The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals, allowing the appellants to move the trial court afresh for any further order in light of the judgement.

case_name: M/S. Mitra Guha Builders (India) Company vs. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited
text: Case: M/S. Mitra Guha Builders (India) Company vs. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited. Date: 8th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main dispute was whether the levy of liquidated damages by ONGC under Clause 2 of the contract was arbitrable or an 'excepted matter' that could not be decided by the arbitrator. The claims included balance payments towards the final bill, amounts allegedly withheld by ONGC, escalation costs, and a declaration that the penalty imposed under Clause 2 was illegal and unwarranted. The Arbitrator allowed some claims of the claimant and disallowed the liquidated damages/compensation imposed by ONGC, considering them as a penalty. The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the Arbitrator's award and the Single Judge's order, holding that the levy of liquidated damages was an 'excepted matter' under Clause 2 read with Clause 25 of the contract, and therefore not arbitrable. The Supreme Court upheld the Division Bench's decision, ruling that the levy of liquidated damages by the Superintending Engineer under Clause 2 was final and not subject to arbitration, and dismissed the appeals. The Supreme Court held that Clause 2 provided a complete mechanism for the determination of liability and that the decision of the Superintending Engineer regarding liquidated damages was final and binding, thus not arbitrable.

case_name: M/S. Nandhini Deluxe vs Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd.
text: Case: M/S. Nandhini Deluxe vs Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd.. Date: 26th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the use of the mark 'NANDHINI' by M/S. Nandhini Deluxe for its restaurants, which the Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd. claimed was deceptively similar to their mark 'NANDINI' used for milk and milk products, leading to potential public confusion. The High Court of Karnataka, in its judgment dated 2nd December 2014, upheld the objections of the Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd. and confirmed the order of the IPAB, which had canceled the registration of the 'NANDHINI' mark for M/S. Nandhini Deluxe. M/S. Nandhini Deluxe argued that their use of the mark 'NANDHINI' since 1989 was honest and in good faith. They also contended that the goods and services offered under their mark were different from those of the respondent, as they run restaurants, while the respondent deals in milk and milk products. The Deputy Registrar of Trade Marks initially allowed the registration of the 'NANDHINI' mark for M/S. Nandhini Deluxe but restricted its use by excluding milk and milk products from the registration, acknowledging the distinctive use of the mark by both parties in different contexts. The IPAB, in its order dated 4th October 2011, ruled in favor of the Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd., stating that the 'NANDINI' mark had acquired distinctiveness and was well-known, and that the 'NANDHINI' mark by M/S. Nandhini Deluxe could cause confusion among consumers. The Supreme Court ruled that there was no likelihood of confusion between the two marks, given the different nature of the businesses and the distinct visual representation of the marks. The Court allowed the registration of the 'NANDHINI' mark for M/S. Nandhini Deluxe, excluding milk and milk products.

case_name: M/S. Panther Security Service Private Limited vs. The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation & Another
text: Case: M/S. Panther Security Service Private Limited vs. The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation & Another. Date: 2nd December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether M/S. Panther Security Service Private Limited was liable to comply with the provisions of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (EPF Act) and to deposit statutory dues as determined by the Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner. The appellant argued that it was not covered by the EPF Act as it merely facilitated providing Chowkidars to its clients, who paid the Chowkidars directly, and thus the appellant did not consider itself the employer of these security guards. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was engaged in specialized and expert services of providing trained security guards, who were its employees, and thus, the appellant was the employer responsible for paying their wages. The balance sheets and other documents revealed a large amount paid towards salaries and wages, indicating that the appellant had more than 20 employees on its rolls, contrary to its claims. This supported the applicability of the EPF Act to the appellant. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant was liable to comply with the EPF Act and deposit the statutory dues as determined. The interim order restraining coercive steps for enforcement of the demand notice was vacated. The judgment discussed the applicability of the EPF Act to establishments rendering expert services and referenced various precedents such as Group 4 Securitas Guarding Ltd. vs. Employees Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal, and provisions of the Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Act, 2005.

case_name: M/S. Patil Automation Private Limited and Ors. vs Rakheja Engineers Private Limited
text: Case: M/S. Patil Automation Private Limited and Ors. vs Rakheja Engineers Private Limited. Date: 17th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The trial court held that the suit was not barred for non-compliance with Section 12A and allowed the case to proceed while directing mediation as per the provisions. The appellants argued that Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, uses the word 'shall,' indicating that pre-litigation mediation is mandatory and failure to comply should lead to rejection of the plaint. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 12A as mandatory, requiring exhaustion of pre-litigation mediation before instituting a commercial suit unless urgent interim relief is sought. The Supreme Court clarified that suits filed without complying with Section 12A should be rejected, but the plaintiff can file a fresh suit after following the mandatory mediation procedure. This decision underscores the importance of adhering to pre-litigation mediation procedures under Section 12A, potentially reducing the burden on commercial courts and encouraging amicable dispute resolution.

case_name: M/S. Shanti Conductors (P) Ltd. & Anr. vs Assam State Electricity Board & Ors.
text: Case: M/S. Shanti Conductors (P) Ltd. & Anr. vs Assam State Electricity Board & Ors.. Date: 23rd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether M/S. Shanti Conductors (P) Ltd. was entitled to claim interest on delayed payments under the Interest on Delayed Payment to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act, 1993, for contracts entered into before the Act came into force. The High Court held that the 1993 Act was not applicable to contracts entered into before the Act came into force, thereby setting aside the trial court's judgment in favor of M/S. Shanti Conductors. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, confirming that the 1993 Act does not apply retroactively to contracts entered into before its enforcement on 23rd September 1992. The Assam State Electricity Board placed supply orders for Aluminium Electrical Conductors on 31st March 1992 and 13th May 1992, with total considerations of Rs. 1.22 crores and Rs. 32.49 lakhs, respectively. M/S. Shanti Conductors filed the suit on 10th January 1997, claiming Rs. 53.68 lakhs as interest on delayed payments under the 1993 Act, arguing that the payments were received late despite the supplies being completed by 4th October 1993. The trial court decreed the suit on 2nd February 2000, awarding M/S. Shanti Conductors Rs. 51,60,507.42 with compound interest at the rate of 23.75% per annum. The Full Bench framed questions regarding the maintainability of the suit for recovery of interest under the 1993 Act, the applicability of the Act to pre-1993 contracts, and whether a supplier could claim interest without reserving the right to do so when accepting delayed payments. The Full Bench of the High Court held that a suit for interest under the 1993 Act was maintainable and that the Act applied to contracts entered into before 23rd September 1992. However, this decision was later overturned by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court emphasized that laws, including the 1993 Act, generally do not have retrospective application unless explicitly stated, and therefore, the provisions of the 1993 Act could not be applied to contracts executed before the Act's commencement date. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by M/S. Shanti Conductors, upheld the High Court's judgment, and confirmed that the 1993 Act did not apply to contracts entered into before its enforcement, thereby denying the claim for interest on delayed payments.

case_name: M/S. Sicagen India Ltd. vs. Mahindra Vadinei & Ors.
text: Case: M/S. Sicagen India Ltd. vs. Mahindra Vadinei & Ors.. Date: 8th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the prosecution based on the second statutory notice after the dishonor of cheques is permissible under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The cheques in question were three cheques issued by the respondents: Cheque No. 316693 dated 20.07.2009 for Rs.1,44,362, Cheque No. 316663 dated 30.07.2009 for Rs.4,26,400, and Cheque No. 316692 dated 10.08.2009 for Rs.4,48,656. The cheques were dishonored and returned with the endorsement 'insufficient funds'. The appellant issued a statutory notice to the respondents on 25.01.2010 demanding the repayment of the amount. When the cheque amount was not paid, the appellant filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The High Court quashed the complaint, holding that the complaint based on the second statutory notice dated 25.01.2010 was not maintainable since it was on the same cause of action as the first notice dated 31.08.2009. The Supreme Court ruled that a prosecution based on a second or successive dishonor of a cheque is permissible and set aside the High Court's judgement. The Supreme Court restored the criminal complaint (CC No. 4029 of 2010) to the file of the Trial Court and directed the Trial Court to proceed with the matter in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court cited the cases of Sadanandan Bhadran v. Madhavan Sunil Kumar and MSR Leathers vs. S. Palaniappan and Another to support its ruling that successive dishonor of cheques allows for fresh statutory notices and complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Supreme Court allowed the respondents to make appropriate applications before the Trial Court for dispensing with their personal appearance, and directed the Trial Court to consider these applications in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court reinforced the principle that the holder of a cheque is entitled to present it multiple times within its validity period and can issue fresh statutory notices and initiate prosecutions based on each successive dishonor.

case_name: M/S. Surendra Trading Company vs. M/S. Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Limited & Ors.
text: Case: M/S. Surendra Trading Company vs. M/S. Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Limited & Ors.. Date: 19th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether the time limit of seven days prescribed in the proviso to sub-section (5) of Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, for removing defects in an application filed by the operational creditor, is mandatory or directory. The NCLAT held that the seven-day period for rectifying defects in an application filed under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, is mandatory. If defects are not removed within this period, the application is liable to be rejected. The Supreme Court ruled that the seven-day period for removing defects in an application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, is directory, not mandatory. The Court emphasized that while applicants should remove defects promptly, they should be given the opportunity to explain delays and not face automatic rejection. Surendra Trading Company, a jute trader, supplied raw jute to Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Limited between 2001 and 2003, for which the corporate debtor owed Rs. 17,06,766.95. The debtor acknowledged this debt in a certificate dated 24th October 2004 but did not pay due to ongoing proceedings under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 (SICA). After the repeal of SICA and enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the creditor sought resolution under the new Code. The Supreme Court reasoned that making the seven-day period mandatory would not serve any practical purpose and could lead to unjust outcomes. The Court highlighted that the intention of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, is to facilitate timely resolution of insolvency cases. However, rigid adherence to the seven-day period could result in meritorious cases being dismissed on technical grounds. Therefore, the Court held that the period should be treated as directory, allowing adjudicating authorities to accept applications if valid reasons for delays are provided.

case_name: M/S. VIJAY INDUSTRIES vs. COMMISSIONER OF INCOME TAX
text: Case: M/S. VIJAY INDUSTRIES vs. COMMISSIONER OF INCOME TAX. Date: 1st March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue addressed was the interpretation of Section 80HH of the Income Tax Act, 1961, particularly whether the deduction is to be computed from 'income' as calculated under the Act or from 'profits and gains' without deducting 'depreciation' and 'investment allowance'. The assessment years involved were 1979-80 and 1980-81. The Income Tax Department's position was that the 20% deduction should be computed after taking into account depreciation, unabsorbed depreciation, and investment allowance. The Supreme Court distinguished between 'profits and gains' and 'income', stating that 'profits and gains' is a broader concept and does not include deductions like depreciation and investment allowance, unlike 'income'. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, overruling the judgment in Motilal Pesticides case, and held that the deduction under Section 80HH should be computed from the 'profits and gains' without considering depreciation and investment allowance.

case_name: M/s Bangalore Club vs. Commissioner of Wealth Tax & Anr.
text: Case: M/s Bangalore Club vs. Commissioner of Wealth Tax & Anr.. Date: 8th September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether M/s Bangalore Club, a social club, was liable to pay wealth tax under Section 21AA of the Wealth Tax Act for the assessment years 1981-82 and 1984-85 to 1990-91. The assessing officer argued that the members of M/s Bangalore Club had rights to its assets, and since the members' shares were indeterminate and the club was not registered as a society or trust, it was liable to pay wealth tax under Section 21AA. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of M/s Bangalore Club, stating that the principle of mutuality applied and that Section 21AA did not apply to the club as it was a social institution. The High Court upheld the tax liability of M/s Bangalore Club, relying on the case of CWT vs. Chikmagalur Club, which ruled that such clubs were liable to wealth tax under Section 21AA. The Supreme Court's judgment clarifies that social clubs without a business or profit-making objective are not liable under Section 21AA, setting a precedent for similar cases.

case_name: M/s Darvell Investment and Leasing (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Others vs The State of West Bengal and Others
text: Case: M/s Darvell Investment and Leasing (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Others vs The State of West Bengal and Others. Date: 8th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was the cancellation of the caste certificate issued to respondent No. 15 and its implications on the sale of land by the respondent's father. The Division Bench of the High Court upheld the order of the Single Judge, which supported the cancellation of the caste certificate issued to respondent No. 15. The certificate was controversial because respondent No. 15's father, who sold land as a general category individual, never claimed to be from a Scheduled Tribe during his lifetime, and respondent No. 15 had sworn affidavits in 2000 claiming to be of general category. The appellants filed an application for the cancellation of the caste certificate issued to respondent No. 15 on 29th March 2012, which was subsequently cancelled by the SDO, Siliguri, on 6th July 2012. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, stating that the appeal should not be sent back to any authority as the facts clearly indicated that respondent No. 15 did not belong to a Scheduled Tribe. The Supreme Court clarified that respondent No. 15's father, who was employed as a driver by the Corporation, was recorded as a general category individual and had never claimed Scheduled Tribe status. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's judgment, concluding that it would be futile to remit the matter back to any authority as there was no merit in the respondent's claim. This decision may ensure stricter scrutiny and validation of caste certificates and reinforce the importance of accurate records and claims regarding caste status in land sales and other legal matters. Individuals should ensure they provide substantial evidence and documentation to support their claims regarding caste status, and be aware that false claims can lead to serious legal consequences and cancellation of certificates. The Supreme Court noted that respondent No. 15 had sworn affidavits in 2000 stating he belonged to the general category, which contradicted his claim of belonging to a Scheduled Tribe and supported the cancellation of his caste certificate. It is likely that authorities will enforce stricter regulations and verification processes for issuing caste certificates to prevent fraudulent claims and ensure compliance with legal standards.

case_name: M/s Gimpex Private Limited vs. Manoj Goel
text: Case: M/s Gimpex Private Limited vs. Manoj Goel. Date: 8th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether parallel prosecutions under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act) for dishonour of cheques could be sustained, specifically in relation to cheques issued before and after a settlement agreement. The dispute arose after ACL issued 18 cheques to Gimpex for part payment of an outstanding liability, which were dishonoured upon presentation, leading to legal notices and complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act. The initial complaints were pending when a settlement agreement was reached. However, the cheques issued pursuant to the settlement agreement were also dishonoured, leading to a second set of complaints. The settlement agreement required ACL to pay Rs. 3 crores immediately and the remaining Rs. 7 crores in three monthly instalments. Post-dated cheques were issued for these payments, and any default would allow Gimpex to file fresh complaints under the NI Act. The High Court quashed the second set of complaints, stating that the cheques issued pursuant to the settlement agreement were not issued for any liability and that the validity of the compromise deed was under challenge in a pending suit. The Supreme Court ruled that parallel prosecutions cannot be sustained and that once a settlement agreement has been entered into, the original complaints must be quashed, and any non-compliance of the settlement gives rise to a fresh cause of action. The Supreme Court emphasized that under Section 139 of the NI Act, there is a presumption that a cheque is issued for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability, which can only be rebutted by the accused during the trial. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order quashing the second set of complaints and quashed the first set of complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act. The trial was to proceed based on the second set of complaints arising from the settlement agreement. The Supreme Court stated that the mere pendency of a suit challenging the validity of the compromise deed did not justify quashing the criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act, as the deed remains valid until set aside by a competent court. case_name: M/s Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Maharashtra and others
text: Case: M/s Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Maharashtra and others. Date: 13th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves M/s Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. filing a complaint against the State of Maharashtra and others regarding forgery and fraudulent sale of the Naziribagh Palace property. The main allegations were forgery and fabrication of a Board Resolution and fraudulent sale of the Naziribagh Palace property to M/s Irish Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. The High Court passed an interim order stating 'no coercive measures shall be adopted' against the original accused concerning the FIR filed. The Sessions Court granted interim protection from arrest to the accused, which was extended multiple times over nearly a year. The appellant argued that the interim protection order restrained the investigating officer from taking necessary coercive measures, thus hampering the investigation. Sections 406, 420, 465, 468, 471, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code were invoked in the FIR. The Supreme Court was critical of the High Court's interim order, suggesting it was not warranted given the nature of the allegations and ongoing investigation. The Supreme Court emphasized that police have a statutory right to investigate cognizable offences without judicial interference unless exceptional circumstances justify such interference. The Supreme Court stated that the inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly and only in the rarest of cases to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice. M/s Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. was concerned that the High Court's order would prevent the proper investigation of serious charges of forgery and fraud against the accused. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's interim order, allowing the investigation to proceed without the restriction of 'no coercive measures' against the accused.

case_name: M/s Peacock Industries Ltd. vs. Union of India and Ors.
text: Case: M/s Peacock Industries Ltd. vs. Union of India and Ors.. Date: 5th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether M/s Peacock Industries Ltd. was entitled to a refund of the excise duty for goods returned by its distributors under Section 173-L of the Central Excise Act, based on the value of the returned goods. The appellant argued that the value of the returned goods should be considered after accounting for their market value as second-hand goods or, alternatively, as raw material for reuse in manufacturing. The Deputy Commissioner valued the returned goods at Rs. 8 to 10 per kg, treating them as scrap, and determined that the value was less than the amount of duty originally paid, thereby denying the refund. The High Court rejected the appellant's challenge, observing that the value determined by the Department was based on appreciation of evidence and the market survey report, and upheld the Deputy Commissioner's decision. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant neither requested a copy of the market survey report nor raised the issue of non-supply during the proceedings before the Tribunal. Therefore, it was not open for the appellant to raise this issue for the first time before the High Court. The Supreme Court interpreted that for the purpose of refund under Section 173-L, the value of the returned goods should be considered as their market value at the time of return, and not the value of the raw material or ex-duty value. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the concurrent findings of the adjudicating authority, the Tribunal, and the High Court that the appellant was not entitled to a refund of the excise duty paid on the returned goods.

case_name: M/s Radha Krishan Industries vs. State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: M/s Radha Krishan Industries vs. State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 20th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the orders of provisional attachment issued by the third respondent against the appellant on 28 October 2020 were in consonance with the conditions stipulated in Section 83 of the Himachal Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (HPGST Act). The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that an alternative remedy was available to the appellant under Section 107 of the HPGST Act. The provisional attachment orders issued on 28 October 2020 by the Joint Commissioner of State Taxes and Excise, Parwanoo, attached the appellant's receivables from its customers, invoking Section 83 of the HPGST Act and Rule 159 of the HPGST Rules. M/s Radha Krishan Industries claimed that the provisional attachment orders violated the procedure established under sub-rule (5) of Rule 159 of the HPGST Rules, which mandates an opportunity of being heard against the provisional attachment. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should not have dismissed the writ petition on the grounds of maintainability, noting that the existence of an alternative remedy does not divest the High Court of its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court concluded that the formation of opinion by the Commissioner under Section 83 of the HPGST Act must be based on tangible material indicating the necessity to protect the interest of the government revenue. Rule 159 prescribes the modalities for effecting a provisional attachment of property, including providing an opportunity for the person whose property is attached to file an objection within seven days and to be heard. The Supreme Court set aside the provisional attachment orders issued against M/s Radha Krishan Industries, holding that the orders did not meet the statutory requirements under Section 83 of the HPGST Act and Rule 159 of the HPGST Rules.

case_name: M/s Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. vs. Commissioner Commercial Taxes & Ors.
text: Case: M/s Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. vs. Commissioner Commercial Taxes & Ors.. Date: 10th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the classification of various products like Mosquito Mats, Coils, Vaporizers, Mortein Insect Killers, Harpic Toilet Cleaner, Lizol Floor Cleaners, and Dettol Antiseptic Liquid under the Kerala VAT Act, 2003 for tax purposes. M/s Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. argued that Mosquito Mats, Coils, Vaporizers, Mortein Insect Killers, Harpic Toilet Cleaner, and Lizol Floor Cleaners should be classified under Entry No. 44(5) of the III Schedule to the Kerala VAT Act as 'pesticides, insecticides' corresponding to HSN Code 3808. The Commissioner of Commercial Taxes classified Mosquito Mats, Coils, and Vaporizers under Entry 66 of Notification SRO 82/06 as 'Mosquito Repellents,' Mortein Insect Killer under the residuary entry with a tax rate of 12.5%, Harpic Toilet Cleaner and Lizol Floor Cleaner under SI No. 27(4) of Notification SRO 82/06, and Dettol Antiseptic Liquid under the residual entry, not as a medicament. The High Court of Kerala dismissed the appeal by M/s Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd., confirming the order passed by the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes regarding the classification of the products. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision regarding Dettol Antiseptic Liquid and held that it would fall under Entry 36(8)(h)(vi) of Schedule III of the Kerala VAT Act as a drug/medicine, liable to be taxed at 4%. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal by M/s Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. It confirmed the classification and tax rates for Mosquito Mats, Coils, Vaporizers, Mortein Insect Killers, Harpic Toilet Cleaner, and Lizol Floor Cleaners as decided by the High Court. However, it ruled that Dettol Antiseptic Liquid should be classified as a drug/medicine under Entry 36(8)(h)(vi) of Schedule III of the Kerala VAT Act and taxed at 4%.

case_name: M/s TRL Krosaki Refractories Ltd. vs. M/s SMS Asia Private Limited & Anr.
text: Case: M/s TRL Krosaki Refractories Ltd. vs. M/s SMS Asia Private Limited & Anr.. Date: 22nd February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the complaint filed by M/s TRL Krosaki Refractories Ltd. under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was valid, considering the authorization and knowledge of the complainant's representative. M/s SMS Asia Private Limited was charged under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for issuing cheques that were dishonoured due to the account being closed. The cheques issued by M/s SMS Asia Private Limited were dishonoured because the account was closed. The respondents argued that the complaint was filed by an incompetent person without the requisite averments, and the complainant's representative did not have knowledge of the transaction. The Supreme Court found that Mr. Subhasis Kumar Das was duly authorized by the Managing Director, who had the power delegated by the Board of Directors, and he had knowledge of the transaction. The prosecution presented the dishonoured cheques, the agreement between the parties, the reconciliation statement, and the notices issued to the respondents. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement quashing the complaint, and restored the complaint for further proceedings. The Supreme Court directed the case to be listed for further proceedings on 15th March 2022 and to be concluded within six months. The respondents were directed to appear before the learned Magistrate on the specified date without expecting fresh summons and to proceed with the trial expeditiously. The Supreme Court imposed costs of Rs. 1,00,000 (Rupees one lakh only) on the respondents, payable to the appellant.

case_name: M/s Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: M/s Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 25th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge to the validity of Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, by M/s Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd., claiming it to be discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the writ petition without deciding the validity of Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income Tax Act, stating that the matter was still sub judice before the Income Tax Authority. The Supreme Court opined that the High Court's decision to dismiss the writ petition without deciding the validity of Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income Tax Act was not sustainable. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should have decided the issue on merits. The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the High Court to decide the writ petition on merits with respect to the challenge to the vires of Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income Tax Act. M/s Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd. argued that the amount deductible in computing income chargeable under the Income Tax Act was not being allowed under Section 40(a)(iib), and this provision was discriminatory as it did not apply to many Central Government undertakings enjoying exemptions. The appellant, M/s Tamil Nadu State Marketing Corporation Ltd., was represented by Senior Advocate Mr. Rakesh Dwivedi, while the respondents, including the Union of India, were represented by Additional Solicitor General Mr. K.M. Natraj. The challenge to Section 40(a)(iib) of the Income Tax Act was based on Articles 14, 19, and 265 of the Constitution of India, which pertain to the right to equality, protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc., and no tax to be levied or collected except by authority of law, respectively.

case_name: M/s Texco Marketing Pvt. Ltd. v. TATA AIG General Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: M/s Texco Marketing Pvt. Ltd. v. TATA AIG General Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 9th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether TATA AIG could rely on the exclusion clause in the insurance policy to deny the claim for a shop situated in the basement, which was destroyed by fire. M/s Texco Marketing Pvt. Ltd. secured a Standard Fire & Special Perils policy from TATA AIG effective from 28th July 2012 to 27th July 2013, meant to cover a shop situated in the basement of a building. TATA AIG denied the claim based on the exclusion clause in the policy, which stated that it did not cover the basement. The State Commission found TATA AIG deficient in service, rejected the insurer's contention, and held that there was no adequate disclosure of the exclusion clause, constituting an unfair trade practice. The National Commission overturned the State Commission's decision, despite acknowledging the insurer's non-compliance with the law, and relied on the exclusion clause to grant a reduced sum of Rs.7.5 lakhs. The Supreme Court ruled that an exclusion clause that destroys the very contract knowingly entered cannot be used by the insurer to avoid liability, especially when the insurer had knowledge of the shop's basement location at the time of contract execution. The Supreme Court applied the principle that exclusion clauses in insurance contracts must be interpreted in the light of the main purpose of the contract and cannot be used to deny claims if the insurer had prior knowledge of the facts leading to the claim. The Supreme Court emphasized that insurers have a duty of utmost good faith, requiring full disclosure and notice of all material facts, and any failure in this duty, especially concerning exclusion clauses, would render such clauses non-enforceable. The judgment sets a precedent that insurers cannot rely on exclusion clauses to deny claims if they had prior knowledge of the circumstances leading to the claim, thereby protecting consumers from unfair trade practices. TATA AIG should ensure full disclosure of all exclusion clauses to policyholders, adhere strictly to IRDA regulations, and provide clear and comprehensive information to avoid future disputes and liability issues. The Supreme Court viewed 'adhesion contracts,' like insurance policies, as standard-form contracts that must be interpreted in favor of the consumer, emphasizing fairness and good faith in their execution and enforcement.

case_name: M/s Thermax Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune-1
text: Case: M/s Thermax Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune-1. Date: 13th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the product manufactured by M/s Thermax Ltd. was classifiable as a heat pump under the heading 84.18 of the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, which would entitle it to a limited exemption from the levy of excise duty. M/s Thermax Ltd. manufactured Modified Vapour Absorption Chillers (MVAC) and described them as heat pumps, which were capable of providing both chilled and hot water as output. The CESTAT concluded that the product was not a heat pump and therefore ineligible for the concessional rate of duty under Sl. No. 2 of Notification No. 155/86-CE dated 1.3.1986. The product was declared a complete machine, not part of a machine, and the value of Lithium Bromide was not to be included in the assessable value of the machine. M/s Thermax Ltd. argued that their MVAC product, capable of producing both chilled and hot water, should be classified as a heat pump. They relied on the Harmonious System of Nomenclature (HSN) Explanatory Notes and industry-related decisions in similar cases involving Blue Star Ltd. and Voltas Ltd. The Supreme Court concluded that MVAC did not satisfy the definition of a heat pump under the HSN, as its primary purpose was to produce chilled water, and the production of hot water was incidental. Thus, MVAC was not classified as a heat pump but as a refrigerating equipment under Sub-heading 8418.10 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. The market parlance test indicated that the product was recognized and purchased as a vapour absorption chiller used for air conditioning and refrigeration, not as a heat pump. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant's website separately identified vapour absorption chillers and heat pumps, reinforcing this distinction. The Supreme Court found that the previous decisions regarding Blue Star Ltd. and Voltas Ltd. were not directly applicable, as they dealt with different issues and classifications. The classification dispute in this case was resolved based on the specific facts and definitions applicable to MVAC.

case_name: M/s Treaty Construction & Anr. vs. M/s Ruby Tower Co-op. Hsg. Society Ltd.
text: Case: M/s Treaty Construction & Anr. vs. M/s Ruby Tower Co-op. Hsg. Society Ltd.. Date: 19th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the deficiency of services by the appellants, including incomplete interior works, failure to obtain Completion and Occupancy Certificates, and illegal collection of charges from the members of the respondent-society. The State Commission directed the appellants to execute the Deed of Conveyance by obtaining Completion and Occupancy Certificates within 90 days, pay Rs. 26,25,000 with interest to the respondent-society, and imposed a penalty of Rs. 1,000 per day for non-compliance. The National Commission modified the order by directing the appellants to pay Rs. 28,00,000 to the respondent-society, upheld the cost of Rs. 50,000, and imposed a lump sum compensation of Rs. 3,00,000 for not obtaining the Occupancy Certificate. The Supreme Court upheld the National Commission's direction for the appellants to pay Rs. 25,00,000 to the respondent-society, as agreed by the appellants in a meeting held on 17th December 2003. No, the Supreme Court set aside the compensation of Rs. 3,00,000 imposed by the National Commission for not obtaining the Occupancy Certificate. text: Case: M/s Writers and Publishers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Dr. A.K. Mishra, Official Liquidator The Cooperative Stores Ltd. Super Bazar. Date: 17th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether M/s Writers and Publishers Pvt. Ltd. (WPL) should be refunded its investment with interest after the failed revival of Super Bazar, and how the assets and claims should be handled following the winding up of Super Bazar. Super Bazar was wound up due to poor management and rising wage bills, which led to significant financial losses, as identified in an inquiry under Section 78 of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002. The Supreme Court decided that WPL should be refunded its entire investment along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum, subject to the deduction of any profits earned during the period it managed Super Bazar. The CAG found that WPL had not fulfilled its commitment to infuse the necessary funds for the revival of Super Bazar and had engaged in questionable financial practices during its management. The Supreme Court held that WPL was entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the entire investment, including the share capital, as part of the overall investment for the revival of Super Bazar. The Supreme Court directed that the refund amount should be calculated by deducting the profits earned by WPL during its management of Super Bazar and that the process should be verified by the CAG. The Supreme Court disposed of the contempt petitions, directed all parties to comply with its interpretation of the earlier directions, and ensured that WPL's entire investment, including interest, would be refunded after adjusting for profits earned.

case_name: M/s. Cheminova India Ltd. & Anr. vs. State of Punjab & Anr.
text: Case: M/s. Cheminova India Ltd. & Anr. vs. State of Punjab & Anr.. Date: 4th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the complaint filed by the Insecticide Inspector against the appellants for misbranding under the Insecticides Act, 1968, was barred by limitation and whether the correct procedure was followed. On 10th February 2011, the Insecticide Inspector inspected the premises of M/s. Navneet Singh and found 60 tins of insecticide (Trizophos 40% E.C.). The samples tested contained 34.70% active ingredient against the labelled 40%, leading to allegations of misbranding. The appellants argued that the complaint was filed beyond the three-year limitation period, and the procedure under Section 24 of the Insecticides Act and Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not followed. The High Court dismissed the petition to quash the complaint for the appellants but allowed it for the Godown Incharge, leading to the appellants filing an appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the limitation period commenced on 14th March 2011, when the initial analysis report was received, and thus, the complaint filed on 25th March 2014 was barred by limitation. The Supreme Court quashed the proceedings against the Managing Director (Appellant No. 2) due to the lack of specific allegations and the presence of an undertaking assigning quality control responsibility to another officer. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part, setting aside the High Court's order regarding the Managing Director and quashing the complaint against him. However, the proceedings against the company were not quashed.

case_name: M/s. Indsil Hydro Power and Manganese Limited vs State of Kerala & Ors.
text: Case: M/s. Indsil Hydro Power and Manganese Limited vs State of Kerala & Ors.. Date: 6th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether M/s. Indsil Hydro Power was liable to pay royalty and charges for controlled water release used for generating electricity, under the terms of its agreement with the Kerala State Electricity Board. The relationship was governed by the INDSIL Agreement, which incorporated the terms of the Kerala Government's policy on hydroelectric projects, including provisions for paying royalty and charges for controlled water release. The Division Bench noted that CPPs like Indsil generate electricity primarily for self-consumption, whereas IPPs generate electricity for sale. This distinction justified different treatment regarding royalty charges. The Supreme Court determined that Indsil benefitted from controlled water releases from the Anayirankal reservoir, which supported smooth electricity generation, obligating it to pay charges as per its agreement. The court directed the Kerala government to reassess and determine royalty charges based on the quantity of water used and the controlled release for electricity generation, aligning with the policy's stipulated formula. The court rejected Indsil's claim of discrimination, holding that Captive Power Producers and Independent Power Producers were rightly treated differently due to their distinct operational objectives and benefits.

case_name: M/s. Indsil Hydro Power and Manganese Limited vs. State of Kerala & Ors.
text: Case: M/s. Indsil Hydro Power and Manganese Limited vs. State of Kerala & Ors.. Date: 6th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue was whether M/s. Indsil Hydro Power and Manganese Limited was liable to pay royalty for controlled release of water used for power generation, as mandated by the policy and agreement with the Kerala State Electricity Board. The relationship was governed by the INDSIL Agreement, which incorporated terms from the Kerala Government’s hydropower policy, including liability for royalties and controlled release charges. The High Court initially ruled that the royalty charges were discriminatory and lacked jurisdiction, quashing the demand order by the Kerala Government. The Division Bench held that the royalty charges were contractual obligations under the agreement, emphasizing the distinction between Captive Power Producers (CPPs) like INDSIL and Independent Power Producers (IPPs). The Supreme Court directed the Kerala Government to recalculate the royalty based on the actual quantity of water used and the formula provided in the policy, rather than on the quantum of energy generated. The Supreme Court emphasized that agreements incorporating policy terms are binding and parties cannot later dispute the agreed-upon obligations unless there is evidence of coercion or illegality. This judgment sets a precedent that CPPs may be subjected to similar royalty charges, provided the terms are explicitly stated in agreements and aligned with the government’s policies. The Supreme Court clarified that CPPs generate electricity for self-consumption, which justifies different regulatory and financial obligations compared to IPPs, which generate electricity for sale. Future challenges may involve disputes over the accuracy of water usage measurements and the application of policy formulas, requiring stricter regulatory frameworks. Hydropower producers should carefully review policy terms incorporated into agreements, ensuring clarity on royalty liabilities and calculation methods to avoid future disputes.
