case_name: M/s. National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. vs M/s. BSCPL Infrastructure Ltd.
text: Case: M/s. National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. vs M/s. BSCPL Infrastructure Ltd.. Date: 7th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case addressed whether an arbitration clause becomes enforceable upon acceptance of the Letter of Award (LOA) or only upon the signing of the final contract agreement. The Delhi High Court held that the arbitration clause contained in the draft agreement was enforceable based on general reference, and it appointed an arbitrator for dispute resolution. The Supreme Court held that the LOA was part of the bidding process and did not itself constitute a binding contract, as critical steps like the signing of the final agreement were pending. The Supreme Court ruled that the arbitration clause contained in the draft agreement was not enforceable as there was no concluded contract between the parties. The Court clarified that the LOA is a preliminary step in the bidding process and does not create enforceable rights or obligations unless followed by the signing of the final contract. The Supreme Court highlighted the need for parties to clearly define when arbitration clauses become binding to avoid similar disputes in the future.

case_name: M/s. Paramount Digital Color Lab & Ors. vs M/s. Agfa India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: M/s. Paramount Digital Color Lab & Ors. vs M/s. Agfa India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 15th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellants were considered 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and whether the respondents were liable for selling a defective photo processing machine to the appellants. The NCDRC dismissed the complaint filed by the appellants and allowed the appeal filed by the respondents, ruling that the appellants were not 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The appellants contended that the photo processing machine purchased from the respondents was defective and did not perform as promised, causing them financial loss. The SCDRC allowed the complaint in part, holding respondent Nos. 2 and 4 responsible for unfair trade practices and directed them to pay compensation to the appellants. The NCDRC based its decision on the finding that the appellants were not 'consumers' as defined under Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, because they were using the machine for commercial purposes. The Supreme Court of India interpreted that a person who buys goods for self-employment and livelihood falls under the definition of 'consumer', even if the goods are used for earning a livelihood. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants, being unemployed graduates who started a business for self-employment, were indeed 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. This judgement might encourage more self-employed individuals to seek redress under consumer protection laws, reinforcing the notion that self-employment and livelihood purposes fall within the definition of 'consumer'. Companies might become more cautious and transparent in their sales practices, ensuring that they provide accurate information about their products and address any defects promptly to avoid liability under consumer protection laws. The appellants claimed the machine was defective because it did not perform up to the promised standards, showing various technical, mechanical, and software problems, and did not provide satisfactory performance. The Supreme Court observed that if a person buys and uses the machine exclusively for earning a livelihood through self-employment, they fall within the definition of 'consumer' and emphasized that each case should be judged based on its specific facts and circumstances.

case_name: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
text: Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III. Date: 10th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether M/s. Saraf Exports was entitled to deductions under Section 80-IB of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for profits earned from Duty Drawback and DEPB (Duty Entitlement Pass Book) schemes. The High Court held that M/s. Saraf Exports was not entitled to the deductions under Section 80-IB for the profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes, based on the judgements of the Supreme Court in Liberty India and Sterling Foods. M/s. Saraf Exports argued that the profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes should be considered as profits derived from the business of the industrial undertaking and therefore eligible for deductions under Section 80-IB. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes are not eligible for deductions under Section 80-IB as they do not constitute profits derived from the industrial undertaking. The Supreme Court reiterated that for profits to be eligible for deductions under Section 80-IB, they must have a 'first degree nexus' with the industrial undertaking. Profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes were deemed to have an indirect nexus and thus not eligible. The Supreme Court distinguished that while Liberty India dealt with export incentives like DEPB and Duty Drawback, which have an indirect nexus with the industrial undertaking, Meghalaya Steels involved subsidies directly reducing the cost of manufacturing, thus having a direct nexus. The final outcome was that M/s. Saraf Exports was not entitled to claim deductions under Section 80-IB for the profits earned from the Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes, as per the Supreme Court's ruling.

text: Case: M/s. Shivali Enterprises vs Smt. Godawari (Deceased) Thr. LRS. and Others. Date: 13th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellant-plaintiff, M/s. Shivali Enterprises, could seek specific performance of the agreement(s) to sell dated 29th October 1983 and 23rd August 1985, despite the non-obtaining of the ITC Certificate and correction of revenue records by the respondents-defendants. The original agreement was for the sale of the suit property situated in the revenue estate of Chak Salarpur, Tehsil Dadri, District Ghaziabad (U.P.), at the rate of Rs. 2900/- per Bigha, with an earnest amount of Rs.50,000/- paid by the appellant-plaintiff. The execution of the sale deed was delayed due to a dispute between the States of U.P. and Haryana, resulting in the property becoming part of Haryana and requiring additional formalities, including obtaining an ITC Certificate and correcting the revenue records. The trial court and the Appellate Court found in favor of the appellant-plaintiff, decreeing the suit for specific performance and recognizing the plaintiff's continuous possession of the suit property since the execution of the agreement(s) to sell. The High Court reversed the decisions on the grounds that the suit for specific performance was premature as the respondents-defendants had not yet obtained the ITC Certificate or corrected the revenue records, and directed that the sale deed be executed at the present prevalent market value. The Supreme Court found fault with the High Court's decision for interfering with the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts, which had found that the appellant-plaintiff was justified in filing the suit due to the respondents-defendants' threats to alienate the property. The respondents-defendants failed to obtain the ITC Certificate and correct the revenue records to reflect their ownership, which were required steps before the execution and registration of the sale deed as per the agreement(s) to sell. The appellant-plaintiff provided evidence of earnest money payments, agreements to sell, and the fact that they were in continuous possession of the suit property since the execution of the agreements, and had made significant improvements to the property. The decision could reinforce the principle that courts should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless there is clear evidence of perversity or error in the application of the law, thus upholding the integrity of the judicial process in similar cases. Parties should ensure that all necessary certificates and corrections to revenue records are obtained in a timely manner, maintain clear documentation of all transactions, and be prepared to take legal action if the other party threatens to breach the agreement. The Supreme Court emphasized this to ensure that a comprehensive evaluation of all available evidence is conducted, maintaining fairness and accuracy in judicial decisions, and preventing the unjust dismissal of legitimate claims based on incomplete assessments.

case_name: M/s. Standard Essential Oil Industries & Anr. vs. Forest Range Officer Kasargod & Ors.
text: Case: M/s. Standard Essential Oil Industries & Anr. vs. Forest Range Officer Kasargod & Ors.. Date: 19th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the confiscation of 125 kgs of sandalwood oil by the Divisional Forest Officer under Section 61A of the Kerala Forest Act was valid. On 16th April 1993, the Kasargod Police conducted a search at 'Rahmith Manzil' and seized 125 kgs of sandalwood oil, which was subsequently reported to the Superintendent, Central Excise, Kasargod, and led to a show cause notice for confiscation under the Kerala Forest Act. The appellants contended that the seized sandalwood oil was accounted stock, with 75 kgs manufactured at their factory and 50 kgs purchased from M/s Punjab Aromatic. They argued that the oil was temporarily stored at the managing partner's residence due to maintenance work at the factory. The High Court of Kerala upheld the order of confiscation, dismissing the appeal filed by the appellants and confirming the order of the single judge. The Supreme Court found that the High Court misdirected itself by framing the issue as related to Section 61A, whereas the confiscation was made under Section 69 of the Act. The Supreme Court held that Section 69 does not give the power of confiscation and is only a rule of evidence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order upholding the confiscation, ruling that the confiscation of sandalwood oil under Section 61A was not valid. The appeal by M/s. Standard Essential Oil Industries was allowed, and the order of confiscation was quashed.

case_name: M/s. Supertech Ltd. vs Rajni Goyal
text: Case: M/s. Supertech Ltd. vs Rajni Goyal. Date: 23rd October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the delay in handing over possession of a flat in the 'Capetown' project, leading to a dispute over compensation and charges demanded by the builder. The scheduled date for possession of the flat was October 2013, with a grace period of six months. Rajni Goyal filed a complaint due to the delay in possession and contested the charges demanded in the Pre-Possession Letter, claiming the builder had not obtained the Occupancy Certificate. The Commission directed the builder to pay compensation in the form of simple interest at 8% per annum from 1st November 2013 until the actual possession date. The builder argued that the delay was due to legal impediments, including orders from the National Green Tribunal, and requested the compensation period to be limited to May 2014 to April 2016. The Supreme Court modified the compensation period to be calculated from May 2014 to April 2016 at the rate determined by the Commission.

case_name: MD. ANOWAR HUSSAIN vs. STATE OF ASSAM
text: Case: MD. ANOWAR HUSSAIN vs. STATE OF ASSAM. Date: 13th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the accused, MD. Anowar Hussain, committed the murder of his 20-year-old wife, Samina Khatun, by inflicting grievous injuries and causing her death by throttling. The cause of death of the victim, Samina Khatun, was asphyxia due to throttling, which was ante-mortem and homicidal in nature. The private witnesses, PW-1 to PW-6, did not support the prosecution and suggested that the victim died in a hospital due to illness. However, their testimony was disbelieved by the Trial Court. The defense presented by MD. Anowar Hussain was that his wife died in a hospital due to illness, and he was arrested while going to get medicines for himself. The Trial Court concluded that the defense was false and that the accused was guilty based on the chain of circumstances proving his guilt. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and life imprisonment sentence of MD. Anowar Hussain. The post-mortem report was significant as it established that the cause of death was asphyxia due to throttling, which contradicted the defense's claim of death due to illness. The appellant claimed he was arrested at Borabara while getting medicines, but this was found to be false. The location of arrest and the absence of medicines supported the prosecution's case. The Investigating Officer (IO), PW-7 Anowar Hussain, provided crucial testimony that helped establish the chain of circumstances leading to the accused's conviction. The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim because the inquest report and other evidence established that the victim's death occurred at home due to throttling, not at a hospital. Given the Supreme Court's dismissal and the strong chain of circumstantial evidence, it is unlikely that future appeals would overturn the appellant's conviction.

case_name: Madan Mohan Mahto & Jagmohan Mahto vs. State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Madan Mohan Mahto & Jagmohan Mahto vs. State of Jharkhand. Date: 7th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the convictions of Madan Mohan Mahto and Jagmohan Mahto under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of Jitu Mahto were justified based on the evidence presented. Madan Mohan Mahto and Jagmohan Mahto were charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of Jitu Mahto. The prosecution alleged that the motive behind the crime was a rivalry between the parties over a land dispute. Madan Mohan Mahto fired three gunshots at the victims, causing them to flee from the field, except for Jitu Mahto who was surrounded and attacked. Jagmohan Mahto cut Jitu Mahto's right palm with a Tangi (a type of axe), contributing to the fatal injuries that led to Jitu Mahto's death. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimonies from Kuila Mahto (PW-2) and Jagran Mahto (PW-1), as well as the post-mortem report confirming the cause of death. The Supreme Court found the testimonies of the eyewitnesses to be consistent and credible, with no material contradictions, supporting the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the convictions and life sentences of Madan Mohan Mahto and Jagmohan Mahto under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. Madan Mohan Mahto and Jagmohan Mahto were sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The Supreme Court concluded that a case of common intention under Section 34 IPC was fully made out, as the accused acted together with the intention to attack the victims, leading to the murder of Jitu Mahto.

case_name: Madan vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Madan vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 9th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Madan, along with other accused, was accused of committing the murder of six persons on account of political rivalry. The FIR was lodged after an incident on 14th October 2003, where Madan and others allegedly fired indiscriminately at Lokendra and his group, resulting in multiple deaths. The motive behind the murders was political rivalry arising from the election of Vimla Devi as Gram Pradhan, supported by Lokendra, which caused enmity with Madan and his family. The main witnesses were Lokendra (PW-1), Irshad Khan (PW-7), Harpal Singh (PW-10), and Sudhir (PW-11). The trial court convicted Madan and other accused under various sections of the IPC, imposing capital punishment on Madan and life imprisonment on others. The High Court dismissed the appeals of Madan and Ishwar, confirming their convictions and sentences, while commuting Sudesh Pal's capital punishment to life imprisonment. The defense argued that the conviction was based on unreliable testimonies, inconsistencies in witness statements, and a lack of independent witnesses supporting the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court considered the consistency and reliability of the eyewitness testimonies, the motive, and the nature of the crime, despite the defense highlighting investigative lapses. The Supreme Court upheld the death penalty for Madan, considering the crime to be of an exceptionally depraved and heinous character, constituting a grave danger to society. The court did not find any mitigating circumstances sufficient to alter the sentence for Madan, noting his criminal history and the brutality of the crime.

case_name: Madhav Prasad Aggarwal & Anr. vs Axis Bank Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: Madhav Prasad Aggarwal & Anr. vs Axis Bank Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The issue was whether the rejection of a plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of CPC could be limited to only one of the defendants, specifically Axis Bank Ltd., without rejecting the entire plaint. The Supreme Court held that the High Court committed a jurisdictional error by allowing the rejection of the plaint against Axis Bank Ltd. alone, as Order 7 Rule 11(d) of CPC mandates rejection of the plaint as a whole or not at all. This judgment clarifies that applications under Order 7 Rule 11(d) must address the entire plaint, preventing piecemeal rejection and ensuring adherence to procedural rules. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, restored the Single Judge's decision dismissing Axis Bank's motion, and emphasized the indivisibility of plaint rejection under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of CPC.

case_name: Madhavi vs Chagan & Ors.
text: Case: Madhavi vs Chagan & Ors.. Date: 9th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the determination of seniority and rightful promotion to the position of Head Master at Shri Samarth Shikshan Sanstha, contested between Madhavi and Chagan based on their qualifications and dates of appointment. Chagan claimed seniority over Madhavi by arguing that he was appointed on a regular basis on 1st August 1985, while Madhavi was appointed on a temporary basis on 16th July 1985, contending that he was thus entitled to be promoted as Head Master. The School Tribunal dismissed Chagan's appeal, holding that Madhavi, who had the qualifications of B.Sc. and B.Ed. at the time of her appointment, was senior to Chagan, who only acquired the necessary qualifications later. At the time of her initial appointment, Madhavi held a B.Sc. and B.Ed. degree, while Chagan had a Senior Secondary Certificate and a Diploma in Education. The High Court initially dismissed Chagan's writ petition but later allowed his review application, setting aside the School Tribunal's order and granting him seniority over Madhavi. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's review order, reinstating the School Tribunal's decision that Madhavi was senior to Chagan based on her qualifications at the time of appointment. The Supreme Court clarified that the seniority rules for primary and secondary schools are different, and in this case, Madhavi was rightly placed in Category 'C' from the date of her appointment, while Chagan was only upgraded to Category 'C' after acquiring his B.Ed. degree in 1999. This judgment reinforces the importance of qualifications at the time of appointment for determining seniority and may influence future disputes in educational institutions, ensuring that initial qualifications are given due consideration. If educational institutions do not adhere to the clarified seniority rules, it could lead to further legal disputes, challenges to administrative decisions, and potential reversals of appointments and promotions. This judgment might prompt private educational institutions to review and possibly revise their appointment and promotion policies to ensure compliance with the legal standards for qualifications and seniority, thus avoiding similar disputes. Teachers should ensure they have the required qualifications at the time of their appointment, as initial qualifications are crucial for determining seniority and future promotion opportunities, as emphasized in this judgment.

case_name: Madhusudan Bhanuprasad Pandya vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: Case: Madhusudan Bhanuprasad Pandya vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.. Date: 1st August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the land declared as excess vacant land under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, should vest in the State or whether the proceedings should abate following the repeal of the Act in 1999. The appellant argued that possession of the excess land was not actually taken by the State despite the panchnama and that the proceedings should abate due to the repeal of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition challenging the declaration of excess land, and the Division Bench affirmed this decision, holding that the land had vested in the State and the possession was validly taken. The Supreme Court found that the possession of the land was validly taken by the State on 24th July 1990, and the proceedings under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, did not abate upon the repeal of the Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the application for exemption under Section 20 was rightly rejected by the State since the land had already vested in the State, and the exemption could not be granted post facto. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the decisions of the Single Judge and the Division Bench of the High Court, affirming that the land had vested in the State and the possession was validly taken.

case_name: Mahabir Industries vs. Principal Commissioner of Income Tax
text: Case: Mahabir Industries vs. Principal Commissioner of Income Tax. Date: 18th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Mahabir Industries was entitled to claim deductions under Section 80-IC of the Income Tax Act for the Assessment Years 2008-09 and 2009-10, beyond the ten-year period allowed under Section 80-IA and Section 80-IB. Section 80-IA provided for deductions in respect of profits and gains from industrial undertakings or enterprises engaged in infrastructure development, subject to certain conditions, for a period of ten consecutive Assessment Years. Mahabir Industries claimed deductions under Section 80-IC after completing substantial expansion of its manufacturing unit in Himachal Pradesh, which qualified it for 100% deductions under the new provision aimed at promoting industrial growth in certain states. The Principal Commissioner of Income Tax argued that the total period for claiming deductions under Section 80-IA and Section 80-IC combined should not exceed ten years, as stipulated by Section 80-IC(6) of the Income Tax Act. The High Court decided that the ten-year period for claiming deductions should start from the first year the deductions were claimed under Section 80-IA, thus denying deductions for the years 2008-09 and 2009-10. The Supreme Court ruled that the ten-year cap under Section 80-IC(6) should not include the years for which deductions were claimed under Section 80-IA, as this provision applied specifically to industries in the North-Eastern Region, which was not the case for Mahabir Industries. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and allowed Mahabir Industries to claim deductions under Section 80-IC for the Assessment Years 2008-09 and 2009-10, recognizing the substantial expansion completed in the Assessment Year 2006-07.

case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. vs. M/s. JSW Steel Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. vs. M/s. JSW Steel Limited & Ors.. Date: 10th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the group of 'captive consumers' are liable to pay additional surcharge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003. The State Commission decided that the additional surcharge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003 is leviable on captive consumers/captive users. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity set aside the State Commission's order and held that the group of captive consumers are not liable to pay additional surcharge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003. Section 9 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that captive generation and use are permitted and do not require permission from the State Commission, thus not subjecting captive users to additional surcharge under Section 42(4). The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 42(4) is applicable only when the State Commission permits consumers to receive electricity from sources other than their distribution licensee, which does not apply to captive consumers who have statutory rights under Section 9. The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Appellate Tribunal, ruling that captive consumers are not liable to pay the additional surcharge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003. The Supreme Court directed that the additional surcharge already recovered from captive consumers should be adjusted in their future wheeling charges bills.

Section 9 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that captive generation and use are permitted and do not require permission from the State Commission, thus not subjecting captive users to additional surcharge under Section 42(4).

The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 42(4) is applicable only when the State Commission permits consumers to receive electricity from sources other than their distribution licensee, which does not apply to captive consumers who have statutory rights under Section 9.
The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Appellate Tribunal, ruling that captive consumers are not liable to pay the additional surcharge under Section 42(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
The Supreme Court directed that the additional surcharge already recovered from captive consumers should be adjusted in their future wheeling charges bills.

case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. vs. The Appellate Authority & Anr.
text: Case: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. vs. The Appellate Authority & Anr.. Date: 15th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (the Board) could levy charges under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 for unauthorized use of electricity detected during an inspection of the respondent's factory. The Board issued a provisional assessment bill after an inspection on 02.08.2003 revealed tampering with the meter seals at the respondent's factory, leading to a revised provisional bill for Rs. 21,38,660/-. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the Board and partly allowed the writ petitions filed by the consumers, setting aside the Appellate Order and remanding the case to the Assessing Authority to follow the provisions of Sections 126 and 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The Supreme Court held that the Electricity Act, 2003 applied to this case as the inspection and the resulting cause of action occurred after the Act came into force on 10.06.2003. The Supreme Court ruled that the respondent had the right to appeal under Section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003 against the provisional/final assessment order made by the Board under Section 126. The Supreme Court directed the authorities to comply with the High Court's directions and pass a consequential order under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 in accordance with the law within three months from the date of the judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Board, upholding the High Court's judgment and directing the authorities to proceed as per the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003.

case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited vs. Ratnagiri Gas and Power Private Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited vs. Ratnagiri Gas and Power Private Limited & Ors.. Date: 9th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether MSEDCL was liable to pay fixed charges to RGPPL for the declared capacity based on RLNG, despite not having given prior consent as required under the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). MSEDCL contended that it was not liable to pay the fixed charges since RGPPL had declared capacity based on RLNG without obtaining MSEDCL's prior consent, as required under Clause 5.9 of the PPA. Both CERC and APTEL held that MSEDCL was liable to pay the fixed charges to RGPPL for the declared capacity based on RLNG, stating that Clause 5.9 did not require prior approval for using RLNG, as it is a primary fuel under Clause 4.3 of the PPA. The Supreme Court agreed with CERC and APTEL, stating that Clause 4.3 permits the use of RLNG as a primary fuel without requiring prior consent from MSEDCL, and that the requirement for consent under Clause 5.9 applies to liquid fuels and not RLNG. The Supreme Court concluded that MSEDCL was liable to pay the fixed charges for the declared capacity based on RLNG, as RGPPL's actions were in accordance with the terms of the PPA. The Supreme Court directed that the execution proceedings pursuant to the execution petition before APTEL should continue. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by MSEDCL, upholding the decisions of CERC and APTEL, and confirmed MSEDCL's liability to pay the fixed charges based on RGPPL's declared capacity using RLNG.

case_name: Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation vs Dilip Uttam Jayabhay
text: Case: Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation vs Dilip Uttam Jayabhay. Date: 3rd January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the punishment of dismissal for the respondent-driver due to an accident causing multiple fatalities was disproportionate and constituted an unfair labour practice under the MRTU & PULP Act, 1971. The Industrial Court set aside the dismissal order, considering it disproportionate to the misconduct proved, and ordered reinstatement without back wages but with continuity of service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and directed the MSRTC to pay back wages to the respondent from 1st November 2003 to 31st May 2018, in addition to confirming the Industrial Court's order of reinstatement with continuity of service. The Supreme Court noted that the acquittal in the criminal case did not impact the disciplinary proceedings, as the standards of proof in criminal and disciplinary proceedings are different. The Court emphasized that the Industrial Court erred in giving undue importance to the acquittal. The Supreme Court concluded that the dismissal was not disproportionate given the gravity of the misconduct, which involved a fatal accident due to the respondent's rash and negligent driving. The Court upheld the dismissal order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgments of the Industrial Court and the High Court, and restored the Labour Court's decision upholding the dismissal of the respondent from service.

case_name: Mahatma Gandhi University and Ors. vs. Rincymol Mathew
text: Case: Mahatma Gandhi University and Ors. vs. Rincymol Mathew. Date: 10th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the past service of the respondent, Rincymol Mathew, in the School of Medical Education should be counted for the purpose of computing benefits under the Career Advancement Scheme (CAS) in accordance with the UGC Regulations. The learned Single Judge directed the Mahatma Gandhi University to count the past service of the respondent in the School of Medical Education for the purposes of the CAS and to grant her the relevant benefits, observing that her appointment followed the due selection process and she was duly qualified. The University revoked the earlier decision to grant CAS benefits on the grounds that the respondent's initial appointment as Lecturer in the School of Medical Education was not to a duly sanctioned post in terms of the Mahatma Gandhi University Statutes. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the writ appeal filed by the University, confirming the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge to count the past service of the respondent for CAS benefits. The Supreme Court held that Regulation 10.1 of the UGC Regulations, which allows the counting of previous regular service for CAS benefits, was applicable in this case. The respondent's continuous service as Lecturer, Assistant Professor, and Associate Professor, following due process and in regular pay-scales, entitled her to the benefits under CAS. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Mahatma Gandhi University, upholding the decisions of the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench of the High Court, thereby confirming the respondent's entitlement to the CAS benefits by counting her past service.

case_name: Mahendra Pratap Singh & Ors vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors
text: Case: Mahendra Pratap Singh & Ors vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. Date: 15th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case revolved around the physical efficiency test conducted for the selection of Ranker Sub-Inspectors in 2011 and whether candidates who were physically unfit due to illness should be allowed a re-test. The appellants claimed they were compelled to participate in the physical efficiency test despite being physically unfit due to illness. The State argued that candidates who participated in the test without raising objections could not be allowed a second chance. The High Court allowed a re-test for candidates who informed about their illness either on the date of the physical efficiency test or earlier. The Supreme Court permitted appellants who had informed the authorities about their illness to approach the competent authority with supporting material for necessary action within one month.

case_name: Mahesh Kumar Agarwal (Dead) By LRS v. Naresh Chandra & Ors.
text: Case: Mahesh Kumar Agarwal (Dead) By LRS v. Naresh Chandra & Ors.. Date: 8th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellant's eviction notice complied with the requirement under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent, and Eviction) Act, 1972. The purchase was made on 4th January 1977 from the previous landlord. The Rent Controller ordered the eviction of the respondents on 16th May 2013. The High Court allowed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant-landlord had not given a six-month notice prior to filing the eviction application, as required under Section 21(1)(a) of the Act. The Supreme Court held that the defective notice could be waived and that the tenant had waived his right by not raising the objection in the initial stages. Therefore, the eviction order by the Rent Controller was restored with a modification. The Supreme Court ordered the appellants to pay a sum of Rs.30,000/- to the respondents within a period of two months.

case_name: Maheshwari Yadav & Anr. vs. The State of Bihar
text: Case: Maheshwari Yadav & Anr. vs. The State of Bihar. Date: 13th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Maheshwari Yadav and Mannu Yadav's convictions under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of Gholti Yadav were justified based on the evidence presented. Maheshwari Yadav and Mannu Yadav were charged under Sections 302 and 325 read with Section 34 of the IPC. The prosecution alleged that the motive was related to a previous incident where the accused no.3, Paro Yadav, was annoyed with the deceased for preventing an assault on Awadhi Yadav. Maheshwari Yadav was standing with a lathi, and Mannu Yadav exhorted accused no.3 to kill the deceased, who then fired a bullet at the deceased, resulting in his death. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimonies from PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4, and PW-5, who all confirmed the presence and actions of the accused during the incident. The defense argued that there was no evidence of common intention shared by the appellants with accused no.3 and that the appellants could not be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The Supreme Court found the testimonies of the eyewitnesses to be credible and consistent, supporting the prosecution's case against the appellants. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentences of the appellants for the murder of Gholti Yadav. Maheshwari Yadav and Mannu Yadav were sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and rigorous imprisonment for three years for the offence under Section 325 read with Section 34 IPC. The Supreme Court directed the appellants to surrender before the Trial Court within one month to undergo the remaining sentence.

case_name: Mahipal vs. Rajesh Kumar @ Polia & Anr.
text: Case: Mahipal vs. Rajesh Kumar @ Polia & Anr.. Date: 5th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case challenged the Rajasthan High Court's decision to grant bail to the accused involved in a murder, questioning whether the High Court exercised proper judicial discretion under Section 439 of the CrPC. The accused allegedly attacked and killed Akhilesh with rods, causing 27 ante-mortem injuries, including severe head trauma, leading to his death. The report noted 27 ante-mortem injuries, with seven on the head, concluding that the cause of death was coma due to head injuries. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court’s order lacked proper reasoning and failed to consider the gravity of the crime and the evidence presented. The High Court granted bail citing the lack of sufficient evidence to directly implicate the accused and the prolonged detention of the accused. The Supreme Court emphasized that bail orders must be supported by clear reasons, especially in serious crimes, to ensure they reflect judicial application of mind. The Supreme Court set aside the bail order, directed the cancellation of the bail bonds, and ordered the accused to be taken into custody immediately. The defense argued that the deceased fell from his bike, resulting in his injuries, and that the accused had been falsely implicated in the FIR. The statements, particularly from Aashish, the sole eyewitness, corroborated the involvement of the accused in the crime, leading the Supreme Court to question the High Court's bail order. The Court reiterated that granting bail in heinous crimes must involve careful judicial discretion, balancing individual liberty with public interest and the administration of justice.

case_name: Major Singh vs. State of Punjab & Anr.
text: Case: Major Singh vs. State of Punjab & Anr.. Date: 16th June 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Major Singh was charged under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of his uncle, Makhan Singh. The incident occurred on 21st July 1998 when Major Singh assaulted his uncle, Makhan Singh, with a wooden 'Bahi' (wooden side of a cot frame) following a quarrel that took place the previous day. The post-mortem report revealed that Makhan Singh sustained eight injuries, including a fatal head injury that led to his death due to shock and hemorrhage. The Trial Court acquitted Major Singh on 13th July 2001, citing reasons such as delay in recording the FIR, lack of credible eyewitness testimony, and contradictory medical evidence. The High Court set aside the acquittal, convicted Major Singh under Section 302 IPC, and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000. The Supreme Court held that the case did not fall under Section 302 IPC but under Section 304 Part II IPC, as there was no intention to kill, and the appellant's actions were provoked by a quarrel the previous day. The Supreme Court modified the conviction to Section 304 Part II IPC and reduced the sentence to the period already undergone. Major Singh was to be released forthwith if not wanted in any other criminal case. The Supreme Court considered the lack of intention to kill, the provocation from the previous day's quarrel, and the fact that Major Singh had already undergone more than eight years of imprisonment. The Supreme Court concluded that intention plays a vital role in distinguishing between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and in Major Singh's case, the intention to kill was absent. The Supreme Court noted that the delay in recording the FIR was due to the priority given to saving the injured Makhan Singh, and it did not affect the credibility of the prosecution's case. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimonies, the recovery of the blood-stained 'Bahi' based on Major Singh's confession, and the post-mortem report indicating the cause of death.

case_name: Malaichamy & Anr. vs. The State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: Malaichamy & Anr. vs. The State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 23rd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants, Malaichamy and another, were rightly convicted under Sections 449 and 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC for the murder of Harish Kumar. The appellants were distantly related to P.W.1, the father of the deceased, Harish Kumar. The prosecution alleged multiple motives including a financial dispute, a failed marriage proposal, and the termination of Accused No.2's employment due to misconduct. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence including the last seen circumstance, motive, and the recovery of two knives based on the confession of Accused No.1. The Supreme Court found the testimonies unreliable due to delays in their statements, contradictions, and their unnatural conduct after the incident. The Supreme Court found the motive weak and unconvincing, stating that the alleged reasons did not strongly connect to the murder of the victim. The Supreme Court acquitted the appellants, giving them the benefit of doubt due to the unreliable evidence and weak motive presented by the prosecution.

case_name: Mallanna & Ors. vs. The State of Karnataka & Anr.
text: Case: Mallanna & Ors. vs. The State of Karnataka & Anr.. Date: 19th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Accused No. 1 was convicted under Sections 354 and 448 IPC read with Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, while Accused Nos. 2, 3, and 4 were convicted under Section 448 read with Section 34 IPC and Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The incident occurred on 27th January 2008, where the complainant alleged that Accused No. 1, Bhikshawath, and others forcibly entered her house, assaulted her, and committed offenses punishable under the IPC and SC/ST Act. Accused No. 1 was sentenced to one year of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 under Section 448 IPC, two years of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 under Section 354 IPC, and two years of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000 under Section 3(1)(xi) of the SC/ST Act. Accused Nos. 2, 3, and 4 were sentenced to one year of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 each under Section 448 read with Section 34 IPC and one year of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 each under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentences of all the appellants as given by the Trial Court. The complainant mentioned that the incident happened due to a misunderstanding and in the spur of the moment. She stated that with the passage of time, relations between her and the appellants had become cordial, and they were now closely related. She expressed that she did not desire the appellants to undergo further imprisonment. The Supreme Court sustained the conviction of Accused No. 1 but limited the sentence to the period already undergone. The convictions of Accused Nos. 2, 3, and 4 were set aside, and they were acquitted of the charges.

case_name: Mallikarjun Kodagali (Dead) represented through Legal Representatives vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.
text: Case: Mallikarjun Kodagali (Dead) represented through Legal Representatives vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.. Date: 12th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether a victim, under the proviso to Section 372 of the CrPC, has the right to appeal against an acquittal even if the alleged offence occurred before the amendment introducing the proviso. The significant provision discussed was the proviso to Section 372 of the CrPC, which grants victims the right to appeal in specific circumstances. The District and Sessions Judge acquitted the accused by a judgment dated 28th October 2013. The High Court dismissed the victim's first appeal, citing that the proviso to Section 372 came into effect after the incident, making the appeal non-maintainable. The victim argued that the right to appeal under the proviso to Section 372 of the CrPC should apply to judgments passed after the amendment's effective date, regardless of the date of the offence. The Supreme Court ruled that the right to appeal under the proviso to Section 372 is applicable to judgments passed after 31st December 2009, regardless of when the offence occurred. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of recognizing victims' rights as a part of social justice and the rule of law, highlighting the need for victims to have a voice in the criminal justice process. The Supreme Court relied on precedents discussing victimology and the progressive recognition of victims' rights under Indian law. The Court recommended considering victim impact statements and psychosocial support as additional measures to ensure justice for victims. The case is significant because it clarified and expanded the right of victims to appeal under Section 372, ensuring their participation in criminal proceedings. The Court emphasized the need to balance the rights of the accused with those of the victim to ensure fairness and justice in criminal proceedings.

case_name: Malluru Mallappa vs. Kuruvathappa & Ors.
text: Case: Malluru Mallappa vs. Kuruvathappa & Ors.. Date: 12th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the plaintiff, Malluru Mallappa, was entitled to specific performance of the agreement to sell dated 30th March 2000, despite the defendants' claim that the suit was barred by limitation and that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. The defendants contended that the suit was barred by limitation and that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. They admitted the execution of the agreement to sell but argued that the plaintiff failed to fulfill his contractual obligations within the specified time frame. The trial court dismissed the plaintiff's suit for specific performance, holding that the suit was barred by time and that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. The court concluded that the plaintiff did not fulfill the necessary conditions stipulated in the agreement. The High Court confirmed the trial court's decision, dismissing the plaintiff's appeal. The High Court agreed with the trial court's findings that the suit was barred by limitation and that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. The plaintiff argued that the High Court passed a cryptic judgment without reappreciating the evidence on record. He contended that the suit was filed within the limitation period prescribed under Article 54 of the Limitation Act and that the High Court failed to properly assess his readiness and willingness to perform the contract. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court failed to properly reappreciate the evidence and did not comply with the provisions of Order XLI Rule 31 of the CPC while deciding the appeal. The Court noted that the High Court's judgment was cryptic and lacked proper examination of the issues. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and remanded the matter back to the High Court for fresh disposal in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to reassess the evidence and address all issues raised by the parties.

case_name: Mamta Rohit vs. Dr. Prafulla Ranjan & Ors.
text: Case: Mamta Rohit vs. Dr. Prafulla Ranjan & Ors.. Date: 26th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellant, Mamta Rohit, met the qualification criteria for the post of Chief General Manager under the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) despite the qualification relaxation by the appointing authority. Her appointment was challenged by some unsuccessful candidates on the grounds that she did not meet the required qualifications for the position, and her appointment was based on a relaxation of qualifications which they argued was not justified. The CAT initially allowed Mamta Rohit to continue in service based on an interim order, but her appointment was later challenged and set aside by the High Court of Delhi. The High Court ruled that there cannot be a deemed relaxation of qualifications and that such relaxation must be based on a proper application of mind considering the specific requirements of the appointment. The Supreme Court noted that Mamta Rohit had resigned from her previous position as Deputy General Manager at IDBI Bank to take up the appointment at PFRDA, and it was not alleged that she misled anyone about her qualifications. The Supreme Court set aside the order canceling Mamta Rohit's appointment and directed that she be reinstated in service with effect from 1st October 2018, treating her service as continuous but without back wages. No, the Supreme Court clarified that its judgement was specific to the peculiar facts and circumstances of Mamta Rohit's case and should not be treated as a precedent for other cases.

case_name: Management of the Barara Cooperative Marketing-cum-Processing Society Ltd. vs. Workman Pratap Singh
text: Case: Management of the Barara Cooperative Marketing-cum-Processing Society Ltd. vs. Workman Pratap Singh. Date: 2nd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case revolves around the termination of Pratap Singh, who was working as a peon, and his subsequent claim for re-employment under Section 25(H) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, after the Management of the Barara Cooperative Marketing-cum-Processing Society Ltd. terminated his services. The Labour Court held Pratap Singh's termination to be illegal and awarded him a lump sum compensation of Rs. 12,500 instead of reinstatement. Pratap Singh sought re-employment after the appellant society regularized the services of two other peons. He claimed that under Section 25(H) of the Industrial Disputes Act, he was entitled to re-employment. The Single Judge of the High Court allowed Pratap Singh's writ petition, setting aside the Labour Court's award, and directed his re-employment. The Division Bench later upheld this decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by the Management of the Barara Cooperative Marketing-cum-Processing Society Ltd., set aside the High Court's orders, and restored the Labour Court's award, holding that Section 25(H) of the Industrial Disputes Act did not apply in this case. The Supreme Court held that Section 25(H) of the Industrial Disputes Act applies to cases where the employer proposes to fill vacancies and must give preference to retrenched employees. In this case, Pratap Singh was not a retrenched employee but had accepted compensation in lieu of reinstatement, and the regularization of other employees did not amount to filling new vacancies.

case_name: Mangilal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Mangilal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 12th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Mangilal's conviction under Section 8(b) read with Section 15(c) of the NDPS Act was justified based on the evidence presented. Mangilal was charged and convicted under Section 8(b) read with Section 15(c) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985. The Additional Sessions Judge convicted Mangilal and sentenced him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment, which was confirmed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. The Supreme Court identified several procedural lapses, including non-compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act, failure to produce seized materials, and reliance on the FSL Report without proper cross-examination of witnesses. The Supreme Court emphasized that compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act is mandatory to ensure fair play in the investigation process and that non-compliance can lead to adverse inferences against the prosecution. P.W.5, a police officer, testified that the seized narcotic substances were in existence at the police station before the alleged occurrence, which was not challenged by the prosecution, thus undermining the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court found that the lower courts mechanically relied on the FSL Report without properly considering the procedural lapses and the fact that key witnesses turned hostile. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitted Mangilal of all charges, and ordered his release, citing serious doubts about the prosecution's case and benefit of the doubt in favor of the appellant. The Supreme Court highlighted that non-production of seized materials can lead to a negative inference against the prosecution, as physical evidence is crucial in NDPS Act cases to establish seizure and recovery. The Supreme Court noted that several key witnesses, including panch witnesses, turned hostile, which significantly weakened the prosecution's case and contributed to the decision to acquit Mangilal. The Supreme Court found that there were too many material irregularities and procedural lapses in the prosecution's case, leading to serious doubts about the evidence and the decision to acquit Mangilal.

case_name: Mani vs State of Kerala and Others
text: Case: Mani vs State of Kerala and Others. Date: 1st April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Mani was primarily charged with an offence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for murder. The FIR was lodged by Vishwanathan, son of Kunchu. The attack was motivated by political enmity between BJP sympathizers (accused) and CPM sympathizers (victims). The trial court convicted Mani under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. Mani stabbed Soman on the chest with a knife, which resulted in Soman's death. Mani argued that he acted in self-defense and that the incident was a sudden fight without premeditation. The Supreme Court ruled that the conviction under Section 302 IPC was not sustainable and modified it to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC. The Supreme Court modified the sentence to the period already undergone by Mani, maintaining a fine of Rs. 20,000. The Supreme Court justified the modification by stating that the incident occurred in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, fitting within Exception 4 of Section 300 IPC. The other accused, Rathnakumar, Praveen, and Selvaraj, were charged under Sections 324 and 341 read with 34 IPC, but were acquitted for the offence under Section 302 IPC.

case_name: Manik Hiru Jhangiani vs State of M.P.
text: Case: Manik Hiru Jhangiani vs State of M.P.. Date: 14th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant could be prosecuted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) for misbranding after the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA) had come into force. The definition of 'misbranded food' under Section 3 of the FSSA came into force on 28th May 2008, and Section 52 of the FSSA, which provides for penalties for misbranding, was brought into force on 29th July 2010. The appellant, Manik Hiru Jhangiani, was a Director of M/s. Bharti Retail Limited, a company operating retail stores under the name 'Easy Day'. The alleged offence was misbranding of food products, specifically biscuit packets, under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA). The High Court dismissed the petition because it noted that the offence of misbranding took place before the repeal of the PFA, and the learned Magistrate was empowered to take cognizance of the offence within the sunset period provided by the FSSA. The appellant argued that after 29th July 2010, the provisions of the FSSA, including Section 52 which provides for penalties for misbranding, would prevail over the PFA, and thus the prosecution under the PFA was not valid. The Supreme Court decided that the provisions of the FSSA would have an overriding effect over the PFA due to Section 89 of the FSSA, which states that the FSSA will prevail in case of any inconsistency between the two laws. The sunset clause in sub-section (4) of Section 97 of the FSSA provides that no court shall take cognizance of an offence under the repealed PFA after the expiry of three years from the commencement of the FSSA. Future prosecutions under the PFA may be affected in that if an inconsistency arises with the FSSA, the provisions of the FSSA will prevail, potentially limiting the applicability of the PFA. Section 89 of the FSSA ensures that the FSSA's provisions will override those of the PFA in the event of any inconsistency, thereby influencing courts to apply the FSSA's penalties and provisions in such cases. The Food Inspector purchased the biscuit packets, drew a panchnama the next day, and sent samples to the State Food Laboratory, Bhopal, for analysis and testing.

case_name: Manju Kumari Singh @ Smt. Manju Singh vs. Avinash Kumar Singh
text: Case: Manju Kumari Singh @ Smt. Manju Singh vs. Avinash Kumar Singh. Date: 25th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the marriage between the appellant (wife) and the respondent (husband) should be dissolved on the grounds of cruelty and desertion. The Family Court dissolved the marriage between the appellant and the respondent on the grounds of cruelty and desertion by the appellant. The High Court of Jharkhand dismissed the appellant's appeal and affirmed the Family Court's decision to dissolve the marriage. The Supreme Court observed that the parties had been living separately for more than a decade, and all attempts at reconciliation had failed. Therefore, there was no chance of them living together, and the marriage was beyond repair. The Supreme Court ordered the respondent-husband to pay a total sum of Rs. 10,00,000 in two installments towards permanent alimony and maintenance to the appellant and their daughter. The Supreme Court directed that all pending cases arising out of the matrimonial proceedings, including the one from which this appeal arose, be disposed of and consigned to the records, putting a quietus to the litigation between the parties. The Supreme Court exercised its power under Article 142 of the Constitution to do substantial justice and declared the dissolution of the marriage, subject to the fulfillment of the financial conditions set out in the judgment.

case_name: Manju Surana vs. Sunil Arora & Ors.
text: Case: Manju Surana vs. Sunil Arora & Ors.. Date: 27th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal question is whether prior sanction for prosecution in cases of alleged corruption against public servants is required before initiating an investigative process under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. The appellant in the case is Manju Surana. The respondents include Sunil Arora, the Principal Secretary to the Government P.H.E.D., Chief Minister, and other officials such as the Superintending Engineer, Chief Engineer, ex Chief Minister, ex Minister of P.H.E.D., Finance Secretary, Deputy Accountant General, and P.S.L. Company through its Managing Director. The appellant alleged that a conspiracy was hatched in the drinking water projects Nos.1 to 8 for personal vested interests through a tender procedure, causing a loss to the Government fund. The Special Judge closed the complaint on 4th February 2014, stating that the accused persons were public servants and no prior sanction had been granted by the competent authority under Section 19 of the PC Act read with Section 197 of the Cr.P.C. The appellant preferred a revision petition against the Special Judge's order, which was dismissed by the High Court on 30th April 2014. Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. allows a Magistrate to order an investigation by the police. The controversy in this case revolves around whether a Magistrate can order such an investigation without prior sanction when public servants are involved. The appellant argued that prior sanction is only required at the stage of taking cognizance of an offence, not at the stage of setting into motion an investigation under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court observed that there is a divergence of opinion on whether prior sanction is needed for directing an investigation under Section 156(3) when public servants are involved. This issue was referred to a larger bench for resolution. The Supreme Court decided that respondent No.1, who was neither the Principal Secretary, PHED, nor the Chief Secretary at the relevant time, should be struck off from the array of parties. However, if material comes to light during an investigation warranting his inclusion, it would be open to do so. The larger question referred to a larger bench is whether the scope of Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. includes the requirement of prior sanction under Section 19(1) of the PC Act for initiating an investigation against public servants.

case_name: Manju vs. State of Delhi
text: Case: Manju vs. State of Delhi. Date: 17th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Manju was rightly convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC for the alleged murder of her newborn baby girl. The prosecution alleged that Manju strangled her newborn baby girl to death shortly after the baby was handed over to her in the hospital on 24th August 2007. Manju's conviction was based on circumstantial evidence, particularly the testimonies of two staff nurses (PW-8 and PW-9) and the post-mortem report indicating death by asphyxia due to ante mortem strangulation. Manju claimed innocence, stating that she was falsely implicated by the police in connivance with hospital authorities to shift the blame from the doctors. She also mentioned being sleepy due to drugs administered after delivery. Manju's counsel highlighted the delayed post-mortem (conducted two days after death), the late registration of the crime (registered on 31st August 2007), and the lack of motive, as Manju already had a male child and was not averse to having a female child. The Supreme Court found no evidence to support the motive attributed to Manju, as she already had a male child and her family was not averse to having a female child. The Supreme Court held that the chain of circumstantial evidence was not complete and sufficient to establish Manju's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court concluded that there was a possibility of natural death, as the baby was on an oxygen mask in an incubator and had not opened her eyes or cried after birth. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the trial court and the High Court, acquitted Manju of the charges, and cancelled her bail bonds. The post-mortem report indicated that the cause of death was asphyxia due to ante mortem strangulation, but the Supreme Court found it insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt in light of other evidence.

case_name: Manno Lal Jaiswal vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Manno Lal Jaiswal vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 25th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The accused were charged under Sections 147, 148, 149, 323, 504, 506, 302, 307, and 34 of the IPC for the murder of Manno Lal Jaiswal's son. The High Court granted bail to the accused, which was contested by the original complainant, Manno Lal Jaiswal. Manno Lal Jaiswal argued that the High Court had applied the wrong facts, stating that the accused were not named in the FIR and that the witness statements under Section 161 Cr.PC were recorded belatedly, both of which were factually incorrect. The Sessions Court observed that the accused were named in the FIR and that the witnesses had given statements supporting the incident. The court noted that all accused persons attacked the deceased with weapons like swords, hockey sticks, and rods. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court had incorrectly noted that the accused were not named in the FIR and that the witness statements were recorded belatedly. The Supreme Court found this to be factually incorrect. The Supreme Court highlighted that the gravity and nature of the offense, the evidence, and the role of the accused should be considered while granting bail. The High Court failed to consider these relevant factors properly. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order granting bail to the accused and directed them to surrender forthwith. case_name: Manoharan vs. State by Inspector of Police, Variety Hall Police Station, Coimbatore
text: Case: Manoharan vs. State by Inspector of Police, Variety Hall Police Station, Coimbatore. Date: 1st August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Manoharan's conviction and death sentence for the rape and murder of two children were justified based on the evidence presented by the prosecution. Manoharan was charged under Sections 302 (murder), 376 (rape), 364-A (kidnapping for ransom), 366-A (procuration of minor girl), and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the Indian Penal Code. The key pieces of evidence included: (i) testimonies from witnesses who saw Manoharan and the co-accused Mohanakrishnan with the children; (ii) the recovery of the children's bodies from the canal; (iii) forensic evidence, including DNA analysis linking Manoharan to the crime; and (iv) Manoharan's confessional statement. The trial court convicted Manoharan under Sections 302, 376, 364-A, 366-A, and 201 of the IPC, sentencing him to death for the offence under Section 302 IPC. The High Court confirmed the trial court's conviction and death sentence for Manoharan, although it set aside his conviction under Sections 120-B and 364-A of the IPC. Manoharan's defense argued that the evidence against him was fabricated, his confession was coerced, and that there were significant discrepancies in the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court found that Manoharan's confession was recorded voluntarily by the Magistrate after ensuring that Manoharan was aware of his rights and that there was no coercion. The Court rejected the defense's claim that the confession was fabricated. The Supreme Court concluded that the forensic evidence, including the DNA analysis linking Manoharan to the crime, was credible and supported the prosecution's case. The presence of Manoharan's DNA on the victim's panties was a crucial piece of evidence. The Supreme Court upheld Manoharan's conviction and death sentence, stating that the nature and gravity of the crime warranted the imposition of the death penalty. The Supreme Court emphasized that in cases of extreme brutality and heinous crimes, the death penalty is justified to serve as a deterrent and to reflect the society's condemnation of such acts.

case_name: Manoj Kumar vs State of Himachal Pradesh
text: Case: Manoj Kumar vs State of Himachal Pradesh. Date: 15th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main charges were under Sections 302, 341, and 323 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Prem Dass. The trial court convicted Manoj Kumar and the other accused under the aforementioned sections and sentenced them to life imprisonment along with fines. The High Court partly allowed the appeal, acquitting some of the accused while upholding the conviction and sentence of Manoj Kumar and two others. The defense argued that there was no premeditation to attack the deceased, and the incident was a result of a sudden quarrel. They also contended that the injuries inflicted did not indicate an intention to kill. The Supreme Court noted that the injuries were not inflicted with sufficient force to show an intention to kill, and the incident appeared to be a sudden fight without premeditation, fitting the criteria for Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. The Supreme Court modified the conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part II IPC, sentencing the appellants to ten years of rigorous imprisonment. As they had already served more than 11 years, they were ordered to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

case_name: Manoj Pratap Singh vs The State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Manoj Pratap Singh vs The State of Rajasthan. Date: 24th June 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Manoj Pratap Singh was charged with offences under Sections 363 (kidnapping), 365 (kidnapping with intent to secretly and wrongfully confine person), 376(2)(f) (rape of a minor), 302 (murder) of the Indian Penal Code, and Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. The victim was a seven-and-a-half-year-old girl who was mentally and physically challenged. The prosecution's case rested on circumstantial evidence including the victim being last seen with the appellant, recovery of the victim's body and other articles at the instance of the appellant, the appellant's failure to explain his whereabouts, and consistent medical and scientific evidence including DNA matches. The medical evidence revealed that the victim had multiple injuries including head injuries that caused her death and signs of brutal rape. The post-mortem report indicated the cause of death as head injury and noted ante-mortem rape. The appellant claimed he was falsely implicated and raised contentions about the impartiality of the investigation, hurried trial, inadequate legal aid, and residual doubts in the chain of circumstances. He did not provide any evidence in his defense. The Supreme Court upheld the death sentence awarded to Manoj Pratap Singh, finding the case to be among the 'rarest of rare' due to the brutal nature of the crime involving the rape and murder of a mentally and physically challenged minor girl. The appellant presented mitigating factors such as his young age, poor socio-economic background, dependent family members, and the possibility of reformation. He also argued that the trial was conducted hurriedly, and he did not get a fair opportunity to present his case. The High Court confirmed the death sentence based on the brutal nature of the crime, where the appellant raped and murdered a mentally and physically challenged minor girl, and his attempt to cover up the crime. The court found it to be a 'rarest of rare case' warranting the death penalty.

case_name: Manoj Suryavanshi vs. State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Manoj Suryavanshi vs. State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 5th March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Manoj Suryavanshi was accused of killing the three minor children of the complainant, Shivlal. The main charges against Manoj Suryavanshi were under Section 302 (murder) and Section 364 (kidnapping or abducting in order to murder) of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution stated that the motive behind the crime was revenge because Manoj Suryavanshi's wife had eloped with the complainant's younger brother. The prosecution presented evidence including eyewitness testimonies, a missing person report, call detail records, and the recovery of the children's bodies based on the accused's disclosure. The defense argued that there was no direct evidence linking Manoj Suryavanshi to the crime and that the prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence which was insufficient. The trial court convicted Manoj Suryavanshi and sentenced him to death. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the conviction and death sentence awarded by the trial court. The defense raised issues such as the lack of a proper hearing on the sentence, the reliance on circumstantial evidence, and alleged procedural errors during the trial. The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had successfully established a complete chain of circumstantial evidence leading to the conclusion that Manoj Suryavanshi was guilty of the crime. This judgement reinforces the importance of a complete chain of circumstantial evidence and sets a precedent for future cases, emphasizing that such evidence can be sufficient for conviction. The Supreme Court's decision highlights the judiciary's stance on the use of the death penalty in cases with heinous crimes and strong circumstantial evidence, potentially influencing future sentencing in similar cases.

case_name: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
text: Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another. Date: 7th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether an offence under Section 326A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is attracted in an acid attack case if the injury caused is simple. Section 326A deals with voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, which includes permanent or partial damage or deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability. Section 326B deals with voluntarily throwing or attempting to throw acid, which includes similar injuries but does not require actual injury to have occurred. The Supreme Court concluded that Section 326A IPC can be attracted even if the injuries caused are simple, as long as they fall under the specified types such as permanent or partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability. The appellant argued that since the injury caused was simple as per the medical report, he should be discharged from the charges under Section 326A IPC. The Supreme Court stated that the nature of injury, whether simple or grievous, is irrelevant for distinguishing between Sections 326A and 326B IPC as long as the injury falls under the specified types mentioned in the sections. The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding the trial court's decision to frame charges under Section 326A IPC despite the injury being simple. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 326A IPC to mean that the provision applies to any of the specified injuries caused by acid attacks, regardless of whether the injuries are simple or grievous. The Supreme Court set the precedent that the severity of the injury (simple or grievous) does not affect the applicability of Section 326A IPC, as long as the injury is one of the types specified in the section. This judgement clarifies that Section 326A IPC can be applied to acid attacks causing simple injuries, ensuring stricter punishment and legal recourse for victims of acid attacks. Legal practitioners should consider that the applicability of Sections 326A and 326B IPC depends on the nature of the act (use of acid) and the type of injury specified, rather than the severity of the injury. Future cases involving simple injuries from acid attacks may see charges framed under Section 326A IPC, following the precedent set by this judgment, ensuring accountability and stricter legal measures against perpetrators.

case_name: Maringmei Acham vs. M Maringmei Khuripou
text: Case: Maringmei Acham vs. M Maringmei Khuripou. Date: 3rd November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the suit filed by the appellant's late father, Maringmei Thaitoungam, seeking a declaration of his right as the village chief (Khullakpa), could continue after his death, considering the failure to implead his legal representatives in time. The High Court held that the suit had abated due to the death of the sole plaintiff, Maringmei Thaitoungam, and the failure to bring his legal representatives on record within the prescribed time. The appellant argued that as per the Rongmei Kabui Customary Law, the post of village chief (Khullakpa) is hereditary, and he, being the eldest son, had the right to continue the suit filed by his father. The Supreme Court concluded that the suit could continue despite the death of the original plaintiff, as the appellant had been brought on record as the legal representative in an appeal arising from an interlocutory order. The Supreme Court directed that both the Original (Declaratory) Suit No. 3 of 2014 and the Original (Injunction) Suit No. 39 of 2014 be consolidated and disposed of as early as possible, within a period of eight months from the date of the judgement. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the consolidation and expedited disposal of the related suits, without making any pronouncement on the merits of the parties' contentions.
