case_name: Mathew Alexander vs. Mohammed Shafi and Anr.
text: Case: Mathew Alexander vs. Mohammed Shafi and Anr.. Date: 13th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the final report from further investigation in Crime No. 1/2015, which stated that the incident was an unavoidable accident not attributable to the negligence of the Appellant's son. The FIR charged the Appellant's son under Sections 279 and 304A of the IPC for a fatal accident involving a gas tanker lorry. The charges against the Appellant's son abated after his death in the accident. The final report concluded that the incident was an unavoidable accident and not due to negligence on the part of the Appellant's son. It stated that the accident occurred as the Alto car tried to overtake a pick-up van, which did not give way, leading to the collision with the tanker lorry. The High Court quashed the final report, stating that the incident was attributable to the rash and negligent driving of the Appellant's son. The court made findings about the son's driving, including the possibility of alcohol consumption and the car going astray to the wrong side. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's findings were unnecessary and incorrect while considering the final report's correctness. The observations made by the High Court were in the nature of findings that should not have been made. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court, stating that the High Court's approach in making findings while considering the final report was incorrect. The appeal was allowed. The Supreme Court noted that the final report would not affect the claim petitions. The negligence of the drivers involved in the accident must be proved in the claim petitions, which are considered based on the preponderance of probabilities, not beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court instructed that the claim petitions should be considered on their own merits, with the burden on the parties to prove negligence. The outcome of the claim petitions would not be influenced by the findings in the quashed final report. The accident occurred when the Appellant's son was driving a Maruti Alto car with friends, and it collided with a gas tanker lorry driven by Ramar. The collision resulted in the deaths of the Appellant's son and five others. The Supreme Court highlighted that the standard of proof in claim petitions is based on the preponderance of probabilities, not beyond a reasonable doubt. This principle guides the determination of negligence in claim petitions for compensation.

text: Case: Maya Gopinathan vs Anoop S.B. & Anr.. Date: 24th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the respondents misappropriated 89 sovereigns of gold jewellery and Rs. 2,00,000 that the appellant alleged were given during the marriage. The High Court found that the appellant failed to prove the misappropriation of jewellery due to lack of documentary evidence and inconsistencies in her testimony, and reversed the Family Court's findings. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision unsustainable, concluding that the evidence on record supported the appellant's claim of entrustment and misappropriation of 89 sovereigns of gold jewellery. The Supreme Court awarded the appellant Rs. 25,00,000 as financial recompense for the misappropriated jewellery and damages, to be paid by the first respondent within six months. The Family Court held that the respondents misappropriated the appellant's jewellery and directed them to pay Rs. 8,90,000 for the jewellery and Rs. 2,00,000 with 6% interest for the amount handed over to the first respondent. The Supreme Court directed the first respondent to pay Rs. 25,00,000 within six months, failing which interest at 6% per annum would accrue until the full payment is made.

case_name: Mayank N Shah vs State of Gujarat & Anr.
text: Case: Mayank N Shah vs State of Gujarat & Anr.. Date: 18th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main allegation was that Mayank N Shah and others conspired to cheat the Central Bank of India by presenting fake transport receipts and fraudulent bills to avail credit facilities, leading to a financial loss of Rs.18,57,064.40 to the bank. Mayank N Shah, serving as Chief Manager (Operations) with M/s. New Russian Automobiles, was responsible for drawing and presenting the fake bills and invoices to the bank, knowing fully well that they were fabricated. The trial court convicted Mayank N Shah under Sections 120B, 161, 166, 420, 468, and 471 of the IPC and Sections 5(1)(d) and 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and sentenced him to various terms of rigorous imprisonment, with the longest being two years, along with fines. The High Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court on Mayank N Shah. The defense argued that the High Court decided the appeal without giving adequate opportunity to the appellant, and that Mayank N Shah was merely a salaried employee following instructions without any direct benefit from the alleged conspiracy. The Supreme Court modified the sentence, reducing the period of rigorous imprisonment to one year for each offence, while confirming the conviction. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently. The Supreme Court ordered Mayank N Shah to surrender within four weeks to serve the remaining period of his sentence, failing which the State was instructed to take steps to take him into custody.

case_name: Md. Mannan @ Abdul Mannan vs. State of Bihar
text: Case: Md. Mannan @ Abdul Mannan vs. State of Bihar. Date: 14th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the death sentence imposed on Md. Mannan for the rape and murder of an eight-year-old girl should be confirmed or commuted to life imprisonment. Md. Mannan was convicted for the rape and murder of an eight-year-old girl on 28th September 2004. He lured the victim by giving her money to buy betel and then took her to a secluded place where he raped and murdered her. The Trial Court sentenced Md. Mannan to death, which was confirmed by the High Court and the Supreme Court. His review petition was dismissed by circulation. The arguments included the failure to conduct a DNA analysis of the spermatozoa, the prolonged solitary confinement causing mental illness, the inadequate legal representation at trial, and the possibility of rehabilitation. The Supreme Court found that Md. Mannan did not receive effective legal representation, especially regarding the opportunity to present mitigating factors during the sentencing phase. The Supreme Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment till his natural death without reprieve or remission, considering the prolonged solitary confinement and the possibility of mental illness as mitigating factors. case_name: Md. Rojali Ali & Ors. vs. The State of Assam
text: Case: Md. Rojali Ali & Ors. vs. The State of Assam. Date: 19th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Md. Rojali Ali and the other appellants were charged under Sections 148, 323, and 302 read with 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of four individuals and causing injuries to another. The prosecution's case was that 26 persons, including the appellants, armed with deadly weapons, trespassed into the house of Md. Aziz Ali, Md. Kutub Ali, Md. Mamud Ali, and Samir Ali, dragged them outside, and assaulted them, resulting in their deaths. Another individual, Md. Atar Ali, was injured in the incident. The Trial Court convicted the appellants under Sections 148, 323, and 302 read with 149 IPC, and the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The defense argued that the eyewitnesses were closely related to the deceased and had a motive to falsely implicate the appellants. They also contended that there were inconsistencies in the eyewitnesses' testimonies and that no weapons were recovered from the appellants. The Supreme Court found the testimonies of the eyewitnesses to be consistent, reliable, and trustworthy. The Court noted that the presence of the eyewitnesses at the scene was natural and that their testimonies were corroborated by the medical evidence. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence imposed by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High Court. The Supreme Court concluded that the motive for the crime, a minor quarrel, was insignificant compared to the gravity of the offence. The Court found that the accused were the aggressors who came with the intention to commit murder and assaulted the deceased without provocation.

case_name: Medical Council of India vs. Jaipur National University Institute for Medical Sciences and Research Centre Jaipur & Another
text: Case: Medical Council of India vs. Jaipur National University Institute for Medical Sciences and Research Centre Jaipur & Another. Date: 4th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the interim order of the Rajasthan High Court allowing Jaipur National University Institute to admit 150 students for the academic year 2018-2019 was justified, despite the Medical Council of India's recommendation against it due to deficiencies. The MCI recommended not to grant renewal of permission for admitting the third batch of MBBS students for the academic year 2018-2019 due to deficiencies in infrastructure, clinical material, and other physical facilities. The High Court's interim order directed the Central Government to allow the respondent institute to admit 150 students in the third batch for the academic year 2018-2019, subject to the condition that if the petition failed, the fees would be refunded to the students. The MCI conducted surprise inspections to verify the respondent institute's claims regarding compliance and removal of deficiencies after the Central Government's renewal of permission for the academic year 2017-2018 despite MCI's negative recommendation. The inspections revealed various deficiencies in infrastructure, clinical material, and other physical facilities at the respondent institute. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's interim order, stating that the High Court was not justified in passing such an order at the interim stage, and emphasized that the matter should be decided on merits without permitting provisional admissions. The Supreme Court reasoned that interim orders allowing provisional admissions subject to the result of the petition could cause tremendous prejudice to students and that the proper course was to hear the matter finally. The Supreme Court directed that the pending matter before the High Court be considered purely on merits and not on the basis of interim orders. The Supreme Court emphasized that courts should avoid passing interim orders that interfere with administrative decisions, especially in matters requiring specialized knowledge, and should allow the issues to be decided on merits. The judgment implies that courts should be cautious in issuing interim orders allowing provisional admissions in educational institutions, as such orders can cause significant prejudice and should only be issued after a thorough consideration of the merits. The Medical Council of India might ensure more rigorous compliance checks and transparent reporting to prevent similar legal challenges and ensure that recommendations are clearly supported by verifiable evidence.

text: Case: Meena Pradhan & Ors. vs Kamla Pradhan & Anr.. Date: 21st September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the Will executed by Bahadur Pradhan on 30th July 1992, and whether the Letter of Administration issued in favor of Kamla Pradhan and her daughter was justified. The Civil Court of Jabalpur concluded that the Will was validly executed by Bahadur Pradhan in the presence of attesting witnesses and issued Letters of Administration to Kamla Pradhan and her daughter. The appellants contended that the Will was forged and raised objections about the authenticity of the document, as well as questioning the testator's mental state and the presence of undue influence during the execution of the Will. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh upheld the validity of the Will, affirming the decision of the Civil Court and dismissing the appellants' contention that the Will was forged. The Supreme Court outlined that the execution of a Will must be proven by fulfilling all formalities under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, including the testator's signature, attestation by two or more witnesses, and the testator's free will and sound state of mind during execution. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that there were no sufficient grounds to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts, and confirmed the validity of the Will and the Letters of Administration issued in favor of Kamla Pradhan and her daughter. No, the Supreme Court did not entertain allegations of bigamy and second marriage, stating that these issues were not relevant to the main issue of the validity of the Will.

case_name: Meenal Bhargava vs. Naveen Sharma & Ors.
text: Case: Meenal Bhargava vs. Naveen Sharma & Ors.. Date: 16th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Naveen Sharma (contemnor) should be punished for contempt of court for failing to comply with the Supreme Court's order to bring his child back to India. Naveen Sharma's defense was that the child could not be brought back to India due to an ongoing forensic investigation in the USA regarding allegations of sexual abuse and the appointment of a Guardian Ad Litem by the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois. The Supreme Court noted that Naveen Sharma showed no signs of remorse and had consistently acted contrary to his assurances to the court, including not applying for the renewal of the child's passport and not making any genuine efforts to comply with the court orders. The Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, appointed a Guardian Ad Litem for the child and was conducting an investigation into allegations of sexual abuse while the child was in India, which Naveen Sharma cited as a reason for not bringing the child back to India. The Supreme Court sentenced Naveen Sharma to six months of simple imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs. 25 lakhs for committing civil and criminal contempt. In default of payment of the fine, he would undergo a further two months of simple imprisonment. The Supreme Court rejected Naveen Sharma's argument that he acted in the best interests of the child, finding that his actions, including discussing litigation with the child and not renewing the child's passport, were contrary to the child's welfare. The Supreme Court directed the Government of India and the Central Bureau of Investigation to take all possible steps to secure Naveen Sharma's presence in India to ensure he undergoes the sentence and pays the fine. The Supreme Court observed that Naveen Sharma had scant respect for the court's orders, as he opposed the request for a mirroring order in the foreign court and misrepresented his submission to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court highlighted that Naveen Sharma attempted to suppress information from the Circuit Court proceedings that could establish his contumacious conduct and defiance of the orders of the Supreme Court of India. The broader implications were that the Supreme Court reinforced the authority of its orders, emphasized the importance of compliance with judicial decisions, and demonstrated a commitment to ensuring justice even in international contexts.

case_name: Mina Pun vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Mina Pun vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 22nd August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the challenge to the conviction of the appellants for offences under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act). The appellants were sentenced to ten years of rigorous imprisonment and fined Rs.1,00,000/-, with an additional two years of rigorous imprisonment in default of payment of the fine. The appellants' counsel claimed a violation of the safeguard provided in Section 50 of the NDPS Act, arguing that the appellants were not informed of their right to be searched before a Magistrate or a Gazetted Officer. The prosecution presented evidence that packets of charas were found on the appellants during a body search conducted by Police Officer Sanjay Singh (PW-4). Police Officer Sanjay Singh admitted that the consent letter did not mention that the appellants were informed about their right to have their body search conducted before a Magistrate or a Gazetted Officer. The Supreme Court, referring to the Constitution Bench decision in Vijaysinh Jadeja vs. State of Gujarat, held that the failure to inform the appellants of their right under Section 50 vitiated the conviction and made the recovery of the illicit articles suspect. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and acquitted the appellants of the offences alleged against them. The Supreme Court directed that if the appellants were already enlarged on bail, their bail bonds should stand cancelled. If the appellants continued to be in custody, they should be set at liberty forthwith. The Supreme Court relied on the legal precedent set by the Constitution Bench in Vijaysinh Jadeja vs. State of Gujarat, which emphasized the mandatory nature of the safeguard under Section 50 of the NDPS Act. The Supreme Court found the recovery suspect because the appellants were not informed of their right to be searched before a Magistrate or a Gazetted Officer, as required under Section 50 of the NDPS Act. This judgement reinforces the mandatory nature of informing suspects of their rights under Section 50 of the NDPS Act, which must be strictly complied with to ensure the validity of any search and seizure operation.

case_name: Mirza Iqbal @ Golu & Anr. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Mirza Iqbal @ Golu & Anr. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 14th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the charges against Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano under Sections 498-A, 323, 504, 506, 304-B of IPC and Sections 3 & 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act should be quashed due to lack of specific allegations and evidence of their involvement. Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano were charged under Sections 498-A, 323, 504, 506, 304-B of IPC and Sections 3 & 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act for dowry harassment and the murder of Rushda Nisar. The prosecution alleged that Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano, along with other family members, continuously demanded dowry and eventually killed Rushda Nisar by hanging her when their demands were not met. Mirza Iqbal's defense was that he was working as a cashier at ICICI Bank in Khalilabad on the date of the incident and was not present at the crime scene in Gorakhpur, which is 40 km away. The Supreme Court observed that the allegations against Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano were vague and lacked specific details, making the prosecution's case weak against them. Mirza Iqbal provided his bank's attendance records, showing his presence at ICICI Bank in Khalilabad on the date of the incident, as well as an affidavit stating the same. The Supreme Court quashed the charges against Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano, finding that there was no specific evidence linking them to the crime and the allegations were general and vague. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in the case of Geeta Mehrotra and Anr. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Anr., where it was held that vague allegations without specific evidence do not justify the prosecution of family members. The key factors included the lack of specific allegations against the appellants, the credible alibi provided by Mirza Iqbal, and the absence of evidence showing their direct involvement in the crime. The final outcome was that the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the charges against Mirza Iqbal and Shamima Bano, and setting aside the High Court's order.

case_name: Mita India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mahendra Jain
text: Case: Mita India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mahendra Jain. Date: 20th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the complaint filed by Mita India Pvt. Ltd. under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was valid, given that it was filed by an authorized representative who was allegedly not properly authorized to do so. The cheques issued by Mahendra Jain to Mita India Pvt. Ltd. were dishonored due to 'stop payment' instructions. Mahendra Jain argued that the complaint was not filed by an authorized person and that Kavindersingh Anand, who was given the power of attorney, had no authority to sub-delegate that power to Ripanjit Singh Kohli, the authorized representative who filed the complaint. The High Court set aside the orders of the trial court and the revisional court, holding that the complaint was not maintainable as it was not filed by a properly authorized person. The Supreme Court held that the power of attorney holder, Kavindersingh Anand, was authorized to sub-delegate his powers to Ripanjit Singh Kohli based on the specific clause in the power of attorney, making the filing of the complaint valid. The Supreme Court relied on principles stating that filing a complaint through a power of attorney holder is legal if the holder has due knowledge of the transactions and that such a holder can depose and verify on oath if they have witnessed the transaction. The Supreme Court found that Kavindersingh Anand had personal knowledge of the transactions, as evidenced by his affidavit, making him competent to depose on behalf of the company. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and restored the orders of the trial court and the revisional court, allowing the complaint filed by the authorized representative to proceed. The Supreme Court directed that the complaint filed by Mita India Pvt. Ltd. through its authorized representative was valid and should be maintained, as it complied with the legal requirements for filing through a power of attorney holder.

case_name: Mohammed Abdul Wahid vs Nilofer & Anr.
text: Case: Mohammed Abdul Wahid vs Nilofer & Anr.. Date: 14th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether a party to a suit, such as the plaintiff or defendant, can be treated as a witness and be subject to the same rules of evidence and cross-examination as other witnesses in the suit. The High Court concluded that a party to a suit, such as the plaintiff or defendant, cannot be equated with a witness. The provisions of Order VII Rule 14(4), Order VIII Rule 1-A(4)(a), and Order XIII Rule 1(3)(a) of the Civil Procedure Code apply only to witnesses, not to parties. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, holding that there is no difference between a party to a suit acting as a witness and other witnesses in terms of the rules of evidence and cross-examination. The Supreme Court ruled that documents can be produced during the cross-examination of both parties to a suit and other witnesses without seeking prior leave of the court, as long as they are intended to refresh the memory or confront the witness. The Supreme Court reasoned that allowing documents to be produced during cross-examination helps to uncover the truth and ensures that the process of cross-examination remains effective and potent. The Court emphasized that both parties and witnesses should be subject to the same rules to maintain fairness. The Supreme Court emphasized that the role of a judge is to hearken to the evidence, ask questions to clear up any overlooked or obscure points, ensure that advocates behave properly, and exclude irrelevancies. The judge must remain impartial and not assume the role of an advocate.

text: Case: Mohammed Salim (D) Through LRS. & Ors. vs. Shamsudeen (D) Through LRS. & Ors.. Date: 22nd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the entitlement of Shamsudeen to a share in the property of Mohammed Ilias, his alleged father, and the legality of the marriage between Mohammed Ilias and Valliamma (Souda Beebi). The respondent, Shamsudeen, claimed that Valliamma was the legally wedded wife of Mohammed Ilias and that he was their son, entitling him to a share in Mohammed Ilias's property. The respondent presented a birth register extract (Exhibit A3) indicating that he was the son of Mohammed Ilias and Valliamma, and a specific pleading that Mohammed Ilias and Valliamma lived together as husband and wife. The appellants argued that Valliamma was not the legally wedded wife of Mohammed Ilias as she was a Hindu at the time of marriage and had not converted to Islam, and thus Shamsudeen was not entitled to any share in the property. The Supreme Court concluded that the marriage was an irregular (fasid) marriage, not void, and therefore Shamsudeen, being their child, was legitimate and entitled to inherit a share in the property of Mohammed Ilias. The Supreme Court held that children born out of an irregular (fasid) marriage are legitimate and entitled to inherit the property of the father, even though the marriage itself is not valid. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's decision that Shamsudeen was the legitimate son of Mohammed Ilias and Valliamma and was entitled to his share in the property.

case_name: Mohammed Zubair vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors
text: Case: Mohammed Zubair vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors. Date: 20th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Mohammed Zubair, co-founder of ALT News, was accused of triggering religious sentiments through his tweets and was charged under various sections of the IPC and FCRA. FIR No. 172 of 2022 was registered on 20th June 2022. On 15th July 2022, Mohammed Zubair was granted regular bail by the Additional Sessions Judge. During the investigation, the charge under Section 35 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010 was added. The Delhi Police conducted a search at Mohammed Zubair's residential premises in Bangalore on 30th June 2022. The petitioner sought the quashing of several FIRs registered against him or, alternatively, the clubbing of these FIRs with FIR No. 172/2022. The Supreme Court directed that all the FIRs against Mohammed Zubair should be transferred to the Special Cell of the Delhi Police and disbanded the SIT constituted by the Uttar Pradesh Police. The Supreme Court granted interim bail subject to Mohammed Zubair filing a personal release bond of Rs 20,000 for each FIR listed in the judgement. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power of arrest must be used sparingly and with justification, and found no reason to keep Mohammed Zubair in continued custody. The Supreme Court ruled against imposing a blanket order preventing the petitioner from tweeting, stating it would be an unjustified violation of his freedom of speech and expression. The court observed that the petitioner was trapped in a vicious cycle of the criminal process, with the process itself becoming a punishment due to multiple investigations across various jurisdictions.

case_name: Mohan Chandra Tamta (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ali Ahmad (D) Thr LRs & Ors.
text: Case: Mohan Chandra Tamta (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ali Ahmad (D) Thr LRs & Ors.. Date: 12th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Mohan Chandra Tamta, who claimed ownership of a property, could evict Ali Ahmad and others who contested the ownership and claimed tenancy under a different owner. The property was originally owned by three brothers in 1872. Over time, the shares were transferred and sold, eventually leading to Lalta Prasad Tamta owning the entire property, which he later sold to Mohan Chandra Tamta. Lalta Prasad Tamta initiated multiple legal actions to secure ownership and possession of the property, including filing suits for eviction and redemption of mortgage portions of the property. The trial court ruled in favor of Mohan Chandra Tamta, confirming his full ownership of the property and decreeing the eviction of the defendants. The High Court reversed the trial court's decision, holding that the defendants' appeal was maintainable and that Mohan Chandra Tamta did not have full ownership of the property. The Supreme Court held that the defendants' appeal was not maintainable as they could not challenge the ownership findings without the original owner (defendant no. 3) challenging the decree. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, restored the trial court's decree, and ruled in favor of Mohan Chandra Tamta, confirming his ownership and ordering the eviction of the defendants.

case_name: Mohandas and Others vs The State of Maharashtra and Others
text: Case: Mohandas and Others vs The State of Maharashtra and Others. Date: 29th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants argued that the reservation lapsed as the authorities failed to acquire the land within ten years of the Development Plan's implementation, as required under Section 127. The Supreme Court found that the Section 127 notices issued by the appellants' predecessors were ineffective because a declaration under Section 126(4) of the Act had already been issued within the ten-year period. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants purchased the land in 2006 knowing it was reserved under the Development Plan and could not claim lapsing of the reservation based on earlier notices issued by the previous owners. The Supreme Court directed the appellants to wait for ten years from 15th May 2012, the date of the revised Development Plan, before issuing a fresh notice under Section 127 of the Act. The Supreme Court declined to invoke Article 142, noting that the appellants were aware of the land's reservation status when they purchased it and the case did not warrant such extraordinary relief.

case_name: Mohar Singh (Dead) through LRS. & Ors. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh Collector & Ors.
text: Case: Mohar Singh (Dead) through LRS. & Ors. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh Collector & Ors.. Date: 7th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The initial compensation granted to the appellants was Rs.70 per sq. yard by the Special Land Acquisition Officer on 1st February 1991. The Reference Court enhanced the compensation to Rs.106 per sq. yard on 6th April 1998. The Supreme Court determined the final compensation to be Rs.150 per sq. yard. The appellants sought condonation of delay due to illiteracy, poverty, inability to arrange court fees, and advice to file appeals in September 2011. The High Court declined to condone the delay and dismissed the appellants' first appeals on 9th March 2016. The Supreme Court allowed the appellants' claim for enhanced compensation to ensure parity with co-villagers, granting Rs.150 per sq. yard but without statutory interest for the delayed period. The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' claim for compensation at par with village Makanpur, stating the High Court had already rejected this claim, and there was no reason to take a different view.

case_name: Mohd. Inam vs. Sanjay Kumar Singhal & Ors.
text: Case: Mohd. Inam vs. Sanjay Kumar Singhal & Ors.. Date: 26th June 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the tenancy of the suit premises was validly transferred to Mohd. Inam after the death of the original tenant, Rashid Ahmed, and whether the premises were rightly declared as vacant by the Rent Control and Eviction Officer. The landlords claimed that Rashid Ahmed had sub-let the suit premises to persons who were not family members, thereby violating the provisions of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The Rent Control and Eviction Officer concluded that the suit premises were indeed sub-let to non-family members and declared the premises as vacant, allowing the landlords to take possession. The High Court of Uttarakhand allowed the writ petition filed by the landlords, upholding the declaration of vacancy and the order of possession in favor of the landlords. Mohd. Inam argued that he, along with his family members, was residing in the suit premises as lawful tenants and that there were no non-family members residing there. The Supreme Court held that the revision petition was maintainable and that the revisional authority had the jurisdiction to entertain the petition against the order declaring the premises as vacant. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the High Court, restoring the order of the District Judge which had set aside the vacancy order and the final order of release. The Court held that the premises were not sub-let and that Mohd. Inam and his family were lawful tenants.

case_name: Mohd. Sahid & Ors. vs Raziya Khanam (D) Thr. LRs & Anr.
text: Case: Mohd. Sahid & Ors. vs Raziya Khanam (D) Thr. LRs & Anr.. Date: 10th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the delay of 349 days in filing an appeal against the ex-parte decree should be condoned. Raziya Khanam filed the suit for cancellation of sale deeds dated 17th February 1979 and 17th May 1979 in favor of the appellants and for a permanent injunction against them over the suit land. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 16th April 1981 against the appellants for not filing a written statement despite being given ample time. The First Appellate Court allowed the appeal because it found that the minor appellant Mohd. Asid had not been properly served, and the case was remanded back to the trial court for a fresh decision. The High Court dismissed the application for condonation of delay, finding the reasons given by the appellants to be self-contradictory and not a sufficient cause for the delay. The appellants claimed they only came to know about the judgment on 6th May 2013 when a constable informed them, but this was found to be incorrect. The trial court records indicated that the appellants were present in court on 14th October 2011, contradicting their claim of not knowing about the proceedings. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because the appellants had full knowledge of the proceedings and had been negligent in pursuing the matter. There was no sufficient cause to condone the delay. The Supreme Court noted that the factual position depicted in paragraphs 6 and 7 of the High Court's order was false and incorrect but did not affect the correctness of the impugned order.

case_name: Mohini Dang vs. State of U.P. & Ors.
text: Case: Mohini Dang vs. State of U.P. & Ors.. Date: 10th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the allotment and subsequent re-allotment of a plot of land to Mohini Dang by the Ghaziabad Development Authority, including the calculation of the amount due for the land based on current market rates. Mohini Dang was originally allotted Plot No.54, Ambedkar Road, Ghaziabad, with an area of 175 sq. mtr. at a price of Rs. 2,000 per sq. mtr. as per the offer letter dated 14th October 1986. Despite an attempt by the Ghaziabad Development Authority to return the money with interest on 24th September 2013, Mohini Dang had not actually received the money. The Supreme Court proposed that Mohini Dang be allotted a new plot, Plot No.AC-15, Ambedkar Road, with an area of 207.11 sq. mtr. She would need to pay the present rate only for the excess land beyond 175 sq. mtr. while other charges would be calculated at the present market rate. Mohini Dang is required to pay the current rate of Rs. 61,500 per sq. mtr. only for the land in excess of 175 sq. mtr., and other charges will be calculated at the present market rate for the entire plot. The amount already offered to her in 2013 will be adjusted accordingly. Mohini Dang must furnish the original documents to the Authority, which will then provide a fresh calculation of the amount due within one month. She is to remit the calculated amount within two months after receiving the communication from the Authority.

case_name: Monika Kumari vs. Abhishek Yadav
text: Case: Monika Kumari vs. Abhishek Yadav. Date: 5th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue in this case is the transfer petitions filed by Monika Kumari seeking the transfer of matrimonial cases filed by her husband Abhishek Yadav from the Family Court in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh to the Family Court in Kota, Rajasthan. On 27th September 2021, the Supreme Court issued an interim order staying further proceedings in the matrimonial cases pending before the Family Court in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh. Monika Kumari sought to transfer (1) CSHM No.100 of 2021, titled 'Abhishek Yadav v. Monika Kumari' and (2) RCSHM No.950 of 2018 / Matrimonial Case No.856 of 2018 titled 'Abhishek Yadav v. Monika Kumari' from the Family Court in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh to the Family Court in Kota, Rajasthan. The Supreme Court allowed the transfer petitions, directing that the cases be transferred from the Family Court in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh to the Family Court in Kota, Rajasthan. The Family Court in Jabalpur was directed to transmit the entire record to the Family Court in Kota immediately. The Family Court in Kota was instructed to explore the possibility of settlement between the parties through mediation. The Registry was directed to send a copy of the Supreme Court's order immediately to both the Family Courts in Jabalpur and Kota for compliance.

case_name: Monthi Menezes (D) by LR vs. Devaki Amma (D) by LR & Anr.
text: Case: Monthi Menezes (D) by LR vs. Devaki Amma (D) by LR & Anr.. Date: 23rd April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Monthi Menezes (D) by LR could claim occupancy rights over 3.07 acres of land in Survey No. 119/2A1 under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961. The Land Tribunal granted occupancy rights to Monthi Menezes (D) by LR over 3.07 acres of land in Survey No. 119/2A1 after finding that the land was used for agricultural purposes and was necessary for cultivating adjacent land. The High Court allowed the writ petition, set aside the Land Tribunal's order, and ruled that the land in question, being Punja land, was not cultivable and therefore could not be classified as agricultural land. The Supreme Court found that the High Court proceeded on irrelevant considerations and ignored relevant aspects of the matter, such as the findings of the Land Tribunal regarding the agricultural use of the land in question. The Supreme Court concluded that the matter should be remanded to the High Court for fresh consideration on merits and in accordance with the law, with a request for early disposal of the writ petition. The Supreme Court ordered that the status quo in relation to the possession of the disputed land should be maintained until the final disposal of the writ petition by the High Court.

case_name: Morgan Securities And Credits Pvt. Ltd. vs. Videocon Industries Ltd.
text: Case: Morgan Securities And Credits Pvt. Ltd. vs. Videocon Industries Ltd.. Date: 1st September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the arbitrator has the discretion to grant post-award interest only on the principal sum due under Section 31(7)(b) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. On 27th January 2003, Morgan Securities And Credits Pvt. Ltd. and Videocon Industries Ltd. entered into an agreement under which Videocon availed of bill discounting facilities, and Morgan Securities disbursed Rs. 5,00,32,656. The dues remained unpaid. The sole arbitrator rendered an arbitral award in favor of Morgan Securities And Credits Pvt. Ltd., decreeing the claim of Rs. 5,00,32,656 with interest at various rates: 21% per annum from the date of default to the date of demand notice, 36% per annum with monthly rests from the date of demand notice to the date of award (pre-award interest), and 18% per annum on the principal amount from the date of award to the date of payment (post-award interest). The appellant contended that the post-award interest of eighteen percent per annum should be granted on the total sum awarded, inclusive of both principal and pre-award interest, rather than just on the principal amount. The Single Judge dismissed the appellant's petition on the grant of post-award interest, holding that the arbitrator had the discretion to restrict the post-award interest to the principal amount. The Division Bench upheld this decision, stating that since the arbitral award was not silent on post-award interest, Section 31(7)(b) of the Act would not be applicable. The Supreme Court concluded that the arbitrator has the discretion to grant post-award interest on a part of the 'sum' as interpreted in Hyder Consulting (UK) Limited v. State of Orissa. The arbitrator's award of post-award interest only on the principal amount did not suffer from an error apparent.

case_name: Mrinalini Padhi vs. Union of India & Others
text: Case: Mrinalini Padhi vs. Union of India & Others. Date: 4th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court directed the District Judge of Puri to submit reports and the temple administration to act on them. The court also ordered the formation of expert committees by the State and Central governments to address deficiencies in management, hygiene, and regulatory measures. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for a queue system for darshan, the construction of adequate toilets and cloakrooms, and the deployment of additional surveillance systems like CCTV cameras. The judgment highlights the need for structured management practices, regular audits, and accountability mechanisms, setting a precedent for better governance of major religious institutions across India. The court acknowledged the hereditary rights of the Sevaks but recommended rationalizing their numbers and providing alternative income sources, such as a percentage of temple donations, while ensuring continuity in rituals. The court directed the temple administration to improve hygiene in the kitchen and Anand Bazar, set up effluent treatment systems, and ensure proper disposal of waste to maintain cleanliness.

text: Case: Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar vs. Thamarasseri Roman Catholic Diocese. Date: 1st April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the property transfers executed by Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar's sister using a general Power of Attorney, which did not explicitly authorize the sale of property, were valid and whether the subsequent sales to the respondent were lawful. The trial court decided that the general Power of Attorney did not confer any power to sell the property and thus the transfers executed by Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar's sister were null and void. The court decreed the suit in favor of Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar. case_name: Ms. Y vs. State of Rajasthan and Anr.
text: Case: Ms. Y vs. State of Rajasthan and Anr.. Date: 19th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the respondent no. 2 accused, who was charged with rape and sexual assault against his minor niece. The appellant-prosecutrix alleged that the respondent no. 2 accused, her uncle, had raped her on multiple occasions and had been sexually assaulting her since 2014. The High Court granted bail without providing detailed reasoning, simply noting the facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions of the counsel. The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court granted bail mechanically without considering the gravity of the offenses and the fact that the respondent no. 2 accused had nearly twenty criminal cases pending against him. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court's order for lacking reasoning and failing to consider the gravity of the offenses and the respondent no. 2 accused's criminal history. The Supreme Court emphasized that every judicial order, especially those granting or refusing bail, must be reasoned to ensure transparency and accountability in the judicial process. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Gurcharan Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), which outlines the parameters for judicial discretion in granting bail, including the nature and gravity of the offense, the position and status of the accused, and the likelihood of the accused fleeing from justice. The Supreme Court noted that the respondent no. 2 accused had nearly twenty criminal cases pending against him, which the High Court failed to consider. This made the High Court's order unsustainable. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's bail order, directed the respondent no. 2 accused to surrender within a week, and allowed the appeal filed by Ms. Y. The Supreme Court directed that if the respondent no. 2 accused failed to surrender within a week, the concerned police authorities should take him into custody.

case_name: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.. Date: 24th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the condition imposed by the Railway Board circular that compassionate appointment cannot be granted to children born from the second wife of a deceased employee is legally sustainable. Jagdish Harijan, an employee of the Indian Railways, had two wives. After his death, his first wife, Gayatri Devi, sought a compassionate appointment for her stepson, Mukesh Kumar, who was born to the second wife. The request was rejected based on a Railway Board circular. The Central Administrative Tribunal, Patna, dismissed the appeal for compassionate appointment, and the High Court of Patna upheld this decision by dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellants. The counsel for the appellants argued that the issue was covered by the Supreme Court's decision in Union of India v. V.R. Tripathi, which held that a child of a second wife of an employee could not be denied compassionate appointment on that ground alone. The Supreme Court held that denying compassionate appointment to children of a second wife solely on that ground is discriminatory and violates Article 16(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits discrimination based on descent. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the authorities to consider Mukesh Kumar's application for compassionate appointment as per the extant policy, within three months. The Supreme Court referred to its own decision in Union of India v. V.R. Tripathi and the decisions of the High Courts in cases like Namita Goldar v. Union of India and Union of India v. Pankaj Kumar Sharma, which held similar views on compassionate appointments for children of second marriages.

case_name: Mukesh Kumar vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
text: Case: Mukesh Kumar vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.. Date: 29th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the failure of the Bihar State Pharmacy Council and the State of Bihar to ensure that only registered pharmacists were allowed to compound, prepare, mix, or dispense medicines in government hospitals, which was alleged to be in violation of the Pharmacy Act, 1948 and the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015. The petitioner sought several reliefs including: (i) preventing non-registered pharmacists from performing duties reserved for pharmacists, (ii) enforcing the Pharmacy Act, 1948 and the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015, (iii) creating necessary posts under the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015, and (iv) constituting an enquiry committee to investigate the functioning of the Bihar State Pharmacy Council. The High Court disposed of the writ petition by noting the submission from the Bihar State Pharmacy Council that a fact-finding committee had been constituted and its report forwarded to the State Government. The High Court suggested that the petitioner individually verify cases of illegality and report them to the relevant authorities. The Supreme Court disapproved of the High Court's casual disposal of the writ petition, emphasizing the serious nature of the allegations and the failure to exercise the powers vested under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court highlighted the importance of addressing the health and safety concerns of citizens. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to consider the writ petition afresh, calling for a detailed report from the State of Bihar and the Bihar State Pharmacy Council on the presence of fake pharmacists and the compliance with the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015. The High Court was instructed to hear the matter within four weeks.

case_name: Mukul Kumar Tyagi vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Mukul Kumar Tyagi vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 16th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the validity of the recruitment process for the post of Technician Grade-II in the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL), specifically regarding the requirement of a Course on Computer Concept (CCC) certificate or its equivalent. The advertisement specified that candidates must have a CCC certificate or an equivalent computer qualification certificate to be eligible for the post of Technician Grade-II. The appellants contended that many candidates included in the select list did not possess the CCC certificate from DOEACC/NIELIT or an equivalent qualification, and the selection process relied on self-certification by candidates without proper verification. The learned Single Judge quashed the select list to the extent it included candidates who did not hold a CCC certificate from DOEACC/NIELIT or an equivalent qualification recognized in law, and directed the Commission to redraw the select list accordingly. The Division Bench set aside the judgement of the learned Single Judge, holding that the reliance on self-certification by candidates regarding their computer qualifications was sufficient, and reinstated the original select list. The Supreme Court held that self-certification by candidates regarding their computer qualifications was not sufficient. The Court emphasized that it was the duty of the recruiting agency to verify and ensure that candidates possessed the required qualifications as per the advertisement. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the judgement of the Division Bench, and upheld the judgement of the learned Single Judge. The Court directed the Commission to redraw the select list, ensuring that only candidates with the requisite CCC certificate or an equivalent qualification are included.

case_name: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai vs M/s. Sunbeam High Tech Developers Private Ltd.
text: Case: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai vs M/s. Sunbeam High Tech Developers Private Ltd.. Date: 24th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether a municipal corporation can demolish a structure in violation of the procedure prescribed and whether the High Court can direct the owner/occupier to reconstruct the demolished structure. Municipal corporations in Maharashtra have the power to demolish structures that violate laws and are built without approved building plans or in violation of laws. However, this power must be exercised fairly, transparently, and by following prescribed rules. The Bombay High Court directed that municipal corporations must follow specific procedures before demolishing structures, including issuing a notice with a 15-day period for the affected party to reply and, if necessary, a short 24-hour notice for structures being constructed or extended without valid permission. The relevant provisions are under Chapter 12 of The Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, including Sections 337, 338, 342, and 351, which govern the erection, alteration, and demolition of buildings. Section 351 provides the procedure for addressing buildings or work commenced contrary to the Act, requiring a designated officer to issue a written notice to the owner/occupier to show cause why the structure should not be removed, altered, or pulled down. The Supreme Court did not approve the High Court's direction for reconstruction of demolished structures, stating that even if the demolition was illegal, allowing the re-erection of an illegal structure would violate the law. The Supreme Court suggested that compensation for demolished structures can be awarded and recovered from the erring officials, but illegal structures should not be permitted to be re-erected. The Supreme Court highlighted the use of Geographic Information System (GIS) for geomapping and geo-photography to monitor and control illegal constructions, directing municipalities in Maharashtra to implement this technology. The Supreme Court directed that all municipal corporations in Maharashtra with populations of 50 lakhs or more must complete geomapping and geo-photography of their areas within one year, including a 10 km radius from the outer boundary. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part, setting aside the High Court's order allowing reconstruction and directing fresh notice to be issued by the municipal corporation for proper legal action.

text: Case: Municipal Corporation, Ujjain vs. BVG India Limited. Date: 28th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the contract awarded to Global Waste Management Cell Private Limited by the Municipal Corporation, Ujjain, for door-to-door collection and transportation of municipal solid waste should be set aside. The High Court set aside the contract awarded to Global Waste Management Cell Private Limited and directed the Municipal Corporation to reconsider the bids, which led to the appeal in the Supreme Court. BVG India Limited contended that the technical evaluation by the Municipal Corporation was flawed, and it should have been awarded higher marks for technical qualifications, which would have made it the lowest bidder. The Supreme Court emphasized that judicial review of administrative actions, particularly in contract awards, is limited to checking for arbitrariness, bias, or malafides and not to reassess the merits of the technical evaluations conducted by experts. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the contract awarded to Global Waste Management Cell Private Limited, finding no arbitrariness or bias in the decision-making process of the Municipal Corporation, Ujjain. The Supreme Court highlighted that judicial review should ensure that the decision-making process is free from arbitrariness, bias, and malafides, and that the government bodies should be allowed a fair degree of discretion in their contractual decisions.

text: Case: Municipal Council Gondia vs. Divi Works & Suppliers, HUF & Ors.. Date: 28th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the cancellation of the work order by the Municipal Council Gondia due to the COVID-19 pandemic and financial constraints was justified. The High Court set aside the Municipal Council's decision to cancel the work order and held that the original writ petitioner No.1 was entitled to make the supply as per the work order dated 7th February 2020. The work order was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in financial constraints and closure of schools. The Government of Maharashtra issued a resolution advising against non-priority expenditure. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in setting aside the Municipal Council's decision. The Court noted that there were no readily available manufactured goods as per the work order specifications and that the High Court should not have issued a writ of mandamus granting specific performance of the contract. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment, but clarified that the original writ petitioners could initiate appropriate proceedings before a civil court for any damages or losses they might have suffered. case_name: Munikrishna @ Krishna etc. vs State by Ulsoor PS
text: Case: Munikrishna @ Krishna etc. vs State by Ulsoor PS. Date: 30th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves the appellants who were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of a 72-year-old man named S. Ramakrishnan in his house at Haudin Road, Ulsoor. The appellants were convicted based on the circumstantial evidence, including their confessional statements to the police and the recovery of stolen items and the weapon used in the crime. The main injury was a 13 cm x 5 cm deep incised wound on the front of the neck, which cut the jugular veins on both sides, leading to death due to shock and hemorrhage. The accused claimed that their confessional statements were obtained under the influence of liquor and were not voluntary. The Supreme Court found that the reliance on the voluntary statements of the accused was misplaced and inadmissible as evidence, as confessions made to the police are not admissible in court. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the Sessions Judge and the High Court, allowing the appeals and ordering the release of the appellants unless they were wanted in some other crime. The post-mortem report indicated that there were seven ante mortem injuries, with the most significant being the incised wound on the neck, which caused excessive loss of blood and immediate death. The recovery of the weapon (knife) and the stolen gold material were found to be doubtful and not conclusively linked to the accused. The inquest report stated that S. Ramakrishnan's body was found in a pool of blood in the kitchen, with a bleeding injury on the neck caused by a sharp weapon, and the cupboards in the living room were open with Rs. 3000 missing. The Supreme Court emphasized that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the entire chain of evidence must be complete, and the conclusions must point towards the culpability of the accused without any reasonable doubt, following well-established principles of criminal jurisprudence. The Supreme Court criticized the lower courts for ignoring established principles of criminal jurisprudence, relying on inadmissible evidence, and failing to scrutinize the circumstantial evidence properly.

text: Case: Munshiya (Dead) Thr LRs vs State of U.P. & Ors. Date: 17th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The issue was whether the appellants were entitled to land compensation at the rate granted to adjacent landowners for the same acquisition notification. The High Court remanded their cases to the Reference Court for fresh consideration, causing delay and uncertainty in their compensation claims. The confusion arose because references for the same acquisition notification were handled by different district courts, leading to inconsistent outcomes. This judgment reinforces the principle that similarly situated landowners should receive consistent compensation for the same acquisition notification. The Supreme Court awarded the appellants land compensation at the rate of Rs. 65 per square yard, matching the rate granted to adjacent landowners.

text: Case: Murali and Rajavelu vs. State rep. by the Inspector of Police. Date: 5th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants' convictions under Sections 324, 341, and 307 of the IPC should be upheld and whether the sentences should be reconsidered in light of an amicable settlement between the parties. Murali was charged under Sections 324 and 341 of the IPC, while Rajavelu was charged under Sections 307 and 341 of the IPC. The incident involved a verbal altercation during a volleyball match, followed by an assault on the victim, Sathya @ Sathiyajothi, by the appellants and others on 9th August 2005. Murali allegedly struck Sathya @ Sathiyajothi on the head with a hockey stick, causing serious injuries. Rajavelu allegedly tried to kill Sathya @ Sathiyajothi by delivering a neck blow with a Veechu Aruval (sharp-edged object), which was blocked by the victim, resulting in severed fingers. Murali was sentenced to three months' rigorous imprisonment under Section 324 IPC and one month under Section 341 IPC. Rajavelu was sentenced to five years' rigorous imprisonment under Section 307 IPC and one month under Section 341 IPC. The appellants sought a reduction in their sentences based on an amicable settlement with the victim, their young age at the time of the incident, and their lack of previous criminal antecedents. The Supreme Court considered the amicable settlement as a relevant factor for reducing the quantum of the sentences, even though the offences were non-compoundable under Section 320(9) CrPC. The Supreme Court reduced the sentences of both appellants to the period already undergone, considering the amicable settlement and other factors. The Supreme Court ordered the release of Murali and Rajavelu, setting them free and discharging their bail bonds.

case_name: Murugan & Ors. vs. Kesava Gounder (Dead) Thr. LRs & Ors.
text: Case: Murugan & Ors. vs. Kesava Gounder (Dead) Thr. LRs & Ors.. Date: 25th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court held that the release deed executed by Lakshmi Ammal did not specifically refer to the alienations made by Balaraman, thus failing to repudiate the sale deeds. The Court directed that any claim on voidable sale deeds must include a prayer to set aside the sale deeds, failing which the suit would not be maintainable. The Court emphasized that void transactions are null from the outset, whereas voidable transactions remain valid until they are annulled by appropriate legal action. The Court held that Article 60, which provides a three-year limitation period for setting aside transfers by a guardian, was applicable, rather than Article 65, which allows 12 years for claims based on title. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming that the suit was barred by limitation and the plaintiffs failed to properly frame their claims by not seeking to set aside the sale deeds.

case_name: Murugan vs. State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: Murugan vs. State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 2nd May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Murugan was charged under Sections 364 and 302/34 of the IPC for kidnapping and murder. The prosecution's case was that Murugan, along with his cousin Kumar, kidnapped and murdered Geetha's father, Murugan, because Kumar's proposal to marry Geetha was not accepted by her father. The motive behind the murder was that Kumar held a grudge against Geetha's father for not agreeing to his proposal to marry Geetha. The High Court dismissed Murugan's appeal and confirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Additional Sessions Judge. The Supreme Court upheld the findings of the lower courts, stating that the concurrent findings were based on due appreciation of evidence and did not warrant interference. The prosecution presented evidence including the testimony of witnesses, the motive for the crime, and the recovery of the murder weapon and other incriminating items. Geetha's testimony was crucial as she witnessed her father being with Murugan and Kumar on the night of the murder and found his body the next morning. Murugan's defense argued that the evidence was circumstantial and did not conclusively prove his involvement in the crime. The Supreme Court viewed the 'last seen' theory as a strong circumstance against Murugan, as he was last seen with the deceased shortly before the murder occurred. The Supreme Court dismissed Murugan's appeal, upholding his conviction and the sentences of life imprisonment and seven years for the respective charges.

case_name: Musstt Rehana Begum vs. State of Assam & Anr
text: Case: Musstt Rehana Begum vs. State of Assam & Anr. Date: 21st January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary allegation was that Musstt Rehana Begum married the second respondent while having a subsisting marriage with another person named Shoukat Ali, thereby committing an offence under Section 495 of the IPC. Musstt Rehana Begum claimed that her marriage with the second respondent occurred on 11th January 1996 and that the allegations of a prior subsisting marriage were false. She also stated that the complaint was a counter-blast to her own complaint against the second respondent for matrimonial abuse. The Family Court declared that the second respondent failed to prove the alleged prior marriage of Musstt Rehana Begum with Shoukat Ali, and hence, the divorce purportedly given by the second respondent was null and void. The Gauhati High Court dismissed the petition under Section 482 of the CrPC, stating that the matter of the alleged prior marriage was highly contentious and required trial. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision and quashed the complaint, ruling that allowing the criminal proceeding to continue would constitute an abuse of process, given the Family Court's conclusive findings. The Supreme Court quashed the complaint on the grounds that the Family Court had conclusively determined that Musstt Rehana Begum did not have a subsisting prior marriage, and this finding had attained finality. The Supreme Court emphasized that quashing of FIRs and complaints should be done sparingly and only in the rarest of rare cases where the continuation of proceedings would result in manifest injustice. Musstt Rehana Begum had lodged a complaint against the second respondent for matrimonial abuse and alleged that the second respondent had produced a forged divorce certificate. The Supreme Court noted that the matter of the forged divorce certificate was part of the ongoing disputes between the parties and highlighted that the Family Court's decision on the invalidity of the divorce had already been made. The Supreme Court stated that the findings of the Family Court, which had jurisdiction to decide on the matrimonial status, should be respected and relied upon in determining the validity of the criminal complaint. The Supreme Court highlighted that the power under Section 482 of CrPC should be exercised with caution and only to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

case_name: N. Jayasree & Ors. vs. Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd.
text: Case: N. Jayasree & Ors. vs. Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd.. Date: 25th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the appropriate amount of compensation payable to the appellants for the death of N. Venugopalan Nair in a motor vehicle accident, which was reduced by the High Court of Kerala from the amount initially awarded by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT). The MACT awarded a total sum of Rs.74,50,971/- to the appellants with interest at 7.5% per annum from the date of the claim petition until realization. This included Rs.73,18,971/- for loss of dependency, based on the deceased's annual salary and a multiplier of '11', after deducting one-fourth of the income towards personal expenses. The High Court reduced the compensation to Rs.48,39,728/- by applying a split multiplier, fixing the deceased's monthly income at Rs.40,000/- and deducting one-third for personal expenses. It awarded separate amounts for pre-retiral and post-retiral periods and excluded the deceased's mother-in-law as a legal representative. The Supreme Court held that the mother-in-law of the deceased, who was residing with him and dependent on him for maintenance, should be considered a legal representative under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Therefore, she was entitled to maintain a claim petition. The Supreme Court decided that the High Court was not justified in applying a split multiplier. The Court emphasized that a standard multiplier should be used to avoid discrepancies and followed the guidelines set in previous judgments such as Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi. The Supreme Court awarded a total compensation of Rs.85,81,815/- to the appellants, including amounts for loss of dependency, loss of estate, funeral expenses, spousal consortium, and parental consortium, with interest at 7.5% per annum from the date of the claim petition until realization.

case_name: N. Manogar & Anr. vs The Inspector of Police & Ors.
text: Case: N. Manogar & Anr. vs The Inspector of Police & Ors.. Date: 16th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in reversing the Trial Court's decision and impleading the appellants as accused persons under Section 319 of the CrPC. The sections involved were Sections 452, 294(b), 323, and 506(1) of the Indian Penal Code. The complaint alleged that the respondents trespassed into the complainant's home, assaulted the complainant and her son, made vulgar comments, and issued threats. The Trial Court rejected the application because there was no specific evidence or allegations against the appellants in the original complaint or during the examination of witnesses. The High Court reversed the decision on the grounds that the statements and examination-in-chief of the prosecution witnesses provided sufficient prima facie evidence to implead the appellants as accused persons. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power under Section 319 of the CrPC is discretionary and extraordinary, to be exercised sparingly and only when there is strong and cogent evidence against a person. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and reinstated the Trial Court's decision to not implead the appellants as accused persons. The Supreme Court's ruling limits the prosecution's case to the original accused, as it prevents the addition of the appellants as accused persons based on insufficient evidence. The decision reinforces the need for strong and cogent evidence before exercising the discretionary power under Section 319, which may result in more stringent scrutiny of such applications in the future. The Supreme Court found that the evidence against the appellants was vague and omnibus, and did not meet the threshold of strong and cogent evidence required for their impleadment as accused persons. The Supreme Court referred to the legal precedent set by the constitution bench in Hardeep Singh v State of Punjab, which outlines the principles for exercising jurisdiction under Section 319 of the CrPC.

case_name: N. Raghavender vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
text: Case: N. Raghavender vs. State of Andhra Pradesh. Date: 13th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. N. Raghavender worked as a Branch Manager in Sri Rama Grameena Bank, Nizamabad Branch from May, 1990 to September, 1995. N. Raghavender was charged under Sections 409, 420, and 477A of the IPC, and Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The Andhra Pradesh High Court dismissed N. Raghavender's appeal against his conviction by the Special Judge, CBI Cases, Hyderabad. The primary allegation was that N. Raghavender abused his position and conspired with others to allow unauthorized withdrawals from the bank accounts, causing a loss to the bank. N. Raghavender allegedly issued loose-leaf cheques and made withdrawals without recording them in the bank's ledger, thus hiding the transactions. The prosecution's evidence included audit reports, testimony from bank officials, and documentary evidence showing unauthorized withdrawals and falsification of records. The defense argued that the premature encashment of FDRs was done with the written request and authorization of the depositor, B. Satyajit Reddy. The court concluded that the appellant had prematurely encashed the FDRs without the proper authorization from the depositor and used the funds for unauthorized transactions. N. Raghavender was sentenced to a total of five years of rigorous imprisonment with various fines for each offence. The main pieces of evidence included audit reports, testimony from bank officials and the auditor, and documentary evidence such as bank records and cheques. The co-accused included a clerk-cum-cashier at the bank and the treasurer of Nishita Educational Academy, who were alleged to have conspired with N. Raghavender in the unauthorized transactions.

case_name: N. Vijayakumar vs. State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: N. Vijayakumar vs. State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 3rd February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. N. Vijayakumar was convicted of offences under Sections 7, 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. N. Vijayakumar was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a penalty of Rs.5000/-. N. Vijayakumar was charged with demanding and accepting illegal gratification of Rs.500/- and a cell phone from Thiru D. Gopal, a Supervisor in a Voluntary Service Organisation called Neat And Clean Service Squad (NACSS), for processing an application for the extension of a sanitation contract. The trial court acquitted N. Vijayakumar on the basis of material contradictions in the testimonies of key witnesses and the absence of proof beyond reasonable doubt regarding the demand and acceptance of the bribe. The appellant's counsel argued that the trial court's judgement was a 'possible view' supported by valid reasons and that the High Court reversed the acquittal without providing cogent reasons, which was not justified. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision erroneous due to material contradictions in witness testimonies, lack of evidence proving the demand and acceptance of the bribe, and the absence of a finding that the trial court's view was not possible. The appellant's counsel highlighted that the High Court's subsequent judgement and conviction for the offence under Section 7 of the Act dated 22.09.2020 and 29.09.2020 was in violation of Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the impugned judgements of conviction dated 28.08.2020 and 22.09.2020, and ordered the release of N. Vijayakumar from custody unless required in connection with any other case. A conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act casts a social stigma on the person in society and has serious consequences on their service rendered. The Supreme Court emphasized that a trial court's acquittal should only be reversed if the conclusion recorded by the trial court is not a possible view, even if the High Court disagrees with the trial court's assessment.

case_name: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha
text: Case: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha. Date: 18th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Family Court proceedings filed by the respondent-husband in Vellore should be transferred to the Family Court in Chennai at the request of the appellant-wife. N.C.V. Aishwarya requested the transfer because she resides in Chennai with her aged parents, who cannot accompany her to Vellore. She has no independent income and is dependent on her parents. The appellant had filed a petition for restitution of conjugal rights and another petition for maintenance under Section 125 of the Cr.P.C. in the Family Court at Chennai. The High Court rejected the transfer petition filed by the appellant, stating that she could travel to Vellore for the court proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the transfer of the case from the Family Court, Vellore, to the Family Court, Chennai. The Supreme Court considered the convenience of the wife, the economic soundness, social strata, and the practical difficulties she would face in traveling to Vellore, along with the desirability of clubbing all related proceedings in one jurisdiction. The Supreme Court directed that the pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of along with the main order.

case_name: N.S. Nandiesha Reddy vs. Kavitha Mahesh
text: Case: N.S. Nandiesha Reddy vs. Kavitha Mahesh. Date: 3rd August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the election of N.S. Nandiesha Reddy from the 151 K.R. Pura Legislative Assembly constituency in Bangalore Urban District should be declared void under Section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The High Court of Karnataka declared the election of N.S. Nandiesha Reddy void and directed the Registrar General to register a complaint against Ashok Mensinkai, the Returning Officer, for giving false evidence before the court. The allegations against Ashok Mensinkai were that he gave false evidence before the court during the election petition proceedings, which led to the direction for his prosecution under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The Supreme Court found that the learned Judge did not provide a definite finding of deliberate falsehood by the Returning Officer and that there was no material to indicate intentional false evidence. Consequently, the direction for prosecution was set aside. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal by N.S. Nandiesha Reddy as infructuous and allowed the appeal by Ashok Mensinkai, setting aside the direction for his prosecution under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code. The Supreme Court's ruling emphasized the importance of ensuring that findings of falsehood or perjury in court proceedings must be supported by clear and deliberate evidence, and that actions against public servants, like Returning Officers, must be justified and not taken lightly.

case_name: NEW OKHLA INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. LT. COL. J.B. KUCHHAL (DEAD) THROUGH LRS. AND ORS.
text: Case: NEW OKHLA INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. LT. COL. J.B. KUCHHAL (DEAD) THROUGH LRS. AND ORS.. Date: 5th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the legality of land acquisition notifications and whether the acquisition of land by the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) was valid under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The State Government issued a preliminary notification on 30th November 1989 under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, proposing to acquire 57.218 acres of land in Village-Bhagel Begumpur. This was followed by a final notification on 16th June 1990 under Section 6(1) of the Act. The High Court quashed the acquisition notifications, citing the Supreme Court's judgment in Daya Ram Tyagi's case, which found the exercise of powers under Section 17 and the dispensation of inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act to be illegal.
