case_name: Prahlad vs. State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Prahlad vs. State of Rajasthan. Date: 14th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Prahlad was charged with offenses under Section 302 IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act for the rape and murder of a minor girl. The prosecution's case was that Prahlad took the minor girl on the pretext of giving her chocolates, and later her body was found with injuries, leading to charges of rape and murder. The trial court convicted Prahlad under Section 302 IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the POCSO Act, sentencing him to capital punishment. The High Court confirmed the trial court's judgement and upheld the death sentence imposed on Prahlad. Prahlad's counsel argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence that was not duly proved, the chain of circumstances was incomplete, and the imposition of capital punishment was not justified. The Supreme Court found ample material against Prahlad to convict him under Section 302 IPC but noted that the evidence did not support a conviction under Sections 3 and 4 of the POCSO Act. The postmortem report revealed five injuries on the victim's thighs, leg, nose, and wrist, and the cause of death was due to hemorrhage shock. No signs of sexual assault were found. The Supreme Court set aside the death sentence and the conviction under the POCSO Act, sentencing Prahlad to life imprisonment for the offense under Section 302 IPC. The Supreme Court considered Prahlad's young age, lack of criminal background, and the probability of his reform and rehabilitation, concluding that the case did not fall under the 'rarest of rare' category. The Supreme Court emphasized that the death penalty should only be imposed in the 'rarest of rare' cases when the alternative option is unquestionably foreclosed, following the guidelines in the case of Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab. The Supreme Court found no reliable material to support the charges under Sections 3 and 4 of the POCSO Act, giving Prahlad the benefit of doubt for these offenses.

case_name: Prakash Corporates vs. Dee Vee Projects Limited
text: Case: Prakash Corporates vs. Dee Vee Projects Limited. Date: 14th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellant (Prakash Corporates) could be granted further time to file its written statement in a commercial suit after the statutory period of 120 days had expired. The two public contract works involved were the 'Construction of Two Laning with Hard Shoulder of Tara-Premnagar-Ramanunjnagar Road Section' and the 'Rehabilitation and Upgradation of NH 111' in Chhattisgarh. The High Court declined to interfere because it held that the Commercial Court had correctly applied the provisions of Order VIII Rule 1 of CPC, as amended by the Commercial Courts Act, which mandated that the defendant's right to file the written statement was forfeited after 120 days. The appellant argued that the period of limitation should be extended in light of the Supreme Court's orders in Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3 of 2020, which extended the period of limitation due to the difficulties caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The Supreme Court held that the orders passed in Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3 of 2020 were applicable, and therefore, the period of limitation for filing the written statement was extended due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the High Court and the Commercial Court, and granted the appellant the opportunity to file the written statement, considering the extraordinary circumstances caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

case_name: Prakash Gupta vs. Securities and Exchange Board of India
text: Case: Prakash Gupta vs. Securities and Exchange Board of India. Date: 23rd July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appeal is against the rejection of an application for compounding an offence under Section 24A of the SEBI Act by the Additional Sessions Judge and subsequently affirmed by the High Court of Delhi. Prakash Gupta was the director and promoter of Ideal Hotels & Industries Limited, which owns a 3-star hotel in Varanasi. In 1995, Ideal Hotels & Industries Limited made an IPO inviting a subscription to 38 lakh equity shares at a par value of Rs 10 per share, aggregating to Rs 380 lakhs. The main allegations were price rigging and insider trading in the shares of Ideal Hotels & Industries Limited, and misutilization of IPO proceeds to purchase its own shares through related entities. SEBI's High Powered Advisory Committee recommended that the offences should not be compounded, and this recommendation was communicated to the Trial Judge. The Supreme Court held that compounding of offences under Section 24A does not require SEBI's consent and remanded the matter back to the Trial Court for reconsideration of the compounding application.

case_name: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar vs. The State of Maharashtra & Anr.
text: Case: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar vs. The State of Maharashtra & Anr.. Date: 21st August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the First Information Report (FIR) against Pramod Suryabhan Pawar for offences under Sections 376, 417, 504, and 506(2) of the IPC and Sections 3(1)(u), (w), and 3(2)(vii) of the SC/ST Act should be quashed. The complainant alleged that Pramod Suryabhan Pawar had promised to marry her and engaged in sexual intercourse with her under this false promise, which she later realized was not genuine. The complainant and Pramod Suryabhan Pawar had known each other since 1998 and had an intimate relationship starting in 2004, with multiple instances of cohabitation and sexual intercourse based on the promise of marriage. Pramod Suryabhan Pawar's defense argued that the relationship was consensual and that the promise of marriage was not false or made in bad faith, and that the complainant was aware of the obstacles to their marriage. The Supreme Court observed that 'consent' under Section 375 of the IPC involves an active understanding of the circumstances and consequences, and that a false promise of marriage must be made in bad faith to vitiate consent. The Supreme Court found that the complainant was aware of the obstacles to the marriage since 2008 and continued to engage in the relationship, indicating that the promise of marriage was not made in bad faith. The Supreme Court found that the allegations regarding WhatsApp messages and words uttered did not constitute offences under the SC/ST Act, as they were not in public view and did not involve assault or domination. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in Bhajan Lal, which provided illustrative examples of where quashing of an FIR may be appropriate, including where allegations do not constitute any offence. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the FIR dated 17th May 2016 against Pramod Suryabhan Pawar, finding no merit in the allegations. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 482 CrPC should be used sparingly and with caution to prevent abuse of the process of law and to ensure that justice is served.

case_name: Pratap Singh @ Pikki vs. State of Uttarakhand
text: Case: Pratap Singh @ Pikki vs. State of Uttarakhand. Date: 12th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellant was a juvenile at the time of the incident on 18th June 1995 and whether his conviction under Section 304 Part II/34 IPC was justified. The charges included offences under Sections 147, 148, 302/149, and 323/149 IPC. The trial court convicted Pratap Singh @ Pikki and Vikas Kirola under Section 304 Part II/34 IPC and sentenced them to 10 years rigorous imprisonment. Pratap Singh @ Pikki argued that he was a juvenile at the time of the incident, based on a birth certificate obtained later which showed his date of birth as 28th June 1977. The High Court relied on the secondary school certificate issued by CBSE in 1993, which recorded Pratap Singh @ Pikki's date of birth as 13th June 1977. The Supreme Court found that Pratap Singh @ Pikki was not a juvenile at the time of the incident, as he was over 18 years of age according to the reliable secondary school certificate. The Supreme Court considered the appellant's young age at the time of the incident, his subsequent conduct, and the fact that the incident took place without premeditation. The Supreme Court altered the sentence to the period already undergone by Pratap Singh @ Pikki, noting that he had served more than three years and five months. The Supreme Court viewed the sentence as excessive and reduced it considering the nature of the crime, the appellant's age, and the lack of criminal antecedents. case_name: Pratibha Manchanda & Anr. v. State of Haryana & Anr.
text: Case: Pratibha Manchanda & Anr. v. State of Haryana & Anr.. Date: 7th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the alleged forgery of documents and fraudulent transfer of ownership of land belonging to the appellants. The main parties involved are the appellants, Pratibha Manchanda and another, and the respondents, State of Haryana and another individual. The High Court granted anticipatory bail to Respondent No. 2 in its order dated 31st May 2022. The appellants accused Respondent No. 2 of forging a GPA and executing a fraudulent sale deed to transfer ownership of their land. The appellants stated that the market value of their land was approximately Rs. 50 crores. The appellants believed the 2022 Sale Deed was fraudulent because it was based on a forged GPA, lacked a PAN number, and did not include the required Tax Deducted at Source (TDS). The appellants alleged that the Sub-Registrar's office officials colluded with Respondent No. 2 and other accused in creating the fraudulent documents. The Supreme Court found that custodial interrogation of Respondent No. 2 and other suspects was imperative to unearth the truth and ensure a thorough investigation. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail to Respondent No. 2. The Supreme Court ordered the Commissioner of Police, Gurugram, to constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to investigate the case thoroughly, including custodial interrogation of suspects.

text: Case: Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. vs. Galaxy Infra and Engineering Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 8th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue addressed was whether there was a valid arbitration agreement between Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. and Galaxy Infra and Engineering Pvt. Ltd. regarding a Consultancy Agreement dated 7th July, 2014. Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. argued that the Consultancy Agreement dated 7th July, 2014, was a concocted document, citing a CFSL report that found discrepancies in the signatures. They also highlighted that subsequent negotiations and a draft agreement indicated the original agreement did not exist. Galaxy Infra and Engineering Pvt. Ltd. claimed that despite the discrepancies, the correspondence and actions between the parties indicated a mutual understanding and existence of a Consultancy Agreement. They argued that Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. had acknowledged and acted upon this agreement. The court concluded that there was insufficient evidence to definitively determine the existence of the arbitration agreement. Therefore, it set aside the Delhi High Court's conclusive finding but upheld the appointment of Justice G.S. Sistani as a Sole Arbitrator to determine this issue as a preliminary matter. The court noted that the CFSL report was inconclusive regarding the authenticity of the signatures on the Consultancy Agreement. This, combined with other inconsistencies, led the court to decide that a deeper examination by an arbitrator was necessary. The court directed that Justice G.S. Sistani, a retired Delhi High Court Judge, would first determine whether an arbitration agreement existed between the parties as a preliminary issue. If such an agreement was found to exist, he would then proceed to decide the merits of the case.

case_name: Prem Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Prem Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 2nd September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal question addressed was whether the period of work-charged service should be included in the qualifying service for pension under the U.P. Retirement Benefit Rules, 1961 and the Civil Services Regulation of Uttar Pradesh. These rules were challenged because they excluded the period of work-charged service from the qualifying service for pension. The decision in Kesar Singh vs State of Punjab was significant because it upheld a similar provision in Punjab that excluded work-charged service from qualifying service for pension. This decision was used as a precedent in the case of Prem Singh. The Supreme Court decided that the period of work-charged service should be counted towards qualifying service for pension, setting aside the exclusions provided by the U.P. Retirement Benefit Rules, 1961 and Regulation 370 of the Civil Services Regulation of Uttar Pradesh. The Supreme Court justified the inclusion by emphasizing that excluding the work-charged service was arbitrary and discriminatory, and it violated the principles of equality enshrined in the Constitution. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was mentioned to highlight that work-charged employees are considered industrial workers and are entitled to certain benefits under this Act. The court noted that treating them differently for pension purposes was unjust. The Supreme Court dismissed the financial burden argument, stating that financial implications cannot be a reason to deny constitutional rights and benefits to the employees. The final outcome was that the Supreme Court directed the State of Uttar Pradesh to count the period of work-charged service as qualifying service for the purpose of pension, benefiting Prem Singh and other similar employees.

case_name: Premchand vs. The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Premchand vs. The State of Maharashtra. Date: 3rd March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case addressed whether the appellant's conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC should be modified based on the evidence and circumstances of the incident. The FIR was registered after Premchand fatally stabbed Nandkishor Korde and injured three others during a scuffle on 26th September 2013. The High Court upheld the Trial Court's decision convicting Premchand under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimonies, the post-mortem report citing stab injuries, and the recovery of a blood-stained knife at the crime scene. Premchand claimed he acted in self-defense during a sudden scuffle initiated by the victim and others, which resulted in injuries on both sides. The case debated the applicability of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, which deals with culpable homicide committed without premeditation in a sudden fight. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction under Section 302 IPC and convicted Premchand under Section 304 Part II IPC, citing the absence of premeditation and sudden provocation. The Court found that the act was committed in the heat of passion during a sudden quarrel without premeditation, fitting the criteria under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. Premchand was sentenced under Section 304 Part II IPC to the period of imprisonment already served, which was more than nine years. The Court emphasized that the right to private defense must be assessed considering the circumstances of the incident, including provocation and imminent danger to life. The Court observed that the police failed to investigate the injuries sustained by Premchand, which indicated a lack of thoroughness in examining the incident.

case_name: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax (Central) - 1 vs. NRA Iron & Steel Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax (Central) - 1 vs. NRA Iron & Steel Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 25th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Judgment dated 05.03.2019 passed ex-parte by the Supreme Court should be recalled due to the Applicant Company not being served with the Notice of the SLP at their registered office. The Applicants contended that the Court Notices were sent to an old address, and they only learned about the Judgment from a news clipping. They argued that their Chartered Accountant, Mr. Sanjeev Narayan, received the documents but misunderstood them due to his cataract condition. The Revenue Department argued that the dasti Notice was duly served on Mr. Sanjeev Narayan, who was the authorized representative of the Applicant - Company and had sufficient time to inform his clients before his cataract surgery. case_name: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
text: Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.. Date: 12th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the waiver of limitation as stipulated in Section 150(2) of the Income Tax Act should be read concerning the date of the issue of notice for reassessment under Section 148, especially in the context of assessments under Section 153A or 153C. The Revenue sought clarification that the waiver of limitation in Section 150(2) applies to the date of issue of notice for reassessment under Section 148. They also sought that the findings in paras 11 and 14 apply to all pending proceedings and that fresh proceedings for reassessment could be initiated based on Section 147/148 read with Section 150. The Supreme Court did not entertain the miscellaneous application, stating that the prayers sought were in the form of a review that requires detailed consideration. The Court relegated the Revenue to file an appropriate review application for the relief sought. The Supreme Court decided not to entertain the miscellaneous application because the relief sought required detailed consideration and was essentially in the form of a review. The Court directed the Revenue to file an appropriate review application to address the issues raised. The Supreme Court directed that as and when the Revenue files an appropriate review application, it should be heard and decided in the open court. The Court also emphasized that it had not entered into the merits of the present application.

case_name: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
text: Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.. Date: 24th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is the scope of assessment under section 153A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, particularly whether the Assessing Officer can assess total income including materials found during a search, and whether such assessment can include completed assessments if no incriminating material is found during the search. The Revenue argued that under section 153A, the Assessing Officer is competent to consider all material available on record, including that found during the search, and make an assessment of total income, even for completed assessments without the necessity of finding incriminating material during the search. The Assessees argued that the assessment under section 153A should be limited to incriminating material found during the search and that completed/unabated assessments should not be reopened unless such material is found during the search. The Supreme Court observed that the legislative intent behind section 153A was to bring to tax the total income, including any undisclosed income found during a search, but it did not intend to permit roving inquiries into completed assessments in the absence of any incriminating material found during the search. The Supreme Court held that in respect of completed/unabated assessments, no addition can be made if no incriminating material is found during the search, thereby dismissing the appeals filed by the Revenue. The Supreme Court relied on precedents set by various High Courts, including the Delhi High Court in the case of Kabul Chawla and the Gujarat High Court in the case of Saumya Construction, which held that no addition can be made in respect of completed/unabated assessments without incriminating material found during the search. The significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it clarifies the interpretation of section 153A, limiting the scope of assessments to incriminating material found during searches, thus providing protection to taxpayers against unnecessary reopening of completed assessments.

case_name: Priti Saraf & Anr. vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
text: Case: Priti Saraf & Anr. vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.. Date: 10th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the criminal proceedings against the second respondent under Sections 420, 406, and 34 of the IPC based on the claim that the allegations did not constitute the stated offenses. Priti Saraf alleged that the second respondent hatched a conspiracy with a broker to cheat and defraud her by breaching an agreement to sell property. She claimed that the second respondent failed to fulfill the agreement's requirements and misappropriated the amounts paid. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the grounds that the allegations constituted a simple breach of contract, which should be dealt with as a civil dispute rather than a criminal offense. The Supreme Court considered the complaint, FIR, charge-sheet, and statements of witnesses. It noted that the complaint included specific allegations of cheating and breach of trust, supported by evidence gathered during the investigation. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 482 CrPC should be used with great caution and only in rarest of rare cases to quash criminal proceedings. It highlighted that the High Court should not have prematurely concluded that the allegations were purely civil without examining the evidence in detail. The Supreme Court stated that just because a dispute involves a commercial transaction does not mean it cannot also involve a criminal offense. The presence of a civil remedy does not preclude criminal prosecution if the allegations indicate elements of cheating or criminal breach of trust. The Supreme Court referred to its judgement in the case of State of Haryana vs. Bhajan Lal, which provides guidelines on when it is appropriate to exercise inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for not considering the charge-sheet filed by the Investigating Officer, which contained substantial material supporting the allegations of cheating and breach of trust against the second respondent. The Supreme Court directed that the trial should proceed expeditiously and that the trial court should not be influenced by the observations made by the High Court or the Supreme Court regarding the merits of the case. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement, and reinstated the criminal proceedings against the second respondent, emphasizing the need for a thorough trial to examine the allegations and evidence.

case_name: Priyanka Jaiswal vs. The State of Jharkhand and Others
text: Case: Priyanka Jaiswal vs. The State of Jharkhand and Others. Date: 30th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The respondents were charged with offenses under Sections 323, 498A, 504, and 506 of the IPC, along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. Priyanka Jaiswal filed a complaint alleging harassment and abuse related to dowry demands by her in-laws and husband. She claimed physical and verbal abuse, including being forcibly restrained from entering her marital home and being physically assaulted. The non-bailable warrants issued against the respondents led to the arrest of respondents 3 and 4. The respondents filed several applications for bail and were partly successful. The High Court quashed the proceedings on three grounds: (i) the arrest of respondents 3 and 4 without following due process, (ii) the allegations in the complaint being omnibus, and (iii) the Court of Jamshedpur lacking jurisdiction. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in quashing the proceedings based on omnibus allegations. The Supreme Court noted that specific allegations of harassment and dowry demands were made against respondents 3, 4, and 8, which warranted investigation. The Supreme Court held that the Jamshedpur Court had jurisdiction, as the appellant was driven out of her matrimonial home and resided at her parental home in Jamshedpur. The Supreme Court cited the appellant's complaint stating her residence at Jamshedpur and the social marriage held there. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order quashing the proceedings against respondents 3, 4, and 8, and affirmed the quashing of proceedings against respondents 5, 6, and 7. The Supreme Court referred to Rupali Devi v. State of Uttar Pradesh to emphasize that a complaint lodged by a wife from the jurisdiction where she resides after being driven out of her matrimonial home is valid. This principle supported the jurisdiction of the Jamshedpur Court. The Supreme Court held that non-compliance with Section 41A of Cr.P.C. could not result in quashing the entire proceedings. The Court noted that at most, the non-bailable warrants issued could have been quashed, not the entire case. The Supreme Court directed that the investigation and trial should continue for respondents 3, 4, and 8, while the proceedings against respondents 5, 6, and 7 remained quashed due to lack of specific allegations against them.

case_name: Pruthiviraj Jayantibhai Vanol vs. Dinesh Dayabhai Vala & Others
text: Case: Pruthiviraj Jayantibhai Vanol vs. Dinesh Dayabhai Vala & Others. Date: 26th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involved an appeal against the High Court's acquittal of respondents who were convicted by the Trial Court for murder under Sections 302, 34, and 120B IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment. The deceased was assaulted with iron pipes, steel rods, and sticks, leading to three stab wounds and nine incised wounds while returning on a motorcycle on 1st October 2003. The High Court found inconsistencies between the medical evidence and eyewitness accounts and doubted the reliability of weapon recovery and witness testimonies. The Supreme Court found the evidence of PW-2 and PW-10 to be credible and consistent with the medical evidence, dismissing the High Court’s doubts. The report noted three stab wounds and nine incised injuries, with injuries to the head deemed sufficient to cause death. The Trial Court held that the iron rod used had a sharp edge capable of causing the injuries observed, aligning with the medical evidence. The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning flawed, stating that the acquittal was based on misappreciation of evidence and overlooking crucial facts. The Supreme Court directed the Director General of Police, Gujarat, to apprehend the absconding accused and submit a report within eight weeks. The Supreme Court held the High Court's acquittal to be perverse and irrational and restored the conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court. The Supreme Court emphasized that ocular evidence should be considered the best evidence unless gross contradictions with medical evidence make it improbable. The Supreme Court directed respondents 1 to 3 to surrender within two weeks to serve the remaining period of their life sentence.

case_name: Pruthvirajsinh Nodhubha Jadeja vs. Jayeshkumar Chhakaddas Shah & Ors.
text: Case: Pruthvirajsinh Nodhubha Jadeja vs. Jayeshkumar Chhakaddas Shah & Ors.. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Jayeshkumar Chhakaddas Shah (JCS) should be impleaded as a plaintiff in the suit concerning the sale of land by Mafaji Motiji Thakor (MMT) through a power of attorney to Pruthvirajsinh Nodhubha Jadeja. The High Court allowed JCS to be impleaded as a plaintiff in the suit, holding that his rights would be vitally affected if he were not made a party to the suit. MMT challenged the sale on the grounds that the power of attorney did not grant the authority to sell the property, and both MMT and his power of attorney denied executing the sale deed. The trial court dismissed JCS's application for impleadment, holding that he was not a necessary or proper party and that he could file a separate suit for his claims. The Supreme Court held that JCS had a vital interest in the suit and was entitled to continue the suit despite the legal heirs of MMT compromising the matter and withdrawing from the suit. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, vacated the interim order dated 06.07.2009, and allowed JCS to be impleaded as a plaintiff, thereby enabling him to continue the suit.

case_name: Pulen Phukan & Ors. vs State of Assam
text: Case: Pulen Phukan & Ors. vs State of Assam. Date: 28th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Pulen Phukan and the other appellants were correctly convicted for the murder of Pradip Phukan and the assault on Robi Phukan under Sections 147, 148, 447, 323, 302, and 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The accused were charged under Sections 147, 148, 447, 323, 302, and 149 of the Indian Penal Code for forming an unlawful assembly, causing hurt, trespassing, and murdering Pradip Phukan. The prosecution alleged that police personnel were present at the scene and did not intervene during the assault, which raised doubts about the prosecution's case. The Trial Court convicted the accused under Sections 147, 148, 447, 323, 302, and 149 IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment for murder and six months' rigorous imprisonment for the other offenses, along with a fine. The defense argued that the prosecution's case was inconsistent and unreliable, pointing to discrepancies in witness testimonies and the unexplained presence of police during the incident. The Supreme Court concluded that the presence of police personnel during the incident and their failure to intervene created serious doubts about the prosecution's version of events. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the convictions and sentences of the accused, and ordered their release, citing insufficient evidence and benefit of doubt. The Supreme Court found that the discrepancies in the testimonies of the eye-witnesses, along with the lack of explanation for the police presence, undermined the prosecution's case and warranted acquittal. This judgment highlights the need for a thorough and transparent investigation, especially when police are present during a crime, to ensure the credibility of the prosecution's case. Legal practitioners should scrutinize the role of police during the incident, challenge any inconsistencies in their involvement, and ensure that their presence or inaction does not unfairly prejudice the accused. If new evidence emerges implicating the accused, the case could potentially be reopened, and the accused could face retrial, depending on the nature and reliability of the new evidence.

case_name: Punalur Paper Mills Ltd. vs. West Bengal Mineral Development and Trading Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Punalur Paper Mills Ltd. vs. West Bengal Mineral Development and Trading Corporation Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 1st March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Section 10B of the West Bengal Requisition Act required that any property requisitioned under the Act be released by the State Government on or before the expiry of a period of 25 years from the date of requisition. For the premises in question, this period ended on 15.08.1998, obligating the State to release the premises, which was not done. The invocation of urgency under Section 17(1) and Section 17(4) was deemed invalid because the Court found no genuine urgency that justified bypassing the Section 5-A inquiry, which allows landowners to object. The urgency was seen as unjustified and not based on immediate necessity, but rather on administrative convenience. WBMDTCL was ordered to pay a sum of Rs. 100 per square foot, per month for the entire period of illegal occupation of the premises. Additionally, WBMDTCL was given four months to vacate the premises and required to pay interim compensation as determined by the arbitrator. The arbitrator, appointed as Shri Soumitra Pal (Retd. Judge, High Court of Calcutta), was tasked with determining the compensation payable by WBMDTCL for the illegal occupation of the premises without any authority of law. The Court quashed the acquisition notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act because it found the invocation of the urgency clause under Section 17 to be unjustified and invalid. The acquisition could not proceed without the necessary inquiry under Section 5-A.

case_name: Puneet Sharma & Ors. vs Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: Puneet Sharma & Ors. vs Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 7th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether degree holders in Electrical Engineering/Electrical and Electronics Engineering are eligible for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical) in the Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board (HPSEB), which required a diploma in the same discipline as the minimum qualification. The HPSEB adopted a neutral position but highlighted that the applicable regulations specified a diploma as the minimum qualification for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical). They asserted that the Himachal Pradesh Staff Selection Commission (HPSSC) was bound to make recruitments in accordance with these regulations. The High Court ruled that a degree in Electrical Engineering/Electrical and Electronics Engineering is not considered a higher qualification in the same line as a diploma in the same discipline. Therefore, degree holders were deemed ineligible for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical). The Supreme Court concluded that the recruitment rules should be interpreted to allow degree holders to be considered eligible for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical). The Court noted that the HPSEB's rules and amendments indicated that degree holders should not be excluded from consideration for the post. The key amendments included the provision that candidates with higher qualifications, such as a degree in Electrical Engineering/Electrical and Electronics Engineering, are eligible for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical). The Supreme Court emphasized that the amendments were clarificatory and intended to apply retrospectively. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment, and directed the HPSEB to process the candidature of all applicants, including degree holders, for the post of Junior Engineer (Electrical). The Court ordered the HPSEB to issue the final selection list based on the relative merits of the candidates.

case_name: Punjab State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. & Anr. vs. M/s Atwal Rice & General Mills
text: Case: Punjab State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. & Anr. vs. M/s Atwal Rice & General Mills. Date: 11th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The agreement was for M/s Atwal Rice & General Mills to process paddy supplied by Punjab State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. into rice and deliver the processed rice to the Food Corporation of India (FCI). The failure to deliver the full quantity of rice caused monetary losses to Punjab State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. and entitled them to recover 1½ times the economic cost of the balance paddy, the cost of balance bags, and applicable taxes and other recoveries. The arbitration award partially allowed the claims of Punjab State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. and awarded them Rs. 10,24,847.15 with interest payable at 21% per annum from 1st January 1999 till realization. M/s Atwal Rice & General Mills raised objections regarding the vagueness of the award, incorrect calculation of interest, lack of competence of the arbitrator to award interest, and other procedural issues. They also claimed that the decreetal amount had been fully satisfied. case_name: Punjab State Power Corporation Limited vs EMTA Coal Limited
text: Case: Punjab State Power Corporation Limited vs EMTA Coal Limited. Date: 21st September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether EMTA Coal Limited had the first right of refusal in the matter of lending of the Mining Lease after the coal block was re-allocated to Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL). EMTA emerged as the successful bidder, leading to the creation of a Joint Venture Company, Panem Coal Mines Limited, for the development of the Pachhwara (Central Block) Coal Mine. The Supreme Court, in the Manohar Lal Sharma-I case, held that all coal block allocations made between 1993 and 2011 were arbitrary, illegal, and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution, except those made through competitive bidding. PSPCL entered into a Transitory Agreement with EMTA for a limited period and later issued a Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) for appointing a Mine Developer-cum-Operator through a competitive bidding process. EMTA argued that they had a legitimate expectation to continue mining operations due to their significant investments and the long-term nature of their initial contract with PSPCL. The High Court ruled in favor of EMTA, holding that they had the first right of refusal in the matter of lending of the Mining Lease. The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 11 gives the successful bidder or allottee the discretion to adopt and continue existing contracts with prior allottees, but it does not mandate them to do so. The Supreme Court found the High Court's judgement erroneous because it forced PSPCL to continue the contract with EMTA despite PSPCL's unwillingness and the discretionary language of Section 11 of the Act. The decision could clarify that successful bidders have the discretion to continue or terminate prior contracts, emphasizing the importance of competitive bidding and proper statutory interpretation in future coal mining contracts. Parties should ensure that all contracts are clearly defined, adhere to competitive bidding processes, and understand that continuance of prior contracts is at the discretion of the new allottees as per statutory provisions. The Supreme Court emphasized plain and literal interpretation to avoid adding words or meaning to the statute that were not intended by the legislature, ensuring that the statutory language is applied as written.

case_name: Purshottam Chopra & Anr. v. State (Govt. of NCT Delhi)
text: Case: Purshottam Chopra & Anr. v. State (Govt. of NCT Delhi). Date: 7th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main accusation against Purshottam Chopra and Suresh was that they caused the death of Sher Singh by setting him on fire after pouring kerosene on him. The key pieces of evidence against the appellants were the dying declarations made by Sher Singh to Dr. Sushma and SI Rajesh Kumar, where he identified Purshottam and Suresh as his assailants. In his dying declaration, Sher Singh identified his assailants by name, stating that Suresh poured kerosene on him and Purshottam set him on fire. The post-mortem examination revealed that Sher Singh died due to shock consequent to 100% ante-mortem flame burns. The defense argued that the dying declarations were unreliable because Sher Singh had 100% burns, including on his thumbs, making it improbable that he could have given a coherent statement or his thumb impression. The prosecution maintained that both dying declarations were credible as they were recorded independently by Dr. Sushma and SI Rajesh Kumar shortly after the incident, and Sher Singh was found to be mentally fit to make the statements despite his critical condition. The trial court concluded that the dying declarations were reliable and formed a valid basis for conviction, noting that there was no evidence of manipulation or fabrication by the recording officers. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and life sentences of Purshottam Chopra and Suresh, agreeing with the lower courts that the dying declarations were reliable and that the prosecution had proven their case beyond reasonable doubt.

case_name: Purushothaman vs State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: Purushothaman vs State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 30th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in canceling the bail of the appellant-accused without providing him a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Purushothaman was convicted by the Trial Court for the offence punishable under Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act). The High Court canceled the bail on the ground that the appellant was enjoying the facility of bail and his advocate sought an adjournment for four weeks. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court's approach cannot be countenanced as it canceled the bail without giving a reasonable opportunity to the appellant to be heard on the issue of cancellation. Section 389(1) CrPC allows the Appellate Court to suspend the execution of the sentence or order appealed against and release the appellant on bail during the pendency of the appeal. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the impugned order of the High Court and restored the earlier order dated 12th January 2018, which granted suspension of sentence and bail to the appellant. The Supreme Court made it clear that if the appellant applies for adjournment on unreasonable grounds, the High Court can proceed with the appeal by appointing an advocate or considering the merits of the appeal. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in the case of Bani Singh v. State of U.P., which suggested that the High Court can appoint an advocate to espouse the cause of the appellant if the appointed advocate refuses to argue on unreasonable grounds. The decision emphasizes the necessity of giving the accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard before canceling bail, which may lead to more careful judicial procedures in future cases. The Supreme Court suggested that the High Court can refuse the adjournment and proceed with the appeal by appointing an advocate to argue the case or by deciding the appeal on merits. The ruling reinforces the rights of the accused to be heard before their bail is canceled, ensuring fair treatment and adherence to due process in the judicial system.

case_name: Pyare Lal vs State of Haryana
text: Case: Pyare Lal vs State of Haryana. Date: 17th July 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Pyare Lal, convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, was eligible for premature release under the State's policy despite having not completed 14 years of actual imprisonment. Pyare Lal was convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for murder and was sentenced to life imprisonment. The State of Haryana applied the policy issued on 2nd August 2019, which allowed for the premature release of convicts who were above the age of 75 years and had completed 8 years of actual sentence, among other criteria. The State justified the release under the special remission policy announced by the Governor on Independence Day, 15th August 2019, which allowed for certain elderly convicts to be released after completing 8 years of actual imprisonment. The Supreme Court noted that the policy did not consider the individual facts and circumstances of each case, such as the severity and impact of the crime, and emphasized that these factors should have been considered before granting remission. The Supreme Court stated that while the Governor's power under Article 161 is not restricted by Section 433-A of the IPC, the exercise of this power must be based on relevant material facts and considerations specific to each individual case. The Supreme Court directed that the matter be referred to a larger bench to decide whether a policy could grant remission without individual case review, thus setting aside the Governor's remission order and reinstating Pyare Lal's life sentence. The conditions included that male convicts above 75 years or female convicts above 65 years, who had completed 8 or 6 years of actual sentence respectively, with satisfactory conduct, could be released, excluding those convicted of specific severe crimes. The Supreme Court considered that the exercise of remission power must include a review of the severity of the crime, the impact on society, and the conduct of the convict, and not be based solely on age or time served under a general policy. The Supreme Court highlighted the need for individual case reviews even under a general remission policy, stating that each case must be evaluated on its own merits and circumstances rather than relying solely on a blanket policy.

case_name: Pyarelal vs Shubhendra Pilania (Minor) through Natural Guardian (Father) Shri Pradeep Kumar Pilania & Ors.
text: Case: Pyarelal vs Shubhendra Pilania (Minor) through Natural Guardian (Father) Shri Pradeep Kumar Pilania & Ors.. Date: 29th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit filed by the appellant, Pyarelal, for declaring a gift deed void and restraining the respondents from alienating the suit property. Pyarelal challenged the orders dated 13th November 2014 and 2nd March 2015 of the Rajasthan High Court, which allowed the revision petition filed by the respondents and dismissed Pyarelal's petition for review, respectively. The High Court allowed the revision petition on the grounds that the suit was barred by the provisions of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, and held that the suit should have been filed in the revenue court rather than the civil court. Pyarelal alleged that the agricultural land devolved upon respondent No. 3 and his sister Kushali Devi in equal shares. Upon Kushali Devi's death, her share devolved upon her children, including Pyarelal. He claimed that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 colluded with the village Sarpanch to record respondent No. 3 as the owner of the land and subsequently executed a gift deed in favor of respondent No. 1. The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the High Court, stating that the civil court did not have jurisdiction to try the suit as the relief sought by Pyarelal required a determination of khatedari rights, which falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the revenue court as per the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The Supreme Court stated that the appellant must first approach the revenue court to have his khatedari rights decreed. Only after such determination by the revenue court could the appellant seek the relief of declaring the gift deed void in the civil court.

text: Case: R. Hemalatha vs Kasthuri. Date: 10th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether an unregistered Agreement to Sell dated 10th September 2013 could be admitted as evidence in a suit for specific performance despite the Tamil Nadu Amendment Act No. 29 of 2012 requiring such agreements to be registered. The High Court of Madras allowed the revision application by Kasthuri and directed that the unregistered Agreement to Sell be received as evidence in the suit for specific performance, relying on the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act. The trial court held the preliminary issue in favor of the defendant, R. Hemalatha, ruling that the unregistered Agreement to Sell dated 10th September 2013 was inadmissible in evidence. R. Hemalatha argued that the Agreement to Sell could not be exhibited in evidence for the main purpose of the suit because it was unregistered, as required by the Tamil Nadu Amendment to Section 17 of the Registration Act. The Supreme Court concluded that as per the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, an unregistered document affecting immovable property may be received as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance, provided it does not fall under Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by R. Hemalatha, upholding the High Court's decision that the unregistered Agreement to Sell could be admitted as evidence in the suit for specific performance.

case_name: R. Muthukumar & Ors. vs. The Chairman and Managing Director TANGEDCO & Ors.
text: Case: R. Muthukumar & Ors. vs. The Chairman and Managing Director TANGEDCO & Ors.. Date: 7th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether TANGEDCO's decision to introduce a viva voce test in the recruitment process for ITI Helper (Trainee) was justified and whether the appellants who were not selected could claim parity with those who were appointed following a compromise order. The appellants challenged the recruitment process on the grounds that the introduction of the viva voce test was arbitrary and that it amounted to changing the rules of the game after the process had started. They argued that they should be given the same benefit as those who were appointed following the compromise order. The High Court upheld TANGEDCO's decision to introduce the viva voce test, stating that it was not arbitrary and was in line with the job requirements. The High Court dismissed the appellants' petitions challenging the recruitment process. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court's compromise order, which directed TANGEDCO to appoint 84 candidates, was not based on the merits of the case but rather on a compromise between the parties. The Supreme Court held that this compromise order could not be used as a basis for extending similar benefits to the appellants. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants could not claim parity with those who benefited from the compromise order, as the compromise was not based on an independent assessment of the merits. The Court emphasized that a wrong decision in one case does not justify repeating the same for others. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the aggrieved appellants, upheld the High Court's order dismissing their petitions, and allowed TANGEDCO's appeals, setting aside the orders that directed the appointment of other candidates based on the compromise order.

case_name: R. S. Sehrawat vs. Rajeev Malhotra & Ors.
text: Case: R. S. Sehrawat vs. Rajeev Malhotra & Ors.. Date: 5th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. R. S. Sehrawat was convicted of committing contempt of court by filing a false affidavit and attempting to mislead the Court. R. S. Sehrawat was sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for 30 days and to pay a fine of Rs. 25,000. The main allegation was that R. S. Sehrawat and other officials had permitted unauthorized construction and later demolished the structure, thus misleading the Court. R. S. Sehrawat presented office submissions, photographs, and reports of the demolition actions taken between March and September 2000. The Committee of Advocates found that the unauthorized structures were still intact during their site visit in January 2001, contradicting the affidavit submitted by R. S. Sehrawat. R. S. Sehrawat argued that the structures could have been reconstructed after the demolition and before the Committee's visit, and that the High Court did not consider his contemporaneous evidence. The Supreme Court observed that R. S. Sehrawat was not served with specific charges and was not given the opportunity to cross-examine witnesses, which violated principles of procedural fairness. R. S. Sehrawat was exonerated in the departmental inquiry, which analyzed the official records and supported his stand. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's judgment, set aside the conviction and sentence, and dropped the contempt charges against R. S. Sehrawat. The Supreme Court emphasized that contempt proceedings require the same standard of proof as criminal cases, where the charges must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

case_name: R. Srinivas Kumar vs. R. Shametha
text: Case: R. Srinivas Kumar vs. R. Shametha. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant-husband, R. Srinivas Kumar, was entitled to a decree of divorce on the grounds of cruelty and irretrievable breakdown of marriage against the respondent-wife, R. Shametha. Both the Family Court and the High Court dismissed the divorce petition filed by R. Srinivas Kumar, holding that he failed to prove the cruelty by the respondent-wife and refused to grant a decree of divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. The appellant-husband argued that both parties had been living separately for 22 years, making it impossible to save the marriage, and sought a decree of divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. He also offered to pay a reasonable permanent alimony to the respondent-wife. The respondent-wife argued that a decree of divorce cannot be granted on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage if either party does not consent to the dissolution. She contended that only mutual consent should lead to divorce on such grounds. The Supreme Court dissolved the marriage between R. Srinivas Kumar and R. Shametha on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, exercising its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. The Court ordered the appellant-husband to pay a lump sum permanent alimony of Rs. 20,00,000 to the respondent-wife within eight weeks. The Supreme Court imposed the condition that until the lump sum permanent alimony of Rs. 20,00,000 is paid, the appellant-husband must continue to pay the maintenance being provided to the respondent-wife.

case_name: RB Dealers Private Limited vs. The Metro Railway, Kolkata
text: Case: RB Dealers Private Limited vs. The Metro Railway, Kolkata. Date: 17th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the solatium as contemplated under sub-section (1) of Section 30 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, should be calculated only on the market value and assets or on the sum total of the market value, assets, and additional 12% per annum on the market value. The land owned by RB Dealers Private Limited was acquired for the construction of the Metro railway under the provisions of the Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978. The Appellate Authority enhanced the compensation amount to Rs. 6,20,52,215 on account of the market value of the land and Rs. 6,75,526 for the value of the structure, along with a further sum at the rate of 12% per annum on the market value and solatium at 100% on the total compensation. The High Court ruled that the solatium payable under sub-section (1) of Section 30 of the 2013 Act has to be calculated only on the market value of the land and assets, excluding the additional 12% per annum on the market value. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's decision, stating that the solatium under sub-section (1) of Section 30 of the 2013 Act should be calculated only on the market value and the value of the assets attached to the land, not including the additional 12% per annum on the market value. The Special Leave Petitions filed by RB Dealers Private Limited were dismissed by the Supreme Court, upholding the High Court's decision regarding the calculation of solatium.

case_name: RISHIPAL SINGH SOLANKI vs. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.
text: Case: RISHIPAL SINGH SOLANKI vs. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.. Date: 18th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant, Rishipal Singh Solanki, was challenging the impugned order dated 12.03.2021 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Revision No.430 of 2021. The incident occurred on 05.05.2020, where Nishant Solanki and other accused allegedly attacked Rishipal Singh Solanki's family, causing serious injuries and the deaths of his father, Bhopal Singh, and his uncle, Kaluram. The Juvenile Justice Board declared Nishant Solanki as a juvenile delinquent on 11.11.2020. The appellant contended that there were contradictions in the evidence regarding Nishant Solanki's date of birth and questioned the genuineness of the documents produced to establish his age. The charges filed against Nishant Solanki and the other accused included sections 147, 148, 149, 323, 307, 302, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant sought a medical test to ascertain the actual and true age of Nishant Solanki, as there were doubts about the authenticity of the documents presented to prove his juvenility. The application for a medical test of Nishant Solanki was dismissed by the Juvenile Justice Board on 14.09.2020. The appellant argued that the school admission form (Ex.A-8) was questionable as it included a requirement for an Aadhaar number, which was not in existence in 2009, and the form bore the signature of Nishant Solanki at the age of four, which seemed unlikely. The court noted discrepancies and doubts about the authenticity of Nishant Solanki's school documents, particularly regarding the dates and signatures. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the decisions of the Juvenile Justice Board and the High Court, which declared Nishant Solanki as a juvenile delinquent.

case_name: Rabari Prabhatbhai Gugubhai & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: Case: Rabari Prabhatbhai Gugubhai & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat & Ors.. Date: 19th April 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appointment of Drivers in the Subordinate Courts in the State of Gujarat and the appellants' non-adjustment due to the peculiar system of operation of the option applied by the High Court. The appellants argued that if the first option was not available, consideration should have been given to the second and third options since the three districts were permitted to be opted. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court had initiated a fresh process of selection for 24 vacancies of drivers and suggested that the appellants could be adjusted to any of these 24 posts. The High Court of Gujarat stated that there were vacancies available and the appellants could be suitably adjusted if the Supreme Court ordered so. The Supreme Court directed the second respondent to adjust the appellants by appointing them as fresh candidates in their respective categories. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to issue a necessary corrigendum regarding the reduction in the number of vacancies within two weeks. The Supreme Court emphasized that the judgment was passed in the peculiar facts of these cases and should not be treated as a precedent. Five of the appellants were selected under the General Category and one was selected under the Socially and Economically Backward Category (SEBC). The Supreme Court ensured that the appellants' interests were protected by directing their adjustment into the newly available 24 vacancies for drivers in the Subordinate Courts of Gujarat.

case_name: Rachit Sinha & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Rachit Sinha & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 11th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the allocation and counseling process for unfilled All India Quota seats in medical colleges, specifically whether these unfilled seats should be reverted to the States or also include deemed/Central institutions. The Supreme Court directed that after the completion of the second round of All India Quota counseling, the unfilled seats would be made over to the States. The words 'and deemed/Central Institutions' were deleted from the order, restricting the directive to the States only. The Supreme Court corrected its order by deleting the words 'and deemed/Central Institutions' from paragraph 9, clarifying that the direction to conduct the second round of counseling was restricted to the States and not to the deemed/Central institutions. The Supreme Court extended the time for the completion of the second round of State counseling for Madhya Pradesh until 15th May 2018 and for the mop-up round until 19th May 2018, due to the State's inability to complete the counseling by the original deadline of 10th May 2018. The applications for directions were dismissed by the Supreme Court, with specific extensions granted for the completion of the counseling rounds in Madhya Pradesh.

case_name: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.
text: Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.. Date: 22nd November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appellant Radha Bai's claim to a share in the ancestral property that had been transferred to the respondents, asserting that she was entitled to a share through her father Saheblal. The Trial Court dismissed the suit filed by Radha Bai, stating that the sale deed executed by Janakram in favor of the respondents was valid and binding. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the respondents, confirming the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, thereby rejecting Radha Bai's claim. The substantial questions of law were: 1) Whether Radha Bai, being a female, had the right to partition the property that belonged to Sukhdeo and devolved upon Janak Ram by survivorship. 2) Whether the suit land inherited by Janak Ram from Sukhdeo became ancestral property for Radha Bai on the date of Sukhdeo's death and Janak Ram's death. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Radha Bai, upholding the High Court's decision that the property devolved upon Janakram and Pilaram equally after Sukhdeo's death, and the appellant Radha Bai had no claim to it. The Supreme Court rejected Radha Bai's claim because her father Saheblal predeceased his father Janakram and grandfather Sukhdeo, meaning he could not have succeeded to the property. Consequently, Radha Bai, being his daughter, could not claim a higher right than her father. The Supreme Court applied the principles of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, specifically Section 6, which deals with devolution of interest in coparcenary property and the rule of survivorship. The partition in 1967 was significant because it led to the suit property coming to the exclusive share of Janakram, who then had the right to sell it, which he did in favor of his grandsons (the respondents).

case_name: Radhey Sham vs. The State of Haryana & Ors.
text: Case: Radhey Sham vs. The State of Haryana & Ors.. Date: 17th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appropriate amount of compensation for land acquired in the villages of Hansi and Dhana, District Hisar, Haryana, for the development of residential and commercial sectors, as determined by the Land Acquisition Collector, the Reference Court, and subsequently modified by the High Court and the Supreme Court. The Land Acquisition Collector awarded compensation by adopting the belting method: Rs. 12,00,000/- per acre for land abutting the G.T. Road (Delhi-Hisar Road) up to a depth of 2 acres, Rs. 10,00,000/- per acre for land abutting the Jind By-pass Road up to a depth of 2 acres, and Rs. 8,00,000/- per acre for the remaining land. The Reference Court determined the compensation to be Rs. 1,000/- per square yard, equivalent to Rs. 48,20,000/- per acre. The High Court increased the compensation to Rs. 4,173/- per square yard, relying on a precedent set by the Supreme Court in the case of Ashrafi and Others v. State of Haryana and Others. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision to award Rs. 4,173/- per square yard, noting the unsafe reliance on an older case with different circumstances. The matter was remanded to the High Court for fresh consideration. The Reference Court reassessed the compensation at Rs. 750/- per square yard, but the High Court, on 4th March 2022, dismissed the landowners' appeals and restored the Land Acquisition Collector's original awards, reducing compensation to Rs. 166/- to Rs. 200/- per square yard. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's decision and held that the landowners were entitled to compensation at Rs. 1,000/- per square yard as per the earlier judgment of the Reference Court on 31st May 2014.

case_name: Radhey Shyam & Ors. vs. State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Radhey Shyam & Ors. vs. State of Rajasthan. Date: 12th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Radhey Shyam and others were charged with offences punishable under Section 148 and Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The main incident was a political rivalry that led to the murder of Raghunath Singh by a group of Ahirs, who attacked him on 16th April 1976. The main eyewitnesses were PW-3 Krishna, the minor daughter of the deceased, and PW-4 Kanwarbai, the mother of the deceased. The defense argued that PW-3 Krishna was a child witness whose testimony needed to be scrutinized cautiously and that PW-4 Kanwarbai failed to identify any accused in court, making their testimonies unreliable. The defense highlighted that there was a delay of three days in sending the FIR to the learned Magistrate, suggesting that false implications could have been made during this period. The Supreme Court found that the identification by PW-3 Krishna was unreliable due to her confusion and the unfair procedure followed in court, making it unsafe to convict the accused based on her testimony. The Supreme Court noted that PW-4 Kanwarbai could not identify any accused in court despite claiming to be an eyewitness, which further weakened the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction of the appellants and set aside the impugned judgements, acquitting the appellants of the charges due to the unreliable identification and insufficient evidence. The Supreme Court stated that the conviction could not be sustained solely based on the alleged recovery of weapons at the instance of the accused. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for careful evaluation of the minor witness's testimony and found it unsafe to convict the accused based solely on such testimony, especially when the other eyewitness could not identify the accused.

case_name: Rafiq vs State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Rafiq vs State of Rajasthan. Date: 19th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Rafiq was appealing against the order dated 12th February 2016 passed by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur in SB Criminal Misc. Second Bail Application No. 2168/2016, which declined to grant him bail. Rafiq had been languishing in jail since 3rd September 2010 before being released on bail by the Supreme Court on 9th March 2017 during the pendency of the trial. The Supreme Court made the interim bail order dated 9th March 2017 absolute and disposed of the criminal appeal. The Supreme Court clarified that the observations made in the interim order regarding maximum punishment were subject to further verification as to the period of punishment. The Supreme Court disposed of the criminal appeal, making the interim bail order absolute, allowing Rafiq to remain out on bail.

case_name: Raghwendra Sharan Singh vs Ram Prasanna Singh
text: Case: Raghwendra Sharan Singh vs Ram Prasanna Singh. Date: 13th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the deed of gift dated 06.03.1981 executed in favor of the appellant was valid, or if it was a showy and sham transaction that did not transfer title and possession to the appellant. The Munsif, Danapur rejected the application filed under Order 7 Rule 11 on the ground that determining the question of limitation required oral evidence and thus could only be adjudicated after both parties had led their evidence. The appellant filed a revision application before the High Court because the Munsif, Danapur had rejected the appellant's application under Order 7 Rule 11, which sought to reject the plaint on the grounds that the suit was barred by the law of limitation. The High Court dismissed the revision application and confirmed the order of the Munsif, Danapur, which had rejected the appellant's application under Order 7 Rule 11. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of both the High Court and the Munsif, Danapur, and rejected the plaint in exercise of powers under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC, finding that the suit was clearly barred by the law of limitation. The Supreme Court rejected the plaint on the grounds that the suit was clearly barred by the law of limitation, as the registered gift deed was executed in 1981 and the suit was filed after more than 22 years, which was beyond the limitation period as per Article 59 of the Limitation Act.

case_name: Rahna Jalal vs. State of Kerala and Another
text: Case: Rahna Jalal vs. State of Kerala and Another. Date: 17th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in declining the prayer for anticipatory bail moved by the appellant under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in a case involving allegations under Section 498-A of the IPC and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. Rahna Jalal was charged with offences under Section 498-A read with Section 34 of the IPC and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, based on allegations made by the second respondent that her husband pronounced triple talaq. The Supreme Court ruled that Section 7(c) of the Act does not impose an absolute bar on the grant of anticipatory bail and that the Magistrate can grant bail after hearing the married Muslim woman upon whom talaq is pronounced and if satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for granting bail. The Supreme Court interpreted that the power to grant anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the CrPC is not barred by Section 7(c) of the Act, provided the court hears the married Muslim woman and is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for granting bail. The Supreme Court found the allegations under Section 498-A of the IPC to be vague and general, lacking details, and therefore not sufficient to deny anticipatory bail to Rahna Jalal. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and granted anticipatory bail to Rahna Jalal, subject to her filing a personal bond of Rs 25,000 and cooperating with the investigation. The Supreme Court imposed conditions that Rahna Jalal should file a personal bond of Rs 25,000 and cooperate with the investigation by the Investigating Officer. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of personal liberty and the presumption of innocence, stating that bail should be granted unless there are reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is guilty. The Supreme Court noted that the Judicial Magistrate First Class-I, North Parur, did not find any substance in the allegations against Rahna Jalal in an order dated 23 October 2020 while deciding an application under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. The Supreme Court stated that the non-obstante clause in Section 7 operates only in the areas covered by clauses (a), (b), and (c), and it does not override the provisions of Section 438 of the CrPC, allowing for anticipatory bail if the court is satisfied with the conditions specified.

case_name: Raj Kumar Bhatia vs Subhash Chander Bhatia
text: Case: Raj Kumar Bhatia vs Subhash Chander Bhatia. Date: 15th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellant, Raj Kumar Bhatia, could amend his written statement in a suit for recovery of possession, arrears of damages, and mesne profits filed by Sharda Rani Bhatia, the mother of both parties. The original dispute was over the possession of a property located on the first floor at 1/6 Ramesh Nagar, New Delhi, which was claimed to be the ancestral joint Hindu Family Property. The High Court of Delhi had set aside the Trial Court's order allowing the amendment of the appellant's written statement, which the appellant challenged in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and affirmed the Trial Court's order allowing the amendment of the written statement. The Supreme Court held that the proposed amendment was an elaboration of what was stated in the original written statement and that the High Court had overstepped its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution by evaluating the merits of the case while considering the amendment application.

case_name: Raj Kumar vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Raj Kumar vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary allegation against Raj Kumar was that he was found selling adulterated milk, with Milk Solid Non-Fat (MSNF) found to be below the prescribed standard. The Public Analyst found that the Milk Fat (MF) was 4.6% and Milk Solid Non-Fat (MSNF) was 7.7%, against the prescribed standard of 8.5%. case_name: Raja Gounder and Others Vs. M. Sengodan and Others
text: Case: Raja Gounder and Others Vs. M. Sengodan and Others. Date: 19th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the plaintiffs were entitled to partition and separate possession of the plaint schedule properties based on their claimed relationship and inheritance from Muthusamy Gounder. The plaintiffs in the original suit were Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, who claimed to be the legal heirs of Muthusamy Gounder. The appellants claimed that Appellant Nos. 1 and 3 were the son and daughter, respectively, of Muthusamy Gounder through Appellant No. 2/Chinnammal, and therefore entitled to a share in the properties. The Trial Court held that Respondent No. 2 and Appellant No. 2 were not legally married to Muthusamy Gounder and thus, their children were not entitled to a share in the coparcenary properties. The High Court dismissed the appeals, agreeing with the Trial Court's view that the marriages of Respondent No. 2 and Appellant No. 2 with Muthusamy Gounder were not established. The appellants argued that even if the marriages of Respondent No. 2 and Appellant No. 2 were void, their children should still be entitled to a share in Muthusamy Gounder's properties based on documentary evidence. The Supreme Court found that the documentary evidence, including the mortgage deed and joint patta, constituted admissions by Muthusamy Gounder that Appellant No. 1 and Respondent No. 1 were his sons, thus entitling them to a share in the property. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the lower courts and passed a preliminary decree of partition, allotting shares to Appellant Nos. 1 and 3, Respondent No. 1, and Respondent No. 3 in Muthusamy Gounder's properties. The Supreme Court emphasized that children from void or voidable marriages are entitled to a share in the property of their parents under the legal framework established by previous case law and statutory provisions. The judgment reinforces that children from void or voidable marriages have legitimate claims to their parents' properties and that admissions by the deceased regarding such children are binding in partition suits. The ruling provides a precedent that children from void marriages can claim a share in their parents' properties, supporting their legal status and inheritance rights in similar disputes.

case_name: Raja Singh & Anr. vs. State of U.P. & Anr.
text: Case: Raja Singh & Anr. vs. State of U.P. & Anr.. Date: 6th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants, who were appointed as District Minority Welfare Officers on a deputation/service transfer basis prior to the enactment of the UP Minority Welfare Department Gazetted Officers Service Rules 2001, had a legal right to be absorbed in the Minority Welfare Department. The High Court held that the appellants had no legal right to claim absorption in the Minority Welfare Department and that their appointment was rightly rejected by the State Government. The appellants claimed that their selection and appointment were made through a proper channel and selection process prior to the coming into force of the Service Rules 2001, and they were not repatriated to their parent departments after two years. The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants' appointments were not mere deputations but service transfers, considering they went through a proper selection process and were appointed before the Service Rules 2001 were enacted. The Supreme Court decided that the appellants, having been appointed before the Service Rules 2001 came into force, should be absorbed as District Minority Welfare Officers and are entitled to the corresponding benefits. The Supreme Court directed the Minority Welfare Department to process and pay all retiral benefits and pensions to the retired appellants as per their entitled position, after adjusting any benefits already paid by their respective parent departments. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, allowed the appeals, and ordered the absorption of the appellants in the post of District Minority Welfare Officer from the date of their original appointment. The Court also provided specific directions regarding the retiral benefits of the retired appellants.

case_name: Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur & Anr. vs Neetu Harsh & Anr.
text: Case: Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur & Anr. vs Neetu Harsh & Anr.. Date: 29th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Neetu Harsh, who had applied for the Rajasthan Judicial Service Examination as a General Category candidate, could be considered for the vacancies reserved for disabled candidates despite not indicating her disability status in the application form. Neetu Harsh claimed that she had inadvertently not indicated her disability status in the application form but requested to be considered under the Differently Abled category as she had 80% disability as per the certificate dated 5th July 2010. The High Court of Rajasthan ordered the appellants to consider Neetu Harsh's candidature for the post of Civil Judge-cum-Judicial Magistrate under the Differently Abled category and to provide her appointment if she was found eligible. The Rajasthan High Court reasoned that the objective of the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights, and Full Participation) Act, 1995 should be kept in view, and Neetu Harsh's subsequent representation indicating her disability should be sympathetically considered. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, stating that Neetu Harsh did not apply under the Differently Abled category initially, and her claim could not be accepted retrospectively after the selection process had concluded. The Supreme Court emphasized that candidates must accurately indicate their category in the application form and submit relevant certificates timely. Failing to do so, and later attempting to change the category, is not permissible. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order, thereby denying Neetu Harsh's claim for consideration under the Differently Abled category and upholding the merit-based selection process as conducted initially.
