case_name: Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur vs. Akashdeep Morya & Anr.
text: Case: Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur vs. Akashdeep Morya & Anr.. Date: 16th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Akashdeep Morya deserved to be appointed to the Civil Judges' cadre despite his involvement in several criminal cases. The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Akashdeep Morya, which challenged the decision of the High Court Committee that he did not deserve the appointment. There were four criminal cases against Akashdeep Morya: FIR No. 81/1999, FIR No. 75/2011, FIR No. 106/2011, and FIR No. 98/2012. The cases involved various charges including assault, cheating, and causing hurt. The Committee initially resolved not to recommend Akashdeep Morya for the Civil Judge Cadre due to his antecedents and involvement in multiple criminal cases, and this decision was reaffirmed after several reexaminations. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment that had allowed Akashdeep Morya's appointment, thereby upholding the decision of the Rajasthan High Court Committee to not appoint him to the Civil Judges' cadre. The Supreme Court found the High Court's judgment erroneous because it did not adequately consider the gravity of the criminal charges against Akashdeep Morya and the fact that his acquittals were not based on a lack of evidence but on compromises.

case_name: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corp. Managing Director & Anr. v. Ramesh Kumar Sharma
text: Case: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corp. Managing Director & Anr. v. Ramesh Kumar Sharma. Date: 16th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the civil suit filed by the workmen for a declaration and permanent injunction against a fine imposed by the appellant management was maintainable, or whether the dispute should be adjudicated under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant argued that the civil court did not have jurisdiction to try the case and that the respondents should be relegated to the remedy under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Both the learned Civil Judge, Jaipur City, and the High Court dismissed the appellant's plea that the plaint was liable to be rejected and that the respondents should be relegated to the remedy under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Supreme Court observed that the workmen had been left without any adjudication on the merits of their claims for the last fifteen years and noted that such a delay in the recourse to justice was unacceptable. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the decisions of the lower courts. It directed the Civil Judge to proceed forthwith with the trial of the Civil Suit No. 774/2005 and to endeavour to complete the trial and pronounce the judgment within six months.

case_name: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur vs. Shri Phool Chand (Dead) Through L.Rs.
text: Case: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur vs. Shri Phool Chand (Dead) Through L.Rs.. Date: 20th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court and the Labour Court were justified in awarding full back wages to the deceased workman after setting aside his dismissal order and directing his reinstatement. Phool Chand was dismissed due to dereliction of duties, specifically his continuous absence from work. The Labour Court converted the punishment of removal from service to stoppage of four annual grade increments without cumulative effect and directed the reinstatement of Phool Chand with full back wages for 13 years. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation and upheld the order of the Labour Court. The Supreme Court modified the impugned order, awarding 50% back wages to Phool Chand's legal representatives instead of full back wages. The Supreme Court noted that the Courts below failed to consider the necessary legal principles and evidence regarding the award of back wages, and therefore awarded 50% of the total back wages based on the facts and circumstances of the case. The Supreme Court directed that the amount be worked out and paid to the respondents after proper verification within three months from the date of the judgment.

text: Case: Rajbir Surajbhan Singh vs The Chairman, Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, Mumbai. Date: 29th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the disqualification of Rajbir Surajbhan Singh from the selection process for the post of Clerk in Public Sector Banks due to the submission of an outdated caste certificate during the interview. His candidature was cancelled because he could not produce a caste certificate issued during the required period (01.04.2013 to 31.03.2015) at the time of the interview. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition, stating that the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection was not a 'State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India and was not amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226. Mr. Gagan Gupta argued that the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection performs public functions and is under the deep and pervasive control of the Government, making it amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection is not amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226 as it does not perform public functions and is not under the control of the Government.

case_name: Rajendhiran vs Muthaiammal @ Muthayee & Ors.
text: Case: Rajendhiran vs Muthaiammal @ Muthayee & Ors.. Date: 3rd January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the sale deed dated 10th February 2011 executed by the first defendant in favor of the second defendant was null and void, and if the suit property belonged to the plaintiffs. The plaintiff No.1 is the wife and plaintiff No.2 is the adopted son of Arunachalam. The first defendant is the daughter of Palaniyappan, and the second defendant is the vendee of the suit property from the first defendant. The plaintiffs claimed that the suit property originally belonged to Avinashi Gounder and was inherited by Arunachalam through an oral partition among the four sons. Arunachalam later executed a will bequeathing the property to the plaintiffs. The defendants argued that there was no oral partition among the sons of Avinashi Gounder and that plaintiff No.2 was not the adopted son of Arunachalam. They also claimed that the suit property had been sold to the second defendant by the first defendant. Both courts found that the plaintiffs failed to prove the existence of the oral partition, the execution of the will by Arunachalam, and that the suit was bad for non-joinder of necessary parties. The High Court relied on Ex.A-3 (Mortgage Deed), Ex.A-4 (Sale Deed), and Ex.B-3 (Sale Deed), which mentioned boundaries, to conclude that an oral partition had taken place. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision because the evidence relied upon by the High Court related to different properties, and the findings were perverse and ignored the material evidence considered by the lower courts. The decision underscores the importance of providing clear and relevant evidence to prove claims of partition and ownership, setting a precedent for future cases to adhere to strict evidentiary standards. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, restored the judgements of the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court, and dismissed the suit of the respondent-plaintiff. Parties should ensure they provide clear, corroborative evidence proving the oral partition and relevant legal documents to substantiate their claims in future litigation. The Supreme Court emphasized this to highlight the necessity of a comprehensive evaluation of all evidence presented to establish the veracity of claims, ensuring a fair and just decision.

case_name: Rajendra @ Rajappa & Ors. vs. State of Karnataka
text: Case: Rajendra @ Rajappa & Ors. vs. State of Karnataka. Date: 26th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appeal was filed by the accused nos. 2 to 5 in Sessions Case No.162 of 2003, Fast Track Court-IV, Gulbarga, against the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 22nd February 2011 in Criminal Appeal No.1812 of 2005 passed by the High Court of Karnataka. The appellants were charged under Sections 143, 147, 148, 324, 326, 307, 302 read with 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The trial court acquitted all the accused from the charges framed against them. The prosecution examined 22 witnesses and presented 15 documents as exhibits. Material objects MO-1 to MO-13 were also marked. The High Court reversed the trial court's decision by finding the testimonies of the key witnesses (PW-1 to PW-3) to be consistent and trustworthy, supporting the prosecution's case. The appellants were sentenced to various terms of rigorous imprisonment for different offences, including life imprisonment and fines. The defense argued that the trial court's view was a possible view and that the High Court committed an error in reversing the well-reasoned judgment of the trial court. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court rightly reversed the trial court's judgment and upheld the conviction of the appellants for the offences they were charged with. The motive behind the crime was a dispute between the parties over the sharing of tapping toddy trees, which led to ill-will against the deceased. PW-1, the complainant and wife of the deceased, provided key testimony supporting the prosecution's case and was considered a truthful and consistent witness by the High Court. The High Court found the medical officer's testimony and the postmortem report consistent with the injuries described by PW-1, supporting the prosecution's case.

case_name: Rajendra Bhagat vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr.
text: Case: Rajendra Bhagat vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr.. Date: 3rd January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court erred in maintaining the conviction of Rajendra Bhagat under Section 498-A IPC despite the parties having settled their marital disputes and leading a happy conjugal life. The allegations were of demand for dowry, mental and physical torture, leading to the lodging of an FIR against Rajendra Bhagat and his family members under Sections 498-A, 323, 417, 34 IPC. The Trial Court convicted Rajendra Bhagat under Section 498-A IPC and sentenced him to three years of simple imprisonment. Other accused persons were acquitted of charges under Sections 417 and 34 IPC and given the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act. The High Court confirmed the conviction of Rajendra Bhagat under Section 498-A IPC but reduced his sentence to the period of imprisonment already undergone, taking note of the settlement between the parties. Two significant events were the sanction of Rajendra Bhagat's dismissal from military service for being convicted under Section 498-A IPC and the submission of a joint application by Rajendra Bhagat and his wife stating they had resolved their disputes and were leading a happy conjugal life. The Supreme Court found that maintaining the conviction would not secure the ends of justice, especially as it would lead to Rajendra Bhagat's loss of job and subsequent financial distress, potentially disrupting the harmony and happy conjugal life of the parties. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing all proceedings arising out of the FIR and setting aside the conviction of Rajendra Bhagat, thereby securing the ends of justice and ensuring the continuation of the parties' happy conjugal life.

case_name: Rajendra Kumar Shrivas vs. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Rajendra Kumar Shrivas vs. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 13th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court of Madhya Pradesh exceeded the 10% quota for appointments through the limited departmental competitive examination as mandated by the Supreme Court in the All India Judges' Association case. The original writ petitioners sought to quash the appointments that exceeded the 10% quota for limited departmental competitive examination and requested the court to direct the respondents to amend the relevant rules to comply with the Supreme Court's order. They also sought a departmental enquiry against the authorities who disobeyed the quota limit. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that the original writ petitioners were not entitled to seek a writ of quo warranto. The High Court did not address the specific reliefs requested by the petitioners regarding the quota for limited departmental competitive examination. The Supreme Court reiterated that from 1st January 2011 onwards, only 10% of seats are to be filled by limited departmental competitive examinations, as directed in the All India Judges' Association case. Any appointments beyond this quota are to be considered in excess and must be adjusted in future recruitments. The Supreme Court directed the High Court of Madhya Pradesh to adhere to the 10% quota for limited departmental competitive examinations from 1st January 2011 onwards. If any recruitments exceeded this quota, the excess appointments must be adjusted in future recruitments. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal, directing the High Court of Madhya Pradesh to comply with the directions issued in the All India Judges' Association case, ensuring that the 10% quota for limited departmental competitive examinations is maintained and any excess appointments are adjusted in future recruitments.

case_name: Rajesh Jain vs. Ajay Singh
text: Case: Rajesh Jain vs. Ajay Singh. Date: 9th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the respondent-accused Ajay Singh issued a cheque in discharge of a debt or liability under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Trial Court acquitted Ajay Singh of the charge under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, stating that the complainant failed to prove the existence of a legally enforceable debt. The High Court upheld the Trial Court's decision because it found that the accused had successfully rebutted the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, raising doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt. Rajesh Jain contended that Ajay Singh had issued a post-dated cheque for Rs. 6,95,204 towards part repayment of an outstanding debt, which was dishonored due to insufficient funds. Ajay Singh claimed that he had not issued the cheque in question, asserting that it was misused by the complainant, who obtained it through his sister-in-law, Gita Sunar. He admitted to borrowing money but contested the debt amount claimed by the complainant. The Supreme Court set aside the concurrent findings of the lower courts, holding that the accused Ajay Singh failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and convicted him, imposing a fine of twice the cheque amount, failing which he would undergo simple imprisonment for one year. The Supreme Court observed that once the presumption under Section 139 is activated, the burden shifts to the accused to rebut it by raising a probable defense. In this case, Ajay Singh failed to discharge this burden satisfactorily.

case_name: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
text: Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana. Date: 18th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Rajesh should be held guilty under Section 306 of the IPC for abetting the suicide of Arvind, who consumed Sulfas tablets allegedly due to harassment by Rajesh and his family members. Rajesh was charged under Section 306 IPC for abetting the suicide of Arvind, who left a suicide note accusing Rajesh, his father Laxmi Narayan, and his sister Indera of harassment and threats related to false dowry allegations. Arvind committed suicide on 23rd February 2002 after being allegedly harassed and threatened by Rajesh and his family. A suicide note was found stating that the harassment and threats were due to false dowry allegations made against him. The Trial Court convicted Rajesh, his father Laxmi Narayan, and his sister Indera under Section 306 IPC, sentencing Rajesh and Laxmi Narayan to five years of rigorous imprisonment and Indera to three years. The High Court dismissed Rajesh's appeal and upheld his conviction, while acquitting his father Laxmi Narayan and sister Indera based on the evidence and the suicide note. The Supreme Court found that the evidence did not warrant Rajesh's conviction under Section 306 IPC. The Court noted that there was no proximate cause linking Rajesh's actions to Arvind's suicide and that the allegations of continuous threats were not substantiated. The Supreme Court interpreted 'instigation' to mean that there must be a direct and proximate cause between the accused's actions and the suicide. The Court found that the evidence did not show that Rajesh provoked or encouraged Arvind to commit suicide. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in convicting Rajesh while acquitting the other accused (Laxmi Narayan and Indera) despite similar allegations and evidence against all three. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside Rajesh's conviction and sentence under Section 306 IPC, and discharged his bail bonds. This judgement emphasizes the need for clear and proximate evidence linking the accused's actions to the suicide, impacting future cases by ensuring that mere allegations of harassment without direct instigation are insufficient for conviction under Section 306 IPC. Legal practitioners should focus on disproving any direct and proximate link between the accused's actions and the suicide, highlighting any lack of substantial evidence of instigation, as illustrated in this case.

case_name: Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh vs. The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.
text: Case: Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh vs. The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors.. Date: 14th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is the custody of the minor children born out of the wedlock between the petitioner-mother, Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh, and the respondent-father, and the petitioner's request to repatriate the children to the USA in compliance with a US court order. Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh sought the issuance of a writ of Habeas Corpus to produce her minor children before the court and deliver their custody to her, to trace the children and produce them before the court, and to repatriate the children to the USA in compliance with a US court order. The US court order dated 30th July 2021 granted temporary custody of the minor children to the petitioner-mother, Rajeswari Chandrasekar Ganesh, and issued a restraint order preventing the removal of the children from the jurisdiction of the Ohio Court. The petitioner alleged that the respondent-father unlawfully detained the children by taking them to India without informing her, taking away all her legal documents, and lodging a false complaint that the petitioner was mentally ill, which prevented her from accessing her children. The Supreme Court directed the respondent-father to cooperate with the petitioner in transporting the minor children to the United States within a specified timeframe and to comply with the US court's custody order. The respondent-father claimed that the children were well-settled in Chennai, attending a good school, and that their welfare would be negatively impacted if they were suddenly taken back to the USA. The Supreme Court noted that India is not a signatory to the Hague Convention, and thus its terms are not binding on Indian courts. However, the welfare of the children remained the paramount consideration. The Supreme Court found the respondent-father's allegations about the petitioner's mental health to be unsubstantiated and noted that the petitioner had successfully managed her children's welfare and education in the USA. The Supreme Court directed the respondent-father to return the children's passports to the petitioner or to arrange for their surrender to the Indian Court or a US Consulate in India. The Supreme Court instructed that the petitioner-mother should be designated as the residential parent and legal custodian of the children, and that the respondent-father should incur all transportation costs for the children's return to the USA, ensuring their welfare and compliance with the US court order. The Supreme Court emphasized that the welfare of the children is the paramount consideration and that their return to the USA and continued education and upbringing in a familiar environment were in their best interests.

case_name: Rajinder Singh vs. Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd
text: Case: Rajinder Singh vs. Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd. Date: 24th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court directed that the compensation withdrawn by Late Rajinder Singh or his legal representatives in the original proceedings or under section 28-A should be refunded along with interest at the rate of 12 percent per annum within 3 months from the judgment date to the appellants/State, and compliance must be reported to the Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by SJVN Ltd. and directed that the question of bona fide transferees should be finally decided in the pending regular first appeal before the High Court. It was stated that if compensation had been paid to transferees, it should not be recovered until the appeal is decided. Civil Suit No.15/1970 was dismissed on merits. In the first appeal, it was withdrawn by Rajinder Singh before the Division Bench on 23.6.1986 after the disputed land was acquired by the State, and compensation was paid. The High Court allowed the withdrawal of the suit with permission to file a fresh suit if necessary. The Supreme Court observed that the principle 'fraud vitiates' was clearly applicable in this case and could not be ignored under the guise of the scope of proceedings under Section 18/30 of the LA Act. It emphasized that fraud cannot be allowed to perpetuate in legal proceedings. The court found that the land had vested in the State under the Abolition Act, and Late Rajinder Singh had already received compensation. It was not open to claim compensation again in the land acquisition case. The court held that Rajinder Singh's title to the land had been extinguished and compensation should not be paid.

case_name: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.
text: Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.. Date: 28th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in allowing the defendant's second appeal and dismissing the plaintiff's suit for permanent injunction in relation to the suit property. The Senior Civil Judge decreed the suit filed by Rajinder Tiwari for permanent injunction against Kedar Nath, as the defendant failed to file a written statement and could not adduce any evidence. The Additional District Judge dismissed the first appeal filed by Kedar Nath and upheld the judgment and decree passed by the Senior Civil Judge. The High Court of Delhi allowed the second appeal filed by Kedar Nath, set aside the judgment of the first Appellate Court, and dismissed the suit filed by Rajinder Tiwari. The Supreme Court found the trial to be unsatisfactory as the defendant was not given an adequate opportunity to file a written statement and adduce evidence. The Court decided to remand the case to the Trial Court for a fresh trial on merits. The Supreme Court directed the Trial Court to allow the respondents (legal representatives of the original defendant) to file their written statement within one month, frame issues based on the pleadings, and allow the parties to adduce their evidence, including additional documents if necessary. The Supreme Court reasoned that all contesting parties must get a fair opportunity to contest the suit on merits, and decisions rendered without such opportunity are not legally sustainable, necessitating a retrial in this case.

case_name: Rajiv Kumar Jindal and Others vs. BCI Staff Colony Residential Welfare Association and Others
text: Case: Rajiv Kumar Jindal and Others vs. BCI Staff Colony Residential Welfare Association and Others. Date: 27th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the validity of the auction process conducted for the sale of assets of M/s Bharat Commerce & Industries Limited (BCI), which was declared a sick company. The auction process and the acceptance of the bid by Rajiv Kumar Jindal and others were challenged on grounds of procedural irregularities and non-compliance with the guidelines set by the Asset Sale Committee (ASC). The allegations included the absence of a competitive bidding process, failure to indicate the reserve price in the auction notice, and the appellants' non-compliance with the ASC guidelines, specifically the failure to furnish a bank guarantee and to pay the sale consideration within the stipulated time. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana set aside the auction held on 24th May 2004, ordered by the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) as the Operating Agency, due to procedural irregularities and non-compliance with the ASC guidelines. The court restored the order of the BIFR dated 24th November 2004 and directed that the property be sold afresh as per the provisions of law. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Rajiv Kumar Jindal and others, upholding the High Court's decision. The Court found that the auction process was defective, and the appellants had failed to comply with the ASC guidelines, including furnishing a bank guarantee and paying the sale consideration in installments. The Supreme Court found the auction process defective because there was no valuation report obtained from an approved valuer, the reserve price was not indicated in the auction notice, and the appellants did not comply with the ASC guidelines. Additionally, the auction received only a solitary bid, which undermined the competitive bidding process necessary to secure the optimum value of the property. The Supreme Court directed that the money deposited by the appellants be refunded in terms of the High Court's order dated 5th February 2010. The Court also directed the Official Liquidator to take all reasonable steps to fetch the optimum value of the property through a fresh auction process.

case_name: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 6th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the premature release of convicts serving life imprisonment, as per the Uttar Pradesh Prisoners (Release on Probation) Act 1938 and the subsequent policies. The Supreme Court issued directions governing the premature release of persons sentenced to life imprisonment, emphasizing the application of the most liberalized policy for considering such cases. The premature release of prisoners is governed by the Uttar Pradesh Prisoners (Release on Probation) Act 1938, the Uttar Pradesh Jail Manual, and the Standing Policy of the State Government. The Standing Policy, as formulated on 1 August 2018 and amended on 27 May 2022, initially prohibited premature release for convicts under the age of 60, but the 2022 amendment lifted this bar, allowing for a more liberalized approach. The Supreme Court observed that the policy should be applied uniformly and transparently, and it should be based on the legal position at the time of conviction or a more beneficial subsequent policy. The Supreme Court directed that all pending cases should be disposed of by 30 April 2023, and a compliance report should be filed by the Director General of Prisons. The Amicus Curiae highlighted that the State was adopting a 'pick and choose' policy instead of uniformly applying the Uttar Pradesh Prisoners Act, 1938, and the Standing Policy for premature release. The affidavit provided district-wise data of convicts eligible for premature release, indicating that 2,228 convicts had completed 14 years of actual imprisonment and were eligible for consideration. The findings indicated that three prisoners were released, one was acquitted, one was released after completing the sentence, two had their premature release rejected, and the remaining cases were pending at various administrative levels. The directive aims to ensure that the State adopts a consistent and transparent approach to the premature release of convicts, adhering to the legal provisions and avoiding arbitrary decisions. The Supreme Court clarified that the policy at the time of conviction should govern the consideration of each case unless a more liberalized policy is subsequently instituted, ensuring fairness and consistency in decisions.

case_name: Rajnish Kumar Rai vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Rajnish Kumar Rai vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 6th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The petitioner argued that he resides in Ahmedabad after retirement, and transferring the case would avoid inconvenience and undue hardship. The Supreme Court refused to invoke its jurisdiction as the Tribunal in Hyderabad was lawfully handling the case, and the transfer was denied due to the case being in its final stage of hearing. The case was cited to emphasize that territorial jurisdiction for judicial review lies with the High Court where the Tribunal's Bench is located, and the petitioner’s transfer plea was influenced by this precedent. The Supreme Court highlighted that the petitioner himself had filed the case in Hyderabad, and transferring the case at its final stage would disrupt judicial efficiency and the Tribunal's functioning. The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petition and upheld the Tribunal's and High Court's decisions, affirming that the transfer application was not justifiable.

case_name: Rajo @ Rajwa @ Rajendra Mandal vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
text: Case: Rajo @ Rajwa @ Rajendra Mandal vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.. Date: 25th August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The petitioner, Rajo @ Rajwa @ Rajendra Mandal, was sentenced to life imprisonment for offenses punishable under Section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 27 of the Arms Act, 1959. The petitioner has been in custody for 24 years and is seeking a direction for his premature release, arguing that he has not been granted remission or parole. The petitioner was convicted for the murder of three persons, including two police personnel and a chowkidar, during a village mela by indiscriminate firing. The Remission Board rejected the petitioner's application twice due to adverse reports from the Presiding Judge and the Superintendent of Police, citing that the petitioner was involved in organized murder and premeditated killing, making him ineligible for premature release under the Bihar Jail Manual. The rule cited for rejection was Rule 529(iv)(b) of the Bihar Jail Manual, which states that prisoners convicted for organized murder in a premeditated manner and in an organized manner are ineligible for premature release. The Supreme Court directed the Remission Board to reconsider the petitioner's application for premature release, taking into account the reports of police and other authorities, the post-prison record of the petitioner, remissions earned, his age, health condition, family circumstances, and his potential for social engagement in a positive manner. The Presiding Judge was instructed to provide an opinion on the petitioner's application for premature release by examining the judicial record and providing adequate reasoning, taking into account the factors laid down in Laxman Naskar, within one month from the date of the judgment.

case_name: Raju Manjhi vs State of Bihar
text: Case: Raju Manjhi vs State of Bihar. Date: 2nd August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Raju Manjhi was accused of participating in a dacoity at the house of Kamdeo Singh in the village Banbareya, during which the assailants stole valuable items and caused injuries to the inhabitants, resulting in the death of Kameshwar Singh. The stolen items included golden ornaments, pants, and cash, with the total value of stolen property amounting to approximately Rs. 25,000. Kamdeo Singh lodged a complaint with the Moffasil police at around 2 am on the night of the incident, leading to the registration of a case under Sections 395/412 of the IPC against unknown persons. The prosecution presented the confessional statement of the accused, the recovery of stolen items, and the testimonies of witnesses including Reena Devi (PW1) and Neeraj Kumar (PW2), who corroborated the occurrence of the dacoity and the involvement of the accused. The defense argued that Raju Manjhi was falsely implicated due to enmity, there was no concrete proof of his participation, and the recovery of Rs. 400 from his possession was not sufficient to prove his involvement in the crime. The Supreme Court noted that while no witness identified Raju Manjhi, the confessional statements and other evidence were sufficient to establish his involvement. The Court held that non-identification by witnesses did not vitiate the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence of Raju Manjhi as passed by the trial court and affirmed by the High Court, finding no infirmity or illegality in the judgments.

case_name: Rakesh Bakshi & Anr. vs State of Jammu and Kashmir & Ors.
text: Case: Rakesh Bakshi & Anr. vs State of Jammu and Kashmir & Ors.. Date: 22nd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the selection and appointment of Junior Engineers (Elect) Grade II by the Services Selection Board of Jammu and Kashmir, which was challenged because the appellants did not possess the requisite qualification by the cut-off date. The Supreme Court set aside the judegment of the Division Bench of the High Court, thereby restoring the appointments of Rakesh Bakshi & Anr. as Junior Engineers, considering their long service and the fact that the writ petitioner did not stand to gain from their ousting. The Division Bench set aside the appointments on the ground that the appellants' results were declared only after the cut-off date for determining eligibility, thus they were not eligible for the posts at the time of the application. The senior counsel argued that the appellants had been working for nearly 18 years, and that setting aside their appointments would be unjust given the efflux of time, their long service, and the fact that the writ petitioner did not have sufficient marks to secure the appointment. The Supreme Court concluded that while the appellants were not eligible as on the cut-off date, considering their long service and the fact that the writ petitioner would not benefit from their ousting, the interests of justice required that their appointments be upheld.

case_name: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.
text: Case: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.. Date: 21st September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the National Law School of India University (NLSIU) could conduct a separate admission entrance examination, the National Law Aptitude Test (NLAT), instead of admitting students through the Common Law Admission Test (CLAT) for the academic session 2020-21. NLSIU issued the admission notification for NLAT due to delays in the CLAT examination caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, aiming to avoid a 'zero year' and ensure that the academic session 2020-21 could commence on time. The petitioners argued that the admission notification for NLAT was in breach of statutory provisions, as it was issued without the recommendation of the Academic Council of NLSIU. They also contended that NLSIU, being a member of the Consortium of National Law Universities, was obligated to admit students through CLAT. The Supreme Court held that the writ petition was maintainable, considering the credentials of petitioner No.2, a former Vice-Chancellor of NLSIU, who was competent to espouse the cause of legal education. The Supreme Court held that the NLAT notification was issued without the recommendation of the Academic Council, which is the statutory authority under the Act, 1986, for admission of students. Hence, the notification was not in accordance with statutory provisions. The Supreme Court set aside the NLAT notification and directed NLSIU to admit students through the CLAT examination scheduled for 28th September 2020, ensuring adherence to the statutory provisions of the Act, 1986.

case_name: Rakesh Malhotra vs. Kamaljit Singh Sandhu & Ors.
text: Case: Rakesh Malhotra vs. Kamaljit Singh Sandhu & Ors.. Date: 16th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the legality of the sale deed executed by the original defendant in favor of Kamaljit Singh Sandhu and others, and whether Rakesh Malhotra had a right to specific performance of an earlier agreement to sell the same property. Rakesh Malhotra sought a declaration that he was the owner in possession of the suit property and that the sale deed executed in favor of the defendants was illegal, null, and void. He also sought specific performance of an agreement to sell and a permanent injunction. The trial court partly decreed the suit in favor of Rakesh Malhotra, granting a decree for recovery of a certain amount with interest but dismissed other reliefs sought by him. The first Appellate Court allowed the appeal, quashing the trial court's judgment and decreeing that the sale deed in favor of the defendants was illegal and that Rakesh Malhotra was entitled to specific performance of the agreement to sell. The High Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the first Appellate Court's judgment and restoring the trial court's judgment, effectively dismissing the suit filed by Rakesh Malhotra for other reliefs. Rakesh Malhotra argued that the High Court erred in quashing the first Appellate Court's judgment and that he had paid the entire sale consideration and stamp duty, and was put in possession of the property based on the agreement to sell. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because the suit did not specifically pray for the relief of specific performance of the agreement to sell, and the issue was not framed in the trial court. The suit was also barred by limitation. The Supreme Court stated that the agreement to sell dated 20.4.1987 was not registered and was not on proper stamp duty, hence it could only be used for collateral purposes and not as a complete sale deed. The Supreme Court ordered that the original defendant nos. 2 and 3 should pay Rs.10,00,000/- ex-gratia to Rakesh Malhotra within six weeks to put an end to the litigation. The judgment emphasizes the importance of explicitly praying for specific performance in the plaint and ensuring that the issue is framed and addressed in the trial court to avoid dismissal on procedural grounds. The Supreme Court noted that the suit was filed in 2004, much later than the execution of the agreement to sell in 1987 and the title deed in 1994, making the suit barred by limitation.

case_name: Rakesh Tiwari vs. Alok Pandey
text: Case: Rakesh Tiwari vs. Alok Pandey. Date: 10th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Rakesh Tiwari was accused of criminal contempt for entering the chamber of the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) during lunch hour without permission, hurling abuses, threatening, and attempting to assault the CJM. The High Court found Rakesh Tiwari guilty of criminal contempt, sentenced him to six months of simple imprisonment, a fine of Rs.2000, and barred him from entering the District Judgeship, Allahabad for six months. Rakesh Tiwari claimed that he did not enter the CJM's chamber on the said date, nor did he abuse or threaten the CJM. He stated that the advocates were on strike, and there was no question of him entering the chamber or using filthy language. The High Court rejected Rakesh Tiwari's defense, finding it to be a concocted story and holding that he, along with 2-3 junior advocates, entered the CJM's chamber, misbehaved, and attempted to assault the CJM. The Supreme Court emphasized that advocates are duty-bound to act with dignity and respect towards the judiciary, and any behavior that undermines the authority of the court must be strictly dealt with. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction for criminal contempt but modified the sentence, suspending the six-month imprisonment for three years subject to good conduct and extending the ban from the District Judgeship, Allahabad for an additional three years. The Supreme Court imposed a condition that Rakesh Tiwari must maintain good conduct and not enter the premises of the District Judgeship, Allahabad from 1st July 2019 to 30th June 2022. Failure to comply could result in the activation of the imprisonment sentence. The Supreme Court expressed concern over the increasing tendency of advocates to make scurrilous allegations against judicial officers and emphasized the need to curb such behavior to maintain the dignity and authority of the judiciary. The Supreme Court's ruling underscored the importance of professional ethics and conduct for advocates, reinforcing that misconduct and attempts to intimidate or undermine the judiciary would be met with strict disciplinary action. The Supreme Court modified the sentence to balance the need for punishment with an opportunity for reform, considering the seriousness of the misconduct while allowing for the suspension of imprisonment contingent on good behavior.

case_name: Ram Chandra vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors.
text: Case: Ram Chandra vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors.. Date: 10th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the legality of Ram Chandra's appointment as a Lecturer (Geology) and subsequent promotion to Reader, which were challenged based on procedural irregularities. The Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court dismissed Ram Chandra's writ petition, upholding the Chancellor's decision to terminate his services due to procedural irregularities in his appointment. The procedural irregularities included the failure of the University to seek nomination of subject experts from the Chancellor for the Selection Committee, which was required by Section 31 of the Uttar Pradesh State Universities Act, 1973. The Hon'ble Chancellor initiated a suo motu enquiry under Section 68 of the 1973 Act and found that Ram Chandra's appointment was not in accordance with the law, leading to the cancellation of his appointments and promotion. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and the Chancellor's order, finding that Ram Chandra's selection process had indeed followed the required procedures, including the presence of Chancellor's nominees in the Selection Committee. The Supreme Court directed that Ram Chandra's termination be set aside and that he be entitled to all terminal benefits as if he had been in continuous service from the date of termination to the date of his retirement, without back wages. The Supreme Court clarified that the presence of two Chancellor's nominees in the Selection Committee was sufficient to satisfy the statutory requirement, and any procedural lapses by the University should not adversely affect Ram Chandra. This decision may ensure stricter adherence to procedural requirements in faculty appointments and reinforce the importance of following statutory provisions to avoid similar disputes. Universities should ensure that Selection Committees are properly constituted with the required subject experts nominated by the Chancellor to avoid procedural challenges and ensure compliance with statutory provisions. The Supreme Court noted that the presence of Chancellor's nominees in the Selection Committee was crucial for validating the selection process, and their absence or procedural lapses by the University should not invalidate the appointment. Universities might implement more rigorous procedures for forming Selection Committees, ensuring timely nominations of subject experts by the Chancellor and strict adherence to statutory requirements to prevent future legal challenges.

case_name: Ram Kishan (Deceased) through Legal Representatives & Anr. vs. Manish Kumar & Anr.
text: Case: Ram Kishan (Deceased) through Legal Representatives & Anr. vs. Manish Kumar & Anr.. Date: 24th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Civil Suit No. 759 of 2018 could be dismissed in light of the Supreme Court's order in Praveen Kumar v. Delhi Cantonment Board, and whether the deletion of issues related to jurisdiction and statutory bars was valid. The appellant contended that the Civil Suit could not proceed due to the Supreme Court's order in Praveen Kumar's case, which directed the Delhi Cantonment Board to handle building plans, asserting this invalidated the plaintiff's claims. The Supreme Court clarified that its order in Praveen Kumar was specific to that case and did not establish any indefeasible rights for the appellant, nor did it bar the ongoing Civil Suit. The Supreme Court predicted that allowing challenges to deletion of irrelevant issues would lead to unnecessary delays in the judicial process. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant had already accepted the jurisdiction of the Delhi Cantonment Board, as recorded in previous proceedings, rendering the issue moot. The Court found no legal basis for the claim, as the issues raised by the appellant were irrelevant to the plaintiff's right to seek relief under the law.

case_name: Ram Manohar Lohia Joint Hospital vs Munna Prasad Saini
text: Case: Ram Manohar Lohia Joint Hospital vs Munna Prasad Saini. Date: 20th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Munna Prasad Saini was an employee of Ram Manohar Lohia Joint Hospital or of the second respondent, Bombay Intelligence Security (I) Ltd. The Labour Court, Lucknow, concluded that Munna Prasad Saini was an employee of Ram Manohar Lohia Joint Hospital, based on the attendance register, duty chart, and other documents. The Labour Court awarded Munna Prasad Saini reinstatement along with compensation of Rs. 20,000 for the period of unemployment and entitlement to full pay from the date of the order. The Supreme Court modified the order by setting aside the direction for reinstatement and instead awarded a lump sum compensation of Rs. 10,00,000 to Munna Prasad Saini. The Supreme Court decided to award lump sum compensation because Munna Prasad Saini was appointed on a contractual basis, not to a regular post, and had not worked since June 2005. The Labour Court relied on the attendance register, duty chart, medicine intend book, salary payment register, joining report, and an affidavit filed by Munna Prasad Saini to determine the employment relationship.

case_name: Ram Naresh vs State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Ram Naresh vs State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 1st December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Ram Naresh shared a common intention with the other co-accused to kill the deceased, Ram Kishore, and whether Section 34 IPC was rightly applied to convict him. Ram Naresh and the other co-accused were charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Ram Kishore. The FIR was lodged by Balram, who alleged that Ram Naresh, Virender, Rajaram, and Jogendra attacked and killed his brother, Ram Kishore, with lathis and an iron rod on 18th October 1982. Both the trial court and the High Court concluded that Ram Naresh, along with the other co-accused, shared a common intention to kill Ram Kishore and were guilty under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The defense argued that there was no evidence to prove that Ram Naresh had a common intention with the other co-accused to kill Ram Kishore, and thus, Section 34 IPC should not apply to convict him. The Supreme Court clarified that common intention can be formed even during the occurrence of the crime and does not require a prearranged plan. The collective actions of the accused in assaulting Ram Kishore indicated their shared common intention. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction of Ram Naresh under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, concluding that the evidence on record sufficiently established his common intention to kill Ram Kishore.

case_name: Ram Sharan Chaturvedi vs The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Ram Sharan Chaturvedi vs The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 25th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ram Sharan Chaturvedi was accused of criminal conspiracy related to the theft of Rs. Six Lakhs from the Guna Branch of Central Bank of India and other related offences. Ram Sharan Chaturvedi was the Head Cashier at the Guna Branch of Central Bank of India and was in custody of one of the keys to the dual locker system. The prosecution alleged that the theft occurred between the evening of 12th June 2004 and the morning of 14th June 2004, and the locks of the building were not broken, indicating the use of actual keys. Based on the information given by the main accused, Pradeep Saxena (A-1), the police recovered Rs. 5,40,000 from a briefcase in A-2's house and Rs. 50,000 from a locker in the same house. The key evidence against Ram Sharan Chaturvedi was that he was in exclusive possession of one set of keys used to open the locks of the main gate, the grill gate of the strong room, and the safe inside the bank. The Trial Court concluded that Ram Sharan Chaturvedi was part of the conspiracy with A-1 and A-2 based on his custody of one set of keys, leading to his conviction under Section 120B of the IPC. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Ram Sharan Chaturvedi but reduced his sentence under Section 477 of the IPC from six years to four years. The Supreme Court found that there was no direct or circumstantial evidence to prove an agreement between Ram Sharan Chaturvedi and the other accused, and that mere possession of one set of keys did not prove his involvement in the conspiracy. The Supreme Court acquitted Ram Sharan Chaturvedi of all charges, stating that the prosecution failed to establish his involvement in the conspiracy beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court reiterated that in cases relying on circumstantial evidence, each circumstance must be clearly established and form a complete chain of events leading to the only conclusion of the accused's guilt, without any reasonable doubt.

case_name: Rama Narang vs. Ramesh Narang and Others
text: Case: Rama Narang vs. Ramesh Narang and Others. Date: 19th January 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is a family dispute over the management and control of Narang International Hotel Limited (NIHL), leading to multiple contempt petitions and legal proceedings between Rama Narang and his sons from his first wife, Ramesh and Rajesh Narang. The consent order intended to settle various disputes within the Narang family by stipulating that the management of NIHL would be shared between Rama Narang and his sons, Ramesh and Rajesh Narang, but disputes continued, leading to further litigation and contempt petitions. Rama Narang alleged that Ramesh and Rajesh violated the consent order by taking unilateral decisions regarding NIHL's management, withholding vital information, and executing high-value contracts without proper authorization. The Facilitator, appointed by the CLB, was responsible for ensuring the smooth functioning of NIHL by mediating disputes among directors and making final decisions on operational matters when the directors could not reach a consensus. The CLB's order on 10th April 2008 appointed Justice Arvind V. Savant as a Facilitator to resolve disputes among NIHL's directors, highlighting the ongoing conflict and need for an external mediator to ensure the company's operations continued smoothly. case_name: Ramabora @ Ramaboraiah & Anr. vs State of Karnataka
text: Case: Ramabora @ Ramaboraiah & Anr. vs State of Karnataka. Date: 10th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main charges were under Sections 143, 144, 148, 147, 448, and 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC for forming an unlawful assembly, trespassing, and committing the murder of Siddaraju. The Sessions Court acquitted all the accused except those against whom the charges abated. The High Court set aside the acquittal of Ramabora @ Ramaboraiah (A-1) and Thimma (A-2) and convicted them under Section 302 IPC, sentencing them to life imprisonment. The acquittal of all other accused was confirmed. The prosecution claimed that A-1 mistook abusive language used by the deceased against his own father as directed towards him, leading to a quarrel and subsequently the murder. The key evidence included the ocular testimony of PW-1 and PW-4, who were the mother and maternal uncle of the deceased, respectively. The Sessions Court acquitted the accused due to inconsistencies and contradictions in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses, as well as the absence of corroborative medical evidence. The Supreme Court found the High Court's judgement to be illogical, noting that the conviction of only 2 out of the 22 accused for the offence under Section 302 IPC was not sustainable given the circumstances and inconsistencies in the evidence. The Supreme Court found discrepancies in the type of weapons used, the role of A-2, and the injuries sustained by PW-1, which were not corroborated by medical evidence. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement convicting the appellants, and ordered their release unless they were required in connection with any other case. The Supreme Court noted that while the principle 'falsus in uno falsus in omnibus' may not have unadulterated application in criminal jurisprudence, the inconsistencies and contradictions in the prosecution's evidence in this case were significant enough to shake the very foundation of the prosecution's case.

case_name: Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti vs State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti vs State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 13th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Criminal Appeal Nos. related to the case were 64-65 of 2022. Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti was convicted for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The main motive behind the crime was Ramanand's extra-marital affair with a married lady named Manju and his desire to marry her, which was opposed by his wife Sangeeta. The FIR was lodged by Shambhu Raidas, who was the brother-in-law of the accused (husband of the accused's sister). Ramanand was sentenced to death under Section 302 of the IPC and was also fined Rs. 20,000, with an additional rigorous imprisonment for one year in default of payment of the fine. The main incriminating circumstances were: discovery of the weapon of offence and blood-stained clothes at the instance of the accused, extra-judicial confession before two prosecution witnesses, strong motive to commit the crime, and false explanation and unnatural conduct by the accused. Ramanand claimed that the injuries on his body were caused by a few individuals from a rival party who committed the murder of his wife and daughters because Sangeeta (deceased) was the sole eyewitness to the murder of Ramanand's brother. The post-mortem reports revealed that Sangeeta and her daughters suffered incised wounds mostly on the head and neck region, with the burn injuries being post-mortem and the incised wounds being ante-mortem. The cause of death was shock and haemorrhage as a result of ante-mortem head injuries.

case_name: Ramesh Bhavan Rathod vs. Vishanbhai Hirabhai Makwana (Koli) & Anr.
text: Case: Ramesh Bhavan Rathod vs. Vishanbhai Hirabhai Makwana (Koli) & Anr.. Date: 20th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the High Court of Gujarat's orders granting bail to six persons implicated in five homicidal deaths arising from a land dispute. The incident involved a violent altercation over a land dispute on 9th May 2020, resulting in the death of five persons, with the accused attacking the victims with firearms and sharp weapons. The accused were charged under Sections 302, 143, 144, 147, 148, 149, 341, 384, 120B, 506(2), and 34 of the IPC, Sections 25(1-b) A, 27, and 29 of the Arms Act, and Section 135 of the Gujarat Police Act. The High Court granted bail based on the accused's long imprisonment duration, the number of witnesses to be examined, and the alleged inconsistencies in the statements of the informant. The Supreme Court found the High Court's bail orders problematic due to the lack of consideration for the gravity of the offenses, the serious nature of the crimes, and the failure to provide adequate reasoning. The Supreme Court viewed the cross FIR as indicating the presence and premeditated actions of the accused to assault the victims, contradicting the High Court's rationale for granting bail. The Supreme Court noted the criminal antecedents of some of the accused, emphasizing that this factor was overlooked by the High Court in its bail decision, further undermining the High Court's orders. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's orders granting bail and directed the accused to surrender forthwith, noting the High Court's failure to consider the severity of the crime and the role of the accused. The Supreme Court disapproved of the High Court's handling due to the absence of adequate reasons, overlooking the gravity of the offenses, and the incorrect application of the parity principle. The Supreme Court highlighted that a judicial order granting bail must include reasons for the decision, ensuring that the discretion is exercised judiciously and in accordance with legal principles. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court misapplied the principle of parity by not considering the individual roles and the specific involvement of the accused in the incident.

case_name: Ramesh Chandra Sharma & Ors. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Ramesh Chandra Sharma & Ors. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 20th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the classification between 'Pushtaini' and 'Gair-pushtaini' landholders for the purpose of compensation in land acquisition. The Full Bench upheld the classification between 'Pushtaini' and 'Gair-pushtaini' landholders, ruling it as reasonable with an intelligible differentia and having a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. 'Pushtaini' refers to ancestral landholders, while 'Gair-pushtaini' refers to those who acquired land after the establishment of the NOIDA authority. 'Pushtaini' landholders were awarded Rs. 322 per sq. yard with additional compensation, while 'Gair-pushtaini' landholders were awarded Rs. 280 per sq. yard without the additional compensation. The appellants cited Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, which does not allow for discrimination between different classes of landholders. The terms 'Pushtaini' and 'Gair-pushtaini' were historically used in the context of ancestry and inclusivity, not exclusion, and this interpretation was considered by the court. The Supreme Court held that the appellants did not forfeit their right to seek revised compensation as the cause of action accrued much after entering into the agreement. The respondents argued that the appellants voluntarily accepted the compensation through an agreement and therefore waived their right to challenge it. No, the Supreme Court found that the classification lacked empirical evidence to justify its reasonableness and was thus discriminatory. The Wednesbury Principle was used to assess the reasonableness of the classification, and it was found that the classification was arbitrary and lacked justification. The proportionality test was applied to determine if the classification had a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved, and it was found lacking, leading to the classification being struck down.

case_name: Ramesh Sanka vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Ramesh Sanka vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 25th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ramesh Sanka sought the issuance of a Writ of Mandamus directing the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to investigate allegations of financial irregularities and other illegal activities committed by Respondent No.12 and its associates. Ramesh Sanka is a former employee and CEO of Respondent No.12, a Limited Company. Ramesh Sanka alleged that Respondent No.12 and its directors and employees committed several financial irregularities and illegal activities in their business dealings with various companies, firms, and individuals, resulting in significant losses to the public exchequer. Respondent No.12 argued that the writ petition was not bona fide and was filed by Ramesh Sanka to settle personal scores, suppressing material facts and pending civil suits between the parties. No, the Supreme Court did not find merit in the allegations and dismissed the writ petition, stating that it was not the appropriate remedy under Article 32 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court directed that the ongoing inquiries by the official respondents (Nos.7 to 11) should continue, and appropriate action should be taken based on the outcome of these inquiries. The Supreme Court suggested that Ramesh Sanka pursue his personal grievances through civil suits or other civil law remedies, as Article 32 was not the appropriate remedy for such issues. The Supreme Court did not entertain the applications filed by other individuals and organizations, suggesting they raise their grievances before the appropriate judicial forum. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition filed by Ramesh Sanka, finding no merit in his allegations and stating that the appropriate legal remedies should be pursued in the proper forums. The Supreme Court observed that a writ petition under Article 32 is not the remedy for agitating personal contractual rights between an employee and employer.

case_name: Ramesh vs. State of Uttarakhand
text: Case: Ramesh vs. State of Uttarakhand. Date: 14th July 2016. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants, Ramesh, Bhola, Paramjeet Singh, and Khalil, were charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC for committing murder. Additionally, Paramjeet Singh and Ramesh were also charged under Section 25 of the Arms Act. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons of all the charges, citing the prosecution's failure to prove the case against them. The High Court overturned the trial court's acquittal, convicting the appellants for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC and sentencing them to life imprisonment. Paramjeet and Ramesh were also convicted under the Arms Act. The Supreme Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It noted inconsistencies and improbabilities in the testimonies of key witnesses (PW-2 and PW-3) and deemed the High Court's approach of reversing the trial court's acquittal on the basis of a 'more probable' version to be erroneous. The Supreme Court highlighted several issues: PW-2's conduct was deemed unnatural and improbable, his presence at the scene was doubtful, and his testimony was inconsistent. Similarly, PW-3's testimony was found to be exaggerated, contradictory, and his presence at the scene was also doubted. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's judgment was unreasonable as it did not provide compelling reasons to overturn the trial court's acquittal. The Supreme Court emphasized that conviction must be based on credible evidence and beyond reasonable doubt, which was not established in this case. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, acquitted the appellants of all charges, and ordered their release on bail, if not required in any other case.

case_name: Ramgopal & Anr. vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Ramgopal & Anr. vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 29th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court had the power to quash non-compoundable offences under Section 482 Cr.P.C. based on a compromise between the accused and the victim. The appellants were involved in an altercation with Padam Singh due to a monetary dispute, where they assaulted him with a pharsa and lathi, resulting in serious injuries including the cutting off of his little finger. The trial court convicted the appellants under Sections 294, 323, and 326 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced them to three years' imprisonment. The Additional Sessions Judge later reduced the sentence to one year upon noticing a compromise between the parties, but upheld the conviction under Section 326 IPC. During the appeal before the Additional Sessions Judge, the appellants and the complainant reconciled and reached a compromise, leading to the compounding of offences under Sections 294 and 323 IPC, but not under Section 326 IPC due to its non-compoundable nature. The Supreme Court invoked its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the criminal proceedings, taking into account the nature of the offence, the voluntary nature of the compromise, and the fact that the parties had amicably settled their dispute. The Supreme Court emphasized that the offences were predominantly of a private nature, did not impact the society at large, and that continuing the proceedings would not serve the ends of justice given the amicable settlement and the time elapsed since the incident. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings and set aside the convictions, directing that the appellants be deemed acquitted of all charges based on the compromise reached between the parties.

case_name: Ramji Singh & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Ramji Singh & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 11th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sarman Singh was threatened by Lakhan Singh while ploughing his field. Later, Sarman Singh was attacked and killed by Lakhan Singh and others while he was at Dasharath Singh's house. Babu Ram (PW-1) lodged the complaint. He was informed about the incident by his nephew, Sarman Singh (the victim). Ramji Singh and Krishna Autar used guns, Laxman Singh and Lala Ram used axes, and Virendra Singh used a pitchfork. The motive was related to a land dispute and strained relations between Sarman Singh and Lakhan Singh, who belonged to different political groups in the village. The Trial Court acquitted the accused on grounds of doubtful medical evidence, withheld material witnesses, lack of independent witnesses, unproven motive, interested witnesses, and failure to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. The High Court set aside the Trial Court's judgement, finding no material contradiction between medical evidence and eyewitness statements, and held that the prosecution had proved the case beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentences of Ramji Singh, Laxman Singh, and Lala Ram. The medical evidence corroborated the prosecution's story, matching the injuries described by eyewitnesses with those found on the deceased's body. The Supreme Court addressed the issue of delayed compliance with Section 157 of the Cr.PC but found sufficient material on record to show that copies of the FIR were sent to other officials as required. Ramji Singh, Laxman Singh, and Lala Ram were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs.10,000 each. The Supreme Court found the eyewitnesses' testimonies reliable and corroborated by medical evidence, despite minor contradictions and their interest in the case.

case_name: Ramji vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Ramji vs. State of Punjab. Date: 27th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court's alteration of Ramji's conviction from Section 304 Part II IPC to Section 302 IPC for the murder of Som Raj was justified based on the evidence. The trial court initially convicted Ramji and his co-accused under Section 304 Part II read with Section 149 IPC, sentencing them to seven years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000 each. Ramji and his co-accused were alleged to have severely beaten Som Raj with deadly weapons, chased him, and ultimately caused his death by inflicting multiple injuries, including pressing his neck until he became unconscious. Ramji, in his SPO uniform, gave repeated kick blows to Som Raj's head, chest, and neck, and pressed his neck with full force, leading to his unconsciousness and subsequent death. The High Court found that Ramji's actions were intentional and exhibited a clear intention to cause death, as evidenced by the severe and repeated blows to vital parts of Som Raj's body. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's decision, noting that the evidence clearly established Ramji's guilt and intention to cause death, thus justifying the conviction under Section 302 IPC. The medical evidence revealed that Som Raj had sustained 15 injuries caused by blunt objects, and the injuries were consistent with the severe beatings described by the witnesses. The Supreme Court noted that Ramji, despite being an SPO expected to uphold the law, took the law into his own hands and engaged in unruly behavior, further demonstrating his culpability. The Supreme Court dismissed Ramji's appeal, upholding the High Court's conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC. The High Court sentenced Ramji and his co-accused to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 20,000 each, in default of which they would undergo further rigorous imprisonment for one year.

The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's decision, noting that the evidence clearly established Ramji's guilt and intention to cause death, thus justifying the conviction under Section 302 IPC.
The medical evidence revealed that Som Raj had sustained 15 injuries caused by blunt objects, and the injuries were consistent with the severe beatings described by the witnesses.
The Supreme Court noted that Ramji, despite being an SPO expected to uphold the law, took the law into his own hands and engaged in unruly behavior, further demonstrating his culpability.
The Supreme Court dismissed Ramji's appeal, upholding the High Court's conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC.
The High Court sentenced Ramji and his co-accused to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 20,000 each, in default of which they would undergo further rigorous imprisonment for one year.

case_name: Ramvir vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Ramvir vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 26th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Sessions Judge acquitted five of the six accused persons of all charges, and convicted the appellant Ramvir (A-1) for the offence under Section 302 IPC, while acquitting him of the charges under Section 149 IPC. Ramvir filed an appeal in the High Court of Allahabad against his conviction under Section 302 IPC by the Sessions Judge. The High Court upheld Ramvir's conviction under Section 302 IPC and additionally convicted him for offences under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC. The Supreme Court acquitted Ramvir based on three main reasons: (1) the Sessions Judge had already acquitted Ramvir of charges under Section 148/149 IPC, and the State did not appeal this acquittal; (2) there was no evidence of any additional unknown persons being part of the unlawful assembly; and (3) there was no evidence to prove that Ramvir fired the gunshot that killed Siyaram, as the ballistic report did not support the prosecution's case and the rifle was surrendered in court, not taken into police custody immediately. On 25th December 1980, around 5 P.M., Ramvir and five others armed with guns/rifles surrounded Siya Ram and fired shots, resulting in Siya Ram's death. The incident occurred in the village of Bishnodi (PS-Patiyali), and the FIR was lodged by Badri (PW-1), the uncle of the deceased. The Supreme Court concluded that the ballistic report did not support the prosecution's case as it opined that the cartridges fired and recovered from the spot could not have been fired from Ramvir's rifle, which was not immediately taken into police custody but was surrendered by Ramvir in court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order, and acquitted Ramvir of the charges framed under Sections 302 read with 148/149 IPC, setting him at liberty unless required in any other case.

case_name: Rana Ayyub vs. Directorate of Enforcement
text: Case: Rana Ayyub vs. Directorate of Enforcement. Date: 7th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge to the summoning order issued by the Special Judge, Ghaziabad, under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act (PMLA) on grounds of lack of territorial jurisdiction. The complaint alleged misuse of funds raised through three crowdfunding campaigns on the platform Ketto during the COVID-19 pandemic. The petitioner argued that the alleged proceeds of crime were deposited in a bank account in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, making Ghaziabad’s jurisdiction invalid under Section 44(1) of the PMLA. A provisional order of attachment was issued for her bank account in Navi Mumbai, along with a show cause notice under the PMLA. The court held that territorial jurisdiction involves questions of fact, such as where the proceeds of crime were concealed, possessed, or acquired, and these require evidence to be determined during the trial. Sections 43 and 44 of the PMLA were discussed, emphasizing that Special Courts are designated for areas where money-laundering offences are committed. The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition, stating that the question of territorial jurisdiction should be raised before the Trial Court as it depends on factual evidence. The petitioner was granted liberty to raise the issue of territorial jurisdiction before the Trial Court. The court emphasized that territorial jurisdiction in criminal cases is governed by Sections 177 to 184 of the CrPC, which outline various contingencies related to the place of commission of the offence. The court directed that the Trial Court must evaluate the evidence and determine the question of jurisdiction based on factual findings.

case_name: Rana Pratap Singh vs. Vittiya Evam Lekha Adhikari, District Basic Education Officer & Ors.
text: Case: Rana Pratap Singh vs. Vittiya Evam Lekha Adhikari, District Basic Education Officer & Ors.. Date: 18th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Rana Pratap Singh's appointment as Junior Accounts Clerk was valid and whether his subsequent re-appointment and right to continue on the post were justified despite challenges and interim orders. The High Court dismissed the initial writ petition on the grounds that it did not have sufficient information about the stay order on the main order affecting Shiv Kumar Rai, and thus, the consequential termination order against Rana Pratap Singh was not properly challenged. The special appeal filed by Rana Pratap Singh was dismissed by the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court on 6th February 2018, which led to the current appeal in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court clarified that the re-appointment order dated 1st January 1993 was in essence a reinstatement due to the interim stay on Shiv Kumar Rai's reversion, allowing Rana Pratap Singh to continue on his post of Junior Accounts Clerk. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench, ruling that Rana Pratap Singh's appointment and continuance on the post of Junior Accounts Clerk were valid. The appeal was allowed, and the previous decisions were quashed. The respondents argued that Rana Pratap Singh's appointment was not made following the prescribed legal procedures and that there was no proper advertisement issued for the vacancy. They also contended that several complaints were filed against him, questioning his appointment and continuance. The Supreme Court viewed the Division Bench's reliance on the dismissal of Shiv Kumar Rai's writ petition as too technical. It emphasized that Shiv Kumar Rai never reverted to his original post and continued in his promoted position until retirement, thus affirming Rana Pratap Singh's right to continue on his post.

case_name: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors
text: Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors. Date: 3rd July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue in this case was the applicability of laws framed by the erstwhile State of Bihar to the newly bifurcated State of Jharkhand, specifically concerning the preparation of the First Register of pharmacists under the Pharmacy Act, 1948, after the bifurcation. The petitioners argued that the First Register of pharmacists prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be deemed the First Register for the State of Jharkhand and that any subsequent registration should comply with the qualifications as per the Education Regulations, 1991. The State of Jharkhand contended that it had the right to prepare a new First Register of pharmacists after its formation, and it constituted a Registration Tribunal to register all persons who possess qualifications in terms of Section 31 of the Pharmacy Act. The High Court of Jharkhand ruled that the State of Jharkhand could not prepare a new First Register and that the First Register of pharmacists prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be deemed the First Register for Jharkhand. It also stated that only those with qualifications as per the Education Regulations could be registered subsequently. The Supreme Court directed that the First Register prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be treated as the First Register for the State of Jharkhand. It allowed the bifurcation of the First Register based on territorial nexus and stated that future inclusions should be made as per Section 32 (2) of the Pharmacy Act, adhering to the Education Regulations. Sections 84 and 85 of the Bihar Reorganization Act were significant as they ensured the continuity of laws applicable in the erstwhile State of Bihar to the newly formed State of Jharkhand until they were modified, repealed, or amended. This included the applicability of the Pharmacy Act and the Education Regulations for the registration of pharmacists.
