case_name: Ranvir Singh vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Ranvir Singh vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 12th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the conviction and sentencing of Ranvir Singh and other appellants under Sections 148, 302/149, and 324/149 of the IPC for the murder of two individuals were justified. The altercation arose from a long-standing enmity over a water dispute, which escalated when the deceased, Hukum Singh, and others were attacked by the accused with weapons, including truncheons and axes, on 25th July 1992. The FIR was recorded by P.W.20, the investigating officer, based on the statement of the deceased Hukum Singh. However, there were discrepancies and doubts about the authenticity and timing of the FIR, including issues with the thumb impression and content written over it. Key contradictions included varying accounts of the incident, the presence and identification of the accused, and the recording of statements. Witnesses like P.W.1 and P.W.4 identified the accused in court without prior test identification parades, and their depositions conflicted with each other and with the FIR. The Supreme Court held that the dying declaration recorded by the investigating officer, P.W.20, was unreliable due to the lack of involvement of a Magistrate or a doctor, and the suspicious nature of the thumb impression and content of the statement. The Supreme Court found that it was unsafe to convict the appellants under Section 149 IPC due to the lack of credible evidence, inconsistencies in witness testimonies, and the questionable recording of the dying declaration. The Court set aside the convictions, conferring the benefit of doubt to the appellants. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the judgments of the Trial Court and the High Court, and directed the immediate release of the appellant, Dhola @ Dholaram, if not required in any other case.

case_name: Rashidul Jafar @ Chota vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr
text: Case: Rashidul Jafar @ Chota vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. Date: 6th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case addressed the premature release of 512 life convicts in Uttar Pradesh based on amendments to the policy governing premature release of prisoners. An amendment on 28th July 2021 introduced a restriction that life convicts must attain the age of sixty years to be eligible for premature release. The Supreme Court ruled that the restriction on age was deleted by a subsequent amendment dated 27th May 2022, making the restriction invalid for this case. The court emphasized Articles 14 and 21, focusing on the right to equality and protection of life and personal liberty. The Court directed that all cases must be processed transparently and expeditiously, ensuring that eligible convicts are not excluded from consideration. DLSAs were tasked with coordinating with jail authorities to monitor and ensure eligible convicts' cases are considered for premature release. The petitioners argued that premature release should be considered based on the policy in effect at the time of conviction, not subsequent amendments. The court mandated that authorities proactively identify and process eligible cases without requiring convicts to file applications. The Court directed that cases of convicts over seventy years or suffering from terminal ailments be prioritized and resolved within two months. The Court aimed to ensure fair treatment, uphold constitutional guarantees, and alleviate the challenges faced by convicts due to prolonged incarceration.

case_name: Rashtreeya Sikshana Samithi Trust vs. Committee For Fixation of Fee Structure Of Private Professional Colleges & Ors.
text: Case: Rashtreeya Sikshana Samithi Trust vs. Committee For Fixation of Fee Structure Of Private Professional Colleges & Ors.. Date: 19th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the orders passed by the Fee Fixation Committee for undergraduate medical courses for the academic years 2004-2005, 2005-2006, and 2006-2007, which were contested by students and private medical colleges in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions filed by the students and dismissed the writ petitions filed by the management of private medical colleges. The Court also ordered the private medical colleges to refund fees to the students in terms of the High Court's order, subject to the condition that the students furnish bank guarantees. The Supreme Court appointed Shri Salman Khurshid as Amicus Curiae to analyze the problem and suggest mechanisms to curb the practice of charging capitation fees. The Court also directed states to furnish information on complaints and actions taken regarding capitation fees and set up a website for public reporting of such practices. The Amicus Curiae suggested creating a web portal for reporting capitation fee demands, ensuring all rounds of counseling are completed before the last date for admissions, making the list of students recommended for stray vacancies public, and prohibiting private medical colleges from charging any fees in cash or additional fees not fixed by the Fee Fixation Committee. The Supreme Court directed the Fee Fixation Committees to fix a price band for different expenses and ensure that no additional fees are charged by the private medical colleges. Any extra charges proposed by the colleges must receive concurrence from the Fee Fixation Committee. The Supreme Court mandated that the names of students recommended for admission in the stray vacancy round be made public along with their NEET ranks. Admissions must be based strictly on merit, and any deviation would lead to action against the medical colleges. Additionally, all admission-related information and updates must be published in both English and vernacular newspapers. The Supreme Court accepted the suggestions of the Amicus Curiae and issued directions accordingly to set up a web portal for reporting capitation fees, complete counseling rounds well before the admission deadlines, ensure transparency in stray vacancy admissions, and prohibit cash payments of fees by private medical colleges.

case_name: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
text: Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.. Date: 22nd November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Ratanlal was the legally adopted son of late Govardhandas Laxmichand Samsuka, which would entitle him to represent himself as Govardhandas's son and claim rights to his estate. The High Court of Judicature at Bombay declared that Ratanlal was not the adopted son of late Govardhandas and consequently restrained him from representing himself as Govardhandas's son or using the name Ratanlal Govardhandas Samsuka. The trial court ruled in favor of Ratanlal's adoption claim based on evidence such as photographs of the adoption ceremony, testimony from the priest who performed the ceremony, and letters and invitations addressed to Ratanlal with his adoptive father's name. The High Court found several issues: non-production of negatives of adoption photographs, lack of proof of any ceremony in the photographs, contradictions in testimonies regarding the adoption, and continuous use of Ratanlal's biological father's name post-adoption. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgement, agreeing that Ratanlal failed to prove the factum of adoption with cogent evidence and noting suspicious circumstances that were not satisfactorily explained. The Supreme Court emphasized that the burden of proving adoption is heavy and requires clear, consistent, and convincing evidence, particularly when the adoption changes the course of succession and affects property rights. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, maintaining that Ratanlal's claim of adoption was not proven and upholding the High Court's ruling that he is not the adopted son of Govardhandas.

case_name: Ratanlal vs. Prahlad Jat & Ors.
text: Case: Ratanlal vs. Prahlad Jat & Ors.. Date: 15th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in allowing the re-examination of witnesses PW4 and PW5 under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. after a significant delay, which the Sessions Judge had previously denied. Prahlad Jat and the other accused were charged under Sections 302, 201, 342, and 120-B of the IPC for the murder of the deceased. The chargesheet was presented on 20th March 2009. PW4 and PW5 claimed in their applications for re-examination that their previous statements were made under the influence of the police, and that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 had no role in the incident. The Sessions Judge dismissed the applications for re-examination, stating that the witnesses had already been cross-examined at length, were not under pressure during their initial statements, and that the applications were filed to favor the accused. The High Court allowed the re-examination of PW4 and PW5 to bring on record the best possible evidence to meet the ends of justice, believing it necessary under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision to be unjustified, as the applications for re-examination were highly belated without satisfactory reasons for the delay, and appeared to be an attempt to assist the accused. The Supreme Court stated that the discretionary power under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised judiciously, with strong and valid reasons, and not arbitrarily. It should be used to prevent failure of justice. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the trial court to proceed with the matter without considering the re-examination evidence of PW4 and PW5 recorded after the High Court's order. The Supreme Court highlighted that the delay in filing the application for re-examination is a crucial factor, and any application under Section 311 must be timely and justified with valid reasons for any delay. The Supreme Court acknowledged that the appellant, being the paternal brother of the deceased and a prosecution witness, had the locus standi to challenge the High Court's order, as the decision directly affected the trial's outcome.

case_name: Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.
text: Case: Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan vs. The State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.. Date: 26th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the summoning order and notice framing under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan was charged under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, for issuing dishonored cheques against a legally enforceable debt or liability. Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the summoning order and the order framing notice, arguing that the cheques were issued as security and not against a legally enforceable debt. The High Court dismissed the petition, stating that the grounds raised by Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan were factual defenses that should be considered during the trial and not in a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court observed that under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there is a presumption that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability, and it is for the accused to rebut this presumption during the trial. The complainant argued that the cheques were issued by Rathish Babu Unnikrishnan for a legally enforceable debt related to the buyback of shares of AAT Academy, and the dishonor of the cheques constituted an offense under Section 138 of the N.I. Act. The appellant contended that the cheques were issued as contingent/security cheques for the buyback of shares and were not meant to be presented for payment until the shares were transferred to the complainant. case_name: Ratnagiri Nagar Parishad vs. Gangaram Narayan Ambekar & Ors.
text: Case: Ratnagiri Nagar Parishad vs. Gangaram Narayan Ambekar & Ors.. Date: 6th May 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Ratnagiri Nagar Parishad could proceed with setting up a Solid Waste Disposal Project on the suit property, despite objections from the local residents regarding potential environmental and health hazards. The local residents opposed the project due to concerns that it would cause severe water pollution, health hazards, and environmental damage, particularly due to the project's location on a rocky, sloping area near a river and the Sheel Dam, which provides water to Ratnagiri city. The trial court dismissed the suit filed by the residents, concluding that they had not provided sufficient evidence to support their claims of potential environmental and health hazards. The first appellate court reversed the trial court's decision, decreeing the suit and prohibiting the Ratnagiri Nagar Parishad from proceeding with the Solid Waste Disposal Project on the suit property. The first appellate court supported the residents' objections based on the potential for severe pollution of the nearby river and dam, which could endanger the health and safety of the residents in Ratnagiri city and the surrounding areas. The Supreme Court of India upheld the first appellate court's decision, agreeing that the potential environmental and health risks justified prohibiting the project at the proposed location. The National Green Tribunal Act was significant because it established that environmental issues should be adjudicated by the National Green Tribunal (NGT), and the Supreme Court noted that the civil court should not have continued with the suit concerning environmental questions, but rather the matter should have been handled by the NGT.

case_name: Raveen Kumar vs. State of Himachal Pradesh
text: Case: Raveen Kumar vs. State of Himachal Pradesh. Date: 26th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Raveen Kumar's conviction under Section 20 of the Narcotics, Drugs, and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, for possessing charas was justified after the High Court reversed his acquittal by the trial court. Raveen Kumar was arrested on 1st November 1994 during a traffic check near the HP-J&K border, where the police found 1 kg 230 gms of charas in his Maruti van hidden under the driver's seat. The trial court acquitted Raveen Kumar, citing reasonable doubt regarding the possession of the prohibited substance, largely due to the testimony of an independent witness who was declared hostile and contradictions in the statements of the police witnesses. The High Court reversed the acquittal, stating that the trial court's reasoning was fallacious, the independent witness's testimony did not significantly undermine the prosecution's case, and the police testimonies were reliable. Raveen Kumar's defense was that the charges were fabricated by the police because he had refused to contribute money towards a sports meet organized by the police, and he denied possession of any prohibited substance. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to convict Raveen Kumar under Section 20 of the NDPS Act but noted that the High Court had shown leniency by sentencing him to two years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 50,000, considering the delay in trial and his dependents. The Supreme Court found the High Court's sentence of two years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 50,000 to be already lenient, given the quantity of charas recovered exceeded the 'commercial quantity' threshold.

case_name: Ravi Chand Mangla vs. Dimpal Solania & Ors.
text: Case: Ravi Chand Mangla vs. Dimpal Solania & Ors.. Date: 18th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the tenants should be evicted from the premises based on grounds such as non-payment of rent, sub-letting, impairment of the property, nuisance, and change of user as per the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973. The grounds for eviction included non-payment of rent for 60 months, sub-letting the property without consent, impairment of the property's value and utility, creating a nuisance in the neighborhood, and changing the use of the property without consent. The Rent Controller dismissed the eviction petition, finding that the arrears of rent were paid, sub-letting was not proven, the value and utility of the property were not impaired, no nuisance was created, and the change of user was within the terms of the rent agreement. The Appellate Authority and the High Court both affirmed the Rent Controller's decision, rejecting the grounds for eviction claimed by Ravi Chand Mangla. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the findings of the lower courts that there was no sufficient ground for eviction and upholding the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court rejected the argument of non-payment of rent because it was clear from the lower courts' judgments that the arrears of rent were paid, and the issue was not raised in the appeal before the Appellate Authority. The tenant argued that the rent agreement allowed for any business activity, not just a sawmill, and hence using the premises for manufacturing grills did not constitute a change of user.

case_name: Ravi Mandal vs The State of Uttarakhand
text: Case: Ravi Mandal vs The State of Uttarakhand. Date: 18th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the evidence presented was sufficient to uphold the conviction of Ravi Mandal and Shabbir for the murder of Chhotu @ Surjeet under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The Trial Court sentenced Ravi Mandal and Shabbir to life imprisonment under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and one year of rigorous imprisonment under Section 201 IPC. Additionally, Shabbir was sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment with a fine under Section 25 of the Arms Act. The primary evidence included testimonies that placed the accused with the deceased Chhotu on the night of the murder, and the recovery of a country-made pistol and a knife from the accused. The High Court upheld the decision because it found the prosecution's evidence reliable and corroborative, affirming the conviction and sentence awarded by the Trial Court. The defense argued that the witnesses were unreliable as they were chance witnesses with delayed disclosures, and that the evidence, including the recovery of weapons, was fabricated or insufficiently supported. The Supreme Court found that the key prosecution witnesses were not credible due to their delayed disclosures and the implausibility of their explanations for being at the crime scene. The Supreme Court found the recovery of the weapons to be unconvincing due to the lack of public witnesses and the delayed preparation of the site plan for the place of arrest and recovery. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgements of the High Court and the Trial Court, and acquitted Ravi Mandal and Shabbir of all charges. The ruling could lead to more stringent scrutiny of the credibility of last seen witnesses and the procedures followed for the recovery of weapons, emphasizing the need for strong and corroborative evidence. The decision reinforces the requirement for the prosecution to provide clear, reliable, and corroborative evidence, ensuring that convictions are based on solid proof rather than on suspicion or weak links in the chain of evidence. The Supreme Court clarified that forensic reports must be put to the accused during their statement under Section 313 CrPC; otherwise, such reports should be eschewed from consideration.

case_name: Ravi Sinha & Ors. vs The State of Jharkhand
text: Case: Ravi Sinha & Ors. vs The State of Jharkhand. Date: 5th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The criminal appeals were filed against the common judgment dated 21st June 2007 of Jharkhand High Court, dismissing criminal appeals related to proceedings under the Criminal Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 1944, which led to the attachment of certain properties. The allegations were that Dr. S.B. Sinha and his family members, including Ravi Sinha, were involved in a conspiracy defrauding the Government of Bihar (now Jharkhand) of several hundred crores through fraudulent transactions in the Animal Husbandry Department and other departments, leading to the attachment of their properties. The key argument was that after the death of Dr. S.B. Sinha on 25th October 1999, the attachment of properties should have been withdrawn as no criminal proceedings could continue against a deceased person, and the properties should not have been attached to the family members who were only name lenders. The Supreme Court concluded that the attachment of properties could continue because Ravi Sinha, a legal heir, was himself accused and convicted in the fodder scam case, and further trials were pending. Therefore, the attachment order making the properties absolute was upheld. The fraud committed was to the tune of Rs. 500 crores in the Animal Husbandry Department and similar fraudulent activities were noted in the Education, Cooperation, and Fisheries Departments. The Supreme Court held that the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi had the jurisdiction to make the ad-interim attachment of properties absolute since the conspiracy and defrauding of government funds involved a larger conspiracy, and legal heirs were also facing trials and had been convicted in related cases.

case_name: Ravinder Singh @ Kaku vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Ravinder Singh @ Kaku vs. State of Punjab. Date: 4th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involved the kidnapping and murder of two children, Aman Kumar and Om, aged 10 and 6 years respectively. Three accused, Anita @ Arti (the mother of the children), Ravinder Singh @ Kaku, and Ranjit Kumar Gupta, were initially sentenced to death by the Trial Court for the offence under Section 302 read with 120B IPC and 10 years of rigorous imprisonment for the offence under Section 364 IPC. The High Court acquitted Anita @ Arti and Ranjit Kumar Gupta while partly allowing the appeal of Ravinder Singh @ Kaku by setting aside the death penalty and sentencing him to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 302 IPC. The High Court's conviction of Ravinder Singh @ Kaku was based on circumstantial evidence, including his intimate relationship with Anita @ Arti, the 'last seen' theory, and the recovery of material objects based on his disclosure statement. The Supreme Court found inconsistencies in the testimonies of key witnesses (PW6 and PW7), contradictions regarding the arrest dates, and discrepancies in the recovery of the school bags, which made the evidence against Ravinder Singh @ Kaku non-conclusive. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by Ravinder Singh @ Kaku, setting aside his conviction under Section 302 and 364 of the IPC, and directed his immediate release unless required in any other case. The Supreme Court found the High Court's inference about the intimate relationship between A1 (Anita @ Arti) and A2 (Ravinder Singh @ Kaku) erroneous due to the lack of direct evidence and the reliance on call records which only indicated a close relationship but did not establish the motive for murder. The Supreme Court emphasized that the electronic evidence (call records) must comply with the certification requirements under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act, and oral evidence cannot substitute the mandatory certification for admissibility.

case_name: Ravindra Kumar vs. State of U.P. & Ors.
text: Case: Ravindra Kumar vs. State of U.P. & Ors.. Date: 22nd February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether non-disclosure of a criminal case in which the candidate was acquitted in the verification form is fatal for the candidate's employment. Ravindra Kumar was charged under Sections 324, 352, and 504 of the IPC. He was acquitted on 13th September 2004, as the key witnesses turned hostile and the prosecution could not prove the charges. His selection was canceled because he submitted an affidavit stating that no criminal case was registered against him, which the authorities later found to be false as he had been involved in a criminal case, albeit acquitted. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that Ravindra Kumar had suppressed material information regarding his involvement in a criminal case, and his subsequent acquittal did not absolve him from the fact that he had suppressed material information. The Supreme Court allowed Ravindra Kumar's appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement and the cancellation order, and directed the respondents to appoint him to the post of Constable, stating that non-disclosure of the criminal case (which ended in acquittal) should not be deemed fatal for his employment. The Supreme Court directed that Ravindra Kumar be appointed as a Constable without entitlement to arrears of salary for the period he was out of service but with all notional benefits, including pay, seniority, and other consequential benefits.

case_name: Reema Salkan vs. Sumer Singh Salkan
text: Case: Reema Salkan vs. Sumer Singh Salkan. Date: 25th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was regarding the quantum of maintenance payable by Sumer Singh Salkan to Reema Salkan. The High Court directed Sumer Singh Salkan to pay maintenance of Rs.9,000 per month to Reema Salkan from 9th December 2010 onwards. Reema Salkan argued that the maintenance amount should not be reduced from the interim maintenance of Rs.20,000 per month granted earlier, as there was no change in circumstances. The High Court observed that Sumer Singh Salkan claimed to be unemployed since 2010 but failed to provide evidence to support his claim, despite being highly educated and able-bodied. The Supreme Court concluded that Sumer Singh Salkan, being highly educated and able-bodied, was capable of earning and thus liable to pay maintenance to his wife. The Supreme Court directed Sumer Singh Salkan to pay Rs.20,000 per month as maintenance from January 2010 and Rs.25,000 per month from 1st June 2018 onwards. The Supreme Court took into account the spiraling inflation rate and high cost of living, which influenced its decision to set the maintenance amount at Rs.20,000 and later Rs.25,000 per month. The Supreme Court disagreed with the Family Court's decision to restrict maintenance only until 8th December 2010 and extended it indefinitely, subject to further orders. The Supreme Court reiterated that an able-bodied husband is duty-bound to maintain his wife, who is unable to maintain herself, as per the personal law arising out of the marital status. The Supreme Court directed Sumer Singh Salkan to clear the arrears of maintenance within eight weeks from the date of the order, after adjusting any amount already deposited in court or paid to Reema Salkan. The Supreme Court highlighted that maintenance laws are meant to support but not enrich, and payments should be fair and just, considering the standard of living and status of the parties involved.

case_name: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.
text: Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.. Date: 17th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Dr. Prabhugouda's Career Advancement Scheme (CAS) promotion should be effective from 01.01.2009 or from 28.10.2013. The High Court declared that the effective date of Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion should be 01.01.2009 and directed the University to grant all consequential benefits from that date. Dr. Prabhugouda argued that he had completed three years of service as an Associate Professor from 01.01.2006 to 01.01.2009, making him eligible for promotion under the CAS from 01.01.2009. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the Trial Court's order, making the effective date of Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion 28.10.2013. The Supreme Court directed that Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion should be effective from 28.10.2013, the date he joined Karnataka University as an Associate Professor. The Supreme Court clarified that the term 'College' in the CAS statute refers only to Constituent Colleges of the University and not affiliated colleges. Dr. Prabhugouda's claim was based on his three years of service as an Associate Professor in J.S.S College, an affiliated college of Karnataka University, from 01.01.2006 to 01.01.2009. This judgment may ensure that only service in constituent colleges of a university is considered for CAS promotions, potentially affecting eligibility criteria for faculty members. Universities should ensure that the service considered for CAS promotions is strictly from constituent colleges and that faculty members meet all criteria specified in the CAS statute. The Supreme Court's decision meant that Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion would be recognized from 28.10.2013, potentially affecting his seniority and related benefits within the university. The Supreme Court interpreted the provisions to mean that the CAS statute's benefits apply only to faculty in constituent colleges, not affiliated colleges, ensuring alignment with the statute's objectives and preamble.

case_name: Religare Finvest Limited vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
text: Case: Religare Finvest Limited vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.. Date: 11th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appeals arise from a final order of the Delhi High Court rejecting a petition for quashing criminal proceedings. Religare Finvest Limited (RFL) and DBS Bank India Limited have challenged the impugned order. Religare Finvest Limited (RFL) alleged that Laxmi Vilas Bank (LVB) misappropriated Fixed Deposits (FDs) furnished as security by RFL and its group companies to secure short-term loans. On 23rd September 2019, Religare Finvest Limited (RFL) lodged a criminal complaint asserting that officials of Laxmi Vilas Bank (LVB) had conspired with RHC Holding and Ranchem, leading to the registration of an FIR by the Economic Offences Wing. Due to Laxmi Vilas Bank's (LVB) unstable financial condition, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) imposed a moratorium on LVB and later directed its non-voluntary amalgamation with DBS Bank India Limited. DBS Bank India Limited filed a Criminal Miscellaneous Case seeking to quash the supplementary chargesheet and the summoning order, arguing that Laxmi Vilas Bank (LVB) had ceased to exist due to the amalgamation, and DBS should not face prosecution for the acts of LVB. The Delhi High Court observed that quashing the summoning order against DBS Bank at that stage might hamper the purpose of the amalgamation scheme and stayed the summoning order until clarification from the RBI. The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings against DBS Bank India Limited, noting that the amalgamation scheme did not intend to transfer criminal liability to the transferee bank.

case_name: Revanasiddayya vs. Gangamma @ Shashikala & Anr.
text: Case: Revanasiddayya vs. Gangamma @ Shashikala & Anr.. Date: 5th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue in the appeal was the possession of the suit land, which the High Court had ordered to be handed over to the respondents (Gangamma @ Shashikala & Anr.) after dismissing the appellant's claim for specific performance of an agreement to sell the land. Veerabasayya, the original owner, agreed to sell the suit land to Revanasiddayya for Rs.1,75,000/-, receiving Rs.1,00,000/- as earnest money and placing Revanasiddayya in possession of the land. The sale deed was to be executed within three months, but Veerabasayya died before it could be completed. The Trial Court declared the respondents as owners of the suit land but did not grant them possession. The court dismissed the appellant's subsequent suit for specific performance of the agreement. The High Court modified the judgment to include a decree for possession of the suit land in favor of the respondents, ruling that they were entitled to reclaim the land from Revanasiddayya. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, ruling that since the appellant's suit for specific performance was dismissed, his possession of the suit land became unauthorized, entitling the respondents to reclaim it. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to refund Rs.1,00,000/- to the appellant within three months, failing which interest at the rate of 6% per annum would apply. The appellant was ordered to restore possession of the suit land to the respondents within three months from the date of the judgment.

case_name: Rima Taipodia vs Arunachal Pradesh Public Service Commission & Ors.
text: Case: Rima Taipodia vs Arunachal Pradesh Public Service Commission & Ors.. Date: 14th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Rima Taipodia met the required minimum disability percentage of 40% for a Group-B post as verified by the State Medical Board. The High Court directed Rima Taipodia to appear before the State Medical Board to assess his disability for the Group-B post he sought appointment for. The State Medical Board assessed Rima Taipodia's disability to be 33.9%, which was below the required 40% for the appointment. The certificate was not issued by the State Medical Board, as required by the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Rules, 1996. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing Rima Taipodia's appeal and validating the requirement for a State Medical Board's assessment. The Supreme Court directed that Rima Taipodia be examined by the State Medical Board to ascertain his disability percentage, which was found to be 33.9%. The Supreme Court clarified that a disability certificate must be issued by a duly constituted State Medical Board, and the assessment must indicate whether the disability is permanent or if there are chances of variation. Since Rima Taipodia's disability was assessed at 33.9%, which is below the required 40%, he was not eligible for the Group-B post he sought, leading to the dismissal of his appeal. This judgment may ensure stricter adherence to the requirement of State Medical Board assessments for disability certifications, potentially affecting the eligibility of candidates in similar employment cases. Future disability assessments will likely follow more rigorous procedures, with State Medical Boards ensuring accurate and compliant evaluations to prevent legal disputes and ensure fairness in employment opportunities. Candidates should ensure their disability certification is obtained from a State Medical Board and meets the required criteria for their desired employment positions to avoid disqualification and legal challenges.

case_name: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 2nd August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether a Magistrate has the authority to compel an accused to give a voice sample during the course of a criminal investigation. Ritesh Sinha was accused of being involved in a scheme with Dhoom Singh to collect money from people on the promise of securing jobs in the police force. The investigating authorities needed Ritesh Sinha's voice sample to verify if the recorded conversations on Dhoom Singh's seized mobile phone were between Dhoom Singh and Ritesh Sinha. The CJM issued a summons on 8th January 2010, directing Ritesh Sinha to appear before the Investigating Officer and give his voice sample. The High Court of Allahabad rejected Ritesh Sinha's challenge to the CJM's order, leading to the present appeal. The two principal questions were: (1) Whether Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India, which protects an accused from being compelled to be a witness against themselves, extends to giving voice samples, and (2) Whether, in the absence of any specific provision in the CrPC, a Magistrate can authorize the recording of an accused's voice sample. The Supreme Court held that Article 20(3) does not extend to protecting an accused from being compelled to give a voice sample, as it does not involve self-incrimination in the sense of conveying personal knowledge of the accused. The Supreme Court concluded that a Magistrate has the implied power under Section 53 of the CrPC to order the taking of voice samples for criminal investigation, filling the statutory gap through judicial interpretation. The Supreme Court emphasized that when there is a significant gap in the statute that affects justice delivery, it is necessary for the judiciary to fill that gap through interpretation until the legislature addresses it. The Supreme Court ruled that a Judicial Magistrate does have the power to order an accused to provide a voice sample for the purpose of investigation, thereby disposing of the appeals and setting the legal precedent. The ruling allows investigative agencies to obtain voice samples from accused persons by seeking authorization from a Magistrate, ensuring that new evidence can be gathered effectively for criminal investigations.

case_name: Riya Bawri vs Mark Alexander Davidson & Ors.
text: Case: Riya Bawri vs Mark Alexander Davidson & Ors.. Date: 23rd August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issues were related to the dishonour of cheques issued for rent payment and the subsequent criminal complaints filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act) and various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The complaints were filed after multiple cheques issued by the respondents to discharge their rental liabilities were dishonoured due to insufficient funds, leading to the issuance of a notice under Section 138 of the NI Act and the subsequent filing of criminal complaints. The High Court of Meghalaya quashed the criminal complaints and the summoning order against respondents Mark Alexander Davidson and Sarita Harish Kanchan, holding that there was insufficient evidence to hold them liable for prosecution. Mark Alexander Davidson argued that he had already resigned from the partnership firm before the issuance of the cheques and provided a Retirement Deed dated 1st April 2018 as evidence. The Supreme Court concluded that the Retirement Deed dated 1st April 2018 could not be taken at face value in the quashing proceedings and should be proved during the trial. The public notice regarding his retirement was issued much later, on 9th February 2022. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order quashing the summoning order and the complaints against Mark Alexander Davidson, reviving the complaints to be tried by the concerned court. The specific allegation was that the respondents were in charge of and responsible for the affairs of the firm and had consented to and connived in the issuance of the dishonoured cheques. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal because the issue of whether Mark Alexander Davidson had indeed resigned from the firm was a matter of evidence to be proved before the trial court, and the High Court's quashing of the complaints was premature. The total amount for which the dishonoured cheques were issued was Rs 1,45,152/- per month, covering multiple months as per the rent agreement. The sections of the IPC invoked in the criminal complaints were Sections 420, 418, 417, 403, 409, and 406, along with Sections 138, 141, and 142 of the NI Act. The appellants argued that the High Court's decision to quash the complaints was based on incomplete and self-serving evidence provided by Mark Alexander Davidson and that the matter should be decided based on full evidence during the trial.

case_name: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.. Date: 7th May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the restructuring of the Tribunal system in India to ensure independence, effectiveness, and accessibility, as per the constitutional scheme and judicial precedents. The Supreme Court noted that the functioning of Tribunals required a review to ensure they provided speedy and inexpensive quality justice, and that they must adhere to principles of independence and separation of powers. Concerns raised included the lack of competence, objectivity, and judicial approach of Tribunal personnel, the need for judicial members to man Tribunals, and the importance of judicial review by High Courts over Tribunal decisions. The recommendations included the creation of a National Tribunal Commission to oversee all Tribunals, ensuring independence and fairness in appointments, and establishing uniform service conditions for Tribunal members. Shri Arvind P. Datar, as amicus curiae, assisted the court by providing a Concept Note suggesting the creation of a regular cadre for Tribunals, national competition for recruitment, and an independent oversight mechanism. The Supreme Court directed the creation of a committee to oversee the restructuring of Tribunals, emphasizing the need for an autonomous body to handle appointments, performance review, and discipline of Tribunal members. Key issues included creating a regular cadre for Tribunals, setting up an autonomous oversight body, amending the scheme of direct appeals to the Supreme Court, and making Tribunal Benches accessible at convenient locations.

case_name: Rupali Devi vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Others
text: Case: Rupali Devi vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Others. Date: 9th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central question is whether a woman forced to leave her matrimonial home due to cruelty can initiate legal proceedings in the jurisdiction where she takes shelter with her parents or other family members. The reference to a larger Bench was made because the opinions of the court on whether a woman can initiate proceedings under Section 498A in the jurisdiction where she takes shelter were sharply divided. The view was that if no specific act of cruelty is committed at the parental home, initiating proceedings under Section 498A in the courts where the parental home is situated is not permissible. The Supreme Court interpreted 'cruelty' to include both physical and mental suffering, recognizing that mental trauma and psychological distress can persist at the parental home due to acts committed in the matrimonial home. Section 178 provides exceptions where the offence is committed partly in one local area and partly in another, where the offence is a continuing one, or where the offence consists of several acts done in different local areas. The Supreme Court decided that courts at the place where the wife takes shelter after leaving the matrimonial home due to cruelty also have jurisdiction to entertain complaints under Section 498A IPC. The Criminal Law (Second Amendment) Act, 1983 amended Sections 174 and 176 of the Cr.P.C. and introduced Section 198A in the Cr.P.C. for the prosecution of offences under Section 498A IPC. It also made the offence cognizable and non-bailable. The decision relates to the concept of continuing offence by recognizing that mental and psychological trauma from acts of cruelty can continue at the parental home, making it a valid jurisdiction for filing complaints. In Sujata Mukherjee v. Prashant Kumar Mukherjee, the court held that if acts of cruelty continue at the parental home, the offence is considered continuing, thus allowing jurisdiction at the parental home under Section 178(c) of the Cr.P.C. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provides a civil remedy for victims of domestic violence, complementing the criminal remedy under Section 498A IPC, and emphasizes the protection of women's mental and physical well-being. The Supreme Court viewed the adverse effects on mental health at the parental home as consequences of cruelty committed in the matrimonial home, amounting to continuing offences under Section 179 Cr.P.C.

case_name: S. Athilakshmi vs The State Rep. by The Drugs Inspector
text: Case: S. Athilakshmi vs The State Rep. by The Drugs Inspector. Date: 15th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether S. Athilakshmi, a registered medical practitioner, violated the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, by stocking medicines for sale without a valid drug license. S. Athilakshmi is a registered medical practitioner, currently working as an Associate Professor and Head of the Dermatology Department at Government Omandurar Medical College, Chennai. During the inspection on 16th March 2016, the Drugs Inspector found various medicines in the inner room of her premises, including lotions and ointments. The prosecution was based on Section 18(c) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, for stocking drugs for sale without a valid license, which is punishable under Section 27(b)(ii) of the Act. The appellant argued that the small quantity of medicines found, mostly lotions and ointments, were for emergency use by her patients and not for sale, as protected under Schedule K of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. The Supreme Court concluded that the small quantity of medicines found did not amount to stocking for sale and that the appellant, being a registered medical practitioner, was protected under the law. The Supreme Court found that the sanction for prosecution was given in a mechanical manner without considering the appellant's explanations and the small quantity of medicines. Schedule K of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, provides exemptions for drugs supplied by a registered medical practitioner to their patients, which was relevant in protecting the appellant from prosecution. The delay in obtaining prosecution sanction suggested non-application of mind and procedural irregularities, which contributed to the Supreme Court's decision to quash the criminal proceedings. This judgment may provide relief to other registered medical practitioners who stock small quantities of medicines for emergency use by their patients, ensuring they are protected under Schedule K. The Supreme Court recognized the importance of legal provisions under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act but emphasized the need to consider the appellant's professional duties and the protective provisions of Schedule K.

case_name: S. Mahesh vs. The Chairman Cum Managing Director, Neyveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. Neyveli Tamil Nadu & Ors.
text: Case: S. Mahesh vs. The Chairman Cum Managing Director, Neyveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. Neyveli Tamil Nadu & Ors.. Date: 29th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether S. Mahesh's appointment and subsequent promotion in Neyveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. (NLC) were valid, considering his inability to produce an original Scheduled Tribe certificate. S. Mahesh initially produced a photocopy of his Scheduled Tribe certificate and requested time to provide the original. He later informed NLC that he could not obtain the original certificate from the Revenue Authorities and requested to be treated as a general category candidate. NLC allowed S. Mahesh to join as a general category candidate and later promoted him to Junior Engineer Grade I, despite his inability to produce the original Scheduled Tribe certificate. NLC issued multiple memos and conducted a Departmental Enquiry, concluding that S. Mahesh submitted a false caste certificate. They imposed a punishment of reduction in rank, but later, in 2010, declared his appointment null and void, which led to legal challenges. The Supreme Court set aside the order of the Division Bench of the High Court, restored the order of the Single Judge, and quashed NLC's order dated 07.07.2010, which declared S. Mahesh's appointment void. The Court held that NLC's actions were arbitrary and unsustainable in law. The Supreme Court reasoned that NLC had condoned the issue by allowing S. Mahesh to join and promoting him, making the caste certificate issue non-significant. It also highlighted that NLC's attempt to revoke the original punishment order after 13 years was legally unsustainable.

case_name: S. Mohammed Ispahani vs. Yogendra Chandak and Others
text: Case: S. Mohammed Ispahani vs. Yogendra Chandak and Others. Date: 4th October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Girdharilal Chandak, the father of Respondent no. 1, lodged a complaint against many persons, including the four appellants, alleging that 50-60 rowdy elements armed with deadly weapons entered his premises, threatened his staff, and damaged and took away valuables like laptops, computers, and other antique articles on 27th April 2007. The appellants, Mehdi Ispahani, Ali Ispahani, and S. Mohammed Ispahani, were the landlords of the premises where the de facto complainant, Girdharilal Chandak, was a tenant. The Small Causes Court, Chennai, directed the eviction of the de facto complainant on 26th February 2007. The de facto complainant's appeal against the eviction order was pending, but no stay of the eviction order was granted. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate dismissed the application under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. because there was no sufficient evidence to proceed against the proposed accused, as none of the prosecution witnesses had implicated the landlords or the bailiff in their testimonies. The High Court allowed the revision petition, setting aside the order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and directing him to implicate the appellants as accused in the case. The appellants' counsel argued that the landlords had taken legal steps to execute the eviction decree, and there was no evidence of conspiracy or involvement in the alleged incident. They emphasized that the police investigation and departmental inquiry had found no involvement of the appellants. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and restored the order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, concluding that there was no strong and cogent evidence against the appellants to summon them as accused persons. The departmental inquiry against the bailiff found him guilty of dereliction of duty for not following the proper procedure while executing the warrants of possession. However, the charge of using rowdy elements and armed persons was not proven in the inquiry. The Supreme Court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution witnesses did not meet the standard of 'strong and cogent evidence' required to summon the appellants under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. The testimonies did not implicate the appellants in any conspiracy or illegal activities.

The Small Causes Court, Chennai, directed the eviction of the de facto complainant on 26th February 2007. The de facto complainant's appeal against the eviction order was pending, but no stay of the eviction order was granted.

The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate dismissed the application under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. because there was no sufficient evidence to proceed against the proposed accused, as none of the prosecution witnesses had implicated the landlords or the bailiff in their testimonies.
The High Court allowed the revision petition, setting aside the order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and directing him to implicate the appellants as accused in the case.

The appellants' counsel argued that the landlords had taken legal steps to execute the eviction decree, and there was no evidence of conspiracy or involvement in the alleged incident. They emphasized that the police investigation and departmental inquiry had found no involvement of the appellants.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and restored the order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, concluding that there was no strong and cogent evidence against the appellants to summon them as accused persons.

The departmental inquiry against the bailiff found him guilty of dereliction of duty for not following the proper procedure while executing the warrants of possession. However, the charge of using rowdy elements and armed persons was not proven in the inquiry.

The Supreme Court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution witnesses did not meet the standard of 'strong and cogent evidence' required to summon the appellants under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. The testimonies did not implicate the appellants in any conspiracy or illegal activities.

case_name: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
text: Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others. Date: 14th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the wrongful arrest and prosecution of S. Nambi Narayanan, a former ISRO scientist, by the Kerala police constituted malicious prosecution and a violation of his fundamental rights. The wrongful arrest and prosecution were triggered by allegations of espionage involving Maldivian nationals and the alleged leak of ISRO secrets, leading to the arrest of Nambi Narayanan and others in 1994. The CBI investigation concluded that the allegations of espionage against Nambi Narayanan and other ISRO scientists were false and unsubstantiated. The CBI filed a closure report, which was accepted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, resulting in the discharge of all accused in 1996. The Kerala High Court initially upheld the State Government's decision not to take disciplinary action against the police officers involved in Nambi Narayanan's wrongful arrest and prosecution, citing a lack of evidence and the passage of time. The Supreme Court criticized the Kerala Government's decision, stating that the wrongful arrest and prosecution of Nambi Narayanan caused immense mental agony and physical suffering. The Court highlighted the failure of the Kerala police to conduct a proper investigation and their wrongful actions against the ISRO scientists. The Supreme Court awarded Nambi Narayanan a compensation of Rs. 50 lakhs for the mental agony and physical suffering caused by his wrongful arrest and prosecution, directing the State of Kerala to pay this amount. The Supreme Court constituted a committee headed by Justice D.K. Jain, a former judge of the Supreme Court, to take appropriate steps against the erring police officers. The committee was tasked with investigating the lapses and ensuring accountability for the wrongful actions taken against Nambi Narayanan.

case_name: S. Ramesh & Ors. vs. State Rep. by Inspector of Police & Ors.
text: Case: S. Ramesh & Ors. vs. State Rep. by Inspector of Police & Ors.. Date: 2nd April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in recalling its earlier orders quashing the criminal proceedings based on a compromise between the parties and subsequently dismissing the criminal original petitions without assigning any reasons. S. Ramesh and the other appellants were charged in various criminal cases under different sections of the IPC, including CC No.1725/2013 arising out of FIR in Crime Case No.3752/2012, CC No.4228/2015 arising out of FIR in Crime Case No.1815/2015, and CC No.6766/2014 arising out of FIR in Crime Case No.3752/2012. The High Court initially allowed the criminal original petitions filed by the appellants under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. and quashed the criminal proceedings based on a compromise arrived at between the parties on 1st March 2018. Respondent No. 2 filed applications for recall of the orders dated 1st March 2018, alleging that the compromise was not genuine and that the High Court had not examined the merits of the cases. The High Court found merit in the grounds urged by Respondent No. 2 and recalled the orders. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's decision to recall its earlier orders quashing the criminal proceedings, as the recall was based on valid grounds presented by Respondent No. 2. The Supreme Court found it problematic because the High Court dismissed the criminal original petitions without assigning any reasons, which was an error in their approach. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order to the extent that it dismissed the criminal original petitions and restored them to their original numbers for disposal on merits in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court emphasized that the High Court should decide the criminal original petitions on merits, strictly in accordance with the law, and uninfluenced by any observations made in the impugned order or the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court opined that it was not necessary to set out the entire factual matrix of the case, as the High Court would decide the cases on merits based on the law.

case_name: S. Rukmini Madegowda vs The State Election Commission & Ors.
text: Case: S. Rukmini Madegowda vs The State Election Commission & Ors.. Date: 14th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the election of S. Rukmini Madegowda as a Councillor for Ward No.36-Yeraganahalli in the Mysore Municipal Corporation should be set aside due to alleged false declarations in her Affidavit of Assets. The allegations were that she falsely declared that her husband did not possess any immovable property and thereby indulged in corrupt practices to benefit from the reservation category of Backward Class-B (Women). The Principal District and Sessions Judge, Mysuru, initially rejected the Election Petition No.4 of 2018 but later, upon remand by the High Court, set aside the election of S. Rukmini Madegowda. The High Court of Karnataka remanded the Election Petition back to the Trial Court for reconsideration in light of the Supreme Court's judgments in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms and Lok Prahari v. Union of India. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision that the false declarations regarding her husband's property constituted corrupt practices, leading to the setting aside of her election. The Supreme Court clarified that the requirement to disclose assets in affidavits, including those of spouses and dependents, was mandated by the notifications issued by the Election Commission following the judgments in Association for Democratic Reforms and Lok Prahari. The Supreme Court interpreted that non-disclosure of assets, as required by the affidavit, amounted to 'undue influence' under Section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which was incorporated into the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act. The decision reinforces the requirement for candidates to make full and accurate disclosures in their affidavits, potentially leading to increased scrutiny and transparency in future elections. Candidates should ensure that they fully disclose all required information, including the assets of their spouses and dependents, to comply with election laws and avoid allegations of corrupt practices. The Supreme Court ruled that the State Election Commission had the power to issue such notifications under Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution, which are in pari materia with Article 324(1) of the Constitution. This judgment may set a precedent for stricter enforcement of disclosure requirements in election affidavits and highlight the importance of transparency and honesty in electoral processes.

case_name: S. Vasanthi & Anr. vs. M/S Adhiparasakthi Engg. College and Another
text: Case: S. Vasanthi & Anr. vs. M/S Adhiparasakthi Engg. College and Another. Date: 11th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. On 22nd May 2010, S. Sathiyanarayan, riding a Bajaj Avenger motorcycle, was hit by a bus owned by M/S Adhiparasakthi Engineering College, resulting in his death. His parents, the appellants, filed a compensation claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The Tribunal awarded Rs. 7,48,052/- with interest at 7.5% per annum, based on a notional monthly income of Rs. 7,000/-, as S. Sathiyanarayan was a student and not earning any salary at the time of the accident. The High Court enhanced the notional income to Rs. 10,000/- per month, increasing the compensation from Rs. 7,48,052/- to Rs. 16,27,000/-, considering the loss of dependency, loss of love and affection, funeral expenses, and granting an additional Rs. 15,000/- as loss of estate. The appellants argued that the notional income should be higher, based on affidavits stating that the deceased's classmates earned around Rs. 40,000/- per month. They contended that S. Sathiyanarayan, being an engineering graduate pursuing an MBA, would have secured a well-paying job. The Supreme Court reassessed the monthly income at Rs. 30,000/-, deducting 50% for personal expenses, resulting in a yearly income of Rs. 2,52,000/-. The total compensation, including conventional heads and loss of consortium, was calculated to be Rs. 46,11,000/-. After deducting the amounts awarded by the Tribunal and High Court, the enhanced compensation of Rs. 29,84,000/- was to be paid to the appellants with interest at 7.5% per annum.

case_name: S.P. Velumani vs Arappor Iyakkam & Ors.
text: Case: S.P. Velumani vs Arappor Iyakkam & Ors.. Date: 20th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the investigation into corruption allegations against S.P. Velumani, a former Cabinet Minister, was conducted properly, and whether he should be provided a copy of the preliminary enquiry report. S.P. Velumani was alleged to have misused his powers as a Minister to influence the tender process and ensure that tenders were awarded to his close aides. The High Court directed that the preliminary enquiry should be conducted by Ms. Ponni, IPS, Superintendent of Police, Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption, and that the progress should be monitored by the Director of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption. The High Court received the status report on 01.11.2019 and granted time to complete the preliminary enquiry. Subsequently, the final report was submitted to the Director of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption on 16.12.2019. The State Government initially accepted the report, which concluded that no cognizable offense was made out. However, after a change in the political dispensation, the State recanted its earlier stand and decided to conduct further investigation based on a CAG report. The High Court permitted the State to conduct further investigation into the matter, despite the earlier conclusion of the preliminary enquiry. The Supreme Court found that the non-disclosure of the preliminary enquiry report was a violation of natural justice and directed that a copy of the report be provided to S.P. Velumani. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to supply a copy of the preliminary enquiry report and other documents to S.P. Velumani, and to restore the writ petition and criminal original petition to its file for disposal on merits. This judgment emphasizes the importance of transparency and natural justice, mandating that accused individuals must be provided with relevant investigation reports to ensure a fair trial. If the State fails to comply, the High Court may take appropriate actions to ensure compliance, and the non-compliance could be viewed as contempt of court, leading to potential legal consequences for the State authorities. Legal practitioners should ensure that all relevant documents and reports are disclosed to the accused to uphold the principles of natural justice, and they should be prepared to challenge any procedural lapses or non-compliance with court directives.

case_name: SAU. Kamal Shivaji Pokarnekhar vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: Case: SAU. Kamal Shivaji Pokarnekhar vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.. Date: 12th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the process issued by the Trial Court against the respondents for alleged forgery and creation of false documents. The complainant alleged that the respondents committed forgery and prepared false documents, leading to the creation of a development agreement dated 11th December 2002, making them liable for prosecution under Sections 420, 465, 467, 468, and 471 read with Section 34 of the IPC. The High Court quashed the process on the grounds that the dispute was of a civil nature and that criminal proceedings against the respondents would be an abuse of the process of law. The Supreme Court stated that the Magistrate is required to apply judicial mind only to determine whether a prima facie case is made out for summoning the accused, without evaluating the merits of the material or evidence in support of the complaint. The Supreme Court held that quashing criminal proceedings is warranted only when the complaint does not disclose any offence or is frivolous, vexatious, or oppressive, and that meticulous analysis of the case is not required before the trial. The Supreme Court found that the High Court acted in excess of its jurisdiction by setting aside the Trial Court's order, as the allegations in the complaint disclosed prima facie offences against the respondents. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the High Court, allowing the appeal, and reinstated the process issued by the Trial Court against the respondents. The Supreme Court emphasized that at the initial stage, the courts should not evaluate the merits of the allegations or the material, as this exercise is reserved for the trial. The only consideration should be whether the allegations make out a prima facie case. The Supreme Court directed the Trial Court to proceed with the trial in accordance with law, based on the process it had initially issued against the respondents.

case_name: SKODA Auto Volkswagen India Private Limited vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: SKODA Auto Volkswagen India Private Limited vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 26th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the FIR registered against SKODA Auto Volkswagen India Private Limited for offences under Sections 34, 471, 468, 467, 420, 419, and 406 IPC should be quashed. The main allegations were that SKODA Auto Volkswagen India Private Limited had installed defeat devices in their vehicles to manipulate emissions tests, leading to higher on-road emissions compared to laboratory tests. The Allahabad High Court refused to quash the FIR but protected the officers of the petitioner against arrest until the submission of the Report under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., provided they cooperated with the investigation. SKODA Auto Volkswagen India Private Limited argued that the Police could not investigate an issue already sub judice before the Supreme Court and that there was a long delay in lodging the complaint, which was based on false particulars. The Supreme Court stated that mere delay in lodging the complaint could not be a ground to quash the FIR and that the questions of fact had to be established during investigation or trial. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition, upholding the High Court's order and stating that the investigation should proceed. The Supreme Court emphasized that quashing of FIRs should be exercised sparingly and only in the rarest of rare cases, and that courts should not interfere with the police investigation unless no cognizable offence is disclosed. The NGT found that Volkswagen had used cheat devices to suppress emissions during laboratory tests, leading to higher NOx emissions on-road, and directed the manufacturers to deposit Rs. 500 crores as compensation for environmental damage. The Supreme Court stated that the NGT proceedings addressed environmental damage broadly, whereas the criminal complaint involved specific allegations by an individual purchaser, making the police investigation appropriate. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to provide interim protection against arrest for the company's officers until the completion of the investigation, provided they cooperated fully with the authorities.

case_name: STATE OF KERALA & ANR. vs. M/S RDS PROJECT LIMITED & ORS.
text: Case: STATE OF KERALA & ANR. vs. M/S RDS PROJECT LIMITED & ORS.. Date: 22nd September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the structural integrity and rehabilitation of the Palarivattom Flyover, which showed distress and cracks within a year of its use, and whether the flyover should be demolished and reconstructed or repaired based on different expert opinions. The IIT Madras recommended repair using carbon fibre fabric composite treatment, while Dr. E. Sreedharan recommended demolishing the existing structure and reconstructing it with a 100-year guarantee for durability. The High Level Committee concluded that the flyover should be demolished and reconstructed as recommended by Dr. E. Sreedharan, citing that this would ensure a 100-year service life and considering the extensive nature of the required repairs. The Kerala High Court directed that a load test should be conducted to ascertain the strength of the existing structure before making any decision on demolition or repair. The Supreme Court set aside the Kerala High Court's directive for a load test, stating that the High Court overstepped its judicial review boundaries by not deferring to the expert committee's recommendations and the State Government's decision. The Supreme Court upheld the State Government's decision to accept the High Level Committee's recommendation for demolishing and reconstructing the Palarivattom Flyover, and set aside the Kerala High Court's judgment and review judgment. The Supreme Court directed that the pending Writ Petitions in the Kerala High Court should be disposed of within six months from the date of the Supreme Court's judgment.

case_name: SVG Fashions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ritu Murli Manohar Goyal & Anr.
text: Case: SVG Fashions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ritu Murli Manohar Goyal & Anr.. Date: 29th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the application filed by SVG Fashions Pvt. Ltd. under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, against M/S Arpita Filaments Pvt. Ltd. was barred by limitation, as determined by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT). The corporate-debtor raised four major objections, including that the claim was barred by limitation. They argued that six cheques issued towards the part payment of liability were lost in March 2017, and 'stop payment instructions' were issued to the bank. They also claimed that the letter dated 28.09.2015 relied upon by the operational creditor was issued by Shree Adeshwar Textiles. The NCLT overruled the objections and held that there was an acknowledgment of liability on the part of the corporate-debtor based on the letter dated 28.09.2015 and the six cheques issued. Consequently, the NCLT ordered the admission of the application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and declared a moratorium in terms of Section 14. The NCLAT held that the debt arose during the period from 11.08.2013 to 02.09.2013 and that the six cheques purportedly issued towards part payment of the liability on 5.12.2017 would not save limitation. The NCLAT further stated that even if the date of default was taken as 7.10.2013, the acknowledgment of liability in terms of Section 18 of the Limitation Act should have occurred on or before 07.10.2016. The Supreme Court observed that the NCLAT failed to discuss the letter dated 28.09.2015 and the six cheques handed over along with it. The Court noted that the NCLAT overlooked the vital aspect of these documents, which were crucial in determining the acknowledgment of liability and the applicability of Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The Supreme Court reiterated that the law relating to the applicability of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, is well settled. The Court emphasized that the acknowledgment of liability must be examined to determine whether it extended the limitation period. The NCLAT's failure to consider this aspect necessitated a remand for fresh consideration. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order of the NCLAT, and remanded the matter back to the NCLAT for fresh consideration in light of the observations and principles of law indicated by the Court. There was no order as to costs.
passages: The primary legal issue was whether the application filed by SVG Fashions Pvt. Ltd. under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, against M/S Arpita Filaments Pvt. Ltd. was barred by limitation, as determined by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

The corporate-debtor raised four major objections, including that the claim was barred by limitation. They argued that six cheques issued towards the part payment of liability were lost in March 2017, and 'stop payment instructions' were issued to the bank. They also claimed that the letter dated 28.09.2015 relied upon by the operational creditor was issued by Shree Adeshwar Textiles.

The NCLT overruled the objections and held that there was an acknowledgment of liability on the part of the corporate-debtor based on the letter dated 28.09.2015 and the six cheques issued. Consequently, the NCLT ordered the admission of the application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and declared a moratorium in terms of Section 14.

The NCLAT further stated that even if the date of default was taken as 7.10.2013, the acknowledgment of liability in terms of Section 18 of the Limitation Act should have occurred on or before 07.10.2016.

The Supreme Court observed that the NCLAT failed to discuss the letter dated 28.09.2015 and the six cheques handed over along with it. The Court noted that the NCLAT overlooked the vital aspect of these documents, which were crucial in determining the acknowledgment of liability and the applicability of Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

The Supreme Court reiterated that the law relating to the applicability of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, is well settled. The Court emphasized that the acknowledgment of liability must be examined to determine whether it extended the limitation period. The NCLAT's failure to consider this aspect necessitated a remand for fresh consideration.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order of the NCLAT, and remanded the matter back to the NCLAT for fresh consideration in light of the observations and principles of law indicated by the Court. There was no order as to costs.

case_name: Sachin Garg vs. State of U.P. & Anr.
text: Case: Sachin Garg vs. State of U.P. & Anr.. Date: 30th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sachin Garg was the Head of Factory at Exide Industries Limited (EIL), situated at Bawal, District Rewari, Haryana. The dispute was over a purchase order for Dissolved Acetylene Gas (DA Gas) and the subsequent amendments to the order, which led to a disagreement over payment. The purchase order dated 1st April 2019 was amended twice: first on 18th July 2019, increasing the rate to Rs. 1.65 per unit, and then on 20th December 2019, decreasing the rate to Rs. 1.48 per unit. Ambika Gases raised an invoice for a total sum of Rs. 9,36,693.18. EIL reconciled the accounts and informed Ambika Gases of alleged foul play regarding the revision of rates, appropriating the amounts claimed by the vendor. Sachin Garg was summoned for trial under Sections 406 (criminal breach of trust), 504 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace), and 506 (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court dismissed the application because it determined that the complaint involved disputed questions of fact that required adjudication. The Supreme Court found that the commercial dispute over the rate revision did not constitute an offence under Section 405 of the IPC, as there was no evidence of dishonest misappropriation or conversion for personal use. The Supreme Court found that the allegations were vague and lacked particulars, constituting mere bald allegations without sufficient detail to support the charge of criminal intimidation. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, quashed the criminal complaint and the summons, and allowed Sachin Garg's appeal.

case_name: Sachit Kumar Singh & Ors. vs The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
text: Case: Sachit Kumar Singh & Ors. vs The State of Jharkhand & Ors.. Date: 28th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the appellants, who applied for the post of Sub Inspector of Police through a limited competitive examination, were rightfully denied eligibility due to not obtaining the minimum qualifying marks in the written examination. The appellants contended that the key answers to nine questions in the written examination were incorrect, and that they should have been awarded marks for those questions, which would have made them eligible for further selection. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petitions, stating that the objections to the key answers were not raised within the stipulated time period provided by the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals, reasoning that even if there were discrepancies in the answers, the discrepancies affected all candidates equally, and thus, no prejudice was caused specifically to the appellants. The Supreme Court decided that the objections to the key answers should be considered on merits and called for the expert's opinion on the disputed questions. The Court found that the High Court had taken a too technical view by dismissing the objections based on the stipulated time period. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the Division Bench of the High Court for fresh consideration of the appeals on merits, with the directive that it may call for the expert's opinion on the disputed questions to determine the correct answers. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals in part, quashing the High Court's judgment that dismissed the Letters Patent Appeals. The case was remitted back to the Division Bench of the High Court for fresh consideration, to be decided within three months.
