case_name: Saeeda Khatoon Arshi vs. State of UP & Anr.
text: Case: Saeeda Khatoon Arshi vs. State of UP & Anr.. Date: 10th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order summoning the second respondent under Section 319 of the CrPC, who was accused of being complicit in the death of Juhi Arshi. The appellant, Saeeda Khatoon Arshi, is the mother of the deceased Juhi Arshi, and the respondents include the State of UP and the second respondent, who was Juhi's husband. On the night of 9th/10th June 2017, Juhi Arshi was found dead in her matrimonial home. The second respondent informed the appellant that Juhi had hanged herself. The appellant saw injury marks on Juhi's body and suspected murder, leading to the filing of an FIR and subsequent exhumation and post-mortem of the body. The post-mortem report, conducted after the body was exhumed, found the body in an advanced stage of decomposition, making it difficult to ascertain the cause of death. However, injury marks were observed on her neck, hands, and legs. The High Court reasoned that the trial was proceeding against another accused under Section 306 IPC, and the trial court's order summoning the second respondent was based on exploring possibilities rather than strong and cogent evidence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, reinstating the trial court's order summoning the second respondent under Section 319 of the CrPC, based on the evidence presented by PW-1 and PW-2 which indicated possible complicity in the crime. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power under Section 319 is discretionary and should be exercised sparingly, only when strong and cogent evidence indicates that a person not originally an accused appears to have committed an offence.

case_name: Sagar Behera @ Banamali @ Dayanidhi vs State of West Bengal
text: Case: Sagar Behera @ Banamali @ Dayanidhi vs State of West Bengal. Date: 4th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sagar Behera was convicted for offences under Sections 302, 394, 323 read with Section 34, and Section 411 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence under Section 302 and rigorous imprisonment for ten years for the offence under Section 394. The incident occurred on 17th April 2001, which led to the conviction of Sagar Behera for multiple offences including murder, robbery, and causing hurt. Sagar Behera raised the plea of juvenility at the time of the offence, relying on a school certificate that indicated he was a minor on the date of the offence. The Supreme Court directed the Sessions Judge, Bhadrak, Odisha, to examine the original school records and record the statement of the Head Master who issued the certificate. The investigation confirmed that Sagar Behera's date of birth was 20th May 1984, making him a minor at the time of the offence. The Supreme Court observed that Sagar Behera had already suffered more than twenty years of incarceration, and his conduct in jail was good. The jail authorities had recommended his premature release/remission of sentence. The Supreme Court directed the release of Sagar Behera from jail on suspension of sentence and instructed the State of West Bengal to consider and decide the request for his premature release/remission within two months.

case_name: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
text: Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another. Date: 10th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the trial court's order that rejected the application to summon the appellant, Sagar, as an accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The incident involved the death of Nitin, who was found in a naked position with an electric wire around his neck in Jagpal's field. The complainant, Ravinder, alleged that his son Nitin was last seen with Jagpal and Sagar before the incident. The trial court rejected the application, finding that the statements of the complainant (PW1) and his father (PW2) did not provide sufficient evidence to summon Sagar as an accused. The court noted that both witnesses were not eye-witnesses to the incident. The High Court set aside the trial court's order and directed the trial court to reconsider the application under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure within two months, allowing sufficient opportunity to the parties. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 319 CrPC is a discretionary and extraordinary power to be exercised sparingly. The Court found that the High Court did not properly consider the principles laid down for invoking Section 319 and set aside the High Court's order. The complainant (PW1) and his father (PW2) mentioned Sagar's presence with Nitin before the incident, and the removal of the electric wire by Sagar was noted. However, the investigating officer did not find sufficient evidence to charge Sagar in the initial investigation. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the High Court's order dated 28th July 2021. The Court upheld the trial court's decision to reject the application to summon Sagar as an accused under Section 319 CrPC. The Supreme Court noted that the evidence needed to invoke Section 319 CrPC should be more than mere probability but short of satisfaction that would lead to conviction if unchallenged. The Court found that such strong evidence was lacking in this case. The Supreme Court highlighted that the power under Section 319 CrPC should be exercised only when strong and cogent evidence is available from the evidence led before the court, ensuring that it is not used in a casual and cavalier manner.

case_name: Sagufa Ahmed & Ors. vs. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Sagufa Ahmed & Ors. vs. Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 18th September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves an appeal against the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)'s decision to dismiss an application for condonation of delay and an appeal as time-barred. The appellants, who hold 24.89% shares in Upper Assam Plywood Products Pvt. Ltd., sought to wind up the company after their petition was dismissed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). The appellants filed an application for condonation of delay because they missed the statutory deadline for filing an appeal against the NCLT's order dated 25th October 2019. They argued that the delay was due to the late receipt of the certified copy of the order and the lockdown imposed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The NCLAT dismissed the application for condonation of delay on the grounds that it had no power to condone delays beyond the statutory limit of 45 days as stipulated by Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. The appellants argued that the limitation period should be computed from the date they received the certified copy of the NCLT order on 19th December 2019, not from the date of the order itself. They also cited the Supreme Court's order extending the limitation period due to the COVID-19 lockdown. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, holding that the appellants could not claim the benefit of the Supreme Court's order extending the limitation period because this order extended only the prescribed period of limitation, not the period within which delays could be condoned. The appellants had not filed the appeal within the permissible period even before the lockdown started. The significance of the Supreme Court's order dated 23rd March 2020, which extended the limitation period due to the COVID-19 pandemic, was that it applied only to the prescribed period of limitation for initiating proceedings. It did not extend the period within which delays could be condoned. Therefore, the appellants' reliance on this order was misplaced.

case_name: Sahib Singh vs. The State of Punjab
text: Case: Sahib Singh vs. The State of Punjab. Date: 31st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the conviction of Sahib Singh under Section 326 IPC for assaulting the deceased, Harbans Singh, with a kirpan was justified. On 26th January 2002, at around 5:30 PM, Sahib Singh along with other accused attacked the deceased, Harbans Singh, and his brother, Jagir Singh, near their tube well outside the village. The appellant's defense was that he was not named in the FIR and thus his conviction was not justified. The courts justified the conviction by noting that Sahib Singh was named in subsequent statements and identified by eyewitnesses, including Jagir Singh (PW-3) and Bachan Singh (PW-4), who were also injured in the incident. The conviction was based on the eyewitness testimonies of Jagir Singh (PW-3) and Bachan Singh (PW-4), who identified Sahib Singh as one of the attackers armed with a kirpan and responsible for assaulting Harbans Singh. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction under Section 326 IPC and finding no reason to interfere with the conclusions reached by the Trial Court and the High Court.

case_name: Sajan Sethi vs. Rajan Sethi
text: Case: Sajan Sethi vs. Rajan Sethi. Date: 2nd March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the partition of the property bearing No.D-1090, New Friends Colony, New Delhi, which was inherited by the parties from their parents through a Will. According to the Will, the ground floor was bequeathed to Rajan Sethi, the first floor to Sajan Sethi, and the second floor was to be divided equally between them, with Sajan Sethi receiving the front half and Rajan Sethi the back half. Rajan Sethi sought the partition and permanent injunction of the second floor and terrace rights of the property. The Trial Court decided that the second floor and terrace rights could not be partitioned by metes and bounds and ordered that the property be put up for sale by auction, with the proceeds to be divided equally between the parties. The High Court set aside the Trial Court's direction for the sale of the second floor and terrace rights and issued new directions, including that Sajan Sethi would not have the right to use the small driveway on the ground floor but would retain easementary rights for water pipes and booster pump access. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision that Sajan Sethi could not use the driveway on the ground floor but retained rights to the water pipes and booster pump. The Court found no merit in Sajan Sethi's appeal and dismissed it. The Supreme Court noted the mother's intention to avoid discord among her children, as expressed in her Will, and emphasized the importance of respecting her wishes for the harmonious division of the property.

case_name: Sajid vs The State of Uttarakhand and Another
text: Case: Sajid vs The State of Uttarakhand and Another. Date: 10th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sajid was convicted under Sections 363 and 366 of the Indian Penal Code for kidnapping and abduction with the intent to compel a woman to marry. Sajid was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of seven years and a fine of Rs. 1,000. The significant development was that the de facto complainant subsequently married another person and they are living happily without any complaint against Sajid. The Supreme Court modified Sajid's sentence to the period already undergone, while confirming the conviction. Additionally, Sajid was directed to pay a fine of Rs. 2,00,000 as compensation to the second respondent within a month. The Supreme Court directed that Sajid should be released forthwith if he was not required in connection with any other case. The appeal was allowed with the modification that Sajid's sentence was limited to the period already undergone, and he was required to pay Rs. 2,00,000 as compensation to the second respondent.

case_name: Sakharam vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Sakharam vs. State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 19th August 2015. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sakharam was initially charged under Section 302 IPC for murder and Section 307 IPC for attempt to murder. The High Court modified Sakharam's conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 325 IPC and sentenced him to seven years of rigorous imprisonment. The incident involved a quarrel where Raju, Tularam, and Vipatlal attacked Ramnath, his brother Badri, and nephew Santu with lathis and a sharp iron rod (Ballam), leading to serious injuries and the death of Badri. The prosecution argued that Sakharam and others attacked Ramnath and his family, causing serious injuries with lathis and Ballam, leading to the death of Badri and injuries to Santu and Ramnath. The Trial Court convicted Sakharam and Tularam under Sections 302 and 307 IPC, sentencing them to life imprisonment and ten years of rigorous imprisonment, respectively. Sakharam's defense argued that the incident was a sudden quarrel without prior intention, and the injuries inflicted on Santu were not grievous as opined by Dr. Moitra (PW-15). The Supreme Court observed that the injuries on Santu's head were grievous, as indicated by the X-ray report showing a fracture of the frontal bone. The Supreme Court reduced the sentence considering the incident was a sudden fight in a fit of passion, and the injuries inflicted were in the heat of the moment. The Supreme Court partly allowed Sakharam's appeal, confirming his conviction under Section 325 IPC but reducing his sentence to three years of rigorous imprisonment.

case_name: Samir Kumar Majumder vs. The Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Samir Kumar Majumder vs. The Union of India & Ors.. Date: 20th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Samir Kumar Majumder, a substitute teacher, was entitled to absorption as an Assistant Teacher in the Higher Secondary Section with continuity of service. Samir Kumar Majumder mentioned that he faced artificial breaks in his service, such as termination before summer vacations and re-engagement after vacations, which he claimed were done to avoid giving him continuous service benefits. The Central Administrative Tribunal dismissed Samir Kumar Majumder's application, relying on a previous order that substitute teachers could not claim regularization as a matter of right and must be selected by the Railway Recruitment Board for regular appointment. The Supreme Court allowed similarly situated candidates to be absorbed on a regular basis through the process of screening by a Screening Committee, without requiring selection by the Railway Recruitment Board, and granted them continuity of service. The main argument was that under the Master Circular dated 29.01.1991, Samir Kumar Majumder, having completed three months of continuous service, should be absorbed as an Assistant Teacher with continuity of service from the date he attained temporary status. The Supreme Court found Samir Kumar Majumder's claim for absorption as an Assistant Teacher in the Higher Secondary Section untenable, as he was appointed as a substitute primary teacher and did not raise this claim in the initial proceedings. case_name: Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: Case: Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.. Date: 22nd April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare, who was disqualified as a Municipal Councillor under Section 44(1)(e) of the Maharashtra Municipal Council, Nagar Panchayat and Industrial Township Act, 1965, for unauthorized constructions carried out by her husband, could be held responsible for the same. The Collector disqualified Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare on the grounds that her husband had carried out unauthorized constructions, and under Section 44(1)(e), a Councillor can be disqualified if their spouse or dependent has constructed any illegal or unauthorized structure. Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare argued that the unauthorized constructions were carried out by her husband, who had deemed permission, and that she should not be held responsible for the actions of her spouse under Section 44(1)(e) of the Act. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 44(1)(e) to mean that a Councillor can be disqualified if their spouse or dependent constructs an illegal or unauthorized structure, regardless of whether the Councillor was directly involved. The provision aims to ensure the highest level of probity by the Councillor and their immediate family. The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, stating that temporary constructions also fall within the mischief of Section 44(1)(e) and can result in disqualification if they are unauthorized. The Court upheld the disqualification based on the temporary constructions carried out by her husband. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the orders of the Collector and the High Court, which had disqualified Sampada Yogesh Waghdhare as a Municipal Councillor due to unauthorized constructions carried out by her husband.

case_name: Sampurna Behura vs Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Sampurna Behura vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 9th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary concern was the virtual non-implementation or tardy implementation of laws beneficial to children, particularly the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 and the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. The Supreme Court appreciated the efforts of Sampurna Behura for highlighting the issues related to the implementation of juvenile justice laws through a Public Interest Litigation and acknowledged the assistance rendered by the learned counsel for the appearing parties. The Chief Justices' Conferences resolved to expedite the setting up of Juvenile Justice Boards, ensure periodic visits to Juvenile Homes by nominated judges, and improve the conditions of these homes and the living conditions of juveniles, among other measures. The Supreme Court highlighted that children are often subjected to official apathy and live in uncomfortable conditions with little or no access to justice. The Court stressed the importance of treating children with dignity and ensuring their fundamental and human rights are protected. The Supreme Court directed that the Chief Justices of High Courts expedite the setting up of Juvenile Justice Boards, ensure regular visits to Juvenile Homes, set up Child Welfare Committees, appoint and train Probation Officers, and improve the living conditions in child care institutions. The Supreme Court stated that judicial intervention was necessary to ensure the enforcement of laws beneficial to children, as State Governments and Union Territories had not fully complied with the provisions of the Juvenile Justice Acts, despite the passage of significant time since their enactment. The Supreme Court observed that the judiciary has a constitutional obligation to act in the best interests of children and ensure that laws beneficial to children are effectively implemented, regardless of criticism of judicial 'activism' or overreach.

case_name: Sandeep Kumar vs. The State of Haryana & Anr.
text: Case: Sandeep Kumar vs. The State of Haryana & Anr.. Date: 28th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the order of the trial court that had summoned three additional accused based on the evidence provided by the complainant (PW-9). The accused were charged under Sections 458, 460, 323, 302, 148, 149, and 285 of the IPC, and Section 25 of the Arms Act for breaking into the complainant's house and committing assault and murder. The complainant (PW-9) provided evidence as an eyewitness, detailing the roles of Ramesh Gandhi, Kalu Jakhar, and Pawan, who were armed and part of the group that broke into his house and assaulted the family members. The trial court decided to summon these individuals based on the evidence presented by the complainant (PW-9), which clearly implicated them in the crime. The High Court set aside the order on the grounds that Ramesh Gandhi was found innocent during the investigation and that there was no evidence of his active participation in the crime, an assertion the Supreme Court found factually incorrect. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for not appreciating the evidence properly and for making uncalled-for presumptions about the innocence of the additional accused without considering the testimony of PW-9. Section 319 of the CrPC allows a court to summon additional persons as accused if it appears from the evidence that they have committed an offence. The Supreme Court emphasized that the trial court was correct in summoning the additional accused based on the evidence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, reinstated the trial court's decision to summon the additional accused, and directed that the trial should proceed expeditiously in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court emphasized that at the stage of summoning additional accused under Section 319 CrPC, the court must only have a prima facie satisfaction that the evidence suggests the person has committed an offence, without delving into the merits of the evidence, which is to be examined during the trial. The Supreme Court viewed the complainant's testimony as credible and significant enough to summon the additional accused, highlighting that the complainant's detailed account provided a clear basis for their involvement in the crime.

case_name: Sandeep alias Kala vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Sandeep alias Kala vs. State of Haryana. Date: 16th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sandeep alias Kala was charged with offences punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 25 of the Arms Act 1959. The Additional Sessions Judge, Sonepat, acquitted Sandeep alias Kala and Ravi Kant, while convicting Arun (A-1) and Sunil (A-3) under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The Additional Sessions Judge acquitted Sandeep alias Kala based on the oral testimony of witnesses and documentary medical evidence that corroborated his alibi of being admitted in a government hospital from 12th February 2005 to 16th February 2005. The High Court allowed the appeals filed by the State of Haryana against the acquittal of Sandeep alias Kala and Ravi Kant, holding them guilty of offences under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs 20,000 each. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Sandeep alias Kala on 5th May 2014, stating that the appeal was devoid of merit. The High Court rejected Sandeep alias Kala's alibi on the grounds that the medical records were not credible, and the documents were prepared to falsely support his alibi. Sandeep alias Kala invoked Article 32 of the Constitution in his writ petition, challenging the deletion of clauses from the Supreme Court Rules and seeking declarations regarding the unconstitutionality of certain provisions. Sandeep alias Kala argued that the deletion of certain clauses from the Supreme Court Rules was contrary to the law laid down by a Constitution Bench and that the absence of guidelines in the 2013 Rules was unconstitutional as it offended the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the deletion of Rule 15(1)(c) was intended to align with the principles laid down by the Constitution Bench in Sita Ram's case, ensuring that appeals under Article 134(1)(a) or (b) or the Enlargement of Jurisdiction Act were not dismissed summarily without notice. The Supreme Court emphasized that the right of appeal in criminal cases is protected under Article 21 of the Constitution, and any procedure that makes this right illusory or its outcome uncertain is unconstitutional.

case_name: Sanjai Tiwari vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Sanjai Tiwari vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 16th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court erred in entertaining a third party's application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to expedite the criminal trial against Sanjai Tiwari. Sanjai Tiwari was accused under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 477A, and 120B of the IPC, and Section 13(1) C/D read with 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The High Court directed the trial court to expedite the trial to ensure a swift conclusion of the criminal proceedings without unnecessary adjournments. Sanjai Tiwari's counsel argued that the High Court erred in entertaining a third party's application, who had no locus standi, and issued the order without notifying the appellant. The Supreme Court observed that the third party, who described himself as a social activist and advocate, had no locus standi to file an application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to expedite the criminal trial. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Janata Dal vs. H.S. Chowdhary, where it was held that third parties do not have the locus standi to intervene in criminal proceedings under the garb of public interest litigants. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, ruling that the application filed by the third party was not maintainable and should not have been entertained. Yes, the Supreme Court emphasized that trials under the Prevention of Corruption Act should be conducted and concluded expeditiously, due to their impact on society and administration. The Supreme Court allowed the trial court to expedite the criminal trial subject to any order passed by the High Court in pending proceedings but dismissed the third party's application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order dated 9th September 2020, and dismissed the application filed by the third party under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

case_name: Sanjay Chaudhary and Anr. vs. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. and Anr.
text: Case: Sanjay Chaudhary and Anr. vs. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. and Anr.. Date: 10th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission allowed the complaint and directed the opposite parties to issue a fresh statement of account, credit delayed compensation of Rs. 2433120/- as on 13.11.2017, and charge interest @9% per annum on the balance amount (except stamp duty and registration charges) from 14.11.2017 till the date of payment. They also directed the opposite parties to execute the conveyance deed and handover possession of the unit to the complainants. The appellants were aggrieved by the direction allowing the respondent-developer to charge interest @9% per annum on the balance amount (except stamp duty and registration charges) from 14th November 2017 till the date of payment from the appellants-homebuyers. The appellants had made payment of 90% of the total sale consideration, which amounted to nearly Rs. 2,21,56,942.42, to the respondent-developer by 23rd June 2014. The scheduled date for the handover of possession of the flat was 16th March 2014. The respondent-developer failed to meet this deadline, leading to the consumer dispute. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the part of the Commission's order that allowed the respondent-developer to charge interest @9% per annum on the balance amount from the appellants. The Court directed the respondents to convey the outstanding amount to the appellants within two months, and the possession of the flat should be handed over within 30 days of the final payment.

case_name: Sanjay Kundu vs. Registrar General, High Court of Himachal Pradesh & Ors.
text: Case: Sanjay Kundu vs. Registrar General, High Court of Himachal Pradesh & Ors.. Date: 12th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge against the High Court's order directing the transfer of Sanjay Kundu from the post of Director General of Police (DGP), Himachal Pradesh, based on allegations of misuse of his official position. The allegations were that Sanjay Kundu, in his official capacity as DGP, intervened in a private civil dispute involving business transactions and attempted to intimidate the complainant, Nishant Sharma, to withdraw his complaints. The criminal writ petition was initiated suo motu by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh based on an email from the complainant, Nishant Kumar Sharma, addressed to the Chief Justice through the Registrar General. The status report indicated that Sanjay Kundu had made 15 missed calls to the complainant on the day of the alleged incident, was in continuous contact with the complainant's business partner 'Y', and placed the complainant under surveillance. The High Court ordered that Sanjay Kundu be shifted out of the post of DGP to ensure a fair investigation into the allegations made by the complainant. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order was passed without giving Sanjay Kundu an opportunity to contest the allegations, leading to a manifest miscarriage of procedural justice. The Supreme Court directed the State Government to constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) consisting of IG level officers to conduct an objective and fair investigation, without reporting to Sanjay Kundu. The complainant alleged that 'Y', a practicing advocate and business partner, used his connections to intimidate the complainant into selling shares in his company, and Sanjay Kundu facilitated these threats. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court improperly assumed disciplinary jurisdiction over Sanjay Kundu, which should have been governed by the rules of service and administrative control. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order transferring Sanjay Kundu from the post of DGP, while directing the State Government to ensure the SIT conducts a fair investigation and provides security to the complainant. The Supreme Court directed the State Government to constitute an SIT of IG level officers who would not report to Sanjay Kundu and to provide adequate security to the complainant and his family based on threat perception.

case_name: Sanjay Patel & Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Sanjay Patel & Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 13th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Sanjay Patel was a juvenile at the time of committing the offence and thus should be tried under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) Act, 2000. Sanjay Patel was convicted by the Sessions Court on 16th May 2006 for the offence punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to life imprisonment. The offence was committed on 8th January 2004. Sanjay Patel filed the application claiming that he was a juvenile at the time of the offence, based on his date of birth being 16th May 1986, which would make him 17 years 07 months and 23 days old on the date of the offence. The Juvenile Justice Board concluded that Sanjay Patel's correct date of birth is 16th May 1986, confirming that he was a juvenile on the date of the offence. Section 7A of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) Act, 2000, allowed Sanjay Patel to raise the claim of juvenility at any stage, even after the final disposal of the case. The Supreme Court allowed the application and directed that Sanjay Patel be forwarded to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate orders. By 1st August 2021, Sanjay Patel had already served 17 years and 03 days in jail. The Supreme Court directed that Sanjay Patel be forthwith set at liberty, provided he was not required to be detained under any other order of a competent court. The decision sets a precedent that juvenility claims can be raised at any stage and emphasizes the importance of adhering to juvenile justice laws, potentially influencing the handling of similar cases in the future. The Supreme Court clarified that under Section 7A, an accused can raise the claim of juvenility at any stage, and if found to be juvenile, the sentence passed by the Criminal Court shall be deemed to have no effect.

case_name: Sanju and Others vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Sanju and Others vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 29th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants' conviction for the murder of Chandrapal Singh and the attempt to murder his brother, Rakesh Kumar, was justified based on the evidence presented. The charges included murder under Section 302 of the IPC and attempt to murder under Section 307 of the IPC. The primary eyewitness was Rakesh Kumar (PW-1), the brother of the deceased Chandrapal Singh. Another purported eyewitness was Ramphal Singh (PW-2), although his testimony was later discarded by the court. The motive was related to a dispute over bricks stored by Chandrapal Singh on Bhagwati Singh's land. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony from Rakesh Kumar (PW-1), medical examination reports of the injuries, the post-mortem report, and the site map prepared by the police. The Supreme Court discarded Ramphal Singh's testimony due to inconsistencies and the late recording of his statement as an eyewitness, which raised doubts about its reliability. The medical examination confirmed that Rakesh Kumar had six injuries, which were consistent with the timeline of the incident, supporting his account of the attack. The Supreme Court found the presence of the appellants at the scene of the crime to be sufficiently established through the credible testimony of Rakesh Kumar (PW-1) and corroborative evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC for the murder of Chandrapal Singh, based on the evidence presented. The Supreme Court did not interfere with the sentences of the appellants, which included life imprisonment and fines for the offences under Sections 302 and 307 IPC. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the convictions and sentences of the appellants for murder and attempt to murder.

case_name: Sankath Prasad vs State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Sankath Prasad vs State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 10th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sankath Prasad was charged with murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the killing of Uma Shanker. The incident occurred on 25th August 1985, when Sankath Prasad allegedly shot Uma Shanker with a country-made pistol during an altercation over the excavation of a mound by Sankath's brother, Durga Prasad. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimonies from Gaya Prasad (PW-1) and Ram Nath (PW-2), who both witnessed the altercation and the shooting. The medical evidence, including the post-mortem report, supported the eyewitness accounts. The High Court dismissed Sankath Prasad's appeal, upholding his conviction under Section 302 IPC and his life imprisonment sentence. The Supreme Court observed that the incident occurred on the spur of the moment during an altercation and was not premeditated. The Court noted that the shooting was a result of a sudden provocation. The Supreme Court converted the conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part I IPC, sentencing Sankath Prasad to ten years of imprisonment instead of life imprisonment.

case_name: Sansera Engineering Limited vs Deputy Commissioner, Large Tax Payer Unit, Bengaluru
text: Case: Sansera Engineering Limited vs Deputy Commissioner, Large Tax Payer Unit, Bengaluru. Date: 29th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the rebate claim filed by Sansera Engineering Limited for the excise duty paid on exported goods was barred by the time limitation prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Sansera Engineering Limited filed claims for rebate of excise duty paid on goods exported between August 2015 and October 2015 and another claim for the period between October 2015 and March 2016, totaling Rs. 29,47,996/-, Rs. 42,27,928/-, and Rs. 1,47,27,766/-. The original authority rejected the rebate claims as they were filed beyond the one-year time limit prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petitions, holding that the rebate claims were made beyond the period of one year prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the judgment of the learned Single Judge that the rebate claims were time-barred under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The appellant's counsel contended that the rebate of duty paid on excisable goods under Rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, is different from a refund of duty under Section 11B, and that the time limit under Section 11B should not apply to rebate claims. The Supreme Court held that Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, applies to rebate claims, as the term 'refund' includes 'rebate of duty' as per Explanation (A) to Section 11B. The Supreme Court stated that Rule 18 and the notification issued under it cannot override the parent statute, Section 11B, and must be read harmoniously with it. The period of limitation under Section 11B is applicable to rebate claims. The Supreme Court decided that the one-year limitation period prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, applies to rebate claims, and any claims made beyond this period are time-barred. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by Sansera Engineering Limited, upholding the decisions of the High Court and the original authority that the rebate claims were time-barred under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Supreme Court reinforced that statutory limitations, such as the one-year period prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, must be strictly adhered to for rebate claims, and subordinate legislation cannot override these statutory provisions.

case_name: Santosh @ Bhure vs. State (G.N.C.T.) of Delhi
text: Case: Santosh @ Bhure vs. State (G.N.C.T.) of Delhi. Date: 28th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Santosh @ Bhure's appeal was dismissed, and his conviction was upheld. The appeal by the State against Neeraj's acquittal was also dismissed. Santosh @ Bhure and Neeraj were charged with offenses under Sections 302 read with 34 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Hari Shankar. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the tenancy of the apartment where the murder occurred, the recovery of a suicide letter, and the discovery of blood-stained clothes and a knife/dagger linked to the accused. The suicide letter, allegedly written by Neeraj, was intended to mislead the investigation. The handwriting expert confirmed that the letter matched Neeraj's handwriting. The court found that the presence of the dead body in Santosh @ Bhure's apartment, along with the circumstantial evidence, pointed towards his involvement in the crime. However, mere tenancy was not sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt without additional evidence. Santosh @ Bhure's defense argued that there was no documentary evidence proving his tenancy, no motive for the murder was established, and his presence in the apartment at the relevant time was not proven.

case_name: Santosh @ Santosh Kumar vs State of Kerala
text: Case: Santosh @ Santosh Kumar vs State of Kerala. Date: 16th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the sentence imposed on Santosh Kumar for the offence under Section 55(a) of the Abkari Act should be reduced. The Additional Sessions Court sentenced Santosh Kumar to five years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1 lakh, with an additional one year of rigorous imprisonment in case of default. The High Court of Kerala reduced the jail sentence from five years to three years but maintained the fine of Rs.1 lakh. The Supreme Court was considering whether the quantum of the sentence awarded to Santosh Kumar by the High Court should be further reduced. The offence involved the illegal storage of spirit in 58 cans found in a residential house and a car parked in the porch of the house. The Supreme Court considered the facts that the incident occurred in 2007, Santosh Kumar had already served around 1 year and 3 months of his sentence, and he was not involved in any other criminal activity. The Supreme Court awarded Santosh Kumar a jail sentence of 'already undergone' and increased the fine to Rs.1,50,000. Failure to pay the fine would result in an additional one year of jail sentence. If Santosh Kumar fails to pay the enhanced fine of Rs.1,50,000, he will have to undergo an additional one year of jail sentence. The ruling finalizes the sentence to 'already undergone' and fine, thereby concluding his legal obligations in this particular case if he pays the enhanced fine. Section 55(a) of the Abkari Act deals with the illegal manufacture, import, export, transport, or possession of liquor or intoxicating drugs, punishable with imprisonment and fine. The Supreme Court considered the duration of the sentence already served, the absence of prior criminal record, and the length of time since the incident occurred.

case_name: Santosh Devi and Ors vs. Mahaveer Singh and Ors
text: Case: Santosh Devi and Ors vs. Mahaveer Singh and Ors. Date: 9th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The legal proceedings were initiated due to a road accident on 30th December 1992, where Puran Chand, husband and father of the appellants, died after a government jeep, driven by the first respondent, collided with his moped. The MACT awarded the appellants Rs. 1,15,200 after assessing the deceased's monthly income at Rs. 1,200 and applying a multiplier of 12, along with interest at 15% per annum. The High Court increased the compensation to Rs. 1,85,000 by applying a multiplier of 15 and reduced the interest rate to 8% per annum. The appellants argued that the High Court should have applied a multiplier of 16, should not have deducted more than 10% for personal expenses, and should have assessed the deceased's income at Rs. 3,500 per month. The Supreme Court assessed the deceased's monthly income at Rs. 2,500 and applied a multiplier of 16, adding 40% towards future prospects. The Supreme Court awarded a total compensation of Rs. 5,23,000 to the appellants, including Rs. 4,48,000 for loss of dependency and Rs. 75,000 for conventional heads, with interest at 9% per annum from the date of the petition until payment.

case_name: Sarabjeet Singh Mokha vs. The District Magistrate, Jabalpur & Ors.
text: Case: Sarabjeet Singh Mokha vs. The District Magistrate, Jabalpur & Ors.. Date: 29th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant is Sarabjeet Singh Mokha, and the respondents are The District Magistrate, Jabalpur & Ors. The primary allegation against the appellant was that he procured fake Remdesivir injections and administered them to patients during the Covid-19 pandemic to make illegal profits, endangering the lives of the general public. The appellant was detained on 12th May 2021 under the National Security Act (NSA). The grounds for detention included allegations of administering spurious Remdesivir injections resulting in untimely deaths, causing public outcry and resentment, and criminal antecedents of the appellant. The Madhya Pradesh High Court rejected the appellant's writ petition on 24th August 2021, upholding the detention order. The Advisory Board reviewed the grounds for detention and submitted a report to the State Government, which opined that there was sufficient cause for the appellant's detention. The appellant raised issues of delay in considering his representation by the Central and State Governments and failure to communicate the rejection of his representation in a timely manner. The Supreme Court found unexplained delays by the State Government in deciding the appellant's representation and failure to communicate the rejection in a timely manner, which invalidated the detention order. No, the Supreme Court did not address the merits of the detention order, as the appellant succeeded on the grounds of procedural violations. The Supreme Court quashed the detention order dated 11th May 2021 and the subsequent extensions, allowing the appeal and setting aside the High Court's judgement.

case_name: Saranya vs Bharathi and another
text: Case: Saranya vs Bharathi and another. Date: 24th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the entire criminal proceedings against Bharathi (respondent no.1) for the offences under Sections 420, 302 read with 109 IPC. Bharathi was accused of introducing Vela alias Velayutham (A1) to Saranya and her deceased husband, and assuring them that Velayutham could secure a government job for a bribe, which led to the husband consuming a poisoned substance and dying. Velayutham (A1) was accused of promising a government job in exchange for money, administering a poisoned substance disguised as 'Prasadam' to Saranya's husband, which led to his death. The prosecution presented evidence including the confessional statement of Bharathi, recovery of Rs. 1.20 lakhs from her house, and call detail records showing communication between Bharathi and Velayutham around the time of the incident. The High Court quashed the chargesheet and the entire criminal proceedings against Bharathi, stating that there was not enough evidence to support the charges under Sections 420, 302 read with 109 IPC. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in quashing the chargesheet against Bharathi, as there was sufficient prima facie evidence to proceed with the trial. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's decision, and directed the trial to proceed against Bharathi based on the evidence. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court improperly assessed the merits of the evidence and entered into an appreciation of the evidence at the stage of quashing the chargesheet, which is not permissible under Section 482 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court noted that while the confessional statement itself may not be admissible, the recovery of money based on that statement and other circumstantial evidence could still be considered during the trial. The decision reinforces the principle that High Courts should not quash chargesheets based on an assessment of evidence merits at the preliminary stage, ensuring that cases with prima facie evidence proceed to trial. If the trial court finds the evidence insufficient during the trial, Bharathi could be acquitted based on the lack of conclusive proof linking her to the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.

case_name: Saravanan vs. State represented by the Inspector of Police
text: Case: Saravanan vs. State represented by the Inspector of Police. Date: 15th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant, Saravanan, was entitled to default bail under Section 167(2) of the Cr.P.C. despite not depositing the amount required by the conditions set by the lower courts. Saravanan was arrested on 31st January 2020 for offences punishable under Section 420 of the IPC in Crime No. 31 of 2019, related to allegations of cheating and dishonesty inducing delivery of property. The Magistrate ordered Saravanan to deposit Rs. 7,00,000 initially and the balance of Rs. 8,67,338 by 6th April 2020 as conditions for granting bail. The High Court granted default bail to Saravanan but imposed a condition to deposit Rs. 8,00,000, considering an earlier undertaking by Saravanan's wife to deposit Rs. 7,00,000. The Supreme Court ruled that the condition to deposit Rs. 8,00,000 was unsustainable and quashed it, stating that such a condition would defeat the purpose of default bail under Section 167(2), Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court modified the conditions, directing Saravanan to cooperate with the investigating officer and report to the concerned police station as and when called for investigation, instead of daily reporting. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Rakesh Kumar Paul v. State of Assam, emphasizing that the accused is entitled to default bail once the statutory period for filing the chargesheet has expired without completion of the investigation.

case_name: Saregama India Limited vs. Next Radio Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Saregama India Limited vs. Next Radio Limited & Ors.. Date: 27th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court found that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by rewriting Rule 29(4) at the interim stage, which was impermissible and undermined the statutory framework of the Copyright Act. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to resolve the constitutional challenge to Rule 29(4) without further interim modifications and ensure compliance with the statutory framework. The Supreme Court stated that while judicial review can evaluate the validity of statutory rules, it cannot supplant or rewrite legislative provisions through judicial interpretation. The Supreme Court interpreted that prior notice under Rule 29(4) is a statutory mandate that ensures transparency and protects the rights of copyright owners, making it non-negotiable. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's interim order, emphasizing that statutory rules must be adhered to unless constitutionally invalidated.

case_name: Sarita Singh vs. M/s Shree Infosoft Private Limited
text: Case: Sarita Singh vs. M/s Shree Infosoft Private Limited. Date: 12th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Sarita Singh was liable to repay expenses incurred by the company during her overseas visit, which the respondent claimed was a deputation requiring a service obligation upon return. The company filed a suit to recover Rs. 5,70,753, citing expenses for Sarita Singh's overseas deputation and her failure to fulfill the service period stipulated in the employment terms. The trial court partially decreed the suit, awarding Rs. 3,14,590 along with interest at 9% per annum, representing expenses incurred during the alleged overseas deputation. The Court clarified that a deputation requires a tripartite agreement, including the consent of the employee, and that Sarita Singh's overseas visit did not meet this criterion. The Court found that Sarita Singh's visit to the US was a business trip, not a deputation, as there was no formal agreement or evidence indicating a deputation arrangement. The Supreme Court dismissed the recovery suit, holding that the respondent failed to provide sufficient evidence to substantiate their claims of a deputation arrangement.

case_name: Sartaj Singh vs State of Haryana & Anr.
text: Case: Sartaj Singh vs State of Haryana & Anr.. Date: 15th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the Trial Court's order summoning the private respondents as additional accused under Section 319 CrPC. The FIR included charges under Sections 148, 149, 341, 323, 324, 307, and 506 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant's application under Section 319 CrPC was based on the evidence given during the trial, particularly his own testimony and that of other eyewitnesses. The High Court quashed the order on the grounds that there was no new evidence against the private respondents except the statement of the appellant, which it found insufficient. The appellant sustained multiple injuries from blows with lathis and gandasis, as detailed in his FIR and testimony. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power under Section 319 CrPC is discretionary and extraordinary, to be exercised sparingly and only when strong and cogent evidence indicates the involvement of the person to be summoned. The Supreme Court found that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by reassessing the evidence on merits and substituting its view for that of the Trial Court. The decision may reinforce the careful and judicious use of Section 319 CrPC, ensuring that additional accused are summoned only when there is substantial evidence against them. The ruling highlights the importance of corroborative evidence and may lead to more stringent scrutiny of witness testimonies before summoning additional accused. The Supreme Court clarified that the power under Section 319 CrPC should be exercised only when the evidence is strong and cogent, and not merely on the basis of the statements of interested or single witnesses. The appellant lodged an FIR detailing the assault, sought medical treatment, and later filed an application under Section 319 CrPC during the trial to summon additional accused based on his and other witnesses' testimonies.

The appellant lodged an FIR detailing the assault, sought medical treatment, and later filed an application under Section 319 CrPC during the trial to summon additional accused based on his and other witnesses' testimonies.

case_name: Sathish Kumar A @ Sathishkumar Anand @ Sathish Kumar Gupta vs. State of Karnataka
text: Case: Sathish Kumar A @ Sathishkumar Anand @ Sathish Kumar Gupta vs. State of Karnataka. Date: 23rd February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sathish Kumar was charged with the offences punishable under Sections 302 (murder) and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Sathish Kumar was convicted for the murder of his wife, Smt. Priyanka Gupta, on 10th August 2010. He created an impression that while he was out jogging, two persons came to their residence, but later it was found that he had strangled her and inflicted incised wounds. The prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, including the timeline of calls between the appellant and his jogging partner, the suspicious behavior of the appellant, and the recovery of bloodstained shoes from his residence. The postmortem report revealed that Priyanka Gupta died due to asphyxia as a result of strangulation, despite having several incised wounds on her neck. Key pieces of evidence included the call records showing suspicious timings, the appellant wearing black leather shoes instead of jogging shoes, and the recovery of sports shoes with bloodstains from the appellant's residence. The Trial Court convicted and sentenced Sathish Kumar to rigorous imprisonment for life under Section 302 IPC and to five years under Section 201 IPC. The High Court affirmed the Trial Court's decision, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentences. The Supreme Court concluded that the circumstances were proved individually and formed a clear chain consistent only with the hypothesis of Sathish Kumar's guilt, excluding any other reasonable hypothesis.

case_name: Satish @ Sabbe vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Satish @ Sabbe vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 30th September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the petitioners, Satish @ Sabbe and Vikky @ Vikendra alias Virendra, were entitled to premature release from life imprisonment for kidnapping under Section 364-A IPC. Satish @ Sabbe and Vikky @ Vikendra were convicted for kidnapping Vishal Sarawat for ransom under Section 364-A of the IPC and were sentenced to life imprisonment. The Allahabad High Court dismissed the appeals of Satish @ Sabbe and Vikky @ Vikendra, confirming their life imprisonment for kidnapping for ransom. The Supreme Court initially declined to interfere with their conviction for kidnapping but issued limited notice regarding their entitlement to premature release. The Supreme Court directed the respondent-State to reconsider the cases of Satish @ Sabbe and Vikky for premature release within four weeks, in accordance with the Jail Manual. The State rejected the petitioners' premature release citing the heinous nature of the crime, their age and potential to reoffend, and serious apprehensions from the informant. The Supreme Court found the State's refusal to release the petitioners to be mechanical and lacking due consideration of their conduct in prison and likelihood to abstain from crime. The Supreme Court emphasized that first-time offenders should be given a chance to reform and integrate back into society, considering their conduct in prison and lack of antecedents. The Supreme Court directed that Satish @ Sabbe and Vikky be released on probation within two weeks, subject to conditions deemed fit by the respondent-State to balance public safety with individual liberty. During his incarceration, Vikky pursued various distance-learning courses, including passing his Intermediate Examination, learning computer hardware, obtaining a Bachelor of Arts degree, and earning certificates in food and nutrition, human rights, and environmental studies.

case_name: Satish Kumar vs The State of Haryana
text: Case: Satish Kumar vs The State of Haryana. Date: 3rd October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Satish Kumar and Dhajja Ram were charged with murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Shamsher, and were also convicted under Sections 506 and 323 read with Section 34 of the IPC. The conflict arose due to objections by Satish Kumar and Dhajja Ram to the relations of a woman belonging to 'Dahiya Gotra' with a man of 'Ohlan Gotra', which led to threats and violence against Shamsher. The key evidence included the dying declaration of Shamsher, statements from witnesses Surender (PW-2), Bharpoor (PW-7), and Sadhu Ram (PW-8), and medical reports from Dr. Jai Mala (PW-3) and Dr. R.K. Nandal (PW-4). The dying declaration and medical report Ex-PC did not mention any head injury, whereas the post-mortem report Ex-PG indicated a head injury and dislocation of the first cervical vertebral joint as the cause of death, leading to inconsistencies in the evidence. The Supreme Court found ambiguity and contradictions in the evidence, leading to a benefit of doubt for Satish Kumar. The Court decided that the conditions under the third clause of Section 300 IPC were not proved beyond doubt. The Supreme Court converted Satish Kumar's conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part I IPC, sentencing him to the period already undergone, and maintaining the convictions and sentences for other offences. No, Dhajja Ram did not appeal the High Court's judgment. It was stated that he may have been released on remission.

case_name: Satish and Another vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Satish and Another vs. State of Haryana. Date: 26th May 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Satish and Anita were convicted under Section 120-B, 302, and 34 IPC for the murder of Anita's husband and sentenced to life imprisonment. Satish was also convicted under the Arms Act. The murder occurred at about 1:30 a.m. on the night of 31st March 2007 to 1st April 2007. PW-1 Sunita, a neighbor, reported the murder to the police the next morning at about 9:00 a.m. after being informed by PW-2 Sahil, the son of the deceased. The postmortem revealed eight incised wounds and seventeen penetrating incised wounds on the deceased's body. The defense argued that the unexplained delay of eight hours in lodging the FIR provided sufficient time for manipulation and false implication of the appellants. The prosecution's key evidence against Anita was an extra-judicial confession made to PW-4, which implicated her in the conspiracy to murder her husband. The Supreme Court observed that an extra-judicial confession is a weak piece of evidence and should be corroborated. In this case, the confession was considered unreliable due to the acquittal of co-accused Ramesh. The Supreme Court found PW-2 Sahil to be a reliable witness despite his young age and the lack of a test identification parade. His testimony was consistent and convincing. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by Satish and Anita, upholding their convictions and sentences as determined by the lower courts. PW-4 was a property dealer who testified that Anita made an extra-judicial confession to him about the conspiracy to murder her husband. The defense argued that PW-4 manipulated the confession to grab her property.

case_name: Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah vs State of Gujarat & Another
text: Case: Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah vs State of Gujarat & Another. Date: 3rd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah was charged under Sections 406, 409, 417, 420, 294(b), and 506(2) of the Indian Penal Code for allegedly cheating and committing a criminal breach of trust by not repaying a loan of Rs. 27,00,000 obtained from the complainant's company. The Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate framed charges against Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah on 4th December 2013, without giving him an opportunity to be heard and in violation of Section 239 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court dismissed Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah's application seeking to quash the order framing the charges and directed the trial court to complete the trial within three months. The defense argued that the allegations were civil in nature, arising out of a loan transaction, and did not constitute criminal offences. They emphasized that the complainant had also filed a summary civil suit to recover the loan amount. The Supreme Court noted that mere inability to repay a loan does not constitute a criminal offence of cheating unless there is fraudulent or dishonest intention from the beginning. The Court emphasized that the complaint lacked the necessary elements to establish criminal breach of trust or cheating. The Supreme Court quashed the charges against Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah, set aside the High Court's judgment, and allowed the application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., thereby dismissing the criminal proceedings initiated based on the FIR.

case_name: Satpal vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Satpal vs. State of Haryana. Date: 1st May 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Satpal's conviction under Section 302 read with Section 201 IPC was justified, based on the last seen theory and circumstantial evidence. Satpal had an altercation with Kapil Kumar a few days before the incident regarding the payment of milk. Satpal was charged under Sections 302 (murder) and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the IPC. The evidence included the last seen theory where PW-7 and PW-9 saw Satpal with the deceased on a bicycle, the recovery of a bicycle and milk can with PW-7's name, and Satpal's absconding after the incident. The defense argued that the dead body was found at a considerable distance from where Satpal was last seen with the deceased, and that the recovery of the bicycle and milk can was planted. Satpal's counsel highlighted inconsistencies in the testimonies of PW-7 and PW-9 regarding the time and manner of the discovery of the dead body and the police reaching the spot. The Supreme Court considered the last seen theory, along with other corroborative evidence, sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused when the accused offers no explanation or a wrong explanation and absconds. The post-mortem report conducted on 12th September 2007 estimated the time of death as 24-36 hours before, coinciding with the time the deceased was last seen with Satpal. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Satpal, finding no reason to interfere with the judgment of the lower courts. The Supreme Court stated that the recovery of the bicycle and milk can, identified by PW-7, were additional incriminating factors completing the chain of circumstances against Satpal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding Satpal's conviction under Sections 302 and 201 IPC.

case_name: Satpal vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Satpal vs. State of Haryana. Date: 5th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Satpal's conviction under Section 302 IPC for the murder of his wife Pooja Rani was justified, based on the evidence and dying declaration presented by the prosecution. Satpal was charged under Section 302 of the IPC for the murder of his wife Pooja Rani. Satpal's conviction was based on the dying declaration of Pooja Rani, in which she stated that Satpal poured kerosene on her and set her on fire, along with supporting witness testimonies. In her dying declaration, Pooja Rani stated that her husband Satpal poured kerosene on her and set her ablaze. Satpal's defense was that Pooja Rani attempted to commit suicide due to a misconception that he had illicit relations with her sister-in-law, Anjali, and he tried to save her by extinguishing the fire. The prosecution argued that the dying declaration was genuine and credible, as it was recorded by a Judicial Magistrate in the absence of the deceased's family members. The testimonies of Pooja Rani's mother (PW-5) and maternal uncle (PW-6) corroborated the prosecution's case, stating that Pooja Rani was tortured by Satpal and his family members. The courts concluded that the presence of Pooja Rani's family members at the hospital did not influence her dying declaration, as it was recorded independently by a Judicial Magistrate. The Supreme Court dismissed Satpal's appeal, upholding his conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC, as the evidence, including the dying declaration and witness testimonies, established his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The key factors included the credibility of the dying declaration, the corroborative testimonies of witnesses, and the lack of any substantial evidence to support the defense's claim of false implication.

case_name: Satvinder Singh @ Satvinder Singh Saluja & Ors. vs. The State of Bihar
text: Case: Satvinder Singh @ Satvinder Singh Saluja & Ors. vs. The State of Bihar. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appellants consumed liquor in a public place under Section 53(a) of the Bihar Excise (Amendment) Act, 2016. The appellants were accused of consuming liquor in a public place under Section 53(a) of the Bihar Excise (Amendment) Act, 2016. The appellants argued that their vehicle, where they were allegedly found consuming liquor, was not a public place as per the definition in the Bihar Excise (Amendment) Act, 2016. The High Court dismissed the application filed by the appellants under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to set aside the order of the Judicial Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence. The Supreme Court allowed the appellants to file an application for discharge before the learned Magistrate, who shall decide the application considering the materials on record, in accordance with law. The prosecution claimed that the appellants were found with a certain quantity of alcohol in their breath when subjected to a breath analyser test at a check post in Rajauli, District Nawada, Bihar. The Supreme Court interpreted that a 'public place' includes a private vehicle when it is on a public road, thus rejecting the appellants' argument that their vehicle was not a public place.

case_name: Satya Deo @ Bhoorey vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Satya Deo @ Bhoorey vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 7th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Satya Deo was a juvenile at the time of the offence on 11th December 1981, impacting his conviction and sentence under the Juvenile Justice Act. Satya Deo was charged with the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for murder, resulting in life imprisonment. The trial court convicted Satya Deo and sentenced him to life imprisonment for the offence of murder. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Satya Deo. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to conduct an inquiry to ascertain if Satya Deo was a juvenile on the date of the offence based on available records. The trial court's inquiry determined that Satya Deo was 16 years, 7 months, and 26 days old on the date of the offence, based on school records and other documents. The Supreme Court interpreted that under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, Satya Deo, being less than 18 years old at the time of the offence, should be treated as a juvenile. The Supreme Court set aside Satya Deo's life imprisonment sentence and directed that he be treated as a juvenile, with the case remitted to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate orders. The Supreme Court directed the Juvenile Justice Board to pass appropriate orders regarding Satya Deo's detention and custody and to determine the appropriate quantum of fine and compensation for the family of the deceased. The Constitutional Bench decision in Pratap Singh's case established that the date of the offence is the determining factor for juvenility, influencing the Supreme Court's decision to treat Satya Deo as a juvenile.

text: Case: Satyajit Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.. Date: 2nd August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the legality and constitutionality of the Jharkhand Government's notification and orders that provided 100% reservation for local candidates in Scheduled Districts for certain posts. The State argued that the reservation policy was within the scope of the Governor's powers under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, aiming to uplift local residents in Scheduled Areas. The appellants claimed that the High Court misinterpreted their case and that their situation involved different advertisements and posts, not the ones contested in the writ petition. The Tribal Advisory Council recommended issuing a notification for 100% reservation for local residents in the Scheduled Districts to improve their socio-economic conditions. The original writ petitioners, who were candidates from Non-Scheduled Districts, argued that the reservation policy violated their fundamental rights under the Constitution. The High Court quashed all appointments made under the contested notifications and directed fresh selection processes for the posts in accordance with the law. The successful candidates contended that the reservation policy was essential for the upliftment of local residents in Scheduled Areas and that it was within the Governor's constitutional powers. The decision might lead to more scrutiny and possible revisions of reservation policies in Scheduled Areas to ensure they comply with constitutional provisions and do not discriminate against candidates from Non-Scheduled Areas. Yes, the reservation policy could potentially be modified to include a more balanced approach that provides opportunities for local residents while also adhering to constitutional mandates against discrimination.

text: Case: Satyama Dubey & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.. Date: 27th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The petitioners raised concern regarding the brutal assault and subsequent death of a 19-year-old girl from Hathras, Uttar Pradesh, and the manner in which she was cremated. The petitioners sought a fair investigation, possibly by transferring the case to the CBI or forming an SIT, and requested the appointment of a sitting or retired Supreme Court or High Court Judge to oversee the matter. The Solicitor General agreed that a fair investigation was necessary and stated that the respondents also desired that the offenders be brought to justice. The court directed that the security for the victim's family and witnesses be provided by the CRPF within a week from the date of the order. The Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench, took suo moto cognizance of the incident and passed a detailed order on 1st October 2020, registering PIL(C) No.16150/2020. The court decided that the Allahabad High Court should continue to monitor the investigation since it had already taken cognizance of the matter. The CBI was directed to report to the Allahabad High Court as per the court's orders from time to time. The court stated that the need for transferring the trial to Delhi would arise after the investigation is complete, and kept the issue open for future consideration. Ms. Indira Jaising contended that the protection provided by the State Police would not be appropriate and requested that the CRPF provide the security instead. The High Court was requested to delete the names and relationships of the victim's family members from the order and to morph the same in the digital records to avoid future disclosures. Ms. Seema Kushwaha and Mr. Raj Ratan were engaged as private advocates on behalf of the victim's family to represent their interests.

The Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench, took suo moto cognizance of the incident and passed a detailed order on 1st October 2020, registering PIL(C) No.16150/2020.
The court decided that the Allahabad High Court should continue to monitor the investigation since it had already taken cognizance of the matter.
The CBI was directed to report to the Allahabad High Court as per the court's orders from time to time.
The court stated that the need for transferring the trial to Delhi would arise after the investigation is complete, and kept the issue open for future consideration.
Ms. Indira Jaising contended that the protection provided by the State Police would not be appropriate and requested that the CRPF provide the security instead.
The High Court was requested to delete the names and relationships of the victim's family members from the order and to morph the same in the digital records to avoid future disclosures.
Ms. Seema Kushwaha and Mr. Raj Ratan were engaged as private advocates on behalf of the victim's family to represent their interests.

case_name: Satyendar Kumar Jain vs. Directorate of Enforcement
text: Case: Satyendar Kumar Jain vs. Directorate of Enforcement. Date: 18th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in rejecting the bail applications of the appellants Satyendar Kumar Jain, Ankush Jain, and Vaibhav Jain in the money laundering case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The allegations were that Satyendar Kumar Jain, while functioning as a Minister of the Delhi Government, acquired disproportionate assets and laundered tainted cash amounts through Kolkata-based shell companies. Ankush Jain and Vaibhav Jain were accused of assisting Satyendar Kumar Jain by making false declarations under the Income Declaration Scheme (IDS) 2016, declaring undisclosed income to shield Satyendar Kumar Jain. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals and upheld the High Court's decision to reject the bail applications of Satyendar Kumar Jain, Ankush Jain, and Vaibhav Jain. The statements recorded under Section 50 of the PMLA were significant as they provided admissible evidence of the involvement of Satyendar Kumar Jain and others in the money laundering activities. The Supreme Court acknowledged the discrepancy but found sufficient material to conclude that Satyendar Kumar Jain was involved in money laundering, and the mistake in the amount mentioned by the ED was considered inadvertent. The Supreme Court noted that the shell companies were used to conceal and project tainted money as untainted, and Satyendar Kumar Jain was found to be the beneficial owner of these companies. The Supreme Court emphasized that the twin conditions under Section 45 of the PMLA, which are mandatory for granting bail, were not satisfied by the appellants. The Supreme Court viewed the declarations under the IDS as false and made to protect Satyendar Kumar Jain, further supporting the allegations of money laundering. The Supreme Court highlighted that the offense of money laundering has a wide reach, capturing every process and activity connected with the proceeds of crime, and emphasized the importance of stringent measures to combat such offenses.

case_name: Sau. Sangeeta W/o Sunil Shinde vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
text: Case: Sau. Sangeeta W/o Sunil Shinde vs. The State of Maharashtra & Ors.. Date: 1st September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the removal of the appellant, Sangeeta Shinde, as the Party Leader of the INCPS Party and the approval of Dr. Vandana Dnyaneshwar Murkute as the new Party Leader by the District Collector, Ahmednagar. The dispute arose when respondent Nos. 3 to 5 filed a complaint alleging that Sangeeta Shinde had not taken the members into confidence and had not convened any meetings of the INCPS Party during her tenure. A meeting was held on 4th January 2020, resulting in a resolution to remove her as Party Leader and appoint Dr. Vandana Dnyaneshwar Murkute as the new leader. The appellant argued that according to the rules and regulations submitted to the District Collector, she was elected as Party Leader for a period of five years and could not be removed before the completion of this term. She contended that the meeting to remove her was convened by an outsider and not by herself, as required. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, upholding the District Collector's decision to approve the appointment of Dr. Vandana Dnyaneshwar Murkute as the Party Leader of the INCPS Party. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, stating that the removal of the appellant and appointment of respondent No. 3 as Party Leader was in accordance with the democratic process and the resolutions passed in the meetings presided over by the President of the Ahmednagar District INC Party. The Supreme Court found the appellant's argument of horse-trading unconvincing, noting that it was the appellant who had acted contrary to the party's wishes by contesting the election for the post of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti with the support of the rival group.
