case_name: State Bank of India & Anr. vs. K.S. Vishwanath
text: Case: State Bank of India & Anr. vs. K.S. Vishwanath. Date: 20th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. K.S. Vishwanath was charged with fraudulently withdrawing Rs. 10 lakhs using a forged letter dated 6th August 1996. The Enquiry Officer found the charges against K.S. Vishwanath to be proved and recommended his dismissal from service. The High Court of Karnataka dismissed the writ appeal filed by SBI, confirming the Single Judge's order setting aside the dismissal of K.S. Vishwanath. SBI argued that the High Court erred in interfering with the findings of the Enquiry Officer and the disciplinary authority, which were based on substantial evidence. The respondent argued that the enquiry was vitiated due to the violation of principles of natural justice and that the evidence was based on conjectures and surmises. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in reappreciating the evidence and interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the Enquiry Officer and the disciplinary authority. The Supreme Court found the dismissal justified due to the serious nature of the misconduct, involving the preparation of a fraudulent letter and the misappropriation of Rs. 10 lakhs. The Supreme Court noted that the acquittal in the criminal case, which was based on the benefit of doubt, did not affect the findings of guilt in the disciplinary proceedings. The Supreme Court quashed the judgements of the High Court and the Single Judge, thereby restoring the order of dismissal passed by the disciplinary authority. The Supreme Court emphasized that the standards of proof required in criminal proceedings are different from those in departmental enquiries, and the findings in one do not necessarily affect the other. The ruling reinforced the principle that High Courts should not reappreciate evidence in disciplinary proceedings and should confine their review to ensuring that the enquiry was conducted according to law and principles of natural justice.

case_name: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
text: Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.. Date: 27th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the principles of natural justice, specifically the rule of audi alteram partem, should be read into the Reserve Bank of India's Master Directions on Frauds before classifying a borrower's account as fraudulent. The borrowers contended that the Master Directions on Frauds violated principles of natural justice because they did not provide an opportunity for borrowers to be heard before their accounts were classified as fraudulent, leading to significant civil consequences. The High Court of Telangana held that the principles of natural justice must be read into the Master Directions on Frauds, requiring that borrowers be given an opportunity to be heard before their accounts are classified as fraudulent. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's directive that mandated a personal hearing before classifying accounts as fraudulent, stating that it was not necessary for the principles of natural justice to include a personal hearing at the pre-decisional stage. The Supreme Court emphasized that classifying an account as fraud has severe civil consequences for borrowers, including their debarment from accessing institutional finance, which could lead to their 'civil death' in the business world. The Supreme Court held that the principles of natural justice, including the rule of audi alteram partem, should be read into the Master Directions on Frauds, requiring that borrowers be given an opportunity to be heard before their accounts are classified as fraudulent. The Supreme Court directed that banks must provide a notice to the borrower, allow them to respond, and consider their representation before classifying their account as fraud, ensuring compliance with the principles of natural justice.

case_name: State Bank of India and Anr vs. New India Assurance Company Limited
text: Case: State Bank of India and Anr vs. New India Assurance Company Limited. Date: 7th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the State Bank of India (SBI) was liable to compensate the borrower for an insurance claim that was denied by New India Assurance Company due to a delay in filing the claim. The SCDRC directed the Bank to forward the insurance claim of the borrower to the insurer, and the insurer to process the claim in accordance with law. It did not hold the Bank liable to pay compensation. The NCDRC held the Bank liable to pay the claim of the borrower with interest, reversing the SCDRC's decision. SBI argued that since the borrower accepted the SCDRC's order and did not appeal, there was no basis for the NCDRC to hold the Bank liable. Additionally, SBI cited a settlement with the borrower in which the borrower agreed to withdraw all claims. The Supreme Court concluded that the NCDRC had no justification to hold the Bank liable, as the borrower had not challenged the SCDRC's order. The Supreme Court set aside the NCDRC's decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appellants to withdraw the amount deposited before the Court, along with any accrued interest.

case_name: State Bank of India vs. M/s. Jah Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: State Bank of India vs. M/s. Jah Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 8th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether a person declared as a wilful defaulter under the Reserve Bank of India's Circulars is entitled to be represented by a lawyer of its choice before such declaration is made. The purpose of the RBI Master Circular is to disseminate credit information about wilful defaulters to caution banks and financial institutions to ensure that further bank finance is not made available to them. The Grievance Redressal Mechanism involves identifying wilful defaulters through a committee, advising the borrower about the proposal to classify them as a wilful defaulter, allowing the borrower reasonable time to represent against the decision, and providing a hearing if the borrower claims wrongful classification. The Supreme Court concluded that there is no unconditional right to be represented by a lawyer in the in-house proceedings under the Revised Circular. However, considering the serious consequences of being declared a wilful defaulter, it incorporated additional procedural safeguards to ensure fairness. The Supreme Court incorporated the requirement for the First Committee to provide its order to the borrower as soon as it is made, allowing the borrower 15 days to make a full representation on facts and law to the Review Committee, which must then pass a reasoned order on the representation and serve it to the borrower. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgement and allowed the appeals, ruling that the Revised Circular dated 01.07.2015 must incorporate the additional procedural safeguards as specified by the Court.

case_name: State Rep. by the Drugs Inspector vs. Manimaran
text: Case: State Rep. by the Drugs Inspector vs. Manimaran. Date: 30th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Manimaran was charged under Sections 27(b)(ii) and 28 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 for storing and selling drugs without a valid drug licence and for not furnishing the name of the supplier of the drugs. During the inspection on 17th December 2008, the Drugs Inspectors found that Manimaran's medical shop, M/s. Sri Balaji Medicals, was storing and selling drugs without a valid drug licence. The trial court convicted Manimaran under Sections 27(b)(ii) and 28 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and sentenced him to one year of rigorous imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs. 5,000 under Section 27(b)(ii) and Rs. 500 under Section 28. The High Court of Madras set aside the conviction of Manimaran, citing the non-examination of the erstwhile owners of the medical shop and questioning the validity of the documents used as evidence. The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's decision because it found that Manimaran had admitted in his statements that he was operating the medical shop without a valid licence, and the non-examination of the previous owners was not fatal to the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court upheld the use of carbon copies as primary evidence under Section 62 of the Indian Evidence Act, dismissing the argument that the evidence was invalid due to being carbon copies. Manimaran claimed that his signatures were obtained on blank papers and that the documents were fabricated. However, the Supreme Court found this defense unconvincing and noted that he did not lodge any complaint about this alleged coercion. The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction under Sections 27(b)(ii) and 28 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act but reduced the sentence of imprisonment from one year to three months while maintaining the fine of Rs. 5,000. The Supreme Court emphasized that the High Court should not have interfered with the concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and the appellate court unless those findings were perverse or ignored material evidence. The Supreme Court directed Manimaran to surrender within four weeks to serve the remaining sentence, failing which he would be taken into custody.

case_name: State Rep. by the Inspector of Police vs. M. Murugesan & Anr.
text: Case: State Rep. by the Inspector of Police vs. M. Murugesan & Anr.. Date: 15th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The State was aggrieved by an order passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras on 24th April 2019, which constituted a Heterogeneous Committee to give recommendations on reforms for the reformation, rehabilitation, and reintegration of the convict/accused person to society and best practices for improving the quality of investigation. The High Court directed the State to furnish data for each District and mandated the Committee to submit a report within eight weeks. The State was also directed to provide office space for the Committee to conduct its meetings and keep the documents and materials in safe custody. The High Court observed that the central aim of criminal law is to reform the offender and rehabilitate him to make him useful to society. It emphasized the need for a thorough revamping of the Criminal Justice system in the State due to the poor record of convictions in serious crimes. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had committed a grave illegality by retaining the file after granting bail to the accused on 18th February 2019. The jurisdiction of the High Court ended when the bail application under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was finally decided. The Supreme Court referred to the case of State of Punjab v. case_name: State Represented by the Deputy Superintendent of Police Vigilance and Anti Corruption, Tamil Nadu vs. J. Doraiswamy & Ors.
text: Case: State Represented by the Deputy Superintendent of Police Vigilance and Anti Corruption, Tamil Nadu vs. J. Doraiswamy & Ors.. Date: 7th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. J. Doraiswamy and the co-accused were charged under Section 7 read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, for demanding and accepting a bribe. The Chief Judicial Magistrate discharged the accused under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, stating that no prima facie case was made out against them. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions and affirmed the order of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, discharging the accused. The primary question was whether the lower courts were justified in allowing the discharge applications filed by the respondents under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Supreme Court set aside the discharge order, dismissed the discharge applications, and remanded the case back to the Special Court (CJM) for trial on merits. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court acted more like an appellate court than a revisionary court, and it erred in appreciating the evidence rather than considering the prima facie case. The Supreme Court directed the Special Court (CJM) to proceed with the trial and conclude it within six months in accordance with the law, without being influenced by observations made by the High Court and the Supreme Court. J. Doraiswamy was working as an Inspector of Police, and the co-accused was a Sub-Inspector of Police in the Tamil Nadu Police Services. The respondents filed applications under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code, claiming that no prima facie case was made out against them under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court found material contradictions in the statements of the prosecution witnesses regarding the date of payment and presence of the accused, which contributed to its decision to discharge the respondents.

case_name: State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs Hemendhra Reddy & Anr.
text: Case: State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs Hemendhra Reddy & Anr.. Date: 28th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in quashing the entire prosecution instituted by the CBI against the accused on the grounds that the CBI could not have undertaken further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC after filing a closure report under Section 173(2). The initial charges were for holding disproportionate assets under Section 13(1)(e) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and Section 109 of the IPC. The case was initially closed because the investigation concluded that the accused could not be prosecuted, and a final report under Section 173 CrPC was accepted by the Special Court. The CBI sought to reopen the case after receiving new evidence that could substantiate the charge of possession of disproportionate assets against the accused persons. The High Court quashed the prosecution on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to permit the CBI to conduct further investigation after accepting the closure report. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in its decision, as further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC is permissible even after a closure report has been accepted, provided new evidence surfaces. The Supreme Court emphasized that while further investigation is permissible, the investigating agency should inform the court and seek formal permission to conduct such an investigation. The ruling clarifies that further investigation is allowed even after a closure report is accepted, ensuring that new evidence can be considered to achieve substantial justice. If new evidence emerges, the investigating agency can seek permission from the court to reopen and conduct further investigation, potentially leading to a supplementary chargesheet. The Supreme Court directed the CBI to conduct further investigation based on the new evidence, allowing them to submit a supplementary chargesheet if necessary. The Supreme Court acknowledged the delay but emphasized that further investigation is crucial for uncovering the truth and ensuring justice, regardless of the time elapsed since the closure report.

case_name: State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs. Sanvlo Naik & Anr.
text: Case: State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs. Sanvlo Naik & Anr.. Date: 7th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sanvlo Naik and S.V. Caeiro were charged with the offense under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, but were acquitted of this charge. They were instead convicted for the offense under Section 304 Part II read with Section 34 IPC. The trial court sentenced S.V. Caeiro to three years of simple imprisonment and Sanvlo Naik to two years of simple imprisonment along with fines for their conviction under Section 304 Part II read with Section 34 IPC. The High Court allowed the appeals, set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court, and acquitted both Sanvlo Naik and S.V. Caeiro. The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's decision to acquit Sanvlo Naik and S.V. Caeiro and considered whether the conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC was correct and if the sentence should be enhanced. The Supreme Court found the plea of alibi raised by the accused to be untenable, as the General Diary entry indicating their departure from the police station was found to be manipulated and there were inconsistencies in their statements. The postmortem report revealed 14 ante-mortem injuries on the deceased's body, which were fatal in the ordinary course of nature, could not be self-inflicted, and were caused by a baton or similar object. The Supreme Court concluded that the accused were responsible for the injuries that caused the death of the deceased while he was in police custody, and their conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC was upheld. The Supreme Court found the sentences imposed by the trial court inadequate given the severity of the offense and enhanced the sentence to ten years of rigorous imprisonment for both accused under Section 304 Part II read with Section 34 IPC. The Supreme Court directed Sanvlo Naik and S.V. Caeiro to surrender forthwith to serve out their enhanced sentences, failing which they would be taken into custody. The Supreme Court emphasized that in cases of custodial deaths, the burden is on the police to explain how the deceased died while in their custody, and failure to provide a cogent explanation indicates their responsibility for the death.

case_name: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra
text: Case: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra. Date: 5th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether +2 lecturers appointed in government and nationalized secondary schools in Bihar, pursuant to Advertisement No. 1/87, should be merged with the Bihar Education Service (BES) Class II, as part of the Bihar Subordinate Education Service (BSES). The High Court ruled that the +2 lecturers appointed pursuant to Advertisement No. 1/87 were always part of the Bihar Subordinate Education Service (BSES) and therefore entitled to be merged with the Bihar Education Service (BES), quashing the notification dated 23rd June 2009 which contradicted this decision. The Bihar Government initially issued a resolution on 7th July 2006 to merge the cadre of BSES (Teaching Branch) with the BES Class-II, but later issued a notification on 6th October 2006 excluding +2 lecturers from this merger, stating that they were never part of the BSES cadre. The Supreme Court noted the Bihar Government's fluctuating and indecisive stance, which led to repeated litigations. The Court criticized the government's attempts to circumvent its earlier decisions and the High Court's decision, emphasizing that the +2 lecturers should be treated as part of the BSES. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, stating that the +2 lecturers appointed under Advertisement No. 1/87 are members of the Subordinate Educational Service and should receive all service benefits as such, dismissing the appeals and granting the state six months to comply with the High Court's directions. The Supreme Court found the notification dated 23rd June 2009 problematic because it encadred +2 lecturers with nationalized secondary school teachers, which was contrary to the legitimate expectations created by the 1985 notification and the 1987 advertisement, thereby denying the +2 lecturers promotional opportunities and fair treatment.

text: Case: State of Gujarat & Anr. vs Narayan @ Narayan Sai @ Mota Bhagwan Asaram. Date: 20th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the respondent, Narayan @ Narayan Sai @ Mota Bhagwan Asaram, should be granted furlough by the High Court despite the objections raised by the prison and police authorities. The charges included offences under Sections 376(2)(c), 377, 354, 344, 357, 342, 323, 504, 506(2), 120-B, 212, 153, and 114 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court granted furlough to the respondent for a period of fourteen days, despite objections from the prison and police authorities. The objections included the respondent's involvement in illegal activities inside the jail, the potential threat to law and order, attempts to bribe public officials, and the possibility of the respondent engaging in criminal activities if released. The Supreme Court noted that the respondent had engaged in illegal activities such as keeping a mobile phone in jail and attempting to make contact with outsiders, which justified the denial of furlough. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting furlough to the respondent, agreeing with the objections raised by the prison and police authorities and highlighting the threat posed to public peace and security.

case_name: State of Gujarat vs Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao. Date: 9th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the order of the sanctioning authority and the charge-sheet filed by the Anti-Corruption Bureau should be set aside due to the alleged non-application of mind by the sanctioning authority. Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao was alleged to have acquired assets disproportionate to his known sources of income while serving as a Sub-Inspector of Borsad Town Police Station, amounting to Rs. 32,68,258, which was more than 40% beyond his known income. The trial court dismissed Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao's application for discharge, stating that the issues raised were questions of fact to be decided during the trial. The High Court set aside the trial court's order and discharged Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao, concluding that the trial court had committed an error by not properly considering the evidence and submissions made by the respondent. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred in its judgment by acting beyond its jurisdiction and by evaluating the defence evidence, which is impermissible at the stage of framing charges. The Supreme Court stated that the trial court must only determine if a prima facie case exists based on the prosecution's evidence without evaluating the defence evidence or holding a mini-trial. The Supreme Court highlighted that the trial court should proceed on the assumption that the prosecution's evidence is true and evaluate whether the facts disclosed constitute the offence alleged. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the trial court to proceed with the trial expeditiously, ideally within one year. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order, and reinstating the trial court's decision to proceed with the trial against Dilipsinh Kishorsinh Rao. The Supreme Court imposed costs of Rs. 50,000 on the respondent, to be paid to the Gujarat State Legal Services Authority.

case_name: State of Gujarat vs Sandip Omprakash Gupta
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs Sandip Omprakash Gupta. Date: 15th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the requirement of 'continuing unlawful activity' under the Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015, necessitated a separate FIR to be registered against a gang member after the Act's promulgation on 1st December 2019. The High Court granted bail to Sandip Omprakash Gupta, relying on the fact that no FIR had been registered against him for any substantive offence after the Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015, came into force. The State of Gujarat argued that the decision in the case of Shiva alias Shivaji Ramaji Sonawane needed a relook, as it frustrated the object of the Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015. The State contended that the previous FIRs were sufficient to establish 'continuing unlawful activity' under the Act. The Supreme Court observed that the term 'continuing unlawful activity' required an activity to have been committed after the promulgation of the Gujarat Control of Terrorism and Organised Crime Act, 2015, and that previous FIRs alone were not sufficient. The Supreme Court emphasized that the Act's provisions required at least one activity to have been committed after its promulgation to qualify as 'continuing unlawful activity,' and previous activities alone could not constitute an offence under the Act. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to grant bail, finding no fault in the reasoning that the provisions of the Act were not met as there was no FIR registered against the accused after the Act came into force.

case_name: State of Gujarat vs. Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs. Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta. Date: 5th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary allegation was that Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta and others hatched a conspiracy to cheat the Government of India by fraudulently remitting over Rs. 104 crores abroad through fake Bills of Entry, causing significant economic losses. The case was initiated following a complaint by the Manager of ICICI Bank against M/s R.A. Distributors Pvt. Ltd. for submitting bogus Bills of Entry and fraudulently opening a current account to remit large sums of money abroad. The High Court of Gujarat set aside the Chief Judicial Magistrate's order that had taken cognizance of the offences and issued summons based on the second supplementary charge sheet, citing insufficient material to connect Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta with the alleged offences. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred in dismissing the supplementary charge sheets without adequately considering the prima facie evidence and statements that implicated Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta in the alleged conspiracy and fraud. Prafulbhai Patel's statement implicated Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta in the collection and illegal transfer of cash, acting as a conduit for remitting funds abroad through hawala transactions. The Supreme Court identified that the High Court had improperly evaluated the merits of the evidence at the stage of issuing summons, which should have been left to the trial stage. The second supplementary charge sheet included significant evidence such as bank transactions, statements of witnesses, and the alleged involvement of Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta in the fraudulent remittance of funds, which warranted taking cognizance of the offences. The Supreme Court directed that the case be remanded to the trial court for a thorough examination of the evidence and for the trial to proceed on its merits, ensuring all procedural requirements are met. The State of Gujarat contended that the High Court erred in quashing the Magistrate's order of issuing summons, arguing that the evidence and materials provided sufficient grounds to proceed against Afroz Mohammed Hasanfatta. The Supreme Court clarified that at the stage of issuing process based on a police report, it is not mandatory for the Magistrate to record detailed reasons, as long as there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused. The Supreme Court stated that determining 'mens rea' or the guilty mind of the accused is not necessary at the stage of issuing summons and is to be established during the trial.

case_name: State of Gujarat vs. Anwar Osman Sumbhaniya and Others
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs. Anwar Osman Sumbhaniya and Others. Date: 27th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Anwar Osman Sumbhaniya was charged with illegal possession of foreign-made firearms and ammunition under TADA, the Arms Act, and related laws. A foreign-made carbine gun, revolvers, a transmitter walkie-talkie set, and several live cartridges were recovered. The Designated Court identified a lack of valid prior approval under Section 20-A(1) and sanction under Section 20-A(2) of TADA. The court observed that the confessional statements were inadmissible due to the invalid sanction. The prosecution claimed that the other accused were involved in the conspiracy and abetment related to the possession of illegal firearms. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for thorough application of mind and detailed evaluation of evidence before granting prior sanction. The court acquitted the respondents due to procedural flaws in obtaining prior approval and lack of admissible evidence. The search and seizure procedures were deemed to be replete with illegalities, affecting the admissibility of evidence. The Supreme Court suggested that the prosecution should ensure compliance with procedural requirements and legal mandates for effective trials. The case highlighted the importance of procedural rigor and judicial oversight in ensuring justice under special laws like TADA.

case_name: State of Gujarat vs. Cadila Healthcare Ltd.
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs. Cadila Healthcare Ltd.. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the product 'KADIPROL' manufactured by Cadila Healthcare Ltd. should be classified as 'Poultry Feed' under Entry 25 of Schedule I of the Gujarat Sales Tax Act (GST Act) or as a 'Drug and Medicine' under Entry 26(1) of Schedule II Part A of the GST Act. The Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax determined that 'KADIPROL' should be categorized as a 'Drug and Medicine' under Entry 26(1) of Schedule II Part A of the GST Act, as it contained preventive medicine. The High Court of Gujarat ruled in favor of Cadila Healthcare Ltd., categorizing 'KADIPROL' as 'Poultry Feed' under Entry 25 of Schedule I of the GST Act, overturning the findings of the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax and the Sales Tax Tribunal. The State of Gujarat argued that the High Court erred in overturning the Tribunal's and Deputy Commissioner's findings, which were based on expert literature. They emphasized that 'KADIPROL' contained medicinal properties and was used as a preventive measure against diseases in poultry, which should classify it as a 'Drug and Medicine'. The Supreme Court noted that while the High Court had relied on previous judgments, it failed to provide detailed reasoning to overturn the Tribunal's findings. case_name: State of Gujarat vs. Reliance Industries Limited
text: Case: State of Gujarat vs. Reliance Industries Limited. Date: 22nd September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the tax credit available under the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003 (VAT Act) should be reduced at the rate of 4% twice for the same goods, under both sub-clauses (ii) and (iii) of Section 11(3)(b). The State of Gujarat contended that the tax credit should be reduced by 4% twice, once under sub-clause (ii) for goods dispatched outside the State as branch transfer and again under sub-clause (iii) for fuels used in the manufacture of goods. The Gujarat Value Added Tax Tribunal decided that the reduction of tax credit should only be at 4% and not twice, rejecting the view that it should be reduced again for the same goods under sub-clause (iii). The High Court of Gujarat upheld the Tribunal's decision, stating that the tax credit should be reduced by 4% only once, not twice. The Supreme Court of India ruled that the reduction of tax credit should indeed be applied at 4% for both sub-clauses (ii) and (iii) separately, except in cases where VAT paid on such raw material is already 4%. For fuels like natural gas and light diesel oil, the reduction should be at 4% under each sub-clause. The Supreme Court explained that the tax credit scheme under the VAT Act is meant to account for taxes paid on raw materials used in manufacturing, and the Legislature's intent was to reduce tax credit by 4% under each applicable provision. This ensures that the benefit of tax credit is proportionately adjusted for both manufacturing and branch transfer activities.

case_name: State of Haryana & Anr. vs Subhash Chander & Ors.
text: Case: State of Haryana & Anr. vs Subhash Chander & Ors.. Date: 10th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the determination and enhancement of compensation for lands acquired in village Kherki, Majra under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The High Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 2,98,54,720 per acre from the previously awarded Rs. 1,56,24,000 per acre. The State of Haryana argued that the High Court erred in taking into consideration the compensation awarded for lands acquired in January 2008 and applying a 12% cumulative increase. The High Court based the enhancement on a previous judgement that awarded Rs. 2,38,00,000 per acre for lands acquired in January 2008, applying a 12% cumulative increase. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's judgement, awarding compensation at Rs. 2,87,98,000 per acre instead of Rs. 2,98,54,720 per acre. The Supreme Court found that a 10% increase was more appropriate based on the market conditions and sale instances produced on record. The Supreme Court considered the sale instances produced from 2007 to 2008 and the gap between the 2008 and 2010 notifications. The decision might lead to more cautious and evidence-based approaches in determining compensation, ensuring fairness and adherence to market trends. Non-compliance could result in further legal challenges and potential contempt of court proceedings, leading to additional financial and reputational costs for the State. The State of Haryana should immediately calculate the compensation at Rs. 2,87,98,000 per acre, including all statutory benefits, and ensure payment to the original landowners within six weeks. The State should adopt a transparent and consistent approach in land acquisition compensation, considering market values and ensuring timely and fair payments to landowners.

case_name: State of Haryana vs Sunder Pal and Ors.
text: Case: State of Haryana vs Sunder Pal and Ors.. Date: 31st October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the acquittal of the respondents under Section 364-A IPC for kidnapping Amit Kumar for ransom was justified. The respondents were charged under Section 364-A IPC for kidnapping Amit Kumar, a nine-year-old boy, for ransom. The High Court acquitted the accused Vikas @ Vicky, Yashpal, Vidya Sagar, Vishav Pal, Pawan Kumar, Sundar Pal, and Jagbir Singh of all charges, but affirmed the conviction of Vinod and Sohan, maintaining their sentence of life imprisonment. The key witness was Amit Kumar (PW-2), the kidnapped boy, who testified that he was forcibly taken by Vinod, Sohan, and Virender and later saw the other accused playing cards near the Sona Arjunpur Railway Station. The Supreme Court found that there was no evidence linking the acquitted accused to the actual kidnapping or conspiracy, as they were only found playing cards near the location where Amit Kumar was taken. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by the State of Haryana, upholding the High Court's acquittal of the accused, finding no grounds for interference. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court's view was plausible and not suffering from any serious infirmity, and thus did not warrant interference. The Supreme Court noted that accused Sunder Pal, Vidya Sagar, and Yashpal had passed away after the filing of the petition and their deaths were verified by the State's counsel. The Supreme Court concurred with the High Court that simply being found playing cards near the kidnapping site was insufficient evidence to convict the accused of kidnapping or conspiracy. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by the State of Haryana, confirming the acquittal of the accused by the High Court and closing the case with no further orders as to costs.

case_name: State of Haryana vs. Krishan & Anr.
text: Case: State of Haryana vs. Krishan & Anr.. Date: 9th June 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Krishan and Som Nath, the respondents, were rightly convicted for their involvement in the 'Kalanwali Hooch Tragedy' under Sections 302, 328 read with Section 120B IPC, and Section 61(1)(a) of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914. The 'Kalanwali Hooch Tragedy' occurred in December 1980, when 36 people died and 44 lost their eyesight after consuming spurious liquor sold from a licensed vend in Village Kalanwali, District Sirsa, Haryana. Krishan and Som Nath were charged with offenses under Section 302 IPC read with Section 120B IPC (for murder), Section 328 IPC read with Section 120B IPC (for causing hurt by means of poison), and Section 61(1)(a) of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914 (for selling spurious liquor). The High Court acquitted Krishan and Som Nath, questioning the prosecution's evidence and finding no direct connection between the respondents and the spurious liquor consumed by the victims. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's decision, noting that there was ample evidence connecting the respondents to the sale of spurious liquor, including witness testimonies and the recovery of liquor bottles containing methyl alcohol. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's conviction of Krishan and Som Nath, finding them guilty of selling spurious liquor that caused deaths and loss of eyesight, and directed them to surrender to undergo the sentences imposed by the trial court. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in acquitting Krishan and Som Nath by not adequately considering the evidence that established their involvement in the sale of spurious liquor.

case_name: State of Haryana vs. M/s. Shiv Shankar Construction Co. & Anr.
text: Case: State of Haryana vs. M/s. Shiv Shankar Construction Co. & Anr.. Date: 14th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The arbitrator increased the rate of compensation from Rs. 1,000 per km per month to Rs. 45,000 per km per month, citing additional expenditure incurred by the contractor due to a substantial increase in traffic volume on the road. The Supreme Court held that awarding compensation for periods after January 2008, when the diversion of traffic ceased, was impermissible and set aside that part of the award. The Supreme Court interpreted that the original contract had estimated a traffic volume of 3,364 PCUs per day, but the actual traffic reached 24,418 PCUs per day due to diversion, justifying a revision of compensation for the period during the increased traffic. The Supreme Court directed that the compensation be recalculated for the period up to January 2008, when the additional traffic existed, and the excess amount awarded beyond this period be quashed. The Court concluded that the arbitrator's decision to revise the contract terms and increase the compensation rate constituted rewriting the contract, which exceeded the arbitrator's authority under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The Supreme Court clarified that arbitrators must adjudicate only within the scope of claims explicitly submitted by the parties and cannot expand or modify the claims unilaterally.

case_name: State of Haryana vs. Rajesh Aggarwal & Anr.
text: Case: State of Haryana vs. Rajesh Aggarwal & Anr.. Date: 20th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in altering the charge against the respondents from Section 302 IPC to Section 304-A IPC for the deaths of seven workers in a factory blast. Rajesh Aggarwal and Anr. were initially charged under Section 302 IPC for the deaths of seven workers in a factory blast. The incident involved a blast in the factory premises of M/s Kee Pharma Private Limited on 27th June 1996, which resulted in a stampede and the deaths of seven workers. The High Court altered the charges from Section 302 IPC to Section 304-A IPC, concluding that the case was one of negligence rather than intentional murder. The respondents filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR registered against them under Section 302 IPC, arguing that the charges were not justified. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's alteration of charges, finding no merit in the appeal and agreeing that the case should proceed under Section 304-A IPC. The Supreme Court directed the Sessions Judge to ensure that the trial is completed on merits within one year from the date of the order, in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court emphasized that the Sessions Judge has the power to alter, amend, or add any charge under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C., notwithstanding the High Court's alteration of charges. The Supreme Court recalled the interim stay order and directed the Registry to send a copy of the order to the concerned Sessions Judge/Police Station for compliance. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State of Haryana, upholding the High Court's decision to alter the charges to Section 304-A IPC.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh & Anr. vs. Vijay Kumar alias Pappu and Anr.
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh & Anr. vs. Vijay Kumar alias Pappu and Anr.. Date: 15th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Vijay Kumar alias Pappu and the co-accused were charged under Section 307/34 IPC for attempting to commit murder by throwing acid on the victim, causing 16% burn injuries. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 307/34 IPC and sentenced them to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000 each. The High Court reduced the conviction from Section 307/34 IPC to Section 326 IPC and reduced the sentence from 10 years to 5 years of rigorous imprisonment, while increasing the fine to Rs. 25,000 each. The victim was 19 years old and sustained 16% burn injuries due to the acid attack. The Supreme Court ordered the accused to pay an additional compensation of Rs. 1,50,000 each and directed the State of Himachal Pradesh to pay compensation under the Victim Compensation Scheme. If the accused failed to pay the additional compensation of Rs. 1,50,000 each within six months, they would have to undergo an additional rigorous imprisonment of six months. The Supreme Court acknowledged the alteration of charges by the High Court but emphasized the importance of providing adequate compensation to the victim for the injuries and emotional distress suffered. The Supreme Court referred to previous judgements, including Laxmi vs. Union of India, which mandated compensation for acid attack victims, and emphasized the need for adequate compensation in such cases. The Supreme Court stated that there is no room for leniency or unwarranted mercy in cases of acid attacks, as such crimes cause severe physical and emotional suffering to the victims. The Supreme Court directed the State of Himachal Pradesh to deposit the compensation amount before the trial court within three months, which would then be disbursed to the victim after proper identification. The counsel for the appellants argued that the trial court's sentence of 10 years was appropriate for the severity of the crime and that the High Court's reduction of the sentence was unjustified.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors. vs. Rajiv and Anr.
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors. vs. Rajiv and Anr.. Date: 24th February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the respondents (Rajiv and Anr.) were entitled to compensation for the land used by the State for the construction of a road without acquiring the land under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The respondents sought a direction for the State to produce records related to the construction of the road, to compensate them for the land used, and if the State was unwilling to compensate, to return the land to them and pay for use and occupation charges from 1996. The State contended that the land was used for road construction with the consent of the respondents, who agreed not to claim any compensation, and that the road was constructed at the request of the public, including the respondents. The learned Single Judge directed the State to initiate the process for acquiring the respondents' land in accordance with the law and to compensate them for the land used for road construction. The Division Bench dismissed the LPA on the grounds of limitation, refusing to condone the delay of 354 days in preferring the appeal. The Supreme Court directed that 17th May 1996 be treated as the deemed date of acquisition and that the respondents be compensated based on the market price as of that date, excluding interest from 17th May 1996 to the filing date of the writ petition due to the 20-year delay.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh vs Achhar Singh
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh vs Achhar Singh. Date: 7th May 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was the appeal by the State of Himachal Pradesh challenging the acquittal of Achhar Singh and Budhi Singh for offences under Sections 302, 452, 326, and 323 of the IPC, which was overturned by the High Court, leading to their conviction. Achhar Singh and Budhi Singh were accused of attacking the complainant's family with axes and other weapons, resulting in the death of Swari Devi and serious injuries to Beli Ram and other family members. The trial court acquitted Achhar Singh and Budhi Singh, citing inconsistencies in the evidence and witness testimonies, as well as prior enmity between the parties. The High Court found that despite inconsistencies, there was a consistent thread of evidence proving that Budhi Singh caused the fatal injury to Swari Devi and Achhar Singh caused serious injuries to Beli Ram, leading to their conviction. The defense argued that the trial court's acquittal was based on a possible view of the evidence and that the High Court erred in overturning it without proving the trial court's judgment to be perverse or unsustainable. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court's judgment as it was perverse and ignored material evidence that consistently pointed to the guilt of Achhar Singh and Budhi Singh. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upheld the High Court's decision to convict Achhar Singh under Sections 452, 326, and 323 IPC and Budhi Singh under Sections 302 and 452 IPC, and directed them to undergo the remainder of their sentences.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh vs Nirmal Kaur @ Nimmo and Others
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh vs Nirmal Kaur @ Nimmo and Others. Date: 20th October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether it is necessary to particularize the species of the contraband recovered (poppy husk, poppy straw, etc.) and if proving the sample of poppy straw without specific species identification is sufficient under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. On 25th July 2003, Sarbjeet Singh (PW-12) along with police officials were informed by Constable Upnesh Kumar (PW-1) that Nirmal Kaur was involved in illicit trading of poppy straw and had stored it in a room with cattle fodder. A subsequent raid led to the recovery of 20 kgs of poppy husk and further discoveries of more poppy husk bags. The Chemical Examiner opined that the samples contained poppy husk. However, the High Court found that the tests conducted to ascertain meconic acid and morphine were not enough to conclude that the samples were poppy straw as defined under the NDPS Act. The trial court found Nirmal Kaur guilty and sentenced her to ten years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 for possessing commercial quantity of poppy straw. The High Court concluded that the tests for meconic acid and morphine alone were insufficient to prove the material as poppy straw within the meaning of the NDPS Act, leading to the acquittal of Nirmal Kaur. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by the State of Himachal Pradesh, upholding the High Court's decision to acquit Nirmal Kaur due to insufficient evidence proving the contraband as poppy straw under the NDPS Act.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh vs. Ravinder Kumar Sankhayan (Dead) and Ors.
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh vs. Ravinder Kumar Sankhayan (Dead) and Ors.. Date: 28th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appeals emanated from the judgments and interim orders passed by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, which addressed the leasing of property by the Municipal Corporation, Shimla to the Himachal Pradesh Tourism Development Corporation (HPTDC) at a rate much lower than the market rate without conducting an auction or tender process. The appeals were filed by the State of Himachal Pradesh and HPTDC against these judgments and orders. The main grievance in the writ petition was that the Municipal Corporation, Shimla had leased out property to HPTDC at a rate much lower than the prevailing market rate without conducting an auction or tender process. Additionally, the Municipal Corporation had failed to recover municipal taxes and rental/lease money from HPTDC, causing a substantial financial loss. The High Court directed the Municipal Corporation to issue a public advertisement for leasing out the subject property, considering that the lease rent payable by HPTDC was significantly lower than an offer made by an intervener. The court opined that the property should be leased out on a public interest basis to the highest bidder. The High Court's interim order was to issue a tender notice for leasing out the property, which resulted in several offers, with the highest bid being Rs.6,51,000 per month, significantly higher than the current lease amount being paid by HPTDC. The High Court directed the Municipal Corporation to lease the property to the highest bidder. The Supreme Court set aside the interim orders passed by the High Court, stating that the High Court had overstepped by passing a mandatory order at an interlocutory stage without addressing the validity of the existing contract between the Municipal Corporation and HPTDC. The Supreme Court emphasized that the High Court should have first determined the legality of the subsisting contract before ordering the tender process.

case_name: State of Himachal Pradesh vs. Trilok Chand & Anr.
text: Case: State of Himachal Pradesh vs. Trilok Chand & Anr.. Date: 17th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the respondents of charges under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act based on discrepancies in the prosecution's evidence. Trilok Chand and the other respondents were charged with offences under Section 20 of the NDPS Act for possession of three gunny bags of charas. The trial court convicted Trilok Chand and the other respondents under Section 20 of the NDPS Act, sentencing them to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 each, with an additional two years of imprisonment in default of payment. Key discrepancies included the contradictory statements of independent witnesses Amar Chand (PW 1) and Kuldip Kumar (PW 2), who denied being present at the scene, and the inconsistent testimonies of police officers regarding the timing and sequence of events, as well as the handling and weighing of the seized contraband. The Supreme Court noted that the discrepancies were significant and went to the root of the prosecution's case. These discrepancies, coupled with contradictory statements by prosecution witnesses, led the Court to conclude that the prosecution failed to establish the offence beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State of Himachal Pradesh, upholding the High Court's decision to acquit Trilok Chand and the other respondents due to the prosecution's failure to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court emphasized that in cases under the NDPS Act, the punishment is stringent and therefore the prosecution's evidence must be scrutinized zealously to exclude every chance of false implication, following the principle 'stringent the punishment stricter the proof'.

case_name: State of Jammu and Kashmir vs. Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan & Ors.
text: Case: State of Jammu and Kashmir vs. Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan & Ors.. Date: 21st November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was the appointment of Respondent No.1, Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan, to the Kashmir Administrative Service, which was challenged by the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The learned Single Judge of the High Court ruled in favor of Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan and later imposed costs of Rs. 20,000 on the State and initiated contempt proceedings. The State's appeal was dismissed by the Division Bench of the High Court. The three main issues remaining were: (i) the order regarding costs, (ii) the fate of the contempt proceedings, and (iii) the payment of arrears to Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan. The Advocate General assured the Supreme Court that the arrears were being worked out and would be paid to Mohammad Mehraj-ud-Din Khan expeditiously, and in any case before his retirement from service. The Supreme Court decided to drop the contempt proceedings and discharge the rule, taking into account the implementation of the judgment in letter and spirit. The Supreme Court vacated the order of costs imposed by the High Court, considering the belated steps taken by the State and its apologetic stand before the Court.

case_name: State of Jharkhand vs Shiv Shankar Sharma & Ors.
text: Case: State of Jharkhand vs Shiv Shankar Sharma & Ors.. Date: 7th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the two Public Interest Litigations (PILs) filed by Shiv Shankar Sharma before the Jharkhand High Court were maintainable, given allegations of large-scale corruption against the Chief Minister of Jharkhand, Hemant Soren. Shiv Shankar Sharma alleged that Hemant Soren, the Chief Minister of Jharkhand, was involved in large-scale corruption, including money laundering through shell companies and misuse of office to secure a mining lease in his own name. The High Court decided to proceed with the matter on its merits, stating that the allegations of large-scale corruption were of serious nature, and even though there might be procedural irregularities, these should not prevent the Court from entertaining the PILs. The Supreme Court held that the procedural compliance under the Jharkhand High Court (Public Interest Litigation) Rules, 2010 was crucial and not merely directory. The non-disclosure of earlier similar efforts and the failure to approach statutory authorities first were significant lapses. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and dismissed the PILs, stating that they were an abuse of the process of the court, filed with unclean hands, and lacked substantial evidence to support the serious allegations made. The Supreme Court emphasized that the bona fides of the petitioner filing a PIL are of extreme importance and must be examined at the very threshold to ensure that PILs are not filed with oblique motives or for personal vendetta.

case_name: State of Jharkhand vs. Sandeep Kumar
text: Case: State of Jharkhand vs. Sandeep Kumar. Date: 6th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sandeep Kumar was charged under Sections 419, 466, 221, 205, 109, and 120-B/34 IPC for making interpolations in an FIR to shield an accused. The High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi granted pre-arrest bail to Sandeep Kumar by order dated 6th July 2022. The case was registered against Sandeep Kumar because he allegedly made interpolations in the FIR to change the father's name of the accused Ranjeet Kumar Saw from Lakhan Saw to Balgovind Saw, thereby arresting the wrong person to shield the actual accused. The Additional Sessions Judge noted that the interpolations in the FIR were clearly visible, and there were sufficient materials indicating Sandeep Kumar's involvement in the alleged offense, leading to the rejection of his initial bail application. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order because it did not record any reasons for granting bail, especially considering the serious allegations against Sandeep Kumar, a senior police officer, which warranted a judicious exercise of discretion. The Supreme Court emphasized that while grant of bail is discretionary, it must be exercised judiciously and not as a matter of course. An order of bail bereft of any cogent reason cannot be sustained. Sanjay Kumar Sharma alleged that Sandeep Kumar changed the father's name of the accused in the FIR and arrested a different person to shield the actual accused, thereby manipulating the investigation. The Supreme Court highlighted the seriousness of the offense, the position held by the accused, the potential for tampering with evidence, and the larger interest of the public as key considerations for granting anticipatory bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail to Sandeep Kumar, and directed that his bail application be considered on its own merits if he is arrested. The Supreme Court believed that granting bail to a police officer facing allegations of manipulating the investigation would send a wrong signal in society and be against public interest.

case_name: State of Karnataka & Anr. vs. State of Meghalaya & Anr.
text: Case: State of Karnataka & Anr. vs. State of Meghalaya & Anr.. Date: 23rd March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary controversy in this case revolves around the interpretation of the expression 'betting and gambling' in Entries 34 and 62 of List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, and whether the states of Karnataka and Kerala have the legislative competence to enact laws imposing taxes on lotteries organized by other states. The key statutes under consideration are the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998, the Karnataka Tax on Lotteries Act, 2004, and the Kerala Tax on Paper Lotteries Act, 2005. The High Courts of Karnataka and Kerala ruled that their respective state legislatures had no legislative competence to enact the Karnataka Tax on Lotteries Act, 2004, and the Kerala Tax on Paper Lotteries Act, 2005, and declared these acts as unconstitutional and invalid. The State of Karnataka contended that the tax imposed by the Karnataka Tax on Lotteries Act, 2004, was a tax on gambling under Entry 62 of List II, not a sales tax or GST, and that the state legislature had the competence to levy such a tax on lotteries. The State of Nagaland argued that the Karnataka legislature had no competence to tax lotteries organized by other states as 'lotteries' fall under Entry 40 of List I, giving exclusive legislative power to the Parliament. The Supreme Court held that the states of Karnataka and Kerala did not have the legislative competence to impose taxes on lotteries organized by other states, affirming the rulings of the High Courts that the Karnataka Tax on Lotteries Act, 2004, and the Kerala Tax on Paper Lotteries Act, 2005, were unconstitutional.

case_name: State of Karnataka vs P. Ravikumar @ Ravi etc.
text: Case: State of Karnataka vs P. Ravikumar @ Ravi etc.. Date: 16th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appeal by the State of Karnataka challenging the acquittal of P. Ravikumar (Accused No. 2) and D.B. Savitha (Accused No. 3) for the offence under Section 302 IPC by the High Court. The prosecution's case was that D.B. Savitha (Accused No. 3) had an illicit relationship with another accused (Accused No. 1), and they, along with P. Ravikumar (Accused No. 2), conspired to murder Savitha's husband, Mohan Kumar, because he used to harass her about the illicit relationship. The trial court convicted all the accused under Section 302 IPC read with 34 IPC and 120(B) IPC, sentencing them for the murder of Mohan Kumar. The High Court acquitted P. Ravikumar and D.B. Savitha due to the lack of compelling evidence against them, particularly because the key witnesses turned hostile and the extra judicial confessions were deemed weak and unreliable. The prosecution relied on an extra judicial confession made to PW-2 (Auto Driver), who was a friend of Accused Nos. 1 and 2, but PW-2 turned hostile during the trial, weakening the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court observed that extra judicial confessions are weak pieces of evidence and require substantial corroboration, which was lacking in this case. The Court found no substantial infirmity in the High Court's order of acquittal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Karnataka, upholding the High Court's decision to acquit P. Ravikumar (Accused No. 2) and D.B. Savitha (Accused No. 3).

case_name: State of Karnataka vs. Prakash & Ors.
text: Case: State of Karnataka vs. Prakash & Ors.. Date: 30th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The accused were charged under Section 87 of the Karnataka Forest Act read with Sections 379 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for illegally transporting sandalwood in their private vehicles. The Trial Court convicted the accused under Section 87 of the Karnataka Forest Act read with Section 34 of the IPC and sentenced them to five years of simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 50,000 each. The High Court acquitted the accused by relying on the non-compliance with Section 62C of the Karnataka Forest Act, which mandates specific procedures for examining and certifying forest produce. The court found that the prosecution failed to prove that the concerned officers were authorized to issue the certificates. The prosecution argued that the High Court erred in acquitting the accused by overemphasizing the non-compliance with Section 62C of the Karnataka Forest Act without properly assessing the facts and evidence presented. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that compliance with Section 62C of the Karnataka Forest Act is mandatory and found that the prosecution failed to prove that the concerned officers were qualified and authorized to issue the necessary certificates for the forest produce. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision to acquit the accused due to the prosecution's failure to comply with the mandatory requirements of Section 62C of the Karnataka Forest Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to provide admissible evidence to prove that the confiscated items were sandalwood billets, as the certificates issued were not valid due to non-compliance with Section 62C of the Karnataka Forest Act.

case_name: State of Karnataka vs. T. Naseer @ Nasir @ Thandiantavida Naseer @ UMmarhazi @ Hazi & ORS.
text: Case: State of Karnataka vs. T. Naseer @ Nasir @ Thandiantavida Naseer @ UMmarhazi @ Hazi & ORS.. Date: 6th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the prosecution could recall a witness and produce a certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act after a delay, in connection with the serial bomb blasts that occurred in Bangalore on 25th July 2008. The prosecution sought to recall M. Krishna (PW-189) to produce a certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act to validate the electronic evidence seized in connection with the bomb blasts. The trial court rejected the application on the grounds of delay, stating that the certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act was sought to be produced six years after the initial evidence submission. The High Court of Karnataka upheld the trial court's decision, agreeing that there was an undue delay in producing the certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act. The Supreme Court held that the certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act could be produced at any stage before the trial concludes, as long as it does not cause irreversible prejudice to the accused. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by the State of Karnataka, setting aside the lower courts' orders and permitting the prosecution to recall the witness and produce the certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act. The Supreme Court reasoned that allowing the production of the certificate would not cause irreversible prejudice to the accused and was necessary to uphold the truth and ensure a fair trial.

case_name: State of Kerala & Anr. vs Joseph & Anr.
text: Case: State of Kerala & Anr. vs Joseph & Anr.. Date: 25th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether 14 acres of land owned by Joseph and his family was exempt from vesting in the State under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, based on their claim of personal cultivation. The Forest Tribunal allowed Joseph's application, granting exemption for the 14 acres of land from vesting in the State, as it was found to be under personal cultivation and within the ceiling limit prescribed by the Act. The High Court initially set aside the Forest Tribunal's decision and dismissed Joseph's application for exemption, but this decision was later set aside by the Supreme Court, which remanded the case back to the High Court for reconsideration. The Supreme Court ruled that Section 3(3) of the Act should be construed liberally and that the intention to cultivate by the landowner could be inferred from both the circumstances on the appointed day (10th May 1971) and subsequent actions indicating the development of the land for cultivation. The Forest Tribunal based its decision on seven findings, including the respondents' acquisition of the land before the appointed day, intention to personally cultivate it, actual cultivation of rubber, coconut, pepper, and coffee, and the fact that the land was within the ceiling limits. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the Forest Tribunal's and the High Court's decisions that exempted Joseph's land from vesting in the State, based on the findings that the land was under personal cultivation and within the ceiling limits. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 3(3) of the Act should be interpreted liberally, taking into account the intention of the landowner to cultivate and the subsequent development of the land for cultivation, rather than strictly requiring actual cultivation on the appointed day.

case_name: State of Kerala vs. M/S Akay Flavours and Aromatics Ltd.
text: Case: State of Kerala vs. M/S Akay Flavours and Aromatics Ltd.. Date: 2nd February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the interpretation of SRO 1727/1993, an exemption notification issued by the State of Kerala, and determining the correct commencement date for the five-year exemption period. The Revenue contended that the exemption period should commence from the date of approval by the Central Government, which was 16th December 1993, when the permission letter was issued, enabling the assessee to import capital goods and start exporting finished products. The assessee argued that the exemption period should commence from the date of commencement of production, which was 1st October 1995, rather than from the date of approval by the Central Government. The Tribunal concluded that the exemption period should not be commuted prior to the setting up of the unit, rejecting the Revenue's contention that the period should start from the date of approval by the Central Government. The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'approval' to mean the unambiguous approval by the Central Government, which in this case was granted on 27th October 1994, when the 'Green Card' was issued, rather than the initial permission letter dated 16th December 1993. The Supreme Court held that the exemption period should commence from the date of final approval by the Central Government, which was 27th October 1994. The appeals were partly allowed, and the date of approval was set as the reckonable date for the grant of exemption under the notification SRO 1727/1993.

The Supreme Court held that the exemption period should commence from the date of final approval by the Central Government, which was 27th October 1994. The appeals were partly allowed, and the date of approval was set as the reckonable date for the grant of exemption under the notification SRO 1727/1993.

case_name: State of Kerala vs. Rajesh
text: Case: State of Kerala vs. Rajesh. Date: 24th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is the challenge against the discretion exercised by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Kerala in granting post-arrest bail to the accused respondents without noticing the mandate of Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. The charges against the accused in Crime No. 14/2018 include possession of 10.202 kgs of hashish oil and currency notes worth Rs. 13,50,000, punishable under Sections 20(b)(ii)(c) and 29 of the NDPS Act. The High Court of Kerala failed to notice the mandate of Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act while granting post-arrest bail to the accused. The prosecution argued that the High Court committed an error by granting post-arrest bail without considering the mandate of Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act, which specifies that bail can only be granted if there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offense while on bail. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court granting bail, cancelled the bail bonds of the accused respondents, and directed that they be taken into custody. The Supreme Court directed the trial Court to proceed and expedite the trial. The accused respondents' bail bonds were cancelled, and they were directed to be taken into custody. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's liberal approach in granting bail under the NDPS Act was uncalled for and that the High Court failed to record a finding mandated under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. Respondent A-5 was previously convicted under Section 55(a) of the Abkari Act in S.C. 235/2005 and had a separate Crime No. 38/2018 registered against him for threatening a witness in Crime No. 14/2018. The High Court justified granting bail by noting that both accused had completed 195 days in judicial custody and their further detention was not necessary as nothing remained to be investigated against them, despite the provisions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The learned senior counsel for the respondents argued that the High Court granted post-arrest bail to other accused persons in Crime No. 14/2018 and that the prosecution had not challenged those decisions, implying that the bail granted to respondent A-5 should also not be interfered with.

case_name: State of M.P. vs Ghisilal
text: Case: State of M.P. vs Ghisilal. Date: 22nd November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the surplus land declared under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, and the possession taken by the State before the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, could be challenged and declared void by the civil court. The respondent, Ghisilal, claimed to be the sole heir and adopted son of Late Padam Singh, and sought a declaration that the surplus land of 16000.32 square meters was exempt under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, as possession had not been taken before the Repeal Act came into force. The appellant, State of M.P., argued that possession of the surplus land was taken following the necessary procedure under the ULC Act and that the land was recorded in the name of the State and utilized for constructing houses for the poor. The trial court decreed the suit in favor of the respondent, holding that possession of the surplus land had not been taken before the Repeal Act came into force, and restrained the State from interfering with the respondent's possession. The High Court dismissed the State's second appeal, confirming the judgements and decrees of the trial court and the first appellate court that possession had not been taken by the State before the Repeal Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the possession of the surplus land had indeed been taken by the State, as evidenced by the panchnama, and the land was utilized for public purposes. Therefore, the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, and the suit itself was not maintainable. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgements and decrees of the lower courts, and dismissed the suit filed by the respondent, ruling that the civil court's jurisdiction was barred by necessary implication and the suit was not maintainable.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. vs. Amit Shrivas
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. vs. Amit Shrivas. Date: 29th September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court emphasized that monetary grants, as specified in the policy, should be uniformly applied to dependents of work-charged employees unless explicitly amended by law. The Court interpreted that the policy categorically excluded work-charged employees from compassionate appointments and replaced such entitlement with a financial grant of Rs. 1,00,000. The Court rejected this argument by distinguishing between 'permanent' and 'regular' status, stating that permanent status only entitled the employee to benefits like pension, not compassionate appointment rights. The Court clarified that such cases must be decided based on the policy in force at the time of the employee's demise, rather than applying the later amendment retrospectively. The Supreme Court denied the claim for compassionate appointment but exercised its powers under Article 142 to increase the monetary grant from Rs. 1,00,000 to Rs. 2,00,000 to provide relief to the respondent.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh and Others vs. Murti Shri Chaturbhujnath and Others
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh and Others vs. Murti Shri Chaturbhujnath and Others. Date: 25th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the correction in revenue records naming the Collector as the 'Manager' of the temple was valid without following the due procedure outlined in Section 115 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959. The State argued that the temple was public property situated on government land and that the Pujaris, being merely caretakers, could not claim ownership rights over the lands. The respondents claimed that the temple lands were owned by the Deity and had been gifted by Syed Mohammad Ali, with the Pujaris managing the temple and using the usufructs for its maintenance. The Supreme Court observed that the correction was made in violation of Section 115 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, as it lacked proper inquiry and notice to the affected parties. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upheld the decisions of the First Appellate Court and the High Court, and held that the correction in revenue records without following due procedure was unsustainable. The court emphasized that any correction in revenue records must comply with the procedure under Section 115 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, which includes proper inquiry and notice to affected parties.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Babbu Rathore & Anr.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Babbu Rathore & Anr.. Date: 17th January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The issue was whether the High Court erred in discharging the respondents from charges under IPC Sections 302/34 and 404/34, as well as Section 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, on procedural grounds. The charges included IPC Sections 302/34 (murder with common intent), 404/34 (dishonest misappropriation of property), and Section 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The High Court upheld the decision because the investigation was conducted by an officer below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, violating the mandatory provisions of Section 9 of the SC/ST Act and Rule 7 of the SC/ST Rules, 1995. The Supreme Court noted that while the investigation under the SC/ST Act was procedurally flawed, the charges under IPC were independently investigated by a competent police officer and should not have been quashed. The Court clarified that procedural lapses in investigating charges under the SC/ST Act do not automatically invalidate charges under the IPC when those charges are independently investigated by a competent officer. The Court emphasized that procedural errors should not allow accused persons to escape charges under other statutes, urging proper compliance with investigative procedures to prevent misuse. The Supreme Court restored the trial for IPC charges under Sections 302/34 and 404/34, directing the trial court to proceed expeditiously in accordance with the law. Key witnesses, including the deceased's wife and others, testified that the deceased was last seen with the respondents, forming the basis for the charges. The Court reiterated the necessity of compliance with Section 9 of the SC/ST Act and Rule 7 of the SC/ST Rules, 1995, to ensure the validity of investigations under the Act. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision to discharge the respondents entirely and reinstated the trial for IPC charges while restricting the quashing to the SC/ST Act charges.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Gangabishan @ Vishnu & Ors.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Gangabishan @ Vishnu & Ors.. Date: 27th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the conviction of the respondents under Sections 302/149 and 325/149 of the IPC and instead convicting only Gangabishan @ Vishnu under Section 304 (Part-I) of the IPC. The respondents were accused of attacking and killing Rajesh with weapons such as lathis and a gun, causing his death, and injuring his brother Dinesh. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 302/149 IPC, sentencing them to life imprisonment, and also under various other sections with corresponding sentences and fines. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of accused Nos. 2 to 9 and convicted Gangabishan @ Vishnu under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC, sentencing him to ten years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The prosecution's case was that the accused, armed with weapons, attacked Rajesh and Dinesh in their field, resulting in Rajesh's death due to a gunshot injury inflicted by Gangabishan @ Vishnu. Gangabishan @ Vishnu fired a gunshot that injured Rajesh, which led to his death. He was convicted under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC for this act. The medical evidence, including the post-mortem report, showed that Rajesh suffered a gunshot injury on his left thigh, and Dinesh had injuries consistent with being hit by a blunt object. The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court's judgment acquitting accused Nos. 2 to 9 and upholding the conviction of Gangabishan @ Vishnu under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC. The dispute arose due to the accused grazing their cattle on the complainant's land, damaging the crops, which led to an altercation and subsequent attack. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court concluded the accused did not have the intention to commit murder but intended to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, justifying the conviction under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC for Gangabishan @ Vishnu.
