case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Harjeet Singh & Anr.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Harjeet Singh & Anr.. Date: 19th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in reducing the conviction of the respondents from Section 307 IPC to Section 324 IPC and acquitting the second respondent. Harjeet Singh was initially charged under Section 307 IPC, while Ramji Lal was charged under Section 307 read with Section 34 IPC. Sukhdev sustained multiple stab wounds, including a deep wound in the chest cavity, incised wounds on the upper region of the right buttocks, sub-scapula region, and illeal region of the left hip. The High Court reduced the conviction because it held that the injuries were on 'unimportant' parts of the body and lacked the intention to commit murder, thus fitting the description of causing simple hurt under Section 324 IPC. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's assessment was incorrect as the chest injury caused bleeding into the lungs, indicating it was on a vital part of the body and could be fatal, fitting the criteria for Section 307 IPC. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, restored the Sessions Court's conviction under Section 307 IPC, and directed Harjeet Singh to undergo the remainder of his five-year sentence. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to acquit Ramji Lal, agreeing that there was a lack of consistency in the prosecution witnesses' statements regarding his role in the crime. The ruling reinforces that injuries inflicted with the intention to cause death, especially on vital parts of the body, should be treated under Section 307 IPC, emphasizing the importance of the intent and severity of injuries. The ruling highlights the need for thorough consideration of medical evidence, especially regarding the impact of injuries on vital organs, to accurately determine the severity and intent behind the assault. The Supreme Court directed Harjeet Singh to surrender before the Sessions Court, Ashok Nagar, Guna, M.P. within two weeks from the date of the judgment to undergo the remainder of his sentence. The independent witness, an advocate (P.W. 3), corroborated the testimonies of the complainant's brothers by stating he saw Sukhdev lying in a pool of blood and was informed that Harjeet Singh had stabbed him multiple times.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Ramji Lal Sharma & Anr.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs Ramji Lal Sharma & Anr.. Date: 9th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main accusation was that Ramji Lal Sharma and the other accused, acting with common intention, attacked and killed Munshilal using firearms and an axe. The incident occurred when the accused assaulted Devendra over a monetary dispute. Later, the accused, armed with weapons, attacked Munshilal, who died from gunshot injuries while being taken to the police station. The trial court convicted all the accused for offences under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment with a fine. The High Court acquitted them by giving the benefit of doubt due to perceived contradictions between the ocular and medical evidence. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court erred in its judgment by not considering the common intention shared by all the accused and the consistency of witness testimonies establishing the presence of the accused. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's acquittal, restored the trial court's conviction of Ramji Lal Sharma and the other accused, and reinstated their sentences.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.. Date: 27th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether R.D. Sharma, who retired as the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF) in 2001, was entitled to have his pension revised to the apex scale of Rs. 80,000/- as per the Indian Forests Service (Pay) Second Amendment Rules, 2008, which came into effect from 27th September 2008. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh held that R.D. Sharma was eligible to get the benefit of Rs. 40,000/- as pension at par with other officers, as per the Indian Forests Service (Pay) Second Amendment Rules, 2008. The State of Madhya Pradesh argued that the amendment rules of 2008 came into force on 27th September 2008, and since R.D. Sharma retired in 2001, he could not be granted the benefit of the apex scale of Rs. 80,000/- which was meant for the upgraded post of Head of Forest Force to be filled by selection from officers holding the post of PCCF in the HAG+ scale. The Supreme Court observed that the principle of 'equal pay for equal work' was not applicable in this case as the upgradation to the apex scale was to be made by selection and not as a matter of course. Therefore, R.D. Sharma, who retired before the 2008 amendments, could not claim the apex scale as a matter of right. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgement, and restored the order of the Central Administrative Tribunal, which had dismissed R.D. Sharma's claim for the apex scale based on 'equal pay for equal work'. The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in the case of K.S. Krishnaswamy & Ors. vs. Union of India & Anr., where it was held that the benefit of upgradation of a post cannot be extended to pensioners who retired before such upgradation.

case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Sabal Singh (Dead) by LRS. & Ors.
text: Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Sabal Singh (Dead) by LRS. & Ors.. Date: 14th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the land recorded as 'Grass' land in the revenue papers before the date of vesting could be treated as Khud-Kasht land of the Ex-Zamindar, thus entitling the plaintiffs to Bhumiswami rights under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code. The plaintiffs, as successors of the Ex-Zamindar, claimed that the land was Khud-Kasht land of their predecessors and sought a declaration of Bhumiswami rights and a permanent injunction to restrain the State of Madhya Pradesh from interfering with their possession of the land. Both the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court dismissed the plaintiffs' suit, concluding that the land was not Khud-Kasht land but was recorded as 'Bir' or 'Grass' land before the abolition of Zamindari. The High Court allowed the plaintiffs' second appeal, declaring them Bhumiswami of the land and granting a permanent injunction against the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in reversing the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court. The Supreme Court restored the Trial Court's judgment, which dismissed the plaintiffs' suit, thus setting aside the High Court's judgment. The key legal provisions discussed include Section 2(c) and Section 4(2) of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, and Section 158 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, which deal with the definition and rights related to Khud-Kasht land and the vesting of land in the State. The Supreme Court reasoned that the land in question was not recorded as Khud-Kasht land in the revenue papers before the date of vesting and therefore did not meet the statutory requirements to be saved from vesting in the State. The land was recorded as 'Bir' or 'Grass' land, and thus, it automatically vested in the State free from all encumbrances.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in reversing the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court. The Supreme Court restored the Trial Court's judgment, which dismissed the plaintiffs' suit, thus setting aside the High Court's judgment.

The key legal provisions discussed include Section 2(c) and Section 4(2) of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, and Section 158 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, which deal with the definition and rights related to Khud-Kasht land and the vesting of land in the State.

The Supreme Court reasoned that the land in question was not recorded as Khud-Kasht land in the revenue papers before the date of vesting and therefore did not meet the statutory requirements to be saved from vesting in the State. The land was recorded as 'Bir' or 'Grass' land, and thus, it automatically vested in the State free from all encumbrances.

case_name: State of Maharashtra & Ors. vs M/s Moti Ratan Estate & Anr.
text: Case: State of Maharashtra & Ors. vs M/s Moti Ratan Estate & Anr.. Date: 4th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the acquisition proceedings for land in village Asarjan, Taluka and District Nanded had lapsed due to the awards under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act not being declared within two years from the date of the declaration under Section 6 of the Act. The High Court quashed the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the awards under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act were not declared within the required two-year period from the date of the declaration under Section 6 of the Act. The State of Maharashtra argued that the delay was due to the pending proceedings and interim stays granted by the High Court, which should be excluded from the calculation of the two-year period for declaring the awards. The Supreme Court ruled that the period during which the interim stay was in operation should be excluded from the two-year period for declaring the awards under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, thereby validating the acquisition proceedings. The Supreme Court held that stay orders affecting some landowners should apply to the entire acquisition scheme, thereby justifying the authorities' decision not to declare the awards until the stay orders were lifted. The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in the case of Raj Kumar Gandhi vs Chandigarh Administration, which stated that when a scheme of acquisition is one, interim stay granted in respect of one pocket of land would operate even with respect to other pockets of land.

case_name: State of Maharashtra vs. Shri Vile Parle Kelvani Mandal & Ors.
text: Case: State of Maharashtra vs. Shri Vile Parle Kelvani Mandal & Ors.. Date: 7th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether charitable education institutions registered under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950, are exempt from paying electricity duty post 1st September 2016, following the enactment of the Maharashtra Electricity Duty Act, 2016. The Bombay High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Shri Vile Parle Kelvani Mandal & Ors., holding that they were exempted from paying electricity duty. Consequently, the court set aside the electricity bills levying the duty on their educational institutions. The State of Maharashtra argued that the High Court erred in holding that charitable education institutions were not liable to pay electricity duty under the Maharashtra Electricity Duty Act, 2016. They contended that the exemption provided under the previous 1958 Act was not carried over to the 2016 Act. The Supreme Court interpreted that the 2016 Act did not provide an exemption from paying electricity duty for charitable education institutions. The Court noted that the specific exemption available under the 1958 Act for such institutions was deliberately omitted in the 2016 Act. The Supreme Court quashed the Bombay High Court's judgment and held that charitable education institutions registered under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950, are not exempt from paying electricity duty under the Maharashtra Electricity Duty Act, 2016. The appeal by the State of Maharashtra was allowed. The Supreme Court emphasized that tax exemption provisions must be interpreted strictly. The clear and unambiguous language of the 2016 Act did not include an exemption for charitable education institutions. The Court highlighted that if the legislature intended to provide such an exemption, it would have explicitly included it in the 2016 Act.

case_name: State of NCT of Delhi vs. Shiv Charan Bansal & Ors.
text: Case: State of NCT of Delhi vs. Shiv Charan Bansal & Ors.. Date: 5th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Delhi High Court was justified in discharging the accused Shiv Charan Bansal, Lalit Mann, Shailendra Singh, and Rajbir Singh from charges under Sections 120B, 302, and 201 read with Section 34 IPC and Sections 25, 27, 54, and 59 of the Arms Act. Shiv Charan Bansal and the other accused were charged with conspiracy, murder, and destruction of evidence under Sections 120B, 302, and 201 read with Section 34 IPC and Sections 25, 27, 54, and 59 of the Arms Act. The case involved the murder of S.N. Gupta, who was shot dead on 21st March 2006. The motive was attributed to financial disputes and business rivalries involving substantial investments in chit funds and business partnerships between the deceased and the accused. The prosecution presented witness testimonies, call detail records, and forensic evidence linking the accused to the crime. This included the recovery of the weapon from Shailendra Singh's office, which matched the bullets recovered from the body of the deceased. Shiv Charan Bansal was alleged to have conspired with his son Sachin Bansal and other accused to murder S.N. Gupta to misappropriate the investments made by the deceased in their chit fund and business partnerships. The Supreme Court found that the Delhi High Court erred in discharging the accused, as there was sufficient material on record to frame charges and proceed with the trial. The Court emphasized that the material on record created a grave suspicion about the involvement of the accused in the conspiracy and murder. The Supreme Court directed the Additional Sessions Judge, Rohini Courts, Delhi, to frame charges against Shiv Charan Bansal, Lalit Mann, and Shailendra Singh under relevant sections and proceed with the trial on a day-to-day basis to conclude within six months. The call detail records revealed continuous communication between the accused before and after the murder, establishing a link and creating strong suspicion about their involvement in the conspiracy to murder S.N. Gupta. The Supreme Court noted that the destruction of committee records by Shiv Charan Bansal and his son created strong suspicion about their conduct and involvement in the conspiracy to murder S.N. Gupta. The forensic and ballistic reports confirmed that the bullets recovered from the body of S.N. Gupta were fired from the unlicensed pistol recovered from Shailendra Singh's office, providing crucial evidence linking the weapon to the murder. The Supreme Court concluded that there was ample material on record to frame charges against the accused and directed the trial court to proceed with the trial against Shiv Charan Bansal, Lalit Mann, and Shailendra Singh for their alleged involvement in the conspiracy and murder of S.N. Gupta.

case_name: State of Odisha & Ors. vs. Manju Naik
text: Case: State of Odisha & Ors. vs. Manju Naik. Date: 4th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case concerns the entitlement of Manju Naik to invalid and family pension benefits following the death of her husband, Sagar Naik, who was a government employee retired on the grounds of mental incapacity. The appellants contended that Sagar Naik, the respondent's husband, did not meet the required ten years of qualifying service for pension under the Orissa Civil Services (Pension) Rules, and hence was not eligible for invalid pension. The Tribunal directed the authorities to sanction invalid pension for Sagar Naik and settle family pension for Manju Naik, despite Sagar Naik not completing the qualifying service period. The High Court dismissed the challenge by stating that the Tribunal's decision was a reasoned order declaring entitlement to invalid pension and left the order undisturbed. The Supreme Court ruled that the qualifying service of ten years under the Pension Rules must be satisfied for invalid pension. It set aside the orders of the Tribunal and the High Court, thereby denying the invalid pension to Sagar Naik. Manju Naik was granted service gratuity, other terminal benefits like GPF and DCRG, and was appointed as a sweeper under the Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme.

case_name: State of Odisha vs. Nirjharini Patnaik @ Mohanty & Anr.
text: Case: State of Odisha vs. Nirjharini Patnaik @ Mohanty & Anr.. Date: 26th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the order of cognizance for offences under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 477A, 120B, and 34 of the IPC against the respondents. The allegations included forging documents to facilitate the illegal transfer of valuable government land to private entities, using forged documents such as Hata Patas, Ekpadia, and rent receipts to manipulate judicial processes and revenue records. The High Court quashed the order due to insufficient evidence of a conspiracy directly implicating the respondents and criticized the thoroughness of the preliminary judicial scrutiny. The Supreme Court found that the evidence suggested a strong prima facie case for further examination, revealing the respondents' critical roles in the misuse of the General Power of Attorney (GPA) and subsequent property transactions. The Supreme Court noted that the GPA was manipulated to misrepresent the authority granted, leading to illegal property transactions at undervalued rates, which caused significant loss to the state. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the trial to proceed expeditiously, allowing a thorough examination of evidence and witnesses to determine the extent of the conspiracy and the respondents' involvement. The Supreme Court emphasized that dismissing the case at the preliminary stage could undermine multiple ongoing investigations and judicial processes related to similar frauds involving government lands. The transactions involved selling substantial portions of government land at rates grossly undervalued, facilitated through forged documents and improper legal proceedings, causing considerable loss to the state. The Supreme Court noted that the respondents' professional positions and influence in the real estate sector were misused to facilitate and conceal the illegal transactions, highlighting their central role in the conspiracy. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to proceed with the trial expeditiously and ensure a thorough examination of the evidence and involvement of the respondents to determine the actual harm caused to the public exchequer.

text: Case: State of Orissa & Anr. vs. Laxmi Narayan Das (Dead) thr. LRs & Ors.. Date: 12th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court found that the record of rights was finalized without any challenges being made within the statutory period, and any subsequent appeals or suits were procedurally barred. The Court dismissed the writ petition due to significant delay, lack of disclosure about the previous civil suit, and the absence of any valid grounds to reopen the finalized record of rights. The Court indicated that errors should have been addressed through revisions filed within one year of the final publication of record of rights under Section 15(b) of the 1958 Act. The Court interpreted that the respondents' claim of adverse possession lacked merit as they had not demonstrated continuous, hostile possession and the claim was belated. The Court predicted that entertaining stale claims like this would disrupt settled records and encourage frivolous litigation.

case_name: State of Orissa vs Santi Kumar Mitra & Another
text: Case: State of Orissa vs Santi Kumar Mitra & Another. Date: 10th May 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether the State of Orissa had the right to resume possession of the leasehold property due to alleged violations of the lease agreement and failure to renew the lease in time. The original lease agreement was for 30 years starting from 29th September 1905 and was later renewed for another 30 years from 26th September 1935. In 1975, the State of Orissa initiated resumption proceedings due to the dilapidated condition of the structures on the property and the occupation by outsiders, leading to the determination of the lease and the resumption of possession. The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration and permanent injunction, challenging the resumption order as illegal and without jurisdiction, and sought renewal of the lease. The State of Orissa must consider the pending renewal application in Lease Renewal Case No. 11/1992 within six months and allow the respondents to challenge any adverse findings in the appropriate forum. The Supreme Court's decision implies that future lease renewals must strictly adhere to the terms of the lease agreement and that any violations could justify the resumption of the leasehold property by the State.

case_name: State of Punjab & Ors. vs Dev Brat Sharma
text: Case: State of Punjab & Ors. vs Dev Brat Sharma. Date: 16th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Dev Brat Sharma was required to make good the deficiency in court fees on the amount of Rs. 20 lakhs claimed by him as compensation for denying the status of freedom fighter and the resultant damages. Dev Brat Sharma alleged that he suffered damages due to being denied the status of a freedom fighter by the defendants and sought Rs. 20 lakhs as compensation for the loss of reputation and other damages. The High Court set aside the Trial Court's order requiring Dev Brat Sharma to make good the deficiency in court fees on the amount of Rs. 20 lakhs, holding that the exact valuation of the relief could not be ascertained at the initial stage. The State of Punjab filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision to set aside the Trial Court's order regarding the payment of court fees. The Supreme Court concluded that the suit for damages and compensation filed by Dev Brat Sharma required the payment of ad valorem court fees based on the amount claimed, which was Rs. 20 lakhs. The Supreme Court clarified that for money suits, including suits for damages and compensation, the court fees should be paid based on the amount claimed, and not on a tentative amount. The decision may ensure that plaintiffs in future suits for damages and compensation properly pay ad valorem court fees based on the actual amount claimed, thus preventing undervaluation of claims. Plaintiffs should ensure that they accurately state the amount of damages claimed and pay the corresponding ad valorem court fees at the time of filing the suit to comply with legal requirements. The Supreme Court directed Dev Brat Sharma to pay the court fees on the amount of Rs. 20 lakhs claimed within four weeks from the date of the judgment. This judgment may set a precedent for stricter enforcement of court fee requirements in suits for damages and compensation, ensuring proper valuation and payment at the initial stage of filing. The Supreme Court directed that Dev Brat Sharma must state the valuation and make the necessary payment of court fees for the appeal before proceeding further in the appellate court.

case_name: State of Punjab vs Baljinder Singh & Anr.
text: Case: State of Punjab vs Baljinder Singh & Anr.. Date: 15th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Baljinder Singh and Khushi Khan were charged with offenses under Section 15 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, for possession of contraband material, specifically poppy husk. The prosecution's case was that on 19th August 2009, during a routine patrol, the police stopped a vehicle driven by Baljinder Singh and accompanied by Khushi Khan. Upon searching the vehicle, they found seven bags containing poppy husk, each weighing 34 kgs. The High Court acquitted Baljinder Singh and Khushi Khan due to the non-compliance with Section 50 of the NDPS Act, which mandates that the accused must be informed of their right to be searched before a Magistrate or a Gazetted Officer. The State of Punjab argued that even though there was non-compliance with Section 50 concerning the personal search of the accused, the recovery of contraband from the vehicle should be considered independently and was valid. The Supreme Court observed that the requirements of Section 50 are applicable only to personal searches and not to searches of vehicles or other containers. Therefore, the non-compliance with Section 50 did not affect the validity of the contraband found in the vehicle. The Supreme Court set aside the acquittal by the High Court and restored the conviction and sentence of Baljinder Singh and Khushi Khan as recorded by the Trial Court. However, it reduced their substantive sentence from 12 years to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court instructed that Baljinder Singh and Khushi Khan should surrender before the concerned police station by 15th November 2019 to undergo their remaining sentence. If they failed to surrender, the police were directed to take them into custody immediately.

case_name: State of Punjab vs Rakesh Kumar
text: Case: State of Punjab vs Rakesh Kumar. Date: 3rd December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the suspension of sentence and grant of bail to the accused respondents who were convicted under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. The respondents were convicted for offences under Sections 21 and 22 of the NDPS Act for possession of manufactured drugs without valid authorization. The High Court granted suspension of sentences and bail to the respondents, reasoning that the drugs in question were manufactured drugs and should be tried under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, not the NDPS Act. The State of Punjab appealed the High Court's decision, arguing that the High Court's order was contrary to law as the NDPS Act does not bar the application of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, and both acts can be applicable. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's decision to try the respondents under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act instead of the NDPS Act was incorrect and not sustainable in law. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order of suspension of sentence and bail, and directed the authorities to take the respondents into custody forthwith. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to expedite the hearings and dispose of the appeals accordingly, considering that some respondents had already undergone a considerable period under incarceration.

case_name: State of Rajasthan vs Banwari Lal and another
text: Case: State of Rajasthan vs Banwari Lal and another. Date: 8th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in reducing the sentence of Banwari Lal from three years rigorous imprisonment to the period already undergone (44 days) after he was convicted under Section 307 IPC for causing grievous injuries to Phool Chand. The High Court reduced Banwari Lal's sentence from three years rigorous imprisonment to the period already undergone, which was 44 days. Phool Chand sustained a lacerated wound of size 10 x 1 cms bone deep extending up to the brain membrane in the center of the skull, with the bone protruding. The grounds included the long passage of time since the offense (26 years), the prolonged trial, and Banwari Lal's age, arguing that he and Mohan Lal had resettled and had not engaged in any criminal activity since. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's decision to reduce the sentence and restored the trial court's sentence of three years rigorous imprisonment for Banwari Lal. The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning insufficient and unsustainable, criticizing its failure to consider the gravity of the offense and the serious injuries caused. The Supreme Court condoned the delay of 1880 days in filing the appeal due to the gravity of the case and the need for proper sentencing. The Supreme Court directed Banwari Lal to surrender before the appropriate jail authority within four weeks to serve the remaining sentence. The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeal against Mohan Lal, as the benefit of probation had been granted by the trial court and was not challenged before the High Court. The Supreme Court emphasized that sentencing should be appropriate, adequate, just, proportionate, and commensurate with the nature and gravity of the crime, and that courts should not be cavalier in their approach to sentencing.

The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's decision to reduce the sentence and restored the trial court's sentence of three years rigorous imprisonment for Banwari Lal.
The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning insufficient and unsustainable, criticizing its failure to consider the gravity of the offense and the serious injuries caused.
The Supreme Court condoned the delay of 1880 days in filing the appeal due to the gravity of the case and the need for proper sentencing.
The Supreme Court directed Banwari Lal to surrender before the appropriate jail authority within four weeks to serve the remaining sentence.
The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeal against Mohan Lal, as the benefit of probation had been granted by the trial court and was not challenged before the High Court.

The Supreme Court emphasized that sentencing should be appropriate, adequate, just, proportionate, and commensurate with the nature and gravity of the crime, and that courts should not be cavalier in their approach to sentencing.

case_name: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
text: Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others. Date: 7th December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Gurbachan Singh was correctly acquitted by the High Court under Section 302 IPC, given the evidence suggesting he shared a common intention with other co-accused in the murder of Teja Singh. Gurbachan Singh and the other accused were charged under Sections 302, 324, 323, and 148 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Teja Singh and injuries caused to Harbhajan Singh. The dispute involved a land partition issue between Teja Singh and the accused. On 6th November 2000, after an altercation, the accused, armed with various weapons, attacked Teja Singh, resulting in his death, and injured Harbhajan Singh. The High Court acquitted Gurbachan Singh under Section 302 IPC, convicting him only under Section 323 IPC for causing injuries to Teja Singh, reasoning that he did not share the common intention to commit murder. The Supreme Court concluded that Gurbachan Singh shared a common intention with the other co-accused to commit the murder, as evidenced by his participation in the attack with a 'lathi' and his continued assault on Teja Singh. The Supreme Court held that common intention could be inferred from the coordinated attack, the weapons used, and the conduct of Gurbachan Singh, establishing his liability under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's sentence of life imprisonment for Gurbachan Singh under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC and upheld his conviction under Section 324 IPC for injuries to Harbhajan Singh. The Supreme Court directed Gurbachan Singh to surrender within 21 days to serve the remaining sentence. If he fails to surrender, the authorities are to take action to detain him. The judgment reinforces that co-accused who share a common intention in a crime can be held equally liable under Section 34 IPC, even if their specific roles in the act differ. Future appeals involving common intention will likely consider this judgment, emphasizing the importance of collective actions and shared intent in establishing liability under Section 34 IPC. Legal practitioners should carefully analyze the coordination, roles, and actions of each accused to establish or refute the presence of common intention, as highlighted by the Supreme Court's reasoning in this case.

case_name: State of Rajasthan vs. Mahesh Kumar @ Mahesh Dhaulpuria & Anr.
text: Case: State of Rajasthan vs. Mahesh Kumar @ Mahesh Dhaulpuria & Anr.. Date: 16th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Mahesh Kumar and the other respondents were charged with offences under Sections 302 (murder), 201 (causing disappearance of evidence), read with Section 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the IPC. The incident involved the discovery of a dead body on 19th October 2002 near the railway line in Kota, Rajasthan. The body had injuries on its head, mouth, and face, and was identified as Bajranglal, a retired constable. The trial court convicted Mahesh Kumar and the other respondents under Sections 302 and 201 read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted the respondents because the circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution was found to be doubtful, contradictory, and unreliable. Many prosecution witnesses were declared hostile, and important witnesses were not produced. The High Court noted that most prosecution witnesses were hostile, many important witnesses were not produced, and there were significant gaps and contradictions in the circumstantial evidence. The chain of events necessary to establish guilt was incomplete. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's evaluation that the prosecution failed to complete the chain of circumstantial evidence, and thus there was no conclusive proof of the respondents' guilt. The High Court's decision to acquit was upheld. The Supreme Court reiterated that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established, consistent with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused, of a conclusive nature, and exclude every other hypothesis except guilt. The prosecution failed to present several key witnesses, including those who identified and handled the dead body, and other witnesses who could have testified about the motive and events leading to the murder. This lack of evidence weakened the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Rajasthan, finding no error in the High Court's judgement of acquitting the respondents due to the insufficiency and unreliability of the prosecution's evidence. The judgement emphasizes that the chain of evidence in circumstantial cases must be complete and must lead only to the conclusion of the accused's guilt, excluding any other reasonable hypothesis. The evidence must be so conclusive that it leaves no room for doubt regarding the innocence of the accused.

case_name: State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs M.S. Viswanathan & Ors.
text: Case: State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs M.S. Viswanathan & Ors.. Date: 20th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the land owned by Smt. Nagarathinam Ammal, which was acquired under the Tamil Nadu Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1978, should be restored to her legal heirs following the repeal of the Act in 1999. The Act required landowners to surrender excess vacant land beyond the ceiling limit to the government. Smt. Nagarathinam Ammal was required to surrender 6750 sq.mts of her land, which was later allotted to the Madras Snake Park Trust and subsequently to the Forest Department. The legal heirs contended that the land was never physically taken over by the government, as evidenced by inspection reports indicating that the land was lying vacant with a compound wall, and therefore, they were entitled to the restoration of the land under the Repeal Act. The letter indicated that Smt. Nagarathinam Ammal voluntarily surrendered and delivered possession of the land to the government. This letter was crucial in establishing that the possession had been taken over by the government, countering the claims of her legal heirs. The Supreme Court concluded that the possession of the land was indeed taken over by the government as per the letter dated 11th November 1980, and therefore, the legal heirs were not entitled to the restoration of the land under the Repeal Act. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench of the High Court, which had granted the benefit of the Repeal Act to the respondents, and dismissed the writ petition filed by the legal heirs of Smt. Nagarathinam Ammal. The Supreme Court observed that the legal heirs had entered into various transactions with realtors, including agreements of sale and power of attorney, which indicated attempts to commercially exploit the land. These actions further undermined their claim for restoration under the Repeal Act.

case_name: State of Tamil Nadu vs. State of Karnataka and Another
text: Case: State of Tamil Nadu vs. State of Karnataka and Another. Date: 14th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary subject matter is a dispute between the State of Tamil Nadu and the State of Karnataka regarding the construction of dams and diversion structures by Karnataka, which Tamil Nadu claims affects the natural flow of the Pennaiyar river and its tributaries, impacting Tamil Nadu's water usage. Tamil Nadu sought a declaration that Karnataka's unilateral construction of dams and diversion structures is illegal, a permanent injunction to restrain Karnataka from further construction, and a direction to ensure the natural flows of the Pennaiyar river to Tamil Nadu. Karnataka argued that the projects were primarily for supplying drinking water to drought-prone areas, were sanctioned and approved by the relevant authorities, and did not require Tamil Nadu's consent under the agreements of 1892 and 1933. The Union of India stated that no formal request for arbitration under the Agreement of 1892 was received from any state government, and thus no action could be taken. It also mentioned that the issue could be addressed by setting up a Water Disputes Tribunal under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, but no request for such a tribunal had been made. The Supreme Court denied interim relief, noting that 75% of the construction work on the disputed projects was already completed, and that the projects were undertaken after receiving all requisite sanctions and permissions. However, the court allowed Tamil Nadu to seek the constitution of a Water Disputes Tribunal by making an appropriate application. Tamil Nadu's counsel argued that Karnataka's actions violated the 1933 Agreement, which requires consent for new structures affecting water flow. They also highlighted that the dispute concerns un-authorized diversions impacting Tamil Nadu's water usage and called for interim relief to maintain the status quo. Tamil Nadu objected to several projects, including the construction of a 500 Mcft capacity reservoir across the Markandeya river near Yargol village, and various schemes for pumping and diverting water in the Pennaiyar river basin.

case_name: State of U.P. & Anr. vs Baleshwar Singh & Ors.
text: Case: State of U.P. & Anr. vs Baleshwar Singh & Ors.. Date: 9th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Baleshwar Singh, an employee of the undivided State of Uttar Pradesh, was entitled to salary and retiral benefits after being relieved from duty and not being allowed to resume his position following the bifurcation of the state. The bifurcation led to complications in the allocation and mutual transfer of employees between the new states, specifically affecting Baleshwar Singh, who was transferred to Uttarakhand but later faced issues in resuming his duties in Uttar Pradesh. The High Court of Allahabad directed the State of Uttar Pradesh to pay salary to Baleshwar Singh from 9th April 2011 until the date of promotion of Mahendra Pratap Singh and to pay the current salary starting from May 2016. The court also ordered that Baleshwar Singh should regain his seniority and be paid arrears within three months. The Supreme Court found that the State of Uttar Pradesh had failed to comply with the High Court's order and directed the state to release the salary and all other consequential benefits to Baleshwar Singh within three months, with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from 30th June 2016. The Supreme Court directed the State of Uttar Pradesh to calculate and release the retiral dues payable to Baleshwar Singh based on his superannuation on 30th June 2016, with simple interest at the rate of 6% per annum from 22nd August 2016. The balance amount must be paid within three months, failing which the interest rate would increase to 9% per annum. The Supreme Court directed that if Baleshwar Singh was entitled to reimbursement of medical expenses incurred, the necessary amount should be released to him within three months in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court directed the State of Uttar Pradesh to pay costs of Rs. 10,000 to Baleshwar Singh within three months. case_name: State of U.P. vs Sonu Kushwaha
text: Case: State of U.P. vs Sonu Kushwaha. Date: 5th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Sonu Kushwaha was guilty of the offence of aggravated penetrative sexual assault punishable under Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012. Sonu Kushwaha was charged under Sections 377 and 506 of the IPC and Section 5 read with Section 6 of the POCSO Act for allegedly committing aggravated penetrative sexual assault on a minor. The prosecution's case was that on 22nd March 2016, Sonu Kushwaha took the 10-year-old victim to a temple, gave him Rs. 20, and forced him to perform oral sex. The victim later reported the incident to his family. The Special Judge convicted Sonu Kushwaha of all three offences and sentenced him to ten years of rigorous imprisonment for the offence punishable under Section 6 of the POCSO Act, seven years for the offence under Section 377 of the IPC, and one year for the offence under Section 506 of the IPC. The High Court held that Sonu Kushwaha was guilty of penetrative sexual assault under Section 4 of the POCSO Act instead of aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 6, reducing his sentence to seven years of rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court found that the offence committed by Sonu Kushwaha was indeed aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 6 of the POCSO Act, as the victim was below twelve years of age. The Supreme Court ruled that the minimum sentence under Section 6 of the POCSO Act is ten years of rigorous imprisonment, and it upheld this sentence for Sonu Kushwaha.

case_name: State of U.P. vs. Gayatri Prasad Prajapati
text: Case: State of U.P. vs. Gayatri Prasad Prajapati. Date: 15th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the interim bail granted to Gayatri Prasad Prajapati by the Allahabad High Court on medical grounds was justified. Gayatri Prasad Prajapati, a former minister in the State of U.P., was accused in case Crime No. 29 of 2017 under Sections 376(D)/376/511/504/506 of the IPC read with Sections 3/4 of the POCSO Act. The FIR was registered against Gayatri Prasad Prajapati after an order was passed by the Supreme Court on 17th February 2017 in a writ petition filed by the complainant. The High Court granted interim bail based on the respondent's medical condition, which included UTI, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, bamboo spine, and seronegative spondylorthropathy. The Court noted that proper treatment was not available at KGMU Hospital, Lucknow, and the COVID-19 pandemic posed a real and imminent threat to his health. The State of U.P. argued that the respondent was receiving adequate treatment at KGMU and SGPGIMS, which are super-speciality hospitals. The State contended that the High Court did not consider the medical board's report and the medical treatment provided at these hospitals before granting interim bail. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting interim bail, stating that the High Court had not considered the medical reports from KGMU and SGPGIMS and the treatment being provided. The Supreme Court emphasized that due medical care was being taken of the respondent. The Supreme Court emphasized that humane treatment to all, including accused persons, is a requirement of law, and that prisoners suffering from ailments must be given due treatment and care while in prison.

case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. vs Akhil Sharda & Ors.
text: Case: State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. vs Akhil Sharda & Ors.. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the criminal proceedings arising out of FIR No. 260 of 2018, which involved allegations of conspiracy and forgery related to the disappearance of trucks loaded with beer. Akhil Sharda & Ors. were accused of being involved in a conspiracy that led to the disappearance of trucks loaded with beer, and were charged under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC. The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings, including the charge-sheet and the summoning order, on the grounds that there was no sufficient evidence to support the charges of conspiracy and forgery. The State argued that the High Court had committed a serious error in quashing the proceedings without properly considering the allegations of a larger conspiracy involving the disappearance of multiple trucks loaded with beer. The Supreme Court held that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by conducting a mini-trial at the stage of deciding the application under Section 482 Cr.P.C., which was not permissible. The Supreme Court noted that the allegations of a larger conspiracy involving the disappearance of trucks loaded with beer were serious and required thorough investigation, which the High Court had failed to appreciate. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order and restored the criminal proceedings before the trial court, directing that the investigation should continue into the allegations of conspiracy and forgery. The Supreme Court emphasized that the FIRs in Case Crime Nos. 260 of 2018 and 227 of 2019 were interconnected and part of a larger conspiracy, thus requiring a comprehensive investigation. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court had delivered its judgment six months after reserving the case for judgment, which was not advisable and could lead to unnecessary speculations and loss of confidence in the judicial system. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the criminal proceedings in Criminal Case No. 5694 of 2019, directing the trial court to proceed with the case.

case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh and Others vs. Shanti Devi
text: Case: State of Uttar Pradesh and Others vs. Shanti Devi. Date: 8th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves the respondent, Shanti Devi, seeking age relaxation for appointment to the post of Mukhya Sevika under the Uttar Pradesh Public Services (Relaxation of the Age limits for Recruitment) Rules 1992. The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the decision of the High Court, which directed the State to consider her claim for age relaxation. The High Court directed the State to consider Shanti Devi's claim for age relaxation, allowing her to participate in the selection process for the post of Mukhya Sevika despite exceeding the upper age limit of 50 years. Shanti Devi sought age relaxation because she had served continuously as an Anganwadi worker since 1987 and believed she was entitled to age relaxation under the Uttar Pradesh Public Services (Relaxation of the Age limits for Recruitment) Rules 1992. The State argued that the Age Relaxation Rules of 1992 did not apply to Shanti Devi because she was not a regular government employee but an Anganwadi worker appointed under a state government scheme. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by the State of Uttar Pradesh, setting aside the High Court's decision, and ruled that Shanti Devi was not eligible for age relaxation under the Uttar Pradesh Public Services (Relaxation of the Age limits for Recruitment) Rules 1992. The Supreme Court denied age relaxation because the Age Relaxation Rules of 1992 apply to regular government service posts and not to honorary positions like that of Anganwadi workers. Additionally, granting age relaxation selectively would lead to arbitrary selections and undermine the uniform eligibility criteria.

case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh vs Hansraj @ Hansu
text: Case: State of Uttar Pradesh vs Hansraj @ Hansu. Date: 12th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Hansraj @ Hansu was charged under Section 20(b)(ii) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act for possession of 300 grams of charas and under Section 60 of the Excise Act for possession of 2700 pouches of country-made liquor. The Trial Court convicted Hansraj @ Hansu under Section 20(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act and sentenced him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000. He was also convicted under Section 60 of the Excise Act and sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment. The High Court acquitted Hansraj @ Hansu, setting aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the Trial Court, primarily on the grounds of delay in sending the sample to the laboratory and lack of evidence on the preservation and handling of the contraband. The High Court cited the delay in sending the sample to the laboratory, lack of evidence on how and in what condition the contraband was kept, and the failure to examine key witnesses who transported the samples to the laboratory as the main reasons for acquitting Hansraj @ Hansu. The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's view was not unreasonable or perverse, as the prosecution failed to provide necessary evidence on the handling and preservation of the contraband, and thus upheld the High Court's acquittal of Hansraj @ Hansu. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by the State of Uttar Pradesh, thereby confirming the acquittal of Hansraj @ Hansu as decided by the High Court.

case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Atul Kumar Dwivedi
text: Case: State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Atul Kumar Dwivedi. Date: 7th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the normalization process adopted by the Uttar Pradesh Police Recruitment and Promotion Board violated the prescribed eligibility criteria of securing 50% marks in each subject for recruitment to various police posts. The Board applied the Standardized Equi-percentile method for normalization of scores across multiple exam sessions, which was contested by candidates who argued it altered the eligibility criteria. The Board reported that 9,158 male candidates and 501 female candidates qualified with raw marks, while 5,229 male candidates and 484 female candidates qualified after normalization. The court addressed whether the term 'marks' referred to raw marks obtained by candidates or normalized scores, ultimately ruling that raw marks should be used for eligibility purposes. The court clarified that normalization could only be applied for preparing the merit list after candidates met the eligibility criteria with raw marks. The Supreme Court directed the Recruitment Board to prepare a new select list based on raw marks and to use normalization only for determining the merit order.

case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Wasif Haider & Ors.
text: Case: State of Uttar Pradesh vs. Wasif Haider & Ors.. Date: 10th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the acquittal of Wasif Haider and other respondents by the High Court for charges under Sections 302, 307, 148 IPC, and Section 7 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act was justified. The charges were filed following a riot on 16th March 2001, during which rioters caused destruction at the Chaubey Gola Temple, and ADM Chandra Prakash Pathak was fatally shot along with his orderly, Ram Chandra, when police attempted to control the situation. The High Court cited various contradictions in prosecution witness testimonies, suspicious identification procedures, and the failure to prove the connection between the accused and the recovered evidence, leading to doubts about the respondents' involvement. The Supreme Court found the TIP to be flawed due to a 55-day delay in conducting it, lack of evidence that the accused were kept concealed, and the possibility that witnesses had seen the accused prior to the TIP, making the identification process questionable. The Supreme Court noted discrepancies between the post-mortem report, which indicated an exit wound, and the forensic report, which claimed a bullet was recovered from the ashes of the deceased, creating doubts about the evidence's reliability. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's acquittal of the respondents, due to investigative lapses and the prosecution's failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court emphasized that suspicion, however grave, cannot replace proof. The prosecution must establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, and any benefit of doubt must be given to the accused.

case_name: State of Uttarakhand & Ors. vs. Kumaon Stone Crusher
text: Case: State of Uttarakhand & Ors. vs. Kumaon Stone Crusher. Date: 15th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the levy of transit fee by the States of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Madhya Pradesh on forest produce, which was challenged by the respondent, Kumaon Stone Crusher. The case scrutinized the rules framed under Section 41 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, including the Uttar Pradesh Transit of Timber & Other Forest Produce Rules, 1978, and similar rules by the States of Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh. Kumaon Stone Crusher contended that once the forest produce (boulders) is converted into commercial commodities like stone grits and chips, it ceases to be forest produce, and no transit fee can be charged. The Uttarakhand High Court allowed the writ petitions, quashing the orders levying the transit fee, holding that once forest produce is processed into commercial commodities, it ceases to be forest produce. The States of Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh filed several appeals challenging the High Court's decision that quashed the levy of transit fee on processed forest produce. The Supreme Court condoned the delay and granted leave to hear the appeals, which were clubbed together for consideration. The case had broader implications for the levy of transit fees on forest produce across different states and the interpretation of when forest produce ceases to be categorized as such after undergoing processing.

case_name: State of Uttarakhand vs. Darshan Singh
text: Case: State of Uttarakhand vs. Darshan Singh. Date: 7th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the appeal against the High Court's acquittal of the respondents for offences under Sections 147, 148, 149, and 302 of the IPC, which was initially convicted by the Trial Court. On 22nd August 1992, Swarn Singh and his family were attacked while traveling on a tractor. The attackers, including Darshan Singh, used firearms and sharp weapons, resulting in the death of Singhara Singh, Swarn Singh's father. The High Court acquitted the accused due to material variations in the evidence of key witnesses, contradictions between ocular and medical evidence, and the fact that important witnesses turned hostile or were not examined. The Supreme Court found that there were significant inconsistencies in the witness testimonies, particularly between PW1 and PW2, and contradictions with the medical evidence regarding the injuries sustained by the deceased. The recovery of weapons based on the accused's statements was noted, but the Supreme Court found that the manner of recovery and the condition of the weapons raised doubts about their probative value. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's acquittal of the accused, finding no substantial and compelling reasons to interfere with the High Court's decision.

case_name: State of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Debasis Das & Ors.
text: Case: State of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Debasis Das & Ors.. Date: 1st September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the selection and appointment to the post of Assistant Investigator in the Bureau of Applied Economics and Statistics, which was delayed due to litigation and changes in recruitment rules. The High Court of Calcutta's order dated 11th February 2016 in W.P.S.T. No. 304 of 2010 was challenged, which pertained to the selection process for the post of Assistant Investigator and the applicability of amended recruitment rules. The Supreme Court directed the State of West Bengal to appoint the six affected candidates as Assistant Investigators within one month, based on the selection already conducted, while applying new rules to the remaining vacancies. The Supreme Court decided to appoint the six affected candidates in the interest of equity, justice, and fairness, considering the prolonged litigation and the fact that these candidates were initially selected before the rule changes. The court directed that the remaining vacancies should be filled under the new recruitment rules, following the appointment of the six affected candidates. No, the Supreme Court clarified that this direction was issued based on the peculiar facts of the case to do complete justice between the parties, and it should not be treated as a precedent for future cases.

case_name: State of West Bengal vs Rakesh Singh @ Rakesh Kumar Singh
text: Case: State of West Bengal vs Rakesh Singh @ Rakesh Kumar Singh. Date: 11th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Rakesh Singh should be granted bail despite being accused under Sections 21(b), 29, and 27A of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (NDPS Act) for allegedly financing illicit trafficking of cocaine and planting it in a vehicle to falsely implicate others. Rakesh Singh was accused of financing the procurement of 76 grams of cocaine and planting it in a vehicle occupied by Prabir Kumar De and Pamela Goswami, with the intention of falsely implicating them due to personal enmity. The High Court concluded that there was no prima facie evidence to support the charge under Section 27A of the NDPS Act against Rakesh Singh, as there was no continuous or regular activity of drug trafficking or financing illicit trafficking established. The High Court imposed stringent conditions for granting bail to Rakesh Singh, including furnishing a bond of Rs. 1,00,000 with four sureties, reporting to the police station once a week, not traveling outside West Bengal without court permission, and surrendering his passport. The prosecution argued that the absence of recovery of contraband from Rakesh Singh's possession did not absolve him of the charges, as the conspiracy involved planting the drugs in the vehicle occupied by others. The Supreme Court noted that the prosecution's story had changed significantly from the initial FIR to the charge-sheet, raising serious doubts about the veracity of the allegations against Rakesh Singh. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to grant bail to Rakesh Singh, agreeing that the case against him was not strong enough to deny bail, especially given the doubts about the prosecution's story. The Supreme Court observed that while Rakesh Singh had a history of criminal cases, none of them involved the NDPS Act, and his past record alone was not sufficient to deny him bail in this case. This judgment underscores the importance of a prima facie assessment of evidence and the veracity of prosecution claims when considering bail under the NDPS Act, especially in cases involving allegations of conspiracy and planting of contraband. Legal practitioners should focus on challenging the prosecution's evidence, especially if there are inconsistencies between the FIR and the charge-sheet, and emphasize the lack of direct recovery of contraband from the accused to strengthen the case for bail. If Rakesh Singh fails to adhere to the bail conditions, the prosecution can seek cancellation of his bail, and he may face additional legal consequences for violating court orders.

case_name: State through Central Bureau of Investigation vs Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava
text: Case: State through Central Bureau of Investigation vs Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava. Date: 4th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the charges framed against Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava under Section 120-B of the IPC and Sections 7, 12, and 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, were justified based on the evidence presented. Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava was charged under Section 120-B of the IPC and Sections 7, 12, and 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, for allegedly obtaining illegal gratification by corrupt means. The prosecution's case was that Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava, along with other officials, conducted an illegal raid at the premises of Dilip Aggarwal and Anand Aggarwal, and through a middleman, Hemant Gandhi, demanded and accepted a bribe of Rs. 60 lakhs. The CBI presented intercepted telephone conversations, witness testimonies, and details of the illegal raid, claiming that Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava was in regular contact with Hemant Gandhi, who acted as a middleman to negotiate and collect the bribe. The High Court quashed the charges against Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava, ruling that there was insufficient evidence to justify the framing of charges, leading to the appeal by the CBI. The Supreme Court found that the intercepted telephone conversations did not conclusively implicate Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava in the conspiracy to demand and accept illegal gratification, as the conversations were ambiguous and lacked direct evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision because the evidence presented by the prosecution, including the intercepted calls and witness statements, was not sufficient to establish a prima facie case against Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava. The Supreme Court highlighted that courts must apply their minds to the entire record and documents placed before them to ensure that a prima facie case is made out before framing charges, and should not conduct a mini-trial at the stage of framing charges. The Supreme Court concluded that there was no material evidence on record to prove Dr. Anup Kumar Srivastava's involvement in the conspiracy, as the intercepted calls were ambiguous and the witness statements were retracted, leading to his acquittal. The ruling may lead to more stringent scrutiny of intercepted communications in corruption cases, emphasizing the need for clear and direct evidence to establish a prima facie case. The decision underscores that circumstantial evidence must be compelling and unambiguous to support criminal charges, ensuring that the rights of the accused are protected against insufficient or ambiguous evidence.

case_name: Station House Officer, CBI/ACB/Bangalore vs B.A. Srinivasan and Anr.
text: Case: Station House Officer, CBI/ACB/Bangalore vs B.A. Srinivasan and Anr.. Date: 5th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main allegations against B.A. Srinivasan included entering into a criminal conspiracy to cheat and defraud Vijaya Bank by sanctioning and disbursing loans based on fake and fabricated documents, violating the bank's rules and regulations, and causing wrongful loss to the bank and corresponding gains to others. The High Court allowed the Criminal Revision Petition filed by B.A. Srinivasan, discharging him of the offences punishable under Sections 419, 420, 467, 468, 471 read with Section 120B of the IPC and Sections 13(1)(d) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The trial court rejected the discharge application filed by B.A. Srinivasan, stating that there were sufficient materials against him for framing charges for the offences punishable under Sections 120B, 420, 471 IPC and under Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The Supreme Court observed that no sanction was necessary under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act if the public servant had retired at the time of cognizance. It also noted that protection under Section 197 of the Code is available only when the act complained of is integrally connected with the discharge of official duty. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court's reasoning, stating that the protection available to a public servant while in service does not extend post-retirement, and the High Court erred in granting discharge based on the lack of sanction. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, restored the trial court's order, and dismissed the discharge application filed by B.A. Srinivasan, directing the case to proceed in accordance with the law.

case_name: Subharti Medical College vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Subharti Medical College vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 8th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the petitioner's application for enhancing MBBS seats from 100 to 150, which was denied by the Medical Council of India (MCI) due to deficiencies noted during an inspection. The MCI inspection report noted several deficiencies, including 55.27% bed occupancy, a shortage of residents by 5.81%, inflated data of clinical material and casualty attendance, and issues with nursing stations and ward visibility. The Competent Authority debarred Subharti Medical College from admitting students for two academic years (2017-18 and 2018-19) and authorized the MCI to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crore. The Supreme Court directed the MCI to send an inspection team within three months to verify the deficiencies, allow the college to rectify any issues, and submit a report to the Competent Authority for further action. The bank guarantee was to be kept alive until a final decision was made. The Supreme Court disposed of the writ petition, allowing the proposal for enhanced seats to be considered for the academic session 2018-19, with inspection and compliance to be verified by the MCI.

case_name: Subhash Kumar vs The State of Bihar & Ors.
text: Case: Subhash Kumar vs The State of Bihar & Ors.. Date: 17th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the relegation of Subhash Kumar from the Bihar Administrative Service to the Bihar Education Service without affording him an opportunity of hearing. The writ petition was filed after Subhash Kumar was relegated to the Bihar Education Service following an order dated 23rd October 2019 by the Supreme Court, which he claimed was done without an opportunity of hearing and in violation of natural justice. The High Court held that an error was committed by the Commission in the evaluation of Baldeo Choudhary's answer script for Paper-II General Studies, which affected his placement in the select list. The Division Bench ruled that while Baldeo Choudhary should be placed in the select list, he would not be entitled to retrospective benefits and would take seniority from the date of his appointment. The Supreme Court clarified that Baldeo Choudhary should be considered qualified for appointment from the date of the Division Bench's judgement, i.e., 29th November 2012, with notional benefits of service but without salary for the intervening period. The Commission revised the recommendations of the 45th Combined Competitive Examination, placing Baldeo Choudhary at Sl. No. 2 and displacing Subhash Kumar from the Bihar Administrative Service to the Bihar Education Service. Subhash Kumar alleged that the order relegating him to the Bihar Education Service was passed without affording him an opportunity of hearing, violating the principles of natural justice. The decision might set a precedent ensuring that any future revisions of select lists must afford affected individuals an opportunity of hearing to avoid violations of natural justice. The State Government could establish clearer procedural guidelines that ensure all affected parties are heard before making any revisions to appointments or reassignments, thus upholding the principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court ruled out the Commission's apprehension because it clarified that Baldeo Choudhary's case was sui generis and his placement should not disturb the existing select list or the appointments made based on it. The Supreme Court quashed the order relegating Subhash Kumar to the Bihar Education Service, finding it unjustified and in violation of natural justice principles.

case_name: Subhash Sahebrao Deshmukh vs. Satish Atmaram Talekar and Others
text: Case: Subhash Sahebrao Deshmukh vs. Satish Atmaram Talekar and Others. Date: 18th June 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the dismissal of a complaint under Section 203 of the Cr.P.C. and the subsequent revision application that restored the complaint. The High Court refused to interfere because it held that no opportunity of hearing was required under Section 398 Cr.P.C. if the direction for further inquiry was being passed after dismissal of the complaint as opposed to a discharge. The complainant, Satish Atmaram Talekar, filed a complaint under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. alleging offences under Sections 420, 467, 468, 120-B, 114, and 34 of the IPC. The police report submitted under Section 173(2) stated that the allegations made in the complaint were false. The protest petition was registered as a complaint case, but the Magistrate, after hearing the respondent, dismissed the complaint under Section 203 Cr.P.C. The Additional Sessions Judge set aside the dismissal order of the Magistrate and directed further inquiry by the Magistrate. The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in Manharibhai Muljibhai Kakadia and another vs. Shaileshbhai Mohanbhai Patel and others, which held that the accused or a person suspected of committing the crime is entitled to a hearing by the Revisional Court. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned orders dated 6th March 2009 and 8th October 2007, and remanded the matter to the Additional Sessions Judge for fresh hearing after notice to the appellant. The Supreme Court directed the Additional Sessions Judge to hear the revision application afresh, provide notice to the appellant, and pass a fresh reasoned and speaking order. The decision in B. Chandrika vs. Santhosh established that a Magistrate has the power to take cognizance of an offense on a complaint or a protest petition even after accepting the final report, and the protest petition must satisfy the ingredients of a complaint before the Magistrate takes cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) CrPC.

case_name: Subhransu Sarkar vs Indrani Sarkar (Nee Das)
text: Case: Subhransu Sarkar vs Indrani Sarkar (Nee Das). Date: 14th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Subhransu Sarkar was entitled to a divorce on the grounds of cruelty and desertion by Indrani Sarkar. Subhransu Sarkar alleged that Indrani Sarkar insisted on living separately from his parents, misbehaved with her in-laws, frequently left the matrimonial home, and physically assaulted him during holidays. Both the Trial Court and the High Court dismissed Subhransu Sarkar's petition for divorce, holding that he could not prove cruelty by Indrani Sarkar. The Supreme Court concluded that the marriage was emotionally dead and there was no point in persuading them to live together any longer. Therefore, it exercised its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India to dissolve the marriage. The Supreme Court directed Subhransu Sarkar to pay an amount of Rs. 25 Lakhs to Indrani Sarkar within a period of eight weeks. This payment was in full and final settlement of all claims. The Supreme Court noted that Indrani Sarkar insisted on continuing the marriage despite living separately for over 16 years and no meaningful effort for reconciliation. However, the Court found the marriage to be irretrievably broken down. The Amicus Curiae, Mr. Ranjan Mukherjee, was appointed to assist the Court on behalf of Indrani Sarkar, as she did not engage an advocate. He informed the Court that she intended to continue living with Subhransu Sarkar but failed to convince the Court due to the unworkable nature of the marriage.

case_name: Sudarsana Rao Gadde vs. Karuna Gadde
text: Case: Sudarsana Rao Gadde vs. Karuna Gadde. Date: 20th February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary dispute revolved around matrimonial issues, including the custody of their minor child Ayush, leading to prolonged litigation. The parties agreed to dissolve their marriage by mutual consent under Section 10A of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, and resolved issues related to visitation and custody rights for their child. The Supreme Court disposed of all pending litigations between the parties in terms of their settlement dated 1st August 2017 and restrained them from filing fresh cases related to the dispute without the Court's permission. The settlement is expected to ensure a peaceful resolution of all matrimonial disputes, including custody matters, and prevent further legal conflicts between the parties. The Supreme Court clarified that all pending cases between the parties, including those in the Family Court at Rangareddy District, were disposed of as per the settlement agreement.

case_name: Sudesh Kedia vs. Union of India
text: Case: Sudesh Kedia vs. Union of India. Date: 9th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sudesh Kedia was charged with offences under Sections 120B/414/384/386/387 of the IPC, Sections 17/18/21 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, Sections 25(1B)(a)/26/35 of the Arms Act, and Section 17(1)(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. The main allegation against Sudesh Kedia was that he was part of a terrorist gang, the Tritiya Prastuti Committee (TPC), and was involved in extorting money from coal traders, transporters, and contractors, and that he had paid a levy to ensure the smooth functioning of his business. Sudesh Kedia's bail application was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner-cum-Special Judge NIA at Ranchi on 14th February 2020, and his criminal appeal was subsequently dismissed by the High Court, upholding the lower court's order. The prosecution argued that Sudesh Kedia was providing financial support to the TPC, a terrorist organization, and that there was sufficient material on record to show his involvement in terror funding and his constant contact with the organization's members. Sudesh Kedia's defense was that he paid the levy under duress to ensure the smooth functioning of his business, and that he was not a member of the TPC or involved in terror funding. He claimed that the payments were made to avoid harm and were not intended to support terrorist activities. The Supreme Court concluded that the main accusation against Sudesh Kedia was payment of extortion money, which does not amount to terror funding. The Court found that there was no prima facie case that he conspired with the TPC to promote their activities, and thus granted him bail. The Supreme Court directed that Sudesh Kedia be released on bail subject to the satisfaction of the Special Court, and clarified that the findings were restricted to the bail application and should not influence the trial court during the trial.

case_name: Sudha Singh vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Sudha Singh vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 23rd April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was the challenge to the bail granted by the Allahabad High Court to an accused involved in serious crimes under the U.P. Gangster and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986. The appellant is Sudha Singh, the wife of the deceased victim Rajnarain Singh, who was allegedly murdered by the accused in conspiracy with others. The main grounds for the appeal were the accused's history of serious crimes, potential threat to witnesses, and the likelihood of the accused repeating his criminal activities if released on bail. The Supreme Court of India set aside the Allahabad High Court's order granting bail to the accused, emphasizing the need to consider the potential threat to witnesses and the community. Key precedents cited included Neeru Yadav vs. State of U.P., Ash Mohammad vs. Shiv Raj Singh, and Prasanta Kumar Sarkar vs. Ashis Chatterjee and Another, which stressed the importance of scrutinizing the accused's criminal antecedents and the potential impact on society.

case_name: Sudhamayee Pattnaik and Others vs. Bibhu Prasad Sahoo and Others
text: Case: Sudhamayee Pattnaik and Others vs. Bibhu Prasad Sahoo and Others. Date: 16th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the subsequent purchasers of the disputed land could be impleaded as defendants in the suit against the wish of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration, permanent injunction, and recovery of possession of the disputed land. The original defendants filed the application to implead subsequent purchasers of the disputed land as party defendants, alleging that the plaintiffs had unlawfully alienated parcels of the land during the pendency of the suit. The trial court allowed the application and directed the impleadment of the subsequent purchasers as defendants to prevent multiplicity of litigation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and confirmed the trial court's order allowing the application under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of both the trial court and the High Court, ruling that subsequent purchasers could not be impleaded as party defendants against the wish of the plaintiffs. However, the Court noted that any risk of not impleading them would be borne by the plaintiffs.
