case_name: Sudhir Kumar @ S. Baliyan vs. Vinay Kumar G.B.
text: Case: Sudhir Kumar @ S. Baliyan vs. Vinay Kumar G.B.. Date: 15th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellant, Sudhir Kumar @ S. Baliyan, should be allowed to file additional documents in a commercial suit for a permanent injunction against the respondent for using the trademarks 'INSIGHT', 'INSIGHT ACADEMY', 'INSIGHT IAS ACADEMY', and 'INSIGHT PUBLICATIONS'. The Commercial Court dismissed the appellant's application to file additional documents under Order VII Rule 14 (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), which was confirmed by the High Court of Delhi. The appellant's counsel argued that the documents were necessary for the just decision of the suit and that the appellant should have been allowed to produce the documents since they were discovered after filing the suit. It was also argued that the application to file additional documents was submitted within 10 days of filing the suit. The Supreme Court observed that Order XI Rule 1, as applicable to commercial suits, mandates the plaintiff to disclose all documents in their power, possession, control, or custody along with the plaint. However, the court noted that additional documents can be allowed with the court's leave if a reasonable cause for non-disclosure at the time of filing is established. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, granting the appellant leave to produce and rely on the invoices mentioned in the application as additional documents, but denied leave to rely on other additional documents that were not produced due to being voluminous. The Supreme Court permitted the appellant to produce and rely on the invoices as additional documents, noting that their non-disclosure at the time of filing was adequately explained.

text: Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. Neeraj Kumar Jain & Ors.. Date: 9th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellant was challenging the award passed by the Lok Adalat before the High Court, where Original Suit No. 68 of 2010 had been compromised between the parties. The appellant argued that he was neither a party to the suit nor to the settlement. The High Court was not inclined to interfere with the award on the ground that the appellant was not an aggrieved party. The core issue regarding the settlement as per the Lok Adalat dated 2nd September 2013 is now pending before the High Court in Misc. Petition (C) No. 497 of 2018, in which both sides are parties. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment dated 11th March 2015 and remitted the matter to the High Court to be taken along with Misc. Petition (C) No. 497 of 2018.

case_name: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. State of Rajasthan
text: Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. State of Rajasthan. Date: 31st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Sudhir Kumar Jain was rightly convicted under Section 302 IPC and Section 3 read with 25 of the Arms Act for the murder of Rajendra Sahu. Rajendra Sahu was shot by an occupant of a Maruti 800 car on 17th April 2003 near Baheti Hospital, resulting in injuries above his navel. He later succumbed to these injuries. The High Court affirmed the conviction based on the dying declaration of Rajendra Sahu, the testimony of a constable who was with the accused, and the recovery of a country-made pistol from the accused. The Supreme Court found serious doubts due to all eyewitnesses turning hostile, inconsistencies in the testimony of the constable, delay in recording his statement, and the recovery of a non-functional country-made pistol. The dying declaration was significant but it did not name the assailants or identify the occupants of the car, which weakened the prosecution's case. The ballistic expert's report indicated that the recovered pistol was not in a serviceable condition, casting further doubt on its use in the crime and undermining the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of Sudhir Kumar Jain under Section 302 IPC and Section 3/25 of the Arms Act, acquitting him of the charges due to lack of reliable evidence.

case_name: Sukhpal Singh vs. State of Punjab
text: Case: Sukhpal Singh vs. State of Punjab. Date: 12th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sukhpal Singh was charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC for committing murder and under Section 201 of the IPC for causing the disappearance of evidence. The trial court convicted Sukhpal Singh under Section 302 of the IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The co-accused was acquitted. The prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory, recovery of the weapon (a .38 caliber gun), and forensic evidence linking the bullet found in the deceased's body to the gun recovered from Sukhpal Singh. The defense argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence and lacked direct evidence. Sukhpal Singh claimed he was falsely implicated, and there was no motive for him to commit the murder. He also stated that he had been suspended and had surrendered his revolver before the incident. The High Court dismissed Sukhpal Singh's appeal and upheld the conviction and life sentence imposed by the trial court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and life sentence. The Court found that the circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory, recovery of the weapon, and forensic evidence, formed a complete chain pointing to Sukhpal Singh's guilt. The Supreme Court stated that while establishing a motive strengthens the prosecution's case, the absence of a motive is not necessarily fatal in circumstantial evidence cases if other circumstantial evidence sufficiently points to the accused's guilt.

case_name: Sultan vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Sultan vs The State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 3rd August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Sultan and Noori were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Khushboo. The trial court based their conviction on the dying declaration of Khushboo, which stated that Sultan and Noori, along with Rukhsana, had poured kerosene oil on her and set her on fire. The High Court upheld the conviction by relying on the dying declaration, Exhibit Ka-3, recorded by Satish Kumar Kushwaha (PW-5), which implicated Sultan and Noori in the murder of Khushboo. The defense argued that there were several gaps and contradictions in the dying declaration, and that Sultan and Noori were residing separately from Khushboo at the time of the incident. The Supreme Court observed that there were several gaps and contradictions in the dying declaration, raising doubts about its veracity and correctness, particularly as it implicated Sultan and Noori. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction of Sultan and Noori under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, giving them the benefit of doubt, and directed their immediate release unless required to be detained in any other case. Rukhsana, the mother-in-law of Khushboo, was also implicated in the dying declaration but did not file an appeal. She was already released due to her old age and the Supreme Court did not examine her conviction.

case_name: Sumedh Singh Saini vs. State of Punjab and another
text: Case: Sumedh Singh Saini vs. State of Punjab and another. Date: 3rd December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Sumedh Singh Saini should be granted anticipatory bail in connection with FIR No. 77 dated 6th May 2020, which included charges under Section 302 IPC. The initial charges against Sumedh Singh Saini in FIR No. 77 included offences under Sections 364, 201, 344, 330, 219, and 120-B of the IPC. The FIR was lodged by Palwinder Singh Multani, brother of the deceased Balwant Singh Multani. The main allegation was that Balwant Singh Multani was illegally abducted, tortured, and killed while in custody by officials acting under the instructions of Sumedh Singh Saini. The Additional Sessions Judge, Mohali, initially granted anticipatory bail to Sumedh Singh Saini for the charges excluding Section 302 IPC. However, upon the addition of Section 302 IPC, his subsequent application for anticipatory bail was dismissed. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed Sumedh Singh Saini's anticipatory bail application for the added charge under Section 302 IPC. Sumedh Singh Saini's defense argued that the FIR was filed with malafide intentions, delayed by 29 years, and was politically motivated. They also contended that the FIR should be quashed as it was based on the same facts as an earlier quashed FIR and lacked jurisdiction. The Supreme Court granted anticipatory bail to Sumedh Singh Saini for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC, considering the delay of 29 years in lodging the FIR and the appellant's cooperation with the investigation.

The Additional Sessions Judge, Mohali, initially granted anticipatory bail to Sumedh Singh Saini for the charges excluding Section 302 IPC. However, upon the addition of Section 302 IPC, his subsequent application for anticipatory bail was dismissed.
The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed Sumedh Singh Saini's anticipatory bail application for the added charge under Section 302 IPC.

Sumedh Singh Saini's defense argued that the FIR was filed with malafide intentions, delayed by 29 years, and was politically motivated. They also contended that the FIR should be quashed as it was based on the same facts as an earlier quashed FIR and lacked jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court granted anticipatory bail to Sumedh Singh Saini for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC, considering the delay of 29 years in lodging the FIR and the appellant's cooperation with the investigation.

case_name: Sumeti Vij vs M/S Paramount Tech Fab Industries
text: Case: Sumeti Vij vs M/S Paramount Tech Fab Industries. Date: 9th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Sumeti Vij, the appellant, was guilty of an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, for issuing cheques that were dishonoured due to insufficient funds. Sumeti Vij purchased non-woven fabric from Paramount Tech Fab Industries and issued two cheques for the amounts Rs.5,07,062 and Rs.5,10,000. These cheques were dishonoured upon presentation due to insufficient funds. The trial court found that the complainant failed to establish that the goods were delivered to Sumeti Vij, and thus, the court acquitted her. The High Court found that the primary burden was discharged by the complainant to prove that the cheques were issued in lieu of material supplied and thus held Sumeti Vij guilty under Section 138 of the Act. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's judgement, noting that Sumeti Vij did not rebut the presumption that the cheques were issued for consideration. The appellant argued that the complainant had the burden to prove the delivery of goods, and merely issuing cheques did not suffice to prove a legally enforceable debt or liability. The Supreme Court noted that proceedings under Section 138 are quasi-criminal in nature and that the burden of proof on the accused is to rebut the presumption by a preponderance of probabilities. The Supreme Court suggested that the standard of proof for the accused to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the Act is 'preponderance of probabilities' and not 'beyond reasonable doubt'. If the appellant decided to make the payment of the stated cheque amount, it could potentially lead to the resolution of the dispute. However, the appellant chose to argue the case on merits. The Supreme Court concluded that the appeals were without substance and dismissed them, upholding the High Court's decision of conviction and directing the appellant to pay the fine or serve the sentence.

case_name: Sumitha Pradeep vs. Arun Kumar C.K & Anr.
text: Case: Sumitha Pradeep vs. Arun Kumar C.K & Anr.. Date: 21st October 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Arun Kumar C.K was alleged to have sexually assaulted his 12-year-old niece by asking her to sit on his lap, hugging her, kissing her cheeks, attempting to kiss her on the lips, and making lewd comments. Arun Kumar C.K was charged under Sections 354A(1)(i),(ii) & (iv), 354A(2), and 354A(3) of the IPC, and Sections 7, 8, 9, and 11 of the POCSO Act. The High Court of Kerala granted anticipatory bail to Arun Kumar C.K with conditions such as appearing before the Investigating Officer for interrogation and not intimidating witnesses. Sumitha Pradeep, the mother of the victim, approached the Supreme Court aggrieved by the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail to Arun Kumar C.K. The Special Judge noted that the victim's statements and the case diary provided sufficient reasons to suspect that the sexual abuse occurred, emphasizing the relationship between the victim and the accused and the trauma faced by the victim. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in granting anticipatory bail as it overlooked the specific allegations and the trauma faced by the victim, thus allowing the Investigating Officer to proceed further in accordance with the law. The incident traumatized the victim to an extent that she slumped in her academic performance, and despite counseling sessions, she initially did not disclose the incident due to fear. The Supreme Court noted that the delay in reporting the crime was justified as the victim was traumatized and fearful, and mere delay in reporting sexual assault on a minor should not discredit the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court emphasized that the need for custodial interrogation should be considered alongside other factors, and even if not required, it should not automatically justify granting anticipatory bail. The Supreme Court highlighted that Section 29 of the POCSO Act mandates a presumption of the commission of the offenses by the accused unless proven otherwise, which should be considered while deciding bail applications.

case_name: Sunil Kumar Gupta and Others vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Others
text: Case: Sunil Kumar Gupta and Others vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Others. Date: 27th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main charges were under Section 302 IPC for the murder of Shilpa, who was allegedly set ablaze by her in-laws due to dowry demands. The trial court issued summons to the appellants under Section 302 IPC based on the evidence presented, including the dying declaration of Shilpa and witness testimonies. The High Court dismissed the revision petition, upholding the trial court's order to summon the appellants for trial under Section 302 IPC. The appellants argued that their names were mentioned in the FIR but were later exonerated by the Investigating Officer in the charge sheet. They contended that the evidence was not strong enough to summon them for trial under Section 302 IPC. The Supreme Court found that the evidence, including the dying declaration, did not strongly implicate the appellants. The Court noted that the prosecution failed to present specific and strong evidence against them, making the summoning under Section 302 IPC unjustified. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and the trial court's decision to summon the appellants under Section 302 IPC, finding that there was no prima facie case against them.

case_name: Sunil Kumar Rai & Ors. vs The State of Bihar & Ors.
text: Case: Sunil Kumar Rai & Ors. vs The State of Bihar & Ors.. Date: 21st February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the constitutional validity of the Bihar government's notification granting Scheduled Tribe status to the Lohar community, which was challenged as unconstitutional and contrary to prior Supreme Court judgments. The petitioners sought the quashing of the Bihar government's notification dated 23rd August 2016 and compensation for alleged wrongful imprisonment and other adverse effects resulting from the notification. The challenge was based on the argument that prior Supreme Court judgments had explicitly excluded Lohars from Scheduled Tribe status, classifying them as Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The Supreme Court found the notification to be unconstitutional and arbitrary, highlighting that the state government ignored authoritative judicial rulings and the English version of the relevant laws. The Supreme Court awarded Rs. 5,00,000 as costs to the petitioners, acknowledging the harm caused by the unconstitutional notification. The Court emphasized the importance of adherence to judicial decisions and statutory provisions, ensuring that state actions do not conflict with established constitutional principles. The Supreme Court clarified that while the Lohara community is recognized as a Scheduled Tribe, the Lohar community is classified as an OBC and cannot be equated with Loharas. Prior judgments were pivotal, as they consistently ruled that the Lohar community is not a Scheduled Tribe, creating a binding precedent for the Court's decision. The judgment restricts the misuse of the 1989 Act by ensuring that only legitimately recognized Scheduled Tribes can invoke its provisions. The decision underscores the need for states to ensure compliance with constitutional provisions and judicial rulings before issuing notifications affecting Scheduled Tribe classifications. The judgment reinforced the principle that arbitrary and unconstitutional government actions cannot override established legal and judicial frameworks.

case_name: Sunil Kumar vs. State of U.P. & Anr.
text: Case: Sunil Kumar vs. State of U.P. & Anr.. Date: 3rd August 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the proceedings against Sunil Kumar, initiated based on a complaint by a co-worker, should be quashed due to the trivial nature of the allegations and the lack of progress in the case since 2015. On 11th September 2014, an altercation occurred between Sunil Kumar, an Assistant Engineer, and the respondent no. 2, a Peon, in the office regarding the distribution of some articles to a consumer, resulting in mutual abuse and threats. The respondent no. 2 alleged that Sunil Kumar had assaulted, abused, and threatened to kill him during the altercation on 11th September 2014. Sunil Kumar sought to quash the chargesheet and proceedings on the grounds that the allegations were trivial and the case had been pending without progress since 2015, causing undue harassment. The Supreme Court quashed the proceedings against Sunil Kumar, stating that continuing the case would amount to persecution and harassment over a petty office incident that should have been resolved amicably on the day it occurred. The Supreme Court noted the trivial nature of the allegations, the long delay in the trial, and the lack of any substantial progress in the case since the chargesheet was filed in 2015, justifying the quashing of proceedings to prevent undue harassment.

case_name: Sunil Kumar vs. The State of Bihar
text: Case: Sunil Kumar vs. The State of Bihar. Date: 25th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The accused, Ramawatar Bhagat and others, were charged with assaulting and killing Shardanand Bhagat, leading to charges under Sections 147, 148, 149, 341, 323, 324, 427, 504, 506, 307, and 302 IPC, and Section 27 of the Arms Act. The FIR was lodged by the appellant, who is the younger brother of the deceased, Shardanand Bhagat. On the day of the incident, the accused, armed with lethal weapons, went to the bamboo clumps of the informant and started cutting bamboos. When Shardanand Bhagat intervened, he was ordered to be killed by Ramawatar Bhagat and subsequently shot by Manish Kumar. Shardanand Bhagat succumbed to the bullet injuries during treatment at the hospital. The Sessions Court rejected the bail application of Ramawatar Bhagat, citing the gravity of the offence and his active participation in the crime. The High Court granted bail to Ramawatar Bhagat, stating that considering the rival submissions and the facts and circumstances of the case, it was inclined to accept the submissions of the petitioner's counsel. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision because it did not provide sufficient reasoning for granting bail, did not consider the gravity of the offence, and failed to account for the accused's criminal antecedents. The Supreme Court emphasized that courts must apply judicial mind and record brief reasons for granting bail, considering factors such as the seriousness of the offence, the accused's antecedents, and the potential impact on witnesses. The Supreme Court directed Ramawatar Bhagat to surrender before the concerned jail authority or the concerned Court forthwith. Ramawatar Bhagat was previously involved in a double murder case, having killed the informant's father and younger brother, with ongoing trials at the evidence stage. The Supreme Court addressed the issue of the High Court not considering the relevant factors and criminal antecedents of the accused while granting bail, leading to an unsustainable decision.

case_name: Sunil Samdaria vs Union of India
text: Case: Sunil Samdaria vs Union of India. Date: 23rd February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The writ petition was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. The respondents were the Union of India through its Secretary, Ministry of Law and Justice, and others. The petitioner challenged the appointments on the grounds that the tenure of the appointments was less than two years, which he argued was a violation of Article 224 of the Constitution of India. The petitioner relied on the Constitution Bench judgement in S.P. Gupta vs. Union of India and another, 1981 Supp SCC 87. The petitioner argued that since the appointed judges had retired from Judicial Service before their appointment, they were not eligible for appointment as Additional Judges of the High Court. The Union of India argued that the appointed judges had held judicial office for at least 10 years and were therefore eligible for appointment under Article 217(2) and Article 224 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court held that appointing judges for less than two years when they are to retire before completing two years is not contrary to Article 224. No, the Supreme Court did not find any merit in the petitioner's submission regarding the tenure of the appointments. The Supreme Court emphasized the necessity of timely appointments to High Courts to cope with the increased workload and to fulfill the object of Article 224(1) of the Constitution. It can be predicted that the process of appointing judges will need more expedition and timely action to prevent delays and ensure efficient judicial administration. The Supreme Court clarified that the term 'held' in Article 217(2)(a) indicates that a person must have held a judicial office for at least 10 years, but it does not require that the person be holding the office at the time of appointment.

case_name: Sunil Todi & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat & Anr.
text: Case: Sunil Todi & Ors. vs. State of Gujarat & Anr.. Date: 3rd December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the cheques issued by the appellants were for a legally enforceable debt or liability under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, given that the cheques were allegedly issued as security. The appellants filed petitions under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the criminal complaint instituted by the second respondent for offences punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The cheques were issued as security for payment under a Power Supply Agreement (PSA) between the appellants' company, R.L. Steels & Energy Limited, and the second respondent for providing uninterrupted power supply at the company's plant. The complaint was initially dismissed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), but the High Court later quashed this order and directed the CJM to reconsider the application filed by the second respondent under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court of Gujarat dismissed the petitions under Section 482 CrPC, stating that the issues pertaining to the issuance of cheques, non-payment of electricity charges, and issuance of Letters of Credit (LCs) were questions of fact to be decided by the trial court. The Supreme Court held that the cheques issued by the appellants were for a legally enforceable debt or liability, as the power supply had been provided by the second respondent and the payments were due under the PSA, despite the cheques being initially labeled as security. The Supreme Court concluded that the Magistrate was required to conduct an inquiry under Section 202 CrPC before issuing process, as the appellants were residing outside the jurisdiction of the Magistrate's court. However, the Court found that the absence of such an inquiry did not invalidate the proceedings. The Supreme Court directed the Trial Court to proceed with the trial, taking into consideration the appellants' arguments during the trial process, and ensuring that the appellants' health conditions and other relevant factors were appropriately considered. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision to allow the criminal complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act to proceed, and directed the trial to continue in accordance with the law. The PSA was significant as it outlined the terms of payment and security for the power supply provided by the second respondent to the appellants' company, R.L. Steels & Energy Limited. The PSA required payments to be made through Letters of Credit, and the cheques issued were initially intended as security for these payments.

case_name: Sunita Devi & Anr. vs The State of Haryana
text: Case: Sunita Devi & Anr. vs The State of Haryana. Date: 2nd December 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellants, Sunita Devi and another, should be granted anticipatory bail in connection with cheating allegations related to land transactions. The allegations against Sunita Devi and the other appellant primarily related to cheating in connection with certain land-related transactions. The High Court refused pre-arrest bail to the appellants on the grounds that they did not meet the necessary criteria for bail at that stage of the investigation. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and granted anticipatory bail to the appellants, stating that custodial interrogation was not necessary as they had cooperated with the investigation. The Supreme Court directed that the appellants be enlarged on bail on such terms as the concerned court may consider fit and proper. The Supreme Court noted that the appellants had joined the investigation and there were no allegations of their non-cooperation at that stage. The Supreme Court allowed the State to apply for the cancellation of bail before the Trial Court if the appellants refuse to cooperate with the investigating agency at any subsequent stage. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's orders, and granted anticipatory bail to the appellants. The Supreme Court directed that any pending applications related to the case also stand disposed of with the granting of anticipatory bail. The significance of the appellants joining the investigation was that it demonstrated their willingness to cooperate, which was a key factor in the Supreme Court's decision to grant anticipatory bail.

text: Case: Superintending Engineer/Dehar Power House Circle Bhakra Beas Management Board (PW) Slapper & Another vs. Excise and Taxation Officer, Sunder Nagar/Assessing Authority. Date: 25th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court, while exercising revisional power under Section 48 of the Himachal Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2005, could condone the delay in filing a revision beyond 90 days. The High Court refused to condone the delay, stating that the provisions of Section 5 of the Limitation Act do not apply to revisions filed under Section 48 of the Himachal Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2005. The Supreme Court examined Section 48 of the Himachal Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2005, and Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963, to determine if the provisions of the Limitation Act were excluded by the special law. The Supreme Court concluded that the provisions of the Limitation Act, including Section 5, were not expressly excluded by the Himachal Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2005, and thus, Section 5 of the Limitation Act could apply. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, holding that the High Court had the power to condone the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, and remanded the case back to the High Court for consideration on merits.

text: Case: Supertech Limited vs Emerald Court Owner Resident Welfare Association. Date: 31st August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the legality of the construction of two towers (T-16 and T-17) in the Emerald Court project, and whether the construction violated building regulations and the rights of existing flat owners. The Allahabad High Court directed the demolition of Towers T-16 and T-17 constructed by Supertech Limited, citing violations of building regulations and the rights of existing flat owners. The main violations included non-compliance with the National Building Code (NBC) and the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) building regulations, specifically regarding the distance between buildings and fire safety norms. The Supreme Court concluded that the construction of T-16 and T-17 reduced the undivided interest of the existing flat owners in the common areas, and their consent was not sought, violating the UP Apartments Act 2010. NOIDA was found to have colluded with Supertech Limited by approving the revised building plans and not ensuring compliance with the building regulations and the UP Apartments Act 2010. The court ordered Supertech Limited to refund the amounts invested by the flat owners in Towers T-16 and T-17 with 14% interest compounded annually. The Supreme Court found clear evidence of collusion between Supertech Limited and NOIDA, which facilitated the unauthorized construction of Towers T-16 and T-17.

case_name: Surajdeo Mahto and Anr. vs The State of Bihar
text: Case: Surajdeo Mahto and Anr. vs The State of Bihar. Date: 4th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case addressed the challenge to the conviction and sentence of Surajdeo Mahto and Prakash Mahto for the murder of Arun under sections 302 read with section 34 and section 120-B of the IPC. The prosecution's case was that on 5th April 1987, Surajdeo Mahto and Raj Kumar lured Arun to watch a cinema and later Arun was found dead in a reservoir near Kakolat on 11th April 1987. The High Court at Patna upheld the conviction and sentence of Surajdeo Mahto and Prakash Mahto for the murder of Arun. Surajdeo Mahto and Prakash Mahto were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 34 of the IPC, section 120-B of the IPC, and Surajdeo Mahto was additionally charged under section 364 of the IPC. The conviction relied heavily on circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory and the testimonies of various witnesses who corroborated the prosecution's case. The motive attributed to Surajdeo Mahto was that Arun was allegedly having an illicit affair with Surajdeo's sister, which led to strained relations between the families. At the crime scene, an iron dagger, two lungis, one pair of slippers, a handkerchief, a knife, and a plastic jerrycan were found near the dead body. The defence argued that the case was based solely on circumstantial evidence, and there were no independent witnesses; they also raised doubts about the reliability of prosecution witnesses. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Surajdeo Mahto but found that the case against Prakash Mahto was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, giving him the benefit of doubt. The Supreme Court considered whether the circumstantial evidence was so impeachable that it established the guilt of the appellants beyond any reasonable doubt. Yes, Surajdeo Mahto raised the plea that he was a juvenile at the time of the incident, but the court found discrepancies in the documents provided to support this claim.

case_name: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India
text: Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India. Date: 29th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court exercised its contempt jurisdiction to maintain the dignity of judicial forums and to address the persistent and inappropriate conduct of the petitioner, Mr. Rajiv Daiya, who sought to justify his existence by making disparaging statements against the judiciary. The original judgment found the litigation initiated by Suraz India Trust to be thoughtless and frivolous. It barred the Trust and its Chairman, Mr. Rajiv Daiya, from filing any public interest petitions in any court and imposed exemplary costs of Rs. 25 lakhs on Mr. Daiya. Mr. Rajiv Daiya sent disparaging communications to the residential offices of Hon'ble Judges, made representations to the President and Prime Minister, and continued to file frivolous petitions despite being barred. He also failed to deposit the imposed costs and attempted to scandalize the court through various communications. The Supreme Court issued notices and directed the Registry to proceed as per law for the recovery of costs. When Mr. Daiya continued to evade and scandalize the court, bailable warrants were issued for his production. The Supreme Court found Mr. Daiya's apology insincere and noted that he continued to make allegations against the judiciary. The Court closed Miscellaneous Application No.1630/2020 by directing the State Government to commence the process of recovering costs as 'arrears of land revenue'. The Supreme Court emphasized that filing public interest litigations is not a birthright and criticized Mr. Daiya for using such petitions as a means to scandalize the court and evade accountability. The Court reaffirmed its earlier order barring the Trust and Mr. Daiya from filing public interest petitions. The decision implies that Mr. Rajiv Daiya and Suraz India Trust are barred from filing public interest petitions and must face the consequences of their actions, including the recovery of imposed costs. The Court's decision underscores the importance of maintaining the dignity of the judiciary and holding litigants accountable for frivolous and scandalous conduct. The Supreme Court observed that persistent contemptuous conduct by litigants must be addressed to uphold the dignity and majesty of the law. The Court emphasized that it is the duty of judges to perform their tasks for the larger good of the institution, even when faced with challenging and scandalous behavior from litigants like Mr. Rajiv Daiya.

case_name: Surender Kumar Gupta & Ors. vs. J.M. Housing Limited & Ors.
text: Case: Surender Kumar Gupta & Ors. vs. J.M. Housing Limited & Ors.. Date: 26th February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the ex-parte order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) was valid and whether the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) was correct in setting aside the order on the grounds of violation of natural justice. The NCLT passed an ex-parte order based on a petition filed by the appellants under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, complaining of oppression and mismanagement. The respondents approached the NCLAT instead of moving the NCLT for vacating or modifying the ad-interim order passed by the NCLT. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's ex-parte order on the grounds that it was passed without providing an opportunity for the respondents to be heard, which violated the principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court held that the NCLAT was incorrect in concluding that the NCLT's ex-parte order should be set aside solely because it was passed without hearing the respondents, as the essence of an ex-parte order is its issuance without hearing the other side in cases of grave urgency. The Supreme Court directed that the appellants should be granted liberty to apply afresh before the NCLT for interim relief based on the same application, allowing the respondents to file their reply within two weeks, and instructed the NCLT to reconsider the application for interim relief after hearing both parties. The Supreme Court instructed the NCLT to take a final decision on the application for interim relief within four weeks from the date a certified copy of the Supreme Court's order is placed on its record. The Supreme Court concluded that the NCLAT failed to address the fundamental issue of whether the respondents had established an urgent case for the grant of ex-parte relief and that its principle was novel to civil jurisprudence, lacking basic legal comprehension.

case_name: Surendra Kumar & Anr. vs. State of U.P.
text: Case: Surendra Kumar & Anr. vs. State of U.P.. Date: 20th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the conviction of Surendra Kumar under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and Ramveer under Section 120B IPC for the murder of Kamla Rani was justified based on the circumstantial evidence presented. The allegations were that Surendra Kumar and Ramveer conspired to murder Kamla Rani, who was shot dead by two armed miscreants while she was traveling on a scooter with Surendra Kumar. The trial court convicted Surendra Kumar under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and Ramveer under Section 120B IPC, sentencing them to life imprisonment for murder and conspiracy. The High Court of Allahabad upheld the conviction and sentence of Surendra Kumar and Ramveer, affirming the trial court's decision. The Supreme Court found that the circumstantial evidence presented was insufficient to conclusively prove the guilt of Surendra Kumar and Ramveer, highlighting several missing components in the chain of evidence. The Supreme Court stated that the burden to prove guilt is always on the prosecution and cannot be shifted to the accused by virtue of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, which the lower courts had incorrectly applied. The Supreme Court found that the testimony of PW1 and PW2, who witnessed the crime and saw two miscreants removing ornaments from the deceased, was not given proper weight by the lower courts, and their failure to implicate Surendra Kumar suggested his innocence. The Supreme Court viewed the alleged motive of Ramveer being unhappy with his wife as insufficient to establish a conspiracy to murder her, especially in the absence of direct or corroborative evidence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, acquitted Surendra Kumar and Ramveer, and directed their immediate release, concluding that the evidence on record did not satisfactorily prove their guilt. The Supreme Court's decision resulted in the acquittal and immediate release of Surendra Kumar and Ramveer, overturning the previous convictions and sentences imposed by the lower courts. The Supreme Court emphasized that proving conspiracy requires solid evidence showing a clear agreement between the accused to commit the crime, which was lacking in this case, thereby leading to the acquittal of Surendra Kumar and Ramveer.

case_name: Surendra Singh & Anr. vs. State of Uttarakhand
text: Case: Surendra Singh & Anr. vs. State of Uttarakhand. Date: 4th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the conviction of Surendra Singh and Ram Singh for the murder of Rajendra Prasad was justified based on the circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution. Surendra Singh and Ram Singh were charged under Sections 457, 380, and 302/34 of the IPC for house trespass, theft, and murder. The motive attributed to the accused was that Rameshwar Singh, one of the co-accused, had developed a grudge against Rajendra Prasad for objecting to his visits to a person involved in unlawful trading. The circumstantial evidence included the accused being last seen near the crime scene, the recovery of stolen articles from their possession, and the discovery of the weapon used in the crime at the instance of Ram Singh. The recovery of stolen articles, such as clothing and cash, from the possession of the accused linked them to the theft and murder of Rajendra Prasad, supporting the prosecution's case. The courts considered the testimony of witnesses who saw the accused in the area before the crime as credible and significant in establishing the presence of the accused near the crime scene. The defense argued that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient and unreliable to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court concluded that the chain of circumstantial evidence was complete and sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused, leading to the affirmation of their conviction. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentences of Surendra Singh and Ram Singh for the murder of Rajendra Prasad. The key factors included credible witness testimonies, recovery of stolen articles, the presence of the accused near the crime scene, and the discovery of the murder weapon, all of which formed a complete chain of evidence supporting the conviction.

case_name: Surendran vs. Sub-Inspector of Police
text: Case: Surendran vs. Sub-Inspector of Police. Date: 30th June 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Surendran was charged under Sections 279, 337, and 338 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for causing an accident while driving a bus, resulting in injuries to the driver of another vehicle. The Judicial First Class Magistrate convicted Surendran under Sections 279 and 338 IPC, sentencing him to six months imprisonment and imposing a fine of Rs. 500 under Section 337 IPC. The Sessions Judge dismissed Surendran's appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence imposed by the Judicial First Class Magistrate. The High Court dismissed Surendran's Criminal Revision petition, leading to the appeal before the Supreme Court. Surendran argued that he was the sole breadwinner for his family, consisting of his wife and four children, and that sending him to jail after more than 21 years would cause irreparable injury to his family. The Supreme Court substituted Surendran's six-month imprisonment under Sections 279 and 338 IPC with a fine of Rs. 1000 each, while maintaining the fine of Rs. 500 under Section 337 IPC. The Supreme Court directed Surendran to deposit the fines totaling Rs. 2000 within one month in the Trial Court.

case_name: Suresh @ Unni @ Vadi Suresh vs The State of Kerala
text: Case: Suresh @ Unni @ Vadi Suresh vs The State of Kerala. Date: 30th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. Suresh @ Unni @ Vadi Suresh was charged with offenses under Sections 302, 307, 143, 147, 148, 324, 326, 427, and 449 read with Section 149 of the IPC, as well as Sections 3(a) and 4(a)(i) of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, and Section 27(1) of the Arms Act, 1958. On 6th March 2006, an unlawful assembly, including the accused, broke into a video shop, attacked Ajeesh (PW-2) and his friend Kapil (the deceased), and hurled country-made bombs, causing grievous injuries and the death of Kapil. The High Court set aside the conviction under the Explosive Substances Act and the Arms Act but confirmed the conviction under various sections of the IPC. It also reduced the sentence for the offense under Section 307 IPC from life imprisonment to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court noted that the identification of the appellant by PW-1 and PW-2 in court, without a prior identification parade, after a lapse of four and a half years from the incident, was insufficient to maintain the conviction. The Supreme Court found the recovery of the iron rod, two years and two months after the incident, implausible due to the presence of blood stains despite the passage of time and exposure to monsoon seasons, thereby doubting the credibility of the recovery evidence. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the convictions and sentences passed by the trial court and the High Court, and acquitted Suresh @ Unni @ Vadi Suresh of all charges, directing his immediate release.

case_name: Suresh Thipmppa Shetty vs. The State of Maharashtra
text: Case: Suresh Thipmppa Shetty vs. The State of Maharashtra. Date: 26th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in upholding the convictions of the appellants for conspiracy and murder under Sections 302 and 120-B of the IPC. The charges against them included conspiracy to abduct and murder Mahendra Pratap Singh, punishable under Sections 302 and 120-B of the IPC. The case involved a business rivalry between the deceased, Mahendra Pratap Singh, and the accused, leading to a conspiracy to abduct and murder Singh on 12th May 1995. The prosecution established involvement through circumstantial evidence, witness testimonies, and the presence of the accused at various key locations related to the crime. PW1 was an eyewitness who accompanied the deceased and testified about the events leading up to the murder, including interactions with the accused. The defence argued that PW7's testimony was unreliable due to the delay in coming forward and inconsistencies in his account of the events. The Supreme Court found reasonable doubt due to the acquittal of the main conspirators, inconsistencies in witness testimonies, and lack of direct evidence linking the appellants to the crime. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the convictions, and directed the appellants to be discharged from their bail bonds. The rivalry was central to the prosecution's theory of motive, but the acquittal of the main conspirators weakened the case against the appellants. The Supreme Court emphasized that reasonable doubt must be resolved in favor of the accused, upholding the presumption of innocence. The Supreme Court directed that any fines paid by the appellants be refunded.

case_name: Suresh Yadav @ Guddu vs. The State of Chhattisgarh
text: Case: Suresh Yadav @ Guddu vs. The State of Chhattisgarh. Date: 25th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Suresh Yadav @ Guddu was accused of causing multiple injuries to the deceased with a pointed knife, leading to her death, because he was enraged seeing her talking to another boy. The prosecution presented the testimony of PW-1, who witnessed the attack, the post-mortem report indicating 12 injuries on the deceased's body, and the recovery of the knife used in the crime based on the appellant's disclosure. The defense argued that PW-1 was not a reliable witness as he neither raised an alarm nor tried to save the deceased, and they also questioned the excessive number of injuries suggesting the involvement of more than one person. The Supreme Court concluded that the evidence of PW-1, being the eyewitness, remained unimpeachable and credible. The Court did not find any reason to discard his testimony solely because he did not raise an alarm or intervene during the incident. The Supreme Court held that the excessive number of injuries did not necessarily imply the involvement of more than one person. The nature and similarity of the injuries suggested that the deceased was repeatedly stabbed by the same person with the same weapon. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the High Court, affirming the conviction and the life imprisonment sentence of Suresh Yadav @ Guddu. No, the Supreme Court clarified that the dismissal of the appeal would not affect the appellant's release under Section 432 CrPC by the Government of Chhattisgarh, as he had already served over 15 years of imprisonment and was released on 7th September 2019.

case_name: Surinder Singh Deswal @ Col. S.S. Deswal and others vs. Virender Gandhi
text: Case: Surinder Singh Deswal @ Col. S.S. Deswal and others vs. Virender Gandhi. Date: 29th May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether the first appellate court is justified in directing the appellants, convicted under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, to deposit 25% of the amount of compensation/fine imposed by the trial court while suspending the sentence pending appeal. The appellants were convicted of the offense under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for dishonoring cheques. The first appellate court directed the appellants to deposit 25% of the amount of compensation/fine awarded by the trial court while suspending their sentence pending appeal. The appellants contended that Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, as amended, should not be applicable to their case as the criminal complaints were filed prior to the amendment's effective date. The Supreme Court interpreted that the amended Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is procedural in nature and applicable to appeals against convictions under Section 138, even for cases filed before the amendment, to prevent delay tactics and ensure the object and purpose of the Act. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision which confirmed the first appellate court's order directing the appellants to deposit 25% of the compensation/fine amount while suspending their sentence pending appeal.

case_name: Suryavir vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Suryavir vs. State of Haryana. Date: 3rd February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Suryavir, along with Devender alias Dhola and Pardeep, was accused of causing the murder of Rajinder alias Raju on 1st October 2008. The prosecution relied on the testimony of Om Prakash (PW-12) and Janki Devi (PW-15), parents of the deceased, who identified Suryavir and others as the assailants. The significant discrepancy was that PW-12 initially stated that the assailants came in a white car, but later it was claimed that they came on motorcycles. The Trial Court convicted Suryavir and Devender of offenses under Section 302 read with 34 IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court acquitted Suryavir because the prosecution failed to establish the identity of the assailants beyond reasonable doubt, as the witnesses' testimonies were based on rumors and not on direct identification. The Supreme Court extended the benefit of acquittal to Devender alias Dhola as well, recalling the earlier order of dismissal and granting him the same relief as Suryavir.

case_name: Sushanta Kumar Banik vs. State of Tripura & Ors.
text: Case: Sushanta Kumar Banik vs. State of Tripura & Ors.. Date: 30th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the detention of Sushanta Kumar Banik under Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 (PIT NDPS Act) was justified. The detention order was based on his involvement in two criminal cases related to narcotic drugs, his habitual engagement in illegal drug trafficking, and the perceived threat to public health and welfare. The two criminal cases were Amtali PS Case No. 2019/AMT/208 dated 5th November 2019 under Sections 22(b)/22(C)/29 of the NDPS Act, 1985, and East Agartala PS Case No. 2021 EAG 052 dated 25th April 2021 under Sections 21(B)/29 of the NDPS Act, 1985. The Supreme Court found the delay problematic because it snapped the 'live and proximate link' between the prejudicial activities and the purpose of detention, and there was no satisfactory explanation for the five-month delay. The Supreme Court noted that the detaining authority was not made aware that Sushanta Kumar Banik had been released on bail in both criminal cases, which was a vital fact that could have influenced the detention decision. The Supreme Court emphasized that the subjective satisfaction required for passing a detention order must be based on complete and accurate information, and any withholding or suppression of vital facts can vitiate the order. The Supreme Court cited the principle that preventive detention orders must be executed promptly to maintain the 'live and proximate link' between the grounds of detention and the purpose of detention. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the detention order passed by the State of Tripura, and ordered the immediate release of Sushanta Kumar Banik from custody unless required in any other case. The decision reinforced the importance of prompt and informed decision-making in preventive detention cases, ensuring that detaining authorities consider all relevant facts and act without undue delay. The Supreme Court criticized both the detaining and sponsoring authorities for their lack of vigilance and failure to provide complete information, which led to an unjustified and delayed preventive detention order.

case_name: Swaati Nirkhi & Ors. vs State (NCT of Delhi) & Ors.
text: Case: Swaati Nirkhi & Ors. vs State (NCT of Delhi) & Ors.. Date: 9th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary request was to transfer Criminal Case No. 3483 of 2017 titled as State v. Swaati Nirkhi & Ors. from the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate 461 North West, Rohini Courts, New Delhi to the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate at Allahabad (Prayagraj), Uttar Pradesh. The main allegations included extortion and false claims of gang rape. Swaati Nirkhi and others were accused of demanding Rs. 5 crores and falsely alleging gang rape to coerce the complainant. The petitioners argued that they had multiple pending cases in Allahabad and that defending the case in Delhi would be financially burdensome and cause hardship. They also cited the health issues of Petitioner No. 2, a senior citizen. The complainant argued that the alleged incidents occurred in New Delhi, and most of the witnesses, including 12 official witnesses, were based in Delhi. Transferring the case to Allahabad would hinder their official duties and cause inconvenience. The Supreme Court dismissed the transfer petition, ruling that the case should be tried in New Delhi where the cause of action arose, and directed the proceedings to be transferred back to the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate 461 North West, Rohini Courts, New Delhi. The Supreme Court found that the petitioners' apprehensions and claimed inconveniences did not constitute exceptional circumstances for transferring the case from Delhi to Allahabad. The convenience of the prosecution, other accused, witnesses, and the larger interest of society were prioritized. The Supreme Court directed the parties to appear before the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate 461 North West, Rohini Courts, New Delhi on 15th April 2021.

case_name: Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd. vs. Loknete Marutrao Ghule Patil Dnyaneshwar Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd. vs. Loknete Marutrao Ghule Patil Dnyaneshwar Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 13th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Industrial Entrepreneur Memorandum (IEM) dated 8th September 2010, granted to Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd., should be de-recognized due to non-compliance with the provisions of Clause 6C of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966. They sought the cancellation of the IEM on the grounds that Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd. failed to set up the sugar factory and commence production within the stipulated time frame and that the proposed sugar factory did not meet the minimum distance requirements set by the State of Maharashtra. The High Court allowed the writ petitions, directing the de-recognition of the IEM granted to Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd. due to non-compliance with the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in its decision, noting that the period spent in litigation should be excluded from the time frame for setting up the sugar factory, as the delays were due to unforeseen circumstances beyond the control of Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and upheld the validity of the IEM granted to Swami Samarth Sugars and Agro Industries Ltd., allowing the extension of time for setting up the sugar factory due to litigation-related delays. The Supreme Court emphasized the principle that delays caused by litigation should not be held against a party, and the period spent in defending litigation should be excluded when considering compliance with statutory time frames.

case_name: Swaminathan Kunchu Acharya vs State of Gujarat & Ors.
text: Case: Swaminathan Kunchu Acharya vs State of Gujarat & Ors.. Date: 9th June 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the custody of the minor child Pranav Acharya, following the death of his parents during the second wave of Covid-19. The appellant, the paternal grandfather, sought custody of the child, which was granted to the maternal aunt by the High Court. The High Court handed over the custody of the minor child Pranav Acharya to the maternal aunt, Hemangini @ Mintu Madanmohan Shuryanvanshi, citing her younger age, better qualifications, and stable employment as reasons. The appellant argued that the High Court did not provide valid reasons for denying custody to the paternal grandparents, did not find any fault in their care during interim custody, and that there should not be a presumption that the younger maternal aunt could take better care of the child. The Supreme Court found that the reasons given by the High Court were not sufficient to presume that the maternal aunt would take better care of the child than the paternal grandparents. The Court emphasized that grandparents could also provide excellent care and emotional support. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed that the custody of Pranav Acharya be continued with the paternal grandparents. The Court also provided for visitation rights for the maternal aunt. The Supreme Court directed the paternal grandparents to ensure the child's education in Ahmedabad and encouraged both families to act jointly and maintain cordial relations for the child's best interest. The Court also provided for regular visitation and video calls between the child and the maternal aunt.

case_name: Swapan Kumar Chatterjee vs. Central Bureau of Investigation
text: Case: Swapan Kumar Chatterjee vs. Central Bureau of Investigation. Date: 4th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in allowing the prosecution to summon the handwriting expert, Mr. H.S. Tuteja, despite repeated failures to produce him in court over a period of thirteen years. Swapan Kumar Chatterjee was accused under Sections 477A, 471, 468, 420, 120B of the IPC, and Sections 5(1)(c)(d) read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, related to economic offences involving forgery and cheating. The trial court initially allowed the prosecution's petition to summon Mr. H.S. Tuteja for examination as a handwriting expert in 2004, but he repeatedly failed to appear in court. The High Court gave the CBI a last opportunity in 2011 to produce Mr. H.S. Tuteja and directed the trial court to proceed without further adjournments if the CBI failed, yet the trial court continued to allow adjournments for his summoning. The Supreme Court criticized the repeated adjournments as an abuse of the process of law, noting that the prosecution's inability to produce the witness for over a decade caused undue delay and prejudice to the accused. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power under Section 311 should be exercised sparingly and only for strong and valid reasons, with great caution and circumspection, to meet the ends of justice. The Supreme Court quashed the orders of the High Court and the trial court, dismissing the application filed by the prosecution to summon Mr. H.S. Tuteja, and directed that the trial proceed without further adjournments. The Supreme Court's decision mandated that the trial court proceed with the trial expeditiously without granting further adjournments for the prosecution to summon Mr. H.S. Tuteja. The Supreme Court conveyed that undue delays and repeated adjournments for summoning witnesses, especially over a prolonged period, undermine the judicial process and cause prejudice to the accused. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should have rejected the prosecution's repeated applications for adjournments and summoning of the witness, thereby ensuring the trial's expeditious conclusion.

case_name: Swarnalatha & Ors. vs. Kalavathy & Ors.
text: Case: Swarnalatha & Ors. vs. Kalavathy & Ors.. Date: 30th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge to the probate granted by the District Court for the Wills of Mannar Reddiar and Adhilakshmiammal, which was set aside by the High Court due to alleged suspicious circumstances. The testators were Mannar Reddiar and Adhilakshmiammal. Adhilakshmiammal's Will, dated 30th January 1995, bequeathed her properties to her two sons, excluding her daughter Kalavathy. Mannar Reddiar's Will, dated 10th December 1998, also excluded Kalavathy and bequeathed his properties to his two sons and grandchildren. The High Court found several suspicious circumstances, including inconsistencies in the execution and registration of the Wills, the testatrix's alleged ailments, the delay in probating the Wills, and the total exclusion of the daughter from the bequest. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's findings were speculative and not supported by evidence. The Court noted that the exclusion of the daughter was explained in the Wills, and there was no convincing evidence of suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the Wills. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the judgment of the Principal District Court, Vellore, which had granted probate of both Wills. The appeal was allowed, and the probate granted by the District Court was upheld.

case_name: Swati Ulhas Kerkar and Ors. vs Sanjay Walavalkar and Ors.
text: Case: Swati Ulhas Kerkar and Ors. vs Sanjay Walavalkar and Ors.. Date: 10th February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central question was whether the invalidation of membership of the appellants solely on the ground that the then Managing Committee on its way out and facing a no confidence motion should not have hastened the admission of new members. The Managing Committee inducted 22 new members (including the appellants) despite objections raised by the Treasurer. The primary allegation was abuse of power and mismanagement by the Managing Committee, resulting in a loss of confidence. The District Registrar declared the induction of the 22 new members as illegal and arbitrary, and set it aside. The High Court upheld the decision because the Managing Committee acted with material irregularity by refusing to convene the Special General Body Meeting (SGBM) demanded by the majority members and hastened the induction of new members, which was seen as an abuse of power. The Supreme Court confirmed that the induction of new members by the Managing Committee during a pending no confidence motion was illegal and arbitrary. The Supreme Court directed that future elections should be conducted under the supervision of an observer appointed by the District Registrar to ensure free, fair, and impartial conduct of elections. The decision reinforces the importance of adhering to democratic principles and ensuring that the Managing Committee acts in the best interests of the Society, avoiding arbitrary decisions, especially during no confidence motions. The Supreme Court clarified that the Managing Committee should refrain from making significant decisions, such as inducting new members, during the pendency of a no confidence motion to avoid potential abuse of power. The Society should establish clear rules and guidelines regarding the induction of new members, the conduct of elections, and the handling of no confidence motions to ensure transparent and fair governance. Other societies should take heed of this ruling to avoid similar legal challenges by ensuring that their governing bodies do not make significant decisions during pending no confidence motions and adhere to democratic principles.

case_name: T.K. David vs. Kuruppampady Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: T.K. David vs. Kuruppampady Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 5th October 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the dismissal of T.K. David by the Kuruppampady Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. was justified, and whether the subsequent reduction in rank by the Cooperative Arbitration Court should stand. The Cooperative Arbitration Court modified the punishment of dismissal to a reduction in rank. The Cooperative Tribunal imposed compulsory retirement with terminal benefits, subject to any liabilities assessed. The High Court dismissed T.K. David's writ petition and upheld the Tribunal's decision of compulsory retirement. The Supreme Court rejected the special leave petition because the earlier Special Leave Petition (C) No. 24231 of 2015 challenging the Division Bench judgment dated 11th March 2015 had already been dismissed, and no relief could be granted in the current petition. The Supreme Court reiterated that special leave petitions challenging orders rejecting review petitions are not maintainable when the main judgment of the High Court is not under challenge.

case_name: T.V. Ramakrishna Reddy vs M. Mallappa & Anr.
text: Case: T.V. Ramakrishna Reddy vs M. Mallappa & Anr.. Date: 7th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether a suit for permanent injunction without seeking a declaration of title was maintainable, given that the plaintiff's title to the property was disputed by the defendants. The plaintiff-appellant claimed to be the absolute owner in possession of the suit property, which he purchased from K.P. Govinda Reddy through a registered sale deed dated 13th April 1992. He alleged that the defendants attempted to demolish his compound wall, prompting him to file the suit for a permanent injunction. The BDA, defendant No.1, argued that the suit was not maintainable due to the plaintiff's failure to serve notice under Section 64 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976. They also contended that the khata issued in the plaintiff's name was merely a revenue entry that did not confer any right, title, or interest in the property. Defendant No.2, M. Mallappa, claimed that he had purchased the suit property through a registered sale deed dated 5th April 1984 from M. Shivalingaiah and had been in peaceful possession since then. He argued that the plaintiff's vendor, K.P. Govinda Reddy, had no right to sell the property, as it belonged to Shivalingaiah's undivided family and had been allotted to Shivalingaiah in a partition. The High Court of Karnataka allowed the appeal filed by M. Mallappa, finding that a suit for permanent injunction without seeking a declaration of title was not maintainable. The High Court set aside the trial court's decree in favor of the plaintiff. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, ruling that in cases where the plaintiff's title is disputed or under a cloud, the proper remedy is to seek a declaration of title. The Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the issue of title must be adjudicated through a comprehensive suit based on evidence. The Supreme Court emphasized that where the plaintiff's title is disputed or under a cloud, a suit for injunction simpliciter is not maintainable. The Court noted that issues of title should be decided through a comprehensive suit for declaration of title, rather than in a suit for mere injunction.

The Supreme Court emphasized that where the plaintiff's title is disputed or under a cloud, a suit for injunction simpliciter is not maintainable. The Court noted that issues of title should be decided through a comprehensive suit for declaration of title, rather than in a suit for mere injunction.

case_name: THE NEW INDIA ASSURANCE CO. LTD. vs. SRI BUCHIYYAMMA RICE MILL & ANR.
text: Case: THE NEW INDIA ASSURANCE CO. LTD. vs. SRI BUCHIYYAMMA RICE MILL & ANR.. Date: 21st January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the damage to the rice mill's boiler unit and other components was caused by a lorry collision, as claimed by Sri Buchiyyamma Rice Mill, or by structural failure due to overloading, as argued by the insurance company. The preliminary surveyor concluded that it was unlikely the incident had occurred in the manner claimed by the insured. The surveyor noted that the damage to the boiling unit structure was not consistent with a lorry collision and suggested that a structural failure might be the real cause of the damage. The structural expert from Andhra University concluded that there was no external impact on the failed columns, the storage capacity of the system had been breached, and the incident resulted from exceeding the load-carrying capacity of the column section, leading to the collapse of the entire paddy boiling structure. The SCDRC dismissed the complaint, agreeing with the insurer's argument that the damage was due to overloading and not an external impact. The SCDRC noted the absence of evidence supporting the collision claim and the findings of the surveyor and structural expert. The NCDRC reversed the decision of the SCDRC, directing the insurer to pay Rs 29,23,503 with interest. The NCDRC found that the survey reports were delayed and breached regulatory guidelines, thus favoring the insured's claim. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the NCDRC's judgment. The Supreme Court upheld the SCDRC's decision, agreeing that the survey reports consistently showed the damage was due to overloading and not a collision, and ruled that the NCDRC had not acted reasonably.

case_name: Tabrez Khan @ Guddu & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Tabrez Khan @ Guddu & Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 5th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the appellants' application to quash the complaint and summoning order issued against them under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. Respondent No. 2 alleged that the appellants committed offences under Sections 498A, 323, 504, 506 of the IPC and Section 3/4 of the DP Act, relating to cruelty, physical assault, and intimidation. Appellant No. 3 is the mother of Mohammad Pervez, the husband of Respondent No. 2, while Appellant Nos. 1 and 2 are the brothers of Mohammad Pervez and brothers-in-law of Respondent No. 2. The High Court declined to quash the Complaint Case No. 3065 of 2016 and the summoning order dated 10.03.2017 issued by the ACJM, Court No. 8, Varanasi. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the complaint filed by Respondent No. 2 against the appellants. The Supreme Court quashed the complaint on the grounds that the averments made in the complaint did not constitute any prima facie case against the appellants. The Supreme Court directed that the complaint against Mohammad Pervez Khan should be decided on its merit by the concerned Magistrate, unaffected by the Court's observations in this case. The Supreme Court found no justification to proceed against the appellants because the facts stated in the complaint did not constitute any case against them, either jointly or severally. The appellants invoked Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. in their application to the High Court, seeking to quash the complaint and the summoning order. The charges against the appellants under the IPC were Sections 498A (cruelty), 323 (voluntarily causing hurt), 504 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace), and 506 (criminal intimidation). They were also charged under Section 3/4 of the DP Act. The Supreme Court described its examination of the case against the appellants as finding no prima facie case or justification to proceed against them based on the facts stated in the complaint.

case_name: Taijuddin vs State of Assam & Ors.
text: Case: Taijuddin vs State of Assam & Ors.. Date: 1st December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Taijuddin's conviction under Section 149 IPC was justified, given his alleged role in pointing out the location of the victim during a mob attack. A land dispute led to the attack. The victim, Abdul Wahab, was attacked by a mob armed with lathis, spears, and daggers while he was trying to escape and hide in a house. Taijuddin was accused of pointing out the house where Abdul Wahab was hiding, which led the mob to find and kill him. The High Court upheld Taijuddin's conviction under Section 149 IPC based on the testimony that he pointed out the location of the victim to the mob. The key evidence against Taijuddin was the testimony of witnesses who stated that he pointed out the location of the victim, Abdul Wahab, to the mob. The Supreme Court noted inconsistencies in the testimonies and highlighted that some key witnesses did not mention Taijuddin at all, casting doubt on the reliability of the evidence against him. The Supreme Court set aside Taijuddin's conviction under Sections 147, 148, 302, 201, and 149 IPC, stating that there was insufficient evidence to prove his involvement beyond reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in Subal Ghorai v. State of West Bengal, which emphasized that passive onlookers should not be falsely implicated as part of an unlawful assembly. The Supreme Court noted that people often gather at the scene of an offense out of curiosity and that such bystanders should not be assumed to share the common object of the unlawful assembly. The Supreme Court ordered that Taijuddin be released forthwith, provided he was not required in any other case.

case_name: Talat Sanvi vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr.
text: Case: Talat Sanvi vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr.. Date: 24th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether interim victim compensation in proceedings for anticipatory bail can be imposed as a condition for the same. The Supreme Court ruled that the imposition of interim victim compensation cannot form part of bail jurisprudence and set aside the impugned order. The Supreme Court referenced the cases of Sahab Alam @ Guddu vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr. and Udho Thakur and Anr. ETC. vs. State of Jharkhand & Anr. The Supreme Court observed that bail cannot per se be granted if a person can afford to deposit the money or has the capacity to pay, and such conditions should not influence the decision to grant bail. The Supreme Court found the use of 'victim compensation' inappropriate in pre-arrest bail proceedings, as these are not meant for money recovery. The Supreme Court provided a historical context on victim compensation, mentioning the 'victimology' movement of the 1960s and the UN Declaration on Basic Principles of Justice for Victims and Abuse of Power adopted in 1985. The provision for victim compensation falls under Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Sub-section (2) of Section 357 imposes a limitation that when fine is imposed in a case subject to appeal, no such payment shall be made before the appeal period has elapsed or the decision of the appeal. The Supreme Court observed that compensation under Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can only arise after the conclusion of trial and should not be a condition for granting bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the condition of interim victim compensation in the impugned order, and maintained the other aspects of the grant of anticipatory bail.

case_name: Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board vs. Sterlite Industries (I) Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board vs. Sterlite Industries (I) Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 18th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the environmental compliance and operation of the copper smelter plant by Sterlite Industries in Tamil Nadu, including the legality of various orders issued by the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) and the National Green Tribunal (NGT). The orders issued by the NGT on 31st May 2013, 8th August 2013, and 15th December 2018, which allowed Sterlite Industries to continue operations despite the TNPCB's closure directives, were challenged. Sterlite Industries was accused of causing severe environmental pollution, including air and water pollution, which led to health issues among local residents. Specific violations included improper management of hazardous waste and emissions exceeding permissible limits. The Supreme Court upheld the NGT's decision allowing Sterlite Industries to resume operations under stringent conditions, but also highlighted the need for comprehensive environmental safeguards and monitoring. Conditions included regular monitoring of air and water quality, proper disposal of hazardous waste, compliance with environmental regulations, and periodic inspections by TNPCB and other authorities. The judgment aimed to balance industrial operations with environmental protection, ensuring that Sterlite Industries' operations did not compromise the health and well-being of local residents. It mandated strict environmental compliance to prevent future violations.
