case_name: Tarak Nath Keshari vs. State of West Bengal
text: Case: Tarak Nath Keshari vs. State of West Bengal. Date: 10th May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Tarak Nath Keshari was accused of possessing mustard oil and vegetable oil in quantities exceeding the permissible limit, in violation of para 3(1) of the West Bengal Pulses, Edible Oil (Dealers Licensing) Order, 1978, under Section 7(1)(a)(ii) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Trial Court sentenced Tarak Nath Keshari to six months of rigorous imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs. 500. Additionally, the sale proceeds of the seized oil were forfeited to the State. The High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from six months of rigorous imprisonment to three months of rigorous imprisonment, while maintaining the fine. The defense argued that since the incident occurred in 1985 and more than 37 years had passed, the sentence of imprisonment should be set aside, and a fine could be imposed in lieu of the sentence. The Supreme Court observed that the incident had taken place over 37 years ago, and considering the passage of time, it was appropriate to consider releasing the appellant on probation. The Supreme Court referred to Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, which allows the court to release an offender on probation of good conduct instead of sentencing them immediately. The Supreme Court decided to release Tarak Nath Keshari on probation under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, on entering into a bond and two sureties to ensure good behavior for the remaining part of his sentence. The Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, being a later enactment, takes precedence, and even if a minimum sentence is provided under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, the provisions of probation can still be invoked. This judgement suggests that in cases involving long-pending offenses, especially those where a significant amount of time has elapsed, courts may consider probation instead of imprisonment, emphasizing rehabilitation over punishment. The Supreme Court highlighted that courts must consider the nature of the offense, the character of the offender, and the circumstances of the case, and may require a probation officer's report before granting probation. If Tarak Nath Keshari fails to maintain good behavior during the probation period, he could be called upon to serve the original sentence as directed by the court.

case_name: Tarlochan Singh @ Rana vs State of Punjab
text: Case: Tarlochan Singh @ Rana vs State of Punjab. Date: 29th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Tarlochan Singh @ Rana was charged under Sections 29 and 30 of the Arms Act for being the license holder of a Double Barrel 12 Bore Rifle used in a murder, and under Section 120-B IPC for criminal conspiracy. The main accusation was that the Double Barrel 12 Bore Rifle, licensed to Tarlochan Singh @ Rana, was used by the co-accused Gurpreet Singh @ Titu to murder Gurdeep Singh. The High Court acquitted Tarlochan Singh @ Rana of the charges under Section 120-B IPC, finding no evidence of criminal conspiracy. The High Court upheld the conviction under Sections 29 and 30 of the Arms Act, sentencing Tarlochan Singh @ Rana to rigorous imprisonment for three years and three months respectively. The Supreme Court observed that there was no evidence to prove that Tarlochan Singh @ Rana willingly handed over the firearm to Gurpreet Singh @ Titu, who took it without his permission. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction under Sections 29 and 30 of the Arms Act, acquitting Tarlochan Singh @ Rana of all charges, as there was no evidence of willful violation of any license conditions or rules. The Supreme Court directed the acquittal of Tarlochan Singh @ Rana from all charges, nullifying the High Court's judgment that upheld his conviction under the Arms Act.

case_name: Tata Power Company Ltd. vs. Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Tata Power Company Ltd. vs. Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 2nd May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary dispute was regarding the payment of standby charges by Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. (formerly Reliance Energy Limited) to Tata Power Company Ltd. for the electricity supplied in the suburbs of Mumbai. The standby charges initially agreed upon were for a monthly firmed demand of 300 MVA, increasing by 50 MVA each year starting from 1st April 1985, to cover Tata Power Company's load growth annually. Tata Power Company Ltd. sought to increase its generating capacity to reduce its offtake of electricity from Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) to zero, which would cause a loss of revenue for MSEB. An arrangement was made where Tata Power Company Ltd. would pay standby charges to MSEB initially for 300 MVA, increasing by 50 MVA each year, up to 550 MVA by 1990. These charges were meant to enable Tata Power Company Ltd. to draw upon MSEB's energy in case of outages or failures in Tata Power's generation capacity. The government of Maharashtra appointed a committee to resolve the issue, which recommended that Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. should pay Rs. 3.5 crores per month to Tata Power Company Ltd. for standby supply for the period 1998-1999, based on various factors such as generation capacity, electricity supply, and financial positions. APTEL directed that Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. should bear 23 percent of the total standby charges incurred by Tata Power Company Ltd. with MSEB, while Tata Power Company Ltd. should bear the remaining charges. It also ordered the refund of the excess amount deposited by Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. under interim orders. The Supreme Court did not interfere with the interim arrangement made by the High Court, which directed Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. to deposit 50 percent of the standby amount as an interim measure, as the final decision on the dispute was expected from the Electricity Regulatory Commission.

case_name: Tehseen Poonawalla vs. Union of India & Anr.
text: Case: Tehseen Poonawalla vs. Union of India & Anr.. Date: 26th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the remarks made against Ms. Indira Jaising in the judgement dated 19th April 2018, indicating that her conduct amounted to contempt or prima facie contempt of court, should be expunged. Ms. Indira Jaising sought an order to expunge or delete the remarks made against her that indicated her conduct amounted to contempt or prima facie contempt of court. The Supreme Court observed that the remarks were made in the context of the conduct of the petitioners and intervenors collectively and were based on the arguments presented during the hearing. The court did not find a basis to expunge the remarks specifically against Ms. Jaising. Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi argued that Ms. Indira Jaising did not intend to make any submissions that would denigrate or scandalize the judiciary and that the remarks made against her were not justified. Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, representing the State of Maharashtra, opposed the application and argued that the submissions attributed to Ms. Jaising were indeed made by her during the proceedings, and the remarks in the judgement were based on those submissions. The Supreme Court noted that prayer clause (c), which sought records from the High Court of Bombay regarding the transfer of Judge Utpat, was indicative of an attempt to revive the controversy settled by the earlier judgement. Dr. Singhvi later submitted that this prayer was being given up. The Supreme Court disposed of the Miscellaneous Application, maintaining the remarks made in the judgement and stating that they pertained to the collective conduct of the petitioners and intervenors, including Ms. Jaising.

case_name: Tejashwi Prasad Yadav vs. Hareshbhai Pranshankar Mehta
text: Case: Tejashwi Prasad Yadav vs. Hareshbhai Pranshankar Mehta. Date: 13th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involved a complaint for defamation filed by Hareshbhai Pranshankar Mehta against Tejashwi Prasad Yadav under Sections 499 and 500 of the IPC, based on statements made by the petitioner alleging that Gujaratis were 'swindlers'. Tejashwi Prasad Yadav made a public statement that 'only Gujaratis could be swindlers' and referenced alleged financial misconduct by individuals from Gujarat. The petitioner clarified that his statements were made in the context of a question about the revocation of the Red Corner Notice against Mehul Choksi and were not intended to defame Gujaratis as a community. Tejashwi Prasad Yadav filed affidavits unconditionally withdrawing the statements made on 22nd March 2023 and stated that he held Gujaratis in high esteem. The Court noted that the petitioner had unconditionally withdrawn his statements, clarified his intent, and expressed regret for any hurt caused to Gujaratis. The Supreme Court quashed the complaint considering the withdrawal of the statements and the petitioner’s explanation, concluding that continuing the prosecution would serve no purpose. The Supreme Court invoked its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India to quash the complaint in the interest of justice. The Court emphasized that defamation cases must balance the right to freedom of speech with the need to protect individuals or communities from unwarranted harm, and prosecutions should not proceed where the alleged harm has been addressed.

case_name: Thangela Narendra @ Chinnu vs The State of Karnataka
text: Case: Thangela Narendra @ Chinnu vs The State of Karnataka. Date: 19th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Thangela Narendra @ Chinnu was charged under Section 498A read with Section 304B of the IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1986. The appellants sought bail from the Supreme Court because the High Court had declined to grant bail despite the fact that the investigation had been completed and they had already been in jail for around a year. The Supreme Court granted interim bail to the appellants at the time of admission and decided to continue their bail during the pendency of the trial, with the condition that the State could seek cancellation of bail if the appellants did not cooperate with the trial. The Supreme Court noted that the investigation had already been completed, which was a significant factor in their decision to grant bail to the appellants. The Supreme Court instructed that it would be open to the State to seek cancellation of bail if the appellants did not cooperate with the trial. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeals, allowing the appellants to remain on bail during the pendency of the trial.

case_name: The Bijnor Urban Cooperative Bank Limited, Bijnor & others vs. Meenal Agarwal & others
text: Case: The Bijnor Urban Cooperative Bank Limited, Bijnor & others vs. Meenal Agarwal & others. Date: 15th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether Meenal Agarwal was eligible for the One Time Settlement (OTS) scheme despite her loan account being classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). The High Court directed the Bank to positively consider Meenal Agarwal's application for the OTS scheme, issuing a writ of mandamus under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The Bank argued that Meenal Agarwal was not eligible for the OTS scheme as her loan account was classified as NPA and there were sufficient assets to recover the loan amount through auction. The Supreme Court ruled that the benefit of the OTS scheme cannot be claimed as a matter of right and is subject to the eligibility criteria and discretion of the Bank. The Supreme Court emphasized that OTS benefits should be granted based on the eligibility criteria specified in the scheme and the Bank's assessment of the chances of recovering the loan amount through other means. The Supreme Court stated that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing a writ of mandamus directing the Bank to positively consider the OTS application, as the decision to grant OTS benefits lies within the Bank's discretion. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's judgment, stating that the Bank was justified in rejecting Meenal Agarwal's OTS application based on the criteria and guidelines of the OTS scheme. This judgment implies that future OTS applications must strictly adhere to the eligibility criteria and that the decision to grant OTS benefits is at the discretion of the financial institution based on their commercial wisdom. Banks should carefully evaluate each OTS application based on the eligibility criteria and ensure that all other recovery measures are considered before granting OTS benefits, maintaining their commercial interests. The judgment underscores that Article 226 cannot be used to compel financial institutions to grant OTS benefits, reinforcing the principle that such decisions are within the commercial discretion of the banks. Borrowers might face stricter scrutiny and must ensure that they meet all eligibility criteria, as banks will be more cautious in granting OTS benefits to avoid potential losses and ensure compliance with guidelines.

case_name: The Chairman V.O. Chidambaranar Port Trust & Ors. vs Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh
text: Case: The Chairman V.O. Chidambaranar Port Trust & Ors. vs Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh. Date: 6th December 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the termination of Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh's appointment as a Pilot Officer by the V.O. Chidambaranar Port Trust was valid, particularly in light of his qualifications and the certification he held from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh possessed a Certificate of Competency as Master issued by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, along with qualifications in MBA (Shipping and Port Management), Master of Human Resource, Advanced Diploma in Maritime Transportation, and Master of Science in Counselling and Psychotherapy. The Port Trust terminated Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh's appointment because they argued that his Certificate of Competency from Singapore was not recognized by the Government of India for performing pilot duties at the port, and thus, he was not eligible for the position. The High Court of Madras set aside the termination order, directing the reinstatement of Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh with back wages, while giving the Port Trust the liberty to re-examine the validity of his certificates by providing him an opportunity for a personal hearing. The Supreme Court held that the Certificate of Competency as Master (Foreign Going) issued by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore was equivalent to the certificate issued by the Government of India. The Court noted that the Port Trust had not raised any objections to this certificate at the time of appointment and had previously sought clarification from the Ministry of Shipping, which did not find any issue with the certification. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's order for reinstatement but modified the back wages to be reduced to 40% from 2012 until the date of his joining. The Court did not find any further necessity to examine the respondent's certificate as the Port Trust had previously accepted his qualifications. The Supreme Court emphasized that the judgment was passed based on the special facts and circumstances of the case and should not be treated as a precedent. Capt. Paul Nadar Bennet Singh was to be reinstated with reduced back wages, taking into account the period he did not work from 2012 until his reinstatement.

case_name: The Commissioner of Central Excise, Vadodara-II vs. Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers Co. Ltd.
text: Case: The Commissioner of Central Excise, Vadodara-II vs. Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers Co. Ltd.. Date: 3rd December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the assessee (Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers Co. Ltd.) was entitled to claim CENVAT credit on duty-paid Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) used as an input for generating steam, which in turn was used to generate electricity for the manufacture of fertilizer, which is exempt from duty. The Commissioner of Central Excise issued two show-cause notices to Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers Co. Ltd., disputing the correctness of their claim to CENVAT credit on LSHS. The Commissioner confirmed the demand for the recovery of the wrongly claimed CENVAT credit, directed the assessee to pay interest on the demanded amount, and imposed penalties. The larger Bench of the Tribunal held that Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers Co. Ltd. was entitled to claim CENVAT credit on LSHS used as an input for producing steam and electricity for the manufacture of fertilizer. The Division Bench of the Tribunal allowed the assessee's appeals, relying on the decision of the larger Bench. The Supreme Court ruled that there is no conflict between the earlier MODVAT rules and the CENVAT Credit Rules of 2002. The principle that CENVAT credit for duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products is not allowable remains consistent. The Court upheld that CENVAT credit is not permissible on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, including fuel inputs like LSHS. The Supreme Court concluded that sub-rule (1) of Rule 6 is plenary and applies to all inputs, including fuel inputs. It restates the principle that CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Sub-rule (2) refers to non-fuel inputs, and the exception in sub-rule (2) does not apply to fuel inputs, which must be governed by sub-rule (1). The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the Commissioner of Central Excise, set aside the Tribunal's order dated 10.04.2008, and reaffirmed that CENVAT credit is not permissible on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The Court emphasized that the CENVAT scheme's principle that credit is not allowed for duty paid on inputs used for exempted goods remains intact.

case_name: The Commissioner, Central Excise and Customs vs. M/S Reliance Industries Ltd.
text: Case: The Commissioner, Central Excise and Customs vs. M/S Reliance Industries Ltd.. Date: 4th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Tribunal held that the extended period of limitation could not be invoked as the assessee had a bona fide belief that its valuation practices were lawful, based on a precedent set by the Tribunal in IFGL Refractories Ltd.'s case. The Supreme Court noted that the Revenue attempted to argue points beyond the written pleadings, such as wrongful clubbing of deemed export clearances, which were neither raised in the show cause notice nor included in the appeal. The Supreme Court emphasized that invoking the extended limitation period requires evidence of deliberate suppression of facts, fraud, or collusion, which was absent in this case, thereby limiting its use in future cases. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals as the demands were time-barred and found no merit in the Revenue's claims of suppression of facts or fraud by the assessee. The Supreme Court clarified that in a self-assessment regime, an assessee cannot be accused of suppression unless there is a legal requirement to disclose specific facts, which was not evident in this case.

case_name: The Commissioner, Commercial Tax, U.P., Lucknow vs S/s Rujhan Studio
text: Case: The Commissioner, Commercial Tax, U.P., Lucknow vs S/s Rujhan Studio. Date: 2nd March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the product sold by S/s Rujhan Studio, described as an 'embroidered ladies suit', should be classified as a 'textile' under Entry 21 of Schedule I of the UP VAT Act 2008, or as an 'other textile made up' under Entry 16 of Schedule II, or be subject to tax under the residuary entry in Schedule V. The Assessing Authority classified the product as an unclassified item under Schedule V of the UP VAT Act 2008, subjecting it to a tax rate of 12.5%. The Additional Commissioner partly allowed the appeal and classified the goods as 'textile made ups', subject to a duty of 4% under Serial Number 16 of Schedule IIA. The Tribunal allowed the appeal filed by S/s Rujhan Studio and rejected the appeal of the Revenue, classifying the product as a 'textile' within the meaning of Entry 21 of Schedule I, thus exempting it from tax. The High Court dismissed the revision because it found no error in the factual findings of the Tribunal and did not interfere with its decision. The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the High Court, Tribunal, and first appellate authority, restoring the order of the Assessing Authority, and classified the product under the residuary entry in Schedule V, subjecting it to a tax rate of 12.5%. The Supreme Court interpreted that the textile material, once subjected to cutting, embroidery, and other processes by S/s Rujhan Studio, ceased to be a 'textile' and assumed the character of an article with a distinct description, thus not falling under Entry 21 of Schedule I. The Supreme Court highlighted that the classification of goods must be based on their description and nature as understood in common parlance, ensuring that specific entries are applied correctly and the residuary entry is used only when no specific entry is applicable. The decision could influence future tax classification disputes by emphasizing the importance of accurately interpreting statutory entries and ensuring that the correct tax rates are applied based on the nature and description of the goods. Businesses should ensure that their products are clearly described, maintain detailed records of their manufacturing processes, and seek clarifications on the applicable tax rates to avoid classification disputes and potential legal challenges. The Supreme Court clarified that 'other textile made ups' must be read ejusdem generis with items like bedsheets and pillow covers, meaning goods of the same class and description, and that unstitched products like those sold by S/s Rujhan Studio do not fall under this entry.

case_name: The ESI Corporation vs. M/s. Radhika Theatre
text: Case: The ESI Corporation vs. M/s. Radhika Theatre. Date: 20th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the ESI Act, specifically the amendment inserting Sub-section (6) of Section 1 effective from 20.10.1989, should apply retrospectively to an establishment that was established prior to the amendment date, and whether demand notices issued by the ESI Corporation post-20.10.1989 were valid. The High Court allowed the appeal by M/s. Radhika Theatre and set aside the demand notices issued by the ESI Corporation for the period post-20.10.1989, holding that the amendment to Section 1 of the ESI Act should not be applied retrospectively. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in its decision and clarified that the amendment to Section 1 inserting Sub-section (6) should apply to all establishments post-20.10.1989, regardless of their establishment date, and the demand notices issued after this date were valid. The ESI Corporation argued that the ESI Act is a social welfare legislation intended for the welfare of workmen, and that Sub-section (6) of Section 1 should apply to all establishments regardless of the number of employees, effective from 20.10.1989. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the demand notices for the period post-20.10.1989, ruling in favor of the ESI Corporation. The High Court interpreted the amendment as not applicable retrospectively, even for periods post-20.10.1989, while the Supreme Court viewed the amendment as applicable to all establishments regardless of their establishment date, effective from 20.10.1989, aligning with the Act's objective of social welfare.

case_name: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.
text: Case: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.. Date: 4th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue addressed was the legality of certain amendments and modifications made by the Central Government to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995, specifically related to the determination of pensionable salary and the impact of the 2014 amendments which capped the salary at Rs. 15,000 for pension calculations. The 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 included raising the maximum pensionable salary to Rs. 15,000 per month, requiring employees drawing more than Rs. 15,000 per month to contribute at an additional rate of 1.16%, and changing the computation of pensionable salary to be based on the average monthly pay drawn during the contributory period of service in the span of 60 months preceding the date of exit. The Kerala High Court ruled that the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 were invalid. The court held that the amendments were arbitrary, especially the capping of the salary at Rs. 15,000 for pension calculations and the requirement for employees to contribute an additional 1.16% on salaries exceeding Rs. 15,000. The court found that these amendments deprived employees of benefits without any justification. The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeals against the High Court judgements, thereby upholding the legality of the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The court acknowledged the financial implications of the scheme and the need for sustainable pension funding, agreeing with the Central Government's amendments. The key arguments made by the employees were that the 2014 amendments were arbitrary and deprived them of their rightful pension benefits. They argued that the capping of the pensionable salary at Rs. 15,000 was unrealistic and deprived them of a decent pension. They also contended that the additional 1.16% contribution lacked statutory backing and that the amendments unfairly penalized employees who had been contributing on actual salaries exceeding the previous cap. The judgement in the case of R.C. Gupta and Others vs. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner was significant as it addressed the issue of entitlement of members whose pensionable salary exceeded the ceiling limit to exercise an option under the proviso to paragraph 11(3) of the scheme. The Supreme Court held that the dates specified in clause 11(3) were not cut-off dates and that a beneficial scheme should not be defeated by a cut-off date, especially when employers had contributed based on actual salaries. The Supreme Court's final decision was to uphold the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The court recognized the financial sustainability concerns raised by the Central Government and found that the amendments were necessary to ensure the continued viability of the pension scheme.

case_name: The Employees State Insurance Corporation vs. M/s Texmo Industries
text: Case: The Employees State Insurance Corporation vs. M/s Texmo Industries. Date: 8th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether 'wages' as defined in Section 2(22) of the Employees State Insurance (ESI) Act would include Conveyance Allowance paid by the Respondent Company to its employees. The inspection revealed discrepancies in wages and consequential short payment towards Employees State Insurance contributions, totaling Rs. 21,52,829/-, including Rs. 9,48,517/- towards Conveyance Allowance. The Respondent Company argued that the Corporation had erroneously included Conveyance Allowance, leave salary, etc., which did not constitute wages as defined in Section 2(22) of the ESI Act. The Employees' State Insurance Court allowed the petition by the Respondent Company and set aside the claim of Rs. 9,48,517/- in respect of Conveyance Allowance, ruling that it did not form part of wages under the ESI Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the Employees' State Insurance Court's order that Conveyance Allowance did not constitute wages under the ESI Act. Section 2(22) of the ESI Act defines 'wages' to include all remuneration paid to an employee, but explicitly excludes any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession. The Court held that Conveyance Allowance is in the nature of travelling allowance and therefore excluded from 'wages'. The Supreme Court held that there is no cogent reason to treat Conveyance Allowance differently from Travelling Allowance, as both serve the purpose of enabling employees to reach their place of work and are excluded from 'wages' under the ESI Act. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition filed by the Employees State Insurance Corporation, upholding the decisions of the High Court and the Employees' State Insurance Court that Conveyance Allowance is not part of 'wages' under the ESI Act.

case_name: The Enforcement Officer vs. Mohammed Akram
text: Case: The Enforcement Officer vs. Mohammed Akram. Date: 17th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. Mohammed Akram was charged under Section 56(1)(ii) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973, for allegedly releasing substantial foreign exchange based on bogus documents. The case involved M/s Pheroze Framrose, an authorized money changer, which allegedly released foreign exchange worth Rs.50 crores based on bogus documents. Mohammed Akram and two others were accused of involvement in this illegal activity. The Special Court dismissed the complaint and acquitted Mohammed Akram on the grounds that the summons issued by the Enforcement Directorate were not duly served on the respondent personally, and the authorities failed to prove the valid service of summons. The High Court dismissed the appeal, following the judgement of the Kerala High Court in the Itty case, holding that disobedience of summons for appearance does not amount to contravention of the provisions of FERA, 1973. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision to be incorrect, stating that disobedience to respond to summons issued under Section 40(3) FERA amounts to an offence under Section 56 of FERA, 1973. The Supreme Court relied on its earlier judgement in Enforcement Director and Anr. v. M.Samba Siva Rao and Ors., which clarified that failure to obey summons under Section 40(1) of FERA amounts to a contravention of the Act and is punishable under Section 56. The Supreme Court noted that the question of service under Section 40(3) of FERA was irrelevant at this point, as Mohammed Akram was represented by an advocate before the trial court, indicating his awareness of the proceedings. The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the High Court and allowed the appeals, thereby reinstating the charges against Mohammed Akram under Section 56 of FERA, 1973. The Supreme Court resolved the divergence by affirming that non-compliance with summons issued under Section 40 of FERA constitutes a contravention of the Act, irrespective of whether it involves a monetary value, thus falling under the ambit of Section 56. The Special Court's findings on the invalid service of summons were significant as they formed the basis for the initial acquittal, which was later overturned by the Supreme Court's decision emphasizing the respondent's representation by an advocate in the trial court.

case_name: The Executive Engineer, M.I.W. vs. Vitthal Damodar Patil & Anr.
text: Case: The Executive Engineer, M.I.W. vs. Vitthal Damodar Patil & Anr.. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the enhancement of compensation for land acquired for the construction of a Minor Irrigation Tank at Village Pimpri, Block Dambhurni, Taluka Pachora, District Jalgaon, Maharashtra. The respondents claimed higher compensation based on the valuation report dated 10th October 1998, prepared by Mr. Ravindra Ghanshyam Chaudhari, and the evidence of the valuer regarding the fruit-bearing trees and the agricultural yield. The appellant argued that the High Court failed to consider the entire evidence properly and mechanically accepted the valuation report of Mr. Ravindra Ghanshyam Chaudhari without proper analysis of his competency and the methodology used in the valuation. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court misapplied the decision in the case of Chindha Fakira Patil and failed to properly analyze the evidence and the cross-examination of the valuer. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and remanded the matter back to the High Court for fresh consideration on its own merits. This judgment underscores the importance of thorough and proper analysis of all evidence, including valuation reports and cross-examinations, in land acquisition compensation cases to ensure just and fair compensation. Future valuation reports should be prepared by qualified and competent valuers, with thorough documentation and evidence to support their methodology and findings, ensuring transparency and accuracy to withstand legal scrutiny.

case_name: The Government of Andhra Pradesh & Ors. vs. Grace Sathyavathy Shashikant & Ors.
text: Case: The Government of Andhra Pradesh & Ors. vs. Grace Sathyavathy Shashikant & Ors.. Date: 1st October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the determination of the exact location of Survey No. 129/45/D in Jubilee Hills, Sheikpet, Hyderabad, and whether the land allotted to Andhra Prabha Publications falls within this survey number. The learned Single Judge held that the Urban Land Ceiling proceedings had abated and ordered a survey to determine if the 8,000 square meters of land allotted to Andhra Prabha Publications was in fact Survey No. 129/45/D. If so, the allotment would be set aside. The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the judgment of the learned Single Judge. However, this decision was later overturned by the Supreme Court on 16th August 2017, which restored the directions of the learned Single Judge. The Supreme Court ordered the Government to demarcate Survey No. 129/45/D within eight weeks. The Court rejected the Committee Report dated 2nd July 2018, which claimed that no such land existed. The final survey report identified that a portion of land now demarcated in Plot No. 129/45/D to an extent of Ac.0-38½ gts and the remaining portion as per the compromise deed in S.A. No. 354/2 of 1954-55 admeasuring Ac. 2-22½ gts. It concluded that the land allotted to Andhra Prabha is located in TS.No. 19/p, Block-K, Ward No. 12 of Shaikpet village. The Supreme Court rejected the second survey report and declared that the land at Survey No. 19/P, marked as 'PQRS' in the survey report, is actually Survey No. 129/45/D. The Court directed Andhra Prabha Publications to deliver the land to the appellants within eight weeks and for the Government to refund any payments made by Andhra Prabha Publications.

case_name: The Greater Mohali Area Development Authority vs. Arminderjit Kaur & Anr.
text: Case: The Greater Mohali Area Development Authority vs. Arminderjit Kaur & Anr.. Date: 26th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the interim orders passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, directing the Greater Mohali Area Development Authority to deposit a certain amount as compensation for land acquisition, which was challenged by the appellant. The Land Acquisition Officer initially offered compensation to the landowners at the rate of Rs. 1.36 crore per acre. The Civil Court (Reference Court) enhanced the compensation payable to the landowners to Rs. 3.8686925 crores per acre. The High Court directed the Greater Mohali Area Development Authority to deposit Rs. 3.50 crores per acre along with statutory benefits within three months, allowing the landowners to withdraw the amount. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's order by directing the Greater Mohali Area Development Authority to deposit the entire awarded sum within three months. The landowners were allowed to withdraw 50% of the amount on furnishing solvent security, with the remaining 50% to be invested in an FDR Scheme in any Nationalized Bank. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to dispose of the appeals finally, preferably within a year.

case_name: The Home Secretary (Prison) vs. H. Nilofer Nisha
text: Case: The Home Secretary (Prison) vs. H. Nilofer Nisha. Date: 23rd January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether a writ of habeas corpus would lie for securing the release of a person undergoing a sentence of imprisonment imposed by a court of competent jurisdiction, on the grounds of some Government orders or rules providing for pre-mature release of prisoners. The Governor of Tamil Nadu issued G.O.(Ms.) No.64 dated 1st February 2018 through the Home (Prison-IV) Department, which framed a scheme for considering the cases of pre-mature release of convicted prisoners on the occasion of the Birth Centenary of Shri M.G. Ramachandran, former Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. The key criteria included the formation of a State level committee headed by the Inspector General of Prisons to examine the cases of life convict prisoners for premature release under Article 161 of the Constitution, in commemoration of the Birthday Centenary of Shri M.G. Ramachandran. The High Court allowed the writs of habeas corpus and ordered the detenus to be released forthwith in terms of G.O.(Ms.) No.64 dated 1st February 2018, unless their presence was required in any other case. The State challenged the High Court's decision on the grounds that the High Court transgressed its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution while issuing the writ of habeas corpus and that the petitioners were convicted of serious offences, including murder, which had been upheld till the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court directed the competent authority to consider the representation of the detenu within six weeks and decide the same, with a reasoned order to be passed if the plea was rejected. The detenu was given the liberty to challenge the order before the High Court.

case_name: The Idol of Sri Renganathaswamy vs P K Thoppulan Chettiar, Ramanuja Koodam Anandhana Trust & Ors.
text: Case: The Idol of Sri Renganathaswamy vs P K Thoppulan Chettiar, Ramanuja Koodam Anandhana Trust & Ors.. Date: 19th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Deed of Settlement dated 8th July 1901 created a specific endowment in favor of The Idol of Sri Renganathaswamy and whether the sale of the trust property could be sanctioned by a civil court or required the approval of the Commissioner under the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959. The Deed of Settlement specified that the property was purchased for performing charitable work related to Sri Renganathaswamy sanctum, including distributing millet porridge and providing water during certain Hindu festivals. It also prohibited the sale or mortgage of the property and directed his descendants to continue the charitable activities from their business income. The Second Additional Subordinate Judge decreed in favor of the first respondent (the trust), allowing the sale of the suit property to the fourth respondent and ruled that the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 did not apply as the trust was a private trust and not a public religious trust. The Principal District Judge, Tiruchirapalli, upheld the decision of the trial court, agreeing that the Deed of Settlement did not vest the property in the appellant idol and that the Act of 1959 did not apply because the trust was a private trust, not a public religious trust. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the High Court and dismissed the suit filed by the first respondent, ruling that the Deed of Settlement created a specific endowment as regulated by the Act of 1959. The Court held that the civil court lacked jurisdiction and that the sale of the trust property required the approval of the Commissioner under the Act of 1959. The Supreme Court specified that any alienation of the suit property by the trust must be sanctioned by the Commissioner under Section 34 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, which requires the Commissioner's approval and consideration of objections and suggestions from interested parties.

case_name: The Joint Labour Commissioner and Registering Officer and Anr vs. Kesar Lal
text: Case: The Joint Labour Commissioner and Registering Officer and Anr vs. Kesar Lal. Date: 17th March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether a construction worker registered under the Building and Other Construction Workers' (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, is a 'consumer' within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Kesar Lal submitted an application for financial assistance of Rs 51,000 under the welfare scheme for the marriage of his daughter. The application was rejected due to technical defects such as incomplete application forms, incorrect birth certificates, and submission after the marriage date, among other issues. The State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission set aside the order of the District Forum and directed the appellants to pay Rs 51,000 to Kesar Lal along with compensation and interest. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission affirmed the State Commission's decision but reduced the rate of interest from 18% to 9% per annum. The appellants argued that the welfare schemes are funded by a cess collected from employers and not by contributions from the beneficiaries, and hence the services provided are not for a 'consideration' making the beneficiaries not 'consumers' under the Act. The Supreme Court held that the construction workers are 'consumers' because they contribute to the welfare fund, and the services provided by the welfare board are not rendered free of charge, thereby falling within the definition of 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the decision to award financial assistance to Kesar Lal and affirming the applicability of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, to the services provided under the welfare scheme.

case_name: The Karnataka Housing Board & Anr. vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.
text: Case: The Karnataka Housing Board & Anr. vs. State of Karnataka & Ors.. Date: 28th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The High Court emphasized that sanctioning of a housing scheme by the State Government under Section 24(2) of the Karnataka Housing Board Act was a mandatory requirement before initiating land acquisition proceedings. The Supreme Court held that Section 33(2) of the Karnataka Housing Board Act allows for the initiation of land acquisition proceedings independently, even before the finalization and sanction of a housing scheme, as long as the land is intended for a contemplated scheme. The Supreme Court predicted that requiring prior scheme sanction could delay the execution of housing projects and undermine the purpose of the Karnataka Housing Board Act to address housing needs efficiently. The respondents argued that the acquisition notifications were issued before the housing scheme was finalized and sanctioned, depriving landowners of the opportunity to effectively raise objections under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act. The Supreme Court clarified that the judgment in Mohammed Yousef's case, which required scheme finalization before land acquisition, was not applicable to the Karnataka Housing Board Act due to differences in statutory provisions.

case_name: The Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. Sri Kalappa M. Sankad (D) Thr. Lrs. & Ors.
text: Case: The Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. Sri Kalappa M. Sankad (D) Thr. Lrs. & Ors.. Date: 12th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the challenge to the termination of Mr. Kalappa M. Sankad's services by the Life Insurance Corporation (LIC) and the subsequent legal battle involving his reinstatement and payment of back wages after his death. The learned Single Judge allowed Mr. Kalappa M. Sankad's writ petition, set aside the termination order, and directed his reinstatement in service. The High Court of Karnataka dismissed LIC's intra-court appeal and upheld the order of the learned Single Judge, which had set aside Mr. Kalappa's termination and directed his reinstatement. The Supreme Court did not interfere with the High Court's decision because it found no good ground to uphold the termination order and agreed with the lower courts that the termination was not justified. The Supreme Court directed LIC to pay back wages amounting to Rs. 20,57,107.18 minus deductions of Rs. 12,59,313.18, resulting in a balance to be paid to the respondents after verification and calculation. The court set a three-month deadline for this payment. The deductions included Provident Fund contribution of Rs. 1,69,771.00, Income Tax of Rs. 4,00,000.00, and recovery against loans and advances availed by Mr. Kalappa amounting to Rs. 2,28,023.00, totaling Rs. 12,59,313.18. The Supreme Court clarified that it did not accept the respondents' claim for arrears of salary based on several pay rises and notional promotions, as it was not legally sustainable in the facts of this case.

case_name: The Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs Babulal Lade & Ors
text: Case: The Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs Babulal Lade & Ors. Date: 4th December 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The issue was whether the employees' dues could take precedence over the claims of the secured creditor, The Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank Ltd., from the proceeds of the sale of the mortgaged assets under the SARFAESI Act. The High Court modified the order to clarify that the recovery certificate issued for employees' dues should be directed to the Collector, who would recover the amount from the sale proceeds held by the Appellant-Bank. The Supreme Court held that Section 529A of the Companies Act, which prioritizes employees' dues, does not apply to co-operative societies as explicitly barred by Section 167 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act. The Court ruled that employees' dues recoverable as arrears of land revenue under Section 50 do not create a paramount charge but take precedence only over unsecured claims. The sale letter indicated that the Appellant-Bank undertook responsibility for employees' dues, which was binding as part of the sale contract and displaced the general distribution order under Section 13(7) of the SARFAESI Act.

case_name: The Manager, Corporate Educational Agency vs. James Mathew & Ors.
text: Case: The Manager, Corporate Educational Agency vs. James Mathew & Ors.. Date: 11th July 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the management of a minority educational institution has the right to appoint a Headmaster of their choice, bypassing senior qualified teachers from the same community. The High Court held that the management of the minority educational institution cannot overlook the qualified and senior teachers belonging to the same community when appointing a Headmaster. The Supreme Court ruled that the management of a minority educational institution has the right to appoint a Headmaster of their choice, and this right is protected under Article 30(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court referred to previous judgments, including Secy. Malankara Syrian Catholic College vs. T. Jose and Others, TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka, and others, to support the management's right to appoint a Headmaster of their choice. The Supreme Court stated that the declaration of minority status by the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions is a recognition of an existing fact and applies retrospectively. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, upheld the minority institution's right to appoint a Headmaster of their choice, and allowed the appeals.

case_name: The Municipal Committee, Barwala vs Jai Narayan & Company & Anr.
text: Case: The Municipal Committee, Barwala vs Jai Narayan & Company & Anr.. Date: 29th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The auction was conducted at a rate of Rs. 2,32,000 per acre, and Jai Narayan & Company emerged as the highest bidder for the land measuring 55 kanals 5 marlas. The Supreme Court found the auction and subsequent decree invalid because the sale was not confirmed by the State Government, as required under the Haryana Municipalities Management of Municipal Properties and State Properties Rules, 1976. The Supreme Court directed the Municipality to take possession of the land immediately and submit a compliance report within three months. The Supreme Court ordered that the amount of Rs. 15,76,150 deposited by the plaintiff be forfeited as damages for the illegal occupation of the land for over 20 years. This judgment underscores the necessity for municipal bodies to secure required approvals from the State Government before finalizing auctions, ensuring adherence to statutory provisions.

case_name: The Municipal Corporation, Faridabad vs Modern School, Faridabad & Ors.
text: Case: The Municipal Corporation, Faridabad vs Modern School, Faridabad & Ors.. Date: 8th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether the Municipal Corporation can levy user charges on the schools for discharging waste water into the municipal sewer system. The office order was issued to regularize tubewells and prevent unauthorized discharges of waste water into the municipal sewer system, and to impose charges based on the diameter of the tubewells. Modern School responded that the tubewell was installed to meet the school's water demand due to insufficient municipal water supply and that it was registered with the Central Ground Water Board. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision unsustainable because the user charges were for municipal services provided for waste water discharge and did not require state approval as per Sections 87 or 88 of the Act. The registration with the Central Ground Water Board signifies that the tubewells were authorized for use, but it does not exempt the schools from paying user charges for discharging waste water into municipal drains. The Municipal Corporation might ensure compliance by strictly enforcing the requirement for prior permission before connecting private drains to municipal drains and by monitoring and regularizing such connections.

case_name: The National Medical Commission vs. Pooja Thandu Naresh & Ors.
text: Case: The National Medical Commission vs. Pooja Thandu Naresh & Ors.. Date: 29th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the National Medical Commission was justified in denying provisional registration to students who had completed part of their medical education, including clinical training, through online mode due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The students argued that they had completed their medical education abroad, qualified the Screening Test, and were therefore eligible for provisional registration to undergo a one-year internship as per the applicable regulations. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court’s decision, stating that it was not within the Court’s domain to modify academic and clinical training requirements prescribed by statutory regulations. The Court highlighted that allowing provisional registration without actual clinical training would compromise the quality of medical education and healthcare standards in the country. The Supreme Court directed the National Medical Commission to create a one-time scheme to allow students to complete their clinical training in India at designated medical colleges, ensuring they meet the required standards. Regulation 4(3) mandates that students must complete their entire medical course, including clinical training, at the same foreign institute to be eligible for provisional registration. The Court found that this requirement was not met by the students. The Supreme Court directed the National Medical Commission to frame a one-time scheme within two months to provide clinical training in India for students who missed such training abroad, followed by an assessment before granting provisional registration. The Supreme Court stated that actions by other medical councils granting provisional registration would not justify similar actions by the National Medical Commission if those actions violated statutory requirements.

case_name: The Periyar District Consumer Co-operative Wholesale Stores Ltd. vs B. Balagopal & Ors.
text: Case: The Periyar District Consumer Co-operative Wholesale Stores Ltd. vs B. Balagopal & Ors.. Date: 2nd March 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the compensation for the use of the leased premises should be increased as sought by the plaintiffs and awarded by the Trial Court. The defendant was The Periyar District Consumer Co-operative Wholesale Stores Ltd. The initial monthly rental amount agreed upon was Rs. 6,500/-. The plaintiffs filed the suit seeking damages at the rate of Rs. 89,000/- per month for the period from 14.07.2000 to 14.07.2003. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the defendant, upholding the Trial Court's judgment and decree. The defendant argued that the enhanced rent awarded by the Trial Court was not justified, and that the defendant had already vacated the premises as agreed in the earlier round of litigation. The Supreme Court suggested that the parties arrive at an amicable settlement to avoid further litigation. The Supreme Court modified the judgment and decree, holding that the defendant should pay a total sum of Rs. 17,50,000/- as lump sum damages for the period from 14.07.2000 to 17.07.2003. The decision might set a precedent for a balanced approach in determining rental compensation, considering both the tenant's financial capacity and the fair market value of the property. If the defendant fails to pay the balance of Rs. 7,50,000/- within three months, the amount will carry an interest rate of 12% per annum from the expiry of three months until the date of payment. The Supreme Court decided to reduce the compensation amount considering the financial position of the defendant, a Consumer Co-operative Wholesale Store, and the need to balance equities.

case_name: The Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-1 vs M/s. Bajaj Herbals Pvt. Ltd.
text: Case: The Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-1 vs M/s. Bajaj Herbals Pvt. Ltd.. Date: 7th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's order dismissing the tax appeal filed by the Revenue, stating that the questions proposed by the Revenue were factual and not substantial questions of law, was correct. The Revenue filed an appeal because the High Court dismissed their tax appeal without providing independent reasoning or addressing the factual matrix of the case, merely stating that the proposed questions were not substantial questions of law. The High Court dismissed the Revenue's appeal by stating that none of the proposed questions by the Revenue could be termed as substantial questions of law and that all the questions proposed were on factual aspects of the matter. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court's order for being a non-speaking and non-reasoned order, lacking independent reasoning and not recording the submissions made on behalf of the Revenue. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order, remanding the matter back to the High Court to decide and dispose of the appeal afresh in accordance with law and on its own merits, and to pass a speaking and reasoned order after recording the submissions made by the respective parties. The Supreme Court allowed the Revenue's appeal to the extent of quashing the High Court's order and remanding the matter back to the High Court for a fresh decision with proper reasoning and consideration of the submissions. The Supreme Court's decision might ensure that High Courts provide detailed reasoning and proper consideration of factual matrices in tax appeals, preventing dismissal of appeals based solely on the nature of questions proposed by the Revenue. The Supreme Court clarified that High Courts must provide independent reasoning and address the factual matrix of the case when determining whether the questions proposed by the Revenue are substantial questions of law. This judgment may prompt High Courts to draft more detailed and reasoned orders in tax matters, ensuring that they thoroughly address the factual and legal issues raised in the appeals. If the High Court does not comply with the Supreme Court's directive, it could result in further appeals and potential reprimand for not adhering to the higher court's instructions, possibly undermining the credibility of its decisions. High Courts should consider providing detailed reasoning and addressing the factual matrices of the case to ensure that their dismissal of tax appeals is based on a thorough examination of the legal and factual issues involved.

case_name: The Project Director, Project Implementation Unit vs. P.V. Krishnamoorthy & Ors.
text: Case: The Project Director, Project Implementation Unit vs. P.V. Krishnamoorthy & Ors.. Date: 8th December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the legality of notifications issued under Section 3A(1) of the National Highways Act, 1956, for the acquisition of specified lands for the development/construction of the Chennai-Krishnagiri-Salem National Corridor. The project associated with the land acquisition was the Bharatmala Pariyojna - Phase I, specifically for the development of the Chennai-Krishnagiri-Salem (National Corridor) and Chennai-Madurai (Economic Corridor). The High Court held that the notifications issued under Section 3A(1) of the National Highways Act, 1956, for land acquisition were illegal and bad in law. The grounds included lack of prior environmental clearance and the allegation that the acquisition was a colorable exercise of power and not for a genuine public purpose. The Bharatmala Pariyojna - Phase I project was conceived to optimize the efficiency of freight and passenger movement across the country by bridging critical infrastructure gaps through the development of economic corridors, inter-corridors, feeder routes, and other key infrastructure. The High Court held that prior environmental clearance was imperative before issuing notifications under Section 3A(1) of the National Highways Act, 1956. The High Court noted that the procedure adopted by the NHAI in appointing the Consultant and making decisions regarding the land acquisition was flawed, lacking proper scrutiny and compliance with standard operating procedures. The High Court allowed the writ petitions, quashed the land acquisition proceedings, and directed that the revenue records be reverted back to the names of the respective landowners.

case_name: The Secretary to Govt. Department of Education (Primary) & Ors. vs. Bheemesh Alias Bheemappa
text: Case: The Secretary to Govt. Department of Education (Primary) & Ors. vs. Bheemesh Alias Bheemappa. Date: 16th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the order passed by the Karnataka State Administrative Tribunal, confirmed by the High Court, directing the appellants to consider the case of the respondent for appointment on compassionate grounds. The respondent's sister, who was employed as an Assistant Teacher in a Government School, died in harness on 8th December 2010, leading the respondent to seek appointment on compassionate grounds. The request was rejected because the amendment to the Karnataka Civil Services (Appointment on Compassionate Grounds) Rules, 2012, which extended benefits to the unmarried dependant brother of an unmarried female employee, was not applicable to the case of the respondent. The Tribunal allowed the respondent's application, holding that the amendment to the Rules on 20th June 2012 would apply retrospectively to cover the respondent's case, even though his sister died in harness on 8th December 2010. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, upholding the Tribunal's decision that the amendment to the Rules was retrospective in nature. The Supreme Court emphasized that appointments on compassionate grounds are an exception to the regular mode of recruitment and must adhere to the mandate of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, providing succor to the family of the deceased Government servant. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the High Court and the Tribunal, and dismissed the respondent's application for compassionate appointment.

case_name: The Secretary, Land & Building Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi & Ors. vs. Om Prakash (Dead) Through LRs. & Ors.
text: Case: The Secretary, Land & Building Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi & Ors. vs. Om Prakash (Dead) Through LRs. & Ors.. Date: 20th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the land acquisition proceedings initiated in 1965 and concluded in 1981 were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. The High Court of Delhi declared that the land acquisition proceedings were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act due to the non-payment of full compensation to the landowners. The land in question was acquired in 1965, with the award declared in 1981. Possession of the land was taken and handed over to the beneficiary department on 23rd September 1981, but the payment of compensation could not be ascertained due to the torn condition of the Naksha Muntzamin. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision unsustainable in light of the Constitution Bench's ruling in the Indore Development Authority case, which clarified that for Section 24(2) to apply, both possession and compensation must not have been taken and paid, respectively. Since possession was taken, the proceedings did not lapse. The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's judgment, ruling that the land acquisition proceedings were valid and had not lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act. The appeals by the Land and Building Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi, and the Delhi Development Authority were allowed. The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set by the Constitution Bench in the Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors. case, which clarified the interpretation of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act and the conditions under which land acquisition proceedings lapse.

case_name: The Silppi Constructions Contractors vs. Union of India and Anr.
text: Case: The Silppi Constructions Contractors vs. Union of India and Anr.. Date: 21st June 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the rejection of the technical bids of The Silppi Constructions Contractors by the tendering authorities, and the subsequent appeals and writ petitions regarding the rejection. The technical bids were rejected because the petitioner did not satisfy the eligibility criteria, and there were adverse remarks against the petitioner's sister company, Silppi Realtors and Contractors Pvt. Ltd. The learned single judge allowed the writ petition, directing the respondents to consider the financial bid of the petitioner. The division bench, however, allowed the writ appeals, emphasizing limited interference in contractual matters and upholding the rejection based on adverse remarks against the sister company. The petitioner argued that the adverse remarks against its sister company should not affect its own bid, as the sister company had not renewed its enlistment and the remarks were not justified. The Supreme Court held that in purely administrative decisions, such as rejecting tenders, the authority is not required to give reasons at every stage, as this could hinder the commercial activities of the state. The Supreme Court found that the petitioner firm was not eligible to submit the tender as it was not an enlisted contractor in the 'SS' Class and did not meet the necessary criteria. The Supreme Court accepted the use of adverse remarks because the petitioner firm and the sister company were related firms with a business relationship, and the sister company had not challenged or addressed the adverse remarks. The Supreme Court stated that making all tenderers parties in a writ petition is not always necessary, especially if the writ petition challenges the rejection of a technical bid at an early stage before any successful tenderer is determined. This judgement could reinforce the principle of limited judicial interference in tender processes, emphasizing that public sector undertakings have the discretion to make administrative decisions without constant judicial scrutiny. The broader implications might include a stricter adherence to eligibility criteria and a heightened scrutiny of business relationships between related firms, potentially leading to more careful compliance by private contractors when dealing with government tenders. The Supreme Court reiterated that judicial review in contract matters should be exercised with great restraint, only intervening in cases of clear arbitrariness, irrationality, mala fides, or bias.

case_name: The State (GNCT of Delhi) Narcotics Control Bureau vs. Lokesh Chadha
text: Case: The State (GNCT of Delhi) Narcotics Control Bureau vs. Lokesh Chadha. Date: 2nd March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the suspension of Lokesh Chadha's sentence by the High Court, which the Narcotics Control Bureau appealed against. Lokesh Chadha was convicted under Sections 23(c) and 25A of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, for offenses involving heroin and pseudoephedrine. The parcels contained 325 grams of heroin and 390 grams of pseudoephedrine. Lokesh Chadha was the proprietor of the courier agency that accepted the parcels for booking to a foreign destination, allegedly acting in complicity with a foreign national. The Special Judge convicted Lokesh Chadha but granted the benefit of doubt to the co-accused, who was an employee acting at Chadha's behest. The High Court suspended the sentence due to the period already served by Chadha, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, and the likely delay in hearing the appeal. The High Court imposed conditions including not leaving the NCT of Delhi without prior permission, appearing before the Court as required, and promptly informing of any change of address. The Bureau argued that under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, bail should only be granted if there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and will not commit further offenses. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, ruling that no case for suspension of sentence under Section 389(1) of CrPC was established. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to take up the appeal for hearing and final disposal by the end of 2021, upon Lokesh Chadha's surrender to the sentence. Section 37 of the NDPS Act stipulates that no person accused of certain offenses shall be released on bail unless there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offense while on bail.

case_name: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane
text: Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane. Date: 26th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the discharge of P. Soupramaniane from service due to his conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude under Section 324 IPC was justified under Section 10(1)(b)(i) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. P. Soupramaniane was discharged from service because he was convicted by a criminal court for an offence involving moral turpitude, specifically under Section 324 IPC for voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons. The Division Bench of the Madras High Court set aside the order of discharge and directed the reinstatement of P. Soupramaniane, with the condition that he would receive 1/4th of his salary as back wages from the date of discharge until reinstatement. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's reasoning, stating that the release on probation by the criminal court did not entitle an employee to claim a right to continue in service if convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude. However, the Supreme Court examined whether the offence under Section 324 IPC involved moral turpitude. The Supreme Court considered factors such as the nature of the act, the motive behind it, whether it shocked the moral conscience of society, and the circumstances of the case. The Court concluded that the offence did not involve moral turpitude. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the High Court, concluding that P. Soupramaniane's offence did not involve moral turpitude, and therefore, he should not be discharged from service. The appeal by the State Bank of India was dismissed.

case_name: The State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs T. Gangi Reddy @ Yerra Gangi Reddy
text: Case: The State Through Central Bureau of Investigation vs T. Gangi Reddy @ Yerra Gangi Reddy. Date: 16th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the bail granted to the accused under Section 167(2) of the Cr.P.C. could be cancelled on merits after the filing of the chargesheet. The charges against T. Gangi Reddy included conspiracy to murder, tampering with evidence, and threatening witnesses in the case related to the death of Y.S. Vivekananda Reddy. The High Court dismissed the CBI's petition to cancel the bail granted to T. Gangi Reddy, stating that once default bail is granted under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C., it cannot be cancelled on merits. case_name: The State by S.P. Through CBI vs. Uttamchand Bohra
text: Case: The State by S.P. Through CBI vs. Uttamchand Bohra. Date: 9th December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Uttamchand Bohra was charged with abetment and conspiracy under Section 120B IPC and Section 109 IPC, along with aiding a public servant in amassing disproportionate assets under Section 13(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The principal accused, A-1, a senior official in the Income Tax Department, was accused of amassing wealth disproportionate to his known sources of income, amounting to ₹2,32,20,296. The sale deed of a property allegedly purchased by A-1 through M/s Raviteja Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. was seized from Uttamchand's residence. Uttamchand Bohra argued that mere possession of the sale deed did not incriminate him, as it did not establish conspiracy or abetment with A-1. The High Court held that possession of the sale deed and the employee's signature on the document did not constitute reasonable suspicion of conspiracy or abetment. The company was allegedly used as a front by A-1 to purchase the property through funds routed from various sources, as part of amassing disproportionate assets. The Supreme Court emphasized that evidence must show a clear agreement to commit an illegal act, supported by either direct or circumstantial evidence. The Supreme Court upheld the decision as there was no material evidence linking Uttamchand Bohra to the money trail or conspiracy, and mere possession of the sale deed was insufficient for framing charges. The Supreme Court reiterated that mere suspicion or surmise, without cogent evidence, cannot be the basis for framing charges or sustaining a criminal trial. The Supreme Court dismissed the CBI's appeal and upheld the High Court's decision to discharge Uttamchand Bohra, citing lack of sufficient evidence.

case_name: The State of Arunachal Pradesh vs. Ramchandra Rabidas @ Ratan Rabidas & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Arunachal Pradesh vs. Ramchandra Rabidas @ Ratan Rabidas & Anr.. Date: 4th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue addressed was whether the Gauhati High Court was justified in directing that road traffic offences should be dealt with exclusively under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and not under the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The Gauhati High Court directed that road traffic offences should be dealt with only under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and held that prosecution under the provisions of the IPC would be unsustainable in law. The Supreme Court held that there is no conflict between the provisions of the IPC and the MV Act and that both statutes operate in different spheres. Therefore, prosecution can lie under both the IPC and the MV Act for road traffic offences. The Supreme Court stated that the punishment under the IPC for road traffic offences is stricter and more proportionate compared to the MV Act. For example, the maximum imprisonment under the IPC for certain offences can go up to 10 years, while under the MV Act, it is up to six months. The Supreme Court noted that offences under Chapter XIII of the MV Act are compoundable, whereas offences under Sections 279, 304 Part II, and 304A of the IPC are not. Therefore, allowing only the MV Act to govern road traffic offences would result in lighter penalties for serious offences. The Supreme Court emphasized that the MV Act is a beneficial legislation aimed at providing a statutory scheme for compensation to victims of motor vehicle accidents. It also stated that the Act was not intended to override the IPC concerning convictions for motor vehicle accidents.

case_name: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
text: Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.. Date: 30th January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the direction by the High Court to provide financial assistance for payment of arrears and current pension to the employees of the Anugraha Narayan Sinha Institute of Social Studies, Patna. The Division Bench ordered the appellant to provide financial assistance for payment of arrears and current pension to the employees of the Institute. The Institute is incorporated by the Anugraha Narayan Sinha Institute of Social Studies Act, 1964, and is governed by a Board of Control, which includes nominees and representatives from the State Government, Indian Council of Social Science Research, University Grants Commission, and other educational institutions. The State Government is mandated to contribute a sum of rupees two lacs in each financial year for the maintenance of the Institute, and it may also contribute additional sums for special items of research, education work, publication, buildings, and proper maintenance and development of the Institute. The High Court allowed the writ petition on the grounds that the State Government had earmarked grants under the pension head in previous years and had provided funds for the payment of pensions, thereby creating a legitimate expectation for the employees that they would receive pensions. The Supreme Court found that the order of the Division Bench of the High Court was not legally sustainable and allowed the appeal, dismissing the writ petition and ruling that the State Government was not obligated to pay the pensions as the retirement benefit scheme was to be operated from the Institute's own resources. The Supreme Court stated that legitimate expectation cannot be claimed as a right and must be founded on the sanction of law or custom or an established procedure. The past payment of pensions by the State did not create an enforceable right for the Institute or its employees.

case_name: The State of Bihar & Ors. vs. M/S. Brahmaputra Infrastructure Limited
text: Case: The State of Bihar & Ors. vs. M/S. Brahmaputra Infrastructure Limited. Date: 22nd March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 (6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was valid, given the existence of the Bihar Public Works Contracts Arbitration Tribunal Act, 2008. The appellant argued that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was excluded by the Bihar Public Works Contracts Arbitration Tribunal Act, 2008, and therefore the appointment of an arbitrator under the Central Act was not valid. The court decided that the Bihar Public Works Contracts Arbitration Tribunal Act, 2008 did not apply in this case because the parties had an agreement that stipulated the applicability of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The court declared this provision as patently unconstitutional, as it was inconsistent with the constitutional scheme, particularly Article 14 of the Constitution of India, and interfered with the impartiality and independence expected from the Arbitration Tribunal. The appeals were dismissed by the court. The court left open the option for the appellant-State to move the High Court for a change of the State Arbitrator if a case for lack of neutrality was made out.
