case_name: The State of Bihar and Others vs Jawahar Lal Ram and Others
text: Case: The State of Bihar and Others vs Jawahar Lal Ram and Others. Date: 10th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the services of the respondents, who were initially engaged by N.I.C.T. and later absorbed by the Bihar Intermediate Education Council, should be regularized after the Council was merged with the Bihar School Education Examination Board. The Division Bench of the High Court reversed the Single Judge's decision and directed that the respondents be taken back to work and granted honorary benefits for the intervening period. The appellants argued that the Division Bench's decision was flawed as the Single Judge had correctly dismissed the writ petitions based on the respondents' failure to meet the conditions of the regularization scheme. The Supreme Court noted that the Division Bench had not provided sufficient reasoning for disagreeing with the Single Judge's findings and emphasized the need for clear justification when overturning a well-reasoned order. The Supreme Court found that the respondents had been continuously working since 1999, initially as employees of N.I.C.T. and later absorbed by the Council, which justified their regularization despite procedural irregularities. The Supreme Court directed that the respondents be absorbed in their respective posts from 2005 and be permitted to rejoin their positions from 1st May 2023, with continuity in service for all purposes including retirement benefits, but without back wages for the period they were out of employment. This decision may set a precedent for the regularization of employees who have been working for extended periods, even if there were procedural lapses, provided they meet certain conditions and their services are essential. Government entities should carefully consider the employees' length of service and contributions before termination, ensuring that procedural requirements are met and any termination is justified with substantial reasoning. The Supreme Court recognized that uprooting the respondents, who had been working since 1999, would have devastating effects on them and their families, which justified a compassionate approach to their regularization. The decision may encourage the creation of more comprehensive and compassionate regularization schemes that take into account long-term service and contributions of employees, ensuring fair treatment even in the presence of procedural irregularities. Non-compliance with the Supreme Court's directives could lead to further legal challenges, potential contempt proceedings, and a loss of credibility for the State Government in handling employment regularization matters.

case_name: The State of Gujarat vs R.J. Pathan and others
text: Case: The State of Gujarat vs R.J. Pathan and others. Date: 24th March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondents, who were initially appointed on a contractual basis for an earthquake redevelopment program, should be regularized and absorbed into government service despite their temporary appointment status. The Division Bench of the High Court directed the State to consider the respondents for regularization and absorption into government service sympathetically, and if necessary, by creating supernumerary posts. The Supreme Court quashed the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court and restored the order of the learned Single Judge, dismissing the writ petition filed by the respondents. The Supreme Court reasoned that the respondents were appointed on a temporary basis for a specific project and not on any regular sanctioned posts. The court held that there was no obligation on the State to regularize or absorb them, especially considering their continued service was due to an interim order by the High Court. The respondents filed a writ petition seeking regularization and absorption into government service after being transferred to the Indian Red Cross Society following the closure of the earthquake redevelopment project they were initially appointed for.

case_name: The State of Gujarat vs. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Gujarat vs. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer & Anr.. Date: 17th July 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the respondents' non-compliance with summons issued under Section 145 of the Central Excise Act, 1944, as made applicable to the service tax and CGST Act 2017, regarding an alleged evasion of Goods and Service Tax Liability. The respondents feared arrest by the concerned officials of the Department. The High Court ruled that the respondents should represent their case before the concerned authority, which was to complete the adjudicatory process within eight weeks, and provided the respondents additional time to fulfill their obligations if necessary. The State of Gujarat appealed because they were dissatisfied with the High Court's order allowing the respondents' writ applications and the stay on the adjudicatory process. The Supreme Court was not convinced with the High Court's disposal and expected the respondents to honor the summons and appear before the authority for interrogation. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power to arrest under the GST Act is statutory, and ordinarily, the writ court should not interfere with such power, especially when the officer has reasons to believe that an offense has been committed. The Supreme Court decided to give the respondents one more opportunity to appear before the authorities for interrogation, failing which the authorities could proceed according to law. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's common order dated 24th December 2018, and disposed of any pending applications. As many as 14 summons had been issued to one of the respondents, but they appeared only once for interrogation. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to appear before the authorities for recording their statements, and if they failed to do so, the authorities could proceed further in accordance with the law.

case_name: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs Hindustan Construction Company Ltd.
text: Case: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs Hindustan Construction Company Ltd.. Date: 15th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the exercise of revisional power under Section 40 of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973, after its repeal by the Haryana Value Added Tax, 2003, was sustainable. The High Court ruled against it because the repeal and saving clause in Section 61 of the Haryana Value Added Tax, 2003, saved only pending proceedings under the former Act, and there were no proceedings pending against the respondent when the new Act came into force. The respondent, Hindustan Construction Company Ltd., argued that the refund was obtained lawfully, and the revisional power exercised by the State to recover the refund was not justified after the repeal of the Act. The Supreme Court concluded that the application of the Punjab General Clauses Act, 1898, was excluded by the express contrary intention manifested in Section 61 of the Haryana Value Added Tax, 2003. The State of Haryana relied on the precedents set in Raymond Ltd. and Anr. vs State of Chhattisgarh & Ors. and Swastik Oil Mills Ltd. vs H.B. Munshi, Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, Bombay, arguing that revisional power should be used to ensure lawful assessments. The State of Haryana issued a show cause notice to Hindustan Construction Company Ltd. on 7th June 2004, regarding the refund ordered earlier, and subsequently, an order for recovery was made on 12th July 2004. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision that the exercise of revisional power under the repealed Act was unsustainable. The decision clarifies that revisional powers cannot be exercised under a repealed statute unless explicitly saved by the new enactment, potentially influencing future cases involving similar circumstances. The Supreme Court clarified that the repeal and saving clause in Section 61 of the Haryana Value Added Tax, 2003, intended to save only pending proceedings and not to reopen matters already closed under the repealed Act. The State of Haryana might ensure that any new enactments clearly articulate the scope of saved proceedings and explicitly address any potential conflicts with the General Clauses Act to avoid similar legal challenges. The Supreme Court found it necessary to consider the factual position to determine if the quality of the land justified the different compensation amounts, emphasizing the importance of accurate factual determination in legal decisions.

case_name: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs. Hira Singh
text: Case: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs. Hira Singh. Date: 2nd May 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the challenge to the High Court's decision declaring that the land acquisition was deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation, and Resettlement Act, 2013. The High Court ruled that the land acquisition was deemed to have lapsed because the compensation amount had not been paid or deposited with the Civil or Reference Court as per Section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The State of Haryana argued that the possession of the lands in question was already taken over and vested with the State Government, and therefore, there should not be any deemed lapse of acquisition. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and remanded the matters back to the High Court to decide afresh in accordance with the law and on its own merits, taking into consideration the law laid down in the case of Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors. The Supreme Court allowed the land owners to make a representation to the State Government under Section 101-A of the Act, 2013, as applicable to the State of Haryana, which should be decided within four months. The Supreme Court requested the High Court to decide and dispose of the writ petitions on remand within nine months from the date of receipt of the order. No, the Supreme Court did not express any opinion on the merits of the case and kept all contentions open for consideration by the High Court in accordance with the law and on its own merits.

case_name: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs. Raj Kumar @ Bittu
text: Case: The State of Haryana & Ors. vs. Raj Kumar @ Bittu. Date: 3rd August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the policies of the State Government regarding remission of sentences for life convicts should apply retroactively and the feasibility of drafting a new policy without leading to discrimination among similarly situated prisoners. The High Court directed the State to consider drafting a new remission policy with retrospective operation while ensuring it does not lead to discrimination among a substantial number of identically situated prisoners. Article 161 of the Constitution grants the Governor of a State the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute the sentence of any person convicted of an offence. The key policies discussed were the policy dated 12th April 2002, which provided for the consideration of premature release after 14 years of actual imprisonment and the policy dated 13th August 2008, which replaced the previous policies and outlined conditions for premature release based on the nature of the crime. The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 433-A restricts the power of the appropriate Government to release a person sentenced to life imprisonment for an offence punishable with death until they have served at least 14 years of imprisonment. The Supreme Court held that the policy dated 13th August 2008, being statutory in nature, supersedes earlier policies and applies to cases of premature release, but the power under Article 161 of the Constitution allows the Governor to grant remission independently of Section 433-A. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's directions and held that the prisoner, having completed 12 years and 25 days of imprisonment, could only be considered for premature release under the policy dated 13th August 2008 after completing 14 years of actual imprisonment, or earlier under Article 161 by the Governor.

case_name: The State of Haryana vs. Anand Kindo & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Haryana vs. Anand Kindo & Anr.. Date: 8th September 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the death sentence imposed by the trial court for the murder of Major General Kailash Chand Dhingra and his wife should be upheld or if a different sentence should be imposed. Anand Kindo and his accomplice brutally murdered Major General Kailash Chand Dhingra and his wife using a hammer and Tava while they were sleeping, driven by greed and the motive of robbery. The trial court sentenced Anand Kindo and his accomplice to death for the murder of Major General Kailash Chand Dhingra and his wife, considering the crime to be of the rarest of the rare category. The High Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, stating that it was not a fit case for the rarest of the rare category. The complainant argued that the brutality of the crime and the aggravating circumstances warranted a fixed term sentence, where the convicts should serve a minimum number of years before being eligible for remission. The Supreme Court considered the brutality of the crime, the premeditated nature of the murder for financial gain, the breach of trust, and the societal impact of such crimes while determining the sentence. The Supreme Court imposed a fixed term sentence of 30 years, stating that this would balance the need for justice with the possibility of rehabilitation for the convicts. The Supreme Court considered the young age of the convicts at the time of the crime and the possibility of their reformation as mitigating factors against imposing the death penalty. The Supreme Court noted that the convicts attempted to escape from prison by digging a tunnel, which indicated a lack of remorse and posed a question on their behavior. The Supreme Court emphasized that the crime committed by trusted employees against their employers sent a wrong signal to society and required a strong response to maintain public trust and justice. The Supreme Court referred to the case of Shankar Kishanrao Khade vs. State of Maharashtra, highlighting that in certain cases, fixed term sentences exceeding 14 years can be imposed to balance justice and rehabilitation.

case_name: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.. Date: 11th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the High Court of Punjab and Haryana correctly set aside the order of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), which had rejected Ashok Khemka's performance appraisal report (PAR) for the period 2016-2017. The key dates were: self-appraisal submitted on 7th June 2017, Reporting Authority's grade of 8.22 on 8th June 2017, Reviewing Authority's upgraded grade of 9.92 on 27th June 2017, and Accepting Authority's downgraded grade of 9 on 31st December 2017. The High Court set aside the CAT's order, expunged the opinion of the Accepting Authority, and restored the opinion and grade awarded by the Reviewing Authority, which was 9.92. The High Court noted that the Accepting Authority failed to appreciate the practical constraints faced by Ashok Khemka, and that the Reviewing Authority had revised the grade in a transparent, fair, and reasoned manner. The Supreme Court found that although the Accepting Authority recorded remarks after the prescribed timeline, it was within the mandatory timeline under Rule 5(1) of the PAR Rules, and therefore, the remarks and grade should not be expunged. The Supreme Court held that the High Court overstepped its jurisdiction by interfering with the CAT's order, as it entered a specialized domain of evaluating an IAS officer's competency without the requisite expertise. The Supreme Court directed the Accepting Authority to take a decision on Ashok Khemka's representation under Rule 9(7B) of the PAR Rules within 60 days from the date of the judgment. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court, directed the Accepting Authority to decide on the pending representation, and allowed the appeal filed by the State of Haryana.

case_name: The State of Jammu & Kashmir vs. Dr. Saleem Ur Rehman
text: Case: The State of Jammu & Kashmir vs. Dr. Saleem Ur Rehman. Date: 29th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings against Dr. Saleem Ur Rehman, including FIR No. 32/2012, and declared Rule 3.16 of the Vigilance Manual, 2008 as ultra vires. Dr. Saleem Ur Rehman was accused of misappropriating government funds by purchasing sub-standard medical kits under the NRHM at exorbitant rates, in violation of supply order conditions. The FIR cited Sections 5(1)(d) r/w 5(2) of the J&K Prevention of Corruption Act, 2006, and Section 120B of the Ranbir Penal Code. The respondent, Dr. Saleem Ur Rehman, as Director of Health Services, was responsible for purchasing drug kits at inflated prices without conducting a market survey or ensuring quality control. The High Court justified quashing the FIR and proceedings due to non-compliance with Section 3 of the J&K PC Act, 2006, lack of prior sanction from a Magistrate, and delay in preliminary verification. The High Court declared Rule 3.16 ultra vires as it was in direct conflict with the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench Judgment in Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, which mandates registration of FIR without preliminary enquiry for cognizable offences. The key discrepancies were that the drug kits were purchased at significantly higher prices than the approved rates from the previous year and from private companies, without proper market surveys or quality checks. The respondent challenged the legal provisions on the basis of Section 3 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, requirement of prior sanction under Section 155 of the J&K Cr.P.C., and the scope of preliminary verification. The High Court viewed the Preliminary Verification as exceeding its scope, entering the domain of investigation, which is not permissible as per the Lalita Kumari judgment. The alleged misappropriation resulted in a financial loss of Rs. 1,04,99,429/- to the state exchequer due to the purchase of substandard items at inflated prices.

case_name: The State of Jammu and Kashmir vs. Farid Ahmad Tak
text: Case: The State of Jammu and Kashmir vs. Farid Ahmad Tak. Date: 2nd May 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the compulsory retirement of Farid Ahmad Tak, based on his alleged involvement in corrupt practices and the subsequent FIR registered against him, was justified and in accordance with the law. Farid Ahmad Tak was accused of abusing his official position to make payments against unexecuted works, recording fraudulent measurements, preparing exorbitant bills for drawal, and causing a huge loss to the State exchequer. An FIR was registered against him by the Vigilance Organisation, Jammu, and the investigation concluded that the allegations were proved. The Committee recommended the compulsory retirement of Farid Ahmad Tak, stating that he had indulged in corrupt practices, caused loss to the State exchequer, and had outlived his utility to the public. The Committee's report highlighted his bad reputation and embezzlement of government money. The Single Judge of the High Court allowed Farid Ahmad Tak's writ petition, holding that the decision to compulsorily retire him was based merely on the registration of an FIR without considering his Annual Confidential Reports (ACRs) and not following the norms evolved by the State. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the State's appeal, affirming the Single Judge's order that the compulsory retirement of Farid Ahmad Tak was not sustainable as it was based on insufficient grounds. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had incorrectly considered the matter from the premise that Farid Ahmad Tak was caught red-handed while demanding and accepting bribe, which was not the case. The Supreme Court also noted that the High Court did not consider the matter from the perspective of Clause (iv) of Article 226(2) of the Regulations. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments and orders of the High Court and remitted the matter back to the Division Bench of the High Court for fresh consideration, directing that the case be dealt with in accordance with the law.

case_name: The State of Jharkhand & Ors. vs. M/s HSS Integrated SDN & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Jharkhand & Ors. vs. M/s HSS Integrated SDN & Anr.. Date: 18th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the termination of the consultancy agreement by the State of Jharkhand was illegal and without following the due procedure as required under the contract. The consultancy agreement was for providing consultancy and supervisory services for the construction of a six-lane Divided Carriage Way of certain parts of Ranchi Ring Road. The agreement was entered into on 28th August 2007, with an original work period from 1st October 2007 to 30th September 2010. The Arbitral Tribunal found that the termination of the contract was illegal and without following the procedure required under the contract. It awarded the respondents a sum of Rs. 2,10,87,304 under various heads. M/s HSS Integrated SDN & Anr. claimed a total sum of Rs. 5,17,88,418 under 13 different heads, excluding interest. The claims primarily involved the unpaid amount for work executed under the contract, loss of profit, and overhead charges. The State of Jharkhand filed a counter-claim for Rs. 6,00,78,736, seeking reimbursement on account of unsatisfactory performance by the respondents. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State of Jharkhand under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act and confirmed the arbitral award. The High Court held that the findings of the Arbitral Tribunal were not perverse or contrary to the evidence on record.

case_name: The State of Jharkhand vs. Brahmputra Metallics Ltd., Ranchi and Anr.
text: Case: The State of Jharkhand vs. Brahmputra Metallics Ltd., Ranchi and Anr.. Date: 1st December 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Brahmputra Metallics Ltd. was entitled to a rebate or deduction of 50% of the amount assessed towards electricity duty for FYs 2011-12, 2012-13, and 2013-14 based on the Jharkhand Industrial Policy 2012 and a statutory notification issued on 8th January 2015. The High Court struck down the last paragraph of the notification dated 8th January 2015, which gave prospective effect to the rebate/deduction from electricity duty, and directed that the notification be deemed effective from 1st April 2011. The court upheld the claim of Brahmputra Metallics Ltd. for a rebate/deduction from electricity duty in terms of the Industrial Policy 2012. Brahmputra Metallics Ltd. based its claim on the Industrial Policy 2012, which provided an exemption from the payment of 50% of electricity duty for five years for captive power plants established for self-consumption or captive use, and the statutory notification issued under Section 9 of the Bihar Electricity Duty Act 1948. The Industrial Policy 2012 aimed to encourage industrialization by providing incentives, including a rebate on electricity duty for captive power plants. The policy stipulated that necessary follow-up notifications would be issued within one month to give effect to its provisions. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, ruling that the notification should be deemed effective from 1st April 2011, as the State government's delay in issuing the notification could not deprive Brahmputra Metallics Ltd. of the benefits promised under the Industrial Policy 2012. The High Court relied on the doctrine of promissory estoppel, which prevents a party from going back on a promise that has been relied upon by another party to its detriment. The court held that the State government's failure to issue the notification in a timely manner was a breach of the promise made under the Industrial Policy 2012.

case_name: The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. vs. Manoj Sharma & Ors.
text: Case: The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. vs. Manoj Sharma & Ors.. Date: 25th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether candidates who obtained their M.Phil. degrees through distance education before 11th July 2009 were eligible for the post of Guest Lecturer despite the University Grants Commission (UGC) Regulations, 2009, which mandated that M.Phil. and Ph.D. degrees obtained through distance education were not valid for such appointments. The High Court decided that the UGC Regulations, 2009, were prospective and did not invalidate M.Phil. degrees obtained through distance education before 11th July 2009. Therefore, candidates with such degrees were eligible for the post of Guest Lecturer. The appellants argued that according to the UGC Regulations, 2009, M.Phil. degrees obtained through distance education were not acceptable for the appointment of Guest Lecturers and that the High Court's decision to allow candidates with such degrees was unsustainable. The Supreme Court interpreted the UGC Regulations, 2009, as prospective, meaning that the regulations applied only to degrees obtained after their publication on 11th July 2009. Therefore, M.Phil. degrees obtained through distance education before this date were valid for consideration for the post of Guest Lecturer. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Madhya Pradesh, upholding the High Court's decision that candidates with M.Phil. degrees obtained through distance education before 11th July 2009 were eligible for the post of Guest Lecturer. The Supreme Court directed that the eligibility of the writ petitioners should be considered taking into account the UGC Regulations, 2009, which were applicable at the time of their application for the post of Guest Lecturer, thereby affirming the validity of their M.Phil. degrees obtained before the enforcement of these regulations.

case_name: The State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Laxmi Narayan and others
text: Case: The State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Laxmi Narayan and others. Date: 5th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was correct in quashing the FIR for non-compoundable offences under Sections 307 and 34 of the IPC based on a compromise between the complainant and the accused. The allegations were that Laxmi Narayan and others attempted to murder the complainant, Charan Singh, by firing at him, causing injuries to his right elbow. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh quashed the criminal proceedings against Laxmi Narayan and others under Sections 307 and 34 of the IPC, based on a compromise between the accused and the complainant. The State of Madhya Pradesh appealed the High Court's decision because it argued that the offences under Sections 307 and 34 IPC are serious crimes against society, and should not be quashed solely based on a compromise between the parties. The Supreme Court stated that offences under Sections 307 and 34 IPC are serious and heinous crimes that impact society at large and should not be quashed based on a private compromise between the complainant and the accused. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision to quash the FIR and directed that the criminal proceedings against Laxmi Narayan and others should continue in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court found the High Court's decision erroneous because it failed to consider the gravity and social impact of the offences, and it mechanically quashed the FIR without proper application of mind. The nature of the offence, being serious and non-compoundable, played a crucial role in the Supreme Court's decision to set aside the High Court's order and direct the continuation of criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court suggested that the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly and with caution, particularly in cases involving serious offences that have a societal impact. The Supreme Court differentiated by stating that crimes such as those under Sections 307 and 34 IPC are against society and have a broader social impact, unlike private disputes which may be settled between parties without affecting societal interests. The Supreme Court's final directive was to allow the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and ensure that the criminal proceedings against Laxmi Narayan and others continue as per the law.

case_name: The State of Odisha & Ors. vs. Radheshyam Agrawal
text: Case: The State of Odisha & Ors. vs. Radheshyam Agrawal. Date: 24th March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the State Government was justified in levying a penalty while granting an extension of time to complete a contracted work when the contractor failed to complete the work within the stipulated period. The contract involved was for the improvement of Khariar Boden Sinapali Road (MDR-121) in the District of Nuapara under NABARD Assistance RIDF-XIII, which was awarded to Radheshyam Agrawal, a special class contractor. The contractor argued that the penalty under para 3.5.5(v) of the OPWD Code could not be imposed as this provision applies only in cases where the contract is terminated due to failure to carry out the work, not in cases of extension of time. The High Court set aside the penalty, agreeing with the contractor's argument that para 3.5.5(v) of the OPWD Code was not applicable since the contract was not terminated but extended. The Supreme Court concluded that neither the contract nor the OPWD Code provided for the imposition of a penalty while granting an extension of time. The penalty imposed was therefore without authority of law and illegal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision to set aside the penalty imposed while granting the extension of time. No, the contractor was not given an opportunity to be heard regarding the penalty before it was imposed, which was another reason the Supreme Court found the imposition of the penalty to be unjustified.

case_name: The State of Orissa vs. Mahimananda Mishra
text: Case: The State of Orissa vs. Mahimananda Mishra. Date: 18th September 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was the appeal against the High Court's decision to grant bail to Mahimananda Mishra, who was accused of conspiring to murder Mahendra Swain. According to the prosecution, Mahendra Swain was murdered on 26th October 2016 by two unknown assailants who hurled bombs at his vehicle and then fired at him. The murder was allegedly committed at the behest of Mahimananda Mishra due to business rivalry. The police found that Mahimananda Mishra had fled to Thailand to avoid arrest, and they recovered weapons and the motorcycle used in the murder. The State also relied on a letter from the deceased expressing fear for his life, which they treated as a dying declaration. The High Court granted bail because it found no prima facie material against Mahimananda Mishra to establish his involvement in the conspiracy, and it did not consider the deceased's undated letter as a dying declaration. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for not exercising its discretion judiciously and for failing to appreciate several crucial factors, such as the risk of Mahimananda Mishra influencing the witnesses and the severity of his criminal antecedents. Mahimananda Mishra was released on bail in May 2018, after being in custody for other cases. There were concerns that he might influence witnesses and obstruct the investigation. The prosecution argued that Mahimananda Mishra, being a powerful and influential person, could intimidate witnesses and influence the investigation. His prior attempt to evade arrest by fleeing to Thailand indicated that he might abscond again. The Supreme Court highlighted that while considering bail applications, courts must account for factors such as the existence of a prima facie case, the gravity of the allegations, the accused's position and status, the likelihood of the accused fleeing from justice, and the possibility of tampering with witnesses. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's bail order, directing that Mahimananda Mishra be taken into custody, as it found that the High Court had not properly considered the risk of him influencing the investigation and witnesses. The Supreme Court justified its intervention by stating that the High Court's decision to grant bail did not judiciously consider the severity of the allegations and the risk posed by Mahimananda Mishra's influence, thereby warranting a reversal of the bail order. The Supreme Court expressed concern that Mahimananda Mishra, due to his power and influence, might tamper with or intimidate witnesses, adversely affecting the trial process.

case_name: The State of Punjab & Anr. vs. Mohinderjit Kaur (D) through L.R.
text: Case: The State of Punjab & Anr. vs. Mohinderjit Kaur (D) through L.R.. Date: 17th August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the family members of government employees transferred to non-pensionable establishments are entitled to family pension under Rule 5.3 of the Punjab Service Rules. Rule 5.3 states that a government employee transferred from a pensionable service to a non-pensionable establishment cannot be granted any pension or gratuity for the qualifying portion of his service until he retires from the non-pensionable establishment. However, it provides options for receiving retirement benefits and specifies conditions under which family pension is not applicable. The State of Punjab argued that the proviso under Rule 5.3(3) exempts the government from the liability of paying family pension to the surviving family members of employees transferred to non-pensionable establishments, even if they receive a monthly pension. The High Court interpreted that the Family Pension Scheme under Rule 6.17, which grants family pension to regular employees in pensionable establishments and those governed by the Family Pension Scheme, 1964, is a special benefit that cannot be overridden by the general rules of Rule 5.3. Therefore, the family members of such employees are entitled to family pension. The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's view that the Family Pension Scheme provides a special benefit that cannot be negated by the general rules of Rule 5.3. The Court upheld the entitlement of family pension for the family members of employees transferred to non-pensionable establishments. The Supreme Court directed that the arrears of pension be disbursed to the respondents within twelve weeks from the date of the judgment. If not disbursed within this period, the arrears would carry an interest rate of 12% from the date of the High Court judgment, and the officers responsible for the delay would be personally liable.

case_name: The State of Punjab vs Jasbir Singh
text: Case: The State of Punjab vs Jasbir Singh. Date: 26th February 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the FIR registered against Jasbir Singh for forging and fabricating documents during legal proceedings was valid and whether the High Court was correct in quashing it. Jasbir Singh was accused under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The FIR was based on allegations that Jasbir Singh had forged and fabricated documents submitted during legal proceedings before the Revenue Courts to claim ownership of property. The High Court quashed the FIR on the grounds that the Deputy Commissioner-cum-Chief Sales Commissioner did not hold a preliminary inquiry or afford an opportunity to Jasbir Singh before ordering the registration of the FIR. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's decision, stating that a preliminary inquiry by the court was not mandatory before filing a complaint under Section 195 of the CrPC. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 340 of the CrPC as not mandating a preliminary inquiry or an opportunity for the accused to be heard before the court files a complaint for offenses related to documents produced in legal proceedings. The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in the case of Pritish vs. State of Maharashtra, which held that a preliminary inquiry and hearing were not mandatory before filing a complaint under Section 195 of the CrPC. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order and reinstating the FIR against Jasbir Singh. The Supreme Court directed that the trial against Jasbir Singh should proceed in accordance with the law, without being influenced by the High Court's previous order quashing the FIR.

case_name: The State of Rajasthan vs Komal Lodha
text: Case: The State of Rajasthan vs Komal Lodha. Date: 13th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the death penalty awarded to Komal Lodha should be commuted to life imprisonment. The Trial Court awarded the death penalty to Komal Lodha. The High Court of Rajasthan commuted the death penalty to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the High Court to reconsider the question of the appropriate sentence for the offence under Section 302 IPC. The High Court made observations on the investigation, noting that certain aspects were not brought to the Supreme Court's notice and that no assistance was provided to the accused to prefer an appeal before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found the High Court's observations in paragraph 42 to be unwarranted and against judicial discipline and propriety. The Supreme Court set aside and expunged paragraph 42 of the High Court's judgment but did not interfere with the decision to commute the death penalty to life imprisonment. The ruling reinforces that the High Court must carefully consider both aggravating and mitigating circumstances before commuting a death penalty and that unwarranted observations against prior court decisions should be avoided. The expunging of paragraph 42 could emphasize the importance of judicial discipline and propriety, ensuring that lower courts respect and follow the judgments and directions of higher courts without making unwarranted observations. The High Court directed a fresh investigation to book certain other accused whose DNA was obtained from the leggings of the deceased for offences of murder, rape, sodomy, and under POCSO. The High Court commuted the death penalty to life imprisonment after considering the aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

case_name: The State of Tamil Nadu & Anr. vs. K. Fazlur Rahman & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Anr. vs. K. Fazlur Rahman & Anr.. Date: 3rd November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the validity of the supersession of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board by the State Government, particularly whether the nomination of two Senior Muslim Advocates as members of the Board affected the composition and functioning of the Board as per the Waqf Act, 1995. The State Government superseded the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board on the grounds that the number of elected members had become less than the number of nominated members, which, according to the government, rendered the Board unable to perform its functions effectively. The High Court held that the supersession of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board was not in accordance with law and set aside the order of supersession, particularly in relation to the election of two members from the Mutawalli category. The High Court allowed the writ petitions filed by Syed Ali Akbar and Dr. Haja K. Majeed. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 14(4) of the Waqf Act, 1995, to mean that the number of elected members of the Waqf Board must always be more than the nominated members. The Court emphasized that this provision incorporates democratic principles and ensures that the Board is predominantly run by elected representatives. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, agreeing that the supersession of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board was not justified under the circumstances. The Court ruled that the fresh election of two members from the Mutawalli category held in 2020 was invalid and that Syed Ali Akbar and Dr. Haja K. Majeed should continue to occupy their office until the end of their five-year term. The Supreme Court stated that it is the responsibility of the State Government to ensure that the composition of the Waqf Board complies with Section 14(4) of the Waqf Act, 1995, and that the number of elected members is always more than the nominated members. Any lapse in fulfilling this requirement cannot be used as a ground for superseding the Board.

case_name: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs G. Hemalathaa & Anr.
text: Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs G. Hemalathaa & Anr.. Date: 28th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondent's Law Paper-1 answer sheet was invalidated due to violating the mandatory instructions of the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission by using a pencil. The High Court granted relief on sympathetic grounds, stating that the violation of instructions was inadvertent and did not provide an unfair advantage to the respondent. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in relaxing the mandatory instructions as it would set a bad precedent and undermine the fairness of the examination process. The Supreme Court stated that mandatory instructions issued by the Commission have the force of law and must be strictly followed to ensure fairness and impartiality in public examinations. The Supreme Court emphasized that making exceptions in such cases would lead to arbitrariness, violating the principles of equality and creating distrust in the selection process. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and upheld the invalidation of the respondent's answer sheet for violating the mandatory instructions.

case_name: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.
text: Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.. Date: 5th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was related to the interpretation of Section 27(f) of the Tamil Nadu Government Servants (Conditions of Service) Act, 2016, specifically the filling of backlog vacancies for the post of Post Graduate Assistants in Chemistry under the Most Backward Class (MBC) and Denotified Community (DNC) quotas. The respondents claimed that meritorious candidates under the MBC quota, who would have been selected irrespective of any reservation, were not considered under the general vacancies but were appointed in the MBC/DNC quota against the backlog vacancies. This caused the respondents not to be appointed. The High Court of Madras quashed the provisional selection list and directed that the meritorious candidates should be adjusted against the general vacancies first, followed by filling the backlog vacancies and then the current vacancies under the quota. The appellants argued that the Section's clear provisions must be given effect, which implied that the backlog vacancies should be filled first based on merit, and then the remaining vacancies should be adjusted against the reserved categories. The Supreme Court interpreted that the merit list should be prepared first without reservation. After that, the backlog vacancies should be filled first, followed by the current year vacancies under the reserved categories. The Court emphasized that the principle of merit should not be compromised. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, agreeing with the High Court's interpretation that meritorious candidates should first be adjusted against the general category, and only thereafter should the backlog and current vacancies for the reserved categories be filled. The Court left the parties to bear their own costs.

case_name: The State of Tamil Nadu vs. Dr. Vasanthi Veerasekaran
text: Case: The State of Tamil Nadu vs. Dr. Vasanthi Veerasekaran. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the acquisition of private land by the State for the implementation of the Mass Rapid Transport System (MRTS) Railway Project and whether the private respondents were entitled to alternative housing sites as displaced persons. The High Court had initially directed the State Government to consider the private respondents' representation for allotment of housing sites as a special category of displaced persons due to the acquisition of their lands for the MRTS Railway Project. The State Government rejected the request because the land was acquired specifically for the MRTS Railway Project and not for housing schemes, and all procedural formalities were completed according to the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The High Court's impugned judgment ordered the State Government to allot alternate land to the private respondents within the Corporation/City limits as a special category of displaced persons due to the acquisition of their land for the MRTS Railway Project. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, ruling that the private respondents were not entitled to alternative housing sites as the land was acquired for the MRTS Railway Project and not for housing schemes. The acquisition was lawful, and there was no legal obligation on the State to provide alternate housing sites. The Supreme Court considered several precedent cases, including State of U.P. vs. Smt. Pista Devi, State of Kerala vs. M. Bhaskaran Pillai, Tamil Nadu Housing Board vs. L. Chandrasekaran, and others, which supported the view that once land is acquired and vested in the State, the owners have no further claim to alternative sites unless there is a specific legal obligation or policy. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the State of Tamil Nadu, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed the writ petitions filed by the private respondents. The decision confirmed that the land acquisition for the MRTS Railway Project was lawful and that there was no obligation to provide alternate housing sites to the displaced landowners.

case_name: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs Principal Abhay Nandan Inter College & Ors.
text: Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs Principal Abhay Nandan Inter College & Ors.. Date: 27th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the judgment of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court dated 19th November 2018, which held that Regulation 101 framed under The Intermediate Education Act, 1921, as amended, was unconstitutional. Regulation 101 pertained to the appointment of non-teaching staff in recognized aided institutions, specifically stating that the appointing authority could not fill any vacancy without prior approval from the Inspector. On 23rd January 2008, the State of Uttar Pradesh decided not to create any new posts in the Class IV category and instead recommended outsourcing the work wherever necessary. The rationale was to regulate and curtail staff expenditure and enhance efficiency, as recommended by the Sixth Central Pay Commission and reiterated by the Seventh Central Pay Commission. The Allahabad High Court's Division Bench concluded that Regulation 101 was unconstitutional, arbitrary, and illegal as it violated Article 14 of the Constitution of India and was contrary to Section 16G of The Intermediate Education Act, 1921. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of Regulation 101, setting aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court, and stated that the regulation was consistent with the policy decision to outsource Class IV employees' work. The Supreme Court directed that respondents recruited contrary to Regulation 101 should be continued with the same scale of pay as if they were recruited prior to 8th September 2010, but the disbursement of their salaries must be made by the institutions alone.

case_name: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs Rajit Singh
text: Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs Rajit Singh. Date: 22nd March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the disciplinary proceedings against Rajit Singh were conducted in violation of the principles of natural justice and whether the order of punishment should be set aside on this ground. Rajit Singh was charged with committing financial irregularities that caused a loss of Rs. 22,48,964.42 to the government while serving as a Junior Engineer at Balia. The Tribunal allowed Rajit Singh's claim petition, setting aside the order of punishment imposed by the Disciplinary Authority on the grounds of the Doctrine of Equality and breach of principles of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the state's writ petition, upholding the Tribunal's decision to set aside the order of punishment imposed on Rajit Singh. The Supreme Court held that the Doctrine of Equality was incorrectly applied by the Tribunal and the High Court, as the charges against the delinquent officer were proven, and the role of each individual officer must be considered separately. The Supreme Court agreed that the disciplinary proceedings were in breach of principles of natural justice because the relevant documents mentioned in the charge sheet were not supplied to Rajit Singh. However, the Court directed a fresh enquiry rather than reinstatement. The Supreme Court directed that a fresh enquiry be conducted from the stage of violation, i.e., after the issuance of the charge sheet, ensuring all necessary documents are furnished to Rajit Singh and following due principles of natural justice. This enquiry must be completed within six months. The state argued that Rajit Singh was given the fullest opportunity to respond to the Enquiry Report and findings before the Disciplinary Authority imposed the punishment. The Supreme Court stated that when an enquiry is vitiated due to violation of principles of natural justice, the appropriate remedy is to remit the case to the disciplinary authority for a fresh enquiry from the point of violation. The Supreme Court held that the exoneration of other officers or no action taken against them cannot be a ground to set aside the order of punishment if the charges against the individual delinquent officer are proven. The Supreme Court allowed the state's appeals, quashed the High Court's judgment, and directed a fresh enquiry into the charges against Rajit Singh, to be completed within six months, ensuring compliance with principles of natural justice.

case_name: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata
text: Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata. Date: 5th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the respondent, Premlata, should be appointed on a Grade-III post on compassionate grounds, despite the deceased employee (her husband) holding a Class-IV post. Premlata's initial application for the post of Assistant Operator was rejected because she did not fulfill the requisite eligibility criteria for that post. After failing the physical fitness examination, Premlata was offered the post of Messenger in the Police Radio Department. The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the Single Judge's order and directed the appellants to consider Premlata's candidature for a Grade-III post on compassionate grounds. The Supreme Court interpreted 'suitable post' as one that should be considered in relation to the post held by the deceased employee, not just based on the qualifications of the candidate. The court emphasized that the post offered should align with the deceased employee's position to maintain the compassionate appointment's purpose. The Supreme Court quashed the Division Bench's decision and restored the Single Judge's order, dismissing Premlata's writ petition and upholding the decision to offer her the post of Messenger.

case_name: The State of Uttarakhand vs. Nalanda College of Education and Others
text: Case: The State of Uttarakhand vs. Nalanda College of Education and Others. Date: 10th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the State Government's decision to not grant recognition to new B.Ed. colleges and to not increase the intake capacity for B.Ed. courses, based on the employment scenario of B.Ed. graduates, was arbitrary. The State Government decided against granting recognition due to the surplus of B.Ed. graduates compared to the demand for teachers. Approximately 13,000 students were passing the B.Ed. course annually against a need for only 2,500 teachers, leading to potential unemployment for the remaining graduates. The Single Judge quashed the State Government's order dated 16th July 2013, which opposed the recognition of new B.Ed. colleges, and directed the NCTE to take an appropriate decision on the college's application to increase the intake seats. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the State's appeal and confirmed the Single Judge's decision to quash the State Government's order and directed the NCTE to take a decision on the college's application to increase the intake seats. The Supreme Court concluded that the State Government's decision was not arbitrary. It held that considering the employment scenario and the surplus of B.Ed. graduates over the actual demand for teachers was a valid basis for the policy decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgments, and upheld the State Government's policy decision to not grant recognition to new B.Ed. colleges and to not increase the intake capacity for B.Ed. courses.

case_name: Thiru K. Palaniswamy vs. M. Shanmugam & Ors.
text: Case: Thiru K. Palaniswamy vs. M. Shanmugam & Ors.. Date: 23rd February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue is related to the internal management and leadership structure of the political party All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), particularly the validity of decisions taken in the General Council meetings and the amendments to the party's byelaws. The legal dispute was triggered by the conflicting views within AIADMK regarding amendments to the party's byelaws, specifically the shift from a system of joint leadership (Co-ordinator and Joint Co-ordinator) to a single leadership structure, and the related decisions taken in the General Council meetings. The Single Judge of the High Court declined to pass any interim order to stop the General Council meeting scheduled for 23rd June 2022, allowing the meeting to proceed but without granting any specific injunction against the amendments proposed. The Division Bench of the High Court allowed the General Council meeting on 23rd June 2022 to proceed but restricted the meeting from taking any decisions on matters other than the 23 items listed in the draft resolution. The Supreme Court stayed the operation of the High Court's order dated 23rd June 2022 and allowed the General Council meeting on 11th July 2022 to proceed in accordance with the law, while leaving it to the Single Judge to decide on any other interim relief. In the General Council meeting held on 11th July 2022, several resolutions were passed, including the abolition of the posts of Co-ordinator and Joint Co-ordinator, the creation of the post of Interim General Secretary, and the election of Thiru E.K. Palaniswamy as the Interim General Secretary. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals by Thiru O. Panneerselvam and others, thereby upholding the validity of the decisions taken in the General Council meeting held on 11th July 2022, which included the move to a single leadership structure.

case_name: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha vs. M/S Prius Auto Industries Ltd. & Ors.
text: Case: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha vs. M/S Prius Auto Industries Ltd. & Ors.. Date: 14th December 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the defendants' use of the trade mark 'Prius' constituted passing off and infringement of the plaintiff's well-known trade marks, including 'Toyota', 'Toyota Innova', 'Toyota Device', and 'Prius'. The plaintiff claimed that it was the first to use the trade mark 'Prius' globally, having launched the Prius car in Japan in 1997 and subsequently in other countries. The plaintiff argued that this use established the mark's goodwill and reputation, including in India, even before the car was officially launched there. The defendants argued that they had registered the trade mark 'Prius' in India in 2002 and had been using it since 2001 for automobile spare parts. They contended that their use of the mark was bona fide and not intended to deceive consumers. The learned trial Judge held that the defendants' use of the trade mark 'Prius' constituted passing off, as the plaintiff was the prior user of the mark globally and had established its reputation and goodwill. The court issued a permanent injunction against the defendants from using the mark 'Prius'. The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the trial court's order, holding that the plaintiff had not established sufficient goodwill and reputation of the 'Prius' mark in the Indian market prior to the defendants' use of the mark in 2001. The court found that the plaintiff had delayed in asserting its rights in India. The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Division Bench of the High Court, concluding that the plaintiff had not established sufficient goodwill and reputation of the 'Prius' mark in India prior to the defendants' use. The court held that the plaintiff's delayed approach to the courts worked to the prejudice of the defendants.

case_name: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited vs. M/S Rain Calcining Limited & Others
text: Case: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited vs. M/S Rain Calcining Limited & Others. Date: 29th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APTRANSCO) had the authority to levy wheeling charges and grid support charges on private power generators under the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Reforms Act, 1998. APTRANSCO proposed a wheeling charge of Rs.1 per Kwh for energy transmitted through its network. The Commission ultimately decided that the wheeling charges for the year 2002-2003 would be Paise 50 per Kwh, effective from 1st April 2002, along with system loss charges of 28.4 percent of energy input by the project developer. The Andhra Pradesh High Court set aside the Commission's order on wheeling charges, declaring it irrational and beyond the Commission's power, and held that the State Government alone was competent to fix wheeling charges as a matter of policy. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court, affirming that the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC) had the authority to fix wheeling charges under the Reforms Act, 1998, as part of its regulatory functions concerning the generation, transmission, distribution, supply, and utilization of electricity. The Supreme Court upheld the APERC's jurisdiction to levy wheeling and grid support charges, stating that the Commission's power to determine tariffs and charges was comprehensive and included the authority to regulate transmission and distribution activities. The Supreme Court directed that the Commission should hold proceedings on revenue calculations and tariff proposals submitted by licensees, consider objections, and notify the licensees of its decisions, ensuring that all parties are heard and due process is followed.

case_name: Travancore Devaswom Board vs. Ayyappa Spices & Ors.
text: Case: Travancore Devaswom Board vs. Ayyappa Spices & Ors.. Date: 6th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Travancore Devaswom Board should be prosecuted for violating the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, as a 'food business operator,' and whether the seized stock of Aravana Prasadam should be destroyed. The High Court directed the destruction because multiple reports, including those from the Government Analyst Laboratory and the FSSAI Office at Kochi, found the cardamom used in the prasadam to be 'unsafe' due to pesticide levels above the permissible threshold. The Supreme Court held that the writ petition should not have been entertained by the High Court because Ayyappa Spices, being an interested party, sought to convert judicial review proceedings for personal gain. The Supreme Court did not find it necessary to consider the applicability of the Act to the Travancore Devaswom Board because the writ petition itself was deemed not maintainable. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the impugned orders of the High Court, and held that there was no illegality or arbitrariness in awarding the contract to respondent no. 2 for the supply of cardamom. The Supreme Court directed the State Government to destroy the existing stock of Aravana Prasadam in an appropriate manner, following the necessary procedure, as the Travancore Devaswom Board decided not to distribute it.

case_name: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Chandra Shekhar & Ors
text: Case: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Chandra Shekhar & Ors. Date: 5th March 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Court directed the appellant to issue fresh notices, allow objections under Section 15 of the 2013 Act, and finalize the award by 30th June 2024. The judgment reinforces the importance of serving notices to all stakeholders and adhering to procedural requirements, ensuring tenure-holders have a fair chance to object. The Court clarified that since the acquisition did not attain finality before 1st January 2014, compensation must be assessed under the 2013 Act, not the repealed 1894 Act. The Court emphasized that delays in acquisition could lead to complications, such as higher compensation under the 2013 Act, and stressed the need for adherence to timelines.

case_name: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Ganga Saran (Dead) Thr. LRS. and Ors.
text: Case: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Ganga Saran (Dead) Thr. LRS. and Ors.. Date: 26th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the compensation amount for the land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for a housing scheme by the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad. The initial notification for land acquisition was issued on 29th September 1979. The Land Acquisition Officer fixed the compensation at Rs.29.08 per square yard. The District Judge, Bulandshahr, increased the compensation amount to Rs.99 per square yard along with statutory benefits. The U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad appealed because they were dissatisfied with the increased compensation amount fixed by the District Judge, Bulandshahr. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, upholding the increased compensation amount of Rs.99 per square yard. The respondents argued that the acquired land was adjacent to residential and commercial buildings, and the market value during the relevant time was supported by sale deeds showing values between Rs.100 to Rs.200 per square yard. U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad filed a special leave petition (SLP) with the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the compensation amount of Rs.99 per square yard as fixed by the District Judge and affirmed by the High Court. The decision may set a precedent for fair market value assessment in future land acquisition cases, ensuring that compensation reflects the true market value based on comparable sales. U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad should proceed with disbursing the enhanced compensation to the respondents-claimants as per the Supreme Court's ruling, ensuring compliance with the judgment.

case_name: U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Ram Singh & Ors.
text: Case: U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad vs Ram Singh & Ors.. Date: 20th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the withdrawal of acquisition under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, by the Uttar Pradesh Government, was valid and lawful. The dispute arose after the Uttar Pradesh Government exempted these plots from acquisition via a notification dated 7th July 2005, citing lack of possession and non-payment of compensation. The Parishad challenged the High Court’s judgment because it annulled the notification canceling the exemption and directed the reinstatement of the acquisition. The Supreme Court held that withdrawal from acquisition under Section 48 requires compliance with natural justice principles, including an opportunity for the beneficiary to present objections. The Supreme Court stated that symbolic possession was insufficient to prevent withdrawal under Section 48, as actual possession must be demonstrated. The Supreme Court clarified that the notification was prospective and could not invalidate prior orders, such as the exemption granted in 2005. The Parishad failed to contest the 2005 exemption notification promptly, only challenging it after adverse High Court orders were issued. The Supreme Court stated that the Parishad could initiate fresh acquisition proceedings for the land in accordance with the law, if required. The High Court found that no notices under Section 9(3) were issued, impacting the validity of possession claims and acquisition procedures. The Supreme Court noted that compensation payment delays did not automatically invalidate the withdrawal but emphasized adherence to procedural correctness. The judgment underscores the need for meticulous adherence to procedural and legal norms, particularly in demonstrating actual possession and compliance with Section 48.

case_name: U.P. Singh vs. Punjab National Bank
text: Case: U.P. Singh vs. Punjab National Bank. Date: 14th December 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the deemed voluntary retirement of the workman, U.P. Singh, by Punjab National Bank was valid under the Bipartite Agreement. The Tribunal accepted the workman's prayer and set aside the Bank's order deeming the workman to have voluntarily retired, directing reinstatement with full back wages and consequential benefits. The Single Judge of the High Court set aside the Tribunal's award, upholding the Bank's order of deemed voluntary retirement. U.P. Singh did not report for duty at the new place of posting due to his suspension and subsequent non-payment of subsistence allowance, leading to his absence and hunger strike. The Supreme Court observed that the workman should have complied with the transfer order or availed of remedies against it, rather than ignoring it and absenting himself from duty. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's order, confirming the validity of the Bank's action of deemed voluntary retirement and dismissing the appeal filed by U.P. Singh.

case_name: UMC Technologies Private Limited vs Food Corporation of India & Anr.
text: Case: UMC Technologies Private Limited vs Food Corporation of India & Anr.. Date: 16th November 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the Food Corporation of India (FCI) was justified in blacklisting UMC Technologies Private Limited for five years and terminating their contract due to alleged negligence in conducting a recruitment examination, resulting in a leak of the question papers. The contract was terminated and UMC Technologies was blacklisted after a police investigation revealed that handwritten documents related to the recruitment examination question papers were found with 50 arrested persons, implicating an employee of UMC Technologies in the leak. UMC Technologies denied any negligence or involvement in the question paper leak, requested forensic analysis of the seized documents, and submitted a detailed observation report explaining discrepancies between the seized documents and the original question papers. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh dismissed the writ petition filed by UMC Technologies, upholding the decision of the Food Corporation of India to terminate the contract and blacklist the company for five years. The Supreme Court found that the show cause notice did not clearly indicate the intention to blacklist UMC Technologies, thereby failing to provide adequate and meaningful opportunity to the company to defend itself against such severe action. The Supreme Court quashed the blacklisting order dated 09.01.2019, holding that it was contrary to the principles of natural justice, and set aside the High Court's order that had upheld the blacklisting. No, the Supreme Court did not remand the matter to the Food Corporation of India for fresh consideration, deeming it unnecessary given the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case.

case_name: Uday Pratap Thakur and Anr. vs The State of Bihar and Ors.
text: Case: Uday Pratap Thakur and Anr. vs The State of Bihar and Ors.. Date: 28th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Larger Bench held that only the period required to meet the shortfall in the qualifying service for pension should be counted from the work charged service, and not the entire period. The original writ petitioners challenged Rule 5(v) because they believed that the entire period of service as work charged employees should be counted for pension, not just a portion. The appellants filed special leave petitions (SLPs) with the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision regarding the counting of work charged service for pension. The decision clarifies that only the necessary portion of work charged service needed to meet the qualifying period for pension will be counted, potentially affecting the pension calculations of other work charged employees in Bihar. The State of Bihar will need to adhere strictly to Rule 5(v) of the Rules, 2013, ensuring that only the necessary portion of work charged service is counted towards meeting the qualifying period for pension. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals because it found that Rule 5(v) of the Rules, 2013, was fair and reasonable, ensuring that work charged service is counted only to the extent necessary to qualify for pension, without equating it entirely with regular service. The Supreme Court directed that the appeals be dismissed, upholding the High Court's decision and Rule 5(v) of the Rules, 2013, and ensured that the service rendered as work charged is counted for qualifying service for pension only to the necessary extent.

case_name: Ude Singh & Ors. vs State of Haryana
text: Case: Ude Singh & Ors. vs State of Haryana. Date: 25th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the appellants abetted the suicide of the complainant's daughter by taunting and humiliating her, leading to her death by hanging. The appellants were accused of taunting and humiliating the complainant's daughter by addressing her with derogatory terms such as 'wife', 'Chachi', and 'Bohoria', which allegedly drove her to commit suicide. The trial court found Ude Singh and the other appellants guilty of abetment of suicide under Section 306 read with Section 34 IPC, sentencing them to four years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 300/-. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana upheld the conviction of the accused but reduced the sentence from four years to two and a half years of rigorous imprisonment. The Supreme Court observed that the continuous taunting and humiliation by the accused were calculated to destroy the self-esteem of the young girl, ultimately driving her to commit suicide. The Supreme Court found that appellant No. 2 was a juvenile at the time of the offence and terminated the proceedings against him, while upholding the conviction of the other appellants. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal for the adult appellants, requiring them to serve the remaining part of their sentence, but allowed the appeal for the juvenile appellant, setting aside his conviction.

case_name: Uma Priyadarshini S. vs. Suchith K. Nair
text: Case: Uma Priyadarshini S. vs. Suchith K. Nair. Date: 6th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the determination of interim maintenance for the appellant and her minor son, including educational expenses, after the High Court reduced the interim maintenance amount set by the subordinate court. The High Court ruled that the appellant was not entitled to any maintenance as she was gainfully employed, and reduced the interim maintenance for her son from Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 15,000 per month. The Supreme Court directed the respondent to pay a lump-sum amount of Rs. 1,00,000 to the appellant towards litigation expenses. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, upheld the subordinate court's interim maintenance decision with modifications, and directed the family court to finalize the maintenance issue expeditiously. The Supreme Court directed the respondent to pay Rs. 30,000 per month for the child's food and clothing expenses and Rs. 11,000 per month for house rent paid by the appellant.

text: Case: Uma Shankar & Ors. vs R. Hanumaiah Since Deceased Through His LRs. & Ors.. Date: 12th May 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the de-acquisition of land by the State Government in favor of R. Hanumaiah was valid, especially in light of previous Supreme Court judgements that had held such de-acquisition to be impermissible. The High Court of Karnataka had set aside the notification dated 13.11.2009, which canceled the de-acquisition of land in favor of R. Hanumaiah, and directed the State to reconsider the matter afresh. The Supreme Court held that the de-acquisition notification issued by the State Government on 14.10.2009 was a misadventure and void, as it violated the binding precedent set by the Supreme Court's earlier judgements in the same matter. The Supreme Court imposed a cost of Rs. 5,00,000 on the LRs of respondent No. 1 to be deposited with the Supreme Court Advocate-on-Record Association within two months from the date of the judgement. The Supreme Court reaffirmed its earlier judgements that the de-acquisition of land after possession had been taken by the State was impermissible under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, and any subsequent notifications attempting to de-acquire the land were void. The Supreme Court noted that the compensation amount had been deposited by the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) with the concerned court on 02.12.2005, and allowed the legal representatives of the respondents to withdraw the same, stating that the BDA's liability for interest ceased after the date of deposit.

case_name: Union Public Service Commission vs. Bibhu Prasad Sarangi & Ors.
text: Case: Union Public Service Commission vs. Bibhu Prasad Sarangi & Ors.. Date: 5th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the first respondent, Bibhu Prasad Sarangi, was correctly denied selection to the IAS due to a disciplinary penalty imposed on him in 2011, and whether the High Court erred in directing the reconsideration of his case for promotion. The Central Administrative Tribunal directed the Union Public Service Commission to reconsider Bibhu Prasad Sarangi's case for promotion to the IAS for the vacancies in 2015, and if found unsuitable, to reconsider him for the years 2016 and 2017. The High Court of Orissa upheld the Tribunal's decision, stating that the Tribunal had elaborately discussed the law and found no jurisdictional error in its order, thereby refusing to interfere with the Tribunal's directions. The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for merely cutting, copying, and pasting from the Tribunal's judgement without providing an independent application of mind or substantive reasoning, which is essential in the judicial process. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement and order of the High Court, restoring the writ petition under Article 226, WP(C) 13029 of 2019, to the file of the High Court for disposal with proper reasoning within four months. The disciplinary penalty imposed on Bibhu Prasad Sarangi on 29th September 2011 was a key factor in the decision to deny him promotion to the IAS, which was contested in the appeals process. Bibhu Prasad Sarangi had retired from service during the pendency of the litigation, making the outcome of the proceedings relevant to his pensionary benefits.

case_name: Union of India & Anr vs Onkar Nath Dhar
text: Case: Union of India & Anr vs Onkar Nath Dhar. Date: 5th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Onkar Nath Dhar, a retired Intelligence Bureau officer and a Kashmiri migrant, was entitled to retain government accommodation indefinitely due to the prevailing conditions in Jammu & Kashmir. Onkar Nath Dhar requested to retain the government accommodation after his retirement in 2006, citing the unsafe conditions in Jammu & Kashmir. His request was initially allowed for one year. The High Court upheld Dhar's right to retain the accommodation indefinitely, considering the unsafe conditions in Jammu & Kashmir and citing a similar case, J.L. Koul v. State of J & K. The Supreme Court ruled that government accommodation is meant for serving officers and not retirees. It set aside the High Court's decision, granting Dhar time until 31st October 2021 to vacate the premises. Dhar challenged the eviction order under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, and initially obtained a stay from the Additional District Judge, Delhi, before moving to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, Faridabad. The Supreme Court stated that the right to shelter does not extend to retaining government accommodation indefinitely. It emphasized that such accommodation is intended for serving officers. The Supreme Court clarified that directions under Article 142, such as those given in J.L. Koul's case, are specific to the facts of the case and should not be treated as general law applicable in all similar circumstances. The decision may lead to the eviction of other retired officials occupying government accommodations and reinforce the policy that such housing is for serving officers only. Retired government employees should vacate government accommodations promptly after retirement and make alternative housing arrangements, as per the applicable policies. The Supreme Court directed the Union of India to submit a report on the action taken against retired officials occupying government accommodations by 15th November 2021. The government should provide temporary transit accommodations or cash compensation to displaced persons while ensuring that permanent government accommodations are reserved for serving officers.
