case_name: Union of India & Anr vs. S. Narasimhulu Naidu (Dead) Through LRs. and Ors
text: Case: Union of India & Anr vs. S. Narasimhulu Naidu (Dead) Through LRs. and Ors. Date: 27th August 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the land measuring 7128.5 sq. yards in Survey No. 299/2, Shaikpet Village, Hyderabad, was lawfully owned by the respondents or had been grabbed by the Union of India. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh on 25.4.2011 did not interfere with the order passed by the Special Court, Hyderabad, under the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982. The applicants claimed the land based on the purchase by their father, Late Sri S.V. Srinivasulu Naidu, through two registered sale deeds dated 12.12.1959 and alleged continuous possession of the land since then. The applicants presented sale deeds (Exhibits A1 and A2) and claimed that no objections were received after a notification was published under Section 8(6) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act in the extraordinary Gazette of Andhra Pradesh on 22.1.2004. The Union of India argued that the land in question had been handed over to them by the Collector, Hyderabad, on 1.4.1958, and that the land was recorded in their possession as defense land, making the Tribunal incompetent to decide the title of defense land. The Tribunal found that the applicants' father and their predecessors-in-title had been in possession of the land since 1949-50 and that the delivery of the land to the defense by the State Government in 1958 was only a paper delivery. The High Court concluded that the father of the applicants had established possession of the land from 1959 to 1964 and that the delivery of the land to the Union of India by the State Government in 1958 was negatived in the suit OS No. 175 of 1970. To comply with the decree in OS No. 175 of 1970 and avoid contempt proceedings, the Union of India proposed an exchange of the defense land with the decretal land, which was accepted, and the decree schedule property was delivered to the decree holders on 14.12.1995. The Union of India argued that the transfer of land by the State of Andhra Pradesh to the Union was valid without the need for a registered instrument, as it was a grant of immovable property by the Government, exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(vii) of the Registration Act, 1908. The Tribunal decided that the applicants had not proven their claim of adverse possession, as they had not taken any steps to get the land restored to them after being dispossessed long ago. If the Union of India continues to assert possession over the disputed land and proves its continuous possession since 1958, the applicants may find it difficult to reclaim the land, especially without the production of the patta document.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs Balwant Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Balwant Singh & Ors.. Date: 3rd September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the judgement in the case of Madishetti Bala Ramul (D) through LRs vs. The Land Acquisition Officer, which pertains to the Land Acquisition Act, could be applied to the National Highways Act, particularly in the context of Section 3G(5) of the latter act, which has a different scheme for determining compensation. The Supreme Court concluded that the judgement in the Madishetti Bala Ramul case, which applied to the Land Acquisition Act, could not be applied to the National Highways Act. The court noted that the scheme under Section 3G(5) of the National Highways Act was fundamentally different from the Land Acquisition Act. The Supreme Court identified that the lower courts erroneously applied the judgement from the Madishetti Bala Ramul case, which pertained to the Land Acquisition Act, to the National Highways Act cases. This misapplication constituted an obvious error. The Supreme Court remanded the cases to be decided under Section 37 jurisdiction of the Arbitration Act by the Punjab & Haryana High Court and requested the Chief Justice of the High Court to constitute an appropriate bench to hear these matters at the earliest. The Supreme Court acknowledged that there were a large number of cases dependent on this judgement and thus requested the Chief Justice of the Punjab & Haryana High Court to ensure these matters are heard at the earliest.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.. Date: 11th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the sentence of 26 years imprisonment given to Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed in Mauritius should be reduced to 10 years in India as per the Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1994. Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed was transferred to India under the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003, after being convicted and sentenced to 26 years imprisonment in Mauritius for possession of heroin. Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed argued that his sentence should be reduced to 10 years in accordance with Section 21(b) of the NDPS Act, which prescribes a maximum of 10 years imprisonment for the quantity of heroin he was found with. The Central Government rejected the reduction of his sentence on the grounds that reducing the sentence by 16 years would not be compatible with Section 13(6) of the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003, and the agreement with Mauritius. The High Court allowed the reduction of Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed's sentence to 10 years, stating that if the offence had been committed in India, the maximum sentence would have been 10 years under the NDPS Act. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, upholding the Central Government's decision to maintain the original sentence of 26 years, stating that the sentence imposed by Mauritius was binding on India. Article 8 of the agreement between India and Mauritius states that the receiving State (India) is bound by the legal nature and duration of the sentence as determined by the transferring State (Mauritius). The Central Government may accept the transfer of a prisoner, issue a warrant to detain the prisoner in India, and ensure the sentence is compatible with Indian law, but bound by the sentence's legal nature and duration as imposed by the transferring State. This judgement reinforces the principle that India must honor the sentence imposed by the transferring State, ensuring the sentence's legal nature and duration are maintained, thus impacting future prisoner transfers. If Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed seeks further legal remedies, he might appeal to a higher court or seek a presidential pardon, but the success of such actions would depend on the legal interpretations and the discretion of the authorities. Legal practitioners should consider the binding nature of sentences imposed by transferring States, the compatibility of such sentences with Indian law, and the specific terms of international agreements governing prisoner transfers.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs Tarsem Singh & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Tarsem Singh & Ors.. Date: 19th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the non-grant of solatium and interest for lands acquired under the National Highways Act, which is available under the Land Acquisition Act, is valid. The Court examined if Section 3J of the National Highways Act violated Article 14 of the Constitution of India. A notification dated 24th December 2004 was issued under Section 3A of the National Highways Act, intending to acquire land belonging to the Respondents for the purpose of four-laning National Highway No.1-A on certain stretches of the Jalandhar-Pathankot section as well as the Pathankot-Jammu section within the State of Punjab. The compensation initially awarded by the competent authority was Rs. 4,219/- per marla or Rs. 6.75 lakhs per acre. The Arbitrator awarded Rs. 1.5 lakhs per marla as compensation. No solatium or interest was awarded because the National Highways Act does not provide for them. The Supreme Court declared that the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act relating to solatium and interest would apply to acquisitions made under the National Highways Act. Consequently, Section 3J of the National Highways Act was declared unconstitutional to the extent that it excluded the payment of solatium and interest.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs. Buddha Tri-Ratna Mission & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India & Anr. vs. Buddha Tri-Ratna Mission & Anr.. Date: 19th May 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the dispute over the allotment and possession of a plot of land in Chittaranjan Park, New Delhi, which was allotted to Buddha Tri-Ratna Mission but led to various rounds of litigation due to non-payment of dues. The plot of land was valued at Rs.80 lakhs per acre as premium and 2.5% thereof as Annual Ground Rent. The respondents failed to pay the dues on time, leading to litigation. The High Court directed the Union of India to hand over possession of the plot to the respondents, Buddha Tri-Ratna Mission, on or before 4th February 2020, provided that a sum of Rs.50,99,163/- was deposited. The Supreme Court ruled that the total dues, including interest, amounted to Rs.78,84,099/- as of 31st May 2022, and directed the respondents to deposit this amount by 31st August 2022. If deposited, possession of the plot would be handed over to them. If the amount was not deposited by 31st August 2022, the dues would cease to be frozen, and the Union of India could consider canceling the allotment of the plot. The Supreme Court's order directed that L.P.A. No.660 of 2019 pending before the Division Bench of the High Court would stand disposed of in terms of the Supreme Court's order.

case_name: Union of India & Anr. vs. Omkar Nath Dhar (D) Through L.Rs.
text: Case: Union of India & Anr. vs. Omkar Nath Dhar (D) Through L.Rs.. Date: 7th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue addressed is the request to recall the judgment of the Supreme Court passed on 5th August 2021 regarding the retention of government accommodation by retired Kashmiri migrants. The recall was sought because the respondent had died on 16th March 2020 and the court had passed an order without seeking substitution of the legal representatives of the deceased respondent. The policy, framed on 28th March 2017 and modified on 19th May 2017, provided alternate residence to retired Central Government employees belonging to the State of Jammu & Kashmir who possess General Pool Residential Accommodation (GPRA) in Delhi. The applicant must be a retired Central Government employee or their spouse, possess GPRA in Delhi, be a permanent resident of Jammu and Kashmir, have no other residence in the country, and not be in a position to return to their native place due to unfavorable conditions. The Supreme Court decided that retired Kashmiri migrants could retain government accommodation for a period of three years from the date of retirement, after which they must make alternative arrangements or move to transit accommodation or avail cash compensation in lieu of it. The applications were dismissed by the Supreme Court, and the time granted to Omkar Nath Dhar to vacate the premises was extended until 30th November 2021. The Union was granted liberty to file an application for modification of the order regarding other retirees covered by the judgment in J.L. Koul. The counsel argued that Kashmiri migrants form a different class as victims of terrorism, facing peculiar hardships, and should be granted protection and residential accommodation as decided in previous judgments, including J.L. Koul. The government highlighted various benefits provided to Kashmiri migrants, including financial assistance, housing repair packages, jobs, and cash relief. It also mentioned the construction of transit accommodations and the movement of migrants back to the Kashmir Valley post the abrogation of Article 370.

The applicant must be a retired Central Government employee or their spouse, possess GPRA in Delhi, be a permanent resident of Jammu and Kashmir, have no other residence in the country, and not be in a position to return to their native place due to unfavorable conditions.

The Supreme Court decided that retired Kashmiri migrants could retain government accommodation for a period of three years from the date of retirement, after which they must make alternative arrangements or move to transit accommodation or avail cash compensation in lieu of it.

The applications were dismissed by the Supreme Court, and the time granted to Omkar Nath Dhar to vacate the premises was extended until 30th November 2021. The Union was granted liberty to file an application for modification of the order regarding other retirees covered by the judgment in J.L. Koul.

The counsel argued that Kashmiri migrants form a different class as victims of terrorism, facing peculiar hardships, and should be granted protection and residential accommodation as decided in previous judgments, including J.L. Koul.

The government highlighted various benefits provided to Kashmiri migrants, including financial assistance, housing repair packages, jobs, and cash relief. It also mentioned the construction of transit accommodations and the movement of migrants back to the Kashmir Valley post the abrogation of Article 370.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. Vs. Managobinda Samantaray
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. Vs. Managobinda Samantaray. Date: 24th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the dismissal of Managobinda Samantaray, a constable in CISF, for misconduct, including sleeping on duty, abusing, misbehaving, and assaulting his superior officer, ASI/Exe B. Panda. Managobinda Samantaray was initially penalized with a reduction in pay by two stages for a period of three years and treated as non-duty for the suspension period from 4th January 2000 until the order receipt. The Appellate Authority issued a show cause notice for enhancing the penalty to dismissal from service, citing the severity of the misconduct and the inadequacy of the initial penalty. The High Court of Odisha set aside the dismissal order on the grounds of violation of natural justice, as the Appellate Authority had failed to consider the respondent's request for an extension of time to reply to the show cause notice. The Appellate Authority, upon re-examination, reaffirmed the dismissal of Managobinda Samantaray, considering the severity of the misconduct and lack of remorse from the respondent. The High Court of Orissa ruled that the punishment of dismissal was shockingly disproportionate to the offense and ordered reinstatement with 50% back wages from 23rd January 2001 to 18th February 2012. The Supreme Court upheld the dismissal order, stating that the punishment was not disproportionate given the gravity of the misconduct, and emphasized the importance of discipline in the CISF. The Supreme Court directed that Managobinda Samantaray be paid subsistence allowance for the period from 4th January 2000 to 15th July 2000, and salary for the period from 16th July 2000 to 23rd January 2001, with interest at 7% per annum for delays in payment. The decision reinforces the importance of strict discipline and integrity within the CISF, setting a precedent for the appropriate handling of severe misconduct and ensuring that the forces maintain high standards of behavior. The ruling may lead to more stringent enforcement of disciplinary actions within the CISF, with a focus on maintaining discipline and integrity, and may discourage misconduct among personnel. The Supreme Court clarified that judicial review in disciplinary actions should ensure compliance with legal procedures and natural justice, but should not replace the discretion of disciplinary authorities unless the punishment is grossly disproportionate.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy. Date: 19th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the punishment of removal from service imposed on M. Duraisamy for committing fraud while serving as a Postal Assistant was justified, or whether it should be modified to compulsory retirement as decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal and upheld by the High Court. M. Duraisamy committed fraud by making fraudulent withdrawals in 85 RD accounts and non-crediting deposits in 71 RD accounts, defrauding a sum of Rs. 16,59,065/-. He was also involved in forging the signatures of depositors and making double payments for RD closures. The departmental enquiry found all charges against M. Duraisamy to be proven, and the Disciplinary Authority imposed the penalty of removal from service, citing the seriousness of the offense and the impact on public trust in the postal service. The Central Administrative Tribunal modified the punishment from removal to compulsory retirement, considering that M. Duraisamy had deposited the entire defrauded amount along with penal interest and had completed nearly 39 years of service. The High Court upheld this modification. The Supreme Court held that the Tribunal and the High Court exceeded their jurisdiction by interfering with the Disciplinary Authority's decision. The Court emphasized that the seriousness of the misconduct and the impact on the department's reputation warranted the original punishment of removal from service. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgments of the Tribunal and the High Court, and restored the Disciplinary Authority's order of removal from service. The Court emphasized that leniency was not warranted given the gravity of the misconduct. The Supreme Court reasoned that the gravity of the misconduct, involving defrauding a significant amount of public money and damaging the department's reputation, justified the severe penalty of removal from service. The Court stated that merely depositing the defrauded amount and having a long service record did not mitigate the severity of the offense.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs Methu Meda
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs Methu Meda. Date: 6th October 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the respondent, Methu Meda, who was acquitted of kidnapping charges, was eligible for appointment as a Constable in the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) despite the acquittal being based on the benefit of doubt. Methu Meda was acquitted because the key witnesses, including the complainant and his wife, turned hostile during the trial, and the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. The Screening Committee decided that Methu Meda was not eligible for appointment in CISF because his acquittal was not an 'honourable acquittal' but was based on the benefit of doubt. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh directed the authorities to issue an order for Methu Meda's appointment and training in CISF, granting him all consequential benefits except back wages. The Supreme Court emphasized that 'honourable acquittal' means a complete exoneration from the charges, and acquittal based on the benefit of doubt does not qualify as 'honourable acquittal'. Thus, the respondent was not automatically entitled to employment. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the High Court, stating that Methu Meda was not eligible for appointment in CISF due to the nature of his acquittal, and emphasized the employer's right to assess the suitability of candidates. The Supreme Court relied on various precedents, including the cases of Avtar Singh vs. Union of India, Mehar Singh, and S. Samuthiram, to highlight that acquittal based on the benefit of doubt does not automatically entitle a person to employment in sensitive positions.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs R. Thiyagarajan
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs R. Thiyagarajan. Date: 3rd April 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether R. Thiyagarajan, a CISF employee, was entitled to deputation allowance while serving in the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) before the formal enforcement of the Disaster Management (National Disaster Response Force) Rules, 2008 on 11th September 2009. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 led to the creation of the NDRF, and the Disaster Management (National Disaster Response Force) Rules, 2008 detailed the organization and administration of the NDRF, including the transfer of control of battalions from various Central Para Military Forces to the NDRF. The Delhi High Court ruled that the petitioner, another CISF employee in the NDRF, was entitled to deputation allowance from the date he joined the NDRF, interpreting that personnel were on deputation from the inception of the NDRF under the Disaster Management Rules. The Union of India contended that deputation allowance was only payable from 14th January 2013, as per an office memorandum, and argued that the personnel of the Central Para Military Forces were not on deputation until the NDRF formed its own battalions on 13th January 2010. The Supreme Court decided that R. Thiyagarajan was entitled to deputation allowance from 11th September 2009, the date when the NDRF took control of the battalions and started paying the personnel, until he was relieved from the NDRF on 7th October 2011. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court of Madras exceeded its jurisdiction by granting relief that had pan-India implications, emphasizing that the High Court should limit its jurisdiction to the territorial boundaries of its state. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, directing that R. Thiyagarajan be paid deputation allowance from 11th September 2009 to 7th October 2011, and clarified that the Delhi High Court should dispose of related petitions in line with this ruling.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. All India Trade Union Congress & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. All India Trade Union Congress & Ors.. Date: 15th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is the regularization and provision of benefits to casual workers in the Border Roads Organization (BRO), which was contested by the Union of India against the directions issued by the High Court of Uttarakhand to regularize these workers and grant them benefits similar to regular employees. The High Court directed the Union of India to regularize the services of casual workers who had worked for more than five years continuously in the BRO and provide them with benefits similar to regular employees, including pay, increments, leave, and other facilities. The High Court ordered benefits including pay scale with DA, HRA, CCA, increments, pro-rata leave, maternity leave for female workers, and implementation of labor laws such as EPF, Gratuity Act, Bonus Act, and Workmen Compensation Act. It also mandated the provision of warm clothes, pre-fabricated houses and medical treatment in Military Hospitals. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and dismissed the writ petition filed by the respondents, stating that the court should not frame schemes but can only direct the government to consider framing an appropriate scheme. The Supreme Court referred to its previous decision in the case of Union of India vs. Vartak Labour Union (2), where it was held that casual employment does not entitle workers to regularization if the original appointment was not as per the relevant rules, and that framing of schemes is the prerogative of the government, not the courts. The Supreme Court concluded that the Union of India had already framed a welfare scheme for casual workers and that the High Court should have considered this instead of issuing its own directives for a new scheme.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Bengal Shrachi Housing Development Limited & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Bengal Shrachi Housing Development Limited & Anr.. Date: 7th November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Union of India, as the lessee, was liable to pay service tax for the commercial premises leased from Bengal Shrachi Housing Development Limited, under the terms of the lease agreement. Clause 6 of the deed of lease stated that the lessor shall pay all rates, taxes, assessments, charges, and other outgoings primarily leviable upon the lessor, while rates and taxes primarily leviable upon the occupier shall be paid by the Government. The Calcutta High Court ruled that the Union of India, as the lessee, was liable to pay service tax for the commercial premises, based on the interpretation that service tax, being an indirect tax, should be borne by the recipient of the service. The Union of India argued that under the Finance Act, 1994, and the Service Tax Rules, 1994, the service tax was primarily leviable on the service provider, i.e., the lessor, and therefore the lessor should bear the service tax. The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'primarily leviable' to mean that the person liable for paying the tax is the service provider, i.e., the lessor, and not the recipient of the service, i.e., the lessee. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court on the grounds of law, but refused to exercise its discretion under Article 136 of the Constitution of India in favour of the Union of India, based on specific letters indicating the Union of India's liability to bear service charges. The sanction letter dated 27th April 2012 and the letter dated 30th April 2012 stated that the Union of India would be liable for registration charges, stamp duty, and service tax, thereby affirming the lessee's responsibility to bear service charges.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.. Date: 3rd January 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue is whether the special pay of Rs. 2,000 per month (w.e.f. 01.01.1996) and Rs. 4,000 per month (w.e.f. 01.01.2006) granted to Scientists in the DRDO, DAE, and DOS should be counted for pension and pensionary benefits under the Central Civil Services Pension Rules, 1972. The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) allowed the original applications filed by the respondents (Scientists) and directed that the special pay of Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 4,000 be treated as part of pay for pensionary benefits. The Union of India argued that the definition of 'pay' under Rule 9(21)(a)(i) of the Fundamental Rules excludes special pay, and therefore, the special pay granted to Scientists should not be included in the computation of pension. The Supreme Court observed that the special pay of Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 4,000 granted to Scientists was not in the nature of special pay as defined in Fundamental Rule 9(25), but was instead in lieu of a separate higher pay scale. Therefore, it should be included in the computation of pension. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Union of India and upheld the decisions of the Central Administrative Tribunals and High Courts, directing that the special pay of Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 4,000 be included in the computation of pension. The significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it clarified the treatment of special pay granted in lieu of a higher pay scale and ensured that such pay is included in the computation of pension for Scientists in the DRDO, DAE, and DOS.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Ex. Naik Ram Singh
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Ex. Naik Ram Singh. Date: 18th July 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the entitlement of Ex. Naik Ram Singh to disability pension for an injury sustained while on annual leave. The Tribunal directed the Union of India to release the disability pension quantified at 80% disability for life to the respondent from the date of his discharge, with arrears restricted to three years immediately preceding the filing of the application and interest at 10% per annum on the arrears. The Union of India argued that there must be a reasonable connection between the injuries sustained by a member of the Armed Forces resulting in disability and the Military service, and that the respondent's accident occurred after he had reached his leave station, thus not entitling him to disability pension. Regulation 173 states that a disability pension may be granted to an individual who is invalidated out of service on account of disability which is attributable to or aggravated by military service in non-battle casualty and is assessed at 20% or over. The Supreme Court interpreted that there must be a reasonable causal connection between the injuries resulting in disability and the military service. In this case, since the respondent's accident occurred after reaching his leave station and had no nexus with military service, he was not entitled to the disability pension. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the Tribunal's judgment dated 23rd December 2010, and dismissed the application filed by the respondent, Ex. Naik Ram Singh, for disability pension.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Gautam Khaitan
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Gautam Khaitan. Date: 15th October 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the Delhi High Court was correct in restraining the Union of India from taking or continuing any action against Gautam Khaitan pursuant to the Order dated 22nd January 2019 under Section 55 of the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015. The Delhi High Court's order restrained the Union of India from taking or continuing any action against Gautam Khaitan under the Black Money Act, based on the retrospective application of the Act from 1st July 2015. The main objectives of the Black Money Act are to unearth black money stashed in foreign countries, prevent unaccounted money from going abroad, punish individuals indulging in illegitimate means of generating money causing loss to the revenue, and prevent illegitimate income and assets from being utilized in ways detrimental to India's social, economic, and strategic interests and national security. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 3 of the Black Money Act as charging tax on undisclosed foreign income and assets for assessment years commencing on or after 1st April 2016, based on the value of the asset in the previous year when it came to the notice of the Assessing Officer. The Supreme Court found the High Court's interim order unsustainable because it incorrectly concluded that the Black Money Act was being applied retrospectively, whereas the Act's provisions were intended to take effect from 1st July 2015 to enable assessees to benefit from the one-time declaration opportunity provided by Section 59 of the Act. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to decide the writ petition on its own merits, uninfluenced by the observations made by the Supreme Court, which were limited to examining the correctness of the interim order.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav. Date: 25th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue is whether the Armed Forces Tribunal was correct in interfering with the punishment of 'Severe Displeasure (Recordable)' awarded to Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav for maintaining unauthorized contact with a foreign national and violating security instructions. Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav maintained unauthorized contact with a foreign national, Ms. Sueli De Oliviera Montilha, through emails, phone calls, and personal meetings, and stayed with her at an Army premises in Goa, violating the 'Instructions on Contact with Foreign Nationals, 1987'. The Armed Forces Tribunal decided that the punishment of 'Severe Displeasure (Recordable)' was excessive and directed the competent authority to reconsider the punishment, suggesting a less severe form of censure. The Supreme Court set aside the Tribunal's decision, reinstating the original punishment of 'Severe Displeasure (Recordable)' awarded by the competent authority, and held that the Tribunal erred in its judgment by undermining the seriousness of the allegations against Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav. The Supreme Court found the Tribunal's interference inappropriate because it overstepped its jurisdiction by substituting its own judgment for that of the competent authority, and failed to appreciate the gravity of Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav's misconduct, which involved serious breaches of security protocols. The Supreme Court upheld the 'Severe Displeasure (Recordable)' punishment because Lt. Col. Kuldeep Yadav's actions constituted a serious breach of security, including unauthorized contact with a foreign national and the potential exposure of official documents, which warranted stern disciplinary action.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. M/s. Hamdard (Waqf) Laboratories
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. M/s. Hamdard (Waqf) Laboratories. Date: 25th February 2016. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the classification of 'Rooh Afza' under the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1986. The respondent claimed it should be classified under sub-heading 2201.90, but the Revenue classified it under sub-heading 2107.91. The Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise and the Commissioner (Appeals) both rejected the respondent's classification claim. The Central Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal upheld these decisions, leading to an appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court decided that 'Rooh Afza' falls under tariff heading 2202.90, classifying it as a non-alcoholic beverage, and directed consequential relief. The respondent filed for a refund of the duty paid, but the Revenue delayed processing the application and did not pay interest on the delayed refund, leading to a writ petition. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision that the respondent is entitled to interest on the delayed refund from 26th November 1999 to 15th November 2000, based on Section 11-BB of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Parashotam Dass
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Parashotam Dass. Date: 21st March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the Armed Forces Tribunal's orders are subject to the writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India by the High Court. The Supreme Court observed that the power of judicial review under Article 226 is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be ousted. The High Courts have the power to review decisions of all courts and tribunals within their jurisdiction. The respondents argued that there could never be a bar to the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 by the High Court, citing the Constitution Bench decision in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, which established that the power of judicial review by the High Courts is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The Supreme Court noted that Section 31 of the Armed Forces Tribunal Act restricts appeals to the Supreme Court only on points of law of general public importance. This leaves many personal service matters without an appellate forum if High Courts are barred from exercising jurisdiction under Article 226. The Supreme Court concluded that the judgment in Major General Shri Kant Sharma & Anr. did not lay down the correct law and was in conflict with previous Constitution Bench judgments. It reiterated that there is no per se restriction on the High Courts' power under Article 226 to review decisions from the Armed Forces Tribunal. The Supreme Court remanded various cases to the respective High Courts for decisions on merits under Article 226, emphasizing the importance of allowing at least two independent judicial scrutinies in administrative jurisprudence.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. R. Karthik
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. R. Karthik. Date: 21st January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the dismissal of R. Karthik from naval service was justified or if the Armed Forces Tribunal's decision to modify the punishment was appropriate. On 29th May 2013, R. Karthik, a sailor, had an altercation with Lt. Abhishek Vardhan, during which Karthik allegedly hit the officer after being provoked by the officer's abusive language. The Armed Forces Tribunal set aside the dismissal order and substituted it with a punishment of 75 days detention and deprivation of the First Good Conduct Badge, citing the provocation by the officer and the disproportionate nature of the original punishment. The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's decision, stating that the Tribunal had the jurisdiction to substitute and mitigate the punishment, and found that the original punishment was disproportionate to the misconduct. The Supreme Court noted that none of the three witnesses deposed regarding the alleged hitting of the superior officer by R. Karthik, and the officer himself was not made available for cross-examination, which influenced the Court's decision to uphold the Tribunal's findings. The Supreme Court directed that R. Karthik be reinstated within two months without any entitlement to back wages from the date of dismissal until reinstatement, but with computation of all consequential benefits including pay fixation.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajib Khan & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajib Khan & Ors.. Date: 16th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether Nursing Assistants in the Border Security Force (BSF) are entitled to receive Nursing Allowance at par with Staff Nurses despite having different educational qualifications and duties. The Gauhati High Court initially dismissed the appeal by the Union of India and others, affirming the Single Judge's decision that Nursing Assistants were entitled to Nursing Allowance similar to Staff Nurses. The Union of India argued that Nursing Assistants have different educational qualifications and experience compared to Staff Nurses, and thus should not receive the same Nursing Allowance. They emphasized that Nursing Assistants only completed a one-year course, while Staff Nurses completed a four-year course and are registered with the State Nursing Council and the Indian Nursing Council. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision on the grounds that different educational qualifications and experience justify different pay scales and allowances. The Court cited previous rulings that support classification based on educational qualifications and upheld the distinction in pay between Nursing Assistants and Staff Nurses. The Supreme Court referred to several precedent cases, including Punjab State Cooperative Milk Producers Federation Limited vs. Balbir Kumar Walia, Director of Elementary Education, Odisha vs. Pramod Kumar Sahoo, and Secretary Department of Personnel Public Grievances & Pension vs. T.V.L.N. Mallikarjuna Rao, to support its decision. The final outcome was that the Supreme Court allowed the appeal by the Union of India, setting aside the High Court's decision, and ruled that Nursing Assistants in the BSF are not entitled to Nursing Allowance at par with Staff Nurses. The original writ petition claiming Nursing Allowance was dismissed.

case_name: Union of India & Ors. vs. V.R. Nanukuttan Nair
text: Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. V.R. Nanukuttan Nair. Date: 7th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether V.R. Nanukuttan Nair was entitled to the service element of disability pension from the date of his discharge from the Navy, despite not having completed the minimum qualifying service of 15 years. The Armed Forces Tribunal held that V.R. Nanukuttan Nair was entitled to the service element of disability pension from the date of his discharge, as he had been invalided from service due to a disability attributable to military service. The appellants argued that V.R. Nanukuttan Nair was not entitled to the service element of disability pension because he was discharged upon completion of his engagement and had not completed the qualifying service of 15 years. They also contended that he was not invalided out of service due to a disability. The Supreme Court interpreted Regulation 105B as allowing the grant of a service element of disability pension to individuals who had completed their engagement period and were found to be suffering from a disability attributable to or aggravated by naval service. The Court rejected the argument that the regulation required completion of 15 years of service. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the Tribunal's decision that V.R. Nanukuttan Nair was entitled to the service element of disability pension from the date of his discharge. The Court directed the appellants to pay the arrears of the service element within four months. The Supreme Court considered Navy (Pension) Regulations, 1964, specifically Regulations 78, 101, 101A, 105B, and 107. The Court also referred to various legal precedents, emphasizing the importance of harmoniously interpreting the regulations to advance the purpose of granting disability pensions.

case_name: Union of India & Others vs. Jogeshwar Swain
text: Case: Union of India & Others vs. Jogeshwar Swain. Date: 5th September 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Jogeshwar Swain, a Constable in the BSF, was accused of clicking pictures of a lady doctor while she was taking a bath, which led to his dismissal from service. The BSF conducted a Summary Security Force Court (SSFC) where Jogeshwar Swain pleaded guilty and was subsequently dismissed from service. The High Court set aside the punishment of dismissal, stating that there were procedural infirmities and lack of substantial evidence against Jogeshwar Swain. It directed that he would be entitled to full consequential benefits except for 50% of his salary. The High Court identified that the SSFC was convened and presided over by the Commandant of Jogeshwar Swain, which violated Rule 60 of the BSF Rules. It also noted that there was no worthwhile evidence against Swain and that the confession obtained was not properly documented. The Supreme Court concluded that the procedural safeguards, such as explaining the consequences of pleading guilty to Jogeshwar Swain and obtaining his signature on the minutes of the proceedings, were not followed properly, thus justifying the High Court's decision to set aside his dismissal. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing the appeals filed by the Union of India and BSF administration, and confirmed that Jogeshwar Swain's dismissal was unwarranted based on the flawed procedural compliance.

case_name: Union of India and Joint Secretary (Cofeposa), Gov. of India, Ministry of Finance vs Dimple Happy Dhakad
text: Case: Union of India and Joint Secretary (Cofeposa), Gov. of India, Ministry of Finance vs Dimple Happy Dhakad. Date: 18th July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the detention orders issued under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange & Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA) were valid. The detention orders were issued because Dimple Happy Dhakad and others were allegedly involved in the smuggling of large quantities of gold into India from UAE. The High Court quashed the detention orders on the grounds that the orders and the relied upon documents were not served on the detenues simultaneously, violating Article 22(5) of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, stating that the statutory period of five days for serving the relied upon documents was adhered to, thus complying with the requirements of COFEPOSA. Dimple Happy Dhakad was alleged to have abetted Nisar Aliyar in smuggling gold and disposed of the smuggled gold through his multiple jewellery outlets. The Supreme Court emphasized that procedural compliance is crucial in preventive detention cases to uphold the detenue's right to personal liberty. No, the Supreme Court found that there was no violation of Article 22(5) since the relied upon documents were served within the statutory period of five days. The case involved the smuggling of over 3300 kgs of gold, valued at approximately Rs. 1000 crores. The Supreme Court upheld the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, stating that the authority had valid reasons to believe the detenues were likely to be released on bail and would continue their prejudicial activities. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in its interpretation of the guidelines, as the statutory requirements were fulfilled within the stipulated period, thus not warranting the quashing of detention orders.

case_name: Union of India and Others vs. Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni
text: Case: Union of India and Others vs. Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni. Date: 23rd March 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the challenge to the orders passed by the Armed Forces Tribunal, which reduced the sentence of Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni from three years rigorous imprisonment and cashiering to dismissal from service. The allegations included irregularities in procurement of various supplies such as Kabuli Chana, Barley, and Gram, as well as issues in the testing and sampling of rations, tendering, and procurement of supplies that were allegedly unfit for human consumption. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal by Union of India and Others, and allowed the Transferred Case (Criminal) No. 1 of 2017 filed by Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni, quashing the orders of the General Court Martial and the Armed Forces Tribunal, thus acquitting him of all charges. Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni was found guilty on charges related to procurement irregularities and failure to ensure quality standards in supplies provided to the Army, including the improper approval of tendering stations and acceptance of substandard supplies. The Supreme Court identified that the General Court Martial was not properly constituted as the members were of ranks lower than Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni, which violated sub-rule (2) of Rule 40 of the Army Rules. The Supreme Court found the findings and sentence of the General Court Martial unsustainable due to lack of proper constitution of the court and because the material factors were either ignored or the evidence was appreciated in a totally erroneous manner. The Armed Forces Tribunal had partly allowed Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni's petition, affirming the findings of the General Court Martial but reducing the sentence from rigorous imprisonment and cashiering to dismissal from service. The Supreme Court did not find any evidence of actual fraud or wrongful gain and held that the acts did not lead to actual loss or wrongful gain, thus acquitting Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni of the charges. Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni was entitled to all pensionary and consequential benefits in accordance with law, and the arrears of such benefits were to be computed and paid to him within three months from the date of the judgment. The anonymous complaint led to an inquiry and subsequent charges against Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni for procurement irregularities, but the Supreme Court found that proper procedures were not followed and that no evidence of fraud or wrongful gain was established. The Supreme Court noted that both the Army Purchase Organization and the Directorate were concurrently responsible for monitoring and examining the progress of the contracts, and found no conclusive evidence of intent to defraud by Lt. Gen. (Retd.) S.K. Sahni.

case_name: Union of India vs Ankit Ashok Jalan
text: Case: Union of India vs Ankit Ashok Jalan. Date: 22nd November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the detention orders issued under COFEPOSA against Ashok Kumar Jalan and Amit Jalan were valid, considering the High Court's decision to quash these orders on grounds of improper examination of the possibility of the detenus being granted bail. The High Court quashed the detention orders on the grounds that there was a lapse and failure by the Detaining Authority to examine and consider the imminent possibility of the detenus being granted bail. The Union of India argued that the Detaining Authority was aware of the detenus being in custody and had properly considered the possibility of their release on bail, and their propensity to indulge in prejudicial activities upon release. The Detaining Authority considered the detenus' involvement in smuggling activities, their self-incriminating confessions obtained under the Customs Act, and the likelihood of their release on bail and continuation of prejudicial activities. The Supreme Court found that the Detaining Authority had adequately considered the imminent possibility of the detenus being released on bail and their propensity to continue engaging in prejudicial activities. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, reinstating the detention orders against Ashok Kumar Jalan and Amit Jalan. The ruling reinforces the importance of the Detaining Authority's thorough consideration of the detenus' likelihood of release and potential for engaging in prejudicial activities, ensuring that detention orders are well-founded. This judgement emphasizes the need for Detaining Authorities to provide clear and detailed reasoning when issuing detention orders, especially regarding the likelihood of the detenus' release and potential continuation of prejudicial activities. The Supreme Court highlighted that Detaining Authorities must be aware of the detenus' custody status, consider the likelihood of their release on bail, and assess their propensity for continuing prejudicial activities, ensuring a well-founded subjective satisfaction. The Detaining Authority's awareness of the detenus' judicial custody and the imminent possibility of their release was significant in establishing the necessity for preventive detention to prevent further prejudicial activities. Following the Supreme Court's decision, Ashok Kumar Jalan and Amit Jalan will remain under preventive detention, which aims to prevent them from engaging in future smuggling and prejudicial activities.

case_name: Union of India vs Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi
text: Case: Union of India vs Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi. Date: 29th July 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi was accused of using criminal force with the intent to outrage the modesty of two women during a medical examination. The Armed Forces Tribunal upheld the conviction but converted the punishment from cashiering from service to a fine of Rs.50,000. Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi argued that the evidence on record was not properly appreciated and that the testimonies of witnesses in his favor were ignored. The Supreme Court found that the evidence of the complainants was clear and convincing, establishing that Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi misbehaved with them during their physical examination. One complainant was suffering from bronchial asthma, and the other had a duodenal ulcer, which required physical examination of their chests and stomachs. The Supreme Court disagreed with the Tribunal's decision to convert the punishment and restored the original punishment of cashiering from service. The Supreme Court directed that the Respondents consider the entire record of service and the advanced age of Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi before initiating proceedings under the Army Pension Regulations. If no proceedings are initiated, he shall be entitled to all pensionary benefits. The Supreme Court restored the punishment of cashiering from service, considering the reprehensible conduct of Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi, who abused his position of trust as a doctor. The Supreme Court noted that Lt. Col. R. Sharma testified that there was no necessity for the Appellant to touch the private parts of the complainants during the medical examination, which supported the charges against Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi. The Supreme Court directed that the amount of Rs.50,000 deposited by Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi be refunded to him with interest accrued therefrom.

The Supreme Court directed that the Respondents consider the entire record of service and the advanced age of Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi before initiating proceedings under the Army Pension Regulations. If no proceedings are initiated, he shall be entitled to all pensionary benefits.
The Supreme Court restored the punishment of cashiering from service, considering the reprehensible conduct of Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi, who abused his position of trust as a doctor.

The Supreme Court noted that Lt. Col. R. Sharma testified that there was no necessity for the Appellant to touch the private parts of the complainants during the medical examination, which supported the charges against Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi.
The Supreme Court directed that the amount of Rs.50,000 deposited by Lt. Col. S. S. Bedi be refunded to him with interest accrued therefrom.

case_name: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India
text: Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India. Date: 1st September 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the definition and payment of Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR) dues by telecom service providers as per the provisions of the Indian Telegraph Act. The Supreme Court mandated that telecom service providers must pay the AGR dues as calculated by the Department of Telecommunications without any reassessment or recalculation. The telecom service providers argued that the insolvency proceedings were initiated bona fide and that the National Company Law Tribunal should decide whether the spectrum/license can be part of the resolution process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The Supreme Court held that the spectrum cannot be subjected to insolvency proceedings as it is not an operational asset but a state-owned asset under the Indian Telegraph Act. The dues towards the spectrum use are not operational dues under the IBC. The Supreme Court provided that telecom operators must pay 10% of their total dues by 31st March 2021 and the remaining amount in yearly installments over the next 20 years. The Supreme Court acknowledged that non-telecom PSUs, such as Powergrid, GAIL, and DMRC, are not involved in providing telecom services to the public and decided to withdraw the demands raised for license fees based on non-telecom revenue.

case_name: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India and Ors.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India and Ors.. Date: 23rd July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case was about the calculation and payment of Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR) dues by telecom operators. The miscellaneous applications were filed for the modification of paragraph 38(i) of the judgment dated 01.09.2020, seeking clarification that the judgment does not bar the Union of India from considering and rectifying clerical or arithmetical errors in the computation of AGR dues. The Supreme Court made it clear that there was no scope for raising any further dispute with respect to AGR dues, and no recalculation or self-assessment could be undertaken. The amounts stated were to be treated as final. The directions included: Telecom Operators cannot raise disputes on AGR dues, must pay 10% of the total dues by 31.03.2021, make yearly payments from 01.04.2021 to 31.03.2031, furnish undertakings to pay arrears, keep existing bank guarantees alive until payment is complete, and report compliance annually by 7th April. The applicants argued that certain arithmetical errors had arisen due to inadvertence on the part of the Department of Telecommunications while computing the dues. They emphasized that they did not intend to reopen issues already decided but sought rectification of these errors. The Supreme Court viewed that correcting arithmetical errors would lead to recalculation, effectively altering the AGR dues specified in the previous order, which was not permissible as per their judgment.

case_name: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.. Date: 22nd August 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the live broadcast signals of cricket matches shared by BCCI with Prasar Bharati should be retransmitted by cable operators, and whether this arrangement was legal under Section 3 of the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007 and Section 8 of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995. The High Court of Delhi ruled that the signals received by Prasar Bharati from BCCI should not be retransmitted by cable operators and that this retransmission was not covered under Section 8 of the Cable Act, 1995. The Union of India argued that the retransmission of live signals by cable operators was necessary to provide access to the largest number of viewers, especially those in remote areas, and that this was in line with the objectives of the Prasar Bharati Act, 1990 and the Sports Act, 2007. The Supreme Court of India upheld the High Court's decision and ruled that the live broadcast signals shared by BCCI with Prasar Bharati should not be retransmitted by cable operators. The court emphasized that the signals were meant for Prasar Bharati's terrestrial and DTH networks only. The Supreme Court interpreted Section 3 of the Sports Act, 2007 as mandating that the live broadcast signals shared with Prasar Bharati should be retransmitted only on Prasar Bharati's terrestrial and DTH networks, and not through cable operators. BCCI argued that retransmitting the live signals through cable operators without proper authorization infringed on their broadcasting rights and revenue, as these signals were exclusively licensed to specific broadcasters under the Media Rights Agreement. The Supreme Court acknowledged the need to balance public access to sports events with the rights of content owners, but ultimately ruled that the statutory mandate under the Sports Act, 2007 should be strictly interpreted to limit retransmission to Prasar Bharati's networks.

case_name: Union of India vs. E Krishna Rao
text: Case: Union of India vs. E Krishna Rao. Date: 28th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether arrears and benefits owed to TV News Correspondents and similarly placed employees should be paid promptly as directed by the Supreme Court in a prior judgment. The Supreme Court directed that arrears for parties involved in the proceedings should be released by 15th March 2022 and benefits for similarly situated employees should be disbursed by 30th June 2022. The Supreme Court ruled that employees who were not parties or intervenors in the earlier proceedings could still claim benefits from the date of the prior judgment on 26th September 2018 without having to initiate separate proceedings. The Court disposed of all miscellaneous applications and contempt petitions, ensuring compliance with its orders regarding arrears and benefits. The Supreme Court clarified that TV Assistant News Editors, in addition to TV News Correspondents and TV Assistant News Correspondents, were entitled to the same benefits as per the prior judgment.

case_name: Union of India vs. Leen Martin & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Leen Martin & Anr.. Date: 1st February 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the appeal against the High Court's decision to acquit Leen Martin of charges under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Leen Martin was charged under Sections 8(c), 20(b)(ii)(c), and 28 read with Section 23 of the NDPS Act for possession and attempted trafficking of narcotic substances. The trial court convicted Leen Martin, sentencing him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 for each charge, to be served concurrently. The High Court acquitted Leen Martin because it found that the prosecution failed to prove the presence of independent witnesses during the seizure, and the evidence presented was inconsistent and contradictory. The Supreme Court found that the evidence from independent witnesses contradicted the statement of the Intelligence Officer, and there was no material to substantiate the case against Leen Martin beyond his retracted statement under Section 67 of the NDPS Act. The Supreme Court concluded that it was not safe to rely solely on the statement of the official witness (PW-1) for convicting Leen Martin, especially when independent witnesses provided a different account. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's acquittal because the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the independent witnesses' statements contradicted the official witness's account. The Supreme Court noted that Leen Martin had already undergone four and a half years of incarceration and was not in the country at the time of the appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's order acquitting Leen Martin. The statements made by independent witnesses (PW-8 and PW-9) were significant because they contradicted the prosecution's account of the seizure and inspection, leading to doubts about the credibility of the evidence. The Supreme Court noted that the statement made under Section 67 of the NDPS Act by Leen Martin was retracted, and without corroborating evidence, it was not sufficient to convict him.

case_name: Union of India vs. Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly
text: Case: Union of India vs. Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly. Date: 1st August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The respondent is Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly. The main issue was Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly's denial of promotion to the position of Director General Medical Services (Army) despite being eligible and senior. The AFT directed the appellants to post Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly as DGMS (Army) as expeditiously as possible and within one month from the date of the judgement. The appellants argued that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly was not found suitable for the position based on an inter se assessment of suitability among eligible officers. The Supreme Court of India upheld the AFT's decision and dismissed the appeal, affirming that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly was entitled to the promotion as DGMS (Army). The Supreme Court highlighted that the criteria included inter se seniority and suitability, and that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly, being the senior most and suitable, should be promoted. The Supreme Court instructed that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly should be appointed to the post of DGMS (Army) without further delay, in accordance with the AFT's decision.

case_name: Union of India vs. Manraj Enterprises
text: Case: Union of India vs. Manraj Enterprises. Date: 18th November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the arbitrator could award pendente lite and future interest on the amounts payable to the contractor, despite a clause in the General Conditions of Contract (GCC) that barred the payment of interest. The arbitrator awarded Manraj Enterprises Rs. 78,81,553.08, along with pendente lite and future interest at the rates of 12% and 18% respectively on the entire awarded amount, except for the earnest money deposit and security deposit. The Union of India argued that as per clause 16(2) of the GCC, no interest was payable on the earnest money deposit, security deposit, or any amounts payable to the contractor under the contract, and thus the arbitrator should not have awarded pendente lite and future interest. The High Court dismissed the Union of India's appeal and confirmed the award made by the arbitrator, including the pendente lite and future interest. The Supreme Court interpreted clause 16(2) of the GCC to mean that no interest was payable upon the earnest money, security deposit, or amounts payable to the contractor under the contract. Therefore, the arbitrator erred in awarding pendente lite and future interest. The Supreme Court set aside the judgments and orders of the High Court and the award of the arbitrator that granted pendente lite and future interest, ruling that the contractor was not entitled to such interest due to the specific bar in clause 16(2) of the GCC.

case_name: Union of India vs. Parmar Construction Company
text: Case: Union of India vs. Parmar Construction Company. Date: 29th March 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The contract involved construction, strengthening, and rebuilding of major bridges between Nadbhai-Idgah (Agra) with a total cost of Rs 3,30,71,724. Parmar Construction Company claimed for Rs 1,07,98,765 for the final bill along with interest and arbitration cost. The High Court appointed an independent arbitrator without adhering to the mutually agreed procedure under the agreement executed between the parties. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in appointing an independent arbitrator without resorting to the procedure prescribed under clause 64(3) of the contract. The contractors claimed refunds for security deposits/bank guarantees, escalation costs, and interests which were unilaterally reduced by the railway establishment. The Supreme Court directed the appellants to appoint an arbitrator within one month as per the agreed terms in clause 64(3) of the agreement.

case_name: Union of India vs. R. Sethumadhavan & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India vs. R. Sethumadhavan & Anr.. Date: 22nd March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the pension of the respondent, who retired as a Train Examiner, should be calculated based on the replacement scale of Rs. 4500-7000 or the revised scale of Rs. 5000-8000 recommended for the re-designated post of Junior Engineer Grade-II. The respondent contended that his post of Train Examiner was re-designated as Junior Engineer Grade-II and that his pension should be based on the revised pay scale of Rs. 5000-8000, as recommended by the 5th Central Pay Commission. The CAT held that the respondent's pension had been correctly fixed based on the replacement scale of Rs. 4500-7000 for the post of Train Examiner, as there was no evidence to suggest that the post was re-designated as Junior Engineer Grade-II. The High Court allowed the writ petition, quashed the CAT's order, and directed that the respondent's pension be recalculated based on the revised scale of Rs. 5000-8000, assuming that the post of Train Examiner was re-designated as Junior Engineer Grade-II. The Supreme Court found no evidence on record to support the High Court's assumption that the post of Train Examiner was re-designated as Junior Engineer Grade-II. The Supreme Court held that the High Court's conclusion was erroneous and not supported by material evidence. The Supreme Court relied on its earlier decision in K.S. Krishnaswamy & Ors. v. Union of India & Anr., which dealt with a similar issue regarding the scale of pay recommended by the 5th Central Pay Commission and the subsequent clarifications issued by the Government of India.

case_name: Union of India vs. Rajendra N Shah & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Rajendra N Shah & Anr.. Date: 20th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the validity of the Constitution (Ninety-Seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, which introduced Part IXB under the chapter 'The Co-operative Societies', and whether it required ratification by half of the State Legislatures under Article 368(2) proviso. The Gujarat High Court declared that Part IXB of the Constitution (Ninety-Seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, was ultra vires the Constitution of India for lack of the requisite ratification by half of the State Legislatures under Article 368(2) proviso. The key components introduced by the amendment included provisions for incorporation, regulation, and winding up of co-operative societies based on democratic principles, member-control, member-economic participation, and autonomous functioning. The Union of India argued that the 97th Constitutional Amendment aimed to achieve significant social and economic objectives regarding the functioning of co-operative societies, and the amendment did not change the legislative power distribution in a manner requiring ratification by the States. The Supreme Court held that the amendment required ratification by half of the State Legislatures as it impacted the legislative powers of the States under Article 246(3) read with Entry 32 of List II (State List). The Supreme Court applied the doctrine of severability, upholding the validity of the amendment concerning multi-State co-operative societies and Union territories but declaring it void concerning co-operative societies within the States due to lack of ratification. The judgment reinforces that the legislative powers concerning co-operative societies remain with the State Legislatures, ensuring that any amendments impacting these powers require ratification by the States. The Supreme Court emphasized that constitutional amendments affecting State legislative powers must comply with the procedural requirement of ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures under Article 368(2) proviso. Future constitutional amendments affecting State powers may face challenges if they do not secure the requisite ratification from the States, ensuring a strict adherence to the federal structure and distribution of legislative powers. Legislative processes should involve thorough consultations with State Legislatures and ensure that any amendments affecting State powers secure the necessary ratification, thereby maintaining the constitutional balance and federal principles. The judgment underscores the importance of preserving the autonomy of co-operative societies by ensuring that any constitutional amendments impacting their governance receive proper ratification, thus protecting the interests of the States and the democratic functioning of these societies.

case_name: Union of India vs. Ranjit Kumar Saha & Anr.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Ranjit Kumar Saha & Anr.. Date: 1st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The first respondent was a Subedar (Building and Road) and the second respondent was a Naib Subedar (Building and Road) in Headquarters-6 Sector, Assam Rifles, Kamrup, Assam. A sting operation carried out by a contractor, Mr. C.C. Mathew, was telecast on Matrabhumi News and 'Tehelka.com' on 24/25th September 2014, alleging corruption in the Assam Rifles. The preliminary objections raised by the respondents were: 1) No opportunity to cross-examine the complainant during the Court of Inquiry and Summary of Evidence; 2) The composition of the GARC was in violation of Section 90 of the 2006 Act; 3) The GARC cannot try a case punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act (PC Act). The Guwahati High Court decided that the GARC cannot try an offence punishable under the PC Act and that only a Special Judge appointed under the PC Act has the jurisdiction to try such offences. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal by stating that the GARC has no jurisdiction to try an offence punishable under Section 7 of the PC Act, which can only be tried by a Special Judge appointed under the PC Act. Mr. Nadkarni argued that the GARC has jurisdiction to try every civil offence, including those under the PC Act, as per Sections 55 and 56 of the 2006 Act. He contended that the 2006 Act should be interpreted to include jurisdiction over offences under the PC Act. The Supreme Court held that Section 4 of the PC Act and Section 55 of the 2006 Act could be harmoniously construed and that the GARC has jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act against members of the Assam Rifles. The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the High Court and allowed the appeal, thereby granting the GARC jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act against members of the Assam Rifles. The decision may set a precedent that grants the GARC jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act, thereby affecting the handling of similar cases involving allegations of corruption within the Assam Rifles. This judgement could influence the interpretation of jurisdiction for other paramilitary forces governed by similar Acts, potentially allowing their respective courts to try offences under the PC Act, thus expanding the scope of their judicial authority. Sections 55 and 56 of the Assam Rifles Act, 2006 were pivotal, as they outline the jurisdiction of the GARC over civil offences and exceptions to this jurisdiction, which the Supreme Court interpreted to include offences under the PC Act.

Mr. Nadkarni argued that the GARC has jurisdiction to try every civil offence, including those under the PC Act, as per Sections 55 and 56 of the 2006 Act. He contended that the 2006 Act should be interpreted to include jurisdiction over offences under the PC Act.

The Supreme Court held that Section 4 of the PC Act and Section 55 of the 2006 Act could be harmoniously construed and that the GARC has jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act against members of the Assam Rifles.
The Supreme Court set aside the judgement of the High Court and allowed the appeal, thereby granting the GARC jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act against members of the Assam Rifles.

The decision may set a precedent that grants the GARC jurisdiction to try offences under the PC Act, thereby affecting the handling of similar cases involving allegations of corruption within the Assam Rifles.

This judgement could influence the interpretation of jurisdiction for other paramilitary forces governed by similar Acts, potentially allowing their respective courts to try offences under the PC Act, thus expanding the scope of their judicial authority.

Sections 55 and 56 of the Assam Rifles Act, 2006 were pivotal, as they outline the jurisdiction of the GARC over civil offences and exceptions to this jurisdiction, which the Supreme Court interpreted to include offences under the PC Act.

case_name: Union of India vs. Uzair Imran & Ors.
text: Case: Union of India vs. Uzair Imran & Ors.. Date: 11th October 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the respondents, including Ankur Gupta, were eligible for appointment as Postal Assistants despite having pursued their intermediate education in the vocational stream, which was excluded by the amended recruitment rules. The CAT decided in favor of the respondents, directing the Union of India to send them for training and appoint them as Postal Assistants, stating that the advertisement did not exclude candidates from the vocational stream. The High Court upheld the CAT's decision, dismissing the Union of India's writ petition and review application, stating that the exclusion of vocational stream candidates was based on an executive order, not a statutory amendment. The Union of India argued that the recruitment rules were amended in 1992 to exclude candidates from the vocational stream and that this amendment was in force before the 1995 recruitment process started, making the respondents ineligible. The Supreme Court observed that the amendment rules were published in the Gazette of India on 15th February 1992, thus making them operational before the recruitment process began in 1995. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, holding that the High Court erred in not considering the amendment rules and the vocational stream exclusion, thus restoring the validity of the exclusion. The Supreme Court emphasized that statutory amendments to recruitment rules prevail over executive orders and that qualifications specified in such amendments must be adhered to in recruitment processes. The Supreme Court directed that Ankur Gupta be offered appointment as a Postal Assistant on probation, subject to satisfactory completion of probation and confirmation in service, with no entitlement to arrears of salary or seniority from the original recruitment date. The judgment reinforces the need for strict adherence to statutory recruitment rules and clarifies that executive orders cannot override such rules, thus guiding future recruitment processes to ensure compliance with established legal frameworks. Candidates should carefully review the statutory recruitment rules and ensure they meet all specified qualifications, avoiding reliance on any executive orders or clarifications that may conflict with these rules. The judgment clarifies that vocational stream qualifications may be excluded from eligibility if specified in statutory recruitment rules, and such exclusions must be clearly communicated and adhered to in the recruitment process.

case_name: University of Delhi vs. Delhi University Contract Employees Union & Ors.
text: Case: University of Delhi vs. Delhi University Contract Employees Union & Ors.. Date: 25th March 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the contractual employees of the University of Delhi were entitled to regularization of their services or not. The Supreme Court decided that the contractual employees were not entitled to regularization in terms of paragraph 53 of the decision in Umadevi. However, the court directed that the contractual employees be given age relaxation and additional marks based on their years of service to compete in the ensuing selection process. The Supreme Court directed that all contractual employees be given age relaxation and additional marks based on their years of service (up to a maximum of 18 marks) in the ensuing selection process. The selection process must include public advertisement, and contractual employees must be given adequate time to prepare and participate. The rationale was to provide a fair opportunity for contractual employees who had served for a significant period and gained valuable experience, allowing them to compete with new applicants on a more level playing field. The Supreme Court directed that contractual employees continue to work in their current positions on a provisional basis until the next round of selections, with the liberty to participate in future selection processes.

case_name: University of Kerala & Anr. vs. Saiful Islam A. & Ors.
text: Case: University of Kerala & Anr. vs. Saiful Islam A. & Ors.. Date: 19th July 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the required teaching experience for appointment to the post of Reader should be pre-Ph.D. or post-Ph.D., with Ph.D. being an essential qualification for the position. The Full Bench of the Kerala High Court held that the required teaching experience for the post of Reader should be post-Ph.D. The Supreme Court modified the High Court's judgment to accommodate the intervening developments, ensuring no recovery of benefits and settling disputes in favor of both parties. The Supreme Court took into account intervening developments such as the retirement of both parties to ensure an equitable resolution under Article 142 of the Constitution. The court addressed whether teaching experience before acquiring a Ph.D. could be counted towards eligibility for the post of Reader, ultimately emphasizing the need for post-Ph.D. experience.
