case_name: University of Kerala and Ors. vs Merlin J.N. and Ors.
text: Case: University of Kerala and Ors. vs Merlin J.N. and Ors.. Date: 17th August 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The central issue was whether the appointment of Dr. Jayakumar as Lecturer in Sociology complied with the University Grants Commission (UGC) regulations, specifically the NET exemption criteria under the 2009/2010 regulations. The High Court set aside Dr. Jayakumar's appointment, ruling that it did not meet the criteria specified under the 2009 UGC regulations. The Supreme Court clarified that the 2016 UGC regulations, which provided exemptions for candidates who obtained their Ph.D. prior to 11th July 2009, were applicable retrospectively, thereby validating Dr. Jayakumar's appointment. The Supreme Court directed that amendments like the 2016 UGC regulations, intended to address ambiguities or hardships, should be considered retrospectively where clear intent is evident, to ensure fairness in appointments. The judgment ensures that pre-2009 Ph.D. holders who met the conditions under the 2016 UGC regulations are entitled to NET exemption and their appointments should not be invalidated retroactively.

case_name: University of Mysore vs. Rajaiah (Dead) By LRS & Ors.
text: Case: University of Mysore vs. Rajaiah (Dead) By LRS & Ors.. Date: 23rd March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The University of Mysore contended that the private respondents, Rajaiah and Chamundi, had no right, title, or interest over the disputed property, as the land was gifted to the President of India and subsequently leased to the University. They argued that the occupancy rights claimed by the respondents were based on forged documents. The High Court of Karnataka dismissed the appeals and writ petitions filed by the University of Mysore, upholding the occupancy rights granted to Rajaiah and Chamundi by the Land Tribunal. The private respondents, Rajaiah and Chamundi, claimed occupancy rights as tenants under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, stating they were granted these rights by the Land Tribunal. They argued that they had been in possession and enjoyment of the land for years. The Supreme Court found the order invalid because it was based on fraudulent documents. The original records showed that the occupancy rights granted by the Land Tribunal were for different lands in Dadadahalli village, not Kurubarahalli. The documents submitted by the private respondents were forged. The Supreme Court held that the University of Mysore was in lawful possession of the disputed land and that the private respondents had no title or possession of it. The Court restored the trial court's judgment, which dismissed the suits filed by the private respondents. Upon discovering the fraud, the University filed writ petitions challenging the Land Tribunal's order and submitted evidence showing that the documents were forged. The University also supported a criminal case filed against the private respondents for forgery and fraud. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the University of Mysore, set aside the judgments of the High Court and the First Appellate Court, and quashed the Land Tribunal's order granting occupancy rights to the private respondents. The Court restored the trial court's decision, which dismissed the suits filed by the private respondents.

case_name: Uppala Bixam @ Bixmaiah vs. The State of Andhra Pradesh
text: Case: Uppala Bixam @ Bixmaiah vs. The State of Andhra Pradesh. Date: 11th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Uppala Bixam's conviction for the murder of Ramesh under Section 302 and Section 201 of the IPC was justified based on the circumstantial evidence. Uppala Bixam was charged under Section 302 for murder and Section 201 for causing the disappearance of evidence. Uppala Bixam was arrested after the deceased Ramesh's family found three of his sheep in possession of Shaik Naseem, who informed them that Lingaiah had sold him the sheep, and Lingaiah in turn stated that Uppala Bixam had sold him the sheep. The prosecution relied on the recovery of the deceased's body based on the appellant's alleged confessional statement and the sale of sheep by the appellant to Lingaiah, which were later found in possession of Shaik Naseem. The trial court convicted Uppala Bixam under Section 302 IPC for murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment, and under Section 201 IPC for causing the disappearance of evidence, sentencing him to six months imprisonment. The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court. The Supreme Court noted that circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain pointing to the guilt of the accused. The Court found that the circumstances presented did not conclusively prove Uppala Bixam's guilt. The Supreme Court highlighted that there was no specific identification mark on the recovered sheep to definitively link them to the deceased Ramesh, weakening the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence of Uppala Bixam, acquitting him of all charges due to insufficient evidence. The Supreme Court reiterated that circumstantial evidence must be cogent, firmly established, and point unerringly towards the guilt of the accused, forming a complete chain with no other plausible explanation. The Supreme Court found the conviction under Section 302 IPC unsustainable because the only strong evidence was the recovery of the body, which raised suspicion but did not conclusively prove Uppala Bixam's involvement beyond reasonable doubt.

case_name: Urmila Devi and Others vs. The Deity, Mandir Shree Chamunda Devi
text: Case: Urmila Devi and Others vs. The Deity, Mandir Shree Chamunda Devi. Date: 10th January 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the specific performance of a contract for the sale of land, which was later transferred to the deity through a gift deed. The agreement involved respondent Nos.2 to 6 selling their 5/16th share in Khasra Nos.430 and 431 for Rs.90,000 to Krishan Lal, the predecessor-in-interest of the appellants. The trial court declared the gift deed as null and void and granted a decree of specific performance in favor of the plaintiff. The High Court modified the decree to order respondent Nos.2 to 6 to pay Rs.90,000 with 9% interest per annum to the plaintiff, instead of granting specific performance. Compensation amounting to Rs.10,03,743 was awarded to defendant No.6, which included compensation for the land and the three shops constructed on it. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in awarding the compensation to defendant No.6 since the gift deed had been declared void and the plaintiff was entitled to the compensation. The Supreme Court directed that Rs.10 lakh should be awarded to the plaintiff-appellants out of the compensation received, and the rest should be given to the landowners (defendant Nos.1 to 5). Section 21 allows the court to award compensation in certain cases where specific performance is not possible, which was applied in this case to grant monetary compensation to the appellants. The appellants argued that they were entitled to the compensation for the land as the gift deed was declared void, and they had a valid agreement to sell the land. The Supreme Court modified the judgement of the High Court, directing a specific distribution of compensation between the plaintiff-appellants and defendant Nos.1 to 5. This judgement clarifies that when specific performance becomes impossible due to land acquisition, courts can award compensation based on the acquisition value, ensuring fairness to the parties involved.

case_name: Usha Chakraborty & Anr. vs. State of West Bengal & Anr.
text: Case: Usha Chakraborty & Anr. vs. State of West Bengal & Anr.. Date: 30th January 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in refusing to quash the FIR registered against the appellants under various sections of the IPC, based on a complaint alleging fraud and misappropriation related to a trust and school management. The respondent alleged that Usha Chakraborty and the other appellants engaged in fraudulent activities by illegally registering a trust deed, removing the respondent from his position as secretary, misappropriating funds, and withholding personal and financial documents. The respondent filed a complaint under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., which led to the registration of the FIR against the appellants, alleging offenses under Sections 323, 384, 406, 423, 467, 468, 420, and 120B of the IPC. The High Court declined to quash the FIR, holding that the case diary and materials presented prima facie made out a case for investigation, and thus, the interim order staying the proceedings was vacated. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, stating that the allegations pertained to a civil dispute over trust management and the respondent had concealed the fact of an ongoing civil suit. The Court emphasized that criminal proceedings should not be used as a tool for harassment in civil disputes. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR No. 189/2017 dated 11.04.2017 and all further proceedings based on it, as they found the allegations to be vague and not constituting the essential ingredients of the alleged offenses. The Supreme Court observed that the criminal proceedings in this case were being used as a weapon of harassment and that the respondent had already availed civil remedies, making the continuation of criminal proceedings an abuse of the process of law.

text: Case: Uttar Pradesh Forest Corporation Lucknow & Ors. vs. Vijay Kumar Yadav & Anr.. Date: 23rd November 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should have maintained the punishment order for the recovery of Rs. 2,46,922.56 since it was proved by the Enquiry Officer, despite the procedural lapse on other charges. The Supreme Court directed that the respondent employee, who has since retired, should receive any further amounts due towards retirement benefits after deducting the recovery amount of Rs. 2,46,922.56.

case_name: V. Lakshmikanthan and Anr. vs Union of India and Ors.
text: Case: V. Lakshmikanthan and Anr. vs Union of India and Ors.. Date: 22nd November 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the Union of India followed the post-based reservation roster as directed in the judgments of R.K. Sabharwal vs State of Punjab and Virpal Singh Chauhan vs Union of India for promotions in the Railway services. In R.K. Sabharwal vs State of Punjab, the court directed that the post-based reservation roster should be followed prospectively from 10th February 1995, and the percentage of reservation should be worked out in relation to the number of posts forming the cadre strength. The appellants' main submission was that the Railways had not followed the post-based reservation roster from 10th February 1995, as mandated by the Supreme Court in the R.K. Sabharwal judgment. The Railways responded that they had issued instructions regarding the introduction of post-based reservation rosters in promotions from Group 'C' to Group 'B' or within Group 'B' with effect from 16th November 2005. The Supreme Court decided that the Railways should have implemented the post-based reservation roster from 10th February 1995, as directed in the R.K. Sabharwal judgment, and not from 16th November 2005. The Supreme Court directed the Railways to examine the case of the appellants for their promotion to the posts of Assistant Executive Engineer and Executive Engineer in light of the judgments referred to and to complete the process within one month. The Supreme Court clarified that promotions already granted to other incumbents would not be affected, but the appellants would be entitled to notional benefits and restoration of seniority if found eligible. The Supreme Court clarified that the post-based reservation roster should be implemented from 10th February 1995, as per the R.K. Sabharwal judgment, and any deviation from this date by the Railways was not justified. If the Railways fail to comply with the Supreme Court's directive within the stipulated time, it could lead to further legal actions, including contempt of court proceedings, and potential disruption in the promotion processes within the Railways. This judgment may lead to stricter adherence to post-based reservation policies in future promotions in government services, ensuring compliance with Supreme Court directives and preventing similar legal disputes. Government departments should ensure that reservation rosters are implemented as per the directives of the Supreme Court, with accurate adherence to the specified dates and guidelines to avoid legal challenges and ensure fair promotions.

case_name: V. Rajaram vs. State Represented by the Inspector of Police CBI/SCB
text: Case: V. Rajaram vs. State Represented by the Inspector of Police CBI/SCB. Date: 26th November 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal of the appellant under Sections 217 and 221 IPC and convicting him for disobedience of law and omission to apprehend offenders. V. Rajaram was charged under Sections 217 and 221 IPC for allegedly disobeying laws with the intention to save the accused and for intentionally omitting to apprehend offenders during an incident at Dinakaran newspaper office. The charges stemmed from an incident on 9th May 2007 when supporters of M.K. Alagiri attacked the Dinakaran newspaper office in response to a poll suggesting M.K. Stalin as the political heir of then Chief Minister M. Karunanidhi, resulting in arson and the death of three employees. The High Court reversed the acquittal based on evidence, including photographs and video footage, that indicated V. Rajaram, as Deputy Superintendent of Police, did not take effective steps to prevent the crime and apprehend the offenders. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court relied on M.O.45-CD and other electronic evidence without proper certification under Section 65-B of the Indian Evidence Act, which raised concerns about the admissibility of such evidence. The Supreme Court concluded that the evidence did not sufficiently prove that V. The appellant argued that the Enforcement Directorate had no authority to seek police custody under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and that the arrest and subsequent remand were illegal and procedurally flawed. The Supreme Court held that the Enforcement Directorate has the power to seek custody for the purpose of interrogation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and that this authority is supported by the relevant legal framework and precedents. The appellant argued that the remand orders were issued without proper consideration of the statutory requirements and procedural safeguards, particularly the conditions under which remand can be granted under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The Supreme Court found that the procedural requirements had been adequately followed and that the appellant's detention and remand were legally justified under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The Supreme Court clarified that the Enforcement Directorate can seek custody within the statutory framework and that the timing of such custody must comply with the procedural safeguards outlined in the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. Future cases will likely see strict adherence to the procedural requirements for custody and remand under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with an emphasis on ensuring that the statutory safeguards are followed. case_name: V.P. Singh vs. The State of Punjab & Ors.
text: Case: V.P. Singh vs. The State of Punjab & Ors.. Date: 24th November 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the charges of abetment to suicide under Section 306 IPC against the appellants were justified in the context of the disciplinary action taken against a student, Gaurav Wahi, who subsequently committed suicide. Gaurav Wahi, a student, committed suicide after being reprimanded for misconduct in class and being suspended, with a requirement to bring his parents to the college. He was allegedly under the influence of alcohol during the class incident. Gaurav Wahi was suspended from the class, required to bring his parents to the college, and asked to deposit a security amount of Rs. 10,000 as part of the disciplinary measures taken by the college administration. Gaurav Wahi's suicide note expressed his love for his mother and stated that his father should not be troubled, indicating a sense of guilt and distress over the incident. The High Court dismissed the criminal revision petitions, allowing the trial to proceed. It did not interfere with the framing of charges against the appellants, although the order was criticized for being cryptic. The Supreme Court found that the evidence, including the charge sheet, did not support the allegations of abetment to suicide. The Court highlighted the lack of independent witnesses and the embellishments in the complaint. The Supreme Court referred to previous judgements, including 'S.S. Chheena vs. Vijay Kumar Mahajan' and 'Sanju Alias Sanjay Singh Sengar vs. State of M.P.', which emphasized the need for clear instigation or provocation for a charge of abetment to suicide under Section 306 IPC. The Supreme Court set aside the order framing charges against the appellants and the High Court's order sustaining the same, thereby discharging the accused from the charges of abetment to suicide. The Supreme Court emphasized that legitimate disciplinary actions necessary for running educational institutions should not be misconstrued as abetment to suicide, and such actions must be seen in the context of maintaining discipline. The Supreme Court conveyed that while the loss of a young life is tragic, the anguish of the affected family should not result in unwarranted legal action against educational institutions for taking necessary disciplinary measures.

text: Case: VVF (India) Limited vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors. Date: 3rd December 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The issue was whether payments made under protest before the assessment order could be considered as part of the mandatory pre-deposit for filing an appeal under Section 26(6A) of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002. VVF (India) Limited paid Rs. 3,64,24,388 under protest, which included Rs. 2,32,37,249 towards tax and Rs. 1,31,87,139 towards interest. The High Court held that amounts paid under protest before an assessment order must be adjusted against the total tax liability, requiring a separate pre-deposit of 10% of the remaining demand to file an appeal. The Court emphasized a strict and literal interpretation of taxing statutes, rejecting any construction based on legislative intent or inference. The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to account for the statutory language, which permits consideration of payments made under protest as part of the deposit.

case_name: Vahitha vs. State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: Vahitha vs. State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 22nd February 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether Vahitha's conviction for the murder of her five-year-old child under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code was justified based on the evidence presented. Vahitha was accused of strangling her five-year-old child to death in her mother-in-law's house while her husband was abroad. The motive was alleged to be her desire to live separately from her mother-in-law. The trial court convicted Vahitha of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced her to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000. The High Court dismissed Vahitha's appeal and upheld the trial court's conviction and sentence. Vahitha's defense was that she was not present at the scene of the crime and was with her father in Kolakkudi at the time of the incident, as testified by her father, who supported her alibi. The prosecution relied on the testimony of witnesses who saw Vahitha with the child before the murder, the post-mortem report indicating death by strangulation, and the recovery of the saree used in the crime. Vahitha's defense highlighted inconsistencies in the statements of key witnesses, particularly regarding the timing and sequence of events on the day of the crime, and discrepancies in the description of the saree used for strangulation. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentence, agreeing with the lower courts that the evidence was sufficient to prove Vahitha's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Vahitha's father's testimony supported her alibi, claiming that she was with him in Kolakkudi at the time of the murder. However, the court found this testimony unreliable compared to the other evidence. The post-mortem report confirmed that the child died of asphyxia due to strangulation, which was consistent with the prosecution's case that Vahitha used a saree to strangle her child. The Supreme Court noted that minor discrepancies in witness testimonies are common and do not necessarily discredit the prosecution's case, especially when the overall evidence strongly indicates the accused's guilt.

case_name: Varadarajan vs. Kanakavalli & Ors.
text: Case: Varadarajan vs. Kanakavalli & Ors.. Date: 22nd January 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The initial order dated 27th November 2007 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in revision petition under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 was challenged in the Supreme Court. The main issue in the revision petition was the order passed by the Executing Court on 19th September 2005, which directed the possession of the suit property to be given to Varadarajan as the legal representative of Umadevi, based on a decree in favor of Umadevi. Umadevi claimed a half share in the suit property as the successor-in-interest of her husband, Manicka Naicker, and filed a suit for partition and separate possession. This suit was decreed on 7th April 1989. The respondents challenged the Will executed by Umadevi, asserting that it was forged and that the son of a sister is not a legal heir as per Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The High Court found that the execution of the Will was surrounded by suspicious circumstances and concluded that the Will had not been proved genuine. Consequently, the legatee under the said Will could not be considered a legal representative to maintain the execution petition. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order was not sustainable in law, set it aside, and restored the order of the Executing Court. The Supreme Court concluded that Varadarajan, as the legal representative of Umadevi, was entitled to execute the decree.

case_name: Varala Bharath Kumar vs. State of Telangana
text: Case: Varala Bharath Kumar vs. State of Telangana. Date: 5th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the criminal proceedings against the appellants under Sections 498A and 406 of the Indian Penal Code should be quashed. The complainant alleged that Varala Bharath Kumar did not come close to her, evaded her, and showed no interest in cohabitation. She also alleged that his family members did not talk to her and that her parents spent a significant amount on the marriage and gold ornaments. The High Court rejected the appellants' plea to quash the proceedings and instead directed Varala Bharath Kumar to file an application under Section 70(2) Cr.P.C. to recall the Non-Bailable Warrant issued against him, and the second appellant to file an application under Section 205 Cr.P.C. to dispense with his presence before the trial court. The Supreme Court found that the allegations did not disclose any demand for dowry or acts of cruelty as defined under Section 498A IPC. The Court also found no evidence of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC. The allegations were seen as instances of unhappiness in the marital relationship rather than criminal conduct. The appellants were charged under Sections 498A (cruelty by husband or relatives) and 406 (criminal breach of trust) of the Indian Penal Code. Section 498A IPC deals with cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards a woman, which includes any willful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury, or harassment with a view to coercing her to meet any unlawful demand for property. Section 406 IPC deals with punishment for criminal breach of trust, which includes dishonestly misappropriating or converting to one's own use property entrusted to someone or violating a direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged. The Supreme Court found no evidence to support the allegations of dowry demand or cruelty. The Court noted that the complainant's allegations were more about personal unhappiness and lack of communication in the marriage rather than any criminal acts. The Supreme Court emphasized that the inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly and only when it is necessary to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the proceedings against both the appellants in CC No. 442 of 2015, pending on the file of XIV Metropolitan Magistrate, Cyberabad at L.B. Nagar.

case_name: Vasant Ganpat Padave (D) By LRs & Ors. vs. Anant Mahadev Sawant (D) Through LRs & Ors.
text: Case: Vasant Ganpat Padave (D) By LRs & Ors. vs. Anant Mahadev Sawant (D) Through LRs & Ors.. Date: 18th September 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case involves a dispute over the right to purchase land under the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, particularly focusing on Section 32-F which deals with the rights of tenants when the landlord is a minor, widow, or disabled person. The key legal issue was the interpretation of Section 32-F of the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, particularly whether tenants of landlords who are minors, widows, or disabled persons must be notified to exercise their right to purchase the land. The court decided that the words 'of the fact that he has attained majority' in Section 32-F(1)(a) should be eliminated to ensure that all tenants of landlords covered by the provision are notified, not just those of minor landlords. The court ruled that the timeline for tenants to exercise their right to purchase the land should begin from the date they are notified of the cessation of the landlord's disability, rather than from the date the disability ceased. The court acknowledged that the tenant's lack of awareness about the landlord's death (who lived in Mumbai while the tenant was in Ratnagiri) was relevant and ruled that the tenant must be informed to exercise the right to purchase effectively. The court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment dated 1st August 2014, and instructed that the tenant's intimation of purchase from 2008 be recorded, leading to the determination of the purchase price and the tenant's eventual ownership of the land.

case_name: Vashist Narayan Kumar vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
text: Case: Vashist Narayan Kumar vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.. Date: 2nd January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the error in the date of birth on the application form, which was inadvertently filled as 08.12.1997 instead of 18.12.1997, was significant enough to disqualify Vashist Narayan Kumar from the selection process for the post of Police Constable. Vashist Narayan Kumar explained that the error occurred while filling out the form at a cyber cafe in a nearby town. The date of birth was entered as 08.12.1997 instead of 18.12.1997, but this error did not provide him any benefit as he met the eligibility criteria regardless. The respondents argued that the advertisement clearly required the date of birth to match the 10th board certificate and that any discrepancies would result in cancellation of the application. They maintained that the appellant did not utilize the correction facility provided in the advertisement. The Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition, citing the error in the application form as a valid reason for disqualification. The Division Bench upheld this decision, noting that the appellant had not sought to quash the result declared on 11.06.2018. The Supreme Court held that the error in the date of birth was trivial and did not constitute misrepresentation or wilful suppression. The Court emphasized that the error did not affect the appellant's eligibility or the selection process and directed the respondents to treat the appellant as having 'passed' the selection process. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to consider the appellant for appointment, treating his date of birth as 18.12.1997, and to issue an appointment letter if he is otherwise not disqualified. The Court also allowed for the adjustment of the vacancy in the next recruitment if there were no current vacancies.

text: Case: Vasudevan Embranthi @ Vasudeva Rao (Dead) By LRS. vs. Gopalakrishnan (Dead) By LRS. & Ors.. Date: 25th October 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was the division of properties following a long-standing litigation that commenced in 1984, involving an application for letters of administration converted into a suit. The initial suit filed by the first respondent was dismissed, but the decree was reversed by the High Court, leading to the appeal by the legal representatives of the first defendant before the Supreme Court. Several attempts were made to find an amicable solution, but they failed due to minor differences between the parties. Both parties submitted proposals and sketches for settlement, which did not tally. The Supreme Court decided to divide the properties in terms of the sketch prepared by Mr. C. K. Venu, as produced by the respondents, despite the objections of the appellants, to do complete justice between the parties under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court's decree included the division of properties as proposed in the sketches, and it made it clear that the two wills (Exhibit A1 & B1) would stand superseded. The decree would be the source of title to the properties of the respective sharers. The Supreme Court directed the trial court to send a copy of the decree to the Sub-Registrar concerned for the purpose of entry in the official records of the Sub-Registrar.

The Supreme Court directed the trial court to send a copy of the decree to the Sub-Registrar concerned for the purpose of entry in the official records of the Sub-Registrar.

case_name: Vasudha Sethi & Ors. vs Kiran V. Bhaskar & Anr.
text: Case: Vasudha Sethi & Ors. vs Kiran V. Bhaskar & Anr.. Date: 12th January 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the custody dispute over the minor child Aaditya Kiran, between the appellant Vasudha Sethi (the mother) and the respondent Kiran V. Bhaskar (the father). Kiran V. Bhaskar filed the habeas corpus petition seeking custody of the minor child, alleging that Vasudha Sethi had detained the child in India against the terms of their agreement. The agreement allowed the child to travel to India for surgery with the mother and specified that the child would return to the USA by 26th September 2019. The High Court directed Vasudha Sethi to return to the USA with the child and hand over custody to Kiran V. Bhaskar, failing which Kiran V. Bhaskar could take custody and return to the USA with the child. The Supreme Court provided Vasudha Sethi an option to travel to the USA with the child and stay there, with Kiran V. Bhaskar bearing all expenses. If she declined, Kiran V. Bhaskar could take the child to the USA. The Supreme Court directed Kiran V. Bhaskar to provide a sufficient monthly amount for their maintenance, arrange for their travel, and ensure health insurance and medical care for the child. The Supreme Court directed that Kiran V. Bhaskar should not enforce the Arkansas court's order for three months after their arrival, allowing Vasudha Sethi to contest the custody proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed Kiran V. Bhaskar to have temporary custody of the child on Sundays and daily video calls for half an hour during the three-month period. The Supreme Court left open the option for the parties to adopt an agreed joint parenting plan for the welfare of the child and to seek further legal remedies as needed. The Supreme Court emphasized that the welfare and best interest of the child were paramount, and all decisions regarding custody and travel should prioritize the child's well-being. The Supreme Court acknowledged Vasudha Sethi's privacy and autonomy, providing her the choice to decide whether to travel to the USA with the child and ensuring support if she chose to do so.

case_name: Vedanta Limited vs The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors
text: Case: Vedanta Limited vs The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. Date: 29th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the closure of Vedanta Limited's copper smelter in Thoothukudi by the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) and the Government of Tamil Nadu due to violations of numerous environmental norms. The violations included operating without proper consent for about sixteen years, lack of hazardous waste management authorization for about ten years, improper disposal of hazardous waste, substantial presence of Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) in the water, dumping large amounts of copper slag leading to air and water pollution, and failure to maintain a mandated green belt. The High Court upheld the closure of Vedanta Limited's copper smelter, finding that the company had committed serious violations of environmental and other laws, justifying the decision to shut down the unit. The Supreme Court held that the High Court did not commit an error of jurisdiction in enquiring into all facets of the matter, including the grounds for the closure of the unit and whether Vedanta Limited was entitled to a renewal of permissions. The Supreme Court rejected Vedanta Limited's argument that the High Court should have confined its enquiry to the five grounds of closure, noting that the petitioner had consented to a full evaluation of the matter by the High Court. The Supreme Court emphasized the principles of sustainable development, the polluter pays principle, and the public trust doctrine, asserting that economic activities should not come at the expense of environmental degradation and public health. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petitions filed by Vedanta Limited, upholding the High Court's decision to close the copper smelter due to serious and repeated environmental violations.

case_name: Vedanta Ltd. (Formerly known as M/s Sesa Sterlite Ltd.) vs. The Goa Foundation & Ors.
text: Case: Vedanta Ltd. (Formerly known as M/s Sesa Sterlite Ltd.) vs. The Goa Foundation & Ors.. Date: 9th July 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the review petitions filed by Vedanta Ltd. and the State of Goa against the judgment in Goa Foundation vs. Sesa Sterlite Limited & Ors., pronounced on 7th February 2018, should be entertained despite significant delays. The review petitions were delayed by 907 days by Vedanta Ltd. and by 650-651 days by the State of Goa. No cogent grounds were furnished for this delay, which occurred well beyond the thirty-day limit prescribed by Rule 2 of Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013. The court disapproved the practice of filing review petitions with significant delays, especially after the retirement of the judges involved in the original decision. This practice was seen as undermining the institutional sanctity of the court's decision-making process. The Supreme Court dismissed the review petitions on the grounds of limitation due to the significant delays in filing. Additionally, the court found no legitimate grounds for reviewing the original judgment in Goa Foundation vs. Sesa Sterlite Limited & Ors. The Supreme Court's decision resulted in the disposal of any pending applications related to the review petitions.

case_name: Velthepu Srinivas and Others vs. State of Andhra Pradesh (now State of Telangana) and Anr.
text: Case: Velthepu Srinivas and Others vs. State of Andhra Pradesh (now State of Telangana) and Anr.. Date: 6th February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for the murder of the deceased, which was challenged in the Supreme Court. The conflict arose due to a political rivalry between the sister of the deceased and the wife of A-4, both of whom contested the Gram Panchayat elections, with the sister of the deceased winning and the wife of A-4 losing. On 15th November 2001, the deceased was traveling in an auto-rickshaw when A-1 stopped the vehicle, dragged the deceased out, and along with A-2, A-3, and A-4, attacked him with various weapons, leading to his death on the spot. A-3 was accused of hitting the deceased on the head with a stone, but the evidence did not support a shared intention to commit murder, leading the Supreme Court to modify his conviction to Section 304 Part II IPC and sentence him to 10 years imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and life sentences of A-1, A-2, and A-4 under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, confirming the findings of the Trial Court and the High Court. The Supreme Court found that A-3 did not share the common intention to commit murder as evidenced by the fact that he did not use the axe like the other accused and only used a stone, thus convicting him under Section 304 Part II IPC instead of Section 302. A-3's conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC was set aside and modified to a conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC with a sentence of 10 years imprisonment.

case_name: Vidyalakshmi @ Vidya vs State of Kerala
text: Case: Vidyalakshmi @ Vidya vs State of Kerala. Date: 15th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants are Vidyalakshmi @ Vidya and Anand Sabariraj @ And, along with others. The main charges were for offences under Section 302 read with Section 34, Section 120B, and Section 114 of the IPC, related to conspiracy and murder. The prosecution's case was that Vidyalakshmi, who was in a relationship with Accused No.1, conspired to murder her husband Anandaraman with the help of Accused No.1 and Accused No.2. The prosecution established the presence of the accused through witness testimonies, mobile phone records showing communication between the accused, and the recovery of items belonging to the deceased from the accused. The trial court convicted the accused under various sections of the IPC, including Section 302 for murder, and sentenced them to life imprisonment along with other penalties. The appellants argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of evidence, and there was no continuing relationship between Vidyalakshmi and Accused No.1 after her marriage. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentences, concluding that the prosecution had successfully established the conspiracy and involvement of the accused in the murder, and that all necessary links in the chain of evidence were proven beyond reasonable doubt.

case_name: Vijay Kumar vs. The State of Jammu & Kashmir
text: Case: Vijay Kumar vs. The State of Jammu & Kashmir. Date: 14th November 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. Vijay Kumar was charged with offenses punishable under Sections 302, 307, 326, 324, and 448 of the IPC for the murder of three minor children and causing serious injuries to Jia Lal, Kamlesh Kumari, and another minor child. The trial court found Vijay Kumar guilty of the charges and sentenced him to death for the offense under Section 302 IPC. Additionally, he was sentenced to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment for the offense under Section 307 IPC, 5 years for the offense under Section 326 IPC, 1 year for the offense under Section 324 IPC, and 1 year for the offense under Section 448 IPC, with all sentences to run concurrently. The High Court confirmed the trial court's judgement and upheld Vijay Kumar's conviction and sentences, including the death sentence for the offense under Section 302 IPC. The Supreme Court's review was limited to the question of the appropriateness of the death sentence imposed by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court. Vijay Kumar's counsel argued that he was not a previous convict or a professional killer, and the crime was driven by a matrimonial dispute where the victims were seen as not supporting the accused in resolving his marital issues. The Supreme Court concluded that the case did not fall within the category of 'rarest of rare' cases warranting the death penalty. The Court converted the death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of remission. The Supreme Court referred to the legal precedents set in the cases of Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh vs. State of Punjab, and Swamy Shraddananda vs. State of Karnataka, which provide guidelines on when the death penalty may be imposed. The aggravating factors included the brutal nature of the crime, where Vijay Kumar murdered three minor children and seriously injured others. However, the Court also considered the mitigating factors, such as his lack of a prior criminal record and the motive related to his matrimonial dispute. The Supreme Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of remission, meaning Vijay Kumar will remain in prison for the rest of his natural life. The Supreme Court stated that while the crime was brutal, the mitigating circumstances, such as the accused's lack of a prior criminal record and the motive related to a personal dispute, made the case fall short of the 'rarest of rare' category required for the death penalty.

case_name: Vijay Raikwar vs State of Madhya Pradesh
text: Case: Vijay Raikwar vs State of Madhya Pradesh. Date: 5th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. Vijay Raikwar was charged with offenses under Section 376(2)(f) and Section 201 of the IPC, as well as Sections 5(i), 5(m), and 5(r) read with Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offenses (POCSO) Act, for the rape and murder of a minor girl aged 7 years. The trial court convicted Vijay Raikwar based on the evidence that he was last seen with the deceased, the presence of the victim's frock and blood-stained mattress and bedsheet in his house, and medical evidence supporting the charges. The High Court dismissed Vijay Raikwar's appeal, confirming the trial court's judgment and upholding the conviction and the death penalty imposed on him. The counsel argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence without an eyewitness, and the chain of evidence did not conclusively prove Vijay Raikwar's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. They also requested to commute the death sentence to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court observed that the prosecution successfully proved the circumstantial evidence, such as the accused being last seen with the victim and the presence of incriminating evidence in his house, leading to his conviction. The Supreme Court confirmed Vijay Raikwar's conviction but commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, considering the mitigating circumstances and determining that the case did not fall under the 'rarest of rare' category warranting the death penalty.

case_name: Vijay Singh Vs. Shanti Devi and Another
text: Case: Vijay Singh Vs. Shanti Devi and Another. Date: 8th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether an ex parte decree, which was later set aside, could be termed as the decree of the court of first instance in a suit for pre-emption. Vijay Singh, as a co-sharer with Roop Chand, filed a suit for possession based on the right of pre-emption granted to a co-sharer under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, after Roop Chand sold the suit land to Shanti Devi. Shanti Devi filed an application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the ex parte decree, claiming she had not received the summons and was unaware of the proceedings until possession was taken. The amendment to Section 15 of the 1913 Act in 1995 took away the right of pre-emption of a co-sharer, retaining the right only with a tenant, which affected Vijay Singh's claim. The appellate court set aside the ex parte decree on the grounds that Shanti Devi had not been properly served, and this decision was upheld by the High Court and Supreme Court. The Supreme Court ruled that setting aside the ex parte decree reverts the parties to their original positions, and the decree passed on contest after the setting aside is treated as the decree of the first court. The trial court, after retrial, dismissed Vijay Singh's suit on 27th November 1999, ruling that the right of pre-emption had been extinguished by the 1995 amendment to the 1913 Act. The Supreme Court stated that an ex parte decree is a valid decree as long as it is not set aside, and once set aside, it ceases to exist and becomes non-est. The judgment clarifies that ex parte decrees, once set aside, are nullified, and the rights of parties are assessed based on the retrial, impacting future pre-emption cases with similar procedural issues. Litigants might focus more on ensuring proper service of summons and be prepared for retrials if ex parte decrees are set aside, adjusting their legal strategies to account for potential procedural challenges. The Supreme Court clarified that once an ex parte decree is set aside, it becomes non-est, and the parties are restored to their original positions before the decree was passed.

case_name: Vijendra vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
text: Case: Vijendra vs. State of Uttar Pradesh. Date: 31st July 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the High Court was justified in affirming Vijendra's conviction under Section 7(1)/16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, for selling adulterated buffalo milk. Vijendra was charged under Section 7(1)/16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, for selling buffalo milk that was found to be deficient in milk fat and non-fatty solids. The complaint was filed after Food Inspector R.C. Kansal found Vijendra selling buffalo milk without a license on 16th October 1979, and subsequent testing revealed the milk to be adulterated. The trial court convicted Vijendra, sentencing him to 6 months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1000, with a default sentence for non-payment of the fine. Vijendra appealed the High Court's decision, arguing that there was non-compliance with Section 10(7) and Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, which affected the validity of the conviction. The Supreme Court noted that there was a failure to prove that the Analyst's report was actually served on Vijendra, which violated his right to seek further analysis by the Central Food Laboratory, thus impacting his defense. The Supreme Court observed that the independent witness, Radhey Shyam, did not support the prosecution's case, which raised doubts about the proper collection and analysis of the milk sample. The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the lower courts, acquitted Vijendra of the charges, and allowed the appeal, citing the failure to prove compliance with mandatory provisions of the Act. The key factors included non-compliance with Section 13(2) of the Act, lack of evidence proving the delivery of the Analyst's report to Vijendra, and the independent witness not supporting the prosecution. The Supreme Court directed that Vijendra be acquitted of the charges under Section 7(1)/16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and ordered his immediate release if he was not required in any other case.

case_name: Vikas Rathi vs. The State of U.P. & Anr.
text: Case: Vikas Rathi vs. The State of U.P. & Anr.. Date: 1st March 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the High Court's order to summon Vikas Rathi as an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. was justified based on the available evidence. The complainant filed an application under Section 319 Cr.P.C. to summon Vikas Rathi as an additional accused based on certain oral allegations made by witnesses PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3 during the trial. The trial court dismissed the application under Section 319 Cr.P.C. for summoning Vikas Rathi as an additional accused, citing lack of sufficient evidence. The High Court quashed the trial court's order and remanded the matter back for fresh examination, directing the trial court to reconsider summoning Vikas Rathi as an additional accused. The appellant argued that the High Court's decision to remand the matter for fresh examination was incorrect, as the evidence available did not support summoning him as an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court emphasized that the power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. is discretionary and should be exercised sparingly, only when strong and cogent evidence is available against the person sought to be summoned. The prosecution presented statements from witnesses, including an eye witness, and a retracted statement recorded under Section 164 of the Cr.P.C., but these were found insufficient to establish Vikas Rathi's involvement in the crime. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and dismissed the application filed by the complainant for summoning Vikas Rathi as an additional accused, finding no strong evidence against him. The Supreme Court highlighted that summoning an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. requires more than a prima facie case and should be based on strong evidence that indicates a near probability of the person's involvement in the crime. The Supreme Court noted that the application was filed towards the end of the trial, and the evidence presented did not justify summoning Vikas Rathi as an additional accused at such a late stage.

case_name: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
text: Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.. Date: 11th February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether Vikash Kumar, who suffers from Writer's Cramp, was entitled to the assistance of a scribe during the Civil Services Examination under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Vikash Kumar requested a scribe because he suffers from Writer's Cramp, a neurological condition that severely affects his ability to write. The UPSC rejected Vikash Kumar's request for a scribe on the grounds that he did not meet the criteria of having a benchmark disability as defined under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. The Supreme Court held that the provision of a scribe should not be limited to candidates with benchmark disabilities and emphasized that reasonable accommodation must be made for all persons with disabilities, including those with specific disabilities like Writer's Cramp. The Supreme Court stated that examining bodies have an obligation to provide reasonable accommodations, such as the assistance of a scribe, to candidates with disabilities to ensure their full and effective participation in examinations. The Supreme Court directed the UPSC to reconsider Vikash Kumar's request for a scribe in light of the broader interpretation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and to make necessary accommodations for his disability. The broader implication of the judgement was the affirmation of the rights of persons with disabilities to reasonable accommodations in competitive examinations, reinforcing the principle of non-discrimination and equal opportunity.

case_name: Vikrant Singh Malik and Others vs. Supertech Limited and Others
text: Case: Vikrant Singh Malik and Others vs. Supertech Limited and Others. Date: 24th August 2020. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) was correct in dismissing a composite complaint filed by twenty-six flat buyers under Section 12(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, due to the lack of commonality among the complainants. The reliefs sought included withdrawing the offer of possession without a valid occupancy certificate, refunding money collected for parking charges and other demands, withdrawing cost escalation and interest charges, cancelling the license granted to the developer, and paying compensation for delayed possession. The NCDRC dismissed the complaint on the grounds that the agreements, flat sizes, costs, dates of agreements, and compensation claimed by the complainants were different, and thus, there was no commonality of interest among them. The Supreme Court found that the NCDRC had erred in its interpretation by not considering the subsequent Full Bench decision in Ambrish Kumar Shukla v. Ferrous Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., which clarified that commonality of interest among consumers does not require identical circumstances. The Supreme Court set aside the NCDRC's decision dismissing the complaint and restored the complaint for reconsideration by the NCDRC, instructing it to examine whether the complainants had a commonality of interest in securing redressal of their grievances. The Supreme Court directed the NCDRC to reconsider the complaint and determine whether the twenty-six complainants had a commonality of interest that would justify a representative action under Section 12(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act. The NCDRC was also instructed to consider any settlements or resolutions that had occurred since the original filing of the complaint.

text: Case: Vinod @ Sai D. Ghogale vs The State of Maharashtra. Date: 3rd October 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue addressed was whether Vinod @ Sai D. The Supreme Court granted bail to Vinod @ Sai D. Ghogale, concluding that he should be released on bail after serving more than seven years of his sentence, similar to his co-accused.

case_name: Vinod Kumar & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Vinod Kumar & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 30th January 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the appellants, who were temporarily appointed as Accounts Clerks under a scheme, should be regularized and absorbed into permanent posts. The Central Administrative Tribunal dismissed the appellants' plea for regularization, stating that their appointments were temporary and scheme-based, and did not entitle them to regularization or absorption into permanent posts. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions, upholding the Central Administrative Tribunal's judgment and stating that the appellants' temporary employment did not confer rights similar to those of permanent employees. The appellants argued that the High Court erred in not recognizing the substantive nature of their duties, which aligned with regular employment rather than temporary or scheme-based roles. They highlighted their continuous service for over 25 years and their selection through a regular recruitment process. The Supreme Court found merit in the appellants' arguments because their continuous service in regular capacities, selection through a process akin to regular recruitment, and the lack of reaffirmation of the temporary nature of their roles warranted a reclassification from temporary to regular status. The Supreme Court distinguished that the appellants' appointments were 'irregular' rather than 'illegal,' as they were made through a proper selection process involving written tests and interviews, and thus deserved consideration for regularization based on their long tenure. The Supreme Court held that the High Court misapplied the Uma Devi judgement, as the specific circumstances of the appellants' employment, including their long tenure and the nature of their duties, distinguished their case from the temporary and casual employees addressed in Uma Devi. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to complete the process of regularizing the appellants within three months from the date of service of the judgement. The judgement implies that temporary employees who have been in continuous service for a long duration and have been selected through proper procedures should be considered for regularization, especially if their duties align with those of regular employees. The Supreme Court's judgement emphasized that denying the appellants regularization despite their long service and regular duties would go against the principles of equity and fairness, as their substantive roles deserved recognition beyond their initial temporary appointments. The broader implications are that employment regulations must consider the evolution of employment roles over time, and long-serving temporary employees performing regular duties should be given fair consideration for regularization to uphold equity and fairness.

case_name: Vinod Singh Negi vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Vinod Singh Negi vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 14th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused during the pendency of their appeals against their conviction for murder. The respondents were Umesh Sharma, Ashok, and Parvinder Singh, who were accused of murdering Manoj, the brother of the appellant, Vinod Singh Negi. The accused were convicted under Section 302/34 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life with a fine of Rs. 50,000 each. The appellant challenged the High Court's order because the High Court did not assign any reasons for granting bail and overlooked the criminal background and pending cases against the accused. The Supreme Court referred to the legal principles laid down in cases like Ajay Kumar Sharma vs. State of U.P., Lokesh Singh vs. State of U.P., Dataram Singh vs. State of U.P., and Mauji Ram vs. State of U.P., which emphasize the need for courts to assign reasons while granting bail. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remanded the case back to the High Court for fresh consideration of the bail applications on their respective merits. The additional grounds were that the appellant and the State filed additional evidence showing the criminal background and pending cases against the accused, which the High Court did not consider. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider the bail applications afresh on merits, keeping in view the legal principles laid down by the Supreme Court and the additional material filed by the appellant and the State. The Supreme Court directed the accused to surrender for being taken into custody and cancelled their bail bonds. The additional evidence, which included details of the criminal background and pending cases against the accused, played a crucial role in the Supreme Court's decision to set aside the High Court's order and remand the case for fresh consideration. The Supreme Court cited precedents such as Ajay Kumar Sharma vs. State of U.P., Lokesh Singh vs. State of U.P., Dataram Singh vs. State of U.P., and Mauji Ram vs. State of U.P. to emphasize the need for reasoned orders while granting bail.

case_name: Vinod Verma vs. Union of India & Ors.
text: Case: Vinod Verma vs. Union of India & Ors.. Date: 2nd April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The case concerns the determination of seniority between Sub-Divisional Engineers (SDEs) promoted through seniority-cum-fitness and those promoted through the Limited Departmental Competitive Examination (LDCE) under the Telecommunications Engineering Service (Group 'B' Posts) Recruitment Rules, 1996. Vinod Verma challenged the seniority list of Sub-Divisional Engineers, arguing that the seniority should be based on the date of joining rather than the notional date of promotion and that the correct application of seniority rules, including the principles of ROTA and quota, was not followed. The CAT, Chandigarh Bench, quashed the seniority list prepared by the department and directed the seniority of officers of TES Group-B to be redrawn based on the date of joining, rather than the notional date of promotion. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed Vinod Verma's petition, relying on the Supreme Court's decision in BSNL vs. S. Sadasivan, which upheld the CAT's decision to base seniority on the date of joining. The Supreme Court dismissed Vinod Verma's appeal, affirming the High Court's decision and the CAT's order to redraw the seniority list based on the date of joining, referencing the earlier decision in BSNL vs. S. Sadasivan and BSNL vs. S.K. Dubey. The Supreme Court reasoned that the issue was already settled by the three-Judge Bench decision in BSNL vs. S.K. Dubey and reaffirmed in BSNL vs. S. Sadasivan, which established that the seniority of Sub-Divisional Engineers should be determined based on the date of joining, not the notional date of promotion, and that the ROTA rule does not apply under the 1996 Rules.

case_name: Vishnu Chandru Gaonkar vs. N.M. Dessai
text: Case: Vishnu Chandru Gaonkar vs. N.M. Dessai. Date: 6th March 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order of the District & Sessions Judge that directed filing a complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of Cr.P.C. against N.M. Dessai. The complaint was filed after allegations that N.M. Dessai committed forgery by verifying and forging the thumb impression of a deceased appellant, Shaba Manju Velip, in the withdrawal application of Civil Appeal No. 91 of 2004. The initial civil suit, No. 4 of 1993, was related to a property dispute between the plaintiffs, Laximan Rama Gaonkar and Janu Narayan Gaonkar, and the defendants, Kusta Naga Gaonkar and Suresh Kust Gaonkar. The Civil Appeal No. 91 of 2004 was withdrawn on 18th July 2006 after the application for withdrawal was filed. The High Court quashed the order of the District & Sessions Judge dated 31st July 2008, which had directed filing a complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of Cr.P.C. The appellant argued that the High Court incorrectly relied on the judgments in Sachida Nand Singh & Anr. vs. State of Bihar & Anr. and Iqbal Singh Marwah & Anr. vs. Meenakshi Marwah & Anr., which were not applicable as the allegations were referable to Section 195(1)(b)(i). The Supreme Court concluded that the allegations made were indeed under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. and upheld the High Court's decision to quash the complaint. The Supreme Court noted that Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. applies only when the offences are committed with respect to a document after it has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding. The Supreme Court did not find any merit in the allegations of misconduct against N.M. Dessai, as the document in question was produced in court with signatures obtained before filing. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Vishnu Chandru Gaonkar, upholding the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to quash the complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. and dismissed the appeal by Vishnu Chandru Gaonkar.

case_name: Vishnu Kumar Shukla & Anr. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
text: Case: Vishnu Kumar Shukla & Anr. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.. Date: 28th November 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. The allegations were that they locked the door of the complainant's shop from inside, broke the wall, and looted various items including wheat, sale money, kerosene oil, goods in stock, all the registers of the shop, documents, and a two-wheeler. They were charged under Sections 448 (house-trespass), 454 (lurking house-trespass or house-breaking in order to commit offence punishable with imprisonment), and 380 (theft in dwelling house, etc.) of the Indian Penal Code. The defense argued that the tenancy agreement presented by the complainant was forged, as it included the Indian Rupee symbol which did not exist at the time the agreement was supposedly made. The Chief Judicial Magistrate, Lucknow rejected the application for discharge filed by the appellants. The High Court upheld the Chief Judicial Magistrate's decision and dismissed the appellants' petition under Section 482 CrPC. The Supreme Court found that the tenancy agreement was prima facie forged as it contained the Indian Rupee symbol that did not exist at the time it was purportedly created. The Supreme Court concluded that the FIR and charges against the appellants amounted to an abuse of the process of law and ordered their discharge. The Supreme Court emphasized the need for courts to ensure that allegations and charges are not based on forged or fabricated documents, and to protect individuals from vexatious and unwarranted prosecutions. This judgement sets a precedent that courts must thoroughly scrutinize allegations based on documentary evidence and protect individuals from prosecution based on forged or fabricated documents. The complainant, Ram Kumar Garg, could face legal consequences for perjury and forgery if further proceedings find that he knowingly filed a false complaint based on fabricated documents. Individuals should ensure that all agreements and documents are properly authenticated, legally valid, and free from any alterations or fabrications to avoid legal complications in property disputes.

Individuals should ensure that all agreements and documents are properly authenticated, legally valid, and free from any alterations or fabrications to avoid legal complications in property disputes.

case_name: Vishram Varu & Co. vs. Union of India
text: Case: Vishram Varu & Co. vs. Union of India. Date: 21st April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was the dismissal of an arbitration petition by the Calcutta High Court on the grounds of being barred by limitation. The appellant was seeking the appointment of an arbitrator to resolve a payment dispute related to excess work executed in 1986. The Calcutta High Court dismissed the petition because it was filed after a period of approximately 32 years from the completion of the work, making it barred by limitation. The appellant argued that the limitation period should start from the date of the legal notice invoking the arbitration clause, not from the date of work completion. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the High Court that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation and stale.

case_name: Vishwabandhu vs. Sri Krishna and Anr.
text: Case: Vishwabandhu vs. Sri Krishna and Anr.. Date: 29th September 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was the recovery of Rs. 22,400/- along with interest, which Respondent No.1 (Sri Krishna) had failed to refund as part sale consideration for a property sale agreement. An ex-parte decree was passed in favor of Respondent No.2, awarding Rs. 22,400/- along with 9% interest, as the defendant (Sri Krishna) failed to appear in court. Respondent No.2 filed for the execution of the decree, leading to the attachment and auction of the property, where Vishwabandhu became the highest bidder. The High Court set aside the ex-parte decree and ordered the trial court to decide the case on merits after giving opportunities to both parties. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's orders dated 21st April 2006 and 18th October 2019, and dismissed the application filed by Respondent No.1 to set aside the ex-parte decree.

case_name: Vishwas Bhandari vs. State of Punjab & Anr.
text: Case: Vishwas Bhandari vs. State of Punjab & Anr.. Date: 3rd February 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Vishwas Bhandari was charged under Sections 363 and 366-A of the Indian Penal Code for allegedly kidnapping a 17 year old girl for the purpose of marriage. The case involved the alleged kidnapping of the complainant's 17 year old daughter by Vishwas Bhandari and another accused, Vikram Roop Rai, on 23rd January 2013. The complainant stated that her daughter was allured and taken away for the purpose of marriage. Vikram Roop Rai was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, as the prosecutrix (the complainant's daughter) testified that she had voluntarily married Vikram and lived with him with the consent of both families. Vishwas Bhandari filed the petition under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash the FIR and subsequent proceedings against him, arguing that there were no allegations or evidence against him in the statements of the complainant and the prosecutrix. The High Court dismissed Vishwas Bhandari's petition, leading to the present appeal in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found that there were no allegations against Vishwas Bhandari in the statements of the complainant and the prosecutrix. The main allegation was against Vikram Roop Rai, who had married the prosecutrix with the consent of both families. The Supreme Court held that the continuation of proceedings against Vishwas Bhandari was an abuse of process of law and quashed the FIR and all subsequent proceedings against him. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the FIR No. 31 of 2013 and all consequent proceedings against Vishwas Bhandari. The Supreme Court emphasized that there was no evidence or allegations against Vishwas Bhandari in the testimonies of the prosecutrix and the complainant, and thus, the proceedings against him were unjustified. The Supreme Court noted that the marriage between the prosecutrix and Vikram Roop Rai was consensual and supported by both families, which further indicated that the allegations against Vishwas Bhandari were baseless.

case_name: Vitthalrao Marotirao Navkhare vs. Nanibai (Dead), through LRs, and others
text: Case: Vitthalrao Marotirao Navkhare vs. Nanibai (Dead), through LRs, and others. Date: 8th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary legal issue was whether the suit properties, including houses and agricultural lands, were joint family properties and if the plaintiff, Vitthalrao Marotirao Navkhare, had a right to partition and separate possession. The Trial Court decreed that the plaintiff was entitled to partition and separate possession of a half-share in the agricultural land at Mouza Shendola, Taluk Teosa, District Amravati, as it was proven to be ancestral property. However, it held that the rest of the properties were the self-acquired properties of late Laxmanrao and not subject to partition. The Appellate Court reversed the Trial Court's decision, holding that the plaintiff had a half-share in all the suit properties and decreed his suit in its entirety. The counter-claim of defendant Nos. 1 to 4 was dismissed. The Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, dismissed the second appeal, upholding the Appellate Court's decision that the suit properties were joint family properties and the business was a joint family business. The review petition was based on the observation that the joint family business commenced only from 1991, which was argued to exclude certain properties from being considered joint family properties. The Supreme Court set aside the review petition's order, holding that the observation regarding the joint family business commencing from 1991 was factually incorrect. The Supreme Court upheld the Appellate Court's judgment that the business was a joint family business and the suit properties were joint family properties.

case_name: Vodafone Idea Cellular Ltd. vs. Ajay Kumar Agarwal
text: Case: Vodafone Idea Cellular Ltd. vs. Ajay Kumar Agarwal. Date: 16th February 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. Ajay Kumar Agarwal filed a consumer complaint alleging deficiency in service after he received a bill of Rs. 24,609.51 for one month, which he claimed was an overcharge compared to his usual bills of approximately Rs. 555. Vodafone Idea Cellular Ltd. argued that the dispute should be resolved through arbitration under Section 7B of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, and that the consumer forum lacked jurisdiction. The NCDRC ruled that the consumer forum had jurisdiction over the case, as Section 7B of the Indian Telegraph Act did not apply to disputes with private telecom service providers. Vodafone Idea Cellular Ltd. argued that as a private telecom service provider, they were subject to arbitration under Section 7B, which ousted the jurisdiction of the consumer forum. The Supreme Court dismissed Vodafone Idea Cellular Ltd.'s appeal and upheld the jurisdiction of the consumer forum to hear the case.

case_name: West Bengal State Election Commission vs Communist Party of India (Marxist) & Ors.
text: Case: West Bengal State Election Commission vs Communist Party of India (Marxist) & Ors.. Date: 24th August 2018. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the nominations for the West Bengal Panchayat elections could be accepted in electronic form, as directed by the Calcutta High Court, despite the State Election Commission not being bound by the Information Technology Act, 2000. The Calcutta High Court directed the State Election Commission to accept nominations submitted in electronic form to facilitate a fair and free election, despite the Commission not being explicitly covered under the Information Technology Act, 2000. The Supreme Court stayed the impugned judgement of the High Court, allowed the Panchayat election to proceed as scheduled, directed the Commission to ensure fair elections, and restricted the notification of results in uncontested constituencies without the Court's leave. The State Election Commission argued that the acceptance of electronic nominations was contrary to the provisions of the Panchayat Elections Act, 2003, and that the High Court had overstepped its jurisdiction by issuing such directions. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's directive, stating that the acceptance of electronic nominations was not supported by the Panchayat Elections Act, 2003, and that any changes to the election process must be made through legislative amendments, not judicial directions. The Supreme Court allowed challenges to the validity of elections for uncontested seats to be pursued through election petitions, extending the period for filing such petitions from the date of the publication of results in the Official Gazette. The Supreme Court upheld the stay on the High Court's judgement, allowing the Panchayat elections to proceed according to the law and directed that the results of uncontested seats could be challenged through election petitions filed within 30 days from the publication of results.

case_name: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. & Ors. vs. M/s. Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
text: Case: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. & Ors. vs. M/s. Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.. Date: 21st August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the provisional assessment made under Section 126(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003, for alleged unauthorized use of electricity involving meter tampering, was valid, especially since parallel criminal proceedings under Section 135 were also ongoing. The provisional assessment was initiated after an inspection revealed tampering with the metering system, including the discovery of foreign material in the meter, leading to allegations of unauthorized energy use and theft. The Supreme Court held that provisional assessments under Section 126 and criminal proceedings under Section 135 could proceed simultaneously as they address different aspects of unauthorized energy use. The judgment clarifies that authorities can pursue both assessment for revenue loss and criminal prosecution for theft simultaneously, providing a precedent for handling similar cases. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision, upheld the validity of the provisional assessment under Section 126, and allowed the appellants to proceed with recovery for unauthorized energy use.

case_name: Western Coalfields Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Trichy/Madurai
text: Case: Western Coalfields Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Trichy/Madurai. Date: 20th February 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the period of limitation of six months applied to the refund claim of central excise duty made by the buyer (Western Coalfields Ltd.) when the duty was paid by the manufacturer (M/s. Fenner (India) Ltd.) under protest. The Tribunal rejected the claim because it was filed beyond the six-month limitation period prescribed under Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944. Western Coalfields Ltd. argued that since the duty was paid by the manufacturer under protest, the six-month limitation period should not apply to their refund claim as per the proviso to Section 11B(1) of the Central Excise Act. The Supreme Court held that the rights of the manufacturer and the buyer to claim a refund under Section 11B are separate and distinct. The limitation period of six months applies to the buyer's refund claim, regardless of the protest by the manufacturer. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals of Western Coalfields Ltd., affirming that the refund claim was time-barred as it was filed beyond the six-month limitation period, and the buyer could not benefit from the protest made by the manufacturer.
