case_name: William Stephen vs The State of Tamil Nadu
text: Case: William Stephen vs The State of Tamil Nadu. Date: 21st February 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main legal issue was whether the conviction of William Stephen and the co-accused under Section 364A read with Section 34 of the IPC for kidnapping with ransom demands was justified. William Stephen and the co-accused were initially charged under Section 364A read with Section 34 of the IPC for kidnapping a child with the intent to demand ransom. The prosecution's case was that William Stephen and the co-accused kidnapped an eight-year-old child and demanded a ransom of Rs. 5 lakhs from the child's parents. The prosecution presented the testimonies of the child's parents (PW-1 and PW-3), the child's own testimony (PW-2), and the evidence of the Investigating Officer (PW-19), along with call records that were later discarded due to lack of certification under Section 65B of the Evidence Act. The High Court upheld the conviction based on the evidence presented by the prosecution, including the testimonies of the witnesses and the circumstances of the kidnapping and ransom demand. The Supreme Court found that the prosecution failed to establish the ransom demand and threat by the accused due to the lack of corroborative evidence and proper certification of call records. The Supreme Court set aside the conviction under Section 364A of the IPC due to insufficient evidence of the ransom demand and threat, but upheld the conviction under Section 363 for kidnapping. The Supreme Court noted the failure of the Investigating Officer to obtain proper certification under Section 65B of the Evidence Act for the call records, which weakened the prosecution's case regarding the ransom demand and threat. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of obtaining proper certification under Section 65B of the Evidence Act for electronic evidence, such as call records, to ensure their admissibility in court. The ruling underscores the need for robust evidence to prove ransom demands and threats, potentially leading to more meticulous investigation and documentation in future kidnapping cases. Following the Supreme Court's decision, William Stephen and the co-accused will remain convicted of kidnapping under Section 363 of the IPC, but their conviction and life imprisonment sentence under Section 364A have been set aside.

case_name: Wipro Finance Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax
text: Case: Wipro Finance Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax. Date: 12th April 2022. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether the loss incurred by Wipro Finance Ltd. due to foreign exchange fluctuation should be treated as revenue expenditure or capital expenditure for the assessment year 1997-98. The ITAT decided that the foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by Wipro Finance Ltd. should be treated as revenue expenditure, allowing the entire claim of Rs. 3,56,57,727/- as a deductible expense. The High Court reversed the ITAT's decision, observing that the ITAT had not recorded sufficient reasons in support of its conclusion and that the conclusion was without any basis. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement, stating that the ITAT's analysis and conclusion were consistent with the exposition of the Court and needed to be upheld. The Supreme Court restored the ITAT's decision in favor of Wipro Finance Ltd. The loan obtained by Wipro Finance Ltd. from the Commonwealth Development Corporation was in foreign currency and was used for financing the existing Indian enterprises for the procurement of capital equipment on hire purchase or lease basis. The Supreme Court concluded that the foreign exchange fluctuation loss should be treated as revenue expenditure, as the loan was wholly and exclusively used for the purpose of the business of financing the existing Indian enterprises. The Supreme Court directed that suitable amends be effected in the final assessment order by treating the entire claim of Rs. 3,56,57,727/- as revenue expenditure and adjusting the consequential benefits such as depreciation availed by Wipro Finance Ltd. in relation to the exchange fluctuation related to leased assets capitalized.

case_name: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
text: Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.. Date: 5th September 2017. Court: Supreme Court of India. The primary issue was whether the order passed by the Union of India, debarring the petitioner medical college from admitting students for two academic sessions (2017-18 and 2018-19) and authorizing the Medical Council of India (MCI) to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crore, was justified. The Union of India debarred the petitioner medical college based on the recommendation from the MCI, which noted several deficiencies in the college during an assessment conducted on 26th-27th October 2016. The MCI noted deficiencies such as a 29.23% shortage of faculty, a 28.26% shortage of residents, 34% bed occupancy on the day of assessment, and other issues such as a lack of patients in ICUs and inadequate library facilities. The OC found that the deficiencies were within acceptable limits, noting that some staff were on leave due to the Diwali festival and others arrived late. The OC's opinion was that there were no significant deficiencies, and it confirmed the Letter of Permission (LOP) for the college. The Supreme Court rejected the argument, noting that the inspection on 26th October 2016, which was three days before Diwali, did not violate the regulations prohibiting inspections two days before or after major festivals. The Supreme Court allowed the students already admitted for the academic session 2016-17 to continue their studies but declined to issue directions for renewal of LOP for the academic session 2017-18. The Court directed the MCI to inspect the college for the academic session 2018-19 and submit a report. The Supreme Court directed the MCI to conduct a fresh inspection within two months, inform the college of any deficiencies, and allow the college time to rectify them. The renewal application for 2017-18 was to be treated as an application for 2018-19, and the bank guarantee was not to be encashed until further orders.

case_name: Yashwant Sinha & Ors. vs. Central Bureau of Investigation
text: Case: Yashwant Sinha & Ors. vs. Central Bureau of Investigation. Date: 10th April 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue raised by the Attorney General was the maintainability of the review petition due to the alleged unauthorized removal and use of three documents from the Ministry of Defence by the petitioners, which were in violation of the Official Secrets Act, 1923. The three documents were: (a) an eight-page note written by three members of the Indian Negotiating Team regarding the Rafale Deal dated 1st June 2016, (b) Note-18 of the Ministry of Defence, marked secret under the Official Secrets Act, and (c) Note-10 written by S.K. Sharma, Deputy Secretary, MoD, Air-III, dated 24th November 2015, also marked secret. The court dismissed the preliminary objections raised by the Union of India, affirming that the review petitions should be adjudicated on their own merit, taking into account the relevance and admissibility of the three documents in question. The respondents did not seriously dispute or contest the fact that the three documents had been published in 'The Hindu' newspaper and were thus available in the public domain. The court held that the unauthorized removal of the documents did not bar their admissibility. The court emphasized that the test of admissibility of evidence lies in its relevancy, and documents in the public domain should not be excluded merely due to the manner in which they were obtained. The court found the claim of privilege under Section 123 of the Indian Evidence Act to be untenable, especially since the documents were already in the public domain and accessible to the entire citizenry. The court noted that the Right to Information Act allows access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to protected interests, even when considering the Official Secrets Act. The court emphasized that transparency and accountability are vital in curbing corruption. The court underscored the importance of the freedom of the press in strengthening democracy. It recognized that the press has the right to publish information, especially when it is in the public domain, and this right is protected under the constitutional guarantee of freedom of speech. The court highlighted that the Right to Information Act serves the public interest by promoting transparency and accountability. It allows for the disclosure of information if public interest outweighs the harm, even when such information is protected under laws like the Official Secrets Act. The court addressed this argument by stating that even if the documents were improperly obtained, their relevancy and public availability justified their consideration. The court emphasized that the manner of obtaining evidence does not preclude its admissibility if it is relevant and in the public interest. The final decision of the court was to adjudicate the review petitions on their own merit, taking into account the relevance and admissibility of the three documents, and to dismiss the preliminary objections raised by the Union of India.

The respondents did not seriously dispute or contest the fact that the three documents had been published in 'The Hindu' newspaper and were thus available in the public domain.

The court held that the unauthorized removal of the documents did not bar their admissibility. The court emphasized that the test of admissibility of evidence lies in its relevancy, and documents in the public domain should not be excluded merely due to the manner in which they were obtained.

The court found the claim of privilege under Section 123 of the Indian Evidence Act to be untenable, especially since the documents were already in the public domain and accessible to the entire citizenry.

The court noted that the Right to Information Act allows access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to protected interests, even when considering the Official Secrets Act. The court emphasized that transparency and accountability are vital in curbing corruption.

The court underscored the importance of the freedom of the press in strengthening democracy. It recognized that the press has the right to publish information, especially when it is in the public domain, and this right is protected under the constitutional guarantee of freedom of speech.

The court highlighted that the Right to Information Act serves the public interest by promoting transparency and accountability. It allows for the disclosure of information if public interest outweighs the harm, even when such information is protected under laws like the Official Secrets Act.

The court addressed this argument by stating that even if the documents were improperly obtained, their relevancy and public availability justified their consideration. The court emphasized that the manner of obtaining evidence does not preclude its admissibility if it is relevant and in the public interest.

The final decision of the court was to adjudicate the review petitions on their own merit, taking into account the relevance and admissibility of the three documents, and to dismiss the preliminary objections raised by the Union of India.

case_name: Yedala Subba Rao & Anr. vs. Union of India
text: Case: Yedala Subba Rao & Anr. vs. Union of India. Date: 17th April 2023. Court: Supreme Court of India. Yedala Subba Rao and his co-accused were charged under Section 120B read with Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, Sections 18, 19, 20, and 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, and Sections 4 and 5 of the Explosives Substances Act, 1908. The incident involved the killing of Shri Kidari Sarveswara Rao, a member of the Legislative Assembly, and Shri Siveri Soma, a former MLA, near the village Livitiputtu on 23rd September 2018, allegedly by members of the Communist Party of India (Maoist). The prosecution's main evidence included the recovery of a landmine at the instance of appellant no.46, call detail records showing communication among the accused, and allegations of providing shelter and logistic support to Maoists. The Supreme Court found the confessional statements recorded in the 'Mediators' Report and Seizure Panchnama' inadmissible, as they were made before the accused's arrest was recorded and contained no new discovery of facts. The Supreme Court did not find a direct connection between the purchase of medicines by accused no.46 in July 2018 and the incident that took place on 23rd September 2018, noting that the alleged Maoist Kiran was in custody at the time. The High Court's decision to grant bail to accused no.84 was significant as it undermined the prosecution's allegations against the appellants, especially the claims of a conspiracy involving frequent communication between the accused. The Supreme Court noted that the appellants had been in custody for four and a half years without the charges being framed and highlighted the improbability of the trial commencing soon due to the large number of witnesses and absconding accused. The Supreme Court suggested that the learned Special Judge for the trial of NIA cases at Vijayawada should impose stringent conditions while granting bail to ensure that the appellants do not abscond or tamper with evidence. The Supreme Court concluded that there were no reasonable grounds to believe that the accusations against the appellants under the UAPA were prima facie true, thus the embargo on the grant of bail under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA did not apply. The Supreme Court directed the respondents to ensure the appellants are produced before the learned Special Judge for NIA cases at Vijayawada within a week and ordered the judge to release the appellants on bail with appropriate conditions.

case_name: Yogesh & Ors. vs. State of Haryana
text: Case: Yogesh & Ors. vs. State of Haryana. Date: 6th April 2021. Court: Supreme Court of India. Yogesh, Anuj, Sumit, and Pardeep were charged with offenses under Sections 302, 364-A, 376, 216 read with Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code for the kidnapping, sexual assault, and murder of a minor girl. According to the prosecution, on 18th August 2004, two boys on a red motorcycle kidnapped a minor girl who was returning home from school. The investigation revealed that the victim was murdered and her body was disposed of in the fields of village Paparwat. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimonies, the recovery of the victim's body and belongings, and a post-mortem report indicating sexual assault and strangulation. Additionally, disclosure statements by the accused led to the recovery of the victim's clothing and tiffin box. Two key witnesses, Neeraj (PW15) and Rajiv (PW12), turned hostile and did not support the prosecution's case. Their testimonies contradicted earlier statements, and they denied that the accused were the individuals who kidnapped the victim. The post-mortem report revealed that the victim had been manually strangled and smothered, resulting in death. The report also indicated forceful penetration of the vagina, consistent with sexual assault. The trial court found Yogesh, Sumit, Pardeep, and Anuj guilty of charges under Sections 302 and 120-B of the IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment. However, the court acquitted them of charges under Sections 364-A and 376 IPC and acquitted the other four accused of all charges. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the convicted accused, upholding the trial court's judgement and sentence of life imprisonment for Yogesh, Sumit, Pardeep, and Anuj. The Supreme Court found that the key eyewitnesses turned hostile, the testimony of PW10 Manoj was unreliable, and there was insufficient circumstantial evidence to conclusively prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court emphasized that circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain linking the accused to the crime, exclude all other hypotheses, and conclusively establish guilt. The Court cited the principles laid down in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the convictions and sentences of Yogesh, Anuj, and Pardeep, and ordered their immediate release unless they were required in connection with any other crime.

case_name: Yogesh @ Sonu Tharu vs. The State
text: Case: Yogesh @ Sonu Tharu vs. The State. Date: 4th April 2024. Court: Supreme Court of India. The appellants, Pradeep Dabas and Yogesh @ Sonu Tharu, were charged with offences under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act, 1959, for the murder of the deceased at a birthday party. The prosecution stated that during a birthday party, an altercation occurred between Yogesh @ Sonu Tharu and the deceased. Pradeep Dabas took a gun and fired at the deceased but missed. Later, Pradeep handed the gun to Yogesh, who shot and killed the deceased. The prosecution relied on the testimony of PW-19, who witnessed the incident, the statement of PW-20, who was informed by PW-19, and the recovery of the body and postmortem report indicating the deceased was intoxicated. The defense argued that the presence of PW-19 was doubtful, his conduct was unnatural, and there was no premeditation involved as the incident occurred under the influence of alcohol. They also contended that A2 (Yogesh) did not instigate A1 (Pradeep) to commit the offence. The Supreme Court found no material to implicate A2 (Yogesh) under Section 34 IPC as he did not shoot the deceased nor instigate A1 to do so. The Court set aside his conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court concluded that A1 (Pradeep) committed an offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC instead of Section 302 IPC, considering the lack of premeditation and the influence of alcohol. The Court modified his sentence to the period already undergone. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by A2 (Yogesh @ Sonu Tharu), setting aside his conviction and sentence. For A1 (Pradeep Dabas), the Court modified the conviction to Section 304 Part I IPC and the sentence to the period already undergone, ordering his release.

case_name: Zonal Manager, Bank of India, Zonal Office, Kochi & Ors. vs. Aarya K. Babu & Anr.
text: Case: Zonal Manager, Bank of India, Zonal Office, Kochi & Ors. vs. Aarya K. Babu & Anr.. Date: 8th August 2019. Court: Supreme Court of India. The main issue was whether candidates possessing a B.Sc. in Forestry degree qualified for the post of Agricultural Field Officer (Scale-1) when the recruitment notification specified a degree in Agro-Forestry. The Supreme Court held that including B.Sc. (Forestry) as an eligible qualification midstream, without prior notification, would be unfair to other candidates who did not apply because they did not meet the original criteria. The Supreme Court directed the Bank of India to provide a fresh appointment to Aarya K. Babu as an Agricultural Field Officer or an equivalent post, treating it as a fresh appointment without retrospective benefits. The judgment reinforces the principle that recruitment criteria must be adhered to as published and that changes during the process must allow equal opportunity for all eligible candidates. The Supreme Court clarified that the High Court's decision to equate B.Sc. (Forestry) with B.Sc. (Agro-Forestry) for eligibility was not justified, as such equivalence should be established by recruitment authorities, not the judiciary.
